docs.title: Promptise Foundry
docs.text:
The production framework for agentic AI systems. Build agents that discover tools, reason with custom patterns, remember context, enforce security, and run autonomously.

pip install promptise

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions="You are a helpful assistant.",
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

You need an API key first

Put it in a .env file in your project (OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...) (Promptise loads it automatically) or pass it in code with Model(...), explained in Models & Providers → In code: Model: Model("gpt-5-mini", provider="openai", api_key="..."). The exact variable name for every provider: Azure AI Foundry, Bedrock, Gemini, Ollama, …, is in Configuration & Secrets → Every provider's variables; self-hosted and inference endpoints are in Models & Providers → Custom, self-hosted and inference endpoints. promptise models env <provider> prints the lines a provider needs.

See the full Quick Start for tools, reasoning patterns, and production features.

docs.title: Already have an API? MCPcast it
docs.text:
Don't hand-write a server for an API that already exists, generate one from its OpenAPI spec:

promptise mcpcast openapi.yaml --name myapi --no-curate --auth env-token  # → myapi-mcp/
export MCPCAST_UPSTREAM_TOKEN="Bearer <your API token>"
claude mcp add myapi -- python myapi-mcp/server.py

Read-only by default; writes, deletes and money-moving calls are only generated when you opt in, and every one of them is approval-gated server-side: so any MCP client can drive your product safely. Drop --no-curate to have a model design a smaller intent-tool surface. Start with MCPcast, end to end: how MCP works, a real API turned into a real server, and the review checklist, then the step-by-step guide and the reference.

docs.text: Subsystem What it does Start here Agent Turn any LLM into a production agent. MCP tool discovery, memory, guardrails, semantic cache, streaming, approval workflows. docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Python 3.10+ required.

pip install promptise

Put your LLM key in a .env file in your project: scripts and the CLI load it automatically (or pass it in code with Model(...); see Configuration & Secrets):

.env
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...

Any other provider (Azure AI Foundry, Bedrock, Gemini, Ollama, …) is one string or one Model(...) away; promptise models env <provider> prints the lines it needs. Verify:

promptise models check openai:gpt-5-mini --ping

docs.title: Promptise Foundry FAQ: Python framework for AI agents and MCP
Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text: Honest, complete answers about Promptise Foundry — the production Python framework for building AI agents, MCP servers, and autonomous runtimes.

docs.title: What is Promptise Foundry?
docs.text: Promptise Foundry is a production-grade Python framework for building AI agents, MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, prompt engineering systems, and autonomous runtimes. It is secure by default, model-agnostic, MCP-native, and designed for teams shipping agentic AI to production. One coherent stack instead of gluing libraries together.

docs.title: Is Promptise Foundry production-ready?
docs.text: Yes. No stub implementations, no half-finished features, no NotImplementedError in shipped code. Built-in: access control, capability-based policies, audit logging, encrypted transport, sandboxed code execution, observability with 8 transporters, crash-recovery via journals. Every backend listed as a parameter option works — if it's documented, it's implemented.

docs.title: Is Promptise Foundry open source?
docs.text: Apache 2.0 — source at github.com/promptise-com/foundry.

docs.title: How do I install Promptise Foundry?
docs.text:
pip install promptise

Python 3.10 or newer required. Optional extras for memory backends, sandboxing, and observability — see Installation Extras.

docs.title: How is Promptise Foundry different from LangChain?
docs.text: LangChain is a general-purpose LLM toolkit with hundreds of integrations. Promptise Foundry is a focused production framework — one coherent stack covering agents, MCP servers, prompt engineering, and autonomous runtime, with built-in access control, audit trails, sandboxing, and governance. Promptise has fewer abstractions, no silent fallbacks (errors raise instead of degrading), is async-first, and uses MCP-native tool discovery instead of manual wiring.

docs.title: How does Promptise Foundry compare to LangGraph?
docs.text: LangGraph is an orchestration layer focused on stateful graphs. Promptise Foundry includes a full Agent Runtime with crash recovery via journals, governance (budget, health, mission), and five trigger types (cron, event, message, webhook, file watch) — built for long-running autonomous agents that survive restarts, not just stateful conversations.

docs.title: How does Promptise Foundry compare to CrewAI?
docs.text: CrewAI focuses on multi-agent role-playing workflows. Promptise Foundry covers single agents, multi-agent coordination through cross-agent delegation (peer agents become ask_agent_<name> tools), plus the production infrastructure — MCP servers, governance, observability, sandboxing — that real deployments need.

docs.title: Which LLM models does Promptise Foundry support?
docs.text: Any model. Use a string like "openai:gpt-5-mini", "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", or "ollama:llama3", or pass any LangChain BaseChatModel directly. Switching providers requires changing one string in build_agent().

docs.title: Does Promptise Foundry support self-hosted or local LLMs?
docs.text: Yes. Use any Ollama model via "ollama:model-name". Local embeddings via SentenceTransformers, local guardrail models (DeBERTa, GLiNER, and Llama Guard through Ollama), and local memory backends (ChromaDB) make air-gapped deployments fully supported.

docs.title: What is MCP and why does Promptise Foundry use it?
docs.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard for connecting LLMs to tools, resources, and prompts. Promptise Foundry is MCP-native — agents auto-discover tools from any MCP server URL, schemas convert to typed tools automatically, and you can build your own MCP servers with the included SDK.

docs.title: Does Promptise Foundry have its own MCP client?
docs.text:
Yes — built from scratch, no third-party MCP client dependencies:

  • MCPClient for single servers
  • MCPMultiClient for connecting to N servers with unified tool list and auto-routing
  • MCPToolAdapter for converting MCP tools to LangChain BaseTool objects with recursive schema handling

Supports HTTP, SSE, and stdio transports. Bearer token and API key authentication.

docs.title: Can I build my own MCP server with Promptise Foundry?
docs.text: Yes — same relationship to MCP that FastAPI has to REST. Decorators for tools, resources, and prompts. Schema auto-generated from type hints. Middleware chain. Authentication, guards, caching, health checks, metrics, exception handlers, webhooks, dependency injection (FastAPI-style Depends), session state, versioning, namespace transforms, OpenAPI tool generation, streaming, elicitation, sampling, and a TestClient for in-process testing. See Building Production MCP Servers.

docs.title: How do I deploy a Promptise Foundry MCP server?
docs.text:
promptise serve myapp:server --transport http --port 8080

Supports stdio, streamable HTTP, and SSE transports with configurable CORS. Auth gate at the transport level. CLI flags: --dashboard (live terminal UI), --reload (hot-reload during development). Kubernetes health probes (liveness, readiness, startup) built in.

docs.title: What is the Agent Runtime?
docs.text: The operating system for autonomous AI agents. Turns stateless LLM calls into persistent, governed processes. Each AgentProcess has lifecycle states (CREATED → STARTING → RUNNING → SUSPENDED → STOPPING → STOPPED/FAILED), trigger queues, heartbeat monitoring, concurrency control, conversation buffer, and journaled state for crash recovery.

docs.title: What's the difference between PromptiseAgent and the Agent Runtime?
docs.text: PromptiseAgent Agent Runtime What Single agent created via build_agent() Wraps an agent in an AgentProcess Invocation await agent.ainvoke(...) or await agent.chat(...) Triggered by events, cron, webhooks, files Lifecycle Stateless between calls Long-running, persistent, recoverable Use case Request/response Autonomous, ambient, scheduled

docs.title: What trigger types can launch an autonomous agent?
docs.text:
Five built-in:

  • CronTrigger — cron expressions
  • EventTrigger — EventBus subscription
  • MessageTrigger — topic-based pub/sub with wildcards
  • WebhookTrigger — HTTP POST with HMAC verification
  • FileWatchTrigger — directory monitoring with glob patterns

Multiple triggers compose on one process. Custom trigger types can be registered.

docs.title: How does Promptise Foundry handle crash recovery?
docs.text: Through journals. InMemoryJournal and FileJournal record every state transition, trigger event, and invocation result. The ReplayEngine reconstructs state from a checkpoint plus replay log. When a process crashes, it restarts from the last known good state — no lost conversations, no lost trigger queue, no data loss.

docs.title: Does Promptise Foundry support distributed deployments?
docs.text: Yes. RuntimeCoordinator for multi-node coordination, with StaticDiscovery and RegistryDiscovery for node discovery. Health checks over HTTP. No etcd or Consul dependency required.

docs.title: What governance does the Agent Runtime provide?
docs.text:
Four subsystems:

Subsystem What it does Budget Per-run and daily limits on tool calls, LLM turns, cost units, irreversible actions Health Anomaly detection — stuck loops, repeating patterns, empty responses, high error rates Mission LLM-as-judge evaluation against success criteria with confidence thresholds Secrets Per-process credentials with TTL expiry, rotation without restart, zero-fill revocation, never serialized to journal

Escalation via webhook POST and EventBus emission. Enforcement: log, pause, stop, or escalate.

docs.title: Does Promptise Foundry handle multi-user access control?
docs.text:
Yes. The MCP server SDK ships:

  • JWTAuth (HS256), AsymmetricJWTAuth (RS256/ES256), APIKeyAuth
  • Capability-based access policies
  • Per-tool permission guards: HasRole, HasAllRoles, RequireAuth, RequireClientId
  • Per-user audit trails (HMAC-chained for tamper detection)
  • CallerContext propagation across the entire stack via async contextvars

Built for multi-tenant production deployments. See Building Multi-User Systems.

docs.title: How does Promptise Foundry handle prompt injection and security?
docs.text:
PromptiseSecurityScanner with six detection heads:

Head Detects DeBERTa Prompt injection (ML model) Regex (69 patterns) PII Regex (97 patterns) Credentials GLiNER Named entities Llama Guard / Azure AI Content safety Custom rules Domain-specific

All models run locally. Input blocking and output redaction built in. Memory retrieval and semantic cache responses are also rescanned.

docs.title: Can I sandbox code execution?
docs.text: Yes. Docker-based sandbox with seccomp syscall filtering, capability dropping (~40 caps), read-only rootfs, resource limits (CPU, memory, time), and network isolation (none, restricted, full). Optional gVisor kernel for stronger isolation. Five agent tools auto-injected when sandbox is enabled — execute, read file, write file, list files, install package. Path traversal and shell injection prevention built in.

docs.title: What memory backends does Promptise Foundry support?
docs.text:
Three providers ship in the framework:

  • InMemoryProvider — testing
  • ChromaProvider — local vector search, persistent
  • Mem0Provider — enterprise-grade graph search

Configured on build_agent(). Before every invocation, the agent auto-searches memory and injects relevant results into the system prompt with prompt-injection mitigation built in.

docs.title: Does Promptise Foundry support conversation persistence?
docs.text:
Yes — ConversationStore protocol with four backends:

  • InMemoryConversationStore
  • SQLiteConversationStore
  • PostgresConversationStore
  • RedisConversationStore

The chat() method handles load → invoke → persist automatically. Session ownership is enforced.

docs.title: Does Promptise Foundry support semantic caching?
docs.text: Yes. SemanticCache with in-memory or Redis backends. Per-user, per-session, or shared scope isolation. Serves cached responses for semantically similar queries. Output guardrails re-scan cached responses. purge_user() deletes one user's cached entries on request. Encrypted-at-rest option available for Redis.

docs.title: Does Promptise Foundry have prompt engineering features?
docs.text:
Yes — prompts as software components:

  • @prompt decorator
  • 8 PromptBlock types (Identity, Rules, OutputFormat, ContextSlot, Section, Examples, Conditional, Composite) with priority-based token budgeting
  • ConversationFlow — system prompts that transform across phases
  • 5 composable strategies: chain_of_thought, structured_reasoning, self_critique, plan_and_execute, decompose
  • 4 built-in perspectives: Analyst, Critic, Advisor, Creative
  • Guards: ContentFilterGuard, LengthGuard, SchemaStrictGuard, custom validators
  • 14 context providers — Tool, Memory, Task, Blackboard, User, Environment, Conversation, Team, Error, Output, Static, Callable, Conditional, World
  • PromptInspector for tracing assembly step-by-step

docs.title: Does Promptise Foundry support multi-agent systems?
docs.text: Yes. Cross-agent delegation: pass peer agents to build_agent(cross_agents={"researcher": CrossAgent(agent=researcher)}) and each becomes an ask_agent_<name> tool. include_broadcast=True adds broadcast_to_agents, which asks several peers in parallel. Delegation runs in the same process, with per-peer timeouts and a max_delegation_depth limit. SuperAgent YAML files declare cross-agent references with cycle detection, and agent processes in the Agent Runtime coordinate through events. See Multi-Agent Coordination.

docs.title: What is a SuperAgent file?
docs.text:
A .superagent YAML file that defines an entire agent declaratively — model, instructions, MCP servers, memory, sandbox, observability, cache, guardrails, cross-agents. Environment variable resolution via ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default}. Loadable via the CLI:

promptise agent file.superagent

docs.title: What is an .agent manifest?
docs.text: A YAML manifest for the Agent Runtime — declares model, instructions, MCP servers, triggers, world state, memory, journal, open mode, budget, health, mission, and secrets. Validated, savable, deployable from the CLI. Distinct from .superagent (one-shot agents); .agent is for runtime processes with triggers and lifecycle.

docs.title: What is Open Mode?
docs.text: Self-modifying agents with 14 meta-tools — modify_instructions, create_tool, connect_mcp_server, add_trigger, remove_trigger, spawn_process, list_processes, store_memory, search_memory, forget_memory, list_capabilities, get_secret, check_budget, check_mission. Guardrails: max instruction length, max custom tools, MCP URL whitelist, mandatory sandbox for agent-written code. Hot-reload without losing conversation state. Rollback to original config.

docs.title: How does observability work?
docs.text: Four levels — OFF, BASIC, STANDARD, FULL. Every LLM turn, tool call, token count, latency, retry, cache hit/miss is recorded. 8 transporters: HTML report, JSON file, structured log, console, Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, webhook, callback. Ring buffer with configurable max entries. Thread-safe.

docs.title: Is there a dashboard for monitoring agents?
docs.text: Yes. Two dashboards — one for the MCP server (six tabs: server overview, tool stats, agents, request log, performance, raw logs) and one for the Agent Runtime (process state, invocation counts, trigger status, context inspection, memory usage, journal history). Both are live terminal UIs.

docs.title: Can I track costs with Promptise Foundry?
docs.text: Promptise Foundry does not estimate or track LLM provider prices — those change weekly and would require constant maintenance. The Budget governance system tracks tool calls, LLM turns, and abstract cost units that you can map to your own pricing model. BudgetConfig(tool_costs={...}) maps tool names to a ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=..., irreversible=...), which sets each tool's cost weight.

docs.title: What about job queues?
docs.text: The MCP server SDK includes MCPQueue with priority scheduling, retry with exponential backoff, progress reporting, and cancellation. Auto-registered tools — queue_submit, queue_status, queue_result, queue_cancel, queue_list. Background tasks supported for fire-and-forget work after a handler returns.

docs.title: How is testing done?
docs.text: For MCP servers: TestClient runs the full pipeline in-process — validation, dependency injection, guards, middleware, handler — with no network. For prompts: mock_llm(), mock_context(), assert_schema(), assert_contains(), assert_latency(), assert_guard_passed() helpers work with pytest.

docs.title: Does Promptise Foundry have a CLI?
docs.text:
Yes:

Command What it does promptise agent <file> Run a .superagent promptise validate Validate a config file promptise list-tools Discover tools from MCP servers promptise run Run a one-shot prompt promptise serve Serve an MCP server

The runtime has its own CLI for managing processes, triggers, and manifests.

docs.title: Where can I find examples?
docs.text: Runnable examples at github.com/promptise-com/foundry/tree/main/examples — covering agents, MCP servers (examples/mcp/), prompt engineering (examples/prompts/), and runtime use cases (examples/runtime/). Every example uses real LLM calls — no mocks, no stubs.

docs.title: How can I contribute?
docs.text: Issues and pull requests welcome at github.com/promptise-com/foundry. Conventional commits required (feat:, fix:, docs:, refactor:, test:, chore:). Type hints on all public APIs (Python 3.10+ syntax), Google-style docstrings, and tests for all new functionality. See Contributing.

docs.title: promptise.agent.build_agent(*, servers=None, model, instructions=None, identity=None, trace_tools=False, cross_agents=None, include_broadcast=False, max_delegation_depth=DEFAULT_MAX_DELEGATION_DEPTH, delegation_timeout=None, sandbox=None, observer=None, observer_agent_id=None, observe=None, memory=None, memory_auto_store=False, memory_max_results=5, memory_min_score=0.0, memory_timeout=5.0, extra_tools=None, flow=None, conversation_store=None, conversation_max_messages=0, optimize_tools=None, guardrails=None, cache=None, approval=None, events=None, on_tool_progress=None, max_invocation_time=0, adaptive=None, context_engine=None, context_compaction=None, agent_pattern=None, pattern=None, graph_blocks=None, node_pool=None, max_agent_iterations=25, tool_summary='off', code_action=None, expose_resources=False, expose_prompts=False) async
docs.text:
Build an MCP-first agent and return a :class:PromptiseAgent.

Discovers tools from the configured MCP servers, converts them into LangChain tools, and builds an agent graph. The result is always a :class:PromptiseAgent with observability and memory as opt-in capabilities.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default servers Mapping[str, ServerSpec] | None

Mapping of server name to spec (HTTP/SSE recommended). Optional: leave it out (or pass {}) for an agent with no MCP tools, e.g. one that only uses extra_tools or just the model and its instructions.

None model ModelLike

REQUIRED. A LangChain chat model instance, a provider id string such as "openai:gpt-5-mini" or "azure:my-deployment" (see :mod:promptise.models for every provider and alias), or a Runnable.

required instructions str | Any | None

Optional system prompt. Defaults to the built-in DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT.

None identity AgentIdentity | None

Optional :class:~promptise.identity.AgentIdentity giving the agent a traceable identity. When provided, every tool call and LLM turn the agent records is attributed to the agent's identifier — its agent_id handle, or, for an IdP-backed identity with no handle, the IdP subject — unless observer_agent_id is set explicitly. A verifiable identity is also presented to HTTP/SSE MCP servers that have no bearer of their own, so the server can authenticate and attribute the calling agent. The credential is requested for each server's audience on every request, so it is renewed before it expires (the session is reopened with the new one) and refreshed once if a server answers 401; a call the server still rejects fails with :class:~promptise.mcp.client.MCPConnectionRejectedError instead of hanging. If the identity cannot supply a credential (the IdP is unreachable), the request is not sent: it fails with :class:~promptise.mcp.client.MCPCredentialError rather than going out unauthenticated. The identity is exposed as :attr:PromptiseAgent.identity.

None trace_tools bool

Print each tool invocation and result to stdout. Covers MCP tools, cross-agent tools, sandbox tools and extra_tools, and calls answered from an earlier result (ContextCompaction(reuse_results=...)), marked as reused.

False cross_agents Mapping[str, CrossAgent] | None

Optional mapping of peer name → CrossAgent. Each peer is exposed as an ask_agent_<name> tool.

None include_broadcast bool

Also add a broadcast_to_agents tool that asks several peers the same question in parallel. Off by default. A peer whose ask_agent_<name> tool needs approval is not reachable through it (unless broadcast_to_agents needs approval too).

False max_delegation_depth int

Most nested delegations one request may make (this agent → peer → peer …). A deeper call, or a call back into a peer that is already working on the request, is refused with a :class:~promptise.cross_agent.DelegationError the model sees as the tool's error. Default 3.

DEFAULT_MAX_DELEGATION_DEPTH delegation_timeout float | None

Seconds to wait for a peer's answer when its :class:CrossAgent sets no timeout of its own. None (default) = no limit beyond the peer's max_invocation_time.

None memory Any | None

Optional :class:~promptise.memory.MemoryProvider. When provided, the agent automatically searches memory before each invocation and injects relevant context as a SystemMessage.

None memory_auto_store bool

When True and memory is provided, automatically store each exchange in long-term memory after invocation. Defaults to False.

False memory_max_results int

Maximum memories injected per invocation (the limit passed to the provider's search). Defaults to 5.

5 memory_min_score float

Drop search results scoring below this relevance (0.0--1.0). Defaults to 0.0 (keep all).

0.0 memory_timeout float

Seconds to wait for the memory search before answering without memory context, and for an auto-store write before returning. A write that takes longer is not cancelled: it finishes in the background, its outcome is logged, and :meth:PromptiseAgent.shutdown waits up to 30 seconds (or memory_timeout, if longer) for it. Defaults to 5.0. Raise it when the provider is slow to start (a ChromaProvider loads its embedding model on first use).

5.0 sandbox bool | dict[str, Any] | None

Optional sandbox configuration (True, a dict of :class:~promptise.sandbox.SandboxConfig fields, a SandboxConfig, or None). Unknown keys raise. The network defaults to "none". When the sandbox cannot be started (no docker package, Docker not running, network="restricted" not enforceable) build_agent raises instead of building an agent without it. agent_pattern="code-action" enables a sandbox automatically.

None observer Any | None

Optional :class:ObservabilityCollector to reuse.

None observer_agent_id str | None

Agent identifier for tool-event recording. Also the agent_id of every event the agent emits (see events).

None observe bool | Any | None

Plug-and-play observability. Can be: - True: Enable with defaults (STANDARD level, HTML report). Writes an HTML report file to ./reports when the agent shuts down; pass an :class:ObservabilityConfig with other transporters or output_dir to change that. - :class:ObservabilityConfig: Full configuration. A config with level=ObserveLevel.OFF records nothing. - A dict of :class:ObservabilityConfig fields (as in a .superagent file's observability: section). - None/False: Disabled (default).

None extra_tools Sequence[BaseTool | Callable[..., Any]] | None

Tools the agent can call next to the MCP-discovered ones: functions made tools with :func:promptise.tool, plain functions (made tools as if decorated with @tool), and LangChain BaseTool instances. Anything else raises TypeError before any server is connected.

None expose_resources bool

Also give the agent the MCP servers' resources: adds a read_resource tool (its description lists the available resources and URI templates) and a list_resources tool. Nothing is added when no server serves resources.

False expose_prompts bool

Also give the agent the MCP servers' prompts: adds a get_prompt tool (its description lists the prompts and their arguments) that returns the rendered prompt for the agent to follow. A generated tool is named mcp_<name> when an MCP server already has a tool with its name. For a server that receives caller tokens (HTTPServerSpec.forwards_caller_token), both send the invoking caller's bearer token, exactly like MCP tool calls; otherwise they use the credentials configured for the server.

False flow Any | None

Optional :class:~promptise.prompts.flows.ConversationFlow instance, subclass, or zero-argument factory. The system prompt then evolves across turns with the flow's phase and active blocks. Each conversation gets its own flow: per session_id (see :meth:PromptiseAgent.chat), else per :class:CallerContext; an instance is deep-copied as a template. Calls with neither get a throwaway flow built from the messages passed in. The flow's prompt comes first, and instructions and the tool list are appended to it in the same system message; with no instructions, the default system prompt is not added.

None conversation_store Any | None

Optional :class:~promptise.conversations.ConversationStore. When provided, the agent's :meth:~PromptiseAgent.chat method automatically loads and persists conversation history.

None conversation_max_messages int

Maximum messages to keep per session when using the conversation store. 0 = unlimited. Oldest messages are dropped when the limit is reached.

0 context_engine Any | None

Optional :class:~promptise.ContextEngine. Its layers (including your add_layer content) are assembled with token budgeting on every call, and what the budget leaves after the instructions and tool definitions bounds the tool loop through context compaction. Its window is taken from the chat model's profile metadata unless you passed model_context_window.

None context_compaction bool | int | Any | None

How long tool loops are compacted (:class:~promptise.engine.ContextCompaction). None or True: the defaults (compact after 6 tool results). False: never compact; the model always sees the full transcript. An int: compact after that many tool results. Applies to nodes with context_scope="auto" (the default ReAct pattern) and the threshold-free settings of "ledger" nodes; a node's own compaction= wins. Compaction never skips a tool call: a repeated call runs the tool, unless its tool is opted in with ContextCompaction(reuse_results=...).

None approval Any | None

Human-in-the-loop approval. An :class:~promptise.approval.ApprovalPolicy gates the agent's own tool calls that match its patterns. Whatever is given — a policy, an :class:~promptise.approval.ApprovalHandler, or a callable — also answers server-side approval gates: MCP servers that ask the client to confirm a gated call through MCP elicitation (ElicitationApprover, MCPcast's default) reach this handler instead of being declined. A bare handler does only the latter. Without approval the agent declares no elicitation support and such servers deny the call. See :func:~promptise.approval.approval_elicitation_callback for the mapping and its fail-closed rules. It also answers the HumanNode steps of the agent's graph; without approval a HumanNode fails the run instead of approving.

None guardrails Any | None

Optional input/output scanner — a :class:~promptise.guardrails.PromptiseSecurityScanner or any object with check_input / check_output. True uses :meth:PromptiseSecurityScanner.default (call warmup() on your own scanner to load its model at startup instead of on the first message). When the scanner has scan_tool_results=True, every tool is wrapped so its result is scanned before the model reads it.

None graph_blocks list[Any] | None

Prompt blocks added ahead of the blocks of every prompt node: those of a pattern given by name, of the default ReAct graph, and of node_pool (the pool's nodes are copied, not changed). A PromptGraph passed as agent_pattern keeps its nodes as they are.

None node_pool list[Any] | None

Nodes for an autonomous graph: the agent picks the next node at each step. Takes precedence over agent_pattern.

None max_agent_iterations int

The most node executions one run may make (the engine's max_iterations). With the default ReAct graph (and "react" / "managed") each execution of the reason node is one model call plus the tool calls it asks for, so N allows at most N model calls (the reason node's limit is N too). Other patterns count each node execution (planner, tools, reflection...), and their nodes keep their own budgets. A run that reaches the limit after the model asked for tools, before it saw their results, raises :class:~promptise.engine.GraphIterationLimitError. Defaults to 25.

25 tool_summary str

Whether the agent's system prompt also lists the offered tools in an "Available tools" block, on top of the tool definitions the provider receives: "off" (default), "names" (one line of names) or "full" (parameters and the first 120 characters of each description; the behaviour before 1.3.4: 25 to 40 tokens a tool). Nodes of a custom graph that set PromptNode(tool_summary=...) keep theirs.

'off' code_action Any | None

Options for agent_pattern="code-action": a :class:~promptise.engine.CodeActionConfig or a dict with exec_timeout (seconds the program may run, default 120), max_repairs (default 1) and max_tool_calls (default 50). Raises ValueError with any other pattern.

None events Any | None

Optional :class:~promptise.events.EventNotifier. The agent emits invocation.*, tool.error, tool.slow, tool.progress (one per progress notification an MCP tool sends), guardrail.*, approval.* and cache.* events to it, whether or not observe is on, and stops it (delivering what is queued) in :meth:~PromptiseAgent.shutdown.

None on_tool_progress Callable[[str, float, float | None, str | None], Any] | None

Optional callback for progress notifications MCP servers send while a tool call runs (ProgressReporter on a Promptise server), called as (tool_name, progress, total, message); sync or async. Progress is requested from servers only when this, events or trace_tools is set.

None adaptive Any | None

Adaptive strategy (learning from failed tool calls): True, an :class:~promptise.strategy.AdaptiveStrategyConfig or a dict of its fields. Requires memory. Independent of observe. Failures and lessons are partitioned per caller by default (scope="per_user"); the manager is available as :attr:PromptiseAgent.adaptive_strategy.

None agent_pattern str | Any | None

The reasoning graph: a :class:~promptise.engine.PromptGraph, or a pattern name from promptise.agent.AGENT_PATTERNS — "react" (the default), "managed", "code-action", "verify", "peoatr", "research", "autonomous", "deliberate" or "debate". Nodes of a custom graph created with inject_tools=True receive the discovered tools. An unknown name raises ValueError.

None pattern str | Any | None

Deprecated alias for agent_pattern.

None

Returns:

Name Type Description A PromptiseAgent PromptiseAgent

Use agent.get_stats(), agent.generate_report(path), and

PromptiseAgent

await agent.shutdown() for observability and cleanup.

docs.title: promptise.function_tools.tool(func=None, /, *, name=None, description=None, timeout=None, read_only=False, idempotent=False)
docs.text:
tool(func: Callable[..., Any]) -> FunctionTool

tool(
    name: str | None = None,
    /,
    *,
    description: str | None = None,
    timeout: float | None = None,
    read_only: bool = False,
    idempotent: bool = False,
) -> Callable[[Callable[..., Any]], FunctionTool]

tool(
    *,
    name: str | None = None,
    description: str | None = None,
    timeout: float | None = None,
    read_only: bool = False,
    idempotent: bool = False,
) -> Callable[[Callable[..., Any]], FunctionTool]

Make a Python function a tool an agent can call.

Works bare (@tool), with options (@tool(name=..., description=..., timeout=...)) and with the name as the only argument (@tool("get_order")), on async def and plain def functions. The result is a :class:FunctionTool; see it for how calls, results and errors work.

Example::

from promptise import ToolError, tool

@tool
async def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID.

    Args:
        order_id: The order ID, for example "A-1001".
    """
    order = await db.orders.get(order_id)
    if order is None:
        raise ToolError(f"No order {order_id}.")
    return order

The tool's name is the function's name. Its description is the docstring without the parameter section, which describes the parameters instead (Google Args:, NumPy Parameters or Sphinx :param:). Annotated[T, Field(description=...)] or Annotated[T, "text"] describe a parameter too, and win over the docstring. Type hints, defaults and Field constraints make the parameter schema, validated before every call.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default func Any

The function (when used bare), or the tool's name (@tool("get_order")).

None name str | None

The tool's name; defaults to the function's name.

None description str | None

The tool's description; defaults to the docstring without its parameter section.

None timeout float | None

Seconds a call may run before the model gets a TIMEOUT error; None (default) for no limit. The error says the call's outcome is unknown, and is retryable only for a tool marked read_only or idempotent.

None read_only bool

The tool only reads data (MCP readOnlyHint): safe to call again, and its answers may be cached.

False idempotent bool

Calling it again with the same arguments has no further effect (MCP idempotentHint): safe to call again.

False

Returns:

Name Type Description A Any

docs.title: promptise.function_tools.FunctionTool
docs.text:
Bases: BaseTool

A tool made from a Python function by :func:tool.

A LangChain BaseTool: pass it to build_agent(extra_tools=[...]) and approval policies, guardrails (scan_tool_results), tracing, events and tool optimization treat it like any other tool.

Calling the tool directly runs the function as it was written: await get_order("A-1001") for an async def, refund(...) for a plain def, with no validation and no injected caller. Use it in unit tests. await get_order.ainvoke({"order_id": "A-1001"}) runs it the way the agent does: validated, with the caller injected, and returns what the model reads.

When the agent calls it, the arguments are validated against :attr:args_schema first (with defaults filled in, and nested objects the model sent as JSON text decoded); invalid ones are answered with a :class:~promptise.tools.ToolArgumentError the model can correct. A synchronous function runs in a worker thread, so it never blocks the event loop. A CallerContext parameter receives the caller of the current agent.ainvoke(..., caller=...) (an empty CallerContext() when there is none, or None when the parameter is CallerContext | None).

Results go to the model as text: a string as it is, None as an empty result, anything else as JSON (dicts, lists, numbers, Pydantic models, dataclasses ...).

Errors: raise :class:~promptise.ToolError to give the model an error it can act on: it sees the same {"error": {"code", "message", ...}} envelope a Promptise MCP server sends (raised to callbacks as :class:FunctionToolError). Any other exception is a tool that failed: the model sees Error: <type>: <message>, as for every tool. With :attr:timeout, a call that runs longer is answered with a retryable TIMEOUT error; a synchronous function's thread can't be stopped, so it finishes in the background and its result is dropped.

Attributes:

Name Type Description timeout float | None

Seconds a call may run, or None for no limit.

Raised by a :class:FunctionTool when its function raises :class:~promptise.ToolError (or another :class:~promptise.mcp.server.MCPError) or runs past the tool's timeout. docs.title: promptise.agent.PromptiseAgent
docs.text:
The unified Promptise agent.

Always returned by :func:build_agent. Observability and memory are opt-in capabilities activated by constructor parameters — disabled features no-op or return sensible defaults, so callers never need to check what type they got back.

.. code-block:: python

# Simple — no observe, no memory
agent = await build_agent(servers=..., model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [...]})
await agent.shutdown()

# With observability
agent = await build_agent(..., observe=True)
result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [...]})
stats = agent.get_stats()
agent.generate_report("report.html")
await agent.shutdown()

# With memory
agent = await build_agent(..., memory=InMemoryProvider())
result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [...]})  # auto-injects context
await agent.shutdown()

Attributes:

Name Type Description collector

The :class:ObservabilityCollector holding recorded events, or None when observability is not enabled.

provider

The :class:~promptise.memory.MemoryProvider instance, or None when memory is not enabled.

docs.text:
Invoke the agent asynchronously.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default input Any

LangGraph-style input dict with messages.

required config dict[str, Any] | None

LangGraph config dict (callbacks, etc.).

None session_id str | None

Optional conversation ID. With a conversation flow, each session (per caller) keeps its own flow state. :meth:chat passes its session_id here.

None caller CallerContext | None

Optional :class:CallerContext with per-request identity. When provided, user_id is used for conversation ownership and the full context is available to guardrails and observability. When omitted, the ambient CallerContext (if one is already active in this task) is inherited, so cross-agent delegation keeps the original human principal: a peer invoked inside another agent's request scopes its cache, memory, guardrails, and conversations to the original user.

None

When memory is enabled, relevant context is searched and injected as a SystemMessage before the inner graph runs. When observability is enabled, a callback handler is attached to capture every LLM turn, tool call, and token count.

docs.title: astream(input, config=None, *, caller=None, **kwargs) async
docs.text:
Stream the agent's run, one chunk per step of its graph.

Each chunk is {"messages": [...]}: the conversation once a node of the agent's graph has finished (LangGraph's stream_mode="values"). The last chunk is what :meth:ainvoke returns. Input guardrails run first (a violation raises), an answer is checked by the output guardrails before its chunk is yielded, and memory and observability work as in :meth:ainvoke. The semantic cache is not consulted.

For token-by-token output and tool activity, use :meth:astream_with_tools.

required config dict[str, Any] | None

None

docs.title: chat(message, *, session_id, user_id=None, caller=None, metadata=None, system_prompt=None) async
docs.text:
Send a message and get a response, with automatic session persistence.

This is the high-level API for building chat applications. The conversation store (if configured) handles loading history, persisting new messages, and session lifecycle automatically.

If no conversation store is configured, this still works — it just has no history beyond the current call.

Ownership enforcement: When user_id (or caller.user_id) is provided and the session already exists, the store checks that the session belongs to that user. If it belongs to a different user, :class:~promptise.conversations.SessionAccessDenied is raised.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default message str

The user's message text.

required session_id str

Unique identifier for this conversation session. Use :func:~promptise.conversations.generate_session_id to create cryptographically secure, non-enumerable IDs.

required user_id str | None

Optional user identifier. Shorthand for caller=CallerContext(user_id=...): it scopes session ownership and the rest of the invocation (per-user memory, cache, guardrails, observability). If both user_id and caller are provided, caller.user_id takes precedence; a caller without a user_id gets this one.

None caller CallerContext | None

Optional :class:CallerContext with per-request identity. Carries user_id, bearer_token, roles, scopes, and metadata through the entire invocation.

None metadata dict[str, Any] | None

Optional metadata to attach to the user message (e.g. source, IP, device).

None system_prompt str | None

Optional per-call system prompt override.

None

Returns:

Type Description str

The assistant's response text.

Raises:

Type Description SessionAccessDenied

If user_id is provided and the session belongs to a different user.

RuntimeError

If the conversation store fails while the session's ownership is being checked. chat() fails closed here: it will not answer in a session whose owner it could not verify. Failures to load or save the history are logged and the call still answers.

from promptise.conversations import generate_session_id

agent = await build_agent(..., conversation_store=store)
sid = generate_session_id()
reply = await agent.chat("Hello!", session_id=sid, user_id="user-42")
reply = await agent.chat("What did I say?", session_id=sid, user_id="user-42")

docs.title: promptise.agent.CallerContext dataclass
docs.text:
Identity and metadata for the caller of an agent invocation.

Pass this to ainvoke() or chat() to carry per-request identity through the entire invocation — guardrails, conversation ownership, observability, and the MCP servers the agent calls.

Attributes:

Name Type Description user_id str | None

Unique user identifier. Used for conversation session ownership and observability correlation.

tenant_id str | None

Organisation / tenant the caller belongs to. When set, it becomes part of :attr:isolation_key, so every per-user isolation surface (semantic cache, memory search, conversation ownership) is scoped per tenant — two tenants with the same user_id can never see each other's data.

bearer_token str | None

JWT or OAuth token for the caller. Sent as Authorization: Bearer <token> on every tool call to an HTTP/SSE MCP server during this invocation, over a session opened for this token — never shared with another caller — so the server authenticates the user, not the credential the agent was built with. A server opts out with HTTPServerSpec(forward_caller_token=False); a server with an API key keeps it unless it sets forward_caller_token=True. stdio servers have no request headers and never receive it. Tool discovery at build time still uses the server spec's credentials.

roles set[str]

Caller's roles (e.g. {"admin", "analyst"}). Available for custom guardrail rules and logging.

scopes set[str]

OAuth scopes (e.g. {"read", "write"}).

metadata dict[str, Any]

Arbitrary key-value metadata (IP, user-agent, etc.).

caller = CallerContext(
    user_id="user-42",
    tenant_id="acme",
    bearer_token="eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...",
    roles={"analyst"},
)
result = await agent.ainvoke(input, caller=caller)
reply = await agent.chat("Hello", session_id=sid, caller=caller)

docs.title: isolation_key property
docs.text:
The identity key used for every per-user isolation surface.

"{tenant_id}::{user_id}" when a tenant is set, otherwise the plain user_id. This single derivation is what the semantic cache, memory scoping, and conversation ownership all key on, so tenant isolation is a structural invariant rather than a convention. None when user_id is unset.

docs.title: promptise.engine.execution.PromptGraphEngine
docs.text:
Adaptive graph traversal engine.

Traverses a PromptGraph by executing nodes and following edges. The graph is copied per invocation so concurrent calls are safe and runtime mutations don't affect the original graph.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default graph PromptGraph

The graph to traverse.

required model BaseChatModel

LangChain BaseChatModel for LLM calls.

required max_iterations int

Maximum node executions per run: N allows exactly N (in the ReAct graph, N model calls).

50 max_node_iterations int | None

Optional engine-wide ceiling on how many times a single node can execute in one run (each tool-loop round counts). None (the default) leaves each node's own max_iterations in charge; with a value, the lower of the two applies. When a node has used its budget, the engine does not run it again: it follows the node's "error" transition, else an __error__ node, else ends the run. A run that ends this way (or on max_iterations) in the middle of a tool loop raises :class:GraphIterationLimitError: the model never answered.

None hooks list[Any] | None

List of hook instances for interception.

None allow_self_modification bool

Allow the LLM to modify the graph via structured output _graph_action fields.

True max_mutations_per_run int

Cap on graph mutations per run.

10 tools list[Any] | None

Tools for nodes with inject_tools=True (build_agent passes the MCP tools it discovered). Tools set on the graph's nodes are added to them.

None compaction Any | None

:class:~promptise.engine.compaction.ContextCompaction settings for nodes that compact (context_scope="auto" / "ledger") and set none of their own.

None tool_summary str | None

The "Available tools" block that PromptNode nodes with tools add to their system prompt when they set no tool_summary of their own: "off" (None, the default), "names" or "full". The model receives the tool definitions either way.

None human_handler Any | None

The async handler(prompt, state) -> bool that HumanNode nodes ask (put in config["_human_handler"] unless the run's config has one). Without a handler a HumanNode fails instead of approving.

None

docs.text: The execution report from the last run (ainvoke() or a stream).

docs.title: ainvoke(input, config=None, **kwargs) async
docs.text:
Run the graph to completion.

Returns {"messages": [...]} matching the LangGraph contract.

docs.title: astream(input, config=None, **kwargs) async
docs.text:
Run the graph, yielding the conversation after every node.

Each chunk is {"messages": [...]} -- the full message list once a node has finished (LangGraph's stream_mode="values"). The last chunk equals what :meth:ainvoke returns. Nodes run exactly as in :meth:ainvoke: one model call per step, tool calls in parallel. A run that ends on a failed node raises :class:GraphExecutionError after its chunks.

docs.title: astream_events(input, *, config=None, version='v2', **kwargs) async
docs.text:
Stream execution events matching LangGraph v2 format.

Yields event dicts consumed by PromptiseAgent.astream_with_tools():

  • on_chat_model_stream -- one per model chunk; data["chunk"] is the AIMessageChunk.
  • on_tool_start / on_tool_end / on_tool_error -- one start and one end per tool call, sharing a run_id. on_tool_end carries data["status"] ("success" or "error" when the tool reported an error, e.g. an MCP ToolError) and data["duration_ms"]; on_tool_error means the tool raised.
  • on_node_start, on_node_end, on_node_error (engine-specific).

Nodes stream through :meth:BaseNode.stream and run exactly once: the events are a view of the same execution :meth:ainvoke does.

docs.title: promptise.engine.execution.GraphExecutionError
docs.text:
Bases: RuntimeError

A graph run ended on a node failure the graph did not recover from.

Raised by :meth:PromptGraphEngine.ainvoke and, after their output, by :meth:PromptGraphEngine.astream and :meth:PromptGraphEngine.astream_events. The provider exception (a rejected API key, a network failure…) is chained as __cause__ when the node recorded one. PromptiseAgent.ainvoke() lets it propagate, so a broken credential is an exception at the call site, never an "answer" that echoes the question.

Attributes:

Name Type Description graph_name

Name of the graph that failed.

node_name

Node whose failure ended the run.

error

The node's recorded error text.

report

The :class:ExecutionReport of the failed run.

docs.title: promptise.engine.execution.GraphIterationLimitError
docs.text:
Bases: GraphExecutionError

A run hit an iteration limit in the middle of a tool loop.

The model asked for tools, the limit stopped the run before it saw their results, so there is no answer: the last message is a tool result. Raised instead of returning that tool result as if it were the agent's answer. A subclass of :class:GraphExecutionError.

Which limit: the node's own budget (PromptNode(max_iterations=...), capped by the engine's max_node_iterations when one is set; the reason node of build_agent's react and managed graphs gets max_agent_iterations) or the engine's max_iterations for the whole run (build_agent(max_agent_iterations=...)).

Attributes:

Name Type Description limit

The limit that was reached.

pending_tools

Names of the tools whose results the model never saw.

docs.title: promptise.engine.execution.GraphStoppedError
docs.text:
Bases: GraphExecutionError

A hook ended a run in the middle of a tool loop.

A hook ends a run by setting state.current_node = "__end__" (:class:~promptise.engine.hooks.CycleDetectionHook, or a custom hook). When that happens after the model asked for tools and before it saw their results, there is no answer: the last message is a tool result. Raised instead of returning that tool result as the agent's answer, like :class:GraphIterationLimitError. A hook stop after the model answered returns the answer as usual.

Attributes:

Name Type Description reason

Why the run stopped (the hook's NodeResult.error when it set one, e.g. "Token budget exceeded: 5078/5000 tokens").

stopped_by

Class name of the hook that ended the run.

pending_tools

Names of the tools whose results the model never saw.

docs.title: promptise.engine.execution.GraphBudgetExceededError
docs.text:
Bases: GraphStoppedError

A :class:~promptise.engine.hooks.BudgetHook stopped a run over its token or cost budget before the model gave an answer.

Bases: GraphExecutionError

A code-action run could not do the whole job within max_tool_calls.

Raised when the last program the model wrote reached the per-program tool-call cap, or when, after a program reached it, the model answered that the job cannot be done in fewer calls. The run has no answer: a partial result computed from part of the data is never returned.

docs.text:
Settings for compacting a long tool loop.

Pass one to build_agent(context_compaction=...) (or True / False / an int for after_tool_results), or to PromptNode(compaction=...) for a single node.

Attributes:

Name Type Description enabled bool

False keeps the full transcript: nodes with context_scope="auto" never compact.

after_tool_results int

"auto" nodes compact once the run has this many tool results.

max_tokens int | None

Also compact once the full transcript is estimated to pass this many tokens, and shrink the ledger until the compacted view fits. None means no token budget. build_agent sets it from a ContextEngine's budget.

keep_result_chars int

Older tool results longer than this are cut to an excerpt of this many characters in the ledger, unless the model made the same call more than once (then it is shown in full).

history_messages int

How many earlier conversation messages the history note keeps.

history_chars int

Each earlier message is cut to this many characters in the history note.

Token counter for max_tokens. Defaults to a 4-characters-per-token estimate.

reuse_results bool | tuple[str, ...]

Answer a repeated call from an earlier result instead of running the tool again. False (the default): every call runs. True: once a node compacts, a call with the same tool and arguments as an earlier successful call in the run gets that call's latest result back. A list of tool names (* wildcards allowed) limits this to those tools. Only for tools whose result cannot change during a run (a lookup by id); never for status, health or queue checks. A reused call is reported like any other (trace_tools, observer, callbacks, stream events), marked as reused.

docs.title: promptise.engine.code_action.CodeActionConfig
docs.text:
Bases: BaseModel

Tuning knobs for the code-action pattern.

Pass it (or an equivalent dict) as build_agent(code_action=...). Unknown keys are rejected.

Attributes:

Name Type Description exec_timeout int

Max seconds the generated program may run in the sandbox. When it expires the program's processes are killed.

max_repairs int

How many times a failed program (it crashed, or it reached max_tool_calls) is fed back to the model for a fix.

max_tool_calls int

Hard cap on the bridged tool calls of each program the model writes. Every call counts, failed ones included. The first program and each repaired one get their own budget, so a run makes at most (max_repairs + 1) * max_tool_calls calls. A program that reaches the cap gets ToolBudgetExceeded for each further call, and its output is never taken as the answer. The model is not told the value, and is told never to skip records to stay under it. A run that cannot do the whole job within the cap raises CodeActionBudgetError (a GraphExecutionError). 0 disables the cap (not advised).

docs.title: promptise.engine.nodes.PromptNode
docs.text:
Bases: BaseNode

A complete reasoning unit in the graph.

Each PromptNode is a self-contained processing pipeline:

Input → Preprocess → Context Assembly → LLM Call → Tool Execution → Postprocess → Guards → Output

Every aspect is configurable: - What the LLM sees (blocks, strategy, perspective, context layers) - What the LLM can do (tools, tool_choice) - What the LLM must produce (output_schema, guards) - How data flows in (input_keys read from state.context) - How data flows out (output_key writes to state.context) - Pre/post processing (preprocessor, postprocessor callables) - Context from previous node (inherit_context_from)

A tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON (LangChain keeps it in AIMessage.invalid_tool_calls) does not run: its ToolMessage is an error that names the tool's parameters, it counts as a failed call (NodeResult.tool_calls, with invalid and raw_args), and the tool loop goes on so the model can call again.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

Unique node identifier.

required blocks list[Any] | None

PromptBlocks to assemble for this node's system prompt.

None strategy Any | None

Reasoning strategy (ChainOfThought, SelfCritique, etc.).

None perspective Any | None

Cognitive perspective (Analyst, Critic, etc.).

None tools list[BaseTool] | None

Tools available at THIS node. None disables tools.

None tool_choice str

"auto" (the model decides, the default), "required" (the model must call a tool), a tool's name (the model must call that tool) or "none" (the model is called without the tools, so it cannot call them). "required" and a tool name apply to the node's first model call; once tool results come back the model decides, so it can answer instead of calling tools until the node's max_iterations.

'auto' inject_tools bool

When True, the engine auto-injects all discovered MCP tools into this node at runtime. Use this when defining custom graphs where nodes should receive tools from build_agent(servers=...) without hardcoding them. The injected tools merge with any tools already set on the node (no duplicates).

False tool_summary str | None

An "Available tools" block in the system prompt, on top of the tool definitions the model receives anyway: "off" (none), "names" (one line of tool names) or "full" (each tool's parameters and the first 120 characters of its description). None (default) uses the engine's setting (PromptGraphEngine(tool_summary=...) / build_agent(tool_summary=...)), which defaults to "off".

None output_schema type | None

Pydantic model for structured output.

None guards list[Any] | None

Guards that validate the output before proceeding.

None context_layers dict[str, int] | None

Extra named context layers with priorities. Merged into the system prompt during assembly.

None max_tokens int | None

Max response tokens for this node's model calls. None (default) keeps the model's own setting.

None temperature float | None

Sampling temperature for this node's model calls. None (default) keeps the model's own setting. Both are set on a copy of the model, under the provider's own field names (max_output_tokens for Google, num_predict for Ollama).

None input_keys list[str] | None

Keys to read from state.context and inject into the system prompt. E.g. ["search_results", "user_query"] makes those values available in the prompt.

None output_key str | None

Key to write this node's output to in state.context: the parsed object with an output_schema, else the reply text. The next node can read it via input_keys.

None inherit_context_from str | None

Name of a previous node whose output should be injected as context. Reads from state.context["{node_name}_output"].

None preprocessor Callable | None

Callable (state, config) (sync or async) that runs before the LLM call. Use for data transformation, enrichment, or validation: when it raises, the node fails without calling the model (NodeResult.error names the exception), and the graph handles that like any node failure.

None postprocessor Callable | None

Callable (output, state, config) → output (sync or async) that runs on the model's reply (not on a step that only calls tools). It receives the parsed object with an output_schema, else the reply text. A value other than None replaces the output; an exception is logged and the output kept.

None include_observations bool

Auto-inject recent tool results from state.

True include_plan bool

Auto-inject current plan/subgoals from state.

True include_reflections bool

Auto-inject past learnings from state.

True context_scope str

How much history the model sees: "full", "auto" (full, compacting once the tool loop gets long), "ledger" (always compacted) or "scoped". See :mod:promptise.engine.compaction.

'full' auto_ledger_after int | None

Tool results before an "auto" node compacts (default 6). Shorthand for compaction=ContextCompaction(after_tool_results=...).

None compaction Any | None

:class:~promptise.engine.compaction.ContextCompaction settings for this node (or True / False / an int). Without it the node uses the settings build_agent passed, else the defaults.

None

docs.title: execute(state, config) async
docs.text:
Execute the full node pipeline:

  1. Preprocessor (custom data transformation)
  2. Context assembly (blocks + input_keys + inherited context + state)
  3. LLM call (with tools if configured)
  4. Tool execution (auto-loop if tools called)
  5. Postprocessor (custom output transformation)
  6. Guards (validate output)
  7. Write output to state.context[output_key]

docs.title: stream(state, config) async
docs.text:
Run the :meth:execute pipeline, streaming as it goes.

One model call per step, exactly as :meth:execute: the call is streamed and its chunks are yielded as on_chat_model_stream events (data["chunk"]; all chunks of one call share data["run_id"]). Each tool call yields on_tool_start and then on_tool_end (data["status"] is "error" when the tool reported an error) or on_tool_error (the tool raised); tool calls run in parallel, as in :meth:execute. The last event is on_node_end with the :class:NodeResult under data["result"].

Nodes with output_schema call the model without streaming (there are no text tokens to stream). A subclass that overrides :meth:execute but not this method streams through :meth:BaseNode.stream, so its own logic is never bypassed.

docs.title: promptise.engine.nodes.ToolNode
docs.text:
Bases: BaseNode

Execute a specific tool or let the engine pick from available tools.

Unlike PromptNode (where tools are called by the LLM), ToolNode executes tools directly based on state context. Useful when tool selection is deterministic rather than LLM-driven.

A call runs as it would in a :class:PromptNode: the engine hooks' pre_tool (may change the arguments, or block the call by raising) and post_tool (may change the result) run around it, the tool is invoked as a tool call (an MCP tool error reaches the model as the server's error envelope, flagged status="error"), and :meth:stream yields on_tool_start / on_tool_end (or on_tool_error) for each call, so astream_events() and astream_with_tools() show it. The node runs one turn's calls one after another, in order. A call whose arguments are not valid JSON (AIMessage.invalid_tool_calls) is answered with an error the model can act on, after the turn's other calls; it does not run.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default tools list[BaseTool] | None

Available tools for this node.

None validate_inputs bool

Check each call's arguments against the tool's parameter schema before calling it (after pre_tool hooks). Invalid arguments do not reach the tool: the call's ToolMessage is an error (status="error") listing each problem by argument path (promptise.tools.ToolArgumentError's message) so the model can correct the call, and callbacks get on_tool_error. As for MCP tools, an explicit null for an optional parameter that cannot be null counts as not given. An MCP tool checks its own arguments the same way, so the node leaves the check to it. With False, the arguments go to the tool as they are.

True deduplicate bool

Run identical (tool, args) calls of one model turn once. Each repeat in that turn still gets its own ToolMessage with the first call's result, and is reported as reused (trace_tools, observer, callbacks, engine hooks' on_tool_reused instead of pre_tool / post_tool, "reused": True in NodeResult.tool_calls and stream events). A call in a later model turn, a later pass of a tool_selector, or another run runs the tool again, so a status check gets the current value. A failed call is never reused. The record lives in the run, never on the node, so sequential and concurrent runs of a graph do not affect each other.

True max_result_chars int

Cap the size of a successful tool result.

4000 tool_selector Callable[[GraphState], tuple[str, dict]] | None

Optional callable that selects which tool to call based on state. If None, runs the tool calls of the most recent AI message that has tool calls.

None

docs.title: stream(state, config) async
docs.text:
Run the :meth:execute pipeline, yielding each call's events.

Each call yields on_tool_start and then on_tool_end (data["status"] is "error" when the tool reported an error, data["reused"] is True for a repeat answered from the turn's earlier result) or on_tool_error (the tool or a hook raised), with the call's run_id and duration_ms -- the events a :class:PromptNode yields for its tool calls. The last event is on_node_end with the :class:NodeResult under data["result"]. A subclass that overrides :meth:execute but not this method streams through :meth:BaseNode.stream.

docs.title: promptise.engine.nodes.AutonomousNode
docs.text:
Bases: BaseNode

dynamically composes its own reasoning path at runtime.

Instead of following a pre-defined graph, the agent:

  1. Sees all available nodes as a menu of capabilities
  2. Decides which node to execute next based on the task
  3. Executes that node (with its tools, blocks, guards)
  4. Evaluates the result
  5. Decides the next node or finishes

The developer provides the LEGO blocks. The agent builds the model.

Usage::

autonomous = AutonomousNode(
    "agent",
    node_pool=[
        web_researcher("search", tools=search_tools),
        data_analyst("analyze", tools=db_tools),
        fact_checker("verify"),
        summarizer("conclude"),
        planner("plan"),
    ],
    planner_instructions="You are a research assistant. "
        "Use the available steps to answer the user's question thoroughly.",
)

graph = PromptGraph("autonomous")
graph.add_node(autonomous)
graph.set_entry("agent")

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default node_pool list[BaseNode] | None

Available nodes the agent can choose from. Each node is fully configured with its own tools, blocks, guards, and instructions.

None planner_instructions str

How the agent should approach selecting and sequencing nodes.

'' allow_repeat bool

Whether the agent can re-use the same node multiple times.

True max_steps int

Maximum nodes the agent can execute per run.

15 entry_node str | None

Pool node to run first, before the agent chooses.

None terminal_nodes list[str] | None

Pool nodes that end the run once they succeed.

None answer_node str | None

Pool node that writes the final answer when the agent finishes without a terminal node having run last. Defaults to the first terminal node; with no terminal node, the node asks the model for the final answer itself.

None

A chosen step runs its whole tool loop — the node is re-run while its model keeps calling tools, up to the node's max_iterations — before the agent chooses again. The routing exchange (the step menu and the model's JSON choice) is never added to the conversation, and the run always ends with a written answer. A tool name given as the next step runs the pool node that has that tool.

docs.title: promptise.engine.code_action.CodeActionNode
docs.text:
Bases: BaseNode

A node that solves a task by writing and running one sandboxed program.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default name str

Node identifier.

required tools list[Any] | None

Tools the generated program may call (bridged to the host). If empty, falls back to the engine's runtime tools (_engine_tools).

None system_prompt str

Base system prompt prepended to the code-writing prompt.

'' blocks list[Any] | None

Accepted for signature parity with other prebuilts (unused in the program prompt — system_prompt carries the instructions).

None sandbox_factory SandboxFactory | None

async () -> SandboxSession. Required at run time; the node creates one session per run and cleans it up.

None model_override Any | None

Optional per-node model: a chat model, a model string ("openai:gpt-5-mini") or a :class:~promptise.models.Model.

None max_repairs int

How many times to feed a failed program (a crash, or a program that reached max_tool_calls) back for a fix.

1 result_marker str

stdout prefix that marks the final answer line.

'RESULT:' exec_timeout int

Max seconds the program may run inside the sandbox.

120 max_tool_calls int

Hard upper bound on the bridged tool calls of each program (the first and each repaired one get their own budget). Every call counts: successful, failed, an unknown tool, or one a hook blocked. Once reached, further calls raise ToolBudgetExceeded in the program instead of executing, a warning is logged, and the program's output is discarded: the model is asked for a program that does the whole job in fewer calls (never one over part of the data), or to reply CANNOT_FINISH_WITHIN_CALL_CAP. That reply, or a budget hit with no repairs left, fails the node, and the engine raises CodeActionBudgetError (a GraphExecutionError). The prompt says the cap exists but not its value, so the model cannot fit the data to it. A hook-independent safety bound so a generated program cannot loop a tool unbounded. Set 0 to disable (not advised).

50

It gives a model the benefit of an explicit verification step at one-turn latency (no multi-call overhead). On models that already reason internally it matches a direct prompt; on weaker models the forced self-check recovers errors a single pass would miss. A good default when you want a self-checking answer without a multi-stage pipeline.

docs.title: promptise.engine.prebuilts.build_managed_graph(tools=None, system_prompt='', *, blocks=None, max_node_iterations=30)
docs.text:
Tool agent with context lifecycle management for long tool chains.

A single tool-using node, but run with context_scope="ledger": instead of feeding the model an ever-growing transcript of tool calls and results (where it loses track and re-queries the same facts dozens of times), each turn it sees the task plus a compact, deduplicated "facts gathered" ledger built from the tool results so far. Context stays bounded and the model stops re-looking-up what it already knows. A call the model does repeat runs the tool again (a status changes); to answer repeats of lookups whose results cannot change from the earlier result, pass build_agent(context_compaction=ContextCompaction(reuse_results=[...])).

Use this for deep multi-tool tasks — traversing a database/graph, gathering many facts then aggregating. It cuts redundant tool calls and bounds token growth on long chains at equal accuracy — an efficiency primitive, not an accuracy claim.

Tools the agent can call.

None system_prompt str

Base system prompt.

'' blocks list[Any] | None

Optional PromptBlocks for the node.

None max_node_iterations int

Tool-loop budget (higher than ReAct's — deep tasks make many calls).

30

Returns:

Type Description PromptGraph

A single-node PromptGraph whose node manages its tool-loop context.

docs.title: promptise.engine.prebuilts.build_code_action_graph(tools=None, system_prompt='', *, blocks=None, sandbox_factory=None, max_repairs=1, exec_timeout=120, max_tool_calls=50)
docs.text:
Code-action reasoning — the model writes one program, not a tool chain.

For aggregation / data-traversal tasks (gather many facts then compute), chaining dozens of conversational tool calls is slow, expensive, and error-prone. code-action changes the action space: in a single LLM turn the model writes one Python program that calls the available tools (bridged into a hardened Docker sandbox) and computes the answer deterministically. Validated on agentic tasks — a large accuracy gain at a fraction of the tokens and latency, in one turn.

Requires a sandbox: build_agent(agent_pattern="code-action") auto-enables it (Docker must be installed and running). The generated code runs with a read-only rootfs, dropped capabilities, seccomp, and no network — it can only reach the outside world through the bridged host tools, so every tool call still passes through the engine's hooks (budget, health, audit).

120 max_tool_calls int

docs.title: promptise.engine.prebuilts.build_peoatr_graph(tools=None, system_prompt='', *, planning_instructions='', acting_instructions='', thinking_instructions='', reflecting_instructions='', blocks=None, max_act_steps=12)
docs.text:
Build a PEOATR (Plan → Act → Think → Reflect → Answer) graph.

Five-stage reasoning pattern where the agent:

  1. Plans subgoals and rates the plan (re-plans below quality 3)
  2. Executes tools to achieve the active subgoal
  3. Analyzes the results (think): another tool call now, or reflect
  4. Reflects on progress and routes: answer, replan, or continue
  5. Writes the final answer

Plan, think and reflect produce structured output, so their routing decisions always reach the engine. Every stage has an iteration budget; a stage that exhausts it hands over to answer (plan hands over to act), so the run always ends with a written answer.

Extra instructions for the Think stage.

'' reflecting_instructions str

Extra instructions for the Reflect stage.

'' blocks list[Any] | None

Optional PromptBlocks shared across all stages.

None max_act_steps int

Budget for the Act stage across the run — each model call (every tool-loop round) counts.

12

docs.text:
Build a Search → Verify → Synthesize research pipeline.

Three-stage pattern for research tasks:

  1. Search: use search tools to gather information, then summarize the findings
  2. Verify: a model checks the findings against the tool results gathered (structured :class:ResearchVerdict). A failed check sends the run back to search with the issues; verify runs at most max_verify_rounds times, then the run moves on to synthesize.
  3. Synthesize: write the final answer from the findings

Every stage has an iteration budget; a search that exhausts its budget hands over to synthesize, so the run always ends with a written answer.

docs.text:
Build a debate graph: Proposer ↔ Critic → Judge → Answer.

The proposer answers (with tools), the critic challenges the answer and sends it back for revision when its severity is above 0.3, the judge renders a verdict (a failed verdict also sends it back), and answer writes the reply. docs.title: promptise.engine.hooks.BudgetHook
docs.text:
Enforces a token and/or cost budget for each graph run.

After every node, the hook adds the node's tokens to the run's total (GraphState.total_tokens, so the budget is per run: one hook on an engine caps every run separately, also concurrent ones). When the run goes over max_tokens or max_cost_usd, the hook ends the run (state.current_node = "__end__") and writes the reason to the node's NodeResult.error.

A run the budget stops after the model asked for tools, before it saw their results, has no answer: the engine raises :class:~promptise.engine.GraphBudgetExceededError instead of returning the last tool result. A run whose model answered on the node that went over budget returns that answer.

docs.title: promptise.conversations.ConversationStore
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Interface for conversation persistence backends.

All methods are async. Implementations must handle their own thread-safety and connection management. Call :meth:close when the store is no longer needed.

Security note: Stores do NOT enforce session ownership internally. Ownership checks happen at the PromptiseAgent layer via _enforce_ownership() before calling store methods. If you use stores directly (outside of build_agent()), you MUST verify session ownership yourself by calling get_session() and checking user_id before load_messages() or delete_session().

Implementing a custom store requires four data methods plus :meth:close::

class MyStore:
    async def load_messages(self, session_id: str) -> list[Message]: ...
    async def save_messages(self, session_id: str, messages: list[Message]) -> None: ...
    async def delete_session(self, session_id: str) -> bool: ...
    async def list_sessions(self, *, user_id=None, limit=50, offset=0) -> list[SessionInfo]: ...
    async def close(self) -> None: ...

docs.title: promptise.config.HTTPServerSpec
docs.text:
Bases: _BaseServer

Specification for a remote MCP server reachable via HTTP/SSE.

Supports two authentication methods:

  1. Bearer token (JWT): pass a pre-issued token via bearer_token and it is automatically injected as Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  2. API key (simple secret): pass a pre-shared key via api_key and it is automatically injected as x-api-key: <key>.

Tokens should be obtained from your Identity Provider (Auth0, Keycloak, Okta, etc.) or from the MCP server's built-in token endpoint (for development/testing). The agent never generates tokens itself.

Attributes:

Name Type Description url str

Full endpoint URL (e.g., http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp).

transport Literal['http', 'streamable-http', 'sse']

"http", "streamable-http", or "sse".

headers dict[str, str]

Extra HTTP headers sent on every request. Values of credential headers (Authorization, Cookie, x-api-key, names containing token, secret, ...) are sent as given but shown as ********** in repr() and in model_dump(mode="json") (a ${VAR} resolved from a manifest never shows up in a dump or a log line). model_dump() in Python mode keeps them, so a spec can be rebuilt from it.

auth str | None

Deprecated and ignored — it was never sent to the server. Setting it emits a FutureWarning; use bearer_token or api_key.

bearer_token SecretStr | None

Pre-issued Bearer token. When set, an Authorization: Bearer <token> header is created automatically.

api_key SecretStr | None

Pre-shared API key. When set, an x-api-key header is created automatically. Use this for simple secret-based auth when JWT is overkill.

forward_caller_token bool | None

Whether an invocation's caller token reaches this server. When it does and the invocation carries a :class:~promptise.CallerContext with a bearer_token, this server's tools are called with Authorization: Bearer <caller token> over a session opened for that caller, so the server sees the user, not whoever built the agent. The caller's token replaces bearer_token (and any Authorization header), which, like the agent identity, is still used for tool discovery and for calls without a caller token.

None (default): forward, unless the server is configured with an API key (api_key or an x-api-key header). An API key is the server's explicit credential and wins: the caller's bearer would be sent next to it, and a gate that checks the bearer first (a Promptise server does) rejects the call with 401. True: always forward, also to an API-key server; the key is still sent, so the server receives both and decides which one counts (a Promptise server checks the bearer first). False: never forward; use it for a third-party server that must not receive your users' tokens, or one that should always see the agent's own credential. See :attr:forwards_caller_token for the resolved value.

Example — Bearer token::

HTTPServerSpec(
    url="http://localhost:8080/mcp",
    bearer_token="eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...",
)

Example — API key::

HTTPServerSpec(
    url="http://localhost:8080/mcp",
    api_key="my-secret-key",
)

Example — manual header::

HTTPServerSpec(
    url="http://localhost:8080/mcp",
    headers={"authorization": "Bearer <token>"},
)
