Conversation Store Memory Provider What it stores Exact chat messages, in order Semantic facts and knowledge How it retrieves By session ID (exact lookup) By similarity search (fuzzy) Scope Per-session Cross-session Purpose "What did they say 3 messages ago?" "What do I know about this user?"

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.conversations import SQLiteConversationStore

store = SQLiteConversationStore("conversations.db")

agent = await build_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    servers={...},
    conversation_store=store,
)

# Each call to chat() automatically loads and saves history
response = await agent.chat("Hello!", session_id="conv-123")
response = await agent.chat("What did I say?", session_id="conv-123")  # Has full context

# Different session = fresh conversation
response = await agent.chat("New topic", session_id="conv-456")

docs.title: InMemoryConversationStore
docs.text:
Dict-backed, no persistence. For testing and prototyping.

from promptise.conversations import InMemoryConversationStore

store = InMemoryConversationStore(
    max_sessions=1000,              # Evict oldest when full (0 = unlimited)
    max_messages_per_session=200,   # Rolling window per session (0 = unlimited)
)

docs.title: PostgresConversationStore
docs.text:
Production store using asyncpg. Auto-creates tables and indexes on first use.

from promptise.conversations import PostgresConversationStore

store = PostgresConversationStore(
    "postgresql://user:pass@localhost/mydb",
    table_prefix="promptise_",     # Safe for multi-app databases
    pool_min=2,                     # Connection pool sizing
    pool_max=10,
    max_messages_per_session=0,    # 0 = unlimited
)

Requires: pip install asyncpg

Auto-created schema:

  • {prefix}sessions: session metadata (id, user, title, timestamps)
  • {prefix}messages: messages with role, content, metadata, timestamps
  • Indexes on (session_id, created_at) and (user_id, updated_at)

docs.title: SQLiteConversationStore
docs.text:
Local development store using aiosqlite. WAL mode enabled for concurrent reads.

from promptise.conversations import SQLiteConversationStore

store = SQLiteConversationStore(
    "conversations.db",            # Or ":memory:" for testing
    table_prefix="promptise_",
    max_messages_per_session=0,
)

Requires: pip install aiosqlite

docs.title: RedisConversationStore
docs.text:
Fast ephemeral sessions using redis.asyncio. Ideal for caching or high-throughput scenarios with optional TTL-based expiry.

from promptise.conversations import RedisConversationStore

store = RedisConversationStore(
    "redis://localhost:6379",
    key_prefix="promptise:",       # Namespace all keys
    ttl=86400,                      # Sessions expire after 24h (0 = no expiry)
    max_messages_per_session=100,
)

Requires: pip install redis

docs.title: The chat() API
docs.text:
agent.chat() is the high-level interface. It handles the full cycle:

  1. Ownership check: verify session belongs to caller (when user_id or caller is provided)
  2. Load history from store (by session_id)
  3. Build LangChain message list with history + new user message
  4. Invoke the agent (with memory injection, prompt context, etc.)
  5. Extract assistant response
  6. Persist updated history to store + assign ownership on new sessions
from promptise.conversations import generate_session_id

# Always use generate_session_id(): never user-controlled or predictable IDs
sid = generate_session_id()  # "sess_a1b2c3d4e5f6..."

# Multi-user: user_id enables ownership enforcement. It is shorthand for
# caller=CallerContext(user_id="user-42"): per-user memory, the semantic cache,
# guardrails and observability see the same user for this call.
response = await agent.chat(
    "Hello",
    session_id=sid,
    user_id="user-42",
    metadata={"source": "web", "ip": "1.2.3.4"},
)

# Same user, same session: works
response = await agent.chat("Follow up", session_id=sid, user_id="user-42")

# Different user, same session: raises SessionAccessDenied
response = await agent.chat("Hack", session_id=sid, user_id="attacker")

# With a per-call system prompt override
response = await agent.chat(
    "Summarize this",
    session_id=sid,
    user_id="user-42",
    system_prompt="You are a concise summarizer. Max 2 sentences.",
)

docs.title: Multi-User Ownership Model
docs.text:
When user_id is provided, every operation enforces ownership:

from promptise.conversations import SessionAccessDenied, generate_session_id

sid = generate_session_id()

# First chat assigns ownership
await agent.chat("Hello", session_id=sid, user_id="alice")

# Alice can continue: same user
await agent.chat("More", session_id=sid, user_id="alice")

# Bob cannot access Alice's session
try:
    await agent.chat("Hello", session_id=sid, user_id="bob")
except SessionAccessDenied as e:
    print(e)  # "User 'bob' denied access to session 'sess_...' (owned by 'alice')"

Ownership rules:

Scenario Behavior user_id provided, session is new Session assigned to that user user_id provided, session belongs to same user Access granted user_id provided, session belongs to different user SessionAccessDenied raised user_id=None, session exists Access granted (no enforcement) user_id provided, session has no owner Access granted (unowned)

Ownership is enforced on chat(), delete_session(), update_session(), and get_session(). The list_sessions() method filters by user_id at the database level: users only see their own sessions.

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
# List sessions for a specific user
sessions = await agent.list_sessions(user_id="user-42")

# Paginate
page2 = await agent.list_sessions(user_id="user-42", limit=20, offset=20)

# Get a specific session (with ownership check)
info = await agent.get_session("sess_abc", user_id="user-42")

# Update session metadata (with ownership check)
await agent.update_session(
    "sess_abc",
    calling_user_id="user-42",  # Verify ownership
    title="Support Chat #42",
)

# Delete a session (with ownership check)
await agent.delete_session("sess_abc", user_id="user-42")

docs.title: Custom Stores
docs.text:
Implement 5 data methods plus close(). The protocol is intentionally small, no auth logic in the store, just data:

from promptise.conversations import ConversationStore, Message, SessionInfo

class MongoConversationStore:
    """MongoDB-backed conversation store."""

    def __init__(self, db):
        self._db = db

    async def get_session(self, session_id: str) -> SessionInfo | None:
        doc = await self._db.sessions.find_one({"_id": session_id})
        if not doc:
            return None
        return SessionInfo(session_id=doc["_id"], **doc)

    async def load_messages(self, session_id: str) -> list[Message]:
        docs = await self._db.messages.find(
            {"session_id": session_id}
        ).sort("created_at").to_list(None)
        return [Message(role=d["role"], content=d["content"]) for d in docs]

    async def save_messages(self, session_id: str, messages: list[Message]) -> None:
        async with await self._db.client.start_session() as session:
            async with session.start_transaction():
                await self._db.messages.delete_many({"session_id": session_id})
                if messages:
                    await self._db.messages.insert_many([
                        {"session_id": session_id, **m.to_dict()}
                        for m in messages
                    ])
                await self._db.sessions.update_one(
                    {"_id": session_id},
                    {"$set": {"message_count": len(messages)}},
                    upsert=True,
                )

    async def delete_session(self, session_id: str) -> bool:
        result = await self._db.sessions.delete_one({"_id": session_id})
        await self._db.messages.delete_many({"session_id": session_id})
        return result.deleted_count > 0

    async def list_sessions(
        self, *, user_id=None, limit=50, offset=0
    ) -> list[SessionInfo]:
        query = {"user_id": user_id} if user_id else {}
        docs = await self._db.sessions.find(query).sort(
            "updated_at", -1
        ).skip(offset).limit(limit).to_list(None)
        return [SessionInfo(session_id=d["_id"], **d) for d in docs]

    async def close(self) -> None:
        pass  # MongoDB client manages its own lifecycle

The agent handles all authorization on top of your store. Your store just reads and writes data: it never needs to know about users or permissions.

docs.title: Combining with Memory
docs.text:
Conversation store and memory provider are orthogonal, use both:

from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.memory import ChromaProvider
from promptise.conversations import PostgresConversationStore

agent = await build_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    servers={...},

    # Long-term semantic memory (cross-session knowledge)
    memory=ChromaProvider(persist_directory=".promptise/chroma"),
    memory_auto_store=True,

    # Per-session chat history (exact message replay)
    conversation_store=PostgresConversationStore("postgresql://localhost/mydb"),
    conversation_max_messages=200,
)

# chat() uses both: memory injects relevant context, store provides exact history
response = await agent.chat("Continue where we left off", session_id="s1", user_id="user-42")

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Session isolation:

  • Ownership enforcement: when user_id is provided, the agent verifies session ownership before every read, write, delete, and update. SessionAccessDenied (a PermissionError) is raised on mismatch.
  • Secure session IDs: generate_session_id() creates 32-character hex tokens using secrets.token_hex(). Non-enumerable, unpredictable.
  • Scoped listing: list_sessions(user_id=...) filters at the database level, never exposing other users' sessions.

Data protection:

  • Table prefix validation: SQL stores reject prefixes containing anything other than [a-zA-Z0-9_] to prevent SQL injection.
  • Parameterized queries: all user data passes through parameterized queries, never interpolated into SQL.
  • Connection pooling: PostgreSQL store uses asyncpg connection pools with configurable min/max.
  • Lazy initialization: database connections are created on first use, not at construction time.
  • Store failures: see When the store fails.

docs.title: When the store fails
docs.text:
chat() treats a store failure differently depending on what it was doing. Verifying ownership fails closed; reading and writing history degrade gracefully:

Step If the store raises (DB down, network error, …) Ownership check (get_session, before anything else) chat() raises RuntimeError("Cannot verify session ownership (store unreachable): ..."). The model is not called: an agent that cannot tell whose session this is must not answer in it. Loading history (load_messages) Logged (Failed to load conversation history); the agent answers without the earlier messages. Saving history (save_messages) Logged (Failed to save conversation history); the reply is returned but this turn is not persisted. Assigning ownership of a new session (update_session) Logged as a warning (Failed to assign session ... to its user); the reply is returned, and the session has no owner until one is assigned, so ownership is not enforced for it.

Handle the RuntimeError the way you handle any other unavailable dependency, for example, return HTTP 503 and let the client retry:

from fastapi import HTTPException
from promptise.conversations import SessionAccessDenied

try:
    reply = await agent.chat(text, session_id=sid, user_id=user.id)
except SessionAccessDenied:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=403)
except RuntimeError:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="Conversation store unavailable")

docs.title: API Summary
docs.text:
Symbol Description ConversationStore Protocol: implement this for custom backends Message A single conversation message: role (user, assistant, system or tool), content, metadata and created_at. Also exported from the top level as promptise.ConversationMessage SessionInfo Session metadata (id, user, title, counts, timestamps) SessionAccessDenied Raised when a user accesses a session they don't own generate_session_id() Create a cryptographically secure session ID InMemoryConversationStore Dict-backed store for testing PostgresConversationStore Production store via asyncpg SQLiteConversationStore Local dev store via aiosqlite RedisConversationStore Ephemeral store via redis.asyncio agent.chat() High-level chat with ownership enforcement and session persistence agent.get_session() Get session metadata with ownership check agent.list_sessions() List sessions with pagination and user filtering agent.delete_session() Delete a session with ownership check agent.update_session() Update session metadata with ownership check

Learn the concept

  • AI Agent Memory in Python: Short-Term and Long-Term: How session history differs from long-term memory.

docs.title: Default System Prompt
docs.text:
An agent built with build_agent without instructions receives a default system prompt that establishes baseline behaviour: tool usage discipline, schema inspection, and result citation. The default prompt lives in a single module so it can be reviewed, overridden, or extended without touching any builder logic.

Source: src/promptise/prompt.py

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent

async def main():
    # Uses the default system prompt automatically
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        servers={},
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, who are you?"}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: The default prompt
docs.text:
The DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT constant contains the following instructions:

You are a capable deep agent. Use available tools from connected MCP servers
to plan and execute tasks. Always inspect tool descriptions and input schemas
before calling them. Be precise and avoid hallucinating tool arguments.
Prefer calling tools rather than guessing, and cite results from tools clearly.

This prompt establishes five key behaviours:

  1. Tool-first mindset: the agent should use tools rather than guess answers.
  2. Schema awareness: always read tool descriptions and input schemas before calling.
  3. Precision: avoid hallucinating tool argument values.
  4. Tool preference: prefer calling a tool over making up a response.
  5. Citation: cite tool results clearly in the final answer.

docs.title: Overriding the prompt
docs.text:
Pass instructions to build_agent to replace the default:

import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        servers={},
        instructions=(
            "You are a financial analyst agent. Use tools to fetch market data. "
            "Always provide numerical evidence and cite your data sources."
        ),
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is AAPL's P/E ratio?"}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Extending the default
docs.text:
To add instructions on top of the default rather than replacing it entirely, import the constant and concatenate:

import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.prompt import DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT

async def main():
    custom_prompt = (
        DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT
        + "\n\nAdditional instructions: Always respond in formal English. "
        "Include a confidence score (0-100) with every answer."
    )
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        servers={},
        instructions=custom_prompt,
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain recursion"}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: API summary
docs.text: Export Type Description DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT str The system prompt an agent gets when you pass no instructions

docs.title: When the default applies
docs.text: build_agent(...) System prompt no instructions, no flow DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT instructions="..." your text only (the default is not added) instructions=Prompt or a PromptBuilder result the rendered prompt flow=ConversationFlow(...) without instructions the flow's prompt only

docs.title: Tips and gotchas
docs.text:
Tip

The default prompt is intentionally short and generic. For production agents, always pass domain-specific instructions that describe the agent's role, available tools, expected output format, and any constraints.

Warning

Replacing the system prompt removes all default instructions, including the "inspect tool schemas before calling" directive. If your custom prompt does not include similar guidance, the LLM may produce more tool-calling errors.

Tip

You can inspect the prompt at any time without reading the source file:

from promptise.prompt import DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT
print(DEFAULT_SYSTEM_PROMPT)

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Building Agents: pass instructions to build_agent
  • Callback Handler: observe how the agent uses the prompt
  • Tools: the tools the prompt tells the agent to inspect

Learn the concept

  • System Prompt Best Practices for AI Agents in Python: What belongs in an agent's system prompt and how to test it.

docs.title: Graph Edges & Transitions
docs.text: Edges define how the graph flows from one node to another. The engine resolves transitions dynamically at runtime using a 7-step priority system.

docs.title: Edge Dataclass
docs.text:
from promptise.engine import Edge, NodeResult


def my_fn(result: NodeResult) -> bool:
    return result.error is None


Edge(
    from_node="plan",       # Source node name
    to_node="act",          # Target node name
    condition=my_fn,        # Optional: (NodeResult) -> bool
    label="ready",          # Optional: label for visualization
    priority=0,             # Optional: higher = checked first
)

docs.title: Edge Helpers
docs.text: All helpers return self for chaining: graph.always("a", "b").always("b", "c").

docs.title: always: Unconditional
docs.text: graph.always("plan", "execute")   # plan always goes to execute

docs.title: when: Conditional
docs.text:
graph.when("review", "fix",
    condition=lambda result: (result.output if isinstance(result.output, dict) else {}).get("quality", 0) < 3,
    label="low_quality",
)

docs.title: on_tool_call / on_no_tool_call: Tool-based routing
docs.text:
graph.on_tool_call("gather", "summarize")   # After a node that made tool calls
graph.on_no_tool_call("gather", "__end__")  # After a node that made none

A PromptNode whose model called tools is re-entered by the engine before any edge is checked (step 1 below), so these edges matter for nodes that record tool calls without asking for that re-entry: a ToolNode, a ParallelNode, a FanOutNode, a custom node. After a PromptNode, on_no_tool_call is the edge that applies once the model answers without tools.

docs.title: on_output: Output key matching
docs.text:
graph.on_output("review", "publish", key="approved", value=True)
graph.on_output("review", "revise", key="approved", value=False)

docs.title: on_error: Error routing
docs.text: graph.on_error("risky_step", "fallback")   # Route to fallback if node errors

docs.title: on_confidence: Confidence threshold
docs.text:
graph.on_confidence("analyze", "conclude", min_confidence=0.7)
# Routes to "conclude" when output["confidence"] >= 0.7

docs.title: on_guard_fail: Guard failure routing
docs.text:
graph.on_guard_fail("validate", "revise")
# Routes to "revise" when any guard fails

docs.title: sequential: Chain multiple nodes
docs.text:
graph.sequential("step1", "step2", "step3", "step4")
# Creates: step1 → step2 → step3 → step4 (always edges)

docs.title: loop_until: Conditional loop with exit
docs.text:
graph.loop_until("refine", "deliver",
    condition=lambda result: (result.output if isinstance(result.output, dict) else {}).get("quality", 0) >= 4,
    max_iterations=5,
)
# Loops "refine" until quality >= 4, then exits to "deliver"
# Exit edge gets priority=10, loop edge gets priority=0

refine runs at most max_iterations times in a run (fewer if its own max_iterations is lower). Once it has used them, the engine exits to deliver even though the condition never held. max_iterations below 1 raises ValueError.

docs.title: Low-level add_edge
docs.text: graph.add_edge("a", "b", condition=my_fn, label="custom", priority=10)

docs.title: Helper reference
docs.text:
Helper Condition Label always(a, b) none "" when(a, b, condition, label="") your (NodeResult) -> bool label on_tool_call(a, b) result.tool_calls is not empty tool_called on_no_tool_call(a, b) result.tool_calls is empty no_tools on_output(a, b, key, value=True) result.output is a dict and output[key] == value key=value on_error(a, b) result.error is set error on_confidence(a, b, min_confidence=0.7) result.output is a dict and float(output.get("confidence", 0)) >= min_confidence confidence>=0.7 on_guard_fail(a, b) result.guards_failed is not empty guard_failed sequential(*names) always between each pair loop_until(node, exit_to, *, condition, max_iterations=5) exit edge (priority 10) + self edge (priority 0) + budget exit_loop / loop

All helpers have priority 0 except the loop_until exit edge. The built-in conditions are EdgeCondition objects (EdgeCondition(kind, key="", value=True, min_confidence=0.0) with kind one of tool_called, no_tool_call, output, error, confidence, guard_failed), so their edges can be saved to YAML; a lambda condition cannot.

result.error includes notes hooks write on a successful node (a TimingHook budget overrun, a BudgetHook stop), so on_error fires on those too. result.output is the reply text for a plain-text reply (None on a step that only called tools), so on_output and on_confidence need a dict: a node with an output_schema, a reasoning node's JSON fields, or a postprocessor that returns a dict.

A condition that raises is treated as not matching (logged at DEBUG), so lambda r: r.output.get("quality") >= 4 silently never fires on a text or None output. Write (r.output if isinstance(r.output, dict) else {}).get(...). Adding a second conditional edge with the same source, target and priority logs a warning, since the first one that matches wins.

Performance

The engine maintains a precomputed adjacency index for O(1) edge lookup per transition (instead of scanning all edges). The index is rebuilt lazily when edges are added or removed.

docs.title: Transition Resolution
docs.text:
When a node finishes, the engine resolves the next node in this order:

graph TD
    NE[Node Executed] --> TC{Tool calls?}
    TC -->|yes| SAME[Re-enter same node]
    TC -->|no| NR{NodeResult<br/>.next_node?}
    NR -->|yes| TARGET2[Go to next_node]
    NR -->|no| LLM{output.route<br/>set?}
    LLM -->|yes| TARGET[Follow that transition<br/>or go to that node]
    LLM -->|no| EDGE{Conditional<br/>edges?}
    EDGE -->|match| TARGET3[Follow edge]
    EDGE -->|no match| TR{Node transitions<br/>match output?}
    TR -->|yes| TARGET4[Follow transition]
    TR -->|no| DEF{default_next?}
    DEF -->|yes| TARGET5[Go to default]
    DEF -->|no| END[__end__]

    style NE fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style SAME fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
  1. Tool loop: If tools were called, re-enter the same node so the LLM sees tool results
  2. NodeResult.next_node: If the node explicitly set the next node in its execute() method (ValidateNode's pass/fail, PlanNode's re-plan)
  3. LLM routing: If output contains route, _next, next_step, or goto naming one of the node's transition keys (follows that transition) or a node in the graph
  4. Graph edges: Conditional edges checked in priority order (highest first)
  5. Node transitions: For a dict output, the first transitions key whose value in the output is True, equals the key, or is any non-empty string
  6. default_next: Fallback node from the node's configuration
  7. end: Graph terminates

docs.title: Edge Priority
docs.text:
When multiple conditional edges exist from the same node, they are checked in priority order (highest first). Use this to ensure exit conditions are checked before loop conditions:

# Exit condition checked first (priority 10)
graph.add_edge("refine", "deliver",
    condition=lambda r: (r.output if isinstance(r.output, dict) else {}).get("done"),
    label="done", priority=10)

# Loop condition checked second (priority 0)
graph.always("refine", "refine")  # default priority=0

docs.title: Dynamic LLM Routing
docs.text:
The LLM can choose the next node by including a routing field in its output. Routing reads a structured output, so give the node an output_schema (a Pydantic model or a TypedDict) with a route field:

from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Decision(BaseModel):
    route: Literal["search", "answer"]
    reason: str


graph.add_node(PromptNode(
    "decide",
    output_schema=Decision,
    transitions={"search": "web_search", "answer": "write"},
))
# The LLM outputs {"route": "search", "reason": "Need more data"}
# → the engine follows the "search" transition to "web_search"

# Supported field names: route, _next, next_step, goto

A route value that is a transition key follows that transition; otherwise it must name a node in the graph (or __end__). When a node without tools has two or more transitions, the engine lists them in the prompt. The "error" transition is reserved: the engine follows it when the node has used its max_iterations, and never offers it to the model.

docs.title: Runtime Graph Mutation
docs.text:
With PromptGraphEngine(allow_self_modification=True) (the default, and what build_agent uses), a node's structured output can carry a _graph_action that changes the run's copy of the graph. The original graph is never modified, and the engine applies at most max_mutations_per_run (default 10) mutations per run, counting these and the GraphMutations nodes return.

Action Output fields What it does add_node _graph_action: "add_node", _node_config: {...} Adds a PromptNode built with PromptNode.from_config(_node_config). Nothing routes to it unless an edge, transition or route names it add_edge _graph_action: "add_edge", _from: "a", _to: "b" Adds an unconditional edge skip_to _graph_action: "skip_to", _target: "node_name" The target node (or "__end__", a normal finish) runs next, ahead of edges and transitions. An unknown target is logged and ignored retry_with _graph_action: "retry_with", _context_update: {...} Merges _context_update into state.context and runs the node again; each retry uses the node's max_iterations budget

add_node and add_edge, like a node's GraphMutations, are offered to the on_graph_mutation hooks first; a blocked one does not count. Before 1.7.0, skip_to to a node was overridden by the normal transition and retry_with did not run the node again.

The model only produces these fields when its output_schema has them (or a reasoning node's JSON reply carries them), so a graph whose schemas don't declare _graph_action is not affected. To rule it out, create the engine with allow_self_modification=False; build_agent has no switch for it.

A node can also return GraphMutations in NodeResult.graph_mutations (add_node, remove_node, add_edge, remove_edge); see GraphMutation.

docs.title: Node Flags
docs.text: Every node in a Reasoning Graph declares its capabilities and behaviors through typed flags. Flags are checked by the engine at runtime to control execution flow, caching, error handling, and observability.

docs.title: Using Flags
docs.text:
from promptise.engine import GraphState, NodeFlag, NodeResult, PromptNode, node

# Set flags on any node
PromptNode("analyze",
    instructions="Analyze the data.",
    flags={NodeFlag.CRITICAL, NodeFlag.OBSERVABLE},
)

# Functional nodes support flags too
@node("validate", flags={NodeFlag.RETRYABLE})
async def validate(state: GraphState) -> NodeResult:
    return NodeResult(output={"ok": True})

# Check flags at runtime (@node returns a node object)
if validate.has_flag(NodeFlag.RETRYABLE):
    ...

docs.title: Execution Control
docs.text: Flag Engine Behavior ENTRY Marks the starting node. Set via is_entry=True. Read by PromptGraph(nodes=[...]) (the first such node becomes the entry) and by from_pool() / build_agent(node_pool=...) (the pool's first step). A node added later with add_node() needs set_entry(). TERMINAL Set via is_terminal=True. Only an AutonomousNode pool reads it: a terminal step that succeeds ends the autonomous loop and writes the answer. In a static graph it does nothing; end a path with default_next="__end__" or an edge to "__end__". CRITICAL If this node errors, the engine aborts the run right away: post-node hooks, mutations and transitions are skipped, the stream gets on_node_error with critical: True, ExecutionReport.error is set, and ainvoke() raises GraphExecutionError (the node's exception is its __cause__). SKIP_ON_ERROR If the previous node's result has an error (including a note a hook wrote, such as a TimingHook overrun), this node does not run: its result is empty with transition_reason="skipped_on_error", and the transitions are resolved from that. Useful for optional enrichment steps. RETRYABLE On failure (a result with an error, or an exception), the engine runs the node again, up to max_iterations attempts in total (default 10), waiting min(0.5 * 2**n, 8) seconds between attempts (0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 8s...). Before each retry state.context["_retry_attempt"] and ["_retry_error"] are set, so the node can adapt; both are removed afterwards. The attempts run through execute(), so a streamed run gets no token chunks from a RETRYABLE node. A RetryNode is never retried this way (it retries itself). REQUIRES_HUMAN Sets state.context["_awaiting_human"] to the node name and awaits on_human_required(node_name, state) on every hook that has it, before the node runs. The node still executes; the flag does not pause anything by itself. An exception in on_human_required is logged and the run goes on (before 1.7.0 it ended the run). For a real approval step, use HumanNode.

docs.title: Context & Memory
docs.text: Flag Engine Behavior NO_HISTORY Before the node runs, the engine keeps only the first message when it is a system message (no messages otherwise). Afterwards the original messages are restored, plus the messages the node added. The node then sees no user question, so give it what it needs through input_keys or inherit_context_from. ISOLATED_CONTEXT The node runs with a state.context holding only its input_keys (empty when it has none). Afterwards the original context is restored, and only the node's output_key and {name}_output values are merged back. CACHEABLE Within one run, a second visit to the node with the same input_keys values returns the first visit's result (output, raw output and next_node; no new messages or tool calls) without executing. The key is the node name plus the input_keys values (only the name for a node without input_keys). The cache lives in state.context["_node_cache"], holds up to 128 results, skips results with an error, and starts empty on every run, so it never carries results between runs.

docs.title: Model Selection
docs.text: Flag Engine Behavior INJECT_TOOLS A PromptNode receives the engine's tools at runtime (the tools build_agent() discovered, or PromptGraphEngine(tools=...)) on top of its own. Set via inject_tools=True. Other node types ignore it. LIGHTWEIGHT If the node has no model_override and the engine was created with a lightweight_model, the engine swaps to that model for this node. build_agent creates the engine without one, so in an agent the flag has no effect; use model_override there. ThinkNode has this flag by default.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Flag Engine Behavior OBSERVABLE After the node runs, awaits on_observable_event(event, state) on every hook that has it, with a NodeEvent(event="on_node_metrics", data={node_name, duration_ms, total_tokens, tool_calls, error}). duration_ms is the node's own measurement (the engine's timing is set afterwards). An exception in the hook is logged and the run goes on (before 1.7.0 it ended the run). VERBOSE Logs the first 2,000 characters of the raw output at DEBUG level on the promptise.engine logger.

docs.title: Output Processing
docs.text: Flag Engine Behavior SUMMARIZE_OUTPUT If raw_output is longer than 1,000 characters, the engine makes one extra model call (the engine's model) to summarize it and replaces NodeResult.raw_output with the summary. The conversation, output and state.context["{name}_output"] keep the full text, so it mainly shortens what hooks and reports see. A failed summary call is logged and ignored. VALIDATE_OUTPUT Validates result.output against the node's output_schema (a Pydantic model, or a dict whose keys must be present). Problems are added to result.guards_failed (an on_guard_fail edge can route on them); a pass adds "output_schema_validation" to guards_passed. Does nothing without an output_schema or with a None output.

docs.title: Concurrency & State
docs.text: Flag Engine Behavior READONLY Declares that this node only reads state. Informational: the engine does not act on it (hooks and your own code can, with node.has_flag()). STATEFUL Declares that this node writes state.context. Informational. PARALLEL_SAFE Declares that this node can run concurrently. Informational: ParallelNode and FanOutNode run their children concurrently whatever their flags.

docs.title: Pre-built Reasoning Node Flags
docs.text:
Each reasoning node ships with sensible default flags:

Node Default Flags Rationale ThinkNode READONLY, LIGHTWEIGHT Pure reasoning, no state writes, smaller model sufficient ReflectNode STATEFUL, OBSERVABLE Writes reflections to state, worth logging ObserveNode STATEFUL Writes entities/facts to state.context JustifyNode READONLY, OBSERVABLE, VERBOSE Audit trail, full logging matters CritiqueNode READONLY, OBSERVABLE Pure analysis, severity worth logging PlanNode STATEFUL, OBSERVABLE Writes to state.plan SynthesizeNode OBSERVABLE Final output, important to capture ValidateNode READONLY, VALIDATE_OUTPUT Quality gate, validates own output RetryNode none Retries itself; the engine does not retry it again FanOutNode PARALLEL_SAFE Designed for concurrent execution

docs.title: Custom Flags
docs.text:
The flag set accepts any hashable value. You can define domain-specific flags:

class MyFlags:
    AUDIT_REQUIRED = "audit_required"
    PII_SENSITIVE = "pii_sensitive"

PromptNode("handle_user_data",
    flags={MyFlags.PII_SENSITIVE, NodeFlag.OBSERVABLE},
)

# Check in hooks
class AuditHook:
    async def post_node(self, node, result, state):
        if node.has_flag(MyFlags.AUDIT_REQUIRED):
            await audit_log.record(node.name, result)
        return result

docs.title: Engine Configuration
docs.text:
from promptise.engine import PromptGraphEngine

engine = PromptGraphEngine(
    graph=graph,
    model=main_model,
    lightweight_model=small_model,  # Used for LIGHTWEIGHT nodes
)

Flags are processed in this order around a node: SKIP_ON_ERROR, CACHEABLE (lookup), NO_HISTORY, ISOLATED_CONTEXT, LIGHTWEIGHT, REQUIRES_HUMAN; then the node runs (with RETRYABLE retries); then the restores, CACHEABLE (store), VERBOSE, OBSERVABLE, SUMMARIZE_OUTPUT, VALIDATE_OUTPUT; then CRITICAL. A skipped or cached node gets none of the post-execute steps.

docs.title: Graph Hooks & Observability
docs.text: Hooks intercept the engine's execution loop at defined points. Use them for logging, metrics, budget enforcement, cycle detection, and custom behavior.

docs.title: Hook Protocol
docs.text:
Hooks implement any subset of these async methods:

class MyHook:
    async def pre_node(self, node: BaseNode, state: GraphState) -> GraphState:
        """Called before each node executes. Can modify state."""
        return state

    async def post_node(self, node: BaseNode, result: NodeResult, state: GraphState) -> NodeResult:
        """Called after each node executes. Can modify result."""
        return result

    async def pre_tool(self, tool_name: str, args: dict, state: GraphState) -> dict:
        """Called before each tool call of a PromptNode or ToolNode. Returns the
        args to call the tool with. Raise to block the call."""
        return args

    async def post_tool(self, tool_name: str, result: str, args: dict, state: GraphState) -> str:
        """Called after each tool call. Returns the result the model sees."""
        return result

    async def on_tool_reused(self, tool_name: str, args: dict, result: str, state: GraphState) -> None:
        """Called instead of pre_tool/post_tool when a call is answered from an
        earlier result without running the tool (tools opted in with
        ContextCompaction(reuse_results=...), and a repeat of an identical call
        in one model turn of a ToolNode(deduplicate=True))."""
        pass

    async def on_observable_event(self, event: NodeEvent, state: GraphState) -> None:
        """Called for nodes with the OBSERVABLE flag after execution."""
        pass

    async def on_human_required(self, node_name: str, state: GraphState) -> None:
        """Called for nodes with the REQUIRES_HUMAN flag."""
        pass

    async def on_error(self, node: BaseNode, error: Exception, state: GraphState) -> str | None:
        """Called when a node fails. Return a node name (or "__end__") to go
        there next, or None for the usual handling."""
        return None

    async def on_graph_mutation(self, mutation: GraphMutation, state: GraphState) -> bool:
        """Called before a graph mutation is applied. Return False to block it."""
        return True

Only implement the methods you need, the engine checks hasattr() before calling. The Hook protocol (from promptise.engine import Hook) describes them for type checking.

on_error gets the exception behind the failure (a RuntimeError with the error text when the node recorded none, for example a RouterNode with no matching route). The first hook that returns the name of a node in the graph, or "__end__", decides where the run goes next, ahead of edges and transitions; returning None leaves the usual handling (on_error edges, then the run raises GraphExecutionError if it ends on the failure). Routing to "__end__" ends the run on the failure, so it still raises. A CRITICAL node aborts the run whatever the hooks return. Before 1.7.0 the engine never called on_error or on_graph_mutation.

When each method runs:

Method When Return value If it raises pre_node Before every node execution (after the node budget check, before flags) The state to use Logged, the run goes on post_node After every node execution (not after a CRITICAL failure), before the next node is chosen The result to use Logged, the run goes on pre_tool Before each tool call of a PromptNode, ToolNode or CodeActionNode program The args to use The call fails (see below) post_tool After each tool call The result text to use The call fails on_tool_reused Instead of the two above, for a reused result ignored Logged on_observable_event After an OBSERVABLE node runs ignored Logged, the run goes on on_human_required Before a REQUIRES_HUMAN node runs ignored Logged, the run goes on on_error After a node fails (it raised or its result has an error), before post_node and routing A node name or "__end__" to route there; None for the usual handling Logged, the next hook is asked on_graph_mutation Before each mutation: a node's graph_mutations and the LLM's add_node / add_edge actions False blocks the mutation (it does not count against max_mutations_per_run) The mutation is blocked (fail closed)

A hook can end a run by setting state.current_node = "__end__" in pre_node or post_node. The node being processed still finishes (from pre_node, it still runs once), then the run ends; mid tool loop that raises GraphStoppedError. post_node runs before NodeResult.duration_ms is final for nodes that do not set it themselves, and before the engine adds the node's tokens to state.total_tokens.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import logging

from promptise.engine import PromptGraphEngine, LoggingHook, MetricsHook, BudgetHook

engine = PromptGraphEngine(
    graph=graph,
    model=model,
    hooks=[
        LoggingHook(level=logging.DEBUG),
        MetricsHook(),
        BudgetHook(max_tokens=50000),
    ],
)

docs.title: Tool Hooks
docs.text:
pre_tool and post_tool run around every tool call of a PromptNode and of a ToolNode, the same way in both:

  1. Each hook's pre_tool(tool_name, args, state), in registration order. It returns the arguments to use, so a hook can change them (the next hook and the tool get what it returned).
  2. The tool runs with those arguments (after a ToolNode(validate_inputs=True) has checked them against the tool's schema).
  3. Each hook's post_tool(tool_name, result, args, state), in registration order, with the arguments the tool got. It returns the result to use: what it returns is what the model sees in the call's ToolMessage.

Blocking a call. A pre_tool hook blocks a call by raising. The tool does not run and no post_tool hook is called for it; the model gets "Error: <exception message>" as the call's result (status="error"), the call counts as failed (NodeResult.tool_calls_failed), and the stream reports it as on_tool_error (ToolEndEvent(success=False, tool_summary="Tool call failed") in astream_with_tools()). The model can then answer, or call something else. A post_tool hook that raises makes the call fail the same way, after the tool ran.

class ReadOnlyHook:
    async def pre_tool(self, tool_name, args, state):
        if tool_name.startswith(("delete_", "drop_")):
            raise PermissionError(f"{tool_name} is not allowed in read-only mode")
        return args

A call answered from an earlier result without running the tool (ContextCompaction(reuse_results=...), or a repeat in one model turn of a ToolNode(deduplicate=True)) gets on_tool_reused instead of pre_tool / post_tool; its result is the earlier call's, as post_tool left it.

docs.title: LoggingHook
docs.text:
Logs every node execution with timing, token counts, tool calls, and errors.

LoggingHook(level=logging.INFO)
Parameter Type Default Description level int logging.INFO Python logging level

Logs on the promptise.engine.hooks logger, so enable that logger (or its parent promptise) at the chosen level to see the lines.

Log output format:

▶ Node 'plan' (iter=0, type=PlanNode)
◀ Node 'plan' → (resolve) (150ms, tokens=340)
◀ Node 'act' → (resolve) (900ms, tokens=1210, tools=2)

The arrow shows NodeResult.next_node when the node set one, else (resolve) (the engine picks the next node after the hooks). tools= and error= appear only when there are tool calls or an error.

docs.title: TimingHook
docs.text:
Enforces per-node time budgets. It measures from pre_node to post_node (the node's whole execution, tool calls included). If a node took longer than its budget, the hook logs a warning and, when the result has no error yet, sets result.error = "Time budget exceeded: 12034ms > 10000ms". It does not interrupt the slow node, and it does not fail the run: the error is a note that an on_error edge, SKIP_ON_ERROR on the next node and MetricsHook (when it runs after TimingHook) all see. For a hard stop, set timeouts on the model and tools.

TimingHook(
    default_budget_ms=30000,
    per_node_budgets={"search": 10000, "synthesize": 60000},
)
Parameter Type Default Description default_budget_ms float 30000 Default time budget per node (30s) per_node_budgets dict[str, float] None Per-node time budget overrides (ms)

docs.title: CycleDetectionHook
docs.text:
Detects infinite loops by tracking patterns in visited node sequences. Forces graph termination when a repeating pattern is detected.

CycleDetectionHook(sequence_length=3, max_repeats=3)
Parameter Type Default Description sequence_length int 3 Length of node sequence to check for repetition max_repeats int 3 Max times a sequence can repeat before forcing end

Example: If visited nodes are [A, B, C, A, B, C, A, B, C], the pattern [A, B, C] has repeated 3 times, the hook sets state.current_node = "__end__". It checks in pre_node, where visited already includes the node about to run; the engine respects a pre_node stop, so that node does not run (it is not in ExecutionReport.nodes_visited).

A node that the engine re-enters for its own tool loop (it called tools and runs again with their results) counts as one step, so a ReAct reason node making many tool calls is not a cycle; bound those with max_iterations / max_agent_iterations. A node that routes back to itself without calling tools still counts every visit. Before 1.7.0 the stopped node ran once more, and a single-node tool loop was ended after 9 model calls with GraphStoppedError.

docs.title: MetricsHook
docs.text:
Collects per-node execution metrics in its metrics dict. Access them via summary() (a copy) after the run. Metrics add up across runs until you call reset(); with concurrent runs on one engine, they mix.

hook = MetricsHook()
engine = PromptGraphEngine(graph=graph, model=model, hooks=[hook])
await engine.ainvoke({"messages": [...]})

metrics = hook.summary()
# {
#     "plan": {"calls": 1, "total_tokens": 450, "total_duration_ms": 1200, "tool_calls": 0, "errors": 0},
#     "act":  {"calls": 3, "total_tokens": 2100, "total_duration_ms": 8500, "tool_calls": 5, "errors": 0},
# }

hook.reset()  # Clear for next run

Tracked metrics per node:

Metric Description calls Number of times this node executed total_tokens Cumulative token usage total_duration_ms Cumulative execution time tool_calls Total tool calls made errors Number of errors encountered

docs.title: BudgetHook
docs.text:
Enforces a token and/or cost budget for each graph run. After every node it adds the node's tokens to the run's total; when the run goes over max_tokens or max_cost_usd, the hook ends the run and writes the reason ("Token budget exceeded: 5078/5000 tokens") to that node's NodeResult.error. The check runs after a node, so a run can go over the budget by up to one node's tokens.

The budget is per run: the total comes from the run's own state, so one hook on an engine caps every run separately (concurrent runs included) and never carries tokens over to the next run.

How the run ends depends on where the budget ran out:

  • In the middle of a tool loop (the model asked for tools and has not seen their results): there is no answer, so the engine raises GraphBudgetExceededError instead of returning the last tool result. It is a GraphStoppedError and a GraphExecutionError, with reason, stopped_by ("BudgetHook"), pending_tools and report. engine.last_report.error holds the same message.
  • On the node that answered: the run returns that answer as usual.
from promptise.engine import BudgetHook, GraphBudgetExceededError, PromptGraphEngine

hook = BudgetHook(
    max_tokens=50000,
    max_cost_usd=0.50,
    cost_per_1k_tokens=0.002,
)
engine = PromptGraphEngine(graph=graph, model=model, hooks=[hook])
try:
    result = await engine.ainvoke({"messages": [...]})
except GraphBudgetExceededError as exc:
    print(exc.reason)          # Token budget exceeded: 50412/50000 tokens
    print(exc.pending_tools)   # ['search']

print(f"Tokens used: {hook.tokens_used}")
print(f"Cost: ${hook.cost_used:.4f}")

Any hook that ends a run the same way (state.current_node = "__end__", e.g. CycleDetectionHook) in the middle of a tool loop raises GraphStoppedError; reason is the NodeResult.error the hook wrote, if any.

Parameter Type Default Description max_tokens int \| None None Maximum tokens per run, summed over all nodes max_cost_usd float \| None None Maximum estimated cost (USD) cost_per_1k_tokens float 0.002 Cost per 1,000 tokens for estimation

Attributes after execution:

Attribute Type Description tokens_used int Tokens of the latest run cost_used float Estimated cost (USD) of the latest run

docs.title: Webhook Notifier
docs.text:
class WebhookNotifier:
    def __init__(self, url: str):
        self.url = url

    async def post_node(self, node, result, state):
        import httpx
        async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
            await client.post(self.url, json={
                "node": node.name,
                "duration_ms": result.duration_ms,
                "tokens": result.total_tokens,
                "error": result.error,
            })
        return result

docs.title: Audit Logger
docs.text:
class AuditHook:
    async def pre_tool(self, tool_name, args, state):
        if tool_name == "delete_user":
            log.warning("AUDIT: delete_user called with %s", args)
        return args

    async def post_tool(self, tool_name, result, args, state):
        audit_log.record(tool_name, args, result)
        return result

docs.title: Human Approval Integration
docs.text:
class HumanApprovalHook:
    async def on_human_required(self, node_name, state):
        approval = await my_approval_system.request(
            node=node_name,
            context=state.context,
        )
        state.context["_human_approved"] = approval

docs.title: ExecutionReport
docs.text:
Every run (ainvoke(), astream(), astream_events()) produces an ExecutionReport:

result = await engine.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize Q3"}]})
report = engine.last_report
print(report.summary())
Field Type Description total_iterations int Total node executions total_tokens int Cumulative token usage total_duration_ms float Total wall-clock time nodes_visited list[str] Ordered node names visited tool_calls int Total tool calls across all nodes graph_mutations int Number of runtime graph mutations guards_passed int Total guards passed across all nodes guards_failed int Total guards failed across all nodes error str \| None Why the run failed or stopped: the error of the node failure the run ended on (any unrecovered failure, not only CRITICAL), or the iteration-limit / hook-stop message of a run stopped mid tool loop. None for a run that answered

summary() returns the report as readable text. The report is also on every engine exception as exc.report. tool_calls counts calls recorded as observations (PromptNode, ToolNode, CodeActionNode programs, and the children of a ParallelNode), failed and reused calls included.

docs.title: NodeResult
docs.text:
Every node execution produces a NodeResult (27 fields, all with defaults) for full traceability:

Category Fields Identity node_name, node_type, iteration Timing duration_ms, llm_duration_ms, tool_duration_ms Tokens prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens Tool Activity tool_calls (list of dicts), tool_calls_deduplicated, tool_calls_failed LLM Output output (the parsed object, or the reply text), raw_output (string), next_node, transition_reason Messages messages_added (messages appended to state) Prompt Trace blocks_used, blocks_dropped, strategy_applied, perspective_applied Guards guards_passed, guards_failed, guard_retries (not set by the built-in nodes; stays 0) Mutations graph_mutations (list of GraphMutation) Error error, error_recovered

All NodeResult objects are stored in state.node_history for full execution replay. tool_calls entries are dicts with name, args, result, success (and reused: True for a reused result). error_recovered=True, set by a hook, makes the engine treat a failed node as recovered.

docs.title: Reasoning Engine Internals
docs.text: How the Reasoning Engine works under the hood, execution flow, transition resolution, autonomous path building, caching, flag processing, and the complete data flow from build_agent() to tool response.

docs.title: The Big Picture
docs.text:
graph TB
    subgraph "build_agent()"
        BA[build_agent] --> NM[Normalize Model]
        BA --> MC[Connect MCP Servers]
        BA --> BG[Build Graph]
        MC --> TD[Discover Tools]
        TD --> TA[Convert to LangChain Tools]
        BG --> |"pattern string"| PB[Prebuilt Pattern]
        BG --> |"PromptGraph"| CG[Custom Graph]
        BG --> |"node_pool"| AP[Autonomous Pool]
        BG --> |"None"| DR[Default ReAct]
        PB --> ENG[PromptGraphEngine]
        CG --> ENG
        AP --> ENG
        DR --> ENG
        NM --> ENG
        TA --> ENG
    end

    ENG --> |"ainvoke(input, caller)"| EXEC[Execution Loop]

    style BA fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style ENG fill:#0e4429,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style EXEC fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff

docs.title: Execution Loop: What Happens on Every ainvoke()
docs.text:
graph TD
    START[ainvoke called] --> COPY[Copy graph per-invocation isolation]
    COPY --> TOOLS[Collect all tools from nodes]
    TOOLS --> STATE[Create GraphState with messages]
    STATE --> LOOP{current_node != __end__?}

    LOOP --> |yes| GET[Get node from graph]
    GET --> |not found| END_ERR[Log error, end]
    GET --> |found| BUDGET{Node budget left?}
    BUDGET --> |"no: loop exit, error transition, __error__ node, or end"| LOOP
    BUDGET --> |yes| PRE_HOOK[Run pre_node hooks]

    PRE_HOOK --> |hook sets __end__| END
    PRE_HOOK --> PRE_FLAG[Pre-execute flags]
    PRE_FLAG --> |SKIP_ON_ERROR + prev errored| SKIP[Return skip result]
    PRE_FLAG --> |CACHEABLE + cache hit| CACHE_HIT[Return cached result]
    PRE_FLAG --> |NO_HISTORY| STRIP[Strip messages, keep system only]
    PRE_FLAG --> |ISOLATED_CONTEXT| ISOLATE[Save context, isolate]
    PRE_FLAG --> |LIGHTWEIGHT| SWAP_MODEL[Swap to lightweight model]
    PRE_FLAG --> |none triggered| EXEC_NODE[Execute node]

    SKIP --> POST_FLAG
    CACHE_HIT --> POST_FLAG
    EXEC_NODE --> |RETRYABLE flag| RETRY[Execute with retry + backoff]
    EXEC_NODE --> |normal| NORMAL[node.execute state, config]
    RETRY --> POST_FLAG
    NORMAL --> POST_FLAG

    POST_FLAG[Post-execute flags] --> |error| ON_ERR[on_error hooks: may pick the next node]
    ON_ERR --> |CRITICAL| ABORT[Abort graph]
    ON_ERR --> MUT
    POST_FLAG --> |NO_HISTORY| RESTORE_MSG[Restore messages]
    POST_FLAG --> |ISOLATED_CONTEXT| RESTORE_CTX[Restore context, merge output_key]
    POST_FLAG --> |CACHEABLE| CACHE_STORE[Store in cache]
    POST_FLAG --> |SUMMARIZE_OUTPUT| SUMMARIZE[LLM summarize if > 1000 chars]
    POST_FLAG --> |VALIDATE_OUTPUT| VALIDATE[Validate against schema]
    POST_FLAG --> MUT[Apply graph mutations the on_graph_mutation hooks allow; skip_to / retry_with pick the next node]
    MUT --> POST_HOOK

    POST_HOOK[Run post_node hooks] --> |hook sets __end__| END
    POST_HOOK --> TRANSITION[Resolve transition, unless a hook or graph action picked the next node]
    TRANSITION --> ITER{iteration >= max_iterations?}
    ITER --> |yes| END
    ITER --> |no| LOOP

    ABORT --> END[Build ExecutionReport]
    END_ERR --> END
    LOOP --> |no| END
    END --> |run ended on an unrecovered node failure| RAISE[raise GraphExecutionError]
    END --> |"limit or hook stopped it mid tool loop"| RAISE2[raise GraphIterationLimitError / GraphStoppedError]

    style START fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style EXEC_NODE fill:#0e4429,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style ABORT fill:#5c1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#fff
    style CACHE_HIT fill:#1a2e3a,stroke:#22d3ee,color:#fff

docs.title: Transition Resolution: How the Engine Picks the Next Node
docs.text:
After every node executes, the engine decides where to go next. This is the 7-step priority chain:

graph TD
    NE[Node finished executing] --> TC{"Tool calls in result and<br/>transition_reason = tool_calls_present?"}
    TC --> |yes| SAME[Re-enter same node]
    TC --> |no| NR{NodeResult.next_node set?}

    NR --> |"yes (reasoning nodes, routers, guards set this)"| TARGET2[Go to next_node]
    NR --> |no| LLM{"output.route / _next / next_step / goto<br/>names a transition key or a node?"}

    LLM --> |yes| TARGET[Follow that transition or go to that node]
    LLM --> |no| EDGE{Edges from this node?}

    EDGE --> |"first match, by priority desc"| TARGET3[Follow matched edge]
    EDGE --> |no match| TR{Node transitions dict match output?}

    TR --> |yes| TARGET4[Follow transition]
    TR --> |no| DEF{node.default_next set?}

    DEF --> |yes| TARGET5[Go to default]
    DEF --> |no| GRAPH_END[__end__]

    SAME --> |"LLM sees tool results, calls again or produces final answer"| NE

    style NE fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style SAME fill:#0e4429,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style GRAPH_END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#fff
    style TARGET fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style TARGET2 fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style TARGET3 fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff

Key insight: Tool-calling nodes re-enter themselves automatically. The LLM calls tools → the node adds ToolMessages to the conversation → the engine re-enters the node → the LLM sees the results → calls more tools or produces a final answer. This loop continues until the LLM stops calling tools or the node's budget (its max_iterations, capped by the engine's max_node_iterations when one is set) is used up.

Before a node runs, the engine checks its budget. A node that has used it is not run again: the engine goes to its loop_until exit, else its "error" transition, else an __error__ node, else ends the run. A run ended that way in the middle of a tool loop raises GraphIterationLimitError.

docs.title: Autonomous Mode: How the AI Builds Its Own Path
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant E as Engine
    participant A as AutonomousNode
    participant LLM as LLM
    participant P as Pool Nodes

    E->>A: execute(state, config)

    loop For each step (up to max_steps)
        A->>LLM: "Here are available nodes:<br/>- plan: Break task into subgoals<br/>- act: Execute tools<br/>- think: Analyze gaps<br/>- reflect: Self-evaluate<br/>- answer: Final synthesis (terminal)<br/><br/>Which should run next?"
        LLM-->>A: {"next_node": "act", "reason": "Need to search for data"}

        alt next_node == "__done__" or terminal node succeeded
            A->>A: Leave the loop
        else Valid node (or a tool of one) selected
            A->>P: Execute chosen node until its tool loop ends
            P-->>A: NodeResult with output
            A->>A: Continue loop
        else Invalid node name
            A->>A: Tell the next routing call, ask LLM again
        end
    end

    opt No terminal node ran last
        A->>P: Run the answer node (first terminal node)
    end
    A-->>E: Return final result

In autonomous mode, the AutonomousNode wraps the pool and orchestrates:

  1. Builds a routing prompt listing all available nodes with descriptions and their tools
  2. Asks the LLM which node to run next: the prompt and reply are sent for that call only, never added to state.messages
  3. Extracts JSON from the response (balanced brace parser for nested objects)
  4. Executes the chosen node, re-running it while its model keeps calling tools (a tool name runs the node that has the tool)
  5. Loops back to step 2 until the LLM chooses __done__ or a terminal node succeeds
  6. When no terminal node ran last, runs the answer node, so the run ends with a written answer

The developer controls the pool composition, what nodes are available. The LLM controls the path, which nodes to use and in what order.

docs.title: PromptNode Execution: The Pipeline
docs.text:
Every execution of a PromptNode is one model call:

graph TD
    START[PromptNode.execute] --> MODEL[1. Resolve model: override or engine model]
    MODEL --> PRE[2. Preprocessor]
    PRE --> |raises| FAIL[Node fails, no model call]
    PRE --> CTX[3. System prompt assembly]
    CTX --> |"instructions + tool summary (off by default) + input_keys + inherited output + context_layers + blocks"| CTX2["+ observations (nodes without tools) + plan + reflections + reasoning-node JSON fields + route choices"]
    CTX2 --> STRAT[4. Strategy wrap + perspective]
    STRAT --> BIND{5. Binding cached for this model, tools, tool choice, schema?}
    BIND --> |yes| REUSE[Reuse bound model]
    BIND --> |no| BUILD[temperature / max_tokens + bind_tools with tool_choice + with_structured_output, cache in config]
    REUSE --> SCOPE[6. Context scope: full, or compacted view]
    BUILD --> SCOPE
    SCOPE --> LLM[7. LLM call]

    LLM --> RESP{8. Response type?}
    RESP --> |AIMessage with tool_calls| TOOL_EXEC[Execute tools]
    RESP --> |AIMessage text only| PARSE["output = text (a reasoning node's JSON object when present)"]
    RESP --> |Structured output| STRUCT[output = dict]

    TOOL_EXEC --> |"2+ calls"| PARALLEL[Run concurrently]
    TOOL_EXEC --> |"1 call"| SEQUENTIAL[Run directly]
    PARALLEL --> TOOL_MSG[Append ToolMessages in call order]
    SEQUENTIAL --> TOOL_MSG
    TOOL_MSG --> |"transition_reason = tool_calls_present"| GUARD

    PARSE --> GUARD[9. Transitions from output, guards]
    STRUCT --> GUARD
    GUARD --> STRAT_PARSE[10. Strategy parse]
    STRAT_PARSE --> POST[11. Postprocessor, on the reply only]
    POST --> WRITE["12. output_key (output) + {name}_output"]
    WRITE --> DONE[Return NodeResult → engine re-enters on tool calls]

    style START fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style LLM fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style PARALLEL fill:#0e4429,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style DONE fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#fff

docs.title: Caching: What Is Reused and When
docs.text:
Item Where Reused while Bound model (sampling settings, tools, structured output) config["_node_cache_{name}"] Same run, same model object (or same model_override), same tool names and tool choice, same output_schema Edge adjacency index graph._edge_index Until an edge is added or removed (lazy dirty flag) Node result (CACHEABLE flag) state.context["_node_cache"] Same run, same input_keys values; up to 128 entries

The system prompt is not cached: it is rebuilt on every execution, since input_keys, plan, reflections, observations and the offered tools can change between steps. The run config is copied per run, so these caches never leak between runs.

docs.title: Flag Processing Order
docs.text:
Flags are processed in two phases around node execution:

graph TD
    subgraph "Pre-execute (before node runs)"
        F1[SKIP_ON_ERROR] --> |"previous errored → skip"| F1R[Return skip result]
        F2[CACHEABLE] --> |"cache hit → return cached"| F2R[Return cached result]
        F3[NO_HISTORY] --> |"save messages, strip to system only"| F3R[Continue]
        F4[ISOLATED_CONTEXT] --> |"save context, give empty/input_keys only"| F4R[Continue]
        F5[LIGHTWEIGHT] --> |"swap config model to lightweight_model"| F5R[Continue]
        F6[REQUIRES_HUMAN] --> |"set flag in state, emit hook event"| F6R[Continue]
    end

    subgraph "Node executes"
        EXEC["node.execute(state, config)"]
        RETRY["If RETRYABLE (not a RetryNode): retry with exp backoff, max 8s cap"]
    end

    subgraph "Post-execute (after node runs)"
        P1[CRITICAL] --> |"error → abort graph immediately"| P1R[Break loop]
        P2[NO_HISTORY] --> |"restore original messages + new ones"| P2R[Continue]
        P3[ISOLATED_CONTEXT] --> |"restore context, merge output_key back"| P3R[Continue]
        P4[LIGHTWEIGHT] --> |"restore original model"| P4R[Continue]
        P5[CACHEABLE] --> |"store result in cache"| P5R[Continue]
        P6[VERBOSE] --> |"log full output at DEBUG"| P6R[Continue]
        P7[OBSERVABLE] --> |"emit metrics event to hooks"| P7R[Continue]
        P8[SUMMARIZE_OUTPUT] --> |"LLM summarize if >1000 chars"| P8R[Continue]
        P9[VALIDATE_OUTPUT] --> |"validate against output_schema"| P9R[Continue]
    end

    style F1R fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
    style F2R fill:#22d3ee,stroke:#0891b2,color:#000
    style EXEC fill:#0e4429,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style P1R fill:#5c1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff

docs.title: Data Flow Between Nodes
docs.text:
graph LR
    subgraph "Node A"
        A_OUT["output_key='findings'"]
    end

    subgraph "state.context"
        CTX["findings: '...data...'<br/>A_output: '...raw...'"]
    end

    subgraph "Node B (reads findings)"
        B_IN["input_keys=['findings']"]
    end

    subgraph "Node C (inherits A)"
        C_IN["inherit_context_from='A'"]
    end

    A_OUT --> CTX
    CTX --> B_IN
    CTX --> C_IN

Three ways nodes pass data:

Method How it works Use when output_key → input_keys Node A writes its output to state.context[output_key] (an output_schema dict, its reply text, a strategy's extracted answer, or a postprocessor's value). Node B gets state.context[input_keys[i]] in its prompt. Named data, structured or text inherit_context_from Node B gets state.context["{A_name}_output"] (A's reply text, or its structured output as JSON) in its prompt. Every PromptNode writes this key. One node directly continues another's work, including plain-text replies state.context direct Node's execute() reads/writes state.context directly. Custom state management in BaseNode subclasses

docs.title: CallerContext → MCP Server Identity Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Your App
    participant Agent as PromptiseAgent
    participant CV as ContextVar
    participant Client as MCPClient
    participant Transport as HTTP Transport
    participant Auth as AuthMiddleware
    participant Guard as HasRole Guard
    participant Handler as Tool Handler

    App->>Agent: ainvoke(input, caller=CallerContext(bearer_token="eyJ..."))
    Agent->>CV: Store caller in async contextvar

    Note over Agent: Reasoning Engine executes graph

    Agent->>Client: Tool call → MCPClient(bearer_token=caller.bearer_token)
    Client->>Transport: Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
    Transport->>Auth: Extract token from headers
    Auth->>Auth: Verify JWT signature (HMAC-SHA256)
    Auth->>Auth: Extract roles, scopes, claims
    Auth->>Auth: Build ClientContext
    Auth->>Guard: Check HasRole("analyst")
    Guard-->>Auth: Pass ✓
    Auth->>Handler: ctx.client = ClientContext(roles, scopes, claims)
    Handler-->>Transport: Result
    Transport-->>Client: Response
    Client-->>Agent: Tool result
    Agent->>CV: Reset contextvar
    Agent-->>App: Final response

docs.title: Hook Execution Points
docs.text:
graph TD
    subgraph "Per-node execution"
        H1["pre_node hooks (state modifiable)"] --> FLAGS_PRE["Pre-execute flags"]
        FLAGS_PRE --> EXEC["node.execute()"]
        EXEC --> FLAGS_POST["Post-execute flags"]
        FLAGS_POST --> H2["post_node hooks (result modifiable)"]
    end

    subgraph "Per-tool execution (PromptNode, ToolNode, CodeActionNode programs)"
        H3["pre_tool hooks (args modifiable)"] --> TOOL["tool.ainvoke()"]
        TOOL --> H4["post_tool hooks (result modifiable)"]
    end

    subgraph "Special hooks"
        H8["on_error (failed nodes)"]
        H9["on_graph_mutation (before each mutation)"]
        H5["on_observable_event (OBSERVABLE nodes)"]
        H6["on_human_required (REQUIRES_HUMAN nodes)"]
        H7["on_tool_reused (reused results)"]
    end

    style H1 fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style H2 fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style EXEC fill:#0e4429,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style TOOL fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff

Hooks run in registration order. A failing pre_node, post_node, on_error, on_observable_event or on_human_required hook is logged and skipped. A pre_tool or post_tool hook that raises fails that tool call (the model gets the error). An on_graph_mutation hook that raises blocks the mutation. A pre_node hook that sets state.current_node = "__end__" ends the run before the node runs. on_error runs for a failed node before post_node; on_graph_mutation before each mutation.

docs.title: Safety Mechanisms
docs.text:
graph TD
    subgraph "Iteration Guards"
        S1["max_iterations (default 50)"] --> |"reached: that many node executions"| S1R["Force graph end"]
        S2["node budget: node.max_iterations (and max_node_iterations when set)"] --> |"used up, node not run again"| S2R["_handle_stuck_node()"]
        S2R --> |"error transition exists"| S2A["Follow error edge"]
        S2R --> |"__error__ node exists"| S2B["Go to error handler"]
        S2R --> |"nothing"| S2C["Force __end__"]
    end

    subgraph "Budget & Health"
        S3["BudgetHook.max_tokens"] --> |exceeded| S3R["Set current_node = __end__; GraphBudgetExceededError if no answer"]
        S4["CycleDetectionHook"] --> |"pattern repeats N times (tool-loop re-entries count once)"| S4R["End before the next node runs"]
        S5["TimingHook"] --> |"node exceeds budget"| S5R["Set error on result"]
    end

    subgraph "Error Recovery"
        S6["CRITICAL flag + error"] --> S6R["Abort immediately, report.error set"]
        S7["RETRYABLE flag + error"] --> S7R["Retry up to max_iterations times"]
        S7R --> |"backoff"| S7B["0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s (capped)"]
        S8["SKIP_ON_ERROR"] --> S8R["Skip node, continue graph"]
    end

    subgraph "Graph Isolation"
        S9["graph.copy() per invocation"] --> S9R["Mutations don't affect original"]
        S10["config = dict(config)"] --> S10R["Concurrent calls don't interfere"]
        S11["max_mutations_per_run (default 10)"] --> S11R["Cap LLM graph modifications"]
    end

    style S6R fill:#5c1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff
    style S7B fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
    style S9R fill:#0e4429,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: The engine's own work per node (copying the graph, looking up edges, flag checks, hooks) is small next to the model and tool calls, which take nearly all of a run's time.

docs.title: Reasoning Graph Nodes
docs.text: Every node in a Reasoning Graph is a complete processing pipeline. Promptise ships with 21 built-in node types, plus three ways to create custom ones.

docs.title: Reasoning Nodes (Pre-built Building Bricks)
docs.text:
These come configured with instructions, context injection settings and default flags. All reasoning nodes inherit from PromptNode (except RetryNode and FanOutNode which inherit from BaseNode), so every PromptNode parameter works on them and overrides the preset (the presets are defaults, set with setdefault).

How a reasoning node reads its fields

ReflectNode, ObserveNode, PlanNode, CritiqueNode, JustifyNode and ValidateNode act on named fields of the reply (route, mistake, subgoals, severity, passes...). Without an output_schema the node adds an instruction to end the reply with a JSON object holding those fields, and parses the last JSON object of the reply into NodeResult.output (and output_key); the reply text stays in the conversation. A reply without a JSON object stays text, and the node then stores and routes nothing. With an output_schema the schema decides and no instruction is added: use one with a model that supports structured output, as the prebuilt patterns do with PeoatrPlan and PeoatrReflection (in promptise.engine.prebuilts). ThinkNode and SynthesizeNode work on plain text. Before 1.7.0 the fields were read from a structured output only.

from promptise.engine import ReflectNode
from promptise.engine.prebuilts import PeoatrReflection

reflect = ReflectNode(
    "reflect",
    output_schema=PeoatrReflection,   # mistake, correction, confidence, route
    transitions={"answer": "answer", "replan": "plan", "continue": "act"},
)

docs.title: ThinkNode
docs.text:
Gap analysis and next-step reasoning. No tools, pure analytical reasoning.

ThinkNode("think")
ThinkNode("think", focus_areas=["data quality", "missing sources"])
Parameter Type Default Description name str "think" Node identifier focus_areas list[str] \| None None Optional areas to focus analysis on **kwargs All PromptNode parameters

Pre-configured behavior:

  • Instructions: analyze the state, name the gaps, rate confidence (1-5), recommend the next step; focus_areas are appended as "Focus on: ..."
  • Injects observations and plan (include_observations=True, include_plan=True, include_reflections=False); no tools
  • Output key: think_output
  • Default flags: READONLY, LIGHTWEIGHT (LIGHTWEIGHT only switches model when the engine has a lightweight_model; build_agent sets none)

docs.title: ReflectNode
docs.text:
Self-evaluation and mistake correction. Auto-stores reflections in state.

ReflectNode("reflect")
ReflectNode("reflect", review_depth=5)
Parameter Type Default Description name str "reflect" Node identifier review_depth int 3 Stored (and saved by save_graph); not used in the prompt **kwargs All PromptNode parameters

Pre-configured behavior:

  • Instructions: assess progress, name mistakes and corrections, rate confidence, pick a route: continue, replan or answer (the route is followed through the node's transitions)
  • Fields read: progress, mistake, correction, confidence, route. With a non-empty mistake, stores {iteration, mistake, correction, confidence, stage: "reflect"} in state.reflections (the last 5 are kept)
  • Injects observations, plan and past reflections
  • Output key: reflection
  • Default flags: STATEFUL, OBSERVABLE

docs.title: ObserveNode
docs.text:
Interprets tool results into structured data. Enriches state with extracted entities and facts.

ObserveNode("observe")
Parameter Type Default Description name str "observe" Node identifier **kwargs All PromptNode parameters

Pre-configured behavior:

  • Instructions: summarize the tool results, extract entities, factual claims and key findings
  • Fields read: summary, entities, facts, key_findings. Appends the entities list to state.context["extracted_entities"] and its facts list to state.context["extracted_facts"] (values that are not lists are ignored)
  • Injects observations only
  • Output key: observation
  • Default flags: STATEFUL

docs.title: PlanNode
docs.text:
Structured planning with subgoal management and quality self-evaluation.

PlanNode("plan", max_subgoals=4, quality_threshold=3)
Parameter Type Default Description name str "plan" Node identifier max_subgoals int 4 Maximum number of subgoals quality_threshold int 3 Plans below this quality score (1-5) trigger re-planning **kwargs All PromptNode parameters

Pre-configured behavior:

  • Instructions: break the task into at most max_subgoals subgoals, pick the first, rate the plan 1-5
  • Fields read: subgoals, active_subgoal, quality_score. Sets state.plan to the subgoals list (cut to max_subgoals). state.completed is not touched; mark progress with state.complete_subgoal() in your own node
  • Reads quality_score (or quality, default 3): below quality_threshold it follows a replan transition, else runs itself again. Give the node a small max_iterations and an "error" transition so weak plans cannot loop (the PEOATR pattern uses max_iterations=3, transitions={"error": "act"})
  • Injects past reflections only
  • Output key: plan_output
  • Default flags: STATEFUL, OBSERVABLE

docs.title: SynthesizeNode
docs.text:
Combines all gathered data into a comprehensive final answer.

SynthesizeNode("answer", is_terminal=True)
Parameter Type Default Description name str "synthesize" Node identifier **kwargs All PromptNode parameters

Pre-configured behavior:

  • Injects observations (the last 5), reflections and plan progress
  • Instructions: answer the original question, support claims with evidence, cite sources
  • default_next="__end__", so the run ends after it unless an edge or transition says otherwise. is_terminal=True only matters to an AutonomousNode pool
  • Output key: synthesis
  • Default flags: OBSERVABLE

docs.title: CritiqueNode
docs.text:
Adversarial self-review with severity-based routing.

CritiqueNode("critique", severity_threshold=0.5)
Parameter Type Default Description name str "critique" Node identifier severity_threshold float 0.5 Severity above this routes to revision (0.0 = perfect, 1.0 = flawed) **kwargs All PromptNode parameters

Pre-configured behavior:

  • Instructions: name weaknesses, counter-arguments and improvements, rate severity from 0.0 to 1.0
  • Fields read: weaknesses, counter_arguments, improvements, severity. A severity above severity_threshold routes to the first of these transitions the node has: revise, improve, retry, replan. Otherwise the normal transition resolution applies
  • Output key: critique
  • Default flags: READONLY, OBSERVABLE

docs.title: JustifyNode
docs.text:
Chain-of-thought justification for audit trail.

JustifyNode("justify")
Parameter Type Default Description name str "justify" Node identifier **kwargs All PromptNode parameters

Pre-configured behavior:

  • Instructions: explain why the last action was taken, step by step, with evidence, a conclusion and a confidence
  • Fields read: reasoning_chain, evidence, conclusion, confidence. Appends {iteration, reasoning, conclusion, confidence} (from reasoning_chain, conclusion, confidence) to state.context["justifications"] (the last 5 are kept)
  • Output key: justification
  • Default flags: READONLY, OBSERVABLE, VERBOSE

docs.title: ValidateNode
docs.text:
LLM-powered quality validation with pass/fail routing.

ValidateNode("validate",
    criteria=["Be accurate", "Cite sources"],
    on_pass="deliver",
    on_fail="revise",
)
Parameter Type Default Description name str "validate" Node identifier criteria list[str] \| None None Validation criteria (defaults to accuracy, evidence, no factual errors) on_pass str "__end__" Node to transition to on pass on_fail str \| None None Node to transition to on fail **kwargs All PromptNode parameters

Pre-configured behavior:

  • Instructions: check the current output against the criteria, list issues and suggestions
  • Fields read: passes (or pass), issues, suggestions, confidence. A true passes routes to on_pass; false routes to on_fail when set, else the normal transition resolution applies
  • Output key: validation
  • Default flags: READONLY, VALIDATE_OUTPUT (the flag checks the output against output_schema, so it does nothing without one)
from pydantic import BaseModel

from promptise.engine import ValidateNode


class Verdict(BaseModel):
    passes: bool
    issues: list[str]


ValidateNode("validate", criteria=["Cites a source"], output_schema=Verdict,
             on_pass="deliver", on_fail="revise", max_iterations=3)

docs.title: RetryNode
docs.text:
Wraps another node with retry logic and error enrichment. Extends BaseNode (not PromptNode).

RetryNode("safe_search", wrapped_node=search_node, max_retries=3, backoff_factor=0.5)
Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier wrapped_node BaseNode required The node to wrap with retry logic max_retries int 3 Retries after the first attempt, so up to max_retries + 1 attempts backoff_factor float 0.5 Wait before retry n (0-based): min(backoff_factor * 2**n, 8) seconds **kwargs All BaseNode parameters (description is set for you)

Behavior:

  • Runs wrapped_node.execute(); a result with an error or a raised exception counts as a failure
  • Between retries, sets state.context["_retry_attempt"], ["_retry_error"] and ["_retry_node"] so the wrapped node can adapt
  • A success comes back under the RetryNode's name; after the last failure the result's error is "All N attempts failed. Last error: ...", with the last exception as the cause of the run's GraphExecutionError
