  • No default flags. The engine does not retry a RetryNode again, even when it carries RETRYABLE (before 1.7.0 the node was RETRYABLE, so the engine's retries multiplied its own: up to 40 attempts with the defaults)

docs.title: FanOutNode
docs.text:
Sends different sub-questions to parallel children with state overrides. Extends BaseNode.

FanOutNode("gather", branches=[
    (PromptNode("web", tools=[web_search]), {"focus": "news"}),
    (PromptNode("docs", tools=[doc_search]), {"focus": "technical"}),
])
Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier branches list[tuple[BaseNode, dict]] None List of (node, state_overrides) tuples merge_strategy str "dict" "dict", "concatenate" or "custom", as for ParallelNode; another value raises ValueError merge_fn Callable \| None None merge_fn({branch_name: output}) for "custom" (required for it) **kwargs All BaseNode parameters (description is set for you)

Behavior:

  • Each branch gets its own GraphState with a copy of the messages and observations and {**state.context, **overrides} as context; changes a branch makes to its state are not copied back
  • All branches run concurrently via asyncio.gather; each runs execute() once, so a branch that calls tools runs them once and does not see their results (there is no tool loop inside a fan-out)
  • output is merged by merge_strategy from {branch_name: branch_output}; a branch that raised gets {"error": "..."} there instead, and the node itself does not fail
  • Tool calls and tokens of the branches are added to the node's result
  • Default flags: PARALLEL_SAFE

docs.title: PromptNode
docs.text:
The core LLM reasoning node. Full prompt-assembly pipeline with tool calling, guards, strategies, and context management.

from pydantic import BaseModel

from promptise.prompts import chain_of_thought
from promptise.prompts.blocks import Identity, Rules
from promptise.prompts.guards import SchemaStrictGuard


class AnalysisOutput(BaseModel):
    summary: str
    complete: bool


PromptNode("analyze",
    instructions="Analyze the data.",
    blocks=[Identity("Analyst"), Rules(["Cite sources"])],
    strategy=chain_of_thought,
    tools=my_tools,
    inject_tools=True,
    output_key="analysis",
    input_keys=["raw_data"],
    inherit_context_from="search",
    preprocessor=enrich_fn,
    postprocessor=format_fn,
    guards=[SchemaStrictGuard()],
    output_schema=AnalysisOutput,
    transitions={"complete": "report", "need_data": "search"},
    model_override="openai:gpt-5-mini",
)

A minimal node you can run on its own, through PromptGraphEngine:

from pydantic import BaseModel

from promptise import resolve_model
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptGraphEngine, PromptNode


class Sentiment(BaseModel):
    label: str
    confidence: float


class PrintOutput:
    async def post_node(self, node, result, state):
        print(result.output)                # {'label': 'positive', 'confidence': 0.95}
        print(state.context["sentiment"])   # the same dict, under output_key
        return result


graph = PromptGraph("classify", nodes=[
    PromptNode("classify", instructions="Classify the sentiment of the message.",
               output_schema=Sentiment, output_key="sentiment",
               is_entry=True, default_next="__end__"),
])
engine = PromptGraphEngine(graph, resolve_model("openai:gpt-5-mini"), hooks=[PrintOutput()])
await engine.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "I love this library!"}]})

A node with an output_schema adds no message to the conversation while the graph goes on (the model's reply is a parsed object, not an AIMessage). When such a node ends the run, the engine appends its output as JSON in a final AIMessage, so ainvoke() returns an answer; end a graph on a node that writes text when the answer should be prose.

Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier instructions str "" Natural-language instructions injected into the system prompt blocks list[Any] None PromptBlock objects (Identity, Rules, OutputFormat, etc.) appended to system prompt strategy Any None A strategy such as chain_of_thought or self_critique (promptise.prompts): its wrap() rewrites the system prompt, its parse() extracts the answer from the reply (when the text changes, NodeResult.output is the extracted answer) perspective Any None A perspective such as analyst or critic (promptise.prompts): its apply() reframes the system prompt; an object with a framing string is put first instead tools list[BaseTool] None Tools bound to the model for this node (@tool functions, MCP tools) tool_choice str "auto" "auto": the model decides. "required": the model must call a tool (sent as LangChain's "any", which providers map to their own value). A tool's name: the model must call that tool. "none": the model is called without the tools. "required" and a tool name apply until tool results come back (the node's first call); then the model decides, so it can answer instead of calling tools until max_iterations inject_tools bool False If True, receives the tools build_agent() discovered (or PromptGraphEngine(tools=...)) at runtime, merged with tools tool_summary str None An "Available tools" block in the system prompt, on top of the tool definitions the model receives anyway: "off", "names" (one line of names) or "full" (parameters and the first 120 characters of each description). None uses the engine's setting (PromptGraphEngine(tool_summary=...) / build_agent(tool_summary=...)), which is "off", see The tool summary output_schema type None Pydantic model or TypedDict for structured output via with_structured_output(). The output is stored as a plain dict (a Pydantic model is dumped), so transitions, edge conditions, route and output_key read it the same way guards list[Any] None Guards with a check_output(text) method (ContentFilterGuard, LengthGuard, ... in promptise.prompts.guards), run on the reply text. A guard that raises is recorded in NodeResult.guards_failed (an on_guard_fail edge can route on it); the node does not retry model_override Any None Per-node model: a chat model, a Model, or a model id string such as "openai:gpt-5-mini" (resolved like build_agent(model=...)) context_layers dict[str, int] None Names of state.context keys to add to the system prompt as name:\nvalue blocks; the priority values are not used max_tokens int \| None None Response token limit for this node's model calls. None keeps the model's own setting. Set on a copy of the model under the provider's field name (max_tokens, max_output_tokens for Google, num_predict for Ollama); a model without such a field logs a warning temperature float \| None None Sampling temperature for this node's model calls. None keeps the model's own setting. Some reasoning models accept only their default temperature input_keys list[str] None Keys from state.context added to the system prompt as "Input data" (key: value; missing keys are skipped) output_key str None Write NodeResult.output to state.context[output_key]: the parsed object with an output_schema, else the reply text (a strategy's extracted answer or a postprocessor's return value when they change it). A step that only calls tools writes nothing inherit_context_from str None Inject another node's output into the prompt: reads state.context["{name}_output"], which every PromptNode writes (its reply text; for an output_schema node, the output as JSON text) context_scope str "full" Context lifecycle mode: "auto" (full→ledger automatically; the ReAct default), "full" (whole transcript), "scoped" (bounded working set), or "ledger" (deduplicated facts ledger), see Context scope auto_ledger_after int None For context_scope="auto": number of accumulated tool results after which the node switches from the full transcript to the compacted view (default 6, or the agent's context_compaction setting) compaction ContextCompaction \| bool \| int None This node's compaction settings; wins over build_agent(context_compaction=...). False keeps an "auto" node on the full transcript preprocessor Callable None Runs before the LLM call: fn(state, config) -> None, sync or async. An exception fails the node before the model is called: NodeResult.error is "Preprocessor failed in node 'x': ...", an on_error edge can route it, and otherwise the run raises GraphExecutionError (so input_validator() stops the node). Before 1.7.0 the exception was logged and the node went on postprocessor Callable None Runs on the model's reply (not on a step that only calls tools): fn(output, state, config) -> Any, sync or async. It receives NodeResult.output (the reply text, or the parsed object with an output_schema); a non-None return value replaces the output. An exception is logged and the output kept include_observations bool True Auto-inject recent tool results from state.observations include_plan bool True Auto-inject current plan/subgoals from state.plan include_reflections bool True Auto-inject past learnings from state.reflections transitions dict[str, str] None Map output keys to next-node names (e.g. {"proceed": "act"}). With two or more keys (other than "error") on a node without tools, the prompt lists them and asks for a route field; see Dynamic LLM routing default_next str None Fallback node if no transition matches max_iterations int 10 Max times this node can execute in one graph run; each tool-loop round counts. An engine max_node_iterations, when set, caps it. Once used up, the node is not run again: the engine follows its "error" transition, else an __error__ node, else ends the run. A run ended this way in the middle of a tool loop (the model never saw its last tool results) raises GraphIterationLimitError flags set[NodeFlag] None Typed flags controlling engine behavior is_entry bool False Shorthand for adding NodeFlag.ENTRY is_terminal bool False Shorthand for adding NodeFlag.TERMINAL

Execution pipeline. One execution of a PromptNode is one model call:

  1. Model: model_override if set, else the engine's model (the lightweight_model for a LIGHTWEIGHT node, when the engine has one)
  2. Preprocessor (an exception fails the node here)
  3. System prompt assembly, in this order: instructions, the optional tool summary, input_keys ("Input data"), inherit_context_from, context_layers, blocks, recent observations (skipped on a node with tools: the results are already in the conversation), plan, past reflections, the JSON fields a reasoning node reads (without an output_schema), and the list of route choices
  4. Strategy wrap(), then perspective
  5. Messages: the conversation with the node's system prompt. When the conversation starts with the agent's prompt, the two are merged into one system message; otherwise the node's prompt is inserted after the first system message (or first)
  6. temperature / max_tokens (on a copy of the model), tool binding (bind_tools() with the tool_choice) and structured output (with_structured_output()); the binding is reused on the next execution of the node in the same run while the model, tool set, tool choice and schema are unchanged
  7. Context scope: "scoped" / "ledger" (and "auto" past its threshold) replace the transcript with the compacted view
  8. The model call (astream() when the run is streamed and the node has no output_schema, else ainvoke())
  9. Tool calls: all calls of the reply run (in parallel when there are two or more), their ToolMessages are appended, and the engine runs the node again so the model sees the results
  10. The output: the parsed object, or the reply text (a reasoning node's JSON object when the reply ends with one)
  11. Transitions read from a dict output, then guards, strategy parse(), postprocessor
  12. state.context[output_key] and state.context["{name}_output"]

The system prompt is rebuilt on every execution, because input_keys, the plan, reflections, observations and the offered tools can change between steps. Tool definitions reach the model through bind_tools(); the "Available tools" block in the prompt is off unless tool_summary asks for it.

docs.title: Context scope
docs.text:
context_scope controls how much accumulated history the node sees on each LLM call, the single most important lever for context-lifecycle management on long or multi-stage tasks. The full transcript grows on every tool call; left unbounded it inflates token cost super-linearly and the model starts losing track of facts it already gathered.

The default ReAct pattern uses "auto", context handling is automatic, with no pattern to choose. The four modes:

Mode What the node sees Use it for "auto" (ReAct default) "full" while the tool loop is short, then "ledger" once it grows past auto_ledger_after (default 6) tool results The smart default, simple tasks unchanged, deep tool loops bounded automatically "full" The whole accumulated transcript When every prior message must always be visible "scoped" The node's system prompt (carrying any inherited/injected distilled state) + the input's system messages + the current user question + only this node's own in-progress tool loop Multi-stage reasoning graphs, drops the verbose intermediate messages produced by other stages so tokens don't grow across stages "ledger" System prompt + the input's system messages + a short note on earlier conversation + the current user question + the most recent assistant turn and its tool results + a compact deduplicated "facts gathered" ledger of older results Long single-node tool loops over an interconnected dataset, where the model otherwise re-queries the same facts dozens of times 
# Default agents already get this: no configuration needed:
PromptNode("reason", inject_tools=True, context_scope="auto", auto_ledger_after=6)

# Multi-stage graph: each stage only sees its own working set.
PromptNode("analyze", instructions="...", context_scope="scoped")

# Force the ledger from turn 0 (deep tool loop you know will be long):
PromptNode("reason", inject_tools=True, context_scope="ledger")

Honest scope of auto

auto is an efficiency / context-bounding default: it keeps tokens and context manageable on deep loops at zero change to short tasks (below the threshold it is byte-for-byte "full"). It does not by itself make the model aggregate gathered facts more accurately; for that, change the action space with code-action.

How "ledger" works:

  • The input's system messages (yours and runtime-injected ones such as [Context State]) and the current user question are always sent. Dict messages ({"role": "user", ...}) are converted to LangChain messages first, so every input form works; with chat history, the question is the last user message and earlier turns become a short note.
  • The ledger is built from the tool calls in the transcript older than the latest exchange, one line per tool(args) = result, last value wins per (tool, args) so duplicates collapse. Results longer than keep_result_chars (2,000) are cut to an excerpt that says how much was cut and names the call; a call the model made more than once is shown in full (it fetched it again for the full text), and is the last to shrink under max_tokens; results shown in the latest exchange are not repeated.
  • It is placed last, immediately before the model's turn, where it is most salient, so the model consults it instead of re-calling a tool.
  • The most recent assistant turn and its tool results (a whole parallel batch) are kept in-flow so the model doesn't lose continuity and loop.
  • Tool execution is unchanged: a repeated (tool, args) call runs the tool again, because its result may have changed (a job's status, a health check). The ledger, not a cache, is what keeps the model from re-fetching facts it already has. For tools whose result cannot change during a run, ContextCompaction(reuse_results=[...]) answers a repeated call from the latest earlier successful result instead of running the tool; such a call is reported to trace_tools, the observer, callbacks, hooks (on_tool_reused) and stream events, marked as reused, and has "reused": True in NodeResult.tool_calls. See Repeated calls run the tool.

This is the mechanism behind the managed prebuilt pattern. It is an efficiency primitive, it bounds token growth and tells the model not to re-fetch what it has; how many calls that saves depends on the model (see the note on managed).

docs.title: ToolNode
docs.text:
Explicit tool execution with input validation and deduplication.

ToolNode("search",
    tools=[search_tool, wiki_tool],
    validate_inputs=True,
    deduplicate=True,
    max_result_chars=4000,
    tool_selector=my_selector_fn,
)
Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier tools list[BaseTool] None Available tools validate_inputs bool True Check each call's arguments against the tool's parameter schema before calling it; invalid arguments do not reach the tool (see below) deduplicate bool True Run identical (tool, args) calls of one model turn once (see below) max_result_chars int 4000 Truncate successful tool results to this length tool_selector Callable None Custom function (state) -> (tool_name, args) to pick which tool to call. Without one, the node runs the tool calls of the most recent assistant message that has tool calls **kwargs All BaseNode parameters

When to use it. A PromptNode runs the tool calls its model asks for itself, so a ToolNode placed after one finds those calls already answered and runs nothing. Use a ToolNode with a tool_selector for a call your code decides (no model turn), or after a custom node that appends an AIMessage with tool calls. A ToolNode uses only its own tools; it does not receive injected tools.

from promptise import tool
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptGraphEngine, ToolNode


@tool
def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Current weather for a city."""
    return f"Sunny in {city}"


graph = PromptGraph("lookup", nodes=[
    ToolNode("weather", tools=[get_weather], is_entry=True, default_next="__end__",
             tool_selector=lambda state: ("get_weather", {"city": state.context.get("city", "Berlin")})),
])
engine = PromptGraphEngine(graph, model=None)    # no model call
result = await engine.ainvoke({"messages": []})
print(result["messages"][-1].content)            # Sunny in Berlin

A call runs as it does in a PromptNode. Whichever node runs a tool, the call goes through the same steps and is reported the same way:

  • The engine hooks' pre_tool run first and may change the arguments; a pre_tool hook that raises blocks the call. Then the tool runs, then post_tool hooks may change the result.
  • The tool is invoked as a tool call, so a tool with an InjectedToolCallId argument gets its id, and a tool that reports an error counts as failed: the model gets an MCP server's own error envelope ({"error": {"code": "TOOL_ERROR", "message": ...}}) in a ToolMessage with status="error". A tool that raises gives "Error: <type>: <message>". Each ToolMessage carries the tool's name.
  • Each call streams: astream_events() yields on_tool_start and then on_tool_end (status, duration_ms, reused) or on_tool_error, and astream_with_tools() turns them into ToolStartEvent / ToolEndEvent with the call's tool_index, duration_ms, success and reused (Streaming). A ToolNode runs one turn's calls one after another, in order, so each call's tool_end comes before the next call's tool_start.
  • A call whose arguments are not valid JSON (LangChain keeps it in the assistant message's invalid_tool_calls) does not run, and neither do the pre_tool / post_tool hooks. Its ToolMessage (status="error", the call's own tool_call_id) says what is wrong and names the tool's parameters (Error: The arguments for 'get_order' were not valid JSON (...). Call the tool again with a JSON object that matches its parameters: order_id (required).), or is the unknown-tool error when the name is not one of the node's tools. The call counts as failed (tool_calls_failed; in NodeResult.tool_calls with success: False, invalid: True, args: {} and the text the model sent as raw_args), callbacks get its start and an on_tool_error with a ToolArgumentError, and the stream shows it with status: "error". The model's next turn can call again; iteration limits apply as for any tool call. A call without an id gets one, on the assistant message as well, so every call has exactly one result.

What validate_inputs=True checks. After the pre_tool hooks, the arguments are validated against the schema the model is offered for the tool (its args_schema without injected arguments). As for MCP tools, an explicit null for an optional parameter that cannot be null counts as not given and is left out. When the arguments do not match, the tool does not run; the call's ToolMessage (status="error") is the same message a promptise.tools.ToolArgumentError gives, which lists each problem by argument path and tells the model to correct the call:

Invalid arguments for tool 'create_order':
- qty: Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer (got "two")
Correct the arguments and call the tool again.

The call counts as failed (tool_calls_failed, success: false in the stream), post_tool hooks see it, and callbacks get its start and an on_tool_error with the ToolArgumentError (code INVALID_ARGUMENTS). An MCP tool (also behind an approval gate or guardrails) checks its own arguments the same way and gives the same message, so the node leaves the check to it, and trace_tools and the observer show the rejected call as for any MCP call. A tool whose schema is a JSON-schema dict rather than a pydantic model is not checked by the node; it validates its own input when it runs. With validate_inputs=False the arguments go to the tool as they are.

What deduplicate=True covers. Only the calls of one model turn (the tool calls of one assistant message). When the model asks for the same tool with the same arguments twice in one turn, the tool runs once and each repeat gets its own ToolMessage with that result, so every tool_call_id has a result. The repeat is reported as reused, like a call answered by ContextCompaction(reuse_results=...): trace_tools prints ↺ Reusing an earlier result for tool: ..., the observer records it with reused: true, LangChain callbacks get its start and end with metadata["promptise_reused"], engine hooks get on_tool_reused (instead of pre_tool / post_tool), stream events have reused: true, and NodeResult.tool_calls has it with "reused": True (tool_calls_deduplicated counts it). The repeat gets the first call's result as the model saw it, after post_tool hooks. A failed call, including one a pre_tool hook blocked or one with invalid arguments, is never reused.

A call in a later model turn, a later pass of a tool_selector, or another run always runs the tool, so a status or health check returns the current value. The record of a turn's calls belongs to the run, not to the node: runs of the same graph, one after another or concurrent, never see each other's calls. If the graph reaches the node again before the model's next turn, calls that already have a result are not run again.

docs.title: RouterNode
docs.text:
LLM decides which path to take from a set of named routes.

from promptise.engine import RouterNode
from promptise.prompts.blocks import Rules

RouterNode("route",
    routes={"search": "search_node", "answer": "synthesize", "clarify": "ask_user"},
    model_override="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    context_blocks=[Rules(["Choose the most relevant path"])],
    default_next="synthesize",
)
Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier routes dict[str, str] None Map of route labels to target node names context_blocks list[Any] None Blocks rendered into the routing prompt (after instructions) model_override Any None Model for routing: a chat model, a Model, or a model id string such as "openai:gpt-5-mini" (resolved like PromptNode's; before 1.7.0 a string made the call fail) **kwargs All BaseNode parameters

How it routes. The node sends the conversation plus one system message ("Choose ONE of these routes: [...] Respond with ONLY the route name"), takes the reply in lower case and picks the first route label (in routes order) that appears in it, as a substring. No match goes to default_next; with no default_next the node fails ("No route matched ..."). Keep labels distinct ("search" also matches a reply of "research"). It makes one model call and binds no tools.

docs.title: GuardNode
docs.text:
Programmatic validation and gating with pass/fail routing.

from promptise.prompts.guards import ContentFilterGuard, LengthGuard

GuardNode("check_quality",
    guards=[LengthGuard(min_length=100), ContentFilterGuard(blocked=["todo"])],
    target_key="draft",
    on_pass="publish",
    on_fail="revise",
)
Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier guards list[Any] None Objects with an async check_output(value) that raises to fail, or plain callables fn(value) -> bool (sync or async; falsy fails) target_key str None Key in state.context to check. None checks the content of the last message that has content on_pass str "__end__" Next node when every guard passes (also when there are no guards) on_fail str \| None None Next node when any guard fails; None falls back to default_next, then to the graph's edges **kwargs All BaseNode parameters

No model call. Every guard runs (a failure does not stop the others); the results land in NodeResult.guards_passed / guards_failed. A failed guard is routing, not an error: the run does not raise. A check_output that returns False without raising counts as a pass.

docs.title: ParallelNode
docs.text:
Run multiple child nodes concurrently and merge results.

ParallelNode("parallel_search",
    nodes=[search_node, wiki_node, docs_node],
    merge_strategy="concatenate",
)
Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier nodes list[BaseNode] None Child nodes to run concurrently merge_strategy str "dict" "dict": output is {child_name: child_output}. "concatenate": one text with a [child_name] section per child that produced output, in child order (dict outputs as JSON). "custom": merge_fn({child_name: child_output}). Another value raises ValueError merge_fn Callable None fn(outputs: dict) -> Any, required for merge_strategy="custom" **kwargs All BaseNode parameters

What the children get. Each child runs execute() once on its own GraphState with copies of the messages, context and observations. A child PromptNode that calls tools runs them once but does not see their results (no tool loop inside a ParallelNode): the successful calls are added to the parent's state.observations, so a following node without tools sees them in its prompt. Context a child writes is not copied back; read the merged output (also in NodeResult.raw_output as text) instead. Before 1.7.0 the default was "concatenate" and it gave the same dict as "dict". A child that raises adds "name: error" to the node's error, which fails the node unless an edge or hook handles it.

docs.title: LoopNode
docs.text:
Repeat a body node until a condition is met.

LoopNode("refine",
    body_node=edit_node,
    condition=lambda state: state.context.get("quality_score", 0) >= 4,
    max_loop_iterations=5,
)
Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier body_node BaseNode None The node to execute on each iteration (it runs on the graph's own state) condition Callable None (state) -> bool, checked before each iteration; the loop exits when it returns True max_loop_iterations int 5 Maximum iterations **kwargs All BaseNode parameters

The whole loop is one execution of the LoopNode for the engine. A body result with an error stops the loop and becomes the node's error. The node's output is state.context["loop_result"], so have the body write its result there. For a loop over graph nodes (with edges in between), use loop_until instead.

docs.title: HumanNode
docs.text:
Pause for human approval with timeout.

HumanNode("approve",
    prompt_template="Approve sending this email?",
    timeout=300.0,
    on_approve="send",
    on_deny="revise",
    on_timeout="cancel",
)
Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier prompt_template str "Approve this action?" Prompt for the human, formatted with state.context ("Send {draft_id}?"); a placeholder missing from the context fails the node timeout float 300.0 Seconds to wait for the handler on_approve str "__end__" Next node on approval on_deny str \| None None Next node on denial; None falls back to default_next on_timeout str "__end__" Next node when the handler does not answer in time **kwargs All BaseNode parameters

The decision comes from the run's human handler: async handler(prompt: str, state: GraphState) -> bool. A truthy return approves; an object with an approved attribute (an ApprovalDecision) counts by that attribute. Give it one of three ways:

  • build_agent(approval=...): the agent's approval handler answers HumanNode steps too. It gets an ApprovalRequest whose context_summary is the node's prompt, tool_name the node name and metadata["source"] "human_node"; a handler error is a denial.
  • PromptGraphEngine(graph, model, human_handler=handler).
  • config={"_human_handler": handler} in PromptGraphEngine.ainvoke() (wins over the engine's).

A handler that raises fails the node.

Changed in 1.7.0: no handler fails the node

Without a handler, HumanNode fails with "HumanNode 'approve' has no human handler ...": the run raises GraphExecutionError unless an on_error edge routes the failure. It never approves on its own. Before 1.7.0 it approved at once ("No human handler configured, auto-approved"), and build_agent set no handler, so an approval step in an agent's graph was skipped. Pass approval= to build_agent, or a handler to the engine, for every graph with a HumanNode.

from promptise.engine import GraphState, HumanNode, PromptGraph, PromptGraphEngine, TransformNode


async def ask(prompt: str, state: GraphState) -> bool:
    print(prompt)                      # Send draft 42?
    return False                       # deny


graph = PromptGraph("approve", mode="static")
graph.add_node(TransformNode("prepare", transform=lambda state: state.context.update(draft_id=42),
                             default_next="approve"))
graph.add_node(HumanNode("approve", prompt_template="Send draft {draft_id}?",
                         on_approve="__end__", on_deny="__end__"))
graph.set_entry("prepare")

engine = PromptGraphEngine(graph, model=None)   # no model call in this graph
await engine.ainvoke({"messages": []}, config={"_human_handler": ask})
print(engine.last_report.nodes_visited)        # ['prepare', 'approve']

docs.title: TransformNode
docs.text:
Pure data transformation without an LLM call.

TransformNode("format",
    transform=lambda state: {"formatted": state.context.get("raw", "").upper()},
    output_key="formatted_data",
)
Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier transform Callable None fn(state) -> Any, sync or async (it gets the state only, no config). Without one the node fails output_key str "transform_result" Where to store the return value in state.context; it is also NodeResult.output **kwargs All BaseNode parameters

An exception in transform fails the node (an on_error edge or "error" handling can route it).

docs.title: SubgraphNode
docs.text:
Embed a complete sub-graph as a single node.

SubgraphNode("research_pipeline",
    subgraph=research_graph,
    inherit_state=True,
)
Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier subgraph PromptGraph None The sub-graph to execute inherit_state bool True True: the sub-graph starts from a copy of the parent's messages, and the messages it adds (its answer included) are appended to the parent's. False: it starts from no messages, and all its messages are appended to the parent's **kwargs All BaseNode parameters

The node runs the sub-graph with a new PromptGraphEngine on the parent's model and max_iterations, and the same run config (tools, compaction); the parent's hooks, max_node_iterations and lightweight_model are not passed on. The sub-graph gets its own GraphState: it does not see or change the parent's context, plan or observations. Its result is NodeResult.output ({"messages": [...]}), and its tokens count toward the parent's. Before 1.7.0, inherit_state=True did not copy the sub-graph's new messages back, so a graph that ended on a SubgraphNode returned no answer.

docs.title: AutonomousNode
docs.text:
Agent dynamically picks which node to execute from a pool.

AutonomousNode("agent",
    node_pool=[think_node, search_node, answer_node],
    planner_instructions="Choose the most productive next step.",
    max_steps=15,
    entry_node="think",
    terminal_nodes=["answer"],
)
Parameter Type Default Description name str "autonomous" Node identifier node_pool list[BaseNode] None Available nodes the agent can choose from planner_instructions str "" Extra instructions for the planning LLM allow_repeat bool True Allow the agent to pick the same node multiple times max_steps int 15 Maximum autonomous steps entry_node str \| None None Force a specific first node terminal_nodes list[str] None Nodes that end the autonomous loop once they succeed answer_node str \| None None Node that writes the final answer when the agent finishes without a terminal node having run last. Defaults to the first terminal node; with none, the node asks the model for the final answer itself

| **kwargs | | | All BaseNode parameters |

A chosen node runs its whole tool loop (re-run while its model keeps calling tools, up to its max_iterations) before the agent picks again. The routing call's prompt and JSON reply ({"next_node": "...", "reason": "..."}) never enter state.messages; a tool name given as the next step runs the pool node that has that tool; "__done__", "__end__", "done" or "finish" ends the loop, and so does a reply with no JSON object. The run always ends with a written answer. NodeResult.output is {"steps": [...], "total": n}.

The whole autonomous loop is one node execution for the engine, so engine hooks (pre_node / post_node), flags and max_iterations apply to the AutonomousNode, not to each pool step; max_steps bounds the steps. Tool hooks (pre_tool / post_tool) still run for every tool call.

You rarely build an AutonomousNode yourself: PromptGraph.from_pool(nodes), build_agent(node_pool=[...]), and build_agent(agent_pattern=PromptGraph("x", nodes=[...])) with two or more nodes and no edges all wrap the pool in one named "orchestrator", taking entry_node from the node with is_entry=True and terminal_nodes from the nodes with is_terminal=True.

docs.title: CodeActionNode
docs.text:
Solves a task by writing one Python program that calls the tools, running it in the sandbox and returning the line the program prints after RESULT:. This is the node behind agent_pattern="code-action"; the Code-Action guide explains when it beats a tool loop.

from promptise.engine import CodeActionNode, PromptGraph

graph = PromptGraph("coder", nodes=[
    CodeActionNode("solve", is_entry=True, is_terminal=True, exec_timeout=60, max_repairs=2),
])
Parameter Type Default Description name str required Node identifier tools list None Tools the program may call (bridged to the host). Empty: the engine's runtime tools system_prompt str "" Instructions put before the code-writing prompt blocks list None Accepted for parity with other nodes; not used in the program prompt sandbox_factory async () -> SandboxSession None Called once per program (the first and each repair), so every program runs in a fresh session, cleaned up afterwards. build_agent(agent_pattern="code-action") sets it from sandbox=. Without one the node fails with "code-action requires a sandbox" model_override Any None Model for this node: a chat model, a Model, or a model id string such as "openai:gpt-5-mini" (resolved like PromptNode's; before 1.7.0 a string made the call fail) max_repairs int 1 How often a failed program (a crash, or one that hit max_tool_calls) is sent back for a fix result_marker str "RESULT:" Prefix of the stdout line that holds the answer (the last such line wins; without one, the last non-empty stdout line is the answer) exec_timeout int 120 Seconds the program may run in the sandbox max_tool_calls int 50 Most bridged tool calls per program. Reaching it fails the program; with no repairs left the engine raises CodeActionBudgetError. 0 disables the cap **kwargs All BaseNode parameters

From build_agent, set exec_timeout, max_repairs and max_tool_calls with code_action={...} or a CodeActionConfig; see Configuration.

CodeActionConfig (a frozen pydantic model, unknown keys rejected):

Field Type Default Constraint exec_timeout int 120 > 0, <= 3600 seconds max_repairs int 1 0 to 10 max_tool_calls int 50 >= 0 (0 disables the cap)

The node writes the answer as an AIMessage, its NodeResult.output, and raw_output. Its prompt holds system_prompt, the system messages of the conversation (memory, flow prompts) and earlier user/assistant turns; tool traffic from earlier turns is left out. It does not stream model tokens.

docs.title: @node decorator
docs.text:
Turn any async function into a graph node.

from promptise.engine import node, GraphState, NodeResult, NodeFlag

@node("fetch_weather", default_next="respond", flags={NodeFlag.RETRYABLE})
async def fetch_weather(state: GraphState) -> NodeResult:
    weather = await api.get(state.context.get("city", "Berlin"))
    state.context["weather"] = weather
    return NodeResult(node_name="fetch_weather", output=weather)

graph.add_node(fetch_weather)

node(name, *, instructions="", transitions=None, default_next=None, max_iterations=10, metadata=None, flags=None, is_entry=False, is_terminal=False) takes the BaseNode parameters except description, which comes from the first line of the function's docstring.

  • The function must be async (a plain function raises TypeError), and can accept (state), (state, config), or ().
  • Return a NodeResult to control everything (an empty node_name is filled in); any other return value becomes NodeResult(output=value).
  • The decorator returns a node object, not a function: add it with graph.add_node(fetch_weather).
  • An exception the function raises fails the node; the engine records it as the node's error.

docs.title: BaseNode subclass
docs.text:
For full control, subclass BaseNode directly.

from promptise.engine import BaseNode, NodeResult, NodeFlag

class DatabaseNode(BaseNode):
    def __init__(self, name, *, query_template, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(name, flags={NodeFlag.RETRYABLE, NodeFlag.STATEFUL}, **kwargs)
        self.template = query_template

    async def execute(self, state, config):
        result = await db.query(self.template.format(**state.context))
        state.context[f"{self.name}_output"] = result
        return NodeResult(node_name=self.name, output=result)

When the graph is streamed (astream(), astream_events(), agent.astream_with_tools()), the engine calls the node's stream(). The default runs execute() once and yields an on_node_end event with the result, so a subclass only overrides stream() to emit events of its own, and then must end with NodeEvent(event="on_node_end", node_name=self.name, data={"result": result}). A stream that ends without the result fails the run; the engine never executes a node twice to get one.

docs.title: BaseNode Parameters
docs.text:
All nodes inherit these parameters from BaseNode:

Parameter Type Default Description name str required Unique identifier within the graph instructions str "" Description of what the node does description str "" Short description for visualization (defaults to first 80 chars of instructions) transitions dict[str, str] None Output key to next-node mapping default_next str None Fallback transition max_iterations int 10 Max executions per graph run, enforced by the engine; when used up, the "error" transition is followed (else __error__, else the run ends) metadata dict None Arbitrary metadata for hooks and observability is_entry bool False Adds NodeFlag.ENTRY is_terminal bool False Adds NodeFlag.TERMINAL flags set[NodeFlag] None Typed flags controlling engine behavior

Every node also has has_flag(flag), the is_entry / is_terminal properties (backed by the ENTRY / TERMINAL flags), execute(state, config) (raises NotImplementedError on BaseNode) and stream(state, config).

NodeProtocol (from promptise.engine import NodeProtocol) is the minimal runtime-checkable protocol: a name attribute plus async execute() and stream(). The engine also reads max_iterations, transitions, default_next, flags and has_flag(), so subclass BaseNode rather than implementing the protocol from scratch.

docs.title: Node Flags
docs.text:
Nodes declare their capabilities through typed NodeFlag enums. The engine processes these flags at runtime to control execution, caching, error handling, and observability.

from promptise.engine import NodeFlag

PlanNode("plan", is_entry=True)                                    # ENTRY flag
PromptNode("act", inject_tools=True)                               # INJECT_TOOLS flag
SynthesizeNode("answer", is_terminal=True)                         # TERMINAL flag
PromptNode("critical_step", flags={NodeFlag.CRITICAL})             # Abort on error
PromptNode("optional", flags={NodeFlag.SKIP_ON_ERROR, NodeFlag.LIGHTWEIGHT})

18 built-in flags cover execution control, context isolation, model selection, observability, and output processing. See Node Flags for the full reference.

docs.title: Skills Library
docs.text:
Pre-configured node factories for common tasks:

from promptise.engine.skills import (
    # Standard skills
    web_researcher, code_reviewer, data_analyst, fact_checker,
    summarizer, planner, decision_router, formatter,
    # Reasoning skills
    thinker, reflector, critic, justifier, synthesizer,
    validator_node, observer_node,
)

graph.add_node(planner("plan", is_entry=True))
graph.add_node(web_researcher("search", tools=search_tools))
graph.add_node(reflector("reflect"))
graph.add_node(synthesizer("conclude", is_terminal=True))

See Skills Library for all 15 skill factories with parameters.

docs.title: Prebuilt Reasoning Patterns
docs.text:
Ten ready-to-use reasoning patterns: nine you can name with build_agent(agent_pattern="...") and PromptGraph.pipeline(...), which takes your nodes. Each factory is a static method on PromptGraph that returns a configured graph; pass it as agent_pattern to build_agent() or run it with PromptGraphEngine.

With a pattern name, build_agent passes its tools, its system prompt (instructions) and graph_blocks to the factory (for research, the tools become search_tools; for code-action, the code_action= settings and a sandbox factory are added). With no agent_pattern at all, the default ReAct graph gets the tools, the system prompt and graph_blocks too (before 1.7.0 it did not get graph_blocks). An unknown name raises ValueError.

Node budgets

Each node runs at most its own max_iterations times per run. Under build_agent, the reason node of react (and of the default graph) and of managed gets max_agent_iterations (default 25) as its budget, so N allows N model calls; the other patterns keep the budgets their factories set, within the run's cap of max_agent_iterations node executions. PromptGraphEngine applies no engine-wide per-node ceiling unless you pass max_node_iterations= (before 1.7.0 it capped every node at 25, so managed's 30 ran as 25).

docs.title: ReAct (Default)
docs.text:
Single PromptNode with tools. The LLM decides when to call tools and when to answer.

graph LR
    A[reason] -->|tool calls| A
    A -->|final answer| END[__end__]

    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
agent = await build_agent(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", servers=my_servers)
# or explicitly:
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="react")

The engine loops: LLM → tools → LLM → tools → ... → final answer.

PromptGraph.react(
    tools=None,              # Tools (@tool functions, MCP tools)
    system_prompt="",        # The reason node's instructions
    blocks=None,             # PromptBlock objects
    max_node_iterations=15,  # The reason node's max_iterations (each model call counts)
)

One PromptNode("reason") with context_scope="auto" and default_next="__end__".

docs.title: Verify (single-pass self-checking)
docs.text:
A single LLM call in which the model must plan, solve, and verify its own answer before responding. It adds the accuracy benefit of an explicit self-verification step at one-turn latency, no multi-call overhead.

graph LR
    A["reason<br/>(plan → solve → verify)"] --> END[__end__]
    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="verify")

PromptGraph.verify(
    tools=None,
    system_prompt="",
    blocks=None,
    max_node_iterations=6,
)

One PromptNode("reason") whose instructions add a PLAN, SOLVE, VERIFY, final-answer structure after system_prompt. It has context_scope="full" (no compaction) and a budget of 6 model calls.

When it helps

The self-check is part of the same generation, so it costs output tokens, not extra calls. It is most useful where a single pass makes careless errors; a model that already reasons carefully may gain little over a direct prompt. Measure it on your own tasks. For multi-stage deliberate reasoning with per-stage context scoping, compose a custom graph (see Custom Graph).

docs.title: Managed (context-managed tool loop)
docs.text:
For deep multi-tool tasks, traversing a database or graph, gathering many facts then aggregating. A single tool-using node run with context_scope="ledger": instead of feeding the model an ever-growing transcript of tool calls and results (where it loses track and re-queries the same facts), each turn it sees the task, its most recent exchange, and a compact deduplicated "facts gathered" ledger. A call the model does repeat runs the tool again (its result may have changed); to answer repeats of lookups whose result cannot change from the earlier result, opt those tools in with context_compaction=ContextCompaction(reuse_results=[...]) (see Repeated calls run the tool).

graph LR
    A["reason<br/>(tool loop + facts ledger)"] --> END[__end__]
    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="managed")

PromptGraph.managed(
    tools=my_tools,
    system_prompt="",
    blocks=None,
    max_node_iterations=30,   # deep tasks make many calls (max_agent_iterations under build_agent)
)

The underlying primitive is PromptNode(context_scope="ledger"), which any custom graph can use on a long-running tool node.

What it does, honestly

The ledger bounds context on long tool chains: the request stops growing with every tool result. Whether it also cuts tool calls depends on the model: models that re-query facts buried in a long transcript make fewer calls with it, others re-read facts the ledger lists. A result the model fetches again is kept in full from then on, so it does not have to re-read it a third time. Measure your own model with ContextCompaction(enabled=False) as the baseline. It is an efficiency primitive: it does not by itself make the model's final answer more correct.

docs.title: Code-Action (one sandboxed program)
docs.text:
For aggregation / data-traversal tasks, the model writes one Python program over your tools in a single LLM turn, instead of chaining dozens of conversational tool calls. The program runs in Promptise's hardened Docker sandbox; its tool calls bridge back to the real host tools, so the model gets code's exactness (loops, sums, filters, joins) while every tool call still keeps its protections, approval gates if configured, plus budget/health/audit hooks when the Agent Runtime has attached them, and the node enforces a hard max_tool_calls cap on each program regardless.

graph LR
    A["reason<br/>(write 1 program)"] --> S["run in sandbox<br/>(tools bridged to host)"]
    S --> END[__end__]
    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="code-action")  # sandbox auto-enabled

# Tune the pattern from build_agent (unknown keys are rejected):
agent = await build_agent(
    ...,
    agent_pattern="code-action",
    code_action={"exec_timeout": 60, "max_repairs": 2, "max_tool_calls": 20},
)

PromptGraph.code_action(
    tools=my_tools,
    system_prompt="",
    blocks=None,
    sandbox_factory=...,   # injected by build_agent
    max_repairs=1,         # re-try once on a failed program, feeding the error back
    exec_timeout=120,      # max seconds the program may run
    max_tool_calls=50,     # hard cap on each program's tool calls
)

The tool-call budget. Every call a program makes counts against max_tool_calls, failed ones included. Once a program reaches it, each further call raises ToolBudgetExceeded in the program without running the tool, a warning is logged, and the program's output is discarded (it is incomplete, even if the program caught the error). The prompt says the cap exists but not its value, and forbids skipping or truncating records to stay under it. After a budget hit the repair asks for a program that does the whole job in fewer calls (it gets a fresh budget, so a run makes at most (max_repairs + 1) × max_tool_calls calls), or for the reply CANNOT_FINISH_WITHIN_CALL_CAP. That reply, or a budget hit with no repair left, fails the node, and the run raises CodeActionBudgetError (a GraphExecutionError) rather than answering from part of the data. MCP tool results that are JSON text reach the program decoded (lists, dicts, numbers), and an MCP tool error raises in the program. ExecutionReport.tool_calls counts the programs' calls. See Code-Action.

The mechanism. In one turn the model writes a program that calls your tools as ordinary Python functions. Inside the sandbox those functions are RPC stubs: each writes a request to the workspace; a concurrent host loop runs the real tool and writes back the response. The sandbox has a read-only rootfs, dropped capabilities, and no network, the program's only outside reach is your bridged tools.

Requirements & honest scope

Requires Docker (auto-enabled for this pattern). It shines when your tools return structured data (lists/dicts/numbers) the program can use directly, and on tasks a conversational loop gets wrong by re-querying and mis-aggregating. It is a pattern, not a replacement, for ambiguous or conversational tasks prefer react/managed. PromptGraph.code_action() without a sandbox_factory builds a graph whose node fails with "code-action requires a sandbox"; build_agent(agent_pattern="code-action") supplies one.

docs.title: PEOATR
docs.text:
Plan → Act → Think → Reflect → Answer. Structured reasoning with specialized nodes.

graph TD
    P[plan] -->|quality < 3| P
    P --> A[act]
    A -->|tool calls| A
    A --> T[think]
    T -->|continue| A
    T -->|reflect| R[reflect]
    R -->|continue| A
    R -->|replan| P
    R -->|answer| ANS[answer]
    ANS --> END[__end__]

    style P fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style A fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style T fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style R fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
    style ANS fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="peoatr")

PromptGraph.peoatr(
    tools=None,                    # Tools for the act node
    system_prompt="",              # Shared system prompt
    blocks=None,                   # Shared blocks
    planning_instructions="",     # Extra instructions for the plan node
    acting_instructions="",       # Extra instructions for the act node
    thinking_instructions="",     # Extra instructions for the think node
    reflecting_instructions="",   # Extra instructions for the reflect node
    max_act_steps=12,             # Act budget per run (each tool-loop round counts)
)

Each stage has its own role:

  • Plan (PlanNode): Create subgoals and rate the plan; a plan rated below 3 is redone
  • Act (PromptNode): Execute tools for the active subgoal, then summarize what it found
  • Think (ThinkNode): Analyze the results: call another tool now (continue) or step back (reflect)
  • Reflect (ReflectNode): Evaluate progress and route: answer, replan or continue
  • Answer (SynthesizeNode): Write the final answer from the gathered results

Plan, think and reflect return structured output (PeoatrPlan, PeoatrThought, PeoatrReflection in promptise.engine.prebuilts), so their routing decisions always reach the engine. Every stage has an iteration budget (plan 3, act and think max_act_steps, reflect 4). A stage that has used its budget hands over to answer (plan hands over to act), so a run always ends with a written answer instead of looping to the engine's step cap.

docs.title: Research
docs.text:
Search → Verify → Synthesize. Three-stage research pipeline with optional verification.

graph LR
    S[search] -->|tool calls| S
    S --> V[verify]
    V -->|pass| SY[synthesize]
    V -->|fail| S
    SY --> END[__end__]

    style S fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style V fill:#3a1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff
    style SY fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="research")

PromptGraph.research(
    search_tools=None,       # Tools for the search node
    synthesis_tools=None,    # Tools for the synthesize node (optional)
    system_prompt="",        # Shared system prompt
    blocks=None,             # Shared blocks
    verify=True,             # Include verification step (set False to skip)
    max_search_steps=12,     # Search budget per run (each tool-loop round counts)
    max_verify_rounds=2,     # How many times verify may run
)
  • Search (PromptNode): Gather information with the tools, then reply with the findings. After a failed check it sees the verifier's issues (state.context["verification"]) and looks up what is missing.
  • Verify (ValidateNode): A model call that checks the findings against the tool results in the conversation and returns a ResearchVerdict (passes, issues; in promptise.engine.prebuilts): every claim backed by a tool result, nothing contradicting the sources or itself, the whole question covered. A failed check routes back to search.
  • Synthesize (PromptNode): Write the final answer from the findings.

Verify runs at most max_verify_rounds times; once it has, and when search has used its budget, the run moves on to synthesize, so it always ends with a written answer. Each check is one extra model call; pass verify=False for search → synthesize without it. For a deterministic check without a model call instead, build the graph yourself with a GuardNode and your own guards in place of verify.

docs.title: Autonomous
docs.text:
Agent receives a pool of configured nodes and dynamically decides which to execute at each step.

graph TD
    AU[AutonomousNode] -->|step 1| N1[reason]
    AU -->|step 2| N2[analyze]
    AU -->|step 3| N3[synthesize]
    AU -->|done| END[__end__]

    N1 -.->|result| AU
    N2 -.->|result| AU
    N3 -.->|result| AU

    style AU fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style N1 fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style N2 fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style N3 fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="autonomous")

PromptGraph.autonomous(
    node_pool=None,          # List of BaseNode instances to choose from
    system_prompt="",        # System prompt for the planner
    tools=None,              # Tools for the default reason node (if no pool provided)
    max_steps=15,            # Maximum autonomous decision steps
    blocks=None,             # PromptBlocks for the default nodes
    max_tool_rounds=10,      # Model calls per reason step in the default pool
)

The LLM sees the node catalog (names, descriptions, the tools each step calls, which steps finish the run) and picks the next step, or __done__. If no pool is provided, the default pool is reason (with the tools), analyze and synthesize, which writes the final answer and is terminal.

  • A step runs its whole tool loop. A chosen node is re-run while its model keeps calling tools (up to the node's max_iterations), so one step can make several tool calls and read their results before the agent picks again.
  • The routing exchange stays out of the conversation. The step menu and the model's JSON choice are sent for that one call and never added to the messages, so they can't pile up or become the reply.
  • Tool names map to steps. A tool name given as the next step runs the pool node that has that tool; an unknown name is reported back to the next routing call.
  • The run ends with an answer. When the agent finishes (__done__, max_steps, or an unparseable choice) without a terminal node having run last, the AutonomousNode's answer_node runs, by default the first terminal node; with none in the pool, the node asks the model for the final answer itself.
  • Streaming. AutonomousNode streams the chosen steps' model chunks and tool events; the routing calls are not streamed.

docs.title: Deliberate
docs.text:
Think → Plan → Act → Observe → Reflect → Answer. Slower, higher-quality reasoning that thinks before acting and observes results carefully.

graph TD
    TH[think] --> PL[plan]
    PL -->|quality < 3| PL
    PL --> AC[act]
    AC -->|tool calls| AC
    AC --> OB[observe]
    OB --> RE[reflect]
    RE -->|continue| AC
    RE -->|replan| PL
    RE -->|answer| ANS[answer]
    ANS --> END[__end__]

    style TH fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style PL fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style AC fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style OB fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
    style RE fill:#3a1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff
    style ANS fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="deliberate")

PromptGraph.deliberate(
    tools=None,              # Tools for the act node
    system_prompt="",        # Shared system prompt
    blocks=None,             # Shared blocks
    max_act_steps=12,        # Act budget per run (each tool-loop round counts)
)

Uses reasoning nodes: ThinkNode → PlanNode → PromptNode (with tools) → ObserveNode → ReflectNode → SynthesizeNode. Plan and reflect return structured output (PeoatrPlan, PeoatrReflection, as in PEOATR), so the plan's quality gate and reflect's continue / replan / answer route always reach the engine. Every stage has a budget (plan 3, act max_act_steps, reflect 4); act and reflect hand over to answer when theirs is used, so the run always ends with the answer stage's written reply.

docs.title: Debate
docs.text:
Adversarial debate. The proposer answers with tools, the critic and the judge send it back until the answer holds up, then answer writes the reply.

graph TD
    PR[proposer] -->|tool calls| PR
    PR --> CR[critic]
    CR -->|severity high| PR
    CR -->|severity low| JU[judge]
    JU -->|fail| PR
    JU -->|pass| ANS[answer]
    ANS --> END[__end__]

    style PR fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style CR fill:#3a1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff
    style JU fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style ANS fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern="debate")  # the proposer gets the agent's tools

PromptGraph.debate(
    system_prompt="",        # Shared system prompt
    tools=None,              # Tools for the proposer
    blocks=None,             # Shared blocks
    max_rounds=3,            # How many times the critic and the judge may each run
    max_proposer_steps=12,   # Proposer budget per run (each tool-loop round counts)
)
  • Proposer (PromptNode): Answers with the tools. On a revision it sees the latest critique and verdict (state.context["critique"], state.context["verdict"]).
  • Critic (CritiqueNode): Returns a DebateCritique (weaknesses, improvements, severity from 0.0 to 1.0); above 0.3 the answer goes back to the proposer.
  • Judge (ValidateNode): Returns a DebateVerdict (passes, issues); a failed verdict goes back to the proposer, a pass goes to answer.
  • Answer (SynthesizeNode): Writes the final reply: the latest proposal, corrected for any issue still listed.

The schemas are in promptise.engine.prebuilts. When the critic has run max_rounds times the run goes to the judge; when the judge or the proposer has used its budget, it goes to answer, so a debate always ends with a written answer.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
Simple sequential pipeline. Chains provided nodes with always edges. No loops, no conditions.

graph LR
    A[step 1] --> B[step 2] --> C[step 3] --> END[__end__]

    style A fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style C fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode

graph = PromptGraph.pipeline(
    PromptNode("extract", instructions="Extract key facts."),
    PromptNode("analyze", instructions="Analyze the facts."),
    PromptNode("format", instructions="Format the results."),
)
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern=graph)

PromptGraph.pipeline(
    PromptNode("extract"),   # Variadic: the nodes to chain, in order
    PromptNode("summarize"),
)

Automatically sets the first node as entry. The last node defaults to __end__.

docs.title: Custom Graph
docs.text:
Build any topology. Pass directly to build_agent().

graph TD
    P[plan] --> S[search]
    S --> A[analyze]
    A -->|quality >= 4| W[write]
    A -->|quality < 4| S
    W --> R[review]
    R -->|approved| END[__end__]
    R -->|rejected| W

    style P fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S fill:#1a2e1a,stroke:#4ade80,color:#fff
    style A fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style W fill:#3a2a0a,stroke:#fbbf24,color:#fff
    style R fill:#3a1a1a,stroke:#f87171,color:#fff
    style END fill:#1a1a1a,stroke:#666,color:#aaa
from pydantic import BaseModel

from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode, GuardNode
from promptise.engine.skills import planner, web_researcher, summarizer
from promptise.prompts.guards import LengthGuard


class Analysis(BaseModel):
    findings: str
    quality: int   # 1-5: is the research good enough to write from?


graph = PromptGraph("custom", mode="static")
graph.add_node(planner("plan"))
graph.add_node(web_researcher("search", tools=search_tools))
graph.add_node(PromptNode("analyze", instructions="Analyze the findings and rate their quality 1-5.",
                          output_schema=Analysis, output_key="analysis", max_iterations=3,
                          transitions={"error": "write"}))
graph.add_node(summarizer("write", input_keys=["analysis"]))
graph.add_node(GuardNode("review", guards=[LengthGuard(max_length=2000)],
                         on_pass="__end__", on_fail="write"))

graph.always("plan", "search")
graph.always("search", "analyze")
graph.when("analyze", "write", lambda r: (r.output if isinstance(r.output, dict) else {}).get("quality", 0) >= 4)
graph.when("analyze", "search", lambda r: (r.output if isinstance(r.output, dict) else {}).get("quality", 0) < 4)
graph.always("write", "review")

graph.set_entry("plan")
assert graph.validate() == []
agent = await build_agent(..., agent_pattern=graph)

Learn the concept

  • AI Agent Reasoning Patterns in Python: 9 Patterns Tested -- How the prebuilt patterns compare on accuracy and cost.
  • Plan-and-Execute Agents in Python: Beyond the ReAct Loop -- Plan, act, verify, reflect, explained on one task.

docs.title: Node Processors
docs.text: Processors are functions that run before (preprocessors) or after (postprocessors) a PromptNode's LLM call. They transform state, parse outputs, and enrich results. The built-in ones are factories in promptise.engine.processors: call them to get the processor.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from promptise.engine import PromptNode
from promptise.engine.processors import (
    chain_postprocessors, context_enricher, state_writer,
)
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Answer(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    confidence: float


node = PromptNode("analyze",
    output_schema=Answer,
    preprocessor=context_enricher(),
    postprocessor=chain_postprocessors(state_writer(fields={"answer": "final_answer"})),
)

What a postprocessor receives

A postprocessor gets NodeResult.output: a dict for a node with an output_schema, the reply text for a plain-text reply (a reasoning node's JSON fields when its reply ends with them), or the extracted answer for a node whose strategy parsed one (for example chain_of_thought when the reply has its answer marker). It runs on the model's reply only, not on a step that only calls tools. So json_extractor() parses the JSON out of a plain PromptNode's reply. A postprocessor's non-None return value becomes the node's output (and is written to output_key). Before 1.7.0 a plain-text reply reached the postprocessor as None.

A preprocessor that raises stops the node

An exception from a preprocessor fails the node before the model is called (fail closed): NodeResult.error is "Preprocessor failed in node 'x': ValueError: ...", an on_error edge or hook can route it, and otherwise the run raises GraphExecutionError with the exception as its cause. So input_validator() is a gate. An exception from a postprocessor is logged on promptise.engine and the output kept. Before 1.7.0 preprocessor exceptions were logged and the node called the model anyway.

docs.title: Preprocessors
docs.text:
Preprocessors run before the LLM call and modify state in place. A preprocessor can be sync or async; the node awaits a coroutine.

Signature: (state: GraphState, config: dict) -> None

docs.title: context_enricher
docs.text:
Adds timestamp and iteration info to state.context.

context_enricher(include_timestamp=True, include_iteration=True)
Parameter Type Default Description include_timestamp bool True Set state.context["_timestamp"] (UTC, ISO 8601) include_iteration bool True Set state.context["_iteration"] (state.iteration) and ["_tools_called"] (state.tool_calls_made)

The values are in state.context; list them in the node's input_keys for the model to see them.

docs.title: state_summarizer
docs.text:
Truncates long string values in state.context to save tokens.

state_summarizer(max_context_chars=2000)
Parameter Type Default Description max_context_chars int 2000 Every string value in state.context longer than this is cut to this length plus "... (truncated)"

It changes the shared state.context for every later node, not only this one's prompt.

docs.title: input_validator
docs.text:
Checks that required keys exist in state.context and raises ValueError naming the missing ones. Inside a node that fails the node before the model is called (see the warning above).

input_validator(required_keys=["query", "data_source"])
Parameter Type Default Description required_keys list[str] required Keys that must be in state.context

docs.title: Postprocessors
docs.text:
Postprocessors run after the LLM call (and after guards and strategy parsing) and transform the output. Sync or async.

Signature: (output: Any, state: GraphState, config: dict) -> Any

docs.title: json_extractor
docs.text:
Parses the first JSON object out of a string output (nested braces work, e.g. {"a": {"b": 1}}). A dict output is passed through, filtered to keys when given. Anything else (including None, or a string with no JSON object) is returned unchanged.

json_extractor()                        # Extract first JSON object from text
json_extractor(keys=["answer", "confidence"])  # Only keep these keys
Parameter Type Default Description keys list[str] \| None None Keep only these keys (missing ones are left out) 
from promptise.engine import GraphState
from promptise.engine.processors import json_extractor

extract = json_extractor(keys=["answer"])
print(extract('Result: {"answer": 42, "notes": "x"}', GraphState(), {}))   # {'answer': 42}

docs.title: confidence_scorer
docs.text:
Adds a _confidence score from hedging words in the output text: max(0.1, 1 - 10 * hedges / words), rounded to two decimals, where hedges counts which of 12 phrases ("might", "maybe", "perhaps", "possibly", "unclear", "uncertain", "not sure", "I think", "could be", "approximately", "roughly", "it seems") appear. A heuristic, not a calibrated probability. A dict output gets a _confidence key; any other output becomes {"text": str(output), "_confidence": ...}.

from promptise.engine import GraphState
from promptise.engine.processors import confidence_scorer

score = confidence_scorer()
print(score("The total is 42.", GraphState(), {}))   # {'text': 'The total is 42.', '_confidence': 1.0}

docs.title: state_writer
docs.text:
Writes specific output fields to state.context keys. Only writes keys that exist in the output dict.

state_writer(fields={"answer": "final_answer", "confidence": "score"})
# output["answer"] → state.context["final_answer"]
# output["confidence"] → state.context["score"]
Parameter Type Default Description fields dict[str, str] required Mapping of output_key → state.context_key

docs.title: output_truncator
docs.text:
Truncates output text to a maximum character length. Appends "..." when truncated.

output_truncator(max_chars=4000)
Parameter Type Default Description max_chars int 4000 Maximum output length in characters

docs.title: chain_preprocessors
docs.text:
Combines multiple preprocessors into one. Runs them in order; sync and async preprocessors mix. The chain stays synchronous until one returns an awaitable, then it returns a coroutine that awaits it and runs the rest (the node awaits it). An exception stops the chain and fails the node. Before 1.7.0 an async preprocessor in a chain never ran.

preprocessor = chain_preprocessors(
    context_enricher(),
    input_validator(required_keys=["query"]),
    state_summarizer(max_context_chars=1000),
)

docs.title: chain_postprocessors
docs.text:
Combines multiple postprocessors into one. Pipes the output through each function in order (each gets the previous one's return value, None included). Sync and async postprocessors mix, as in chain_preprocessors: each step's awaitable is awaited before the next step gets its value.

postprocessor = chain_postprocessors(
    json_extractor(keys=["answer", "confidence"]),
    confidence_scorer(),
    state_writer(fields={"answer": "final_answer"}),
)

docs.title: Custom Processors
docs.text:
Write your own processors using the same signatures:

import re
from typing import Any

from promptise.engine import GraphState, PromptNode
from promptise.engine.processors import chain_preprocessors, context_enricher


# Custom preprocessor
def inject_user_profile(state: GraphState, config: dict) -> None:
    user_id = state.context.get("user_id")
    if user_id:
        state.context["user_profile"] = db.get_user(user_id)

# Custom postprocessor
def extract_citations(output: Any, state: GraphState, config: dict) -> Any:
    if isinstance(output, str):
        citations = re.findall(r'\[(\d+)\]', output)
        return {"text": output, "citations": citations}
    return output

# Use them
PromptNode("personalized",
    preprocessor=chain_preprocessors(inject_user_profile, context_enricher()),
    postprocessor=extract_citations,
)

docs.title: Graph Serialization & YAML
docs.text: Save and load graphs as YAML files or Python dicts. A saved graph loads back as the same graph: every node setting round-trips, or saving refuses with an error that names the node and the setting.

docs.title: Save a Graph
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel

from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode, ValidateNode
from promptise.engine.serialization import save_graph


class Verdict(BaseModel):
    passes: bool
    issues: list[str]


graph = PromptGraph("checked-answer", mode="static")
graph.add_node(PromptNode("answer", inject_tools=True, default_next="verify"))
graph.add_node(ValidateNode(
    "verify", output_schema=Verdict, on_pass="__end__", on_fail="answer", max_iterations=3,
))
graph.set_entry("answer")

save_graph(graph, "my-agent.yaml")

The file is written only if the whole graph can be represented (see What can't be saved).

docs.title: Load a Graph
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel

from promptise.engine.serialization import load_graph


class Verdict(BaseModel):   # the class the saved graph references (__main__:Verdict)
    passes: bool
    issues: list[str]


# tools=agent.tools when the graph names tools; this one only uses inject_tools
graph = load_graph("my-agent.yaml", tools=[], refs=[Verdict])
print(graph.describe())
Argument What it's for tools Tools are saved by name. Pass the tools to resolve them against, a list (typically agent.tools) or a {name: tool} mapping. A name that isn't provided raises. refs Python objects the file references by import path, output_schema models, processors, edge conditions, @node functions. Pass them as a list (or a {"module:QualName": obj} mapping). References into promptise itself resolve without it. allow_imports Import any other reference instead of requiring refs. Importing a module runs its code, only for files you trust. Default False.

The file may hold the graph at the top level or under a graph key.

docs.title: What Round-Trips
docs.text:
Setting Stored as Instructions, transitions, default_next, max_iterations, metadata Plain data Every node type's own settings: input_keys, output_key, inherit_context_from, context_scope, temperature, on_pass/on_fail, max_subgoals, … Plain data Flags (including inject_tools, is_entry, is_terminal) flags: [inject_tools, ...] compaction (a ContextCompaction, or True/False/an int) Its fields, e.g. compaction: {after_tool_results: 3} or compaction: {reuse_results: [get_user]} (a custom count_tokens as an import reference) Tools Tool names, resolved from tools= on load output_schema, preprocessor, postprocessor, transform, merge_fn, tool_selector, a LoopNode condition Import reference "module:QualName" model_override given as a string The model id Nested nodes (ParallelNode, LoopNode, RetryNode, FanOutNode, AutonomousNode pool) and subgraphs Nested configs An @node function A reference to the module-level node Graph name, mode, entry, edges Plain data Edges from on_tool_call, on_no_tool_call, on_output, on_error, on_confidence, on_guard_fail A condition: mapping Edges from when(...) / loop_until(...) with a module-level function condition: {ref: "module:function"} loop_until(..., max_iterations=...) budgets loops: {refine: {max_iterations: 5, exit_to: deliver}}

Values a node would get by default are left out, so a saved graph stays short and picks up improved defaults (for example a reasoning node's built-in instructions).

docs.title: What Can't Be Saved
docs.text:
These are Python objects with state of their own. Saving a graph that uses them raises GraphSerializationError; remove them before saving and set them in code after loading:

  • A lambda, or a function or class defined inside another function (as an output_schema, processor or edge condition), move it to module level. An object defined in the script you run is saved as __main__:Name; pass it in refs= when loading.
  • blocks, strategy, perspective, guards, a RouterNode's context_blocks.
  • A model_override that is a model object rather than a model id string (it may carry credentials).
  • A node class that isn't registered (see Custom Node Types).
from promptise.engine.serialization import GraphSerializationError, save_graph

try:
    save_graph(graph, "agent.yaml")
except GraphSerializationError as exc:
    print(exc)
    # Edge act → verify condition: can't be saved, it is a lambda or defined
    # inside a function. Define it at module level in an importable module, ...

Loading is just as strict: an unknown node type, an unknown field, a tool that wasn't provided or a reference that can't be resolved raises GraphSerializationError (a ValueError).

docs.title: YAML Format
docs.text:
version: 2
name: plan-act-verify
mode: static
entry: plan
nodes:
  plan:
    type: plan
    instructions: Plan how to answer with the sales tools.
    output_schema: my_agent.schemas:Plan
    flags: [observable, stateful]
  act:
    type: prompt
    instructions: Work through the plan with your tools, then write the answer.
    flags: [inject_tools]          # receives the agent's tools at run time
    max_iterations: 8
  verify:
    type: validate
    output_schema: my_agent.schemas:Verdict
    on_pass: __end__
    on_fail: reflect
    max_iterations: 3
    flags: [readonly, validate_output]
  reflect:
    type: reflect
    input_keys: [validation]
    flags: [observable, stateful]
edges:
  - from: plan
    to: act
  - from: act
    to: verify
  - from: reflect
    to: act
  - from: verify
    to: reflect
    condition: {kind: output, key: passes, value: false}

A node with flags: [inject_tools] (or inject_tools: true) gets the agent's tools when the graph runs, so the file doesn't need to name them. Hand-written files may also use is_entry: true / is_terminal: true.

docs.title: Edge Config Format
docs.text:
Field Type Required Description from str Yes Source node name to str Yes Target node name label str No Label for visualization priority int No Priority for condition checking (higher = checked first) condition mapping No {kind: tool_called}, {kind: no_tool_call}, {kind: error}, {kind: guard_failed}, {kind: output, key: ..., value: ...}, {kind: confidence, min_confidence: 0.7}, or {ref: "module:function"}

The built-in conditions are EdgeCondition objects (from promptise.engine import EdgeCondition), so graph.when("a", "b", condition=EdgeCondition("output", key="done", value=True)) saves too.

docs.title: Python Dict Format
docs.text:
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode
from promptise.engine.serialization import graph_from_config, graph_to_config

graph = PromptGraph("two-step", mode="static")
graph.add_node(PromptNode("draft", instructions="Draft the answer."))
graph.add_node(PromptNode("polish", instructions="Polish it.", default_next="__end__"))
graph.on_no_tool_call("draft", "polish")
graph.set_entry("draft")

config = graph_to_config(graph)                    # plain data, with "version": 2
print(config["edges"])   # [{'from': 'draft', 'to': 'polish', 'label': 'no_tools', 'condition': {'kind': 'no_tool_call'}}]
graph = graph_from_config(config, tools=[], refs=[])   # tools=agent.tools, refs=[...] as needed

node_to_config(node) and node_from_config(config, tools=..., refs=..., allow_imports=...) do the same for a single node.

docs.title: Node Type Registry
docs.text:
All built-in node types are registered:
