docs.title: Code Sandbox for Agents
docs.text:
Execute untrusted code safely in isolated Docker containers with resource limits and network controls.

from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.config import HTTPServerSpec

# Simple: enable sandbox with defaults
agent = await build_agent(
    servers={"tools": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8000/mcp")},
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    sandbox=True,
)

# Detailed: configure resource limits (the network stays off unless you set it)
agent = await build_agent(
    servers={"tools": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8000/mcp")},
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    sandbox={"memory_limit": "512M", "cpu_limit": 2},
)

Install

The sandbox needs the Docker Python client: pip install "promptise[sandbox]". Docker itself must be installed and running on the host.

No silent fallback

If the sandbox cannot be started (the docker package is missing, the Docker daemon is not running, gVisor is requested but runsc is not installed, or network="restricted" cannot be enforced), build_agent raises instead of building an agent without it. To run without a sandbox, leave sandbox unset (or pass None/False).

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The sandbox provides a secure execution environment for agent-generated code. When an agent creates or runs code (especially in Open Mode), the sandbox ensures that code runs inside an isolated container with:

  • Resource limits -- CPU, memory, process count, workspace size, and execution time
  • Network isolation -- no network by default; restricted (DNS and ports 80/443 to any host) or full when you ask for it, optionally on a Docker network of your own (for an egress proxy that allows only some hosts)
  • Filesystem isolation -- read-only root, size-capped writable workspace
  • A non-root user -- code runs as nobody (uid 65534) unless you set user="root"
  • Capability dropping -- ~40 Linux capabilities dropped, no-new-privileges always set
  • Syscall filtering -- Docker's default seccomp profile; optional gVisor kernel
  • Timeouts that stop the code -- a command that exceeds its timeout is killed

docs.title: SandboxConfig
docs.text:
SandboxConfig controls every aspect of the sandbox environment.

Field Type Default Description backend str "docker" Container backend: "docker", "gvisor" image str "python:3.11-slim" Base container image cpu_limit int 2 Maximum CPU cores (1-32) memory_limit str "4G" Maximum memory (e.g. "512M", "4G") disk_limit str "1G" Size of the writable workspace (a tmpfs at workdir; counts toward memory_limit). /tmp and /var/tmp are capped at the same size or less. pids_limit int 256 Maximum processes and threads (contains fork bombs) network NetworkMode NONE Network isolation mode docker_network str \| None None Name of an existing Docker network to attach the container to instead of Docker's default bridge. Needs network "full" or "restricted". See Allowing only some hosts. persistent bool False Keep the container after the session ends timeout int 300 Default per-command timeout in seconds (1-3600) workdir str "/workspace" Working directory inside container env dict[str, str] {} Additional environment variables (HOME defaults to workdir) allow_sudo bool False Keep CAP_SETUID/CAP_SETGID so sudo works in images that ship it user str "65534:65534" User the container and every command run as: "uid[:gid]" or a user name from the image. The default is nobody. Set "root" to run as root. runtime str \| None None Docker runtime (e.g., "runsc" for gVisor) read_only_rootfs bool True Read-only root filesystem

Unknown keys are rejected with a hint, so a misspelled option fails loudly instead of being ignored:

SandboxConfig.from_dict({"network_mode": "none"})
# ValidationError: Unknown sandbox option(s): 'network_mode': use 'network'
# ("none", "restricted" or "full"). Valid options: backend, image, ...

There is no option to pre-install tool ecosystems: use an image that already contains what the code needs (for example node:22-slim, or your own image built FROM python:3.11-slim with the packages baked in).

docs.title: NetworkMode
docs.text:
Mode Description NetworkMode.NONE No network interface besides loopback (default) NetworkMode.RESTRICTED Outbound DNS (port 53) to any host and TCP 80/443 to any host outside the link-local range; everything else dropped, IPv4 and IPv6 NetworkMode.FULL Full unrestricted network access

The network is "none" unless you set network explicitly, for sandbox=True, for a custom dict, and for agent_pattern="code-action".

"restricted" is enforced with iptables/ip6tables rules installed in the container before any sandboxed code runs. It fails closed: if the image does not ship iptables and ip6tables (the default python:3.11-slim does not), the container is removed and the session refuses to start. Use an image that includes them, or choose "none" or "full" explicitly.

"restricted" filters ports, not hosts. Exactly what it allows:

  • loopback;
  • DNS (UDP and TCP port 53) to any server, so DNS queries can carry data out;
  • TCP ports 80 and 443 to any host on the internet (example.com, pypi.org, an attacker's server alike), and to private addresses the container can route to;
  • nothing on the link-local ranges 169.254.0.0/16 and fe80::/10 and on fd00:ec2::254 (other than DNS), so code can't read cloud instance metadata and credentials from 169.254.169.254.

Everything else (other ports, UDP other than DNS, ICMP) is dropped. Use it to keep code off databases, SSH and other services on non-web ports, not to stop it from sending data to a web server.

docs.title: Allowing only some hosts
docs.text:
To let sandboxed code reach only some hosts (a package index, one API), put an egress proxy that allows those hosts between the sandbox and the internet, and attach the sandbox to a Docker network whose only way out is that proxy:

# A network with no route out, and a proxy on it and on the default bridge
docker network create --internal agent-egress
docker run -d --name egress-proxy --network bridge my-allowlist-proxy
docker network connect agent-egress egress-proxy

config = SandboxConfig(
    network="full",                 # no port filter; the network has no route out
    docker_network="agent-egress",  # created above
    env={"HTTPS_PROXY": "http://egress-proxy:3128", "HTTP_PROXY": "http://egress-proxy:3128"},
)

On an --internal network the container has no route to the internet, so code that ignores the proxy settings can't connect anywhere directly; the proxy decides which hosts a CONNECT may reach. The network must exist before the sandbox starts (the session refuses to start otherwise). docker_network also works with network="restricted", which adds the port filter on top (then the proxy must listen on port 80 or 443). The sandbox never joins the host's network or another container's: docker_network can't be "host", "none" or "container:…".

from promptise.sandbox.config import SandboxConfig, NetworkMode

config = SandboxConfig(
    backend="gvisor",
    cpu_limit=4,
    memory_limit="8G",
    pids_limit=512,
    network=NetworkMode.FULL,
    timeout=600,
)

docs.title: SandboxManager
docs.text: SandboxManager is responsible for creating and managing sandbox sessions. It normalizes configuration from bool, dict, or SandboxConfig and provides an async context manager for lifecycle management.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
SandboxManager(config: SandboxConfig | dict | bool)
  • SandboxConfig -- used directly.
  • dict -- converted to SandboxConfig via field mapping.
  • bool -- True creates a SandboxConfig with defaults; False disables sandboxing.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Return Type Description create_session() SandboxSession Create a new isolated sandbox session (container). cleanup_all() None Stop and remove all sessions created by this manager.

SandboxManager also supports use as an async context manager, which calls cleanup_all() on exit.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from promptise.sandbox import SandboxManager, SandboxConfig

config = SandboxConfig(image="python:3.11-slim", cpu_limit=2, memory_limit="4G")
async with SandboxManager(config) as manager:
    session = await manager.create_session()
    result = await session.execute("python -c 'print(42)'")
    print(result.stdout)  # "42\n"
    await manager.cleanup_all()

docs.title: SandboxSession
docs.text: SandboxSession manages a persistent sandbox session for command execution. It provides a high-level interface for running commands, reading/writing files, and installing packages.

docs.title: Creating a Session
docs.text:
Sessions are typically created by SandboxManager.create_session(). They support async context managers for automatic cleanup:

async with sandbox_session as session:
    result = await session.execute("python --version")
    print(result.stdout)
# Container is automatically cleaned up on exit

docs.title: Method Reference
docs.text:
Method Signature Description execute execute(command, timeout=None, workdir=None) -> CommandResult Run a shell command inside the container. read_file read_file(path) -> str Read a file from the sandbox filesystem. write_file write_file(path, content) Write a file into the writable workspace (or /tmp). Missing parent directories are created. list_files list_files(directory="/workspace") -> list[str] List files in a directory inside the sandbox. install_package install_package(package, tool="python") -> CommandResult Install a package using the specified ecosystem (python, node, rust, go). cleanup cleanup() Kill and remove the container (it is removed at once, so it gets no graceful-stop grace period). If persistent=True, the container keeps running for reuse.

SandboxSession also supports use as an async context manager, which calls cleanup() on exit.

docs.title: Full Example
docs.text:
async with session:
    # Execute a command
    result = await session.execute("python -c 'print(42)'", timeout=30)
    print(result.stdout)       # "42\n"
    print(result.exit_code)    # 0
    print(result.success)      # True

    # File operations
    await session.write_file("/workspace/script.py", "print('hello')")
    content = await session.read_file("/workspace/script.py")
    files = await session.list_files("/workspace")

    # Install a package
    await session.install_package("requests")

docs.title: Executing Commands
docs.text:
result = await session.execute("python script.py", timeout=30)

if result.success:
    print(result.stdout)
else:
    print(f"Failed (exit code {result.exit_code}): {result.stderr}")

When a command exceeds its timeout, every process it started is killed inside the container (children and background jobs included) and the result has timeout=True. If the processes cannot be killed individually (for example a fork bomb has used up pids_limit), the container is restarted, which also empties the workspace.

docs.title: File Operations
docs.text:
# Write a file into the sandbox (works with the read-only root filesystem)
await session.write_file("/workspace/script.py", "print('hello')")

# Read a file from the sandbox
content = await session.read_file("/workspace/script.py")

# List files in a directory
files = await session.list_files("/workspace")

docs.title: Installing Packages
docs.text:
# Python packages
result = await session.install_package("pandas", tool="python")

# Node.js packages
result = await session.install_package("lodash", tool="node")

# Supported ecosystems: "python", "node", "rust", "go"

Packages are installed into the writable workspace (HOME points at it, so pip falls back to a user install under /workspace/.local; npm installs into /workspace/node_modules). Downloading needs network access, which the default network="none" does not provide. For packages the code always needs, build a custom image with them pre-installed instead.

docs.title: CommandResult
docs.text:
Every command execution returns a CommandResult dataclass.

Field Type Description exit_code int Process exit code (0 = success) stdout str Standard output stderr str Standard error timeout bool Whether the command timed out duration float Execution time in seconds success bool Computed property: True if exit_code == 0 and not timed out 
result = await session.execute("python -c 'import sys; sys.exit(1)'")
assert not result.success
assert result.exit_code == 1

docs.title: SandboxBackend
docs.text: SandboxBackend is the abstract base class that defines how containers are managed. The framework ships with DockerBackend (which optionally supports gVisor via the runsc runtime).

docs.title: Abstract Methods
docs.text:
Method Description create_container() Create and start a new container from the configured image. execute_command() Execute a command inside a running container. read_file() Read a file from the container filesystem. write_file() Write a file into the container filesystem. stop_container() Stop a running container. remove_container() Remove a stopped container. health_check() Return whether the backend is available and functional.

kill_container() (not abstract) stops a container without a grace period; SandboxSession.cleanup() uses it before removing a non-persistent container. The default calls stop_container(); DockerBackend sends SIGKILL (the container's /bin/bash ignores SIGTERM, so a graceful docker stop always waited out its timeout).

ensure_available() (not abstract) raises with the actual reason the backend cannot run containers; SandboxManager.create_session() calls it, so a missing gVisor runtime is reported as such rather than as "Docker is not running".

docs.title: DockerBackend
docs.text:
DockerBackend is the default backend. It communicates with the Docker daemon to create isolated containers. When the runtime field in SandboxConfig is set to "runsc", Docker uses gVisor for additional kernel-level isolation.

from promptise.sandbox.config import SandboxConfig

# Standard Docker
config = SandboxConfig(backend="docker")

# Docker with gVisor runtime (equivalent to backend="gvisor")
config = SandboxConfig(backend="docker", runtime="runsc")

If runsc is not registered with Docker, create_session() raises RuntimeError: ... gVisor runtime 'runsc' is not registered with Docker (available runtimes: ...). The sandbox never falls back to the default runtime.

docs.title: Simple Boolean
docs.text:
agent = await build_agent(
    servers={"tools": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8000/mcp")},
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    sandbox=True,  # Uses SandboxConfig defaults
)

docs.title: Detailed Configuration
docs.text:
Pass a dict to customize sandbox settings:

agent = await build_agent(
    servers={"tools": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8000/mcp")},
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    sandbox={
        "image": "node:22-slim",  # an image with the tools the code needs
        "memory_limit": "512M",
        "cpu_limit": 2,
        "pids_limit": 128,
        "timeout": 120,
        # "network": "full",      # only if the code must reach the network
    },
)

When the sandbox is enabled, five tools are added to the agent: sandbox_exec, sandbox_read_file, sandbox_write_file, sandbox_list_files and sandbox_install_package. With trace_tools=True their calls are printed like any other tool call.

docs.title: Security Layers
docs.text:
What every sandbox container gets, and what it does not:

Layer What is applied Network No network interface besides loopback by default (network="none", see NetworkMode) Seccomp Docker's default seccomp profile, which blocks ~44 syscalls such as mount, reboot, kexec_load and kernel module loading. Promptise does not ship a custom profile. AppArmor Docker's docker-default profile on hosts with AppArmor enabled. Promptise does not load a custom profile. Capabilities ~40 capabilities dropped, including CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_PTRACE and CAP_SETUID/CAP_SETGID (kept only with allow_sudo=True). CAP_SYS_ADMIN is never re-added. User Code runs as nobody (user="65534:65534"), not as the image's default user (root in python:*-slim). The workspace is owned by (or writable for) that user. Root only with user="root". Privileges no-new-privileges always set; never a privileged container Filesystem Read-only root; writable size-capped tmpfs at workdir, /tmp and /var/tmp (/tmp and /var/tmp are noexec) Resources cpu_limit, memory_limit (swap disabled), pids_limit, disk_limit Time Per-command timeout; the command's processes are killed when it expires Kernel Optional gVisor (backend="gvisor") for a user-space kernel

The egress filter for network="restricted" and the kill of a timed-out command run as short privileged execs issued by the host-side backend; the sandboxed code itself never gains those privileges.

Upgrading from 1.5.0

Before 1.5.1 the sandbox did not set a user, so code ran as the image's default user, which is root in the default python:3.11-slim image. It now runs as nobody. The workspace (also HOME) and /tmp are writable, and pip install installs into the workspace as before. Code that writes outside them, or a custom image that expects a particular user, needs user= set: the image's user name, or user="root" for the old behaviour.

agent = await build_agent(..., sandbox={"user": "root"})  # 1.5.0 behaviour

docs.title: Open Mode Sandboxing
docs.text:
When using Open Mode, agent-created tools can be sandboxed automatically:

from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, ExecutionMode, OpenModeConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    execution_mode=ExecutionMode.OPEN,
    open_mode=OpenModeConfig(
        allow_tool_creation=True,
        sandbox_custom_tools=True,  # Agent-written code runs in sandbox
    ),
)

When sandbox_custom_tools=True, any Python tools the agent creates at runtime are executed inside the sandbox with restricted builtins, preventing access to the host filesystem, network, and system resources.

Docker required

The sandbox requires Docker to be installed and running on the host machine and the promptise[sandbox] extra. The gvisor backend requires additional setup (install runsc).

docs.title: Path-Scoped Skill Activation
docs.text:
Register reasoning-graph skills with glob patterns so they only activate when the agent is working in a matching directory. A TypeScript review skill stays hidden when the agent operates in a Python repo.

from promptise.engine import Skill, SkillRegistry
from promptise.engine.skills import code_reviewer

reg = SkillRegistry()
reg.register(
    Skill(
        name="ts-reviewer",
        description="Reviews TypeScript / React code.",
        paths=["**/*.tsx", "**/*.ts"],
        factory=lambda **kw: code_reviewer("ts_review", **kw),
    )
)

# Only activates when cwd contains .tsx or .ts files
active = reg.activate_for(cwd=".")

docs.title: Why path scoping?
docs.text: Modern agents have many skills (web research, code review, data analysis, summarization, etc.). Including all of them in every prompt wastes tokens and confuses the LLM. Path scoping is a cheap, declarative way to keep the active set small and contextual, no code changes needed when the agent moves between projects.

docs.title: Skill dataclass
docs.text:
@dataclass
class Skill:
    name: str                          # unique identifier
    description: str = ""              # shown to the agent
    paths: list[str] = []             # glob patterns, empty = always active
    factory: Callable[..., Any] = None # returns a node, tool, or any effect
    metadata: dict[str, Any] = {}     # extra frontmatter fields

matches_cwd(cwd) returns True if any file under cwd matches any of the globs: first Path(cwd).glob(pattern) (so **/*.ts searches subdirectories), then fnmatch on every path relative to cwd, where * also matches /, so *.ts finds src/app.ts too. The walk stops at the first match, but a tree with no match is walked in full. Before 1.7.0 the fnmatch pass stopped after the first entry, so *.ts in practice matched the top level only. Empty paths = always active (global skill). A cwd that is not a directory matches nothing.

create(**kwargs) calls factory(**kwargs) and returns what it returns; a skill without a factory raises ValueError.

docs.title: SkillRegistry
docs.text:
Method Returns Description register(skill) None Add a skill; a name that is already registered raises ValueError unregister(name) bool Remove by name; False when it was not registered get(name) Skill \| None Look up by name all() list[Skill] Every registered skill, in registration order activate_for(cwd=".") list[Skill] The skills whose paths match under cwd (or are empty) names_active_for(cwd=".") list[str] Their names, sorted load_directory(directory) int Load skill files (below); returns how many were registered len(reg), "name" in reg Count and membership

The registry holds no execution state, so one instance can be shared by several agents.

docs.title: File-based loading with frontmatter
docs.text:
Write a .py file that starts with a YAML-ish docstring header and defines a create() function. The header must be the first thing in the file: a comment, an import or from __future__ above it means the file is not read as a skill.

skills/ts_review.py
"""
name: ts-reviewer
description: Reviews TypeScript / React code.
paths:
  - src/**/*.tsx
  - src/**/*.ts
"""

def create(**kwargs):
    from promptise.engine.skills import code_reviewer
    return code_reviewer("ts_review", **kwargs)

Load an entire directory:

from pathlib import Path

from promptise.engine import SkillRegistry

skills_dir = Path("skills")
skills_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(skills_dir / "ts_review.py").write_text('''"""
name: ts-reviewer
description: Reviews TypeScript / React code.
paths:
  - src/**/*.tsx
  - src/**/*.ts
"""


def create(**kwargs):
    from promptise.engine.skills import code_reviewer
    return code_reviewer("ts_review", **kwargs)
''')

reg = SkillRegistry()
loaded = reg.load_directory(skills_dir)
print(f"Loaded {loaded} skills")                 # Loaded 1 skills
print(reg.names_active_for(cwd="."))             # [] until the cwd has src/**/*.ts files

How load_directory() treats files:

  • Only *.py files directly in the directory (no subdirectories), in name order. A missing directory raises FileNotFoundError.
  • A file without a recognizable header is skipped silently (it is not a skill file).
  • The file is imported to get create, so its code runs: load only directories you trust. A file that fails to import or has no callable create is logged and skipped; so is a name that is already registered.
  • name defaults to the file name without .py; a single paths string becomes a one-item list.

The frontmatter parser is built in, so no YAML library is needed. It recognizes name, description, paths (as a list), and passes any extra keys through as metadata. Scalars are converted: true/yes/on, false/no/off, null, integers and floats; quotes around a value are removed. Lines starting with # are ignored, and an empty line ends a list.

The same parser is public as parse_frontmatter(source). It reads the first triple-quoted docstring of a Python source string and returns its key: value lines (and - item lists under a key) as a dict, or None when there is no docstring or no recognizable key:

from promptise.engine import parse_frontmatter

source = '''"""
name: ts-reviewer
description: Reviews TypeScript / React code.
paths:
  - src/**/*.tsx
  - src/**/*.ts
"""
'''
print(parse_frontmatter(source))
# {'name': 'ts-reviewer', 'description': 'Reviews TypeScript / React code.',
#  'paths': ['src/**/*.tsx', 'src/**/*.ts']}
print(parse_frontmatter("# a comment first\n" + source))   # None

docs.title: Using with PromptGraph
docs.text:
from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, Skill, SkillRegistry
from promptise.engine.skills import summarizer

reg = SkillRegistry()
reg.register(Skill(name="summary", description="Summarize findings.",
                   factory=lambda **kw: summarizer("summarize", **kw)))   # no paths: always active

graph = PromptGraph("assistant")
for skill in reg.activate_for(cwd="."):
    graph.add_node(skill.create())
print(list(graph.nodes))   # ['summarize']

activate_for() checks the file system on every call, so call it when the working directory changes (each run, or each project the agent switches to), not once at startup.

docs.title: Streaming with Tool Visibility
docs.text:
Stream agent execution with real-time tool activity: see which tools are being called, their results, and the LLM generating text token by token.

async for event in agent.astream_with_tools(
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Check my order status"}]},
    caller=CallerContext(user_id="user-42"),
):
    match event.type:
        case "tool_start":
            print(f"🔧 {event.tool_display_name}...")
        case "tool_end":
            print(f"   → {event.tool_summary}")
        case "token":
            print(event.text, end="", flush=True)
        case "done":
            print(f"\n✅ Done in {event.duration_ms:.0f}ms")

Output: 

🔧 Searching orders...
   → Found: Order #4521, shipped March 20
🔧 Getting tracking info...
   → Status: In transit, ETA March 25
Your order #4521 shipped on March 20 and is currently in transit.
Expected delivery: March 25.
✅ Done in 2340ms

docs.title: Event Types
docs.text:
Type Class When Key Fields tool_start ToolStartEvent Tool begins executing tool_name, tool_display_name, arguments, tool_index tool_end ToolEndEvent Tool finishes tool_name, tool_summary, duration_ms, success, tool_index, reused token TokenEvent LLM generates a token text, cumulative_text done DoneEvent Agent finished full_response, tool_calls, duration_ms, cache_hit error ErrorEvent Something went wrong message, recoverable

done and error are always the last event of a run.

Every class derives from StreamEvent (from promptise import StreamEvent), which carries type and timestamp; event.to_dict() gives a JSON-ready dict, for example to send over Server-Sent Events.

docs.title: What a Streamed Run Does
docs.text:
A streamed run executes exactly the steps ainvoke() would: the stream is a view of that run, not a second one:

  • One model call per step. Each step's model call is streamed as it is generated. A question answered without tools is one model call; with a tool it is two (the call that asks for the tool, and the answer).
  • The answer after a tool streams too. Its tokens arrive after the tool_end events, and full_response is that answer.
  • full_response is the final answer: the text of the run's last model call, the same text ainvoke() returns as the last message. Text a model writes before calling a tool ("Let me look that up.") streams as tokens and is in cumulative_text, but not in full_response.
  • Tool calls run in parallel, as in ainvoke(). When the model asks for several tools at once, every tool_start comes first, then each tool_end as that call finishes: possibly out of order. In a custom graph whose calls a ToolNode runs, the calls of one turn run one after another, so each tool_end comes before the next call's tool_start.
  • Every node's tool calls stream. Calls a ToolNode runs stream exactly like the ReAct agent's (PromptNode) calls, with the same fields, including calls it answers from an earlier result and calls a pre_tool hook blocked or that validate_inputs rejected (both success: false).
  • tool_index and duration_ms belong to the call. A tool_end has the same tool_index as its tool_start, and duration_ms is how long that call ran.
  • Failed calls are success: false. A tool that reports an error: an MCP server's ToolError, which the server returns with isError set: ends with success: false and the error's message as tool_summary. A tool that raises ends with success: false and tool_summary "Tool call failed" (the exception text is not streamed). The model sees the error either way and answers from it.
  • Reused results are reused: true. Only for tools you opted in with ContextCompaction(reuse_results=...), and for a repeat of an identical call in one model turn of a ToolNode(deduplicate=True): a repeated call answered from the earlier result of the same call, without running the tool, still streams its tool_start and tool_end, and the tool_end has reused: true.

examples/mcp/stream_tool_calls.py shows both against a real model:

>>> Where are my orders A-1001 and A-1002?
  1.5s  tool_start #0 Getting order status {'order_id': 'A-1001'}
  1.5s  tool_start #1 Getting order status {'order_id': 'A-1002'}
  2.5s  tool_end   #0 ok in 1006 ms: order_id: A-1001, status: shipped, carrier: DHL (+1 more)
  2.5s  tool_end   #1 ok in 1006 ms: order_id: A-1002, status: processing, carrier: None (+1 more)
  6.2s  answer streaming: Here's the current status: ...
  6.8s  done (308 characters in full_response)

>>> Where is my order Z-9999?
  1.3s  tool_start #0 Getting order status {'order_id': 'Z-9999'}
  2.3s  tool_end   #0 FAILED in 1006 ms: No order found with ID Z-9999.
  4.9s  answer streaming: I couldn't find an order with ID Z-9999 ...
  5.9s  done (816 characters in full_response)

docs.title: Server-Sent Events (FastAPI + EventSource)
docs.text:
The browser's EventSource only sends GET requests, so the endpoint is a GET that takes the question as a query parameter:

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

from promptise import CallerContext

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/chat")
async def chat(q: str, user=Depends(current_user)):
    # current_user is your auth dependency. EventSource sends the page's
    # cookies but cannot set headers, so authenticate with the session cookie.
    async def event_stream():
        async for event in agent.astream_with_tools(
            {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": q}]},
            caller=CallerContext(user_id=user.id),
        ):
            yield f"data: {event.to_json()}\n\n"

    return StreamingResponse(
        event_stream(),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache", "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"},
    )

docs.title: Frontend (JavaScript)
docs.text:
const source = new EventSource(`/chat?q=${encodeURIComponent(question)}`);

source.onmessage = (e) => {
  const event = JSON.parse(e.data);
  switch (event.type) {
    case "tool_start":
      showToolIndicator(event.tool_index, event.tool_display_name);
      break;
    case "tool_end":
      updateToolResult(event.tool_index, event.tool_summary, event.success);
      break;
    case "token":
      appendText(event.text);
      break;
    case "done":
      source.close();  // the run is over: stop EventSource from reconnecting
      finishResponse(event.full_response);
      break;
    case "error":
      source.close();
      showError(event.message);
      break;
  }
};

source.onerror = () => {
  // A dropped connection: don't let EventSource silently re-ask the question.
  source.close();
  showError("Connection lost.");
};

Always close the EventSource on done and error

When the server ends the response, EventSource treats it as a dropped connection and reconnects about 3 seconds later: the same GET, so the agent runs the question again (more model calls, more tool calls) and the page receives a second answer. Call source.close() when the done or error event arrives, and in onerror.

Use the event's tool_index to match a tool_end to its tool_start: parallel calls can finish in any order.

docs.title: POST with fetch()
docs.text:
To send the question in a request body (long prompts, or a bearer token in a header), use a POST endpoint: the same handler with @app.post and a request model, and read the stream with fetch() instead of EventSource. A fetch stream does not reconnect on its own:

const response = await fetch("/chat", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  body: JSON.stringify({ message: question }),
});
const reader = response.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader();
let buffer = "";
for (;;) {
  const { value, done } = await reader.read();
  if (done) break;
  buffer += value;
  const frames = buffer.split("\n\n");
  buffer = frames.pop();  // keep an incomplete frame for the next chunk
  for (const frame of frames) {
    if (frame.startsWith("data: ")) handleEvent(JSON.parse(frame.slice(6)));
  }
}

docs.title: Tool Display Names
docs.text:
Tool names are automatically converted to human-readable strings:

Raw Name Display Name search_customers Searching customers get_order_status Getting order status hr_list_employees Listing employees create_ticket Creating ticket deploy_service Deploying service

Override with custom names:

async for event in agent.astream_with_tools(
    input,
    tool_display_names={
        "pg_query": "Querying database",
        "s3_upload": "Uploading to cloud storage",
    },
):
    print(event)

docs.title: Tool Result Summaries
docs.text:
Tool results are automatically summarized for display:

  • JSON dicts: "name: Alice, status: active (+3 more)"
  • JSON lists: "Found 5 result(s)"
  • Plain text: truncated to 120 characters
  • Failed calls: the error message ("No order found with ID Z-9999."), or "Tool call failed" when the tool raised

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description input dict required Agent input (same as ainvoke) caller CallerContext None Per-request identity include_arguments bool True Include tool arguments in events tool_display_names dict[str, str] None Custom display name overrides

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Argument redaction: Tool arguments are run through guardrails before streaming. PII and credentials are replaced with labels.
  • Error sanitization: ErrorEvent.message is always generic: no internal stack traces, file paths, or database URLs.
  • Stream cancellation: Closing the SSE connection cancels the agent's async task. No wasted LLM calls.
  • No cumulative arguments: TokenEvent.cumulative_text only contains LLM text, never tool arguments.

docs.title: Integration
docs.text:
astream_with_tools() runs the full agent pipeline: same guarantees as ainvoke():

  • ✅ Input guardrails (block injection → ErrorEvent)
  • ✅ Memory injection (relevant context before LLM call)
  • ✅ Output guardrails (PII redaction on full_response; tokens are streamed as the model generates them, before the check)
  • ✅ Observability (callback handler records timeline)
  • ✅ Event notifications (invocation.start/complete emitted)
  • ✅ CallerContext propagation (multi-user safe; the ambient caller is inherited when none is passed)
  • ✅ Adaptive strategy (failed tool calls are recorded, learned lessons injected)

docs.title: tool_display_name()
docs.text:
Convert raw MCP tool names to human-readable labels:

from promptise.streaming import tool_display_name

tool_display_name("search_customers")      # "Searching customers"
tool_display_name("get_order_status")      # "Getting order status"
tool_display_name("deploy_production")     # "Deploying production"
Parameter Type Description tool_name str Raw tool name (e.g. "search_customers") overrides dict[str, str] \| None Custom name mappings (tool_name → display text) Returns str Human-readable display name

docs.title: tool_summary()
docs.text:
Summarize tool output for the stream:

from promptise.streaming import tool_summary

tool_summary('{"results": [...100 items...]}')  # '{"results": [...100 items...]}'[:120]
tool_summary(None)                               # "Done"
tool_summary("")                                 # "Done"
Parameter Type Description result str \| None Raw tool output max_length int Truncation limit (default: 120) Returns str Summarized output

docs.title: tool_error_summary()
docs.text:
Summarize a failed tool call: the message of an MCP ToolError:

from promptise.streaming import tool_error_summary

tool_error_summary('{"error": {"code": "TOOL_ERROR", "message": "No order A-9."}}')  # "No order A-9."
tool_error_summary("Error: Unknown tool 'x'")                                      # "Error: Unknown tool 'x'"

docs.title: Event Serialization
docs.text:
All stream events support serialization:

event.to_dict()  # Returns dict
event.to_json()  # Returns JSON string (for SSE)

docs.title: Streaming the Conversation: astream()
docs.text:
agent.astream() streams at a coarser grain: one chunk per step of the agent's graph, each the whole conversation so far: {"messages": [...]}. The last chunk is what ainvoke() returns. Use it to process intermediate messages (tool calls and their results) in code; use astream_with_tools() for a chat UI.

async for chunk in agent.astream({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]}):
    last = chunk["messages"][-1]
    print(type(last).__name__, last.content[:60])
# ToolMessage {"order_id": "A-1001", "status": "shipped", ...}   step 1: tool call + result
# AIMessage Your order A-1001 has shipped with DHL ...           step 2: the answer

docs.title: Testing Agents
docs.text:
An agent's behavior depends on what the model answers, and a real model costs money, needs an API key and answers differently from run to run. promptise.testing.ScriptedModel takes the model's place: you write its replies in advance, the agent runs exactly as it would with a provider (tools are bound and called, results go back to the model, streaming works), and the model records every request it received so you can assert on it.

Nothing leaves the process, so these tests run in CI without secrets, and you don't import LangChain to write them.

Source: src/promptise/testing.py

docs.title: A first test
docs.text:
Script one tool call and the final answer, run the agent, and check both the answer and what the model was sent:

import asyncio
import json

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall

ORDERS = {"A-1001": {"order_id": "A-1001", "status": "shipped"}}


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID.

    Args:
        order_id: The order ID, for example "A-1001".
    """
    return ORDERS[order_id]


async def ask(model: ScriptedModel, question: str) -> str:
    agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order])
    try:
        result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}]})
    finally:
        await agent.shutdown()
    return result["messages"][-1].content


def test_agent_looks_up_the_order():
    model = ScriptedModel([
        ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),
        "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
    ])

    answer = asyncio.run(ask(model, "Where is order A-1001?"))

    assert answer == "Order A-1001 has shipped."
    # The model was called twice, with the get_order tool bound both times.
    assert [call.tools for call in model.calls] == [["get_order"], ["get_order"]]
    # The second call carried the tool's result.
    assert model.calls[1].messages[-1].content == json.dumps(ORDERS["A-1001"])

Run it with pytest. The test wraps the agent in asyncio.run(), so it needs no plugin; with pytest-asyncio you can write async def tests and await the agent directly.

Each model call takes the next reply. The first reply asks for get_order, the agent runs the real tool, and the second reply is the answer. The tool itself is not mocked: only the model is scripted.

docs.title: Replies
docs.text:
A reply is one model turn. It can be:

Reply The model's turn "text" Text with no tool calls: the agent's answer ToolCall(name, args) One tool call [ToolCall(...), ToolCall(...)] Several tool calls in one turn (the agent runs them in parallel); a string in the list is the turn's text Malformed.tool_call_as_text(...) A tool call written into the text instead of sent as one Malformed.unparseable_arguments(...) A tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON an AIMessage That LangChain message, as it is

ToolCall(name, args, id=None) takes the tool's name and arguments. Leave id out and the model numbers its calls call_1, call_2, ... in the order it sends them, so the ids in a test are always the same.

A reply that isn't one of these raises TypeError when the model is created, so a typo in a script fails at once rather than in the middle of a run.

docs.title: Assert on what the model received
docs.text:
model.calls holds a ModelCall for every request, in order:

Attribute What it holds messages The messages the model was sent (system prompt, conversation, tool results) tools The names of the tools bound for that call tool_schemas Those tools as the model was offered them (OpenAI-style function definitions) reply The message the model answered with (None when it had no reply left)

model.remaining is the number of replies not yet sent. Checking it at the end of a test shows that the agent made as many model calls as you expected:

import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel([ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}), "Shipped."])
    agent = await build_agent(
        model=model,
        instructions="You answer questions about orders.",
        extra_tools=[get_order],
    )
    await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]})
    await agent.shutdown()

    first = model.calls[0]
    print(first.messages[0].type, "|", first.messages[0].content[:33])
    print(first.messages[-1].type, "|", first.messages[-1].content)
    print(first.tool_schemas[0]["function"]["parameters"]["required"])
    print(model.calls[1].messages[-1].type, model.calls[1].messages[-1].tool_call_id)
    print("replies left:", model.remaining)


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

system | You answer questions about orders
human | Where is A-1001?
['order_id']
tool call_1
replies left: 0

The messages are LangChain message objects: .type is "system", "human", "ai" or "tool", and .content is the text. A tool result also has .tool_call_id and .status ("success" or "error").

docs.title: Test failure handling
docs.text: Small and local models get tool calling wrong more often than large hosted ones: they invent tool names, send arguments that don't match the schema or aren't JSON, or write the tool call into their text. Scripting these replies tests what your agent does when it happens, without waiting for a model to make the mistake.

docs.title: A tool name the agent doesn't have
docs.text:
Script a ToolCall with a name the agent has no tool for. The agent doesn't fail: the model gets an error result that names the tools it can call, and its next turn can use the right one.

import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


@tool
def refund_order(order_id: str, amount: float) -> str:
    """Refund part of an order."""
    return f"Refunded {amount:.2f} EUR on {order_id}."


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel([
        ToolCall("get_order_status", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),  # invented name
        ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),         # the model corrects it
        "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
    ])
    agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order, refund_order])
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]})
    await agent.shutdown()

    error = model.calls[1].messages[-1]
    print(error.status, "|", error.content)
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

error | Error: Unknown tool 'get_order_status'. Call one of the available tools: get_order, refund_order.
Order A-1001 has shipped.

The error lists the agent's tools with the names closest to the one called first, at most 20 of them, followed by how many more there are. When the name looks like a misspelling of a tool's name (get_ordr, getOrder), the error also asks "Did you mean 'get_order'?". A name that only shares a word with a tool, such as cancel_order, gets no suggestion, so the model isn't pointed at a tool that does something else.

docs.title: Invalid arguments
docs.text:
Arguments that don't match the tool's schema are a ToolCall too. A @tool function checks its arguments before it runs, and the model gets the problems to correct:

import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel([
        ToolCall("get_order", {"id": "A-1001"}),        # wrong argument name
        ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),
        "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
    ])
    agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order])
    await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]})
    await agent.shutdown()

    print(model.calls[1].messages[-1].content)


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

Invalid arguments for tool 'get_order':
- order_id: Field required
Correct the arguments and call the tool again.

docs.title: A tool call written as text
docs.text:
Some models answer with the tool call as JSON in their text instead of as a tool call. Malformed.tool_call_as_text(name, args) sends that reply, in one of three styles:

style Text of the reply "json" (default) {"name": "get_order", "arguments": {"order_id": "A-1001"}} "tagged" The same object inside <tool_call> and </tool_call> lines "fenced" The same object in a Markdown json code block

The reply has no tool call, so the agent takes the text as the answer and no tool runs. A test can check that your code catches such an answer, for example a check that rejects answers that look like JSON:

import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import Malformed, ScriptedModel


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


def looks_like_a_tool_call(answer: str) -> bool:
    text = answer.strip().strip("`").removeprefix("json").strip()
    return text.startswith(("{", "<tool_call>")) and '"name"' in text


async def main():
    for style in ("json", "tagged", "fenced"):
        model = ScriptedModel([
            Malformed.tool_call_as_text("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}, style=style),
        ])
        agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order])
        result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]})
        await agent.shutdown()
        answer = result["messages"][-1].content
        print(style, looks_like_a_tool_call(answer))


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

json True
tagged True
fenced True

docs.title: Arguments that aren't JSON
docs.text:
Malformed.unparseable_arguments(name, raw_args) sends a tool call whose argument text can't be parsed, such as a Python-style dict with single quotes (the default). LangChain keeps such a call in the message's invalid_tool_calls, not its tool_calls, as it does for a provider's reply. The agent doesn't run a call it can't read. It answers the call with a tool error (status="error", the call's own tool_call_id) that says what is wrong and names the tool's parameters, and the loop goes on, so the model can call the tool again:

import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import Malformed, ScriptedModel, ToolCall


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel([
        Malformed.unparseable_arguments("get_order", "{'order_id': 'A-1001'}"),
        ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),  # the model calls again
        "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
    ])
    agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order])
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]})
    await agent.shutdown()

    error = model.calls[1].messages[-1]
    print(error.status, error.tool_call_id)
    print(error.content)
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

error call_1
Error: The arguments for 'get_order' were not valid JSON (Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes at line 1 column 2). Call the tool again with a JSON object that matches its parameters: order_id (required).
Order A-1001 has shipped.

Such a call counts as a failed tool call: NodeResult.tool_calls records it with success: False, invalid: True and the text the model sent under raw_args, callbacks get its start and an on_tool_error (ToolArgumentError), and astream_with_tools() yields a ToolEndEvent with success=False. Each retry is a model call, so max_agent_iterations still ends a model that never sends valid arguments. A call that names a tool the agent doesn't have gets the unknown-tool error instead.

When this reply is streamed, LangChain reads the arguments as a partial JSON object, as it does for a provider's stream: a cut-off object such as '{"order_id"' becomes a tool call with the arguments read so far ({}), while text that can't start a JSON object stays an invalid call and gets the same error. A streamed run (astream_with_tools()) recovers the same way.

docs.title: When the replies run out
docs.text:
A model call after the last reply raises ScriptExhaustedError, which says which call it was and how many replies the script has. In an agent run it fails the run: ainvoke() raises GraphExecutionError, whose __cause__ is the ScriptExhaustedError. An agent that makes more model calls than you scripted is usually the bug a test is looking for, so this is the default.

import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.engine import GraphExecutionError
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ScriptExhaustedError


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel(["Hello!"])
    agent = await build_agent(model=model)
    ask = {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hi"}]}
    await agent.ainvoke(ask)
    try:
        await agent.ainvoke(ask)
    except GraphExecutionError as exc:
        assert isinstance(exc.__cause__, ScriptExhaustedError)
        print(exc.__cause__)
    finally:
        await agent.shutdown()


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

ScriptedModel has no reply for model call 2: the script has 1 reply. Add a reply, or pass on_exhausted='repeat_last' to repeat the last one.

The call is still recorded in model.calls, with reply=None, so you can see what the agent asked for.

ScriptedModel(replies, on_exhausted="repeat_last") answers every call after the last reply with the last reply again, for a test that calls the agent many times with the same answer. A script with no replies raises either way.

docs.title: Streaming and sync calls
docs.text:
The model streams too. Its text comes word by word and each tool call as one chunk, so astream_with_tools() and astream() emit the same events as with a provider:

import asyncio

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall


@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel([
        ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),
        "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
    ])
    agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order])
    async for event in agent.astream_with_tools(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]}
    ):
        if event.type == "token":
            print(f"token {event.text!r}")
        else:
            print(event.type)
    await agent.shutdown()


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

tool_start
tool_end
token 'Order '
token 'A-1001 '
token 'has '
token 'shipped.'
done

model.invoke() and model.stream() work as well, for code that calls a chat model synchronously:

from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel

model = ScriptedModel(["Bonjour", "Hello there"])
print(model.invoke("Say hello in French").content)
print([chunk.content for chunk in model.stream("Now in English") if chunk.content])

Output:

Bonjour
['Hello ', 'there']

docs.title: Where to use it
docs.text:
ScriptedModel is a LangChain chat model, so it goes wherever a model instance is accepted: build_agent(model=...), every agent pattern (agent_pattern="react", "peoatr", your own PromptGraph), a FallbackChain and a graph node's model. Tools are bound with bind_tools() as for a provider model, and calls records the tools of each call.

Things to know:

  • The replies don't depend on the input. A script fixes the order of the model's turns, not what it reads. Assert on model.calls to check what the agent sent; to make a reply depend on the conversation, script an AIMessage you build in the test, or subclass the model.
  • There is no token usage. Replies carry no usage data, so budgets and cost reports see zero tokens.
  • An AgentProcess runs on it too. Pass it as the process's model, ProcessConfig(model=ScriptedModel([...])) or AgentProcess(name, config, model=...), and inject a TriggerEvent: the process runs the agent on the script without a provider (The agent's model).
  • Concurrent runs share the script. Each call takes the next reply whichever run makes it, so give each concurrent run its own model.

docs.title: API summary
docs.text:
Name What it is ScriptedModel(replies, *, on_exhausted="raise") The chat model; calls, remaining ToolCall(name, args={}, id=None) A tool call in a reply Malformed.tool_call_as_text(name, args=None, *, style="json") A tool call written as text Malformed.unparseable_arguments(name, raw_args="{'arg': 'value'}", *, id=None) A tool call whose arguments are not JSON ModelCall One recorded request: messages, tools, tool_schemas, reply ScriptExhaustedError Raised by a call after the last reply (a RuntimeError)

All of them are imported from promptise.testing.

docs.title: Tool Optimization
docs.text:
Reduce the token cost of MCP tool definitions sent to the LLM with every invocation.

from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.config import HTTPServerSpec

agent = await build_agent(
    servers={"tools": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8000/mcp")},
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    optimize_tools=True,  # "minimal": shorter tool definitions, same tools
)

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: When an agent connects to MCP servers, every tool's full name, description, and JSON Schema is sent to the LLM on every invocation via function-calling. With 20-50+ tools, this costs 5,000-15,000+ tokens per call: just for tool definitions. This is the single largest token cost after the conversation itself.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Tool optimization operates at two layers:

Layer 1: Static optimization (applied once at build time), reduces the per-tool token cost without changing which tools are available:

  • Schema minification: strips description metadata from Pydantic Field schemas. The LLM still sees field names, types, and required status, but not verbose per-field descriptions.
  • Description truncation: caps tool-level descriptions at N characters, ending on a whole sentence when that keeps most of the budget, otherwise at a word boundary with a single ....
  • Depth flattening: replaces deeply nested objects with dict beyond a configurable depth.

Layer 2: Semantic tool selection (applied before every model call), the biggest optimization. Instead of sending all 50 tools, only the most relevant ones are offered:

  1. At build time, every tool's name and description is embedded with a small local model.
  2. Before each model call (not just once per ainvoke()), a query is built from the recent conversation: the latest user message, the assistant reply it answers, the tool calls of the previous and current turn, and earlier user turns, and compared against the tool embeddings. A follow-up like "Yes, go ahead." therefore keeps the tools of the request it confirms, and the selection follows the agent as it calls tools.
  3. The model is offered the semantic_top_k most relevant tools, plus every tool in preserve_tools, tools already called in the previous or current turn, and the request_more_tools fallback.
  4. If the right tool is missing, the model calls request_more_tools; the tools it returns are offered from the next model call on.

docs.title: One-liner
docs.text:
agent = await build_agent(
    servers=servers, model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    optimize_tools=True,  # Uses "minimal" preset
)

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Static optimization (True, "minimal", "standard") needs nothing extra. Semantic selection embeds tools with sentence-transformers:

pip install "promptise[tool-optimization]"   # also included in promptise[all]

Without it, build_agent(optimize_tools="semantic") raises an ImportError that names this extra, before connecting to any server.

docs.title: Preset levels
docs.text:
# Static optimization only: safe, no behavioral change
agent = await build_agent(servers=servers, model="openai:gpt-5-mini", optimize_tools="minimal")

# Deeper minification + nested description stripping
agent = await build_agent(servers=servers, model="openai:gpt-5-mini", optimize_tools="standard")

# Full semantic selection: biggest savings, per-invocation tool filtering
agent = await build_agent(servers=servers, model="openai:gpt-5-mini", optimize_tools="semantic")

docs.title: Fine-grained control
docs.text:
from promptise import ToolOptimizationConfig, OptimizationLevel

agent = await build_agent(
    servers=servers,
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    optimize_tools=ToolOptimizationConfig(
        level=OptimizationLevel.SEMANTIC,
        max_description_length=100,
        semantic_top_k=5,
        preserve_tools={"critical_payment_tool", "auth_tool"},
    ),
)

docs.title: Three Preset Levels
docs.text:
Setting minimal standard semantic Schema minification Yes Yes Yes Max description length 200 chars 150 chars 100 chars Strip nested descriptions No Yes Yes Max schema depth No limit 3 2 Semantic selection No No Yes Semantic top-K - - 8 Fallback tool - - Yes Measured savings (see below) 14% 14% 90%

The savings are tool-definition tokens per model call, measured on one server: 90 tools with flat schemas (string parameters with one-line descriptions, tool descriptions under 200 characters). Static optimization saves what your schemas spend on parameter descriptions, long tool descriptions and nesting, so expect more on verbose or deeply nested schemas and less on terse ones; standard only pulls ahead of minimal when schemas are nested. Semantic selection's saving grows with the number of tools, since the model sees about semantic_top_k of them whatever the total. Measure your own payload with observability before relying on a number.

docs.title: ToolOptimizationConfig
docs.text: Field Type Default Description level OptimizationLevel \| None None Preset level. Any explicit field overrides the preset. minify_schema bool \| None from preset Strip description from Pydantic Field metadata max_description_length int \| None from preset Truncate tool descriptions at N chars strip_nested_descriptions bool \| None from preset Remove descriptions from nested model fields max_schema_depth int \| None from preset Flatten nested objects beyond this depth to dict semantic_selection bool \| None from preset Select tools semantically before every model call (needs promptise[tool-optimization]) semantic_top_k int \| None from preset (8) Most-relevant tools offered per model call; preserved, recently called and unlocked tools and the fallback come on top semantic_context_turns int \| None from preset (3) Recent user turns that make up the selection query always_include_fallback bool \| None from preset Include the request_more_tools fallback embedding_model str \| None "all-MiniLM-L6-v2" Model name or local path for sentence-transformers preserve_tools set[str] \| None None Tool names that are never optimized and always offered

docs.title: OptimizationLevel
docs.text: Level Value OptimizationLevel.MINIMAL "minimal" OptimizationLevel.STANDARD "standard" OptimizationLevel.SEMANTIC "semantic"

docs.title: Embedding model
docs.text: Semantic selection embeds tool descriptions using sentence-transformers. The default model is all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384 dimensions, no API key needed). On first use it downloads from HuggingFace Hub and caches locally at ~/.cache/huggingface/. After that, it runs fully offline.

docs.title: Local / air-gapped deployments
docs.text:
For enterprises that cannot access external networks, download the model files once and point to a local directory:

# Download the model on a machine with internet
python -c "from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer; SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2').save('/models/all-MiniLM-L6-v2')"

# Use the local model: zero network calls
agent = await build_agent(
    servers=servers,
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    optimize_tools=ToolOptimizationConfig(
        level=OptimizationLevel.SEMANTIC,
        embedding_model="/models/all-MiniLM-L6-v2",
    ),
)

You can also use any other sentence-transformers-compatible model:

optimize_tools=ToolOptimizationConfig(
    level=OptimizationLevel.SEMANTIC,
    embedding_model="BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5",  # or any local path
)

docs.title: The request_more_tools fallback
docs.text:
When semantic selection is active, every model call is also offered a fallback tool (turn it off with always_include_fallback=False):

Tool: request_more_tools(query?: str, tool_names?: list[str])
"Call this when none of your current tools can do what is needed. Describe the
 capability in `query` (or give exact `tool_names`); the matching tools are
 returned and you can call them on your next step. Without arguments it returns
 the next few tools most relevant to the conversation; call it again for more."
  • query searches the index and returns the semantic_top_k best matches.
  • tool_names returns exactly those tools (unknown names are reported), at most 32 per call; the reply says how many were left out.
  • No arguments returns the next semantic_top_k tools most relevant to the conversation that the model was not offered yet. Each further argument-less call pages on to the next semantic_top_k. It never enables the whole catalogue: on a server with hundreds of tools that would break the next model call (OpenAI accepts at most 128 tools per request).

One call returns at most 32 tools, and a model call is offered at most 100 of the indexed tools (preserve_tools first, then tools already called, then tools request_more_tools returned, then the most relevant ones). Tools the index doesn't manage, such as the fallback itself, come on top, so a request stays under OpenAI's 128-tool limit.

Every tool the call returns is offered on the agent's next model call, and stays offered for the rest of that turn and the next one. Nothing is stored on the agent: the selection is recomputed from the request_more_tools call in the conversation, so concurrent requests never see each other's tools.

A tool call the model makes for a tool that exists but wasn't offered on that step still runs: selection decides what the model is shown, it is not access control. Use approval or server-side guards to restrict what may run.

docs.title: preserve_tools
docs.text:
Tools listed in preserve_tools are:

  1. Never optimized: the full tool description and every parameter description are kept
  2. Offered on every model call by semantic selection, on top of the semantic_top_k relevant tools

Use this for critical tools that the agent must always have access to:

optimize_tools=ToolOptimizationConfig(
    level=OptimizationLevel.SEMANTIC,
    preserve_tools={"process_payment", "verify_identity"},
)

docs.title: The tool summary in the system prompt
docs.text:
The model always receives each offered tool as a tool definition (name, description and parameter schema), which is what the savings above measure. Promptise can also list the tools in the system prompt, in an "Available tools" block. It repeats the definitions, so it is off by default since 1.3.4 (before that, every node with tools added the "full" block):

agent = await build_agent(
    servers=servers,
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    tool_summary="names",   # "off" (default), "names" or "full"
)
tool_summary What the system prompt gets Tokens on the 40-tool test server "off" (default) Nothing 0 "names" Available tools: hr_list_employees, hr_get_employee, ... 178 "full" One line per tool: - hr_get_employee(employee_id: string*): Get detailed... (parameters, * = required, and the first 120 characters of the description) 997

Measured with tiktoken's o200k_base encoding on the first request of a build_agent run against the 40 tools of tests/_e2e_40tool_server.py (one-line descriptions): the tool definitions are 3,043 tokens, so "full" adds a third on top of them. With longer descriptions the block costs more (about 40 tokens a tool on a 48-tool server). The summary lists the tools offered on that call, so with semantic selection it shrinks with the selection. Turn it on only if a model picks tools or parameters better with it. In a custom graph, PromptNode(tool_summary=...) sets it per node and PromptGraphEngine(tool_summary=...) for every node that sets none.

docs.title: Combining with Other Features
docs.text:
Tool optimization composes with all other agent features:

agent = await build_agent(
    servers=servers,
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    optimize_tools="standard",
    observe=True,           # observability still tracks all tool calls
    memory=provider,        # memory injection happens before tool selection
    sandbox=True,           # sandbox tools keep full schemas
)

Static optimization applies to tools discovered from MCP servers. Semantic selection covers every tool the agent has: MCP, extra_tools, sandbox and cross-agent tools, and applies to ainvoke(), chat(), astream() and astream_with_tools().

docs.title: Checking selection offline with ToolIndex
docs.text:
ToolIndex (in promptise.tool_optimization) is the index semantic selection uses. Build one over an agent's tools to check, before paying for any model call, whether each of your typical requests would be offered the right tool, and to compare embedding models or description lengths:

from promptise.tool_optimization import ToolIndex, build_selection_query

tools = [t for t in agent.tools if t.name != "request_more_tools"]
index = ToolIndex(tools, model_name_or_path="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

for request, expected in [("Suspend user u_42, she left.", "suspend_user")]:
    offered = [t.name for t in index.select(request, top_k=8)]
    print(request, "->", "ok" if expected in offered else f"missed (got {offered[:3]})")

# The query the agent would use for a whole conversation:
query = build_selection_query(messages, user_turns=3)

index.select(query, top_k=8, preserve=None) returns the top_k most relevant tools followed by the preserved ones (which don't take a relevance slot). Embeddings of repeated queries are cached.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Does optimization affect tool call quality?

Schema minification removes per-field descriptions but keeps field names, types, and required status. Most LLMs infer field purpose from well-named parameters (e.g., user_id, email, start_date). For tools with ambiguous parameter names, use preserve_tools to exempt them.

What if semantic selection picks the wrong tools?

The model can call request_more_tools, and the tools it returns are offered on the next model call. To catch misses before they cost anything, check your typical requests with ToolIndex. The two most effective fixes are longer tool descriptions in the index (raise max_description_length: the semantic preset truncates descriptions to 100 characters, and those truncated descriptions are what gets embedded) and adding must-have tools to preserve_tools.

Does this work with all LLM providers?

Yes. Tool optimization modifies the tool definitions before they reach LangChain: it works with OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, and any other provider.

Learn the concept
