docs.title: 1 · Foundations: build and shape an agent
Building AI Agents
docs.text: Build a production agent in twelve runnable steps: Python tools, an MCP server, conversations, memory, guardrails, human approval, observability, a code sandbox, delegation to other agents, a reasoning pattern and a .superagent file. One function call creates it; every capability is opt-in. You'll learn: build_agent(), @tool, MCP servers, chat() and conversation stores, memory, guardrails, ApprovalPolicy, observability, sandbox, CrossAgent, agent_pattern, SuperAgent files.

docs.title: Cookbook
docs.text: Short, copy-paste recipes for the tasks you reach for most, each with a link to the full reference.

docs.title: Prompt Engineering
docs.text: Build reliable, testable system prompts with typed blocks, token budgeting, composable reasoning strategies, runtime guards, and dynamic context injection. You'll learn: PromptBlocks, strategies, perspectives, guards, context providers, ConversationFlow, registry, testing.

docs.title: Context Lifecycle Management
docs.text: Keep deep tool loops token-efficient. The default agent handles context automatically (context_scope="auto"); go further with scoped and ledger for multi-stage graphs. You'll learn: context_scope (auto/full/scoped/ledger), the facts-ledger loop, bounding token growth.

docs.title: Code-Action: Agents that Write Programs
docs.text: For aggregation and data-traversal, have the model write one Python program over your tools (a single LLM turn instead of dozens of tool calls) run in a hardened Docker sandbox. You'll learn: agent_pattern="code-action", the sandbox tool-bridge, max_tool_calls, when to reach for it.

docs.title: 2 · Build the tools your agents use
Building Production MCP Servers
docs.text: Build a production-grade MCP server: tool registration, Pydantic validation, JWT auth with structured client context, scope-based authorization, routers, middleware, caching, and request tracing. You'll learn: MCPServer, tool/resource/prompt decorators, AuthMiddleware, ClientContext, guards, on_authenticate, MCPRouter, tracing.

docs.title: MCPcast an Existing API
docs.text: Already have an API? Don't hand-write the server. promptise mcpcast turns an OpenAPI 3.x or Swagger 2 spec into a curated, safe, agent-ready MCP server emitted as editable code: read-only by default, with every write gated by human approval the server enforces, so any MCP client can drive your product. You'll learn: promptise mcpcast, risk classification, safety profiles, LLM curation with code-enforced post-conditions, the plan file, auth modes, server-side approval, Agent Readiness Score.

docs.title: Make Your Python API MCP-Ready
docs.text: You have an app, not a spec. Find the OpenAPI URL your framework already serves (FastAPI, Django Ninja, DRF, Flask, Litestar), rewrite the spec so a model can read it, generate the MCP server from the running app, map auth, wire up Claude and Cursor, gate writes behind approval, and ship with a CI guard and a Dockerfile. You'll learn: operation_id/summary/Field descriptions as the tool surface, env-token vs passthrough vs api-key auth, server-side approval, the readiness score as a quality bar.

docs.title: Building Multi-User Systems
docs.text: End-to-end identity: a user's JWT flows from your backend through the agent to the MCP server; conversation ownership, per-user cache/memory isolation, guardrails, and tamper-evident audit are all wired to that identity. You'll learn: CallerContext, JWT/OAuth flow, guards, conversation ownership, per-user isolation, audit.

docs.title: CallerContext: Agent → MCP Identity
docs.text: The focused reference for how identity crosses the wire: what the bearer token carries, what the server extracts, and how guards see it. You'll learn: CallerContext fields, JWT propagation, server-side extraction, guard evaluation.

docs.title: Secure Multi-Tenant Platform
docs.text: The enterprise capstone: one server serving many customer orgs with provable tenant isolation, role-based access, server-side human approval for destructive tools (four-eyes), fair per-tenant usage, and tamper-evident audit. You'll learn: tenant_id isolation invariant, require_tenant, RequireTenant/HasTenant, requires_approval + ApprovalGateMiddleware, PendingApprover, tenant-stamped audit.

docs.title: Building Agentic Runtime Systems
docs.text: Autonomous, long-running agents that react to events, persist state, recover from crashes, enforce governance, and scale across machines. You'll learn: AgentProcess, triggers, journals, governance (budget/health/mission/secrets), AgentRuntime, distributed coordination.

docs.title: Multi-Agent Coordination
docs.text: Systems where agents collaborate: sharing tools, delegating, communicating through events, and coordinating through shared state. You'll learn: a shared MCP server with per-agent roles, CrossAgent delegation, InProcessEventBus and event triggers, shared state, supervisor and pipeline patterns.

docs.title: Hands-On Labs
docs.text:
Domain-specific, copy-paste-ready tutorials. Each includes a pre-built MCP server, a specialized reasoning pattern, and runnable code.

  • Customer Support Agent: issue classification, KB search, policy validation, human escalation. (Classify → Investigate → Draft → Validate → Respond)
  • Data Analysis Agent: questions → SQL, cross-table joins, accurate reports. (Plan → Execute → Observe → Verify → Report)
  • Code Review Agent: security review via adversarial self-critique with line-referenced claims. (Read → Analyze → Critique → Justify → Synthesize)
  • Pipeline Observer Agent: an autonomous runtime agent that watches a pipeline, reacts to events, and escalates.
  • MCPcast Your SaaS API: a storefront API turned into agent tools end to end: risk-classified tools, a real agent completing a business task, a refund held by the server-side approval gate, and an Agent Readiness Score before and after fixing the plan.

docs.title: Guide Structure
docs.text:
Every guide follows the same progression:

  1. What You'll Build: A concrete description of the end result
  2. Concepts: The key ideas before any code
  3. Step-by-Step: Progressive implementation with working code at each step
  4. Complete Example: Full working code you can copy and run
  5. What's Next: Links to reference docs for deeper exploration

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
All guides assume:

  • Python 3.10+
  • pip install promptise (or pip install "promptise[all]" for all extras)
  • An OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable set (or another LLM provider)

See Installation and Model Setup if you need help getting started.

docs.title: What You'll Build
docs.text: A production-grade autonomous agent system that monitors data pipelines, reacts to events, persists state across invocations, recovers from crashes, enforces governance policies, and scales across multiple machines. You'll start with a single agent and progressively add capabilities until you have a governed, mission-driven, distributed multi-agent operations center.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
An agentic runtime is the infrastructure that turns a stateless LLM into a persistent, autonomous process. Without a runtime, an agent exists only for the duration of a single request: you call it, get a response, and it disappears. A runtime wraps that same agent in a long-running process with scheduling, event handling, persistent memory, crash recovery, and governance.

Think of the relationship like a web application versus a web framework: you could handle HTTP requests manually, but a framework gives you routing, middleware, sessions, and error handling. The Agent Runtime does the same for AI agents: it provides the infrastructure so you can focus on what the agent should do, not how to keep it running.

The runtime is built in layers. Each layer adds capabilities without requiring changes to the layer below:

Layer 5: Governance                  Budget, health, mission, secrets
         |
Layer 4: Distributed Coordination    Multi-node clusters with transport & discovery
         |
Layer 3: AgentRuntime                Multi-process manager with lifecycle control
         |
Layer 2: AgentProcess                Single autonomous agent with triggers & state
         |
Layer 1: build_agent()          Stateless LLM agent with MCP tool access

You can stop at any layer. Most projects need Layer 2 (a single autonomous agent). Add Layer 3 when you need multiple agents working together. Layer 4 is for production deployments across multiple machines. Layer 5 is for autonomous agents that need guardrails.

docs.title: Step 1: Single Autonomous Agent
docs.text:
Start with an AgentProcess wrapping a stateless agent in a persistent process.

import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import AgentProcess, ProcessConfig, TriggerConfig

process = AgentProcess(
    name="pipeline-monitor",
    config=ProcessConfig(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions=(
            "You monitor data pipelines. When triggered, check pipeline "
            "health and report any anomalies."
        ),
        servers={
            "pipeline_api": {
                "url": "http://localhost:8080/mcp",
                "transport": "streamable-http",
            },
        },
        triggers=[
            TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *"),
        ],
    ),
)

async with process:
    # Process runs autonomously, waking on every cron tick
    await asyncio.sleep(3600)  # Run for 1 hour

The process handles the full lifecycle: build the agent, connect MCP servers, discover tools, start triggers, and invoke the agent on each trigger event.

docs.title: Step 2: Add Triggers
docs.text:
Triggers wake the agent in response to events. Compose multiple triggers to create responsive agents.

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="You respond to pipeline events and scheduled checks.",
    triggers=[
        # Wake every 5 minutes for health checks
        TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *"),

        # Wake on incoming webhooks (e.g., from CI/CD)
        TriggerConfig(
            type="webhook",
            webhook_path="/pipeline-events",
            webhook_port=9090,
        ),

        # Wake when config files change
        TriggerConfig(
            type="file_watch",
            watch_path="/etc/pipeline/config",
            watch_patterns=["*.yaml", "*.json"],
            watch_events=["modified"],
        ),

        # Wake on events from other agents
        TriggerConfig(
            type="event",
            event_type="alert.critical",
        ),

        # Wake on inter-agent messages
        TriggerConfig(
            type="message",
            topic="pipeline.alerts.*",
        ),
    ],
)

Each trigger type fires a TriggerEvent with type-specific payload data that the agent receives as context.

Trigger Wakes On Payload cron Schedule expression scheduled_time, cron_expression webhook HTTP POST request Request body (JSON or text) file_watch File system changes path, filename, event_type event EventBus events event_type, source, data message MessageBroker messages topic, sender, content

docs.title: Step 3: Persistent State and Context
docs.text:
AgentContext gives each process a persistent key-value state with audit trail, long-term memory, environment variables, and file mounts.

from promptise.runtime.config import ContextConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="You track pipeline health over time.",
    context=ContextConfig(
        # Pre-populate state
        initial_state={
            "alert_count": 0,
            "last_healthy": None,
            "known_issues": [],
        },

        # Give the agent an update_state(key, value) tool, limited to these keys
        state_tool=True,
        writable_keys=["alert_count", "last_healthy", "known_issues"],

        # Long-term memory (persists across restarts)
        memory_provider="chroma",
        memory_collection="pipeline_memory",
        memory_persist_directory=".promptise/memory",
        memory_auto_store=True,

        # Short-term conversation buffer
        conversation_max_messages=50,

        # Expose environment variables matching prefix
        env_prefix="PIPELINE_",

        # Logical names for paths your tools look up (no file I/O by the context)
        file_mounts={
            "config": "/etc/pipeline/config.yaml",
            "runbook": "/docs/runbook.md",
        },
    ),
    triggers=[
        TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *"),
    ],
)

The context state is injected into every agent invocation as a system message. With state_tool=True the agent can also write the keys in writable_keys through its update_state tool; without it, only your code, triggers and the API write state. See Agent Context.

State access in code:

process = AgentProcess(name="monitor", config=config)
await process.start()

# Read state programmatically
ctx = process.context
alert_count = ctx.get("alert_count", 0)
snapshot = ctx.state_snapshot()

# Write state with audit trail
ctx.put("alert_count", alert_count + 1, source="external")

# View audit history for a key
history = ctx.state_history("alert_count")
for entry in history:
    print(f"  {entry.timestamp}: {entry.value} (by {entry.source})")

docs.title: Step 4: Crash Recovery with Journals
docs.text:
The journal records every state transition, context write and run result (and, at level="full", every trigger event and tool call). When a process with the same name starts again after a crash or a redeploy, it restores its context state, conversation, budget counters and mission from the last checkpoint by itself (JournalConfig.recover_on_start, on by default).

from promptise.runtime.config import JournalConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Critical monitoring agent.",
    journal=JournalConfig(
        level="full",                          # "none", "checkpoint", or "full"
        backend="file",                        # "file" or "memory"
        path=".promptise/journal",             # Persist to disk
    ),
    max_consecutive_failures=3,              # FAILED after 3 failed runs in a row
    restart_policy="on_failure",             # Auto-restart on failure
    max_restarts=5,                          # Max restart attempts
    triggers=[
        TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *"),
    ],
)

Recovery flow: the process does this on its first start(), and process.recovered reports what came back. To look at what a process would recover without starting it, use the ReplayEngine yourself. Entries are filed under the process name:

from promptise.runtime.journal import FileJournal, ReplayEngine

journal = FileJournal(base_path=".promptise/journal")
engine = ReplayEngine(journal)

recovered = await engine.recover(process_id="monitor")
print(f"Recovered state: {recovered['context_state']}")
print(f"Last lifecycle state: {recovered['lifecycle_state']}")
print(f"Entries replayed: {recovered['entries_replayed']}")

With restart_policy="on_failure", the runtime automatically attempts to restart failed processes up to max_restarts times.

docs.title: Step 5: Governance (Autonomy Budget)
docs.text:
Without a budget, an autonomous agent can loop indefinitely, call expensive APIs without limit, or take irreversible actions at 3am. The autonomy budget defines the envelope within which the agent operates freely.

from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, BudgetConfig, EscalationTarget, ToolCostAnnotation

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Process customer support tickets.",
    budget=BudgetConfig(
        enabled=True,

        # Per-invocation limits
        max_tool_calls_per_run=20,
        max_llm_turns_per_run=10,
        max_cost_per_run=25.0,
        max_irreversible_per_run=2,

        # Daily limits (reset at midnight UTC)
        max_tool_calls_per_day=500,
        max_cost_per_day=100.0,

        # Per-tool cost annotations
        tool_costs={
            "stripe_charge": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=5.0, irreversible=True),
            "send_email": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=2.0, irreversible=True),
            "search": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=0.5),
        },

        # What happens when a limit is hit
        on_exceeded="escalate",   # "pause", "stop", or "escalate"
        inject_remaining=True,     # Show budget in agent context

        escalation=EscalationTarget(
            webhook_url="https://hooks.slack.com/services/...",
        ),
    ),
    triggers=[
        TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *"),
    ],
)

When inject_remaining=True, the agent sees its remaining budget before every turn, so it can prioritize actions and avoid hitting limits.

cost_weight is abstract, not dollars

cost_weight values are budget units you define, not real money. The framework does not track LLM API costs (token pricing). max_cost_per_day=100.0 with cost_weight=5.0 on stripe_charge means "the agent can make 20 Stripe charges per day", not "$100/day." Use max_llm_turns_per_run to limit LLM usage. See Autonomy Budget for full details on designing your cost scale.

docs.title: Step 6: Governance (Behavioral Health)
docs.text:
System monitoring watches CPU and memory. Nobody watches whether the agent is actually doing what it should be doing. Behavioral health catches stuck agents, infinite loops, empty responses, and high error rates, without making any LLM calls.

from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, HealthConfig, EscalationTarget

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Monitor data pipelines.",
    health=HealthConfig(
        enabled=True,
        stuck_threshold=3,         # 3 identical calls = stuck
        loop_window=20,            # Check last 20 tool calls for loops
        loop_min_repeats=2,        # 2+ repeats of a pattern = loop
        empty_threshold=3,         # 3 consecutive short responses = anomaly
        empty_max_chars=10,        # At most 10 chars = trivial response
        error_rate_threshold=0.5,  # 50%+ failed runs = anomaly
        on_anomaly="pause",        # "log", "pause", "escalate" or "stop"
        cooldown=300,              # 5 min before the same anomaly is reported again
        escalation=EscalationTarget(
            webhook_url="https://hooks.slack.com/services/...",
        ),
    ),
    triggers=[
        TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *"),
    ],
)

Four anomaly detectors run automatically:

Anomaly Detection Example Stuck The same tool with the same arguments N times in a row within one run Agent calling get_status("pipeline-3") 5 times in a row Loop Repeating subsequence in tool call history Agent cycling through check → fix → check → fix endlessly Empty response N consecutive final replies of at most empty_max_chars characters Agent returning "" or "ok" repeatedly High error rate Share of failed runs in the last error_window runs at or above the threshold 6 of the last 10 runs raised

docs.title: Step 7: Governance (Mission-Oriented Execution)
docs.text:
Standard agents run on a trigger, do something, stop. A mission-oriented agent runs until a goal is achieved, accumulating context across invocations, with LLM-as-judge evaluation and automatic completion.

from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, MissionConfig, EscalationTarget

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Migrate all database tables to v2 schema.",
    mission=MissionConfig(
        enabled=True,
        objective="Migrate all database tables to v2 schema",
        success_criteria="All tables pass v2 schema validation with zero errors",
        eval_every=3,               # Evaluate after every 3rd successful run
        confidence_threshold=0.7,   # Below this: pause the mission and escalate
        timeout_hours=24,           # Fail after 24 hours
        max_invocations=50,         # Fail after 50 successful runs
        auto_complete=True,         # Stop when mission succeeds
        eval_model="openai:gpt-5-mini",  # Separate model for evaluation
        escalation=EscalationTarget(
            webhook_url="https://hooks.slack.com/services/...",
        ),
    ),
    triggers=[
        TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/10 * * * *"),
    ],
)

The mission tracker:

  1. Prepends the objective and progress into every agent invocation context
  2. Every N successful runs, runs an LLM-as-judge evaluation against the success criteria (or your own success_check first)
  3. If achieved=True and auto_complete=True, stops the process
  4. If the mission is not achieved and confidence < confidence_threshold, pauses the mission (the process keeps running its triggers) and notifies escalation
  5. If timed out or over the run limit, fails the mission; later runs are skipped

docs.title: Step 8: Governance (Scoped Secrets)
docs.text:
Environment variables are shared across all agents on the same host. Secret scoping gives each process its own isolated credential context with automatic expiry and access logging.

from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, SecretScopeConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Process payments.",
    secrets=SecretScopeConfig(
        enabled=True,
        secrets={
            "stripe_key": "${STRIPE_API_KEY}",    # Resolved from env at startup
            "db_password": "${DB_PASSWORD}",
            "static_token": "tok-abc123",          # Literal value
        },
        default_ttl=3600,           # 1 hour default
        ttls={
            "stripe_key": 1800,     # 30 min for payment credentials
        },
        revoke_on_stop=True,        # Zero-fill on process stop
    ),
    triggers=[
        TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *"),
    ],
)

Key security properties:

  • Values live only in memory: encrypted, and redacted ([REDACTED]) from the journal, checkpoints, conversation history, hook data and API responses
  • TTL-based expiry: secrets become inaccessible after their TTL expires
  • Access logging: every access is logged in the journal (name only, never the value)
  • Zero-fill revocation: on process stop, all values are overwritten with zeros and removed
  • Crash recovery: secrets are resolved from the environment again on start, never from the journal

docs.title: Step 9: Multi-Agent Runtime
docs.text:
AgentRuntime manages multiple AgentProcess instances with centralized lifecycle control.

import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import AgentRuntime, InProcessEventBus, ProcessConfig, TriggerConfig

# Shared channels: InProcessEventBus for "event" triggers. A "message" trigger
# needs a broker object you provide (subscribe(topic, handler) / unsubscribe(id)).
event_bus = InProcessEventBus()
broker = MyMessageBroker()

async with AgentRuntime(event_bus=event_bus, broker=broker) as runtime:
    # Register agents
    await runtime.add_process("monitor", ProcessConfig(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions="Monitor pipelines and report failures.",
        triggers=[
            TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *"),
        ],
    ))

    await runtime.add_process("analyst", ProcessConfig(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions="Analyze alerts and determine root cause.",
        triggers=[
            TriggerConfig(type="event", event_type="alert.critical"),
        ],
    ))

    await runtime.add_process("responder", ProcessConfig(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions="Execute remediation based on analysis.",
        triggers=[
            TriggerConfig(type="message", topic="analysis.complete"),
        ],
    ))

    # Start all agents
    await runtime.start_all()

    # Monitor status
    status = runtime.status()
    for name, proc_status in status["processes"].items():
        print(f"  {name}: {proc_status['state']}")

    # Run until interrupted
    await asyncio.sleep(3600)

Agent-to-agent communication happens through two channels:

  • Event bus: broadcast events that any listening process receives. Use TriggerConfig(type="event", event_type="...") to subscribe.
  • Message broker: topic-based messaging (wildcards are up to your broker). Use TriggerConfig(type="message", topic="...") to subscribe.

An agent has no built-in tool to publish on the bus or the broker. The events come from your code (a web handler, a scheduler), from an MCP tool you give the agent, or from a runtime hook that publishes when a run finishes; see the staged pipeline in Multi-Agent Coordination.

Loading from manifests:

# Load all .agent files from a directory
loaded = await runtime.load_directory("agents/")
print(f"Loaded: {loaded}")  # ["monitor", "analyst", "responder"]

await runtime.start_all()

docs.title: Step 10: Distributed Coordination
docs.text:
For multi-node deployments, RuntimeTransport exposes each node's runtime over HTTP, and RuntimeCoordinator manages cluster membership.

import os

from promptise.runtime import AgentRuntime
from promptise.runtime.distributed import RuntimeTransport, RuntimeCoordinator

TOKEN = os.environ["PROMPTISE_NODE_TOKEN"]  # required for a non-loopback bind

# Node 1: primary
runtime_1 = AgentRuntime()
transport_1 = RuntimeTransport(
    runtime_1,
    host="0.0.0.0",
    port=9100,
    node_id="node-1",
    auth_token=TOKEN,
)
await transport_1.start()

# Node 2: secondary
runtime_2 = AgentRuntime()
transport_2 = RuntimeTransport(
    runtime_2,
    host="0.0.0.0",
    port=9101,
    node_id="node-2",
    auth_token=TOKEN,
)
await transport_2.start()

# Coordinator tracks all nodes
coordinator = RuntimeCoordinator(
    health_check_interval=15.0,
    node_timeout=45.0,
    auth_token=TOKEN,  # sent as a bearer token to every node
)
coordinator.register_node("node-1", "http://node-1:9100")
coordinator.register_node("node-2", "http://node-2:9101")

Each node exposes a REST API for remote management. Every endpoint except /health requires Authorization: Bearer <token>; binding a non-loopback address without auth_token raises ValueError (see Discovery and Transport).

Endpoint Method Description /health GET Health check with process count /status GET Full runtime status /processes GET List all processes /processes/{name}/start POST Start a process /processes/{name}/stop POST Stop a process /processes/{name}/event POST Inject a trigger event

docs.title: Step 11: Production Hardening
docs.text:
Combine governance, failure handling, and resource limits for a production deployment:

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Production agent.",

    # Concurrency control
    concurrency=3,                    # Up to 3 parallel invocations

    # Health monitoring
    heartbeat_interval=10.0,          # Idle and lifetime checks every 10s
    idle_timeout=300.0,               # Suspend after 5 min idle; the next event resumes it
    max_lifetime=86400.0,             # Stop after 24h (recycled instead with restart_policy="always")

    # Failure handling
    max_consecutive_failures=3,       # FAILED after 3 failed runs in a row
    restart_policy="on_failure",      # Auto-restart on failure
    max_restarts=5,                   # Max 5 restart attempts

    # Governance
    budget=BudgetConfig(
        enabled=True,
        max_tool_calls_per_day=1000,
        on_exceeded="pause",
    ),
    health=HealthConfig(
        enabled=True,
        on_anomaly="escalate",
        escalation=EscalationTarget(webhook_url="https://hooks.slack.com/..."),
    ),
    mission=MissionConfig(
        enabled=True,
        objective="Keep all pipelines healthy",
        success_criteria="Zero critical alerts for 24 consecutive hours",
        eval_every=10,
        timeout_hours=48,
    ),
    secrets=SecretScopeConfig(
        enabled=True,
        secrets={"api_key": "${PIPELINE_API_KEY}"},
        default_ttl=3600,
        revoke_on_stop=True,
    ),
)

Monitoring:

# Global runtime status
status = runtime.status()
print(f"Processes: {status['process_count']}")

# Per-process status (includes governance info)
for info in runtime.list_processes():
    print(f"  {info['name']}: {info['state']}")

# Detailed process status
detail = runtime.process_status("monitor")
print(f"  Invocations: {detail['invocation_count']}")
print(f"  Failures: {detail['consecutive_failures']}")
print(f"  Uptime: {detail['uptime_seconds']:.0f}s")

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
A three-agent system with full governance: a monitor watches pipelines with a budget and health checks, an analyst diagnoses issues, and a responder executes fixes with a mission objective. Each agent records its result with its state tool, and one runtime hook passes that result on as the next agent's event.

import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import (
    AgentRuntime, BudgetConfig, EscalationTarget, HealthConfig, HookContext, HookEvent,
    HookManager, InProcessEventBus, MissionConfig, ProcessConfig, SecretScopeConfig, TriggerConfig,
)
from promptise.runtime.config import ContextConfig, JournalConfig

PIPELINE = {"pipeline": {"url": "http://localhost:8080/mcp", "transport": "streamable-http"}}
# Which state key a process fills, and which event announces it
HAND_OFF = {"monitor": ("alert", "alert.critical"), "analyst": ("analysis", "analysis.complete")}


async def main():
    bus = InProcessEventBus()
    hooks = HookManager()
    slack = EscalationTarget(webhook_url="https://hooks.slack.com/services/...")
    runtime = AgentRuntime(event_bus=bus, hooks=hooks)

    @hooks.on(HookEvent.TASK_COMPLETED)
    async def hand_off(ctx: HookContext) -> None:
        if ctx.data["outcome"] != "success" or ctx.process_id not in HAND_OFF:
            return
        key, event_type = HAND_OFF[ctx.process_id]
        context = runtime.get_process(ctx.process_id).context
        if context.get(key):
            asyncio.create_task(bus.emit(event_type, {key: context.get(key)}, source=ctx.process_id))
            context.put(key, None, source="hand_off")   # announce each result once

    await runtime.add_process("monitor", ProcessConfig(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions=(
            "You monitor data pipelines. If a pipeline is unhealthy, describe the problem "
            "with update_state('alert', ...)."
        ),
        servers=PIPELINE,
        triggers=[TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *")],
        context=ContextConfig(
            initial_state={"alert": None},
            state_tool=True,
            writable_keys=["alert"],
            memory_provider="chroma",
            memory_auto_store=True,
        ),
        journal=JournalConfig(level="full", backend="file"),
        budget=BudgetConfig(enabled=True, max_tool_calls_per_day=500, on_exceeded="pause"),
        health=HealthConfig(enabled=True, stuck_threshold=5, on_anomaly="escalate", escalation=slack),
    ))

    await runtime.add_process("analyst", ProcessConfig(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions="Find the root cause of the alert. Save it with update_state('analysis', ...).",
        triggers=[TriggerConfig(type="event", event_type="alert.critical", event_source="monitor")],
        context=ContextConfig(state_tool=True, writable_keys=["analysis"]),
    ))

    await runtime.add_process("responder", ProcessConfig(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions="Execute the pipeline remediation the analysis calls for.",
        servers=PIPELINE,
        triggers=[TriggerConfig(type="event", event_type="analysis.complete", event_source="analyst")],
        restart_policy="on_failure",
        mission=MissionConfig(
            enabled=True,
            objective="Restore all pipelines to healthy status",
            success_criteria="All pipeline stages pass health checks for 3 consecutive runs",
            eval_every=3,
            confidence_threshold=0.6,
            timeout_hours=4,
            auto_complete=True,
            escalation=slack,
        ),
        secrets=SecretScopeConfig(
            enabled=True,
            secrets={"pipeline_admin_key": "${PIPELINE_ADMIN_KEY}"},
            default_ttl=1800,
            revoke_on_stop=True,
        ),
    ))

    await runtime.run_forever()   # starts all three; Ctrl+C or SIGTERM stops them cleanly


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

run_forever() starts every process and, on shutdown, stops and closes them. Check runtime.status() (or promptise runtime status when you start it from manifests) to see each process's state, counters and governance status.

docs.title: Building AI Agents
docs.text:
Build a production agent in twelve small steps. Each step adds one capability to the same agent: Python tools, MCP servers, conversations, memory, guardrails, human approval, observability, a code sandbox, delegation to other agents, a reasoning pattern and, at the end, the whole agent as a .superagent file.

Start here

Every step is a complete script you can run. For the full reference of each feature, follow the links at the end of each step, or start from Building Agents.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
pip install promptise

A .env file in your project with your model key (Promptise loads it automatically):

.env
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...

Any other provider works the same way: see Model Setup. promptise models check openai:gpt-5-mini --ping tells you whether the key works.

docs.title: How a Promptise agent is put together
docs.text:
• One function builds it. build_agent() takes a model, tools and optional features, and returns a PromptiseAgent. Every feature is a keyword argument and off unless you pass it.
  • Tools come from two places. Python functions you decorate with @tool, and the tools of the MCP servers you connect. The agent treats both the same way.
  • The model is a string or a Model. "openai:gpt-5-mini", "anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", "ollama:llama3.1", or Model("gpt-5-mini", provider="openai", api_key=...). Changing it changes nothing else.

docs.title: Step 1: A minimal agent
docs.text:
import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions="You are a support assistant for an online shop. Be brief.",
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in five words."}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

ainvoke() takes the conversation as a list of messages and returns the state after the run; the last message is the answer. Always await agent.shutdown() when you are done: it closes MCP connections, stores and background tasks.

docs.title: Step 2: Give it Python tools
docs.text:
Put the shop's tools in their own module, so the next steps can import them:

shop_tools.py
from promptise import CallerContext, ToolError, tool

ORDERS = {
    "A-1001": {"order_id": "A-1001", "status": "shipped", "total": 120.0, "customer": "alice"},
    "A-1002": {"order_id": "A-1002", "status": "processing", "total": 42.5, "customer": "bob"},
}

@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID.

    Args:
        order_id: The order ID, for example "A-1001".
    """
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if order is None:
        raise ToolError(f"No order {order_id}. Ask the customer to check the ID.")
    return order

@tool
def refund_order(order_id: str, amount: float, caller: CallerContext) -> str:
    """Refund part or all of an order.

    Args:
        order_id: The order to refund.
        amount: Amount to refund, in EUR.
    """
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if order is None:
        raise ToolError(f"No order {order_id}.")
    if amount > order["total"]:
        raise ToolError(f"Refund {amount} is more than the order total {order['total']}.")
    return f"Refunded {amount:.2f} EUR on {order_id} (requested by {caller.user_id})."

Then pass them with extra_tools:

import asyncio
from promptise import CallerContext, build_agent
from shop_tools import get_order, refund_order

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions="You are a support assistant for an online shop.",
        extra_tools=[get_order, refund_order],
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the status of order A-1001?"}]},
        caller=CallerContext(user_id="alice"),
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

What happens:

  • The tool's name is the function name, its description is the docstring, and its parameters come from the type hints and the Args: section.
  • Arguments are validated before the function runs. Invalid arguments go back to the model as a tool error it can correct.
  • raise ToolError("...") sends that message to the model instead of a stack trace.
  • A parameter typed CallerContext is not shown to the model: the agent fills it in with the caller= you pass to ainvoke() or chat().

See Tools (@tool) for every option (name=, description=, timeout=, Annotated constraints, sync and async functions).

docs.title: Step 3: Connect an MCP server
docs.text:
Tools that other agents or apps should also use belong in an MCP server. Here the order lookup moves into a server that the agent starts as a subprocess:

shop_server.py
from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer

server = MCPServer("shop")

@server.tool()
async def list_open_orders(customer: str) -> list[str]:
    """List the IDs of a customer's orders that have not shipped yet."""
    return ["A-1002"] if customer == "bob" else []

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server.run(transport="stdio")

import asyncio
import sys
from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.config import StdioServerSpec
from shop_tools import get_order

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        servers={
            "shop": StdioServerSpec(command=sys.executable, args=["shop_server.py"]),
        },
        extra_tools=[get_order],
    )
    print(agent.tool_names)  # ['list_open_orders', 'get_order']
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Which orders of bob are still open?"}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

build_agent() connects to every server in servers, lists its tools and converts their JSON Schemas. A remote server is an HTTPServerSpec:

from promptise.config import HTTPServerSpec

servers = {
    "crm": HTTPServerSpec(url="https://crm.internal/mcp", bearer_token="..."),
}

Tool names are not namespaced

When two servers expose a tool with the same name, the server listed last in servers wins and a warning names both. Give the tools distinct names on the servers, for example with MCPRouter(prefix="billing"), which names a router's tools billing_<name>.

See Server Configuration for every server option (headers, API keys, per-caller tokens, transports) and MCP Server SDK for building servers.

docs.title: Step 4: Keep conversations
docs.text:
For a chat application, the agent should load a session's history, answer, and store the new messages. Give it a conversation store and use chat():

import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.conversations import SQLiteConversationStore, generate_session_id
from shop_tools import get_order

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        extra_tools=[get_order],
        conversation_store=SQLiteConversationStore("conversations.db"),
        conversation_max_messages=200,  # keep the last 200 messages per session; 0 keeps all
    )
    sid = generate_session_id()  # unpredictable "sess_..." ID

    print(await agent.chat("Where is my order A-1001?", session_id=sid, user_id="alice"))
    print(await agent.chat("And what was its total?", session_id=sid, user_id="alice"))

    sessions = await agent.list_sessions(user_id="alice")
    print([s.session_id for s in sessions])
    await agent.update_session(sid, calling_user_id="alice", title="Order A-1001")
    await agent.delete_session(sid, user_id="alice")
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

The first chat() with a user_id makes that user the session's owner; later calls from another user raise SessionAccessDenied. Generate session IDs on the server (never take them from the client unchecked).

Store Backend Use InMemoryConversationStore Python dict Tests SQLiteConversationStore aiosqlite (installed with Promptise) One process, local apps PostgresConversationStore asyncpg (pip install asyncpg) Production, several processes RedisConversationStore redis Sessions with a TTL

See Conversations.

docs.title: Step 5: Add memory
docs.text:
A conversation store replays one session. Memory is different: before each run the agent searches a memory provider for text related to the user's message and adds the best matches to the system prompt.

import asyncio
from promptise import InMemoryProvider, build_agent

async def main():
    memory = InMemoryProvider()
    await memory.add("Alice prefers refunds as store credit.", metadata={"user": "alice"})

    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        memory=memory,
        memory_max_results=5,    # at most 5 memories per run (default 5)
        memory_auto_store=False, # True also stores each exchange (default False)
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "How does Alice like her refunds?"}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())
Provider Search Persistence Extra InMemoryProvider Keyword match Process only none ChromaProvider Vector similarity Disk with persist_directory= promptise[all] Mem0Provider Vector and graph Mem0 backend promptise[all]

Memory is shared by default

Providers are created with scope=MemoryScope.SHARED: every caller reads the same memories. For a multi-user agent create the provider with scope=MemoryScope.PER_USER and pass a CallerContext with a user_id. See Memory scopes.

docs.title: Step 6: Add guardrails
docs.text:
Guardrails scan the user's message before the model sees it and the answer before it is returned. This scanner uses regular expressions only, so it downloads no model:

import asyncio
from promptise import (
    Action, CredentialDetector, CustomRule, GuardrailViolation, PIICategory,
    PIIDetector, PromptiseSecurityScanner, build_agent,
)

async def main():
    scanner = PromptiseSecurityScanner(
        detectors=[
            PIIDetector(categories={PIICategory.CREDIT_CARDS, PIICategory.EMAIL}),
            CredentialDetector(),
        ],
        custom_rules=[
            CustomRule(name="internal_codename", pattern=r"\bPROJECT-ORION\b", action=Action.BLOCK),
        ],
        redact_input=True,  # also redact PII and keys in the user's message
    )
    agent = await build_agent(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", guardrails=scanner)

    # The key is replaced with [AWS_ACCESS_KEY] before the model sees it.
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Is AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE a valid key format?"}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)

    # A BLOCK finding stops the run before the model is called.
    try:
        await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is PROJECT-ORION?"}]})
    except GuardrailViolation as exc:
        print("Blocked:", exc)
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

What each part does:

  • PII and credentials in the answer are always replaced with labels such as [CREDIT_CARD] or [AWS_ACCESS_KEY].
  • In the input they are only recorded unless redact_input=True.
  • A finding whose action is Action.BLOCK (the prompt-injection classifier, or your own CustomRule) raises GuardrailViolation and the model is never called.

guardrails=True uses PromptiseSecurityScanner.default(), which adds the prompt-injection classifier (a local model from Hugging Face, downloaded on first use). See Guardrails for every detector and action.

docs.title: Step 7: Ask a human before sensitive tools run
docs.text:
An ApprovalPolicy pauses the run when the agent calls a matching tool and asks a handler for a decision. A denied call returns a DENIED result to the model, which then adapts.

import asyncio
from promptise import ApprovalDecision, ApprovalPolicy, CallerContext, build_agent
from shop_tools import get_order, refund_order

async def approve(request):
    print(f"Approve {request.tool_name}({request.arguments})?")
    ok = request.arguments.get("amount", 0) <= 50  # your UI or rule goes here
    return ApprovalDecision(approved=ok, reason="" if ok else "Over 50 EUR needs a manager.")

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        extra_tools=[get_order, refund_order],
        approval=ApprovalPolicy(tools=["refund_*"], handler=approve, timeout=300),
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Refund 100 EUR on order A-1001."}]},
        caller=CallerContext(user_id="alice"),
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

tools takes glob patterns. Handlers can be an async function, a WebhookApprovalHandler (HTTP with HMAC signatures) or a QueueApprovalHandler (your own UI). See Approval (HITL); to enforce approval inside an MCP server for every client, see Approval Gates.

docs.title: Step 8: Observe every run
docs.text:
import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent
from shop_tools import get_order

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", extra_tools=[get_order], observe=True)
    await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Status of A-1002?"}]})

    stats = agent.get_stats()
    print(stats["total_tokens"], stats["llm_call_count"], stats["tool_call_count"], stats["error_count"])
    agent.generate_report("report.html", title="Support agent")
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

observe=True records LLM turns, tool calls, tokens, latency and errors at the standard level. For more control pass an ObservabilityConfig:

from promptise import ObservabilityConfig, ObserveLevel, TransporterType

observe = ObservabilityConfig(
    level=ObserveLevel.FULL,          # OFF, BASIC, STANDARD (default), FULL
    session_name="support",
    transporters=[TransporterType.HTML, TransporterType.STRUCTURED_LOG],
    output_dir="./reports",
    log_file="./logs/agent.jsonl",
)

The eight transporters are HTML, JSON, STRUCTURED_LOG, CONSOLE, PROMETHEUS, OTLP, WEBHOOK and CALLBACK. See Observability.

docs.title: Step 9: Run code in a sandbox
docs.text:
When the agent should write and run code, give it a Docker sandbox. It needs Docker running and pip install "promptise[sandbox]".

import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        sandbox={"memory_limit": "512M", "cpu_limit": 1, "timeout": 60},  # network stays "none"
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Use Python to compute the 30th Fibonacci number."}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

sandbox=True uses the defaults. The agent gets five tools: sandbox_exec, sandbox_read_file, sandbox_write_file, sandbox_list_files and sandbox_install_package. The container runs as an unprivileged user with a read-only root file system, dropped capabilities and no network unless you set "network": "restricted" or "full". Unknown keys raise an error, and when the sandbox cannot start build_agent() raises instead of building an agent without it. See Sandbox.

docs.title: Step 10: Delegate to other agents
docs.text:
A peer agent becomes a tool named ask_agent_<name>:

import asyncio
from promptise import CrossAgent, build_agent
from shop_tools import get_order

async def main():
    policy_expert = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions="You know the shop's refund policy: refunds within 30 days, store credit or card.",
    )
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        extra_tools=[get_order],
        cross_agents={
            "policy": CrossAgent(agent=policy_expert, description="Answers refund policy questions.", timeout=60),
        },
    )
    print(agent.tool_names)  # ['get_order', 'ask_agent_policy']
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Can I still get a refund after 3 weeks?"}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)
    await agent.shutdown()
    await policy_expert.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

Delegation runs in the same process. include_broadcast=True adds a broadcast_to_agents tool that asks several peers at once, and max_delegation_depth (default 3) limits chains of agents asking agents. See Cross-Agent Delegation.

docs.title: Step 11: Choose a reasoning pattern
docs.text:
The default is a tool loop ("react"). Other patterns change how the agent thinks:

import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent
from shop_tools import get_order

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        extra_tools=[get_order],
        agent_pattern="verify",  # plan, solve, then check the answer before replying
    )
    result = await agent.ainvoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Is order A-1001 shipped, and what did it cost?"}]}
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)
    await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

Pattern names: react (default), verify, managed, code-action, peoatr, research, autonomous, deliberate, debate. Any other string raises ValueError. You can also pass your own PromptGraph:

from promptise.engine import PlanNode, PromptGraph, PromptNode, SynthesizeNode

graph = PromptGraph("support", nodes=[
    PlanNode("plan", is_entry=True),
    PromptNode("act", inject_tools=True),
    SynthesizeNode("answer", is_terminal=True),
])
# build_agent(..., agent_pattern=graph)

See Reasoning Patterns and the Reasoning Graph.

docs.title: Step 12: Put the agent in a .superagent file
docs.text:
The same agent can live in a YAML file that you check in and run from the CLI:

support.superagent
version: "1.0"
agent:
  model: openai:gpt-5-mini
  instructions: |
    You are a support assistant for an online shop. Be brief.
servers:
  shop:
    type: stdio
    command: python
    args: ["shop_server.py"]
memory:
  provider: in_memory
observability:
  level: standard
  transporters: [html]
  output_dir: ./reports

promptise validate support.superagent
promptise agent support.superagent

Or build it in Python:

from promptise import build_superagent

agent = await build_superagent("support.superagent")

${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} in the file are read from the environment (and .env). See SuperAgent Files for every key.

docs.title: Limits and errors
docs.text:
agent = await build_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    max_agent_iterations=25,   # most model calls per run (default 25); raises GraphIterationLimitError
    max_invocation_time=120,   # seconds per run (default 0, no limit); raises TimeoutError
)
What fails What you see An MCP server cannot be reached at build time build_agent() raises MCPClientError naming the server The model provider is missing a key ModelSetupError with the variable to set A guardrail blocks the input GuardrailViolation from ainvoke() A tool raises The model gets the error as the tool result and continues Too many model calls GraphIterationLimitError

print(agent.tool_names) shows the tools the agent actually has.

docs.title: Run it from the CLI
docs.text:
promptise agent support.superagent                                 # chat with a .superagent file
promptise validate support.superagent                              # check the file
promptise list-tools --stdio "name=shop command=python args='shop_server.py'"  # list a server's tools
promptise run agent.py:create_agent                                # chat with the agent a factory returns
promptise run agent.py:create_agent --devtools                     # the same, with live traces and cost

See the CLI Reference and Projects & promptise run.

docs.title: Code-Action: one program beats a 20-call tool loop
docs.text:
For tasks that gather many facts and then compute (sum a department's salaries, average a metric across a graph, join records across sources), a conversational tool loop is the wrong tool. The transcript grows on every call, the model loses the thread, re-queries the same facts, and aggregates them unreliably in its head. Costs climb, latency climbs, accuracy drops.

agent_pattern="code-action" changes the action space: in a single LLM turn the model writes one Python program over your tools and runs it in a sandbox. Code computes exactly (loops, sums, filters, joins), so the answer is deterministic, cheap, and fast.

Runnable example

examples/reasoning/code_action_agent.py. Real LLM, real Docker. Set OPENAI_API_KEY and have Docker running.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from promptise import build_agent, tool

EMPLOYEES = {
    "Ada": {"department": "Engineering", "salary": 210_000},
    "Grace": {"department": "Engineering", "salary": 195_000},
    "Linus": {"department": "Sales", "salary": 120_000},
}


@tool("list_employees")
def list_employees() -> list:
    """Return a list of every employee name."""
    return list(EMPLOYEES)


@tool("get_employee")
def get_employee(name: str) -> dict:
    """Return {name, department, salary} for an employee."""
    return {"name": name, **EMPLOYEES[name]}


agent = await build_agent(
    servers={},                          # or your MCP servers
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    agent_pattern="code-action",         # sandbox auto-enabled (Docker required)
    extra_tools=[list_employees, get_employee],
)

result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content":
    "What is the combined salary of everyone in Engineering?"}]})
print(result["messages"][-1].content)    # 405000
await agent.shutdown()
# The model wrote ONE program: list → look up each → filter → sum → print.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use code-action Use react / managed instead Sums, averages, counts over a dataset Open-ended Q&A Multi-hop joins / graph traversal Ambiguous or conversational tasks "Gather N facts, then compute" A single tool call answers it You can run Docker No container runtime available

It is a pattern, not a replacement. On tasks that are genuinely conversational, a normal loop is better.

docs.title: Best practice: structured tools
docs.text:
Code-action is at its best when your tools return structured data (lists, dicts, numbers) that the program can use directly:

@tool("get_employee")
def get_employee(name: str) -> dict:          # ✅ program does emp["salary"]
    return {"name": name, "department": "Engineering", "salary": 210000}

@tool("get_employee")
def get_employee(name: str) -> str:           # ⚠️ program must parse prose
    return f"{name}: department=Engineering; salary=210000"

The bridge preserves the return values, so a @tool that returns a dict arrives in the program as a dict (not a stringified blob), and a list as a list. Prose-string tools still work (the model is told to parse them), but structured returns are more reliable.

MCP tools (servers=...) answer with the text of the server's result, and a server sends lists and dicts as JSON text. The bridge decodes it: when an MCP tool's text result is valid JSON, the program gets the data (list_orders("2026-09") returns a list, a number returns an int or float); any other text arrives as a str. A tool error (an MCP error result, or a Promptise {"error": {"code": ..., "message": ...}} envelope) raises in the program, with the server's code and message (RuntimeError: MCPToolError: NOT_FOUND: ...). Python tools are not decoded: a str they return stays a str. A ToolError raised by a @tool raises in the program the same way (RuntimeError: FunctionToolError: TOOL_ERROR: ...).

docs.title: The security model
docs.text:
The model writes code, so the code runs contained:

  • Hardened sandbox: the program executes in Promptise's Docker sandbox: read-only rootfs, dropped capabilities, Docker's default seccomp profile, CPU/memory/process limits, and network="none". The network stays off even when you pass your own sandbox={...} without a network key. When exec_timeout expires the program's processes are killed.
  • No direct host access: the program's only reach to the outside world is your tools, via the bridge. It can't touch the host filesystem or network.
  • Tools keep their protections: each bridged call invokes the real BaseTool on the host. If you wrapped tools with an approval gate (build_agent(..., approval=...)), bridged calls trigger it too. When you run the agent under the Agent Runtime, its governance hooks (budget / health / audit) apply to each bridged call. Without the runtime, a plain agent has no budget hook attached, so code-action enforces its own hard, hook-independent max_tool_calls cap on each program (default 50) so a generated program can never loop a tool unbounded (see The tool-call budget).

Honest enterprise note

The bridge is a deliberate capability hole: the program can call any tool the agent has, programmatically. The containment (above) means the model's code can't escape; it does not make your tools safe on its own. For untrusted input or multi-tenant use: keep code-action's tool set least-privilege, wrap mutating tools with approval, set max_tool_calls conservatively, and prefer the gVisor backend (sandbox={"backend": "gvisor", "network": "none"}) for kernel-level isolation. There is no per-run cost budget unless you run under the Agent Runtime. That, and a global concurrency limit on sandbox sessions, are the pieces to add before high-throughput untrusted production.

graph LR
    M[LLM writes 1 program] --> P["program (in sandbox, no network)"]
    P -->|"req file"| B[host bridge loop]
    B -->|"real tool + hooks"| T[your BaseTool]
    T -->|"resp file"| P
    P -->|"RESULT: ..."| A[answer]
    style P fill:#2d1b4e,stroke:#c084fc,color:#fff
    style B fill:#1e3a5f,stroke:#60a5fa,color:#fff

docs.title: How the bridge works
docs.text:
The program runs inside the container while a host loop services its tool calls over the writable /workspace tmpfs:

  1. The generated promptise_tools.py turns each of your tools into a stub: it writes a request file (req_<id>.json) and blocks.
  2. A concurrent host loop sees the request, runs the real tool (with hooks), and writes the response (resp_<id>.json + a .done marker so reads never race a partial write).
  3. The stub unblocks and returns the value to the program.

No network is involved, the channel is the shared filesystem, which is why the sandbox can stay fully network-isolated.

docs.title: Repair on failure
docs.text: If the program crashes, code-action feeds the stderr back to the model for a bounded number of fixes (max_repairs, default 1) before giving up. This recovers the common "off-by-one in the parsing" class of errors without an unbounded loop. A program that reaches the tool-call budget is a failure too (below). When no repair is left, the node fails and the run raises GraphExecutionError (CodeActionBudgetError when the budget was the reason); ExecutionReport.error says why the last program failed.

docs.title: The tool-call budget
docs.text:
max_tool_calls (default 50) caps the tool calls of each program:

  • Every call counts: successful ones, failed ones (a tool that raised, an MCP error), calls to an unknown tool, and calls a pre_tool hook blocked.
  • Reaching it is an error, never a quiet result. Once a program has made max_tool_calls calls, its next call raises ToolBudgetExceeded (a RuntimeError, importable in the program) without running the tool, and so does every later call. The node logs a warning, and the program's output is discarded, even if the program caught the error and printed an answer: it is incomplete.
  • The model is never asked to fit the data to the cap. The prompt says each program has a cap on function calls, but not its value, and tells the model to use all the data the question needs: never skip, sample or truncate records, never count its own calls or stop early, and let ToolBudgetExceeded raise. (Told "at most N calls", models wrote if calls >= N: break or orders[:N-1], and the partial result came back as the answer.) The error a refused call raises in the program does not give the value either.
  • A repair must do the whole job. After a program reaches the cap, the model is asked for a program that does the whole job with fewer calls (a tool that returns many records at once, no repeated fetches), never one over part of the data, or to reply CANNOT_FINISH_WITHIN_CALL_CAP if it can't. The repaired program gets its own max_tool_calls, so a run makes at most (max_repairs + 1) × max_tool_calls calls. When an answer comes from a program written after a budget hit, a warning is logged on promptise.engine.code_action.
  • A job that doesn't fit fails. If the model replies CANNOT_FINISH_WITHIN_CALL_CAP, or the last program also reaches the cap, the run raises CodeActionBudgetError (a GraphExecutionError, so existing handlers still catch it) with max_tool_calls, attempts and the report; ExecutionReport.error names max_tool_calls. Raise max_tool_calls, or give the agent a tool that returns many records per call.
from promptise.engine import CodeActionBudgetError

try:
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}]})
except CodeActionBudgetError as exc:
    print(f"needs more than {exc.max_tool_calls} tool calls per program")

What Promptise can and can't check

Promptise sees every call a program makes, so a program that reaches the cap is always caught, even if it catches the error. It cannot see whether a program that finished within the cap read all the data: a model that ignores the instructions and slices the data itself still returns a partial answer. Hiding the cap's value and forbidding truncation makes that unlikely (it removes the number a model would fit to); set max_tool_calls well above the calls the job needs.

ExecutionReport.tool_calls (engine.last_report when you run the graph with PromptGraphEngine, exc.report on an engine exception) counts the calls the programs made, failed ones included; refused calls never ran and are not counted.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
From build_agent, pass code_action= (a dict or a promptise.engine.CodeActionConfig; unknown keys are rejected):

agent = await build_agent(
    servers=my_servers,
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    agent_pattern="code-action",
    code_action={
        "exec_timeout": 60,    # seconds the program may run (default 120)
        "max_repairs": 2,      # self-repair attempts after a failed program (default 1)
        "max_tool_calls": 20,  # hard cap on each program's bridged tool calls (default 50)
    },
    sandbox={"memory_limit": "1G"},  # optional; network stays "none"
)

For a custom graph, use the factory directly:

from promptise.engine import PromptGraph

PromptGraph.code_action(
    tools=my_tools,
    system_prompt="",
    sandbox_factory=...,   # async () -> sandbox session; build_agent injects one, a custom graph supplies its own
    max_repairs=1,         # self-repair attempts after a failed program
    exec_timeout=120,      # seconds the program may run inside the sandbox
    max_tool_calls=50,     # hard cap on each program's bridged tool calls
)

docs.title: Honest limits
docs.text:
• Needs Docker. build_agent(agent_pattern="code-action") raises a clear error if a sandbox can't be initialized, there is no silent fallback, because running model-written code outside a sandbox would be unsafe.
  • Latency floor. Each program runs in a fresh container: starting it, running the program and removing it takes about 1 s on a warm Docker host, plus the program's own time (each repair adds another container, and build_agent starts one once to check the sandbox works). The token and accuracy wins dominate on real aggregation tasks, but for a one-shot lookup a plain react call is snappier.
  • Not magic on reasoning. Code-action makes the computation exact; it does not make the model's plan smarter. If the task is ambiguous, clarify it first.

docs.title: Context Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
The single biggest reason long-running agents get slow, expensive, and wrong is context bloat. Every tool call appends its request and result to the transcript. On a deep task the model ends up re-reading a growing wall of its own past calls, it loses the thread, re-queries facts it already has, and pays for thousands of redundant tokens on every turn.

Promptise bounds this for you: the default agent compacts a tool loop once it gets long, and you can tune or turn that off, or choose per node how much history it sees. This guide shows the problem, how compaction works, the modes of context_scope, the two ready-made patterns built on them, and a decision table for picking the right one.

Runnable example

Everything here is demonstrated end-to-end in examples/reasoning/verify_and_managed.py. Real LLM calls, just set OPENAI_API_KEY.

docs.title: The problem: transcripts grow, models drown
docs.text:
A naive tool-calling loop feeds the model the entire conversation on every turn:

turn 1:  [system, user]
turn 2:  [system, user, ai→tool, tool_result]
turn 3:  [system, user, ai→tool, tool_result, ai→tool, tool_result]
...
turn 12: [system, user, + 22 more messages]   ← the model re-reads ALL of this

For a task that needs ~13 distinct facts, a naive loop can make dozens of tool calls, repeatedly looking up the same employee or record because the relevant result is buried far back in the transcript. Tokens grow super-linearly, latency climbs, and accuracy can drop as the signal gets lost in the middle.

docs.title: The lever: context_scope on PromptNode
docs.text:
Every PromptNode accepts a context_scope argument controlling what it sees on each LLM call. A node you create yourself defaults to "full"; the default ReAct agent that build_agent() builds uses "auto".

Mode What the node sees Use it for "full" (PromptNode default) The whole accumulated transcript Short tasks, or when every prior message matters "auto" (the ReAct default) "full" while the tool loop is short, then the compacted view once the run has 6 tool results (or passes a token budget) The default: simple tasks are unchanged, deep tool loops stay bounded "ledger" The compacted view on every call Long single-node tool loops that gather many facts then aggregate "scoped" Pinned messages + the current question + only its own in-progress tool loop Multi-stage reasoning graphs: drops the verbose output of other stages so tokens don't grow across stages 
from promptise.engine import PromptNode

# Multi-stage graph: each stage only sees its own working set.
PromptNode("analyze", instructions="...", context_scope="scoped")

# Deep tool loop: compact from the first call.
PromptNode("reason", inject_tools=True, context_scope="ledger")

docs.title: How compaction works
docs.text:
Once a node compacts ("ledger", or "auto" past its threshold), each model call gets a bounded view instead of the transcript:

  1. Pinned, always sent: every system message in the input, such as instructions you or the runtime added ([Context State], mission, budget), and the node's own system prompt.
  2. Earlier conversation: chat history before the current question (what agent.chat() loads from the session) becomes a short note: the last 6 messages, 400 characters each.
  3. The current question, exactly as you passed it. A {"role": "user", ...} dict, a HumanMessage and a ("user", ...) tuple all work: input messages are converted to LangChain messages first.
  4. The latest exchange, verbatim: the model's last tool call(s) and their results, so it sees the outcome of its last action in flow. A parallel batch is kept whole.
  5. A ledger of older results, last: one line per earlier tool(args), last value wins per (tool, args). A result longer than 2,000 characters is cut to its first 2,000 with a note that says how much was cut and that the model may call the tool once more for the rest. A call the model made more than once is shown in full from then on, so a result it fetched again for its full text is not cut again (with max_tokens, such results are the last to shrink). Results already shown in the latest exchange are not repeated. The ledger's header tells the model to use these facts and call again only for a cut result or when it is waiting for something to change, such as a job's status.

No LLM summarization

Compaction is deterministic: it cuts and drops, it never asks a model to summarize, and it costs no extra calls. A fact in the part of an old result that was cut is only back in view if the model calls the tool again. If your tools return large results that must stay verbatim, raise keep_result_chars, return leaner results (a summary tool instead of a raw dump), or turn compaction off.

docs.title: Repeated calls run the tool
docs.text:
Compaction changes what the model sees, never what a tool call does. When the model calls a tool again with the same arguments, the tool runs again: a job's status, a health check or a queue length can change between two calls, so an agent that polls queue_status(job_id) sees the job complete. The ledger shows the model the facts it already has, each as it was when its call ran, so it has no reason to fetch a fact again unless the value can change.

A model that keeps repeating a call is stopped by the node's iteration limit (max_iterations; 15 on the ReAct agent's reason node, or the run's max_agent_iterations when that is lower). A run stopped that way in the middle of a tool loop raises GraphIterationLimitError (a GraphExecutionError); it never returns the last tool result as the answer.

For tools whose result cannot change during a run, such as a lookup by id, you can have a repeated call answered from the earlier result instead of running the tool:

from promptise.engine import ContextCompaction

agent = await build_agent(
    ...,
    context_compaction=ContextCompaction(reuse_results=["get_employee", "lookup_*"]),
)

reuse_results takes tool names (* wildcards allowed), or True for every tool; it is False by default. It applies once the node compacts, to a call with the same tool and arguments as an earlier successful call in the run, and returns that call's latest result. A failed call is never reused. A reused call is reported like any other, marked as reused: trace_tools prints ↺ Reusing an earlier result for tool: ..., the observer timeline and observe=True record it with reused: true in the metadata, LangChain callbacks get its start and end with metadata["promptise_reused"], engine hooks get on_tool_reused, and astream_with_tools() ends it with a ToolEndEvent whose reused is True.

Only for results that cannot change

Never list a status, health, queue or search tool. MCP's idempotentHint says that repeating a call has no further side effects, not that it returns the same result, so no tool annotation turns reuse on.

docs.title: Tune it, or turn it off
docs.text:
build_agent(context_compaction=...) sets compaction for the whole agent:

from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.engine import ContextCompaction

# Never compact: the model always sees the full transcript.
agent = await build_agent(..., context_compaction=False)

# Compact after 10 tool results instead of 6.
agent = await build_agent(..., context_compaction=10)

# Full control.
agent = await build_agent(
    ...,
    context_compaction=ContextCompaction(
        after_tool_results=10,     # "auto" threshold
        keep_result_chars=8_000,   # older results longer than this are cut
        max_tokens=60_000,         # also compact past this many tokens, and
                                   # shrink the ledger until the view fits
        history_messages=6,        # earlier messages in the history note
        history_chars=400,         # characters per earlier message
        reuse_results=False,       # see "Repeated calls run the tool"
    ),
)

False keeps "auto" nodes on the full transcript; nodes you set to "ledger" or "scoped" keep that choice. A node's own PromptNode(compaction=...) wins over the agent's setting.

With a ContextEngine, the budget the engine has left after your instructions and tool definitions becomes max_tokens, so the engine keeps bounding the context on every call of the tool loop, not only the first.

See Context scope for the node-level reference.

docs.title: Two ready-made patterns
docs.text: You rarely need to wire a node by hand, two built-in agent_pattern values package these levers for the common cases.

docs.title: verify: accuracy via a one-turn self-check
docs.text:
A single node that must plan, solve, and re-check its own answer within one generation. You get the accuracy benefit of an explicit verification step at one-turn latency, no multi-call pipeline.

from promptise import build_agent

agent = await build_agent(
    servers={},                      # no tools needed for pure reasoning
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    agent_pattern="verify",
    instructions="Give only the final answer at the end.",
)

result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [
    {"role": "user", "content":
     "A bat and a ball cost $1.10. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. "
     "How much is the ball?"}
]})
# The VERIFY step catches the intuitive-but-wrong $0.10 and corrects to $0.05.

Honest scope

verify helps where a single pass makes careless errors that a forced self-check catches. A model that already reasons carefully may gain little over a plain prompt, so treat it as a cheap safety net and measure it on your own questions.

docs.title: managed: efficiency for deep tool chains
docs.text:
A single tool-using node run with context_scope="ledger". Best for traversing a database or graph: gather many facts, then aggregate.

from promptise import build_agent

agent = await build_agent(
    servers={"company": my_server_spec},  # or pass extra_tools=[...]
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    agent_pattern="managed",
    instructions=(
        "Answer by calling tools. A ledger of facts you already gathered is "
        "provided each turn, consult it and don't re-fetch a fact you have "
        "unless you are waiting for it to change (a job's status, for example)."
    ),
    max_agent_iterations=30,          # the run's cap on node executions
)

Under build_agent, max_agent_iterations is the managed node's budget and the run's: max_agent_iterations=30 allows 30 model calls (the default is 25). PromptGraph.managed(...) run with PromptGraphEngine uses its own budget of 30 model calls (max_node_iterations= on the factory changes it).

Honest scope

managed is an efficiency primitive. On long chains it bounds token growth; whether it also cuts tool calls depends on the model (see the note on managed). It does not by itself make the model's final answer more correct; for computing over many facts, see code-action.

docs.title: Which one should I use?
docs.text: Situation Reach for Short Q&A, short tool loops Default react (context_scope="auto": full until the loop gets long) Every tool result must stay verbatim build_agent(..., context_compaction=False) One question that's easy to get subtly wrong verify A long tool chain over a dataset (gather → aggregate) managed A multi-stage custom graph where stages pile up tokens A custom graph with context_scope="scoped" on each stage You need both bounded context and a custom topology Build a custom graph and set context_scope per node

docs.title: Composing it yourself
docs.text:
context_scope is a node-level primitive, drop it onto any node in a custom graph, mixing modes per stage:

from promptise.engine import PromptGraph, PromptNode

graph = PromptGraph("research", mode="static")
graph.add_node(PromptNode("gather", inject_tools=True, context_scope="ledger",
                          instructions="Gather the facts with the tools, then summarize them."))
graph.add_node(PromptNode("write", context_scope="scoped",
                          inherit_context_from="gather", default_next="__end__"))
graph.sequential("gather", "write")
graph.set_entry("gather")

agent = await build_agent(servers=my_servers, model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
                          agent_pattern=graph)

Here gather runs a bounded tool loop (ledger), then write sees only the distilled output it inherits plus the task (scoped), neither stage drowns in the other's raw messages.

docs.title: Key takeaways
docs.text:
• Context is a resource to manage, not a side effect. On deep tasks it is the deciding factor for cost, latency, and reliability.
  • The default agent compacts long tool loops ("auto"): short tasks see the full transcript; past 6 tool results the model sees the pinned messages, the current question, its latest exchange and a ledger. Tune it with context_compaction, or set it to False.
  • Compaction never drops the question or your system messages, and it never summarizes with a model: older results are cut, not rewritten.
  • A repeated call runs the tool, so a status the agent polls is current. Answering repeats from the earlier result is an opt-in for lookups whose result cannot change (reuse_results), and it is never silent.
  • verify is the accuracy lever; managed is the efficiency lever. Be honest about which problem you have, they solve different ones.
