docs.title: Advanced MCP Server Patterns
docs.text: Patterns for evolving, composing, and extending MCP servers: tool versioning for backwards compatibility, controlling which tools each caller sees, server composition for gateways, OpenAPI bridging, batch execution, streaming results, elicitation, and sampling.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: You ship search to production and agents depend on its arguments. Now you want to add a filters parameter without breaking the agents that use the old shape.

docs.title: @server.tool(version=...)
docs.text:
Register each version of the tool with version=. Every version is served under a pinned name, search_v1_0 and search_v2_0, and the bare name search runs the highest version:

from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer

server = MCPServer(name="search-api")

DOCS = [{"id": 1, "title": "Refund policy", "score": 0.9}, {"id": 2, "title": "Shipping", "score": 0.4}]

@server.tool(version="1.0")
async def search(query: str) -> list[dict]:
    """Full-text search."""
    return [d for d in DOCS if query.lower() in d["title"].lower()]

@server.tool(version="2.0")
async def search(query: str, min_score: float = 0.0) -> list[dict]:
    """Full-text search with an optional minimum score."""
    return [d for d in DOCS if query.lower() in d["title"].lower() and d["score"] >= min_score]

# tools/list: search (runs 2.0), search_v1_0, search_v2_0

An agent that binds to search_v1_0 keeps the old contract when you ship 3.0; agents that use search move to each new version. How it behaves:

  • Pinned names are <name>_v<version>, with every run of characters other than letters and digits replaced by _ ("2.1-beta" gives search_v2_1_beta). They use only characters LLM providers accept in function names, so agents can call them. MCP has no per-tool version field, so the version lives in the name.
  • The bare name is a copy of the highest version: same description, schema, guards and settings. Versions are compared numerically per dot-separated part: "2.0" > "1.0", "1.10" > "1.9" (a non-numeric part counts as 0), not by registration order.
  • Each version is its own tool: its own input schema and validation, auth, roles, rate_limit and other options, as given on its decorator.
  • Every registration of a versioned name needs version=. Registering the same version twice, a version next to an unversioned tool of the same name (in either order), or a version with no letter or digit raises ValueError.
  • Routers: @router.tool(version=...) works the same; the router's prefix applies to all names (billing_charge, billing_charge_v1_0).

New optional parameters with defaults (like min_score above) are backwards compatible on their own: an agent that doesn't send them gets the old behaviour, so a version is only needed for a breaking change (a renamed or removed parameter, a different result shape).

docs.title: VersionedToolRegistry
docs.text:
VersionedToolRegistry is the registry behind version= (server._tool_versions). It also works on its own for code that keeps several ToolDef versions under one base name, for example a gateway that builds its own tool list, and resolves name@version there:

from promptise.mcp.server import VersionedToolRegistry, ToolDef

async def handler(query: str) -> list:
    return []

v1 = ToolDef(name="search_v1_0", description="v1", handler=handler, input_schema={"type": "object"})
v2 = ToolDef(name="search_v2_0", description="v2", handler=handler, input_schema={"type": "object"})

vr = VersionedToolRegistry()
vr.register("search", "1.0", v1)
vr.register("search", "2.0", v2)

print(vr.get("search").description)      # "v2": the highest version
print(vr.get("search@1.0").description)  # "v1"
print(vr.list_versions("search"))        # ["1.0", "2.0"]
print(vr.has("search"))                  # True
print(len(vr.list_all()))                # 2: every registered version

Registering the same version twice raises ValueError; get() returns None for an unknown name or version. Registering a ToolDef in a registry you created yourself does not serve it; use @server.tool(version=...) for that.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: You want different agents to discover different tools: prefixed names, hidden admin tools, only public tools, descriptions rewritten for one audience.

docs.title: server.add_transform()
docs.text:
A transform changes the tool list clients discover. server.add_transform(transform) adds one; transforms run in the order they were added, on every tools/list and on the docs://manifest resource, each on the output of the previous one (after hide_unauthorized_tools filtering).

from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer, NamespaceTransform, TagFilterTransform

server = MCPServer(name="analytics")

@server.tool(tags=["public"])
async def query(sql: str) -> list[dict]:
    """Run a read-only query."""
    return []

@server.tool(tags=["admin"], roles=["admin"])
async def reset() -> str:
    """Reset the warehouse."""
    return "reset"

server.add_transform(TagFilterTransform(required_tags={"public"}))
server.add_transform(NamespaceTransform(prefix="analytics"))
# tools/list: analytics_query
Transform What it does NamespaceTransform(prefix) Lists every tool as <prefix>_<name>. A call by the prefixed name runs the tool; the registered name keeps working too. TagFilterTransform(required_tags) Lists only tools with at least one of the tags. VisibilityTransform(hidden={name: predicate}) Leaves out a tool when predicate(ctx) returns true. A predicate that raises hides its tool.

Each transform receives the listing request's context. When the server has an AuthMiddleware, the context is authenticated from the request's headers first, so ctx.client_id, ctx.client and ctx.state["roles"] describe the caller (they are empty for a caller whose credentials don't verify):

from promptise.mcp.server import APIKeyAuth, AuthMiddleware, VisibilityTransform

server.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware(APIKeyAuth({"sk-ops": "ops", "sk-bi": "bi-team"})))
server.add_transform(VisibilityTransform(hidden={"analytics_reset": lambda ctx: ctx.client_id != "ops"}))

Transforms change discovery, not access

A tool a transform leaves out can still be called by its name: a client with an old tool list, or one that guesses the name, reaches it. Put access decisions in guards (roles=, guards=), as reset above does with roles=["admin"], and use transforms to keep each caller's list short and relevant. MCPServer(hide_unauthorized_tools=True) lists only the tools a caller's guards allow, without a transform.

docs.title: Writing a transform
docs.text:
A transform is any object with apply(tools: list[ToolDef], ctx: RequestContext | None = None) -> list[ToolDef] (the ToolTransform protocol); apply may be async. Return copies made with dataclasses.replace, never change the definitions you receive. A transform that renames tools also defines resolve_name(name) -> str | None, which returns the registered name for a listed one (or None when the name is not one of its renamings), so that calls by the listed name reach the tool:

from dataclasses import replace

from promptise.mcp.server import RequestContext, ToolDef

class AudienceNote:
    """Add a note for one audience to every description."""

    def apply(self, tools: list[ToolDef], ctx: RequestContext | None = None) -> list[ToolDef]:
        return [replace(t, description=f"{t.description} Results are in EUR.") for t in tools]

server.add_transform(AudienceNote())

The transform classes also work on their own, on any ToolDef list (a custom gateway, tests): TagFilterTransform(required_tags={"public"}).apply(tools).

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: Your company has separate teams building separate MCP servers: payments, users, analytics. You want to expose them all through a single gateway server so agents only connect to one endpoint.

docs.title: mount()
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer, mount

# Team 1: Payment tools
payments = MCPServer(name="payments")

@payments.tool()
async def charge(customer_id: str, amount_cents: int) -> dict:
    """Charge a customer's payment method."""
    return await stripe.charge(customer_id, amount_cents)

@payments.tool()
async def refund(charge_id: str) -> dict:
    """Refund a charge."""
    return await stripe.refund(charge_id)

# Team 2: User tools
users = MCPServer(name="users")

@users.tool()
async def get_user(user_id: str) -> dict:
    """Get user profile."""
    return await db.get_user(user_id)

@users.tool()
async def update_user(user_id: str, name: str | None = None) -> dict:
    """Update user profile."""
    return await db.update_user(user_id, name=name)

# Gateway: compose into one server
gateway = MCPServer(name="api-gateway", version="1.0.0")
mount(gateway, payments, prefix="pay")
mount(gateway, users, prefix="usr")

# Agents see: pay_charge, pay_refund, usr_get_user, usr_update_user
if __name__ == "__main__":
    gateway.run(transport="http", port=8080)

docs.title: What gets mounted
docs.text:
mount() copies everything from the child into the parent:

Registry Behavior Tools Names prefixed with {prefix}_ Resources Copied as-is (no prefix) Prompts Copied as-is Exception handlers Merged into parent Input models Re-mapped to prefixed tool names docs://manifest Skipped (the parent serves its own)

mount(parent, child, *, prefix="", tags=None) returns the number of tools mounted. It copies the child's registrations at the time you call it; later registrations on the child are not seen. Each copy keeps its auth, roles, guards and router middleware.

The child's server middleware is not mounted

Middleware added with child.add_middleware(...) (authentication, rate limits, audit) does not come along: mounted tools run through the parent's middleware chain. Add the middleware to the gateway. Name clashes (two tools with the same final name) raise ValueError.

docs.title: Adding tags during mount
docs.text:
# Tag all payment tools for filtering
mount(gateway, payments, prefix="pay", tags=["payment", "billing"])
mount(gateway, users, prefix="usr", tags=["user-management"])

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text:
You have an existing REST API with an OpenAPI (or Swagger 2) spec and want agents to call it through MCP.

OpenAPIProvider registers one tool per operation. Each tool's input schema is the operation's parameters (path-level ones included) plus its JSON request body, with every $ref inlined; calls are validated against it and each argument is sent where the spec puts it: path (URL-encoded), query, header, cookie or body. Arguments the caller leaves out are not sent, so the API applies its own defaults.

import os

from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer, OpenAPIProvider

server = MCPServer(name="petstore-bridge")
provider = OpenAPIProvider(
    "./openapi.json",
    prefix="pets_",
    auth_header=("Authorization", "Bearer " + os.environ["PETSTORE_TOKEN"]),
)
count = provider.register(server)   # one tool per operation

Annotations come from the HTTP method: GET/HEAD are read-only, DELETE is destructive, GET/HEAD/PUT/DELETE are idempotent, and every tool has open_world_hint=True; the title is the operation's summary. A JSON object body contributes its properties as arguments (a parameter with the same name wins); any other JSON body (an array, a string) is the single body argument. Only application/json bodies are mapped. The tool returns the response's JSON, or {"status": ..., "body": ...} when the response is not JSON, whatever the status code.

For a curated, typed server (descriptions written for agents, selected operations, generated tests), use MCPcast (promptise mcpcast ./openapi.yaml) instead.

OpenAPIProvider(spec, *, base_url=None, prefix="", include=None, exclude=None, auth_header=None, tags=None) and provider.register(server) -> int (the number of tools):

Parameter Default Description spec (required) URL (fetched with httpx), file path (JSON, or YAML with .yaml/.yml), JSON string, or dict base_url From spec Override the API base URL (servers[0].url, or Swagger schemes/host/basePath) prefix "" Prepended to tool names as given (include your own _) include All Only these operation IDs exclude None Skip these operation IDs auth_header None (header_name, value) sent on every request tags [] Tags for all generated tools

Tool names are the operationId (or <method>_<path>) with - and / replaced by _. A spec URL or base URL that resolves to a private or loopback address is refused.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: An agent needs to fetch 20 user profiles. Without batching, that's 20 sequential MCP round-trips. With a batch tool, it's one request that executes all 20 in parallel.

docs.title: register_batch_tool()
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer, register_batch_tool

server = MCPServer(name="user-api")

@server.tool()
async def get_user(user_id: str) -> dict:
    """Get a user by ID."""
    return await db.get_user(user_id)

@server.tool()
async def get_team(team_id: str) -> dict:
    """Get a team by ID."""
    return await db.get_team(team_id)

# Register the batch meta-tool
register_batch_tool(server, name="batch_call", max_parallel=10)

Agents call it like this:

{
  "tool": "batch_call",
  "arguments": {
    "calls": [
      {"tool": "get_user", "args": {"user_id": "u-001"}},
      {"tool": "get_user", "args": {"user_id": "u-002"}},
      {"tool": "get_team", "args": {"team_id": "t-100"}}
    ]
  }
}

Response:

[
  {"tool": "get_user", "status": "ok", "result": ["..."]},
  {"tool": "get_user", "status": "ok", "result": ["..."]},
  {"tool": "get_team", "status": "ok", "result": ["..."]}
]

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description name "batch_call" Name of the batch tool description "Execute multiple tool calls in parallel." Description max_parallel 10 Maximum concurrent executions

register_batch_tool(server, *, name="batch_call", description="Execute multiple tool calls in parallel.", max_parallel=10). A batch larger than max_parallel * 2 calls is refused with a single {"status": "error", "error": "Batch size ... exceeds max ..."} entry. Each sub-call runs through the server's full pipeline (middleware, guards, validation) with the caller's request headers, so authentication and permissions apply per sub-call. Failed individual calls return {"tool": ..., "status": "error", "error": "..."} without failing the batch; result holds the text of each content item.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: Your tool processes a large dataset or streams search results. Instead of accumulating everything in memory and returning a flat dict, you build up results incrementally and return them with metadata.

docs.title: StreamingResult
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer, StreamingResult

server = MCPServer(name="search-api")

@server.tool()
async def search_products(
    query: str,
    max_results: int = 50,
) -> StreamingResult:
    """Search the product catalog.

    Returns results as they're found, with search metadata.
    """
    result = StreamingResult()
    result.set_metadata("query", query)

    async for hit in catalog.stream_search(query):
        result.add({
            "id": hit.id,
            "name": hit.name,
            "price": hit.price,
            "score": hit.relevance_score,
        })
        if len(result) >= max_results:
            break

    result.set_metadata("total_available", await catalog.count(query))
    return result

The framework serializes StreamingResult as JSON:

{
  "items": [
    {"id": "p-001", "name": "Widget", "price": 999, "score": 0.95},
    {"id": "p-002", "name": "Gadget", "price": 1499, "score": 0.87}
  ],
  "count": 2,
  "metadata": {
    "query": "electronics",
    "total_available": 1250
  }
}

docs.title: Batch adding
docs.text:
result = StreamingResult()

# Add one at a time
result.add({"id": 1, "name": "Alice"})

# Add many at once
result.add_many([
    {"id": 2, "name": "Bob"},
    {"id": 3, "name": "Charlie"},
])

# Attach metadata
result.set_metadata("source", "users_table")
result.set_metadata("cached", False)

len(result)         # → 3
result.items        # → [{"id": 1, ...}, {"id": 2, ...}, {"id": 3, ...}]
result.metadata     # → {"source": "users_table", "cached": False}

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: Your tool is about to deploy to production or delete data. You want to ask the user for confirmation during tool execution, not before.

docs.title: Elicitor
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer, Elicitor, Depends

server = MCPServer(name="deploy-api")

@server.tool()
async def deploy_to_production(
    service: str,
    version: str,
    elicit: Elicitor = Depends(Elicitor),
) -> dict:
    """Deploy a service version to production.

    Asks the user for confirmation before proceeding.
    """
    # Show what's about to happen and ask for confirmation
    answer = await elicit.ask(
        message=(
            f"About to deploy {service} v{version} to production.\n"
            f"Current production version: {await get_current_version(service)}\n"
            f"Confirm deployment?"
        ),
        schema={
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "confirm": {
                    "type": "boolean",
                    "description": "Set to true to proceed with deployment",
                },
                "reason": {
                    "type": "string",
                    "description": "Optional: reason for deployment",
                },
            },
            "required": ["confirm"],
        },
    )

    if not answer or not answer.get("confirm"):
        return {"status": "cancelled", "reason": (answer or {}).get("reason", "User declined")}

    deploy_id = await deploy(service, version)
    return {"status": "deployed", "deploy_id": deploy_id, "version": version}

docs.title: Graceful degradation
docs.text:
ask() sends the request through the SDK's ServerSession.elicit, waits up to its timeout (default from the Elicitor), and returns the response content only when the user accepts. If the client does not support elicitation (not all MCP clients do), declines, cancels, or the request times out, ask() returns None and logs the reason at WARNING. Design your tools to handle this:

@server.tool()
async def delete_project(project_id: str, elicit: Elicitor = Depends(Elicitor)) -> dict:
    """Delete a project after the user confirms."""
    answer = await elicit.ask(
        f"Delete project {project_id}?",
        schema={"type": "object", "properties": {"confirm": {"type": "boolean"}}, "required": ["confirm"]},
    )
    if answer is None:
        # The client can't elicit, or the user declined: don't act
        return {"error": "This action requires confirmation. Please confirm and retry."}
    if not answer.get("confirm"):
        return {"status": "cancelled"}
    return {"status": "deleted", "project_id": project_id}

elicit.last_failure says why the last ask() returned None (for example "the client did not declare the elicitation capability" or "the client answered 'decline'"), so a tool can tell the user.

ask(message, schema=None, *, timeout=None); without a schema the request is a bare confirmation (an empty object form). Over the initialize handshake, elicitation needs a session that can send requests to the client, so it doesn't work for handshake clients of a server served with asgi_app(stateless=True). 2026-07-28 clients are asked in input rounds instead: see Elicitation on the 2026-07-28 protocol.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Parameter Default Description timeout 60.0 Seconds to wait for user response (handshake connections only)

docs.title: Elicitation on the 2026-07-28 protocol
docs.text:
How ask() reaches the client depends on the protocol version the client connected with (on the mcp 2.x SDK; with the 1.x SDK every client uses the handshake):

Connection What ask() does Per-session state (SessionState) initialize handshake (1.x clients, Promptise's MCPClient, 2.x clients with mode="legacy") Sends elicitation/create and waits up to timeout for the answer Kept for the connection 2026-07-28 (2.x clients by default) Ends the call with an InputRequiredResult holding the question; the client asks its user and calls the tool again with the answer, and the tool runs again from the start, where ask() now returns the answer None: the tool answers SESSION_REQUIRED A stateless server (asgi_app(stateless=True)) with a handshake client No elicitation (no way back to the client): ask() returns None None: the tool answers SESSION_REQUIRED

On 2026-07-28, the tool runs once per question, so code before ask() runs again on every round. Put side effects after the answer:

@server.tool()
async def delete_project(project_id: str, elicit: Elicitor = Depends(Elicitor)) -> str:
    """Delete a project after the user confirms."""
    project = await load_project(project_id)          # read-only: fine to repeat
    answer = await elicit.ask(f"Delete {project.name}?", schema=CONFIRM)
    if not answer or not answer.get("confirm"):
        return f"Not deleted: {elicit.last_failure or 'not confirmed'}"
    await really_delete(project_id)                   # runs once, after the answer
    return "Deleted"

A tool that asks several questions takes one round per question. The answers to earlier questions travel in the result's request_state, which the server encrypts and binds to the tool, its arguments and the server's name (the SDK's RequestStateBoundary), so a client can only send back state this server minted for that call. By default the key is made at startup and held by the process: a round answered by another worker, or after a restart, is refused with Invalid or expired requestState. With several workers or replicas, share a key:

from mcp.server.request_state import RequestStateSecurity

server = MCPServer(
    name="deploy-api",
    request_state_security=RequestStateSecurity(keys=[os.environ["MCP_STATE_KEY"]]),  # 32+ bytes
)

A client that did not declare the elicitation capability gets no question: ask() returns None and last_failure says why. The approval gate's ElicitationApprover works the same way: the client approves in an input round, and a client that can't answer is denied with that reason. Sampler is not available on 2026-07-28 (the spec deprecates sampling) and returns None with a warning.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: Your tool needs to call an LLM to process data (summarize text, classify content, extract entities) but the client controls which LLM to use. MCP sampling lets the server request completions through the client's model.

docs.title: Sampler
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer, Sampler, Depends

server = MCPServer(name="content-api")

@server.tool()
async def summarize_document(
    document_url: str,
    sampler: Sampler = Depends(Sampler),
) -> dict:
    """Summarize a document using the client's LLM.

    The server fetches the document; the client provides the model.
    """
    content = await fetch_document(document_url)

    summary = await sampler.create_message(
        messages=[
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize this document in 3 bullet points:\n\n{content[:5000]}"},
        ],
        max_tokens=500,
        system="You are a professional document summarizer. Be concise and factual.",
        temperature=0.3,
    )

    if summary is None:
        return {"error": "Sampling not supported by client"}

    return {
        "url": document_url,
        "summary": summary,
        "model": "client-provided",
    }

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
result = await sampler.create_message(
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}],
    max_tokens=1024,          # Maximum tokens to generate
    model="claude-sonnet-4-20250514",      # Model hint (client may ignore)
    system="You are...",      # System prompt
    temperature=0.7,          # Sampling temperature
    stop_sequences=["\n\n"],  # Stop sequences
)

The client controls which model actually runs. The model parameter is sent as a model preference hint; the client can override it based on cost, availability, or policy. Message roles other than "assistant" are sent as "user" (MCP sampling has no system role; use system=). create_message() returns the generated text, or None when the client doesn't support sampling or the request fails (logged at WARNING). Like elicitation, sampling needs a session that can send requests to the client.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: A client makes several calls in one conversation and a tool needs to remember something between them: a cart, a selected project, a cursor.

docs.title: SessionState
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer, SessionState, Depends

server = MCPServer(name="cart-api")

@server.tool()
async def add_item(item: str, session: SessionState = Depends(SessionState)) -> dict:
    """Add an item to this session's cart."""
    items = session.get("items", [])
    items.append(item)
    session.set("items", items)
    return {"count": len(items)}

@server.tool()
async def cart(session: SessionState = Depends(SessionState)) -> list[str]:
    """List the items in this session's cart."""
    return session.get("items", [])

SessionState is a small key-value store: get(key, default=None), set(key, value), delete(key), clear(), keys(), to_dict() and key in session. The server keeps one store per MCP connection (in a SessionManager), in memory.

Limits in 1.6.0

  • State lives in the server process: it is lost on restart and not shared between replicas or workers.
  • Stores are not removed when a session ends, so a long-running HTTP server keeps one per connection it has served. Don't put large values in it.
  • The store is keyed by the connection object's Python id(). After a connection is closed and garbage-collected, a later connection can receive the same id and see the old store. Don't keep secrets or per-user data that must not leak between sessions in SessionState; key such data by ctx.client.client_id in your own store instead.
  • Without a session (asgi_app(stateless=True), or TestClient) each call gets a fresh store.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: You want agents to introspect your server (discover all tools, their schemas, tags, auth requirements, and rate limits) without calling each tool individually.

docs.title: register_manifest()
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer, register_manifest

server = MCPServer(name="my-api", version="2.0.0", auto_manifest=False)

@server.tool(tags=["math"], roles=["user"])
async def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two numbers."""
    return a + b

@server.tool(tags=["math"], auth=True)
async def divide(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Divide two numbers."""
    return a / b

register_manifest(server)

# MCPServer(auto_manifest=True), the default, registers docs://manifest when the
# server is built. Call register_manifest() yourself only with auto_manifest=False.

Agents read the manifest via MCP's resource protocol:

{
  "server": {"name": "my-api", "version": "2.0.0", "instructions": null},
  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "add",
      "description": "Add two numbers.",
      "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"a": {"type": "integer"}, "b": {"type": "integer"}}},
      "tags": ["math"],
      "auth_required": true,
      "roles": ["user"],
      "guards": ["HasRole"]
    },
    {
      "name": "divide",
      "description": "Divide two numbers.",
      "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"a": {"type": "number"}, "b": {"type": "number"}}},
      "tags": ["math"],
      "auth_required": true
    }
  ],
  "resources": [],
  "resource_templates": [],
  "prompts": []
}

Each entry lists only the fields that apply: tags, auth_required, roles, guards (class names), rate_limit, timeout. With MCPServer(hide_unauthorized_tools=True) the manifest is filtered per caller like the lists.

docs.title: Programmatic access
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import build_manifest

manifest = build_manifest(server)
print(manifest["tools"])  # All registered tools with metadata

build_manifest(server, tools=None, *, resources=None, resource_templates=None, prompts=None): pass any of the lists to describe a subset instead of every registration.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: You're developing an MCP server and want to see changes immediately without restarting manually. Hot reload watches your Python files and restarts the server when you save.

docs.title: hot_reload()
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import MCPServer, hot_reload

server = MCPServer(name="dev-server")

@server.tool()
async def greet(name: str) -> str:
    """Greet someone."""
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    hot_reload(
        server,
        transport="http",
        port=8080,
        watch_dirs=["src/"],       # Directories to watch
        poll_interval=1.0,          # Check every second
    )

--- Starting server (pid will follow) ---
    Watching: src/
    Poll interval: 1.0s

MCP server running on http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp

--- Detected changes in 1 file(s) ---
    src/tools.py
--- Restarting server ---

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The parent process watches *.py files for modification time changes
  2. When a change is detected, the child server process is terminated
  3. A new child process is started with the updated code
  4. If the server crashes on startup (syntax error), it waits for the next file change

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description transport "http" Transport for the child server host "127.0.0.1" Bind host port 8080 Bind port watch_dirs ["."] Directories to watch poll_interval 1.0 Seconds between checks dashboard False Enable dashboard in child allowed_hosts None Host allow-list for the child (see Deployment) allowed_origins None Origin allow-list for the child

hot_reload() restarts the script you ran (sys.argv) in a child process, so call it from the if __name__ == "__main__": block of the file that defines the server. A child that exits with an error waits for the next file change before restarting. Changes are detected by modification time of *.py files under watch_dirs.

Development only

Hot reload is for development. In production, use a process manager like systemd, supervisord, or Kubernetes.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: You've built an MCP server in a Python module but don't want to add if __name__ == "__main__" boilerplate. The CLI serve command runs any server from the command line.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Run with stdio transport (default)
promptise serve myapp.server:server

# Run with HTTP transport
promptise serve myapp.server:server --transport http --port 8080

# With hot reload (development)
promptise serve myapp.server:server --transport http --reload

# With live dashboard
promptise serve myapp.server:server --transport http --dashboard

docs.title: Target format
docs.text:
The target uses module:attribute format:

# module.path:attribute_name
promptise serve myapp.server:server     # myapp/server.py → server variable
promptise serve myapp.api:app           # myapp/api.py → app variable
promptise serve tools:tool_server       # tools.py → tool_server variable

docs.title: CLI options
docs.text:
Flag Default Description --transport, -t stdio Transport: stdio, http, or sse --host 127.0.0.1 Bind host --port, -p 8080 Bind port --dashboard off Enable live dashboard (HTTP/SSE only; ignored with a warning on stdio) --reload off Enable hot reload --allowed-host HOST none Host header value to accept (repeatable); see Deployment --allowed-origin ORIGIN none Origin header value to accept for browser clients (repeatable; needs --allowed-host on a non-loopback bind)

The current directory is put on sys.path, so promptise serve server:server finds ./server.py. A target that is not module:attribute, can't be imported, or is not an MCPServer exits with code 1 and a message on stderr (stdout stays clean for the stdio protocol).

docs.title: Approval Gates (Server-Side HITL)
docs.text:
Human-in-the-loop enforced where the tool lives. A tool declared with requires_approval=True cannot execute (for any MCP client) until a human (or a policy acting for one) approves the call. Denied by default on timeout. Every outcome is visible to the audit chain.

Why server-side

Agent-side approval (ApprovalPolicy) governs Promptise agents, but an enterprise MCP server is called by clients the server team doesn't control. A gate in the server's middleware chain makes approval a property of the tool, not a courtesy of the caller.

docs.title: Declare, gate, done
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import (
    ApprovalGateMiddleware, AuthMiddleware, MCPServer, PendingApprover,
)

server = MCPServer(name="billing")
server.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware(auth))          # identity first
approver = PendingApprover(server, approver_role="approver")
server.add_middleware(ApprovalGateMiddleware(approver, timeout=300))

@server.tool(auth=True, requires_approval=True)
async def refund(order_id: str, amount: float) -> dict:
    """Refund an order — requires human sign-off."""
    ...

An ungated declaration refuses to build

If any tool declares requires_approval=True and no ApprovalGateMiddleware is installed, the server raises at build time (and TestClient raises on call). A declared approval that silently doesn't enforce would be worse than none.

Install the gate after AuthMiddleware so approval requests carry the verified caller identity (client id, tenant, JWT subject).

The gate checks the tool's guards first

Before requesting a human decision, the gate evaluates the tool's own guards (RequireAuth, HasRole, HasTenant, …). A caller the guards would reject is denied immediately and never reaches a reviewer, so unauthorized callers can't spam approvers or fill the pending queue. Pair requires_approval=True with auth=True/guards so there is an identity to check; a gated tool left fully unauthenticated can be triggered by any client (the server owner's explicit choice).

docs.title: Gate semantics: fail closed everywhere
docs.text:
Event Outcome Decision approved=True Call proceeds; approval logged Decision approved=False ApprovalDeniedError (APPROVAL_DENIED, not retryable); reviewer_id + approval_request_id in details, the reviewer's reason in the message No decision within timeout Denied by default (on_timeout="allow" opts out, explicitly) Decision carries modified_arguments Denied: the server-side gate cannot rewrite bound arguments, and executing the original args after a reviewer changed them would run something they didn't approve Handler crash Denied via the error pipeline

ApprovalGateMiddleware(handler, *, timeout=300.0, on_timeout="deny", include_arguments=True):

Parameter Default Description handler required A PendingApprover, an ElicitationApprover, any ApprovalHandler, or a bare callable returning bool / ApprovalDecision timeout 300.0 Seconds to wait for a decision on_timeout "deny" "allow" lets the call run when no decision arrives in time include_arguments True Show the validated arguments to reviewers; False for tools whose arguments are too sensitive

The gate only acts on tools declared with requires_approval=True; every other call passes through.

docs.title: PendingApprover: independent four-eyes review
docs.text:
PendingApprover(server=None, *, approver_role="approver", max_pending=100, max_pending_per_client=None, max_pending_per_tenant=None). Gated calls block in a pending store. A human holding approver_role reviews them through two auto-registered, role-guarded admin tools:

approvals_list()                          → pending requests: tool, args,
                                            caller, tenant, age
approvals_decide(request_id, approve,     → release or deny; the reviewer's
                 reason)                     client_id is recorded

Separation of duties is enforced: approvals_decide rejects an approval whose reviewer client_id equals the request's original caller: you cannot approve your own call, even if you also hold approver_role (denying your own is always allowed). The store is process-local (like the in-memory job queue); calls that outlive the gate timeout are denied by default. Three caps bound the store, and beyond any of them a call is denied immediately rather than parked:

Cap Counts Default max_pending every waiting call 100 max_pending_per_tenant calls whose tenant_id metadata (stamped by the gate from the authenticated client) is the same; requests without a tenant share one bucket none max_pending_per_client calls from one caller: caller_user_id, else the request's client_id / tenant_id metadata, else agent_id; anonymous callers share one bucket none

max_pending_per_client stops a single client from filling the queue for everyone else; max_pending_per_tenant is the cap that matters on a multi-tenant server, because the per-client cap counts client ids and a tenant holding several API keys could otherwise still take the whole store. The caps nest (max_pending_per_client ≤ max_pending_per_tenant ≤ max_pending, else the constructor raises ValueError) and the denial reason names the cap that was hit (per-tenant pending approval cap reached for tenant 'acme' (40 per tenant), per-client pending approval cap reached for 'alice' (20 per client)).

docs.title: ElicitationApprover: confirm with the human behind the client
docs.text:
ElicitationApprover(*, message_template=None). The message shown to the user defaults to "Approval required: call tool '{tool_name}' with arguments {arguments}. Approve?"; pass message_template with the same {tool_name} and {arguments} placeholders to change it. Uses MCP elicitation (ServerSession.elicit) to ask the calling client's user to confirm ({"approve": bool, "reason": str}). Right for destructive-but-personal operations ("really delete this?"). Fail-closed: if the transport has no live MCP session (e.g. TestClient), the client does not support elicitation, the user declines or cancels, or the request times out, the call is denied with a clear reason, never silently allowed. The denial is logged at WARNING with the cause, so an unexpected "client declined" is diagnosable.

Promptise's own clients answer through an approval handler. build_agent(approval=...) routes the request to the agent's handler, and MCPClient(elicitation_callback=approval_elicitation_callback(handler)) does the same without an agent. Without one they declare no elicitation support, and the call is denied. See Server-side approval gates.

docs.title: Callbacks and existing handlers: bring your own channel
docs.text:
The gate accepts any ApprovalHandler: the same protocol as agent-side approval, so the existing handlers plug in directly:

# Bare callable (bool or ApprovalDecision, sync or async)
ApprovalGateMiddleware(lambda request: request.arguments.get("amount", 0) < 100)

# The agent-side handlers work as-is:
from promptise.approval import WebhookApprovalHandler   # HMAC-signed + polling
ApprovalGateMiddleware(WebhookApprovalHandler(url="https://approvals.internal/hook",
                                              secret=os.environ["APPROVAL_SECRET"]))

docs.title: What reviewers see
docs.text: Each request is a promptise.approval.ApprovalRequest: tool name, the validated arguments (unless include_arguments=False), and metadata with client_id, tenant_id, JWT subject/issuer, and the MCP request id: enough to decide without grepping logs.

docs.title: Audit visibility
docs.text: Approval outcomes flow through the standard pipeline: a denial surfaces as a structured APPROVAL_DENIED error, and grants proceed to the normal audited tool call. With AuditMiddleware installed before the gate, a denial is recorded like any error outcome: "status": "error" and "error": "ApprovalDeniedError: Approval denied for tool 'issue_refund'" (plus the reviewer's reason, when one was given). The approval request id and reviewer id are in the error's details, which the client receives; they are not written to the audit entry. To correlate the two, use the gate's own log lines (logger promptise.server), which record every requested/granted/denied decision with its request_id, tool, client and reviewer.

docs.title: Combining with tenancy
docs.text: Approval requests carry tenant_id, and the admin tools are ordinary guarded tools, so on a require_tenant=True server, reviewers themselves must present tenant identity, and approvals_list shows which tenant each pending call belongs to.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Argument modification is not supported server-side: approve or deny only. (Agent-side ApprovalPolicy supports modified_arguments.)
  • The PendingApprover store is process-local: pending calls don't survive a restart (they are denied by the gate timeout), and replicas don't share a queue. Run one replica for gated tools, or use an ApprovalHandler backed by your own shared store (for example a WebhookApprovalHandler to an approval service).
  • Elicitation requires a client + transport that support it; everything else fails closed.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:

  • Multi-Tenancy: tenant identity the gate records
  • Authentication & Security: the identity the gate relies on

Learn the concept

docs.title: MCP Server Authentication & Security
docs.text: Secure your MCP servers with JWT tokens, API keys, role-based guards, and dependency injection.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import (
    MCPServer, AuthMiddleware, JWTAuth, HasRole, Depends, LoggingMiddleware,
)

jwt_auth = JWTAuth(secret="my-secret-key")

server = MCPServer(name="secure-api")
server.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware(jwt_auth))
server.add_middleware(LoggingMiddleware())

@server.tool(auth=True, roles=["admin"])
async def delete_user(user_id: str) -> str:
    """Delete a user (admin only)."""
    return f"Deleted {user_id}"

@server.tool(auth=True)
async def list_users() -> list[str]:
    """List users (any authenticated client)."""
    return ["alice", "bob"]

@server.tool()
async def health() -> str:
    """Public health check (no auth required)."""
    return "ok"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server.run(transport="http", host="127.0.0.1", port=8080)

Only tools with auth=True require authentication. Unauthenticated clients can still call health.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The auth system has three layers:

  1. Auth providers (JWTAuth, APIKeyAuth, AsymmetricJWTAuth) verify credentials and extract client identity.
  2. AuthMiddleware runs in the middleware chain, calling the provider for tools that require auth. On success, it populates ctx.client with a structured ClientContext containing identity, roles, scopes, JWT claims, IP address, and user-agent.
  3. Guards (RequireAuth, HasRole, HasAllRoles, HasScope, HasAllScopes, RequireClientId, RequireTenant, HasTenant) enforce fine-grained permissions after authentication. When a guard denies access, the error message explains why, which roles or scopes were required vs. what the client has.

After authentication, everything you need is on ctx.client:

@server.tool(auth=True)
async def my_tool(ctx: RequestContext) -> str:
    ctx.client.client_id   # "agent-007"
    ctx.client.roles       # {"admin", "analyst"}
    ctx.client.scopes      # {"read", "write"} (from JWT "scope" claim)
    ctx.client.issuer      # "https://auth.example.com" (JWT "iss")
    ctx.client.audience    # "my-api" (JWT "aud")
    ctx.client.subject     # "agent-007" (JWT "sub")
    ctx.client.ip_address  # "192.168.1.42"
    ctx.client.user_agent  # "MCP-Client/1.0"
    ctx.client.extra       # {} (populated by on_authenticate hook)
    ctx.client.claims      # Full JWT payload dict
    return "ok"

docs.title: JWTAuth
docs.text:
Validates HS256 JWT tokens from request metadata. Verified tokens are cached in an LRU to avoid repeated crypto operations on the hot path.

from promptise.mcp.server import JWTAuth

jwt_auth = JWTAuth(
    secret="my-secret-key",               # Shared secret for HS256 verification
    audience="api://crm",                 # Required "aud" (a string or a list)
    issuer="https://auth.example.com",    # Required "iss"
    meta_key="authorization",             # Key in request metadata (default)
    cache_size=256,                       # Max cached tokens (0 to disable)
)

Every token must be signed with secret, carry an exp in the future, and not have an nbf in the future. audience and issuer are optional; when set, they are checked too:

  • audience: the token's aud (a string or a list) must include one of the configured values. A token without aud is rejected. Set it whenever the secret is shared by more than one service, so a token minted for one of them is refused by the others.
  • issuer: the token's iss must equal it exactly. A token without iss is rejected.

create_token() adds the (first) configured audience and the issuer when the payload does not set them, so test tokens verify against the same provider.

Clients send tokens via the Authorization: Bearer <token> header. The provider strips the Bearer prefix automatically. Only HS256 tokens are accepted (a token whose header names another algorithm is rejected), and a token without exp is rejected.

Parameter Default Description secret required Shared HS256 secret audience None Accepted aud value or list of values issuer None Required iss value meta_key "authorization" Lower-case header name that carries the token cache_size 256 Verified tokens kept in the LRU cache; 0 disables it

Token payload format:

{
  "sub": "agent-admin",
  "roles": ["admin", "finance"],
  "exp": 1717200000
}

The sub (or client_id) claim becomes ctx.client_id. The roles array is extracted by AuthMiddleware into ctx.state["roles"].

Utility methods:

# Create a token (for testing)
token = jwt_auth.create_token(
    {"sub": "test-agent", "roles": ["admin"]},
    expires_in=3600,  # 1 hour
)

# Verify a token without a request context
is_valid = jwt_auth.verify_token(token)

docs.title: APIKeyAuth
docs.text:
Pre-shared key authentication with optional role support. Maps API keys to client identifiers.

Simple format: key maps to a client ID string:

from promptise.mcp.server import APIKeyAuth

api_auth = APIKeyAuth(
    keys={
        "sk-abc123": "frontend-app",
        "sk-xyz789": "backend-service",
    },
    header="x-api-key",  # Header name (default)
)

Rich format: key maps to a config dict with roles for guard compatibility:

api_auth = APIKeyAuth(
    keys={
        "sk-admin-abc": {"client_id": "admin-agent", "roles": ["admin", "write"]},
        "sk-read-xyz":  {"client_id": "viewer-agent", "roles": ["read"]},
    },
)

Rich keys automatically populate ctx.state["roles"], so role-based guards (HasRole, HasAllRoles) work out of the box, with no JWT required. A rich entry may also carry "tenant_id": "acme", which becomes ctx.client.tenant_id for tenant guards.

Clients send their key via the x-api-key header (configurable via header). The matching client ID becomes ctx.client_id. Keys are compared in constant time.

The header name is matched case-insensitively, as HTTP header names are: header="X-Custom-Key" and header="x-custom-key" read the same header. With MCPServer(require_auth=True), the transport gate reads the API key from the same header.

docs.title: AsymmetricJWTAuth
docs.text:
For production deployments using RS256 or ES256 (asymmetric) JWT tokens: common with Auth0, Keycloak, and other identity providers:

from promptise.mcp.server import AsymmetricJWTAuth, AuthMiddleware

# RS256 with a PEM public key
auth = AsymmetricJWTAuth(
    public_key="-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----\nMIIBI...\n-----END PUBLIC KEY-----",
    algorithm="RS256",  # or "ES256" for ECDSA
)

server.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware(auth))

Load the key from a file:

auth = AsymmetricJWTAuth(
    public_key=open("/path/to/public.pem").read(),
    algorithm="RS256",
)

AsymmetricJWTAuth(public_key, *, algorithm="RS256", audience=None, issuer=None, meta_key="authorization", cache_size=256) uses the same interface as JWTAuth: it works with AuthMiddleware, guards, and ctx.client_id. public_key is a PEM string or the path to a PEM file; algorithm must be "RS256" or "ES256" (anything else raises ValueError). Set audience for IdP-issued tokens: without it, a token that carries an aud claim is rejected. Requires the PyJWT and cryptography packages (optional dependencies).

docs.title: JwksAuth
docs.text:
For tokens issued by an identity provider whose signing keys rotate and are published at a JWKS endpoint: Microsoft Entra, Okta, Auth0, Keycloak, any OIDC provider. This is the server-side counterpart to Agent Identity: an agent presents an IdP-issued identity credential, and JwksAuth verifies it against the IdP's public keys (fetched on demand and cached, so key rotation needs no reconfiguration):

from promptise.mcp.server import JwksAuth, AuthMiddleware

auth = JwksAuth(
    jwks_url="https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/discovery/v2.0/keys",
    issuer="https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0",
    audience="api://my-mcp-server",   # the resource agents target
)
server.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware(auth))

The validated token's sub and claims are surfaced on ctx.client (subject, issuer, audience, claims), so guards (RequireClientId, HasRole) and audit logs can see which agent called. Requires the PyJWT and cryptography packages.

Parameter Default Description jwks_url required The IdP's JWKS endpoint audience required Expected aud; an empty value raises ValueError issuer None Expected iss (recommended) algorithms ("RS256", "ES256") Accepted signing algorithms (asymmetric only) meta_key "authorization" Header carrying the bearer token leeway 60.0 Seconds of clock skew allowed on exp, nbf and iat

Keys are cached for five minutes; a token signed with an unknown kid triggers an immediate re-fetch (at most once per key id per minute), so a rotated key works on first use.

audience is required

JwksAuth verifies the aud claim on every token. This is what stops an agent from replaying a token it was legitimately issued for a different resource of the same IdP. Set audience to the resource this server represents.

You can let the JWKS endpoint be discovered from the issuer's OIDC metadata ({issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration) instead of passing jwks_url:

auth = JwksAuth.from_discovery(
    issuer="https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0",
    audience="api://my-mcp-server",
)

The discovery document is fetched once (lazily, on the first verified call) and its issuer is checked against the configured one before its jwks_uri is trusted. from_discovery(*, issuer, audience, algorithms=("RS256", "ES256"), meta_key="authorization", request_timeout=5.0, leeway=60.0).

docs.title: Custom auth provider
docs.text:
Implement the AuthProvider protocol for custom authentication (OAuth2 introspection, mTLS, etc.): verify the credential, return the client id, and store the verified claims in ctx.state["jwt_payload"]. AuthMiddleware builds ctx.client from those claims exactly as it does for a JWT: roles, scope, the tenant claim, and iss / aud / sub / iat / exp.

from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable

from promptise.mcp.server import AuthenticationError, RequestContext


class OAuth2Introspection:
    """Verify opaque tokens with your IdP's introspection endpoint (RFC 7662)."""

    def __init__(self, introspect: Callable[[str], Awaitable[dict]]):
        self._introspect = introspect  # e.g. a call to your IdP's /introspect

    async def authenticate(self, ctx: RequestContext) -> str:
        token = ctx.meta.get("authorization", "").removeprefix("Bearer ")
        if not token:
            raise AuthenticationError("Missing authentication token")
        claims = await self._introspect(token)
        if not claims.get("active"):
            raise AuthenticationError("Token is not active")
        ctx.state["jwt_payload"] = claims  # roles, scopes and tenant for ctx.client
        return claims["sub"]

Install it like any provider: server.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware(OAuth2Introspection(introspect))). A tool declared with roles=["admin"] then passes for a token whose claims include "roles": ["admin"]. Without the jwt_payload claims the caller is authenticated but has no roles or scopes.

docs.title: AuthMiddleware
docs.text:
AuthMiddleware wraps an auth provider and runs it for tools, resources and prompts marked with auth=True:

from promptise.mcp.server import AuthMiddleware

server.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware(jwt_auth))

AuthMiddleware(provider, *, on_authenticate=None, tenant_claim="tenant_id"):

Parameter Default Description provider required Any AuthProvider: an object with async def authenticate(ctx) -> str (the client id). verify_token(token) -> bool is optional and used by the transport gate on_authenticate None OnAuthenticateHook: sync or async (client: ClientContext, ctx: RequestContext), called after a successful authentication tenant_claim "tenant_id" JWT claim copied to ctx.client.tenant_id (string values only)

When a tool has auth=True:

  1. The middleware calls provider.authenticate(ctx).
  2. On success, ctx.client_id is set and ctx.client is populated with a full ClientContext: identity, roles, scopes, JWT claims (iss, aud, sub, iat, exp), client IP address, and user-agent.
  3. On failure, an AuthenticationError is returned to the client.

Tools without auth=True pass through the middleware without authentication checks. roles=[...] and the built-in identity guards (RequireAuth, HasRole, HasAllRoles, HasScope, HasAllScopes, RequireClientId, RequireTenant, HasTenant) imply auth=True, since they can only pass once the caller is identified. A custom guard does not: give its tool auth=True if the guard reads ctx.client.

docs.title: Identity is resolved per request
docs.text:
On the HTTP and SSE transports an MCP session spans many HTTP requests. The credential the provider verifies, and everything ctx.client reports (client id, tenant, roles, IP address, user-agent), come from the HTTP request that carries this tools/call, never from the request that opened the session:

  • A call that presents a different valid credential than the one that opened the session runs as that credential's principal, with its own tenant and roles.
  • A call with no credential is unauthenticated, even inside a session opened with a valid one: auth=True tools answer AuthenticationError.
  • With MCPServer(require_auth=True) the transport gate goes one step further and binds the session to the credential that created it: a different credential on a known mcp-session-id is answered 404 Session not found. See Transport-level auth gate.

TestClient behaves the same way: headers passed to one call_tool apply to that call only.

docs.title: Client enrichment hook
docs.text:
Use on_authenticate to load additional client metadata (org, tenant, plan tier) from your database after authentication:

async def enrich_client(client: ClientContext, ctx: RequestContext):
    """Called after successful authentication."""
    org = await db.get_org_for_client(client.client_id)
    client.extra["org_id"] = org.id
    client.extra["plan"] = org.plan
    client.extra["rate_limit_tier"] = org.rate_limit_tier

server.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware(jwt_auth, on_authenticate=enrich_client))

The hook receives (ClientContext, RequestContext) and can be sync or async. Mutate client.extra to attach custom metadata that's available to all handlers and middleware for the rest of the request.

@server.tool(auth=True)
async def my_tool(ctx: RequestContext) -> str:
    org_id = ctx.client.extra["org_id"]
    plan = ctx.client.extra["plan"]
    return f"Handling request for org {org_id} on {plan} plan"

docs.title: ClientContext
docs.text:
After successful authentication, ctx.client is a ClientContext dataclass with typed fields:

Field Type Source client_id str JWT sub (else client_id claim) or API key mapping; "anonymous" before authentication tenant_id str \| None JWT claim named by tenant_claim, or the API key's tenant_id roles set[str] JWT roles claim + provider roles scopes set[str] JWT scope claim (space-separated per RFC 8693) claims dict Full JWT payload (empty for API key auth) issuer str \| None JWT iss claim audience str \| list \| None JWT aud claim subject str \| None JWT sub claim issued_at float \| None JWT iat claim (Unix timestamp) expires_at float \| None JWT exp claim (Unix timestamp) ip_address str \| None Client IP from transport layer user_agent str \| None User-Agent header extra dict Custom metadata from on_authenticate hook

Helper methods: has_role(), has_any_role(), has_all_roles(), has_scope(), has_any_scope().

docs.title: Force auth on all tools
docs.text:
Set require_auth=True on the server constructor to force auth=True on every tool, resource and prompt, including those registered without the flag (and those from routers, mounts, OpenAPI imports and include_prompts()):

server = MCPServer(name="locked-down", require_auth=True)

docs.title: Guards
docs.text: Guards check fine-grained permissions after authentication. They run after middleware (so AuthMiddleware has already populated ctx.client_id and ctx.state["roles"]).

docs.title: RequireAuth
docs.text:
Denies access if ctx.client_id is not set:

from promptise.mcp.server import RequireAuth

@server.tool(auth=True, guards=[RequireAuth()])
async def protected() -> str:
    return "authenticated"

docs.title: HasRole
docs.text:
Grants access if the client has any of the specified roles:

from promptise.mcp.server import HasRole

@server.tool(auth=True, guards=[HasRole("admin", "manager")])
async def manage_team() -> str:
    return "team managed"

The roles=["admin", "manager"] shorthand on @server.tool() creates a HasRole guard automatically:

# These two tools are protected the same way:
@server.tool(auth=True, roles=["admin", "manager"])
async def manage_team_shorthand() -> str:
    return "team managed"

@server.tool(auth=True, guards=[HasRole("admin", "manager")])
async def manage_team_explicit() -> str:
    return "team managed"

docs.title: HasAllRoles
docs.text:
Grants access only if the client has all of the specified roles:

from promptise.mcp.server import HasAllRoles

@server.tool(auth=True, guards=[HasAllRoles("admin", "finance")])
async def approve_budget() -> str:
    return "budget approved"

docs.title: RequireClientId
docs.text:
Grants access only to specific client identifiers:

from promptise.mcp.server import RequireClientId

@server.tool(auth=True, guards=[RequireClientId("cron-service", "admin-agent")])
async def run_migration() -> str:
    return "migration complete"

docs.title: HasScope
docs.text:
Grants access if the client has any of the specified OAuth2 scopes (from the JWT scope claim):

from promptise.mcp.server import HasScope

@server.tool(auth=True, guards=[HasScope("read", "admin")])
async def get_data() -> str:
    return "data"

JWT only

Scopes are extracted from the JWT scope claim. When using APIKeyAuth without JWT, ctx.client.scopes will be empty and scope guards will always deny. Use role-based guards (HasRole) for API key auth.

docs.title: HasAllScopes
docs.text:
Grants access only if the client has all of the specified scopes:

from promptise.mcp.server import HasAllScopes

@server.tool(auth=True, guards=[HasAllScopes("read", "write")])
async def update_data() -> str:
    return "updated"

docs.title: Descriptive guard errors
docs.text:
When a guard denies access, the error message explains why:

# HasRole denial:
"Requires any of roles [admin, manager], but client has [viewer]"

# HasAllRoles denial:
"Requires all roles [admin, analyst, ops], client has [admin], missing [analyst, ops]"

# HasScope denial:
"Requires any of scopes [read, write], but client has [(none)]"

This makes debugging auth issues straightforward: you see exactly which roles or scopes are required, which the client has, and what's missing.

docs.title: Custom guards
docs.text:
Implement the Guard protocol: async def check(ctx) -> bool, plus an optional describe_denial(ctx) -> str for the error message (the default names the guard class). A custom guard does not imply auth=True; set it on the tool when the guard reads ctx.client:

from promptise.mcp.server import Guard, RequestContext

class IPAllowlist(Guard):
    def __init__(self, allowed_ips: set[str]):
        self._allowed = allowed_ips

    async def check(self, ctx: RequestContext) -> bool:
        return ctx.client.ip_address in self._allowed

    def describe_denial(self, ctx: RequestContext) -> str:
        return (
            f"Client IP '{ctx.client.ip_address}' is not in the "
            f"allowlist [{', '.join(sorted(self._allowed))}]"
        )

docs.title: Request Tracing
docs.text:
Every request gets a unique request_id. If the client sends an X-Request-ID header, that value is used; otherwise one is generated automatically. The header is read from the HTTP request carrying each call, so every tools/call in a session carries its own id. This ID is available to all middleware, handlers, and audit logging:

@server.tool()
async def my_tool(ctx: RequestContext) -> str:
    ctx.logger.info("Processing", extra={"request_id": ctx.request_id})
    return "done"

Propagate the X-Request-ID from your upstream services to enable end-to-end distributed tracing through your MCP tools.

docs.title: ToolResponse: response metadata
docs.text:
Handlers can return a ToolResponse to attach metadata for audit, observability, and middleware:

from promptise.mcp.server import ToolResponse

@server.tool()
async def search(query: str, ctx: RequestContext) -> ToolResponse:
    results = await db.search(query)
    return ToolResponse(
        content=results,
        metadata={
            "source": "primary_db",
            "result_count": len(results),
            "cache": "miss",
        },
    )

The content is serialized normally (the agent sees the results). The metadata is stored on ctx.state["response_metadata"] for downstream use by audit middleware, webhook middleware, or custom logging. The agent never sees the metadata: it's for your infrastructure.

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text: Use Depends() to inject shared resources into tool handlers: database connections, HTTP clients, configuration, or any callable.

docs.title: Basic injection
docs.text:
from promptise.mcp.server import Depends

async def get_db():
    db = await Database.connect()
    try:
        yield db       # Yielded value is injected
    finally:
        await db.close()  # Cleanup runs after the handler

@server.tool()
async def query(sql: str, db: Database = Depends(get_db)) -> list:
    """Run a SQL query."""
    return await db.execute(sql)

docs.title: Supported dependency types
docs.text: Type Example Lifecycle Async generator async def dep(): yield val Cleanup after handler Sync generator def dep(): yield val Cleanup after handler Async callable async def dep(): return val Called once per request Sync callable def dep(): return val Called once per request Class Depends(MySettings) Constructor called per request

docs.title: Request-scoped caching
docs.text:
By default, the same dependency is resolved once per request (cached by identity). Disable with use_cache=False:

# Resolved once per request (default):
db: Database = Depends(get_db, use_cache=True)

# Resolved fresh each time (e.g., for unique IDs):
request_id: str = Depends(generate_id, use_cache=False)

docs.title: Injecting RequestContext
docs.text:
Handler parameters typed as RequestContext are injected automatically:

from promptise.mcp.server import RequestContext

@server.tool(auth=True)
async def whoami(ctx: RequestContext) -> dict:
    """Return the authenticated client's identity."""
    return {
        "client_id": ctx.client.client_id,
        "roles": sorted(ctx.client.roles),
        "scopes": sorted(ctx.client.scopes),
        "issuer": ctx.client.issuer,
        "ip": ctx.client.ip_address,
    }

docs.title: Token Endpoint (Dev/Testing)
docs.text:
For development and testing, enable a built-in /auth/token endpoint that issues JWT tokens:

jwt_auth = JWTAuth(secret="dev-secret")
server.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware(jwt_auth))

server.enable_token_endpoint(
    jwt_auth=jwt_auth,
    clients={
        "agent-admin":  {"secret": "admin-secret",  "roles": ["admin", "finance"]},
        "agent-viewer": {"secret": "viewer-secret", "roles": ["viewer"]},
    },
    path="/auth/token",           # HTTP path (default)
    default_expires_in=86400,     # Token lifetime in seconds (default: 24h)
)

Clients request tokens with a standard OAuth 2.0 client_credentials request (RFC 6749, form-encoded):

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/auth/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials \
  -d client_id=agent-admin \
  -d client_secret=admin-secret

The client can authenticate with HTTP Basic instead (curl -u agent-admin:admin-secret -d grant_type=client_credentials ...). Any OAuth 2.0 client library works, and so does MCPClient.fetch_token(). A JSON body ({"client_id": ..., "client_secret": ...}, where grant_type defaults to client_credentials) is still accepted for older clients.

Response:

{"access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...", "refresh_token": "prf_...", "token_type": "bearer", "expires_in": 86400}

Exchange the refresh token for a new pair with grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=prf_...; each refresh token works once and expires after 30 days. Refresh tokens are kept in memory, so a restart invalidates them. Errors use the OAuth 2.0 shape: {"error": "invalid_client", "error_description": "..."}.

enable_token_endpoint(jwt_auth, clients, *, path="/auth/token", default_expires_in=86400). Each client entry needs "secret" and may set "roles" (list), "expires_in" (seconds, overrides the default) and "claims" (extra JWT claims, for example {"tenant_id": "acme", "scope": "read write"}). The issued token has sub = the client id and roles, plus the provider's audience and issuer. The endpoint is served on the HTTP and SSE transports and by asgi_app(). The settings are held in a TokenEndpointConfig(jwt_auth, clients, *, path="/auth/token", default_expires_in=3600, refresh_token_ttl=2592000); enable_token_endpoint() builds it for you.

Not for production

The built-in token endpoint is a convenience for development. In production, use a proper Identity Provider (Auth0, Keycloak, Okta) and pass tokens to clients via bearer_token.

docs.title: Complete Auth Setup
docs.text:
A full example combining JWT auth, guards, dependency injection, and the token endpoint:

from promptise.mcp.server import (
    MCPServer, MCPRouter, AuthMiddleware, JWTAuth,
    LoggingMiddleware, TimeoutMiddleware, ConcurrencyLimiter,
    BackgroundTasks, Depends, RequestContext, get_context,
)

server = MCPServer(name="hr-api", version="1.0.0")

# Auth
jwt_auth = JWTAuth(secret="production-secret")
server.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware(jwt_auth))
server.add_middleware(LoggingMiddleware())
server.add_middleware(TimeoutMiddleware(default_timeout=30.0))
server.add_middleware(ConcurrencyLimiter(max_concurrent=50))

# Dev token endpoint
server.enable_token_endpoint(
    jwt_auth=jwt_auth,
    clients={
        "agent-admin":  {"secret": "s3cret", "roles": ["admin"]},
        "agent-viewer": {"secret": "v1ewer", "roles": ["viewer"]},
    },
)

# Public tool (no auth)
@server.tool()
async def ping() -> str:
    """Health check."""
    return "pong"

# Read tools (any authenticated user)
@server.tool(auth=True, roles=["admin", "viewer"])
async def list_items() -> list[str]:
    """List all items."""
    return ["item-1", "item-2"]

# Write tools (admin only, with background tasks)
@server.tool(auth=True, roles=["admin"])
async def delete_item(
    item_id: str,
    bg: BackgroundTasks = Depends(BackgroundTasks),
) -> dict:
    """Delete an item (admin only)."""
    ctx = get_context()
    bg.add(log_audit, "DELETE", ctx.client_id, item_id)
    return {"deleted": item_id}

async def log_audit(action: str, client: str, target: str) -> None:
    print(f"AUDIT: {action} by {client} on {target}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server.run(transport="http", host="127.0.0.1", port=8080)

docs.title: Connecting from Promptise Agents
docs.text:
When a Promptise agent connects to your MCP server, identity flows automatically:

# Agent side — CallerContext carries the JWT
from promptise.agent import CallerContext

caller = CallerContext(
    user_id="user-42",
    bearer_token=jwt_token,  # This gets sent to your server
)
result = await agent.ainvoke(input, caller=caller)

The agent's MCPClient sends the bearer_token as an Authorization: Bearer <token> header. Your server's AuthMiddleware validates it and populates ctx.client: the handler never sees the raw token.

# Server side — handler receives validated identity
@server.tool(auth=True, roles=["analyst"])
async def query_data(sql: str, ctx: RequestContext) -> str:
    # ctx.client.client_id = "user-42" (from JWT 'sub' claim)
    # ctx.client.roles = {"analyst"} (from JWT 'roles' claim)
    # The raw bearer_token is NOT accessible here — only parsed claims
    return await db.query(sql, user_id=ctx.client.client_id)
Agent side (CallerContext) Wire Server side (ClientContext) bearer_token → Authorization: Bearer header → JWT validated, claims extracted user_id (not sent) Extracted from JWT sub claim roles (not sent) Extracted from JWT roles claim scopes (not sent) Extracted from JWT scope claim

See CallerContext: Agent to MCP Identity for the complete flow with examples.

docs.title: API Summary
docs.text:

Method Enable built-in dev token endpoint

Guard composition

Pass multiple guards to a tool's guards list. They are checked in order after the middleware chain; the first failure short-circuits and returns an ACCESS_DENIED error with the guard's describe_denial() text.

Secret management

Never hardcode JWT secrets in source code. Use environment variables or a secrets manager. The ServerSettings class supports loading secrets from env vars with a configurable prefix.

Token caching

JWTAuth caches verified tokens in a thread-safe LRU (default: 256 entries). This avoids repeated HMAC-SHA256 computation when the same token is reused across requests, which is the common case for agent sessions.
