docs.title: PromptBuilder
docs.text: Fluent API for constructing prompts programmatically at runtime. Use PromptBuilder when prompt configuration depends on runtime conditions: user input, feature flags, A/B tests, or dynamic model selection.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.builder import PromptBuilder
from promptise.prompts.context import UserContext, BaseContext, user_context, world_context
from promptise.prompts.strategies import chain_of_thought, analyst
from promptise.prompts.guards import content_filter, length

prompt = (
    PromptBuilder("analyze")
    .system("You are an expert data analyst.")
    .user(UserContext(expertise_level="expert"))
    .world(project=BaseContext(name="Alpha", deadline="March 2026"))
    .context(user_context(), world_context("project"))
    .strategy(chain_of_thought)
    .perspective(analyst)
    .constraint("Must include confidence scores")
    .guard(content_filter(blocked=["secret"]), length(max_length=5000))
    .template("Analyze in under 150 words: {data}")
    .model("openai:gpt-5-mini")
    .build()
)

result = await prompt(data="quarterly figures...")

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The PromptBuilder provides a fluent (chainable) API where every method returns self. This lets you incrementally configure a prompt, then call .build() to produce the final Prompt instance.

Key differences from the @prompt decorator:

  • Runtime configuration: you can build prompts based on runtime conditions instead of static decoration.
  • Dynamic templates: set templates from variables, databases, or user input.
  • Programmatic composition: loop through configurations, conditionally add guards, etc.

The builder extracts {variable} names from the system text and template, in order of first appearance, and creates a synthetic async function with one parameter per name. Every parameter is a str that defaults to "", so the prompt can be called positionally or with keywords, and a missing argument renders as an empty string. With no variables, the function accepts any keyword arguments and ignores them. The resulting Prompt behaves like one created with @prompt.

build() raises ValueError when the builder name or a variable name is not a valid Python identifier (for example PromptBuilder("my-prompt")).

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Builder
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.builder import PromptBuilder

builder = PromptBuilder("my_prompt")

The name is used for logging, observability traces, and the PromptInspector.

docs.title: Step 2: Set System Text and Template
docs.text:
builder.system("You are a senior financial analyst.")
builder.template("Analyze the following report:\n{report}\nFocus: {focus}")

The system text and the template are joined with a blank line into one template; the result is sent as a single system message. Both support {variable} placeholders and the template syntax. Calling .system() or .template() again replaces the earlier text.

docs.title: Step 3: Configure the Model
docs.text:
builder.model("openai:gpt-5-mini")

The default model is openai:gpt-5-mini if not explicitly set.

docs.title: Step 4: Add World Context
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.context import UserContext, EnvironmentContext, BaseContext

builder.user(UserContext(name="Alice", expertise_level="expert"))
builder.env(EnvironmentContext(platform="linux", timezone="UTC"))
builder.world(
    project=BaseContext(name="Q1 Report", deadline="March 2026"),
    team=BaseContext(size=5, department="analytics"),
)

docs.title: Step 5: Add Context Providers
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.context import user_context, world_context

builder.context(user_context(), world_context("project", header="## Project"))

World contexts are only the data. A provider such as user_context() or world_context(key) turns them into prompt text (see Context).

docs.title: Step 6: Set Strategy and Perspective
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.strategies import chain_of_thought, analyst

builder.strategy(chain_of_thought)
builder.perspective(analyst)

docs.title: Step 7: Add Constraints and Guards
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.guards import content_filter, length

builder.constraint("Must include confidence scores", "Cite data sources")
builder.guard(content_filter(blocked=["confidential"]), length(max_length=5000))

docs.title: Step 8: Add Lifecycle Hooks
docs.text:
async def log_before(ctx):
    print(f"About to call: {ctx.prompt_name}")

async def log_after(ctx, result):
    print(f"Got result: {len(str(result))} chars")

async def handle_error(ctx, error):
    print(f"Error: {error}")

builder.on_before(log_before)
builder.on_after(log_after)
builder.on_error(handle_error)

docs.title: Step 9: Set Output Type
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class AnalysisResult(BaseModel):
    summary: str
    confidence: float
    recommendations: list[str]

builder.output_type(AnalysisResult)

docs.title: Step 10: Build and Use
docs.text:
prompt = builder.build()
result = await prompt(report="Revenue grew 15%...", focus="trends")

docs.title: Chaining Everything
docs.text:
Since all builder methods return self, you can chain the entire configuration:

from promptise.prompts.builder import PromptBuilder
from promptise.prompts.strategies import chain_of_thought
from promptise.prompts.guards import length

prompt = (
    PromptBuilder("quick_summary")
    .system("Expert summarizer")
    .template("Summarize in {max_words} words: {text}")
    .model("openai:gpt-5-mini")
    .strategy(chain_of_thought)
    .constraint("Be concise")
    .guard(length(max_length=1000))
    .build()
)

result = await prompt(text="long article...", max_words="100")

docs.title: Dynamic Prompt Construction
docs.text:
The real power of PromptBuilder is in dynamic, conditional construction:

from promptise.prompts.builder import PromptBuilder
from promptise.prompts.strategies import chain_of_thought, self_critique
from promptise.prompts.guards import content_filter, length

def create_analysis_prompt(user_level: str, strict_mode: bool) -> "Prompt":
    builder = (
        PromptBuilder("analysis")
        .template("Analyze: {data}")
        .model("openai:gpt-5-mini")
    )

    # Adjust strategy based on user level
    if user_level == "expert":
        builder.strategy(chain_of_thought + self_critique)
        builder.constraint("Include statistical confidence intervals")
    else:
        builder.strategy(chain_of_thought)
        builder.constraint("Explain in simple terms")

    # Add guards in strict mode
    if strict_mode:
        builder.guard(
            content_filter(blocked=["confidential", "internal"]),
            length(max_length=2000),
        )

    return builder.build()

# Usage
prompt = create_analysis_prompt(user_level="expert", strict_mode=True)
result = await prompt(data="quarterly revenue figures...")

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
.observe() makes the built prompt record every call with a PromptObserver: start, end, errors, guard blocks and context providers, as timeline events. .observe(True) records to the prompt's own collector; pass an ObservabilityCollector (or a PromptObserver) to record somewhere shared:

from promptise.observability import ObservabilityCollector

collector = ObservabilityCollector()
prompt = (
    PromptBuilder("tracked_prompt")
    .template("Process: {input}")
    .model("openai:gpt-5-mini")
    .observe(collector)
    .build()
)
# After a call: [e.event_type for e in collector.get_timeline()]

docs.title: API Summary
docs.text:
Method Returns Description PromptBuilder(name="builder_prompt") PromptBuilder Create a new builder; name becomes the prompt's name .system(text) self Set system/instruction text .template(text) self Set prompt template with {variable} placeholders .model(name) self Set the LLM model identifier .observe(enabled=True) self Record calls with a PromptObserver (True, a collector or an observer; False turns it off) .output_type(t) self Set output type for structured parsing .user(user_ctx) self Set world["user"] .env(env_ctx) self Set world["environment"] .world(**contexts) self Add named world contexts .context(*providers) self Add context providers .strategy(s) self Set reasoning strategy .perspective(p) self Set cognitive perspective .constraint(*texts) self Add constraint strings .guard(*guards) self Add input/output guards .on_before(fn) self Set pre-execution hook .on_after(fn) self Set post-execution hook .on_error(fn) self Set error-handling hook .build() Prompt Construct the final Prompt instance

Builder vs. decorator

Use @prompt for static, declarative prompt definitions. Use PromptBuilder when you need to construct prompts based on runtime conditions. Both produce Prompt objects with the same methods.

Blocks, inspector and description

The builder has no methods for blocks, an inspector or a description. Add them to the built prompt: builder.build().with_blocks(Identity("Analyst")).with_inspector(inspector). .observe() is the builder's way to attach a PromptObserver; .with_observer(...) works on the built prompt too.

Template is required

If neither .system() nor .template() is called, the template is "Respond to the user's request." Always set an explicit template for production prompts.

Default model

If .model() is not called, the builder defaults to openai:gpt-5-mini. This keeps quick prototyping fast without specifying a model every time.

docs.title: Prompt Chaining
docs.text: Compose prompts into multi-step pipelines with sequential chains, concurrent execution, conditional branching, retry logic, and fallback strategies.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts import prompt
from promptise.prompts.chain import chain, parallel, retry

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def extract_facts(text: str) -> str:
    """Extract key facts from: {text}"""

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def analyze_facts(text: str) -> str:
    """Analyze these facts: {text}"""

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def write_summary(text: str) -> str:
    """Write an executive summary: {text}"""

pipeline = chain(extract_facts, analyze_facts, write_summary)
result = await pipeline("Raw quarterly data...")

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The chaining module provides five composition operators:

Operator Behavior chain Sequential: output of each step feeds the next parallel Concurrent: all prompts run at once on the same input branch Conditional: route to different prompts based on a predicate retry Resilience: retry a prompt with exponential backoff fallback Graceful degradation: try alternatives on failure

All operators return async callables: await op(*args, **kwargs). They are not Prompt objects (no with_*(), render() or name), but any operator can be used where another operator expects a prompt, so you can nest them.

docs.title: Chain (Sequential)
docs.text:
chain(*prompts) executes prompts in order. Each prompt's output is passed as input to the next prompt. The final prompt's output is returned.

from promptise.prompts.chain import chain

pipeline = chain(extract_facts, analyze_facts, write_summary)
result = await pipeline("Raw data...")

The data flow:

  1. extract_facts("Raw data...") returns extracted facts.
  2. analyze_facts(extracted_facts) returns analysis.
  3. write_summary(analysis) returns the final summary.

docs.title: How Output Feeds Input
docs.text:
• String output: passed as the first positional argument to the next prompt.
  • Dict output: unpacked as keyword arguments to the next prompt.
  • Other types: converted to string via str() and passed as the first argument. This includes Pydantic models and lists from typed prompts, so the next prompt receives their str() text, not JSON. Return a dict, or convert the result yourself, when the next step needs structured input.
# String -> positional arg
# {"key": "value"} -> **kwargs
# 42 -> str(42) -> positional arg

Chain requires at least 2 prompts

Calling chain() with fewer than 2 prompts raises ValueError.

docs.title: Parallel (Concurrent)
docs.text:
parallel(**prompts) executes multiple prompts concurrently on the same input. Returns a dict mapping prompt names to their results.

from promptise.prompts.chain import parallel

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def analyze_sentiment(text: str) -> str:
    """Analyze the sentiment of: {text}"""

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def extract_topics(text: str) -> str:
    """Extract main topics from: {text}"""

multi = parallel(sentiment=analyze_sentiment, topics=extract_topics)
results = await multi("Great product launch, revenue up 40%!")

print(results["sentiment"])  # Sentiment analysis
print(results["topics"])     # Topic extraction

All prompts receive the same arguments and run concurrently with asyncio.gather. If one fails, the exception propagates and the other results are lost; wrap individual prompts in retry() or fallback() when partial failure matters.

Parallel requires at least 2 prompts

Calling parallel() with fewer than 2 named prompts raises ValueError.

docs.title: Branch (Conditional)
docs.text:
branch(condition, routes, default=None) routes to different prompts based on a condition function. The condition receives the same arguments as the prompts and must return a string key that matches one of the routes.

from promptise.prompts.chain import branch

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def technical_response(text: str) -> str:
    """Provide a technical explanation: {text}"""

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def simple_response(text: str) -> str:
    """Explain in simple terms: {text}"""

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def default_response(text: str) -> str:
    """Respond to: {text}"""

def classify_input(text: str) -> str:
    if any(term in text.lower() for term in ["api", "algorithm", "protocol"]):
        return "technical"
    return "simple"

router = branch(
    condition=classify_input,
    routes={
        "technical": technical_response,
        "simple": simple_response,
    },
    default=default_response,
)

result = await router("Explain the TCP protocol")
# Routes to technical_response

The condition is a plain (sync) function called with the same arguments as the prompts. If it returns a key not in routes and no default is set, a ValueError is raised.

docs.title: Retry (Exponential Backoff)
docs.text:
retry(target, max_retries=3, backoff=1.0) wraps a prompt with automatic retry on failure. The backoff doubles after each attempt.

from promptise.prompts.chain import retry

resilient = retry(analyze_facts, max_retries=3, backoff=1.0)
result = await resilient("data...")

Any exception triggers a retry: an LLM error, a GuardError, a ValidationError from a typed return. max_retries counts retries after the first attempt (max_retries=3 means up to 4 calls; 0 means no retry; negative raises ValueError).

Backoff schedule with backoff=1.0:

Attempt Wait before retry 1st failure 1.0 seconds 2nd failure 2.0 seconds 3rd failure 4.0 seconds 4th failure (raises the exception)

If all retries are exhausted, the last exception is raised.

docs.title: Fallback (Try Alternatives)
docs.text:
fallback(primary, *alternatives) tries prompts in order until one succeeds. The first successful result is returned.

from promptise.prompts.chain import fallback

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def fast_analyze(text: str) -> str:
    """Quick analysis: {text}"""

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def thorough_analyze(text: str) -> str:
    """Detailed analysis: {text}"""

safe = fallback(fast_analyze, thorough_analyze)
result = await safe("quarterly data...")

If the primary fails, each alternative is tried in order. Errors from all but the last are swallowed; if the last fails, its exception is raised.

docs.title: Combining Operators
docs.text:
Operators are composable. Build complex pipelines by nesting them:

from promptise.prompts.chain import chain, parallel, retry, fallback

# Retry the extraction step, then branch into parallel analysis
pipeline = chain(
    retry(extract_facts, max_retries=2),
    parallel(
        sentiment=analyze_sentiment,
        topics=extract_topics,
    ),
)

result = await pipeline("Raw data...")
# result is {"sentiment": "...", "topics": "..."}

docs.title: API Summary
docs.text:
Function Returns Description chain(*prompts) Callable Sequential execution, output feeds next input (at least 2) parallel(**prompts) Callable Concurrent execution, returns dict of results (at least 2) branch(condition, routes, default=None) Callable Conditional routing based on a predicate retry(target, max_retries=3, backoff=1.0) Callable Exponential backoff retry fallback(primary, *alternatives) Callable Try alternatives on failure

Retry + Fallback together

Combine retry and fallback for maximum resilience: fallback(retry(primary, max_retries=2), backup_prompt). This retries the primary prompt, then falls back to a backup if all retries fail.

No shared state between steps

Each prompt in a pipeline builds its own PromptContext, so nothing but the return value travels from one step to the next. To pass extra data, return a dict whose keys match the next prompt's parameters (it is unpacked as keyword arguments).

docs.text:

  • Guards: Input/output validation
  • Testing: Test your prompt pipelines

docs.title: Prompt Context System
docs.text: The context system gives your prompts dynamic awareness of their world: who the user is, what tools are available, what errors occurred previously, and any custom data you need. Context providers fire on every invocation and inject relevant text into the prompt automatically.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts import prompt
from promptise.prompts.context import context, user_context, env_context, UserContext, EnvironmentContext

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
@context(user_context(), env_context())
async def analyze(text: str) -> str:
    """Based on available context, analyze: {text}"""

personalized = analyze.with_world(
    user=UserContext(name="Alice", expertise_level="expert"),
    environment=EnvironmentContext(timezone="Europe/Zurich"),
)
print(await personalized.render_async(text="quarterly revenue figures"))   # no LLM call
result = await personalized("quarterly revenue figures")

The providers read the world (with_world(), PromptBuilder.world(), a suite's default_world, or a YAML file's world:) and append a Markdown section such as ## User Context to the prompt. World data with no provider that reads it is not added to the prompt.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The context system has three layers:

  1. BaseContext: an extensible key-value container. Predefined subclasses (UserContext, EnvironmentContext, etc.) add typed fields but never restrict what you can store.
  2. PromptContext: the complete world available during prompt execution. It carries the world dict (containing BaseContext instances), input args, agent references, and extensible state.
  3. ContextProvider: a pluggable protocol that generates context text at runtime. Providers receive the PromptContext and return a markdown string to inject into the prompt.

docs.title: BaseContext
docs.text: The foundation for all context data. Accepts arbitrary keyword arguments.

docs.title: Creating Contexts
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.context import BaseContext, UserContext, EnvironmentContext

# Use a predefined subclass with typed fields
user = UserContext(user_id="123", name="Alice", expertise_level="expert")

# Add custom fields -- no subclassing needed
user = UserContext(user_id="123", department="eng", clearance="high")

# Entirely custom context
project = BaseContext(sprint="2026-Q1", budget=50000, deadline="March 2026")

docs.title: Accessing Data
docs.text:
project = BaseContext(sprint="2026-Q1", budget=50000)

# Attribute access
project.sprint          # "2026-Q1"

# Dict-style access
project["budget"]       # 50000

# Safe access with default
project.get("missing")  # None
project.get("missing", "fallback")  # "fallback"

# Extend after creation
project.deadline = "March 2026"

docs.title: Merging Contexts
docs.text:
Merge two contexts into a new one. Values from the second context override the first:

base = BaseContext(sprint="2026-Q1", budget=50000)
override = BaseContext(budget=75000, team_size=5)

merged = base.merge(override)
# merged.sprint == "2026-Q1"
# merged.budget == 75000
# merged.team_size == 5

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
data = project.to_dict()   # {"sprint": "2026-Q1", "budget": 50000}
keys = project.keys()      # dict_keys(["sprint", "budget"])

docs.title: BaseContext Methods
docs.text:
Method Returns Description get(key, default=None) Any Retrieve a value by key with optional default to_dict() dict Shallow copy of stored data merge(other) BaseContext New context with merged data (other overrides self) keys() KeysView All context keys

ctx.missing returns None for an unknown key, while ctx["missing"] raises KeyError; "key" in ctx tests membership, and an empty context is falsy. Field names starting with _ can't be read or set as attributes. merge() keeps the class of the left-hand context.

docs.title: Predefined Context Classes
docs.text: All predefined classes accept additional **kwargs for custom fields.

docs.title: UserContext
docs.text:
Who the agent is serving.

from promptise.prompts.context import UserContext

user = UserContext(
    user_id="u-123",
    name="Alice",
    preferences={"format": "markdown"},
    expertise_level="expert",  # "beginner", "intermediate", "expert"
    language="english",
    # Custom fields
    department="engineering",
    clearance="high",
)
Field Type Default Description user_id str "" Unique user identifier name str "" Display name preferences dict {} User preference dict expertise_level str "intermediate" Beginner, intermediate, or expert language str "english" Preferred language

docs.title: EnvironmentContext
docs.text:
Runtime environment information.

from promptise.prompts.context import EnvironmentContext

env = EnvironmentContext(
    timezone="America/New_York",
    platform="linux",
    available_apis=["openai", "anthropic"],
)
Field Type Default Description timestamp float time.time() Epoch timestamp timezone str "" IANA timezone string platform str "" OS platform available_apis list[str] [] Available API identifiers

docs.title: ConversationContext
docs.text:
Conversation history and state.

from promptise.prompts.context import ConversationContext

conv = ConversationContext(
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Analyze Q1 data"},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "Here is my analysis..."},
    ],
    turn_count=2,
    summary="User asked for Q1 analysis.",
)
Field Type Default Description messages list[dict] [] Message history turn_count int 0 Number of turns summary str "" Compressed summary

docs.title: TeamContext
docs.text:
Other agents in the team.

from promptise.prompts.context import TeamContext

team = TeamContext(
    agents=[
        {"name": "researcher", "role": "data collection", "capabilities": ["web_search"]},
        {"name": "writer", "role": "content creation", "capabilities": ["markdown"]},
    ],
    completed_tasks=[
        {"agent": "researcher", "task": "gather Q1 data", "result_preview": "Revenue: $2.3M"},
    ],
)

docs.title: ErrorContext
docs.text:
Previous errors for retry awareness.

from promptise.prompts.context import ErrorContext

errors = ErrorContext(
    errors=[{"type": "ValidationError", "message": "Missing field: revenue"}],
    retry_count=1,
    last_error="Missing field: revenue",
)

docs.title: OutputContext
docs.text:
Expected output format and constraints.

from promptise.prompts.context import OutputContext

output = OutputContext(
    format="json",
    schema_description="Object with summary, confidence, and recommendations fields",
    examples=[{"summary": "...", "confidence": 0.9}],
    constraints=["Must include confidence score"],
)

docs.title: PromptContext
docs.text:
The complete world available during prompt execution. Every context provider, strategy, perspective, guard, and hook receives this object.

from promptise.prompts.context import PromptContext, UserContext, BaseContext

ctx = PromptContext(
    prompt_name="analyze",
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    input_args={"text": "quarterly data"},
    world={
        "user": UserContext(name="Alice"),
        "project": BaseContext(sprint="2026-Q1"),
    },
)

# Convenience properties
ctx.user          # UserContext if "user" key exists in world
ctx.environment   # EnvironmentContext if "environment" key exists
ctx.conversation  # ConversationContext if "conversation" key exists
ctx.team          # TeamContext if "team" key exists
ctx.errors        # ErrorContext if "errors" key exists
ctx.output        # OutputContext if "output" key exists

docs.title: PromptContext Fields
docs.text:
Field Type Description prompt_name str Name of the prompt prompt_version str Version string model str LLM model identifier input_args dict Arguments passed to the prompt rendered_text str Rendered prompt text agent Any The agent, set when the prompt is an agent's instructions; None in a standalone call task Any A task object for task_context(); None unless you build the context yourself blackboard Any A blackboard with get_section(prefix) for blackboard_context(); None unless you build the context yourself world dict[str, BaseContext] Named context instances state dict Free-form state for your providers and hooks (a new, empty dict on every call)

All fields have defaults (prompt_version="0.0.0", everything else empty or None). A standalone call builds a new PromptContext from the arguments and the prompt's world on every call, so nothing in it carries over to the next call.

docs.title: The ContextProvider Protocol
docs.text:
Implement a single async method to create a custom provider:

from promptise.prompts.context import ContextProvider, PromptContext

class WeatherContextProvider:
    async def provide(self, ctx: PromptContext) -> str:
        # Return empty string to skip injection
        if not ctx.user:
            return ""
        return "## Current Weather\nSunny, 22C in New York"

docs.title: Built-In Providers
docs.text:
Provider Factory Injects UserContextProvider user_context() ## User Context: name, expertise, language (when not English), preferences and custom fields of world["user"] (a UserContext) EnvironmentContextProvider env_context() ## Environment: platform, timezone, available APIs and custom fields of world["environment"] (an EnvironmentContext) ConversationContextProvider conversation_context(last_n=10) ## Conversation History: summary and the last last_n messages of world["conversation"] TeamContextProvider team_context() ## Team Context: members and the last 5 completed tasks of world["team"] ErrorContextProvider error_context() ## Previous Errors: retry count, last error and the last 3 errors of world["errors"] OutputContextProvider output_context() ## Expected Output: format, schema, first 3 examples and constraints of world["output"] WorldContextProvider world_context(key, header=None) Every non-empty field of world[key], under header (default ## <Key>) StaticContextProvider static_context(text, header=None) Fixed text block CallableContextProvider callable_context(fn, header=None) The string your sync or async fn(ctx) returns (nothing when it returns an empty value) ConditionalContextProvider conditional_context(condition, provider) The inner provider's text when condition(ctx) is true MemoryContextProvider memory_context(limit=5, min_score=0.3) ## Relevant Context: memories from ctx.agent.provider scoring at least min_score; only when the prompt is an agent's instructions and the agent has a memory provider TaskContextProvider task_context() ## Task Context: goal (or name), description, expected_output, priority of ctx.task BlackboardContextProvider blackboard_context(prefix="result.") ## Prior Results: entries of ctx.blackboard.get_section(prefix) ToolContextProvider tool_context(include_schemas=False) Nothing. A placeholder kept for compatibility: tools reach the model as tool definitions. include_schemas is ignored

The typed providers check the class: user_context() reads world["user"] only when it is a UserContext (likewise EnvironmentContext, ConversationContext, TeamContext, ErrorContext, OutputContext). For a plain BaseContext, use world_context(key).

docs.title: Using the @context Decorator
docs.text:
Attach providers to a prompt with the @context() decorator:

from promptise.prompts import prompt
from promptise.prompts.context import context, tool_context, memory_context

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
@context(tool_context(), memory_context())
async def analyze(text: str) -> str:
    """Based on available context, analyze: {text}"""

docs.title: StaticContextProvider
docs.text:
Inject a fixed text block on every invocation:

from promptise.prompts.context import static_context

rules = static_context(
    "Always respond in JSON format.\nNever include PII.",
    header="## Output Rules",
)

docs.title: CallableContextProvider
docs.text:
Wrap any async callable as a context provider:

from promptise.prompts.context import callable_context

async def fetch_latest_data(ctx):
    # Fetch from database, API, etc.
    return f"Latest revenue: $2.3M"

data_provider = callable_context(fetch_latest_data, header="## Latest Data")

Sync callables also work:

def get_timestamp(ctx):
    import time
    return f"Current time: {time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M')}"

time_provider = callable_context(get_timestamp)

docs.title: ConditionalContextProvider
docs.text:
Only run the inner provider when a condition is met:

from promptise.prompts.context import conditional_context, memory_context

# Only search memories when the prompt runs inside an agent
smart_memory = conditional_context(
    condition=lambda ctx: ctx.agent is not None,
    provider=memory_context(limit=10),
)

docs.title: WorldContextProvider
docs.text:
Read any custom BaseContext from the world dict and format it as markdown:

from promptise.prompts.context import world_context

project_provider = world_context("project", header="## Project Info")

This reads ctx.world["project"] and formats all its fields into a markdown section.

docs.title: Context Classes
docs.text: Class Description BaseContext(**kwargs) Extensible key-value container UserContext(...) User identity and preferences EnvironmentContext(...) Runtime environment ConversationContext(...) Conversation history TeamContext(...) Team composition ErrorContext(...) Previous errors OutputContext(...) Expected output format PromptContext(...) Complete world during execution

docs.title: Provider Factories
docs.text: Factory Description tool_context(include_schemas=False) No-op placeholder memory_context(limit=5, min_score=0.3) Relevant memories (agent instructions only) task_context() Current task metadata blackboard_context(prefix="result.") Prior results from a blackboard user_context() User identity env_context() Environment information conversation_context(last_n=10) Conversation messages team_context() Team members and completed tasks error_context() Previous errors output_context() Output format static_context(text, header=None) Fixed text callable_context(fn, header=None) Any callable conditional_context(condition, provider) Conditional world_context(key, header=None) Custom world context

docs.title: Decorators
docs.text:
Decorator Description @context(*providers) Attach context providers to a prompt (below or above @prompt; both add)

Prompt.with_context(*providers) and PromptBuilder.context(*providers) add providers without the decorator.

Empty string skips injection

If a context provider returns an empty string, nothing is injected. This lets providers gracefully handle missing data without cluttering the prompt.

Custom fields without subclassing

You never need to subclass BaseContext. Just pass extra keyword arguments: UserContext(user_id="123", department="eng", clearance="high"). All fields are accessible via attribute access, dict-style access, and get().

Provider ordering

Providers execute in the order they are passed to @context(), and their sections appear in that order after the template text. In a PromptSuite, suite-level providers run first; a suite provider is skipped when the prompt already has a provider of the same class.

Providers that need an agent

memory_context() returns nothing in a standalone call because ctx.agent is None. It works when the prompt is passed as build_agent(instructions=...) and the agent has a memory provider. task_context() and blackboard_context() need ctx.task / ctx.blackboard, which only a PromptContext you build yourself and pass to render_async(ctx) sets.

docs.text:

  • Guards: Input/output validation

docs.title: Layer 2: ConversationFlow
docs.text: Build conversation agents where the system prompt evolves across phases: different blocks activate as the conversation progresses.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.flows import ConversationFlow, TurnContext, phase
from promptise.prompts.blocks import Identity, Rules, Section, OutputFormat

class SupportFlow(ConversationFlow):
    base_blocks = [
        Identity("Customer support specialist", traits=["empathetic", "patient"]),
        Rules(["Never blame the customer", "Keep responses to 2-3 sentences"]),
    ]

    @phase("greeting", initial=True)
    async def greet(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
        ctx.activate(Section("greet", "Ask how you can help today."))

    @phase("investigate")
    async def investigate(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
        ctx.deactivate("greet")
        ctx.activate(Section("investigate", "Ask clarifying questions."))

    @phase("resolve")
    async def resolve(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
        ctx.deactivate("investigate")
        ctx.activate(OutputFormat(format="markdown"))
        ctx.activate(Section("resolve", "Propose a concrete solution."))

flow = SupportFlow()
prompt = await flow.start("Hi")                    # Enter greeting phase with the first message
prompt = await flow.next_turn("My app crashed")    # Process user message
await flow.transition("investigate")               # Move to investigate
prompt = await flow.next_turn("It crashes on login")

A flow instance holds the state of one conversation. To use a flow in an agent, pass it to build_agent(), which keeps a separate copy per session (Integration with build_agent).

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
A ConversationFlow is a state machine where:

  • Phases define distinct conversation stages (greeting, investigation, resolution)
  • Base blocks are always included in the prompt regardless of phase
  • Phase handlers activate and deactivate blocks as the conversation evolves
  • The system prompt is not static: it is reassembled every turn with the currently active blocks

Each call to next_turn() or transition() runs the current phase handler, which can modify the active block composition, then returns a freshly assembled AssembledPrompt.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> greeting: start()
    greeting --> investigation: transition("investigate")
    investigation --> resolution: transition("resolve")
    resolution --> farewell: transition("farewell")
    farewell --> [*]

docs.title: Subclass ConversationFlow
docs.text:
Set base_blocks as a class variable for blocks that are always active:

from promptise.prompts.flows import ConversationFlow
from promptise.prompts.blocks import Identity, Rules

class MyFlow(ConversationFlow):
    base_blocks = [
        Identity("Helpful assistant"),
        Rules(["Be concise", "Ask before making assumptions"]),
    ]

docs.title: Define Phases with @phase
docs.text:
Use the @phase decorator on async methods. Mark exactly one phase as initial=True:

from promptise.prompts.flows import phase, TurnContext
from promptise.prompts.blocks import Section, OutputFormat

class MyFlow(ConversationFlow):
    base_blocks = [Identity("Assistant")]

    @phase("greeting", initial=True)
    async def greet(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
        ctx.activate(Section("greet", "Welcome the user warmly."))

    @phase("working", blocks=[OutputFormat(format="json")])
    async def work(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
        ctx.deactivate("greet")
        ctx.activate(Section("work", "Focus on completing the task."))

The @phase decorator accepts:

Parameter Type Description name str Phase name (used for transitions) initial bool Whether this is the starting phase (exactly one required) blocks list[Block] Blocks auto-activated on phase entry, auto-deactivated on exit on_enter Callable Callback invoked when entering this phase on_exit Callable Callback invoked when leaving this phase

Signature: phase(name, *, initial=False, blocks=None, on_enter=None, on_exit=None). on_enter and on_exit are called with no arguments (sync or async); use the phase handler when you need the TurnContext. On a transition the old phase's blocks are removed and its on_exit runs, then the new phase's blocks are added and its on_enter runs, then its handler runs.

Phase is a plain record

promptise.prompts.Phase(name, blocks=[], on_enter=None, on_exit=None) is a dataclass describing a phase. ConversationFlow does not take Phase objects: phases are always declared with @phase on a subclass.

docs.title: TurnContext
docs.text: Every phase handler receives a TurnContext that provides methods to manipulate the prompt and control flow.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Property Type Description turn int Current turn number (0-based) phase str Current phase name state dict[str, Any] Arbitrary flow state dict: mutate freely history list[dict] Conversation message history (read-only copy)

docs.title: Block Manipulation
docs.text:
@phase("investigate")
async def investigate(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
    # Remove a block from the active composition
    ctx.deactivate("greeting_instructions")

    # Add a new block
    ctx.activate(Section("investigate", "Ask clarifying questions."))

    # Fill a ContextSlot by name
    ctx.fill_slot("user_info", "Premium customer since 2023")
Method Description activate(block) Add a block to the active prompt composition deactivate(name) Remove a block by name fill_slot(name, value) Fill a ContextSlot block by name transition(phase_name) Request a phase transition (happens after handler completes) get_prompt() Assemble the current prompt without advancing the turn

docs.title: In-Handler Transitions
docs.text:
Call ctx.transition() inside a phase handler to request a transition after the current handler completes:

@phase("greeting", initial=True)
async def greet(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
    if ctx.state.get("returning_customer"):
        ctx.transition("working")  # Skip to working phase
    else:
        ctx.activate(Section("greet", "Welcome! How can I help?"))

docs.title: Starting the Flow
docs.text:
start() enters the initial phase, runs its handler, and returns the first assembled prompt. Pass the conversation's first user message so the initial phase handler can act on it (it is recorded in ctx.history as turn 0):

flow = SupportFlow()
prompt = await flow.start("Hi, my app keeps crashing")
print(prompt.text)              # Full prompt with base + greeting blocks
print(prompt.included)          # ["identity", "rules", "greet"]

start() with no argument still works and starts the flow before any message arrives.

docs.title: Processing Turns
docs.text:
next_turn() records the user message in history, runs the current phase handler, and returns the updated prompt:

prompt = await flow.next_turn("My app keeps crashing")
print(prompt.text)  # Prompt reflects current phase blocks

Optional parameters:

prompt = await flow.next_turn(
    "Details about the crash",
    assistant_message="I understand, let me help.",  # Record assistant reply
    transition_to="resolution",   # Force a phase transition before processing
)

docs.title: Explicit Transitions
docs.text:
transition() moves to a new phase, runs the new phase handler, and returns the updated prompt. It does not advance the turn counter:

prompt = await flow.transition("resolution")

A transition to an unknown phase raises ValueError. If the handler run by transition() itself calls ctx.transition(), the flow enters that next phase and runs its handler too, in the same call, as start() and next_turn() do. Transitions requested by those handlers are followed the same way. One call runs at most 5 phases: circular transitions (a → b → a ...) raise RecursionError.

docs.title: Reading the Current Prompt
docs.text:
get_prompt() assembles the current state without advancing the turn counter:

prompt = flow.get_prompt()

docs.title: Resetting
docs.text:
reset() clears all state, history, active blocks, and the turn counter:

flow.reset()
# Flow is now back to its initial state, ready for start()

docs.title: Token Budget
docs.text:
Cap the assembled prompt with token_budget, as a class attribute or a constructor argument. Over budget, blocks are dropped lowest-priority first, exactly as in PromptAssembler. Dropped blocks are listed in prompt.excluded.

class SupportFlow(ConversationFlow):
    token_budget = 1500          # every instance
    ...

flow = SupportFlow(token_budget=800)   # or per instance

docs.title: Inspecting a Flow
docs.text:
Give the flow a PromptInspector and every start(), next_turn() and transition() records a trace with the blocks included and excluded, the token estimate, the prompt text, and flow_phase / flow_turn:

from promptise.prompts.inspector import PromptInspector
from promptise.prompts.flows import ConversationFlow, TurnContext, phase
from promptise.prompts.blocks import Identity, Section

class SupportFlow(ConversationFlow):
    base_blocks = [Identity("Customer support specialist")]

    @phase("greeting", initial=True)
    async def greet(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
        ctx.activate(Section("greet", "Ask how you can help today."))

inspector = PromptInspector()
flow = SupportFlow(inspector=inspector)   # or set `inspector = ...` on the class
await flow.start("Hi")
trace = inspector.last()
print(trace.prompt_name, trace.flow_phase, trace.flow_turn)   # SupportFlow greeting 0

docs.title: Integration with build_agent
docs.text:
Pass a flow to build_agent() and the system prompt evolves with each message:

import asyncio
from promptise import build_agent
from promptise.config import HTTPServerSpec

async def main():
    agent = await build_agent(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        servers={"support": HTTPServerSpec(url="http://localhost:8080/mcp")},
        flow=SupportFlow(),
        instructions="Use the tools to look up orders.",   # optional
    )
    try:
        reply = await agent.chat("My mug arrived broken.", session_id="sess-1", user_id="dana")
        reply = await agent.chat("The order is A-1001.", session_id="sess-1", user_id="dana")
        print(agent.get_flow("sess-1", user_id="dana").get_prompt().included)
    finally:
        await agent.shutdown()

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: One flow per conversation
docs.text:
A flow carries one conversation's phase, history, ctx.state and slot fills, so the agent never shares one between conversations. The flow you pass is a template: each conversation gets its own deep copy. You can also pass the class (flow=SupportFlow) or any zero-argument factory (flow=lambda: SupportFlow(business_customer=True)), which is called once per conversation. If your flow holds something that can't be deep-copied (a client, a lock), pass a factory: build_agent() raises TypeError otherwise.

The agent picks the conversation from the call:

Call Flow state kept per agent.chat(msg, session_id=...) session, scoped to its caller / user_id agent.ainvoke(input, session_id=...) session, scoped to its caller agent.ainvoke(input, caller=CallerContext(user_id=...)) caller (tenant and user) agent.ainvoke(input) with neither nothing kept: a fresh flow built from the messages in input

When the agent first sees a conversation, it starts a new flow and feeds it every user message in the input, in order: the first message goes to start(), the rest to next_turn(). After that, each call feeds only the newest user message. So a conversation whose history is passed in (from a conversation store after a restart, or a full messages list with no session_id) resumes in the right phase. The agent keeps up to 10,000 flows; the least recently used is dropped and rebuilt the same way when that conversation continues. delete_session() drops the session's flow.

Phase handlers replay

Rebuilding a flow runs its phase handlers once per earlier user message. Keep handlers free of side effects (they should only read ctx.history and ctx.state and change blocks), or pass a session_id so the flow is built once.

Use agent.get_flow(session_id, caller=..., user_id=...) to read a conversation's flow, for example its phase (flow.current_phase) or its current prompt (flow.get_prompt()). The template you passed to build_agent() is never advanced.

docs.title: What the model receives
docs.text:
The model gets one system message: the flow's prompt for this turn, then your instructions, then the list of available tools. Without instructions, nothing is added to the flow's prompt; the generic default system prompt is only used when there is no flow.

Not on streaming calls

Flows run on ainvoke(), invoke() and chat(). astream() and astream_with_tools() don't advance a flow, and neither does an agent built with a context_engine.

docs.title: Full Example: Customer Support Agent
docs.text:
import asyncio
from promptise.prompts import prompt
from promptise.prompts.blocks import Identity, Rules, Section, OutputFormat
from promptise.prompts.flows import ConversationFlow, TurnContext, phase

class SupportFlow(ConversationFlow):
    base_blocks = [
        Identity(
            "Customer support specialist for TechCorp",
            traits=["empathetic", "patient", "solution-oriented"],
        ),
        Rules([
            "Never blame the customer",
            "Acknowledge frustration before problem-solving",
            "Keep responses to 2-3 sentences",
        ]),
    ]

    @phase("greeting", initial=True)
    async def greet(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
        ctx.activate(Section(
            "greeting_instructions",
            "Warmly greet the customer. Ask how you can help today.",
        ))

    @phase("investigation")
    async def investigate(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
        ctx.deactivate("greeting_instructions")
        ctx.activate(Section(
            "investigation_instructions",
            "Ask clarifying questions: what happened, when, what they tried.",
        ))

    @phase("resolution")
    async def resolve(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
        ctx.deactivate("investigation_instructions")
        ctx.activate(Section("resolution_instructions", "Propose a concrete fix."))
        ctx.activate(OutputFormat(format="markdown"))

    @phase("farewell")
    async def farewell(self, ctx: TurnContext) -> None:
        ctx.deactivate("resolution_instructions")
        ctx.deactivate("output_format")
        ctx.activate(Section("farewell_instructions", "Thank the customer."))

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def respond(system_prompt: str, conversation: str) -> str:
    """{system_prompt}

Conversation so far:
{conversation}

Respond as the support agent:"""

async def main():
    flow = SupportFlow()
    assembled = await flow.start()

    # Greeting
    response = await respond(
        system_prompt=assembled.text,
        conversation="(Customer just connected)",
    )
    print(f"Agent: {response}")

    # Customer describes issue -> transition to investigation
    assembled = await flow.next_turn(
        "My app crashes on file upload",
        transition_to="investigation",
    )
    response = await respond(
        system_prompt=assembled.text,
        conversation="Customer: My app crashes on file upload",
    )
    print(f"Agent: {response}")

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: ConversationFlow
docs.text: Method Returns Description ConversationFlow(*, token_budget=None, inspector=None) Create a flow; both default to the class attributes start(user_message=None) AssembledPrompt Enter initial phase (with the first message) and return first prompt next_turn(user_message, ...) AssembledPrompt Process a turn and return updated prompt transition(phase_name) AssembledPrompt Transition to a new phase get_prompt() AssembledPrompt Get current prompt without advancing turn reset() None Reset to initial state current_phase str \| None Current phase name (property), None before start()

docs.title: TurnContext
docs.text:
Method Description activate(block) Add a block to the active composition deactivate(name) Remove a block by name fill_slot(name, value) Fill a ContextSlot transition(phase_name) Request a deferred phase transition get_prompt() Assemble and return current prompt

One initial phase required

Exactly one phase must be marked initial=True. Two initial phases raise ValueError when the flow is created; phases with no initial one raise ValueError on start(). A flow with no phases at all is allowed: start() returns the base blocks.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use ctx.state to track conversation metadata (e.g., questions_asked, issue_category) across phases.
  • Phase handlers run on every turn within that phase: use them to dynamically adjust blocks based on conversation progress.
  • Blocks from @phase(blocks=[...]) are automatically activated on phase entry and deactivated on exit. Blocks added via ctx.activate() persist until explicitly deactivated.
  • Use ctx.history inside handlers for a copy of the recorded messages ({"role": ..., "content": ...} dicts). Only start() and next_turn() record messages; the assistant reply is recorded only when you pass assistant_message=.
  • Run a flow by hand (as in the full example) when you drive the model yourself. Create one flow per conversation and keep it with that conversation.

docs.title: Prompt Guards
docs.text: Runtime enforcers that validate and transform input before the LLM call and output after it. Guards protect your prompts from bad data going in and bad data coming out.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts import prompt
from promptise.prompts.guards import guard, content_filter, length

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
@guard(
    content_filter(blocked=["secret", "password"]),
    length(max_length=2000),
)
async def analyze(text: str) -> str:
    """Analyze in at most three sentences: {text}"""

result = await analyze("Quarterly revenue grew 15%...")

If the input contains a blocked word, the guard raises GuardError before the LLM is ever called. If the output exceeds 2000 characters, the guard raises after the call returns.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Guards implement two async methods:

  • check_input(input_text): runs before the LLM call. Returns the (possibly transformed) text or raises GuardError to reject.
  • check_output(output): runs after the LLM call, on the parsed result (a string, or your Pydantic model / dict / list for a typed return). Returns the (possibly transformed) output or raises GuardError to reject.

Guards are attached to prompts via the @guard() decorator, with_guards(), PromptBuilder.guard() or a suite's default_guards. Every guard is registered on both sides: its check_input and its check_output both run. Multiple guards execute in order, each guard's output feeding the next.

What check_input receives depends on how the prompt runs:

Mode check_input receives check_output receives Standalone call (await my_prompt(...)) The full rendered prompt text: blocks, template, context, perspective, strategy, constraints, schema instructions The parsed result Agent instructions (build_agent(instructions=my_prompt)) Each user message The agent's reply text

Input guards see your own prompt text in standalone calls

content_filter(blocked=["password"]) on a standalone prompt also rejects the call when your own blocks, template or constraints contain "password". Keep blocked words out of your instructions, or check only the user-supplied value in an input_validator.

docs.title: ContentFilterGuard
docs.text:
Block or require specific words (case-insensitive) in both input and output.

from promptise.prompts.guards import content_filter

# Block dangerous words in input AND output
safe = content_filter(blocked=["secret", "password", "ssn"])

# Require specific words in output
quality = content_filter(required=["recommendation", "conclusion"])

# Combine both
strict = content_filter(
    blocked=["confidential"],
    required=["summary"],
)

docs.title: LengthGuard
docs.text:
Enforce character length bounds on output.

from promptise.prompts.guards import length

# Maximum length only
concise = length(max_length=500)

# Minimum length only
detailed = length(min_length=200)

# Both bounds
bounded = length(min_length=100, max_length=2000)

docs.title: SchemaStrictGuard
docs.text:
Validates that LLM output is well-formed JSON. Raises GuardError if the output cannot be parsed as JSON. Non-string outputs (a parsed Pydantic model, dict or list) are passed through unchanged. schema_strict() takes no arguments: it does not check a schema and does not retry.

from promptise.prompts.guards import schema_strict

strict = schema_strict()

Prefer a typed return for structured output

With a str return type, a reply wrapped in a Markdown code fence fails schema_strict(). Annotating the return type with a Pydantic model (-> Analysis) adds the JSON schema to the request, strips fences, extracts the first JSON value and validates it; a reply that doesn't validate raises ValidationError. Wrap the prompt in retry() to try again.

docs.title: InputValidatorGuard
docs.text:
Wrap any callable (sync or async) as an input-only validator. The callable receives input text and must return text or raise an exception.

from promptise.prompts.guards import input_validator, GuardError

def require_revenue_data(text: str) -> str:
    if "revenue" not in text.lower():
        raise GuardError("Input must mention revenue", guard_name="require_revenue")
    return text

revenue_guard = input_validator(require_revenue_data)

Async validators work the same way:

async def check_against_blocklist(text: str) -> str:
    # Could call an external API here
    return text

async_guard = input_validator(check_against_blocklist)

docs.title: OutputValidatorGuard
docs.text:
Wrap any callable (sync or async) as an output-only validator. The callable receives the LLM output and returns the (possibly transformed) value.

from promptise.prompts.guards import output_validator

def clean_whitespace(output: str) -> str:
    return output.strip().replace("  ", " ")

clean_guard = output_validator(clean_whitespace)

docs.title: Using the @guard Decorator
docs.text:
Attach one or more guards to a prompt with the @guard() decorator. Stack it below @prompt:

from promptise.prompts import prompt
from promptise.prompts.guards import guard, content_filter, length, schema_strict

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
@guard(
    content_filter(blocked=["secret"]),
    length(max_length=2000),
    schema_strict(),
)
async def summarize(text: str) -> str:
    """Summarize as a JSON object with a "summary" key: {text}"""

The @guard decorator can be applied before or after @prompt: it detects whether it is decorating a Prompt object or a plain function and adds the guards either way.

docs.title: Custom Guards
docs.text:
Implement the Guard protocol for full control over both input and output:

import re
from typing import Any
from promptise.prompts.guards import GuardError

class PiiRedactionGuard:
    """Redact SSNs from input before sending to the LLM."""

    async def check_input(self, input_text: str) -> str:
        return re.sub(r"\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}", "[REDACTED]", input_text)

    async def check_output(self, output: Any) -> Any:
        if isinstance(output, str):
            return re.sub(r"\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}", "[REDACTED]", output)
        return output

Attach your custom guard the same way:

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
@guard(PiiRedactionGuard(), content_filter(blocked=["password"]))
async def process(text: str) -> str:
    """Process: {text}"""

docs.title: Handling GuardError
docs.text:
When a built-in guard rejects input or output, it raises GuardError(message, guard_name="") with the message in reason (and str(e)) and the guard's name in guard_name ("content_filter", "length", "schema_strict"). Exceptions raised by your own validators propagate as they are; raise GuardError yourself to get the same shape. The prompt's on_error hook runs before the exception reaches you, and an attached inspector lists the guard in guards_failed.

from promptise.prompts.guards import GuardError

try:
    result = await analyze("Contains secret data")
except GuardError as e:
    print(f"Guard '{e.guard_name}' rejected: {e.reason}")
    # Guard 'content_filter' rejected: Input contains blocked word: 'secret'

docs.title: API Summary
docs.text:
Factory / Class Description content_filter(blocked=[], required=[]) Block or require specific words (case-insensitive) length(min_length=None, max_length=None) Enforce output character length bounds schema_strict() Reject a string output that is not valid JSON input_validator(fn) Wrap any callable as an input-only validator output_validator(fn) Wrap any callable as an output-only validator guard(*guards) Decorator that attaches guards to a Prompt GuardError Exception raised when a guard rejects Guard Protocol with check_input() and check_output() methods

Guards are transformers, not just validators

Guards can transform data, not just reject it. Use InputValidatorGuard to sanitize input (redact PII, normalize whitespace) and OutputValidatorGuard to clean up output (strip extra whitespace, fix formatting) before it reaches your application.

Guard ordering matters

Guards execute in the order they are passed to @guard(), and a transforming guard changes what the next one sees. Put redaction before a content_filter that would otherwise reject the unredacted text.

Built-in guard classes

The factories return ContentFilterGuard(blocked=None, required=None), LengthGuard(min_length=None, max_length=None), SchemaStrictGuard(), InputValidatorGuard(fn) and OutputValidatorGuard(fn), all importable from promptise.prompts.guards. content_filter matching is a case-insensitive substring test, so blocked=["ssn"] also matches "lessons". required words are checked on output only, and length checks output only.

  • Structured Outputs: Get Reliable JSON from an LLM: Get reliable JSON from an LLM.

docs.title: Prompt Inspector & Observability
docs.text: See how your prompts are assembled: which blocks made it in, token estimates, what was dropped, guard results, and the exact text sent to the LLM.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.inspector import PromptInspector
from promptise.prompts import prompt
from promptise.prompts.blocks import blocks, Identity, Rules

inspector = PromptInspector()

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", inspect=inspector)
@blocks(Identity("Analyst"), Rules(["Be precise"]))
async def analyze(text: str) -> str:
    """Analyze: {text}"""

result = await analyze("quarterly data")

trace = inspector.last()
print(trace.prompt_name)            # "analyze"
print(trace.blocks_included)        # ["identity", "rules"]
print(trace.total_tokens_estimated) # estimate for the assembled blocks
print(trace.input_text)             # Full prompt sent to LLM
print(trace.latency_ms)             # Execution time in ms

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The prompt framework has two observability tools:

  • PromptInspector: local debugging and tracing. Records detailed traces of every prompt assembly and execution. Designed for development and testing.
  • PromptObserver: production telemetry. Records structured events to a pluggable ObservabilityCollector. Designed for metrics, monitoring, and dashboards.

Both can be used simultaneously. The inspector records everything locally; the observer emits events to your telemetry pipeline.

docs.title: Recording Traces
docs.text:
Attach the inspector to a prompt with @prompt(inspect=...) or prompt.with_inspector(inspector). A ConversationFlow takes inspector= too:

from promptise.prompts.inspector import PromptInspector

inspector = PromptInspector()

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", inspect=inspector)
async def summarize(text: str) -> str:
    """Summarize: {text}"""

result = await summarize("long article text...")

Each standalone call, each render_async() (also when the prompt is an agent's instructions), and each flow start() / next_turn() / transition() records one PromptTrace. One inspector can be shared by many prompts.

docs.title: Reading Traces
docs.text:
# Most recent trace
trace = inspector.last()

# All recorded traces
all_traces = inspector.traces

# Human-readable summary
print(inspector.summary())

docs.title: PromptTrace Fields
docs.text: Field Type Description prompt_name str Name of the prompt model str Model used timestamp float Unix timestamp blocks list[BlockTrace] Per-block details total_tokens_estimated int Estimated tokens of the assembled blocks (not the whole prompt) blocks_included list[str] Blocks included in assembly blocks_excluded list[str] Blocks not included context_providers list[ContextTrace] One entry per context provider that ran: class name, characters it added, time it took input_text str Final text sent to the LLM (after input guards) output_text str Raw LLM response after the strategy's parse() (standalone calls only) latency_ms float Execution time in milliseconds (standalone calls only) guards_passed list[str] Guards that passed every check they ran, each listed once (a guard attached with @guard or with_guards() checks both the input and the output) guards_failed list[str] Guards that rejected the input or output flow_phase str Conversation flow phase (if used) flow_turn int Conversation flow turn number

docs.title: ContextTrace Fields
docs.text: Field Type Description provider_name str Name of the context provider chars_injected int Characters injected into the prompt render_time_ms float Time to render the context

docs.title: Summary Report
docs.text:
print(inspector.summary())

Produces a human-readable report covering all recorded prompt traces, including blocks, context providers, and guards.

docs.title: Inspector API
docs.text:
Method / Property Returns Description last() PromptTrace \| None Most recent prompt trace traces list[PromptTrace] All recorded prompt traces (a copy) last_graph() GraphTrace \| None Most recent graph trace graph_traces list[GraphTrace] All recorded graph traces (a copy) summary() str Human-readable summary report clear() None Discard all recorded traces

Recording methods (auto-called by @prompt; available for custom integrations):

Method Description record_assembly(assembled, prompt_name, model) Record how the prompt was assembled record_execution(trace, output, latency_ms) Record LLM output and latency record_context(trace, provider_name, chars_injected, render_time_ms) Record a context provider contribution record_guard(trace, guard_name, passed) Record guard pass/fail record_graph(graph_name, node_traces, total_duration_ms, path, iterations, final_state) Record a graph run as a GraphTrace (with NodeTrace entries)

Guard names in traces are the guard's name attribute, or its class name (ContentFilterGuard, LengthGuard, ...).

docs.title: PromptObserver
docs.text: PromptObserver(collector) turns prompt lifecycle events into timeline events on an ObservabilityCollector. Recording failures are logged at debug level and never raise.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.observe import PromptObserver
from promptise.observability import ObservabilityCollector

collector = ObservabilityCollector()
observer = PromptObserver(collector)

A prompt records its calls with an observer when you ask for it: @prompt(observe=...), PromptBuilder.observe(...), observe: true in a YAML prompt file, or with_observer(...) on any prompt:

from promptise.observability import ObservabilityCollector
from promptise.prompts import prompt

collector = ObservabilityCollector()

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", observe=collector)   # or observe=observer
async def analyze(text: str) -> str:
    """Analyze: {text}"""

result = await analyze("Q3 revenue $3.2M")
print([e.event_type for e in collector.get_timeline()])
# [<TimelineEventType.PROMPT_START: 'prompt.start'>, <TimelineEventType.PROMPT_END: 'prompt.end'>]
observe= Events go to False (default) Nowhere; prompt.observer is None True The prompt's own ObservabilityCollector: analyze.observer.collector.get_timeline() An ObservabilityCollector That collector (share one between prompts, or with an agent's collector) A PromptObserver That observer

Each standalone call (await analyze(...)) records PROMPT_START when it starts, PROMPT_CONTEXT for each context provider, PROMPT_GUARD_BLOCK when a guard rejects the input or output, then PROMPT_END on success or PROMPT_ERROR on failure. Copies made with with_*() record to the same observer. Rendering without an LLM call (render_async(), a prompt used as agent instructions) records nothing; the agent's own observability covers those runs. An observer that raises is logged at debug level and never fails the call.

You can also call the observer yourself, for example from lifecycle hooks, with the methods below.

docs.title: Events Recorded
docs.text:
Method Event Data record_start(prompt_name, model, input_text) PROMPT_START prompt_name, model, input_length record_end(prompt_name, model, latency_ms, output_length) PROMPT_END prompt_name, model, latency_ms, output_length record_error(prompt_name, error) PROMPT_ERROR prompt_name, error_type, error_message record_guard_block(prompt_name, guard_name, reason) PROMPT_GUARD_BLOCK prompt_name, guard_name, reason record_context(prompt_name, provider_name, chars_injected) PROMPT_CONTEXT prompt_name, provider, chars_injected

Each event uses the prompt name as its agent_id.

docs.title: Observer API
docs.text:
Method Description record_start(prompt_name, model, input_text) Record prompt execution start record_end(prompt_name, model, latency_ms, output_length) Record prompt execution end record_error(prompt_name, error) Record prompt execution error record_guard_block(prompt_name, guard_name, reason) Record a guard blocking execution record_context(prompt_name, provider_name, chars_injected) Record context provider execution

Inspector for debugging, Observer for production

Use PromptInspector during development to understand exactly how your prompts are assembled. Use PromptObserver in production to feed metrics into your monitoring pipeline. They serve different purposes and can run simultaneously.

Inspector stores traces in memory

The inspector keeps all traces in memory. Call inspector.clear() periodically in long-running processes to avoid unbounded memory growth.

docs.text:
