docs.title: Prompt Loader & Templates
docs.text: Load prompts from .prompt YAML files, save prompts back to YAML, and use the built-in template engine for variable interpolation, conditionals, loops, and includes.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
# prompts/analyze.prompt
name: analyze
version: "1.0.0"
description: Expert data analysis prompt
author: team-data
tags: [analysis, reporting]

template: |
  Analyze the following data: {text}
  Focus area: {focus}

arguments:
  text:
    description: The data to analyze
    required: true
  focus:
    description: Specific area to focus on
    required: false
    default: general

strategy: chain_of_thought
perspective: analyst
constraints:
  - Must include confidence scores

from promptise.prompts.loader import load_prompt

prompt = load_prompt("prompts/analyze.prompt")
result = await prompt(text="quarterly figures...", focus="revenue trends")

docs.title: File Extensions
docs.text:
The loader accepts three extensions:

  • .prompt
  • .prompt.yaml
  • .prompt.yml

docs.title: Loading a Single Prompt
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.loader import load_prompt

prompt = load_prompt("prompts/analyze.prompt")
result = await prompt(text="quarterly figures...")

The register parameter auto-registers the loaded prompt into the global PromptRegistry:

prompt = load_prompt("prompts/analyze.prompt", register=True)
# Now available via registry.get("analyze", "1.0.0")

docs.title: Loading from a URL
docs.text:
Fetch a .prompt file from any HTTP(S) URL:

from promptise.prompts.loader import load_url

prompt = await load_url(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/org/prompts/main/analyze.prompt",
    register=True,
)
result = await prompt(text="quarterly figures...")

load_url() is async. It refuses URLs whose host resolves to a private, loopback or link-local address (PromptFileError), uses a 30-second timeout, and wraps HTTP errors in PromptFileError. It needs httpx, which Promptise installs.

docs.title: Loading a Directory
docs.text:
Recursively load all .prompt files from a directory into a local PromptRegistry:

from promptise.prompts.loader import load_directory

local_registry = load_directory("prompts/")

# Retrieve prompts from the local registry
analyze = local_registry.get("analyze")
summarize = local_registry.get("summarize", "2.0.0")

Pass register=True to also register each prompt in the global registry. load_directory() scans **/*.prompt, **/*.prompt.yaml and **/*.prompt.yml recursively. Suite files are loaded (so they are validated) but not added to the returned registry, and a second file with the same name and version is skipped. A missing directory raises PromptFileError.

docs.title: Saving a Prompt to YAML
docs.text:
Export any Prompt instance back to a .prompt file:

from promptise.prompts.loader import save_prompt

save_prompt(
    my_prompt,
    "prompts/exported.prompt",
    version="2.0.0",
    author="data-team",
    description="Improved analysis prompt",
    tags=["analysis", "v2"],
)

The version, author, description, and tags parameters override the prompt's stored metadata. save_prompt() writes the template, arguments (from the function signature), built-in strategies and perspectives, constraints, the built-in guards, world contexts and a non-default model. Blocks, context providers, hooks, custom strategies, custom guards and the return type are not saved.

docs.title: Complete YAML Schema
docs.text:
All supported fields for a .prompt file:

# --- Required ---
name: "my_prompt"              # Unique prompt name; must be a Python identifier
template: "..."                # Prompt template with {variable} placeholders

# --- Model ---
model: "openai:gpt-5-mini"    # LLM model (can be overridden at runtime)

# --- Metadata ---
version: "1.0.0"              # Semantic version
description: "..."            # Human-readable description
author: "team-name"           # Author or team
tags: [tag1, tag2]            # Searchable tags

# --- Arguments (replace the signature taken from the template) ---
arguments:
  variable_name:
    description: "What this argument is"
    required: true             # default true
    default: "fallback"        # string; used when required is false (else "")

# --- Return type (default: str) ---
return_type: "str"             # str, int, float, bool, list, dict

# --- Reasoning ---
strategy: "chain_of_thought"   # Built-in strategy name
perspective: "analyst"         # Built-in perspective name

# --- Constraints ---
constraints:
  - "Be concise"
  - "Under 500 words"

# --- Guards ---
guards:
  - type: "length"
    max_length: 500
  - type: "content_filter"
    blocked: ["secret", "password"]
  - type: "schema_strict"      # no options

# --- Observability ---
observe: false                 # true: record calls with a PromptObserver (prompt.observer.collector)

# --- World context ---
world:
  user:
    type: UserContext          # UserContext, EnvironmentContext, ConversationContext,
    name: "Alice"              # TeamContext, ErrorContext, OutputContext or BaseContext
    expertise_level: "expert"
  project:                     # no type: BaseContext
    sprint: "2026-Q1"
    budget: 50000

Unknown top-level keys are rejected (PromptValidationError, with the pydantic errors in .errors and the path in .file_path). A single prompt needs template; a suite needs prompts. Defaults: version: "0.0.0", model: openai:gpt-5-mini. The file has no keys for blocks or context providers: put that text in the template, or add them in code with with_blocks() / with_context() after loading. World contexts are only read by a context provider, which you add in code.

docs.title: Available Strategy Names
docs.text:
chain_of_thought, structured_reasoning, self_critique, plan_and_execute, decompose

Composite strategies use a list:

strategy: ["chain_of_thought", "self_critique"]

docs.title: Available Perspective Names
docs.text:
analyst, critic, advisor, creative

Custom perspectives use a dict:

perspective:
  role: "security auditor"
  instructions: "Focus on OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities."

docs.title: Available Guard Types
docs.text: content_filter (blocked, required), length (min_length, max_length), schema_strict (no options). Other keys on a guard entry are ignored; an unknown type raises PromptFileError.

docs.title: Suite Format
docs.text:
When suite: true, the file defines multiple prompts sharing defaults:

name: data_suite
suite: true
description: Data analysis prompt suite
author: team-data

defaults:
  strategy: "chain_of_thought"
  perspective: "analyst"
  constraints:
    - "Be concise"

prompts:
  summarize:
    template: "Summarize: {text}"
  analyze:
    template: "Analyze: {data}"
    strategy: "structured_reasoning"  # Per-prompt override

In a suite file, defaults are merged into every entry of prompts (the entry wins), and each entry may use any single-prompt key. load_prompt() returns a PromptSuite instance whose prompts are attributes; register=True is ignored for suites.

docs.title: Environment Variable Resolution
docs.text:
Every string value in the file (not only the template) supports ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default}, resolved from the environment when the file is loaded:

template: |
  API endpoint: ${API_BASE_URL:-https://api.example.com}
  Analyze: {text}

docs.title: Template Engine
docs.text: The built-in TemplateEngine provides variable interpolation, conditionals, loops, and template includes. It is intentionally minimal, not a Jinja2 replacement.

docs.title: Variable Interpolation
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.template import render_template

result = render_template(
    "Summarize in {max_words} words: {text}",
    {"text": "long article...", "max_words": 100},
)

docs.title: Conditionals
docs.text:
result = render_template(
    "{% if formal %}Use formal language.{% endif %}\nAnalyze: {text}",
    {"formal": True, "text": "data..."},
)

With else branches:

result = render_template(
    "{% if detailed %}Provide a detailed analysis.{% else %}Be brief.{% endif %}\n{text}",
    {"detailed": False, "text": "data..."},
)

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
result = render_template(
    "{% for topic in topics %}Discuss: {topic}\n{% endfor %}",
    {"topics": ["AI safety", "Alignment", "Governance"]},
)

docs.title: Includes
docs.text:
Register reusable template fragments, then reference them with {% include "name" %}:

from promptise.prompts.template import TemplateEngine

engine = TemplateEngine(includes={
    "header": "You are a {role} assistant.",
    "rules": "Rules:\n- Be concise\n- Cite sources",
})

result = engine.render(
    '{% include "header" %}\n{% include "rules" %}\n\nAnalyze: {text}',
    {"role": "research", "text": "quarterly data..."},
)

docs.title: Literal Braces
docs.text:
Use {{ and }} to output literal curly braces:

result = render_template(
    "Return JSON like: {{\"key\": \"value\"}}\nInput: {text}",
    {"text": "data..."},
)
# Output: Return JSON like: {"key": "value"}
# Input: data...

docs.title: Processing Order
docs.text:
The engine processes templates in this order:

  1. {% include "name" %}: resolved from the includes registry (unknown name: ValueError)
  2. !`cmd`: shell interpolation, only when a shell_executor is set (see Shell Context Injection); the output is literal text, braces included
  3. {% if %}...{% else %}...{% endif %}: truthiness of the variable (missing counts as false)
  4. {% for item in items %}...{% endfor %}: iteration (missing collection: KeyError)
  5. {{ / }}: literal brace escapes
  6. {variable}: interpolation (missing variable: KeyError; {a.b} or {a[0]}: ValueError)

Conditions and loops take a bare variable name (no expressions, no nesting of the same tag). Inside a loop, only {item} is replaced; filters and loop indexes are not supported.

docs.title: Loader Functions
docs.text: Function Returns Description load_prompt(path, *, register=False) Prompt \| PromptSuite Load from a .prompt YAML file await load_url(url, *, register=False) Prompt \| PromptSuite Load from a public HTTP(S) URL save_prompt(prompt, path, *, version=None, author=None, description=None, tags=None) None Save a Prompt to a YAML file load_directory(path, *, register=False) PromptRegistry Load all .prompt files from a directory

docs.title: Template Functions
docs.text: Function / Class Description render_template(template, variables, includes=None, *, shell_executor=None) Convenience function to render a template TemplateEngine(includes=None, *, shell_executor=None) Template engine with an include registry TemplateEngine.render(template, variables) Render a template with variables

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Exception Description PromptFileError Error loading or saving a .prompt file (missing file, wrong extension, YAML error, unknown strategy, perspective, guard or return type) PromptValidationError Schema validation failed; a PromptFileError subclass with .errors (list of dicts) and .file_path

Portable prompts

YAML prompt files are model-agnostic. Define the prompt structure in YAML, choose the model at runtime, and share prompts across teams and projects.

Missing variables raise KeyError

If a template references {variable} and it is not in the variables dict, a KeyError is raised. A prompt loaded from YAML without an arguments section gives every template variable a default of "", so a missing argument renders as an empty string; with arguments, a required: true argument must be passed. Use required: false and a default for optional variables.

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text:
• Suite & Registry: Group and version prompts
  • PromptBuilder: Fluent API for runtime prompt construction
  • Inspector: Trace how prompts are assembled

docs.title: Shell Context Injection in Templates
docs.text:
Inject live system context into prompt templates by running shell commands at render time. The !cmd`` syntax executes a command and replaces itself with stdout.

from promptise.prompts import TemplateEngine, SubprocessShellExecutor

engine = TemplateEngine(
    shell_executor=SubprocessShellExecutor(timeout=2.0),
)

out = engine.render(
    "Today is !`date +%Y-%m-%d`. Branch: !`git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`.",
    {},
)
# "Today is 2026-04-11. Branch: main."

docs.title: Disabled by default
docs.text:
Without an explicit shell_executor, the !cmd` syntax is left as **literal text**: there is no implicit shell access.@prompttemplates,PromptBuilderand.promptfiles render without an executor, so shell interpolation only happens where you callTemplateEngineorrender_template(..., shell_executor=...)` yourself.

# No executor → syntax stays literal
engine = TemplateEngine()
out = engine.render("Today is !`date`", {})
# "Today is !`date`"

docs.title: SubprocessShellExecutor
docs.text:
The built-in executor runs commands via the system shell with a configurable timeout:

from promptise.prompts import SubprocessShellExecutor

executor = SubprocessShellExecutor(
    timeout=5.0,          # max seconds per command (default 5)
    shell=True,           # run via /bin/sh -c (default True; ignored with an allowlist)
    cwd="/path/to/repo",  # working directory (default: inherited)
    env={"API_KEY": "x"}, # extra env vars (merged with os.environ)
)

With shell=False the command line is tokenized like a terminal would (shlex.split) and its executable resolved on PATH. Unless cwd is set, the process is started without fork() (CPython's posix_spawn path): a forked child of a multithreaded process that has used macOS system frameworks (any httpx client does) can die with SIGSEGV before exec, which surfaces as exited -11. Setting cwd forces the fork path, so prefer running the command with an absolute path over changing directory.

docs.title: Allowlist
docs.text:
When allowlist is set, a command runs only if its first word is one of the allowlisted executable names, and it never runs through a shell, whatever shell says. The command line is split into words like a shell would (shlex.split, so quotes work), and the program is started directly:

from promptise.prompts import ShellExecutionError, SubprocessShellExecutor, TemplateEngine

executor = SubprocessShellExecutor(allowlist={"git", "date"})
engine = TemplateEngine(shell_executor=executor)

print(engine.render("Branch: !`git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`", {}))   # Branch: main

for command in ["rm -rf /tmp/x", "git status; rm -rf /tmp/x"]:
    try:
        engine.render(f"!`{command}`", {})
    except ShellExecutionError as exc:
        print(exc)
# command 'rm' not in shell executor allowlist
# shell operator ';' is not allowed with a shell executor allowlist (allowlisted commands run without a shell)

What the allowlist enforces:

  • Shell syntax is refused, not passed on. An unquoted ;, |, &, &&, ||, <, >, ( or ) raises ShellExecutionError, so a second command can't be chained, piped or substituted ($(...)). Quoted, these characters are ordinary text in an argument (git log --grep 'a;b'). $HOME and globs such as * are not expanded.
  • The first word must match exactly: {"git"} allows git ... (found on PATH) but not /usr/bin/git or ./git.
  • Programs only: shell builtins can't be allowlisted, since no shell runs them (echo works on Linux and macOS, where it is also a program, but not on Windows, where it is a cmd.exe builtin).
  • Arguments are not checked. Allowlist only programs that can't do harm whatever arguments they get: git -c core.pager=..., find -exec or an interpreter (python -c) run other code.

docs.title: Custom executors
docs.text:
Any synchronous callable (str) -> str works as a shell executor (the ShellExecutor protocol):

from promptise.prompts import TemplateEngine

# Dry-run executor for testing
engine = TemplateEngine(shell_executor=lambda cmd: f"[would run: {cmd}]")
print(engine.render("Status: !`git status --short`", {}))
# Status: [would run: git status --short]

The engine calls the executor synchronously, so an async def executor does not work: its coroutine would be inserted as text. Run async work before rendering and pass the result as a variable instead.

docs.title: Processing order
docs.text:
Shell interpolation runs after template includes and before conditionals and variable substitution. A variable's value is never executed, because commands run before variables are substituted. This means:

  1. {% include "name" %}: resolved first (included templates can contain !cmd``)
  2. !cmd``: executed, stdout replaces the block
  3. {% if %}, {% for %}: conditionals and loops
  4. {variable}: variable interpolation

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
• Non-zero exit code → raises ShellExecutionError
  • Timeout → raises ShellExecutionError
  • Command not in allowlist, or shell syntax with an allowlist → raises ShellExecutionError

All errors propagate to the caller: there is no silent fallback. A command that can't start (unknown executable with shell=False, unbalanced quotes) also raises ShellExecutionError. Empty commands render as an empty string.

Command output is literal text: braces in it are kept as they are and never read as {variable} or {% if %} syntax, so output such as {"ok": true} renders unchanged and can't pull a template variable into the prompt.

docs.title: Parameter reference
docs.text:
SubprocessShellExecutor(*, timeout=5.0, shell=True, cwd=None, env=None, allowlist=None)

Parameter Default Description timeout 5.0 Seconds before the command is killed (ShellExecutionError) shell True Run through /bin/sh -c; False splits with shlex and runs the executable directly. Ignored with an allowlist (never a shell) cwd None Working directory (inherits the caller's) env None Variables merged over os.environ allowlist None Set of allowed executable names. The command runs without a shell; any other first word, or an unquoted shell operator, raises ShellExecutionError

The executor returns stdout with surrounding whitespace stripped. A non-zero exit raises ShellExecutionError with the exit code and up to 500 characters of stderr.

docs.title: Prompt Strategies & Perspectives
docs.text: Strategies control how the agent reasons. Perspectives control from where the agent reasons. They are orthogonal and composable: any strategy pairs with any perspective, and strategies compose via the + operator.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts import prompt
from promptise.prompts.strategies import chain_of_thought, self_critique, analyst

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def analyze(text: str) -> str:
    """Analyze the following text: {text}"""

# Apply strategy + perspective
configured = (
    analyze
    .with_strategy(chain_of_thought + self_critique)
    .with_perspective(analyst)
)

result = await configured("Quarterly revenue grew 15% year-over-year...")

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• Strategy = HOW to reason (step-by-step, critique, decompose). Strategies implement wrap() to inject reasoning instructions before the LLM call, and parse() to extract the final answer from the raw output.
  • Perspective = FROM WHERE to reason (analyst, critic, advisor). Perspectives implement apply() to prepend or inject cognitive framing into the prompt text.

Both are composable and orthogonal: any strategy can pair with any perspective.

docs.title: ChainOfThoughtStrategy
docs.text:
Step-by-step reasoning with an answer marker. Instructs the LLM to think step-by-step, then produce a final answer after ---ANSWER---.

from promptise.prompts.strategies import chain_of_thought

result = await analyze.with_strategy(chain_of_thought)("Complex problem...")

docs.title: StructuredReasoningStrategy
docs.text:
Multi-step structured reasoning with customizable phases. Default phases: Understand, Analyze, Evaluate, Conclude.

from promptise.prompts.strategies import structured_reasoning, StructuredReasoningStrategy

# Use defaults
result = await analyze.with_strategy(structured_reasoning)("Evaluate this proposal")

# Custom phases
security_review = StructuredReasoningStrategy(
    steps=["Threat Model", "Attack Surface", "Mitigations", "Risk Rating"]
)
result = await analyze.with_strategy(security_review)("Review this API design")

docs.title: SelfCritiqueStrategy
docs.text:
Generate, critique, and improve. Supports multiple critique rounds.

from promptise.prompts.strategies import self_critique, SelfCritiqueStrategy

# Single round (default)
result = await analyze.with_strategy(self_critique)("Write a recommendation")

# Multiple rounds
deep_critique = SelfCritiqueStrategy(rounds=3)
result = await analyze.with_strategy(deep_critique)("Design a system architecture")

docs.title: PlanAndExecuteStrategy
docs.text:
Plan first, then execute each step, then synthesize.

from promptise.prompts.strategies import plan_and_execute

result = await analyze.with_strategy(plan_and_execute)("Create a marketing strategy")

docs.title: DecomposeStrategy
docs.text:
Break into subproblems, solve each independently, then combine.

from promptise.prompts.strategies import decompose

result = await analyze.with_strategy(decompose)("Optimize this distributed system")

docs.title: Strategies Summary Table
docs.text: Strategy Import Behavior chain_of_thought strategies.chain_of_thought Step-by-step reasoning with ---ANSWER--- marker structured_reasoning strategies.structured_reasoning Phases: Understand, Analyze, Evaluate, Conclude (customizable) self_critique strategies.self_critique Generate, critique, improve (configurable rounds) plan_and_execute strategies.plan_and_execute Plan steps, execute each, synthesize decompose strategies.decompose Break into subproblems, solve each, combine

docs.title: Composing Strategies
docs.text:
Strategies compose with the + operator. wrap() applies left-to-right, parse() applies right-to-left:

from promptise.prompts.strategies import chain_of_thought, self_critique

combined = chain_of_thought + self_critique
result = await analyze.with_strategy(combined)("Complex optimization problem")

You can compose any number of strategies:

triple = chain_of_thought + self_critique + decompose

The CompositeStrategy class handles the composition. It flattens nested composites automatically.

docs.title: Custom Strategies
docs.text:
Implement the Strategy protocol with wrap() and parse() methods:

from promptise.prompts.strategies import Strategy
from promptise.prompts.context import PromptContext

class StepBackStrategy:
    """Take a step back before answering."""

    def wrap(self, prompt_text: str, ctx: PromptContext) -> str:
        return (
            f"{prompt_text}\n\n"
            "Before answering, take a step back and consider the broader context.\n"
            "What assumptions might be wrong? What is the bigger picture?\n"
            "After your reasoning, write '---ANSWER---' then your final answer."
        )

    def parse(self, raw_output: str, ctx: PromptContext) -> str:
        if "---ANSWER---" in raw_output:
            return raw_output.split("---ANSWER---", 1)[1].strip()
        return raw_output

    def __add__(self, other):
        from promptise.prompts.strategies import CompositeStrategy
        return CompositeStrategy([self, other])

Custom strategies compose with built-in strategies via +:

step_back = StepBackStrategy()
combined = step_back + chain_of_thought

docs.title: AnalystPerspective
docs.text:
Evidence-based analysis. Focuses on data, patterns, measurable outcomes, and evidence-based conclusions.

from promptise.prompts.strategies import analyst

result = await analyze.with_perspective(analyst)("Evaluate this investment proposal")

docs.title: CriticPerspective
docs.text:
Critical evaluation. Challenges assumptions, identifies weaknesses, stress-tests ideas.

from promptise.prompts.strategies import critic

result = await analyze.with_perspective(critic)("Review this architecture design")

docs.title: AdvisorPerspective
docs.text:
Balanced advisory. Provides balanced recommendations with trade-off analysis and actionable next steps.

from promptise.prompts.strategies import advisor

result = await analyze.with_perspective(advisor)("Should we migrate to microservices?")

docs.title: CreativePerspective
docs.text:
Creative exploration. Explores unconventional solutions, novel combinations, and challenges conventional thinking.

from promptise.prompts.strategies import creative

result = await analyze.with_perspective(creative)("How can we improve user engagement?")

docs.title: Perspectives Summary Table
docs.text: Perspective Framing analyst Evidence-based, data patterns, quantifiable metrics critic Challenge assumptions, identify weaknesses, stress-test advisor Balanced recommendations, trade-off analysis, actionable steps creative Unconventional solutions, novel combinations, innovation

docs.title: Custom Perspectives
docs.text:
Use the perspective() factory function for quick custom perspectives:

from promptise.prompts.strategies import perspective

security_auditor = perspective(
    role="security auditor",
    instructions="Focus on OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities and missing authorization checks.",
)

result = await analyze.with_perspective(security_auditor)("Review this API code")

Or implement the Perspective protocol directly:

class DomainExpertPerspective:
    def __init__(self, domain: str):
        self.domain = domain

    def apply(self, prompt_text: str, ctx: PromptContext) -> str:
        return (
            f"You are a domain expert in {self.domain}. Apply deep domain "
            f"knowledge and industry-specific best practices.\n\n{prompt_text}"
        )

fintech_expert = DomainExpertPerspective("financial technology")

docs.title: Combining Strategy + Perspective
docs.text:
Strategies and perspectives are orthogonal. Use both on the same prompt:

from promptise.prompts.strategies import chain_of_thought, analyst

configured = (
    analyze
    .with_strategy(chain_of_thought)
    .with_perspective(analyst)
)

result = await configured("Evaluate quarterly performance data")

docs.title: Strategy Protocol
docs.text: Method Description wrap(prompt_text, ctx) -> str Inject reasoning instructions into the prompt parse(raw_output, ctx) -> str Extract the final answer from the raw LLM output

docs.title: Perspective Protocol
docs.text: Method Description apply(prompt_text, ctx) -> str Prepend cognitive framing into the prompt

docs.title: Built-In Singletons
docs.text: Name Type Description chain_of_thought ChainOfThoughtStrategy Step-by-step reasoning structured_reasoning StructuredReasoningStrategy Multi-phase reasoning self_critique SelfCritiqueStrategy Generate-critique-improve plan_and_execute PlanAndExecuteStrategy Plan then execute decompose DecomposeStrategy Subproblem decomposition analyst AnalystPerspective Evidence-based analysis critic CriticPerspective Critical evaluation advisor AdvisorPerspective Balanced advisory creative CreativePerspective Creative exploration

docs.title: Factories
docs.text:
Function Returns Description perspective(role, instructions="") CustomPerspective Create a custom perspective StructuredReasoningStrategy(steps=[...]) StructuredReasoningStrategy Custom reasoning phases SelfCritiqueStrategy(rounds=1) SelfCritiqueStrategy Multi-round critique CustomPerspective(role, instructions="") CustomPerspective The class behind perspective() CompositeStrategy(strategies) CompositeStrategy The class behind a + b; nested composites are flattened

SelfCritiqueStrategy.parse() falls back to the text after the last **Improved Answer**: heading when the marker is missing; the other strategies return the whole reply.

Use the ---ANSWER--- marker

All built-in strategies use the ---ANSWER--- marker to separate reasoning from the final answer. The parse() method strips the reasoning and returns only the answer. Custom strategies should follow this convention for consistency.

Pairing strategies and perspectives

Pair chain_of_thought with analyst for data-driven step-by-step reasoning, or self_critique with critic for a stricter review of the draft answer. Compare the outputs on your own inputs before settling on a pair: each strategy adds instructions and output tokens.

Composite strategy ordering

In a composite A + B, wrap() applies A first, then B wraps the result, so A's instructions come right after the prompt text and B's are appended after A's. parse() runs in reverse: B first, then A. Because every built-in strategy asks for the same ---ANSWER--- marker, combining two of them gives the model two sets of instructions for one marker; check the result on your prompts.

docs.title: Where strategies and perspectives apply
docs.text:
On every render and call, the perspective is applied first (its framing is prepended), then the strategy wraps the text (its instructions are appended), then constraints and schema instructions are added. After the LLM call, only the strategy's parse() runs. A Strategy is any object with wrap(prompt_text, ctx) -> str and parse(raw_output, ctx) -> str; a Perspective is any object with apply(prompt_text, ctx) -> str. Perspectives don't compose with +: a prompt has one perspective, and with_perspective() replaces it.

The same objects work in the reasoning engine (PromptNode(strategy=..., perspective=...)) and in .prompt files by name.

docs.title: Prompt Suite & Registry
docs.text: Group related prompts with shared configuration via PromptSuite, and version-control prompts with PromptRegistry.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts import prompt
from promptise.prompts.suite import PromptSuite
from promptise.prompts.strategies import structured_reasoning, critic

class SecurityAudit(PromptSuite):
    default_strategy = structured_reasoning
    default_perspective = critic
    default_constraints = ["Reference OWASP categories"]

    @prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
    async def scan_code(self, code: str, language: str) -> list[str]:
        """Scan for security vulnerabilities in this {language} code:
        {code}"""

    @prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
    async def suggest_fixes(self, vulnerabilities: list[str]) -> str:
        """Suggest fixes for: {vulnerabilities}"""

suite = SecurityAudit()
results = await suite.scan_code(code="def login(): ...", language="python")

docs.title: PromptSuite Concepts
docs.text:
A PromptSuite bundles related prompts that share a common configuration. When you define a suite subclass:

  1. Set class attributes for shared defaults (strategy, perspective, constraints, guards, context providers, world contexts).
  2. Decorate methods with @prompt(...) to define individual prompts.
  3. Suite defaults merge with per-prompt configuration: per-prompt settings override suite defaults.

The merge rules are:

  • Context providers: suite providers come first, then prompt-level providers. A suite provider is skipped when the prompt already has a provider of the same class.
  • Strategy / Perspective: prompt-level wins if set; otherwise suite default applies.
  • Constraints: suite constraints are prepended to prompt-level constraints.
  • Guards: suite guards are prepended to prompt-level guards.
  • World contexts: suite world is the base; prompt-level world entries override matching keys.

Defaults are applied once, when the subclass is created, by changing the Prompt objects defined on the class. Methods take self for readability, but self is removed from the prompt's signature: call them as suite.summarize(data=...) or DataAnalysisSuite.summarize(data=...); every instance shares the same prompts.

docs.title: Suite Class Attributes
docs.text: Attribute Type Description context_providers list[ContextProvider] Shared context providers default_strategy Strategy \| None Default reasoning strategy default_perspective Perspective \| None Default cognitive perspective default_constraints list[str] Default constraint strings default_guards list[Guard] Default guards default_world dict[str, BaseContext] Default world contexts

docs.title: Full Suite Example
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts import prompt
from promptise.prompts.suite import PromptSuite
from promptise.prompts.context import tool_context, memory_context, BaseContext
from promptise.prompts.strategies import chain_of_thought, analyst
from promptise.prompts.guards import content_filter

class DataAnalysisSuite(PromptSuite):
    context_providers = [tool_context(), memory_context()]
    default_strategy = chain_of_thought
    default_perspective = analyst
    default_constraints = ["Include confidence scores", "Cite data sources"]
    default_guards = [content_filter(blocked=["confidential"])]
    default_world = {
        "project": BaseContext(name="Q1 Report", deadline="March 2026"),
    }

    @prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
    async def summarize(self, data: str) -> str:
        """Summarize this data: {data}"""

    @prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
    async def forecast(self, data: str, horizon: str) -> str:
        """Based on this data, forecast trends for {horizon}: {data}"""

suite = DataAnalysisSuite()
summary = await suite.summarize(data="Revenue: $2.3M, Growth: 15%...")
forecast = await suite.forecast(data="...", horizon="next quarter")

docs.title: Discovering Prompts in a Suite
docs.text:
The prompts property returns a dict mapping prompt names to Prompt instances:

suite = DataAnalysisSuite()

for name, p in suite.prompts.items():
    print(f"{name}: {p}")
# forecast: <Prompt name='forecast', model='openai:gpt-5-mini', ...>
# summarize: <Prompt name='summarize', model='openai:gpt-5-mini', ...>

docs.title: Rendering the Suite
docs.text:
Render a combined system prompt from all suite prompts, or render asynchronously with a context:

# Static rendering (no context providers)
system = suite.system_prompt()

# Async rendering with context providers
from promptise.prompts.context import PromptContext
rendered = await suite.render_async(PromptContext())

Both join each prompt's rendered text under a ## <prompt name> heading. Templates are rendered without variables, so {data} placeholders stay as they are. A suite can be an agent's instructions: build_agent(instructions=DataAnalysisSuite()) injects render_async() on each turn and runs the guards of all its prompts.

docs.title: Suite Methods
docs.text: Method Returns Description system_prompt() str Render a combined system prompt from all suite prompts render_async(ctx) str Async render all prompts with context providers prompts dict[str, Prompt] All Prompt instances on this suite (property)

docs.title: PromptRegistry Concepts
docs.text:
The PromptRegistry stores versioned prompts keyed by (name, version). "Latest" is the version registered last, not the highest version number, and version strings are not parsed. It supports:

  • Registration of prompts at specific semantic versions.
  • Retrieval by name (latest) or by name + version.
  • Rollback to remove the latest version and revert to the previous one.
  • Listing all registered prompts and their versions.

A module-level singleton registry is available for convenience. The @version() decorator auto-registers prompts into this singleton; it works above or below @prompt. load_prompt(path, register=True) registers into it too. The registry is process-local and in memory.

docs.title: Versioning Prompts
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts import prompt
from promptise.prompts.registry import registry, version

@version("1.0.0")
@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def summarize(text: str) -> str:
    """Summarize: {text}"""

@version("2.0.0")
@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini")
async def summarize(text: str) -> str:
    """Provide a concise summary with key takeaways: {text}"""

docs.title: Retrieving Prompts
docs.text:
# Get the latest version
latest = registry.get("summarize")

# Get a specific version
v1 = registry.get("summarize", "1.0.0")

# Check the latest version string
ver = registry.latest_version("summarize")  # "2.0.0"

docs.title: Rolling Back
docs.text:
Remove the latest version and revert to the previous one:

rolled_back = registry.rollback("summarize")
# Removes v2.0.0, returns the v1.0.0 Prompt

Rollback requires at least two versions

Calling rollback() when only one version is registered raises KeyError.

docs.title: Listing All Prompts
docs.text:
registry.list()
# {"summarize": ["1.0.0", "2.0.0"]}

docs.title: Using a Custom Registry
docs.text:
You can create isolated registries instead of the global singleton:

from promptise.prompts.registry import PromptRegistry

team_registry = PromptRegistry()
team_registry.register("analyze", "1.0.0", my_prompt)
team_registry.register("analyze", "1.1.0", improved_prompt)

latest = team_registry.get("analyze")

docs.title: PromptSuite
docs.text: Attribute / Method Type / Returns Description context_providers list[ContextProvider] Shared context providers default_strategy Strategy \| None Default reasoning strategy default_perspective Perspective \| None Default cognitive perspective default_constraints list[str] Default constraints default_guards list[Guard] Default guards default_world dict[str, BaseContext] Default world contexts prompts dict[str, Prompt] All prompts in the suite system_prompt() str Render combined system prompt render_async(ctx) str Async render all prompts

docs.title: PromptRegistry
docs.text: Method Returns Description register(name, ver, prompt) None Register a prompt at a version get(name, ver=None) Prompt Retrieve by name; ver=None returns latest; unknown name or version: KeyError latest_version(name) str Get the latest version string rollback(name) Prompt Remove latest version, return new latest; KeyError with fewer than two versions list() dict[str, list[str]] List all prompts and their versions clear() None Remove all registered prompts

docs.title: Decorators
docs.text:
Decorator Description @version(ver) Register a prompt in the global registry at version ver

Suite + Registry together

Define your prompts in a PromptSuite for shared configuration, then register each suite prompt in the PromptRegistry for version management. Use suite.prompts to iterate and register.

Duplicate version protection

Registering the same name + version twice raises ValueError. This prevents accidental overwrites in production.

docs.title: Prompt Testing
docs.text: A small test helper for prompts. PromptTestCase provides mocked LLM calls, context injection, and assertions for content, result type, latency and guards.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
import pytest
from promptise.prompts import prompt, PromptInspector
from promptise.prompts.testing import PromptTestCase
from promptise.prompts.context import context, user_context, UserContext

inspector = PromptInspector()

@prompt(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", inspect=inspector)
@context(user_context())
async def analyze_sentiment(text: str) -> str:
    """Analyze the sentiment of this text: {text}"""

class TestSentiment(PromptTestCase):
    prompt = analyze_sentiment

    async def test_positive(self):
        with self.mock_llm("positive"):
            result = await self.run_prompt("I love this product!")
            self.assert_contains(result, "positive")

    async def test_with_context(self):
        with self.mock_context(user=UserContext(expertise_level="expert")):
            with self.mock_llm("strongly positive"):
                await self.run_prompt("Great product")
        # The mocked model ignores the prompt; check what would have been sent
        assert "**Expertise:** expert" in inspector.last().input_text

mock_llm() returns your fixed text whatever the prompt says, so assertions on the result only test parsing, strategies and guards. To test what the prompt sends, attach a PromptInspector and assert on trace.input_text, or call await prompt.render_async(...).

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
PromptTestCase is a plain base class (not a unittest.TestCase). With pytest, use pytest-asyncio (asyncio_mode = "auto", or mark each test). With unittest, also inherit from unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase so async def test_* methods run. Key features:

  • mock_llm(response): mock the LLM call to return a fixed string, eliminating API costs during testing.
  • mock_context(**contexts): temporarily inject world contexts into the prompt under test.
  • Specialized assertions: purpose-built for prompt validation (schema, latency, guards, content).
  • Stats access: retrieve PromptStats from the last call for latency assertions.

docs.title: Configure the Prompt Under Test
docs.text:
Set the prompt class attribute to the Prompt you want to test:

from promptise.prompts.testing import PromptTestCase

class TestMyPrompt(PromptTestCase):
    prompt = my_analysis_prompt

docs.title: Running Prompts
docs.text:
Use run_prompt() to execute the prompt:

async def test_basic(self):
    with self.mock_llm("expected response"):
        result = await self.run_prompt("input text")
        assert result == "expected response"

Use run_with_stats() to get both the result and execution stats:

async def test_with_stats(self):
    with self.mock_llm("response"):
        result, stats = await self.run_with_stats("input text")
        self.assert_latency(stats, max_ms=5000)

docs.title: Mocking LLM Calls
docs.text:
mock_llm(response) patches the chat model factory used by standalone prompt calls (promptise.prompts.core.init_chat_model) so the model returns a fixed string. No API calls are made, and no API key is needed. It does not affect agents built with build_agent():

async def test_mocked(self):
    with self.mock_llm("The sentiment is positive."):
        result = await self.run_prompt("I love it!")
        self.assert_contains(result, "positive")

docs.title: Mocking Context
docs.text:
mock_context(**contexts) temporarily adds world contexts to the prompt:

from promptise.prompts.context import UserContext, BaseContext

async def test_with_user(self):
    with self.mock_context(
        user=UserContext(name="Alice", expertise_level="expert"),
        project=BaseContext(name="Q1 Report"),
    ):
        with self.mock_llm("Expert-level analysis..."):
            result = await self.run_prompt("quarterly data")
            self.assert_contains(result, "Expert")

The original world contexts are restored when the context manager exits. mock_context() changes the shared Prompt object while it is active, so don't run tests that use it on the same prompt concurrently. World contexts only reach the prompt text through a context provider such as user_context().

docs.title: Combining Mocks
docs.text:
Stack mock_llm and mock_context for isolated tests:

async def test_full_isolation(self):
    with self.mock_context(user=UserContext(expertise_level="beginner")):
        with self.mock_llm("Simple explanation of the data."):
            result = await self.run_prompt("complex technical data")
            self.assert_contains(result, "Simple")
            self.assert_not_contains(result, "error")

docs.title: Content Assertions
docs.text:
# Assert result contains a substring
self.assert_contains(result, "recommendation")

# Assert result does NOT contain a substring
self.assert_not_contains(result, "error")

docs.title: Schema Assertions
docs.text:
Check the result's type with isinstance (works with dataclasses, Pydantic models, and basic types; it does not validate field values):

from pydantic import BaseModel

class Analysis(BaseModel):
    summary: str
    confidence: float

self.assert_schema(result, Analysis)
self.assert_schema(result, str)
self.assert_schema(result, dict)

docs.title: Latency Assertions
docs.text:
result, stats = await self.run_with_stats("test input")

# Assert latency is within limit
self.assert_latency(stats, max_ms=5000)

stats is the prompt's last_stats, a PromptStats:

Field Type Description prompt_name str The prompt's name model str The model string latency_ms float Wall time of the call, including guards input_tokens / output_tokens int From the model's reply (LangChain usage_metadata); 0 when the provider reports no usage context_providers_used list[str] \| None Class names of the attached context providers strategy / perspective str repr() of the strategy and perspective, or ""

docs.title: Context Provider Assertions
docs.text:
Verify that a context provider of a given class was attached to the prompt (it checks stats.context_providers_used, not whether the provider produced text):

self.assert_context_provided(stats, "UserContextProvider")

docs.title: Guard Assertions
docs.text:
Assert that the result was not blocked by a guard. Guards raise, so this only checks that the result is not None; test a rejection with pytest.raises(GuardError) as below:

self.assert_guard_passed(result)

docs.title: Testing with Real LLM Calls
docs.text:
For integration tests that validate actual LLM behavior (requires API key):

import os
import pytest

class TestRealLLM(PromptTestCase):
    prompt = analyze_sentiment

    @pytest.mark.skipif(
        not os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
        reason="Requires OPENAI_API_KEY",
    )
    async def test_real_sentiment(self):
        result = await self.run_prompt("I absolutely love this product!")
        self.assert_contains(result, "positive")

docs.title: Testing Guard Behavior
docs.text:
from promptise.prompts.guards import GuardError

class TestGuards(PromptTestCase):
    prompt = guarded_prompt

    async def test_blocked_input(self):
        with self.mock_llm("should not reach here"):
            with pytest.raises(GuardError) as exc_info:
                await self.run_prompt("Contains secret data")
            assert exc_info.value.guard_name == "content_filter"

    async def test_clean_input(self):
        with self.mock_llm("Analysis complete"):
            result = await self.run_prompt("Clean input data")
            self.assert_guard_passed(result)

docs.title: Testing Different User Contexts
docs.text:
class TestExpertiseAdaptation(PromptTestCase):
    prompt = adaptive_prompt

    async def test_beginner_response(self):
        with self.mock_context(user=UserContext(expertise_level="beginner")):
            with self.mock_llm("Here is a simple explanation..."):
                result = await self.run_prompt("Explain neural networks")
                self.assert_contains(result, "simple")

    async def test_expert_response(self):
        with self.mock_context(user=UserContext(expertise_level="expert")):
            with self.mock_llm("The gradient descent optimization..."):
                result = await self.run_prompt("Explain neural networks")
                self.assert_contains(result, "gradient")

docs.title: PromptTestCase
docs.text: Method Returns Description run_prompt(*args, **kwargs) Any Execute the prompt under test run_with_stats(*args, **kwargs) tuple[Any, PromptStats] Execute and return result + stats

docs.title: Context Managers
docs.text: Method Description mock_llm(response) Mock the LLM to return a fixed string mock_context(**contexts) Temporarily inject world contexts

docs.title: Assertions
docs.text:
Method Description assert_schema(result, expected_type) Assert isinstance(result, expected_type) assert_contains(result, substring) Assert substring is present assert_not_contains(result, substring) Assert substring is absent assert_latency(stats, max_ms) Assert latency within limit assert_context_provided(stats, name) Assert a provider class name is in stats.context_providers_used assert_guard_passed(result) Assert the result is not None

All assertions raise AssertionError. run_prompt() and mock_context() raise ValueError when the prompt attribute is not set.

Mock for speed, real for confidence

Use mock_llm() in unit tests for fast, deterministic feedback loops. Use real LLM calls in integration tests (guarded by API key checks) for end-to-end validation.

pytest compatibility

Define your test classes with PromptTestCase as a base, use async def test_* methods, install pytest-asyncio, and run with pytest --asyncio-mode=auto.

Set the prompt attribute

Calling run_prompt() without setting the prompt class attribute raises ValueError. Always set prompt = my_prompt on your test class.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: Every environment variable Promptise reads, what it does and its default. Variables are read from the process environment, and from a .env file that Promptise loads for scripts and the CLI (see Configuration & Secrets). A .env file never overrides a variable that is already set.

docs.title: Model providers
docs.text:
Each provider reads its own key and endpoint variables, for example OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY with AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT and OPENAI_API_VERSION, GROQ_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY or GOOGLE_API_KEY, MISTRAL_API_KEY, DEEPSEEK_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, TOGETHER_API_KEY, XAI_API_KEY, FIREWORKS_API_KEY, AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK with AWS_REGION, GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT with GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION, AZURE_INFERENCE_ENDPOINT with AZURE_INFERENCE_CREDENTIAL, HF_TOKEN (Hugging Face Inference Providers), OLLAMA_HOST, and OPENAI_BASE_URL for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

The exact set for every provider is in Every provider's variables. Two commands print it for you:

promptise models env azure            # the lines a provider needs, ready for .env
promptise models check azure:chat-prod   # what is still missing for a model string

A key passed in code with Model(..., api_key=...) wins over the environment.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text: Variable Default Effect PROMPTISE_NO_DOTENV unset Any non-empty value turns off automatic .env loading, for scripts and the CLI. Use it when your platform injects secrets and a stray .env must not be read.

docs.title: Agent features
docs.text: Variable Default Effect PROMPTISE_CACHE_KEY unset Fernet key for SemanticCache(encrypt_values=True). Without it a key is generated at start-up (a warning is logged) and cached values cannot be read after a restart. Create one with python -c "from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())". See Semantic Cache.

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text: Variable Default Effect PROMPTISE_AUDIT_SECRET unset HMAC key AuditMiddleware signs the audit chain with when you pass no hmac_secret, and the key promptise audit verify checks with (--key-env names another variable). See Observability & Monitoring.

docs.title: promptise run
docs.text:
Variable Default Effect PROMPTISE_SERVE_TOKEN unset Bearer token clients must send to promptise run --serve. The [serve] table's auth_token_env names this variable by default; a token is required when the server binds a non-loopback host. PROMPTISE_RUN_SCRIPT set by Promptise The name of the [scripts] entry being run. PROMPTISE_PROJECT_ROOT set by Promptise The directory that holds the manifest (promptise.toml or pyproject.toml). PROMPTISE_INIT_CWD set by Promptise The directory you ran promptise run from (the program itself runs in the project root).

See Projects & promptise run.

docs.title: Agent Runtime CLI
docs.text:
Variable Default Effect PROMPTISE_RUNTIME_STATE_DIR ~/.promptise/runtime Where promptise runtime start records running runtimes (name, API address, token) for status, stop, logs and restart. PROMPTISE_RUNTIME_TOKEN random per start Bearer token for the control API that promptise runtime start serves, and the token the other runtime commands send to a --url target. PROMPTISE_HOOK_EVENT set by Promptise Given to a shell hook command: the event that fired it. PROMPTISE_PROCESS set by Promptise Given to a shell hook command: the process name.

See Runtime CLI Commands.

docs.title: Agent identity
docs.text:
AgentIdentity.auto() picks a platform from the first of these groups that has a variable set:

Order Platform Variables that select it 1 Microsoft Entra ID AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE, AZURE_CLIENT_ID 2 AWS AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_NAME, AWS_EXECUTION_ENV, EKS_POD_NAME, AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE, PROMPTISE_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE 3 Google Cloud GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT, K_SERVICE, GCE_METADATA_IP 4 SPIFFE / SPIRE SPIFFE_ENDPOINT_SOCKET

PROMPTISE_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE is also the token file the AWS projected mode presents: AgentIdentity.from_aws(mode="auto") (the default) uses projected mode when it is set, and STS otherwise. See Agent Identity and Architecture.

docs.title: MCPcast
docs.text:
Read by promptise mcpcast while it parses a spec and runs the readiness eval:

Variable Default Effect MCPCAST_FETCH_SECONDS 60 Wall-clock limit for downloading a spec from a URL. MCPCAST_MAX_SPEC_BYTES 20 MiB Largest spec download. MCPCAST_MAX_SPEC_NODES 2000000 Most YAML/JSON nodes after aliases are expanded. MCPCAST_EVAL_AUTHORIZATION placeholder Credential the --eval live reads send upstream, for example Bearer <token>. MCPCAST_EVAL_HEADERS unset JSON object of headers for the --eval live reads; replaces the default header.

Read by a generated server (<name>-mcp/config.py):

Variable Default Effect MCPCAST_UPSTREAM_TOKEN unset Upstream credential in --auth env-token mode, for example Bearer <token>. Read on every call, so rotating it needs no restart. MCPCAST_UPSTREAM_TOKENS unset JSON object {"<tenant_id>": "<credential>"} for --auth api-key mode. Read on every call. MCPCAST_CLIENT_KEYS unset JSON object mapping each client API key to {"client_id", "tenant_id", "roles"} in api-key mode. Read at start-up. MCPCAST_BASE_URL the spec's server Points the server at another environment without regenerating. Must be a plain http(s):// URL without credentials, query or fragment. MCPCAST_TIMEOUT 30 Seconds one upstream call may take in total. MCPCAST_APPROVAL_TIMEOUT 300 Seconds a gated call waits for a reviewer. MCPCAST_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES 1048576 Largest upstream response body passed to the agent. MCPCAST_ERROR_EXCERPT_CHARS 500 How much of an upstream error body the agent sees (0 hides it). MCPCAST_MAX_PENDING 100 Gated calls waiting for review at once, in approval mode pending. MCPCAST_MAX_PENDING_PER_TENANT 40 The same cap per tenant. MCPCAST_MAX_PENDING_PER_CLIENT 20 The same cap per client key. The caps must nest (client, tenant, store) or the server refuses to start. MCPCAST_ALLOW_INSECURE_HTTP unset 1 sends the upstream credential to a plain http:// host that is not loopback. MCPCAST_PUBLIC unset 1 lets a server without MCP-level authentication bind a non-loopback address (what --public sets, for containers).

See the MCPcast reference.

docs.title: Set by Promptise, do not set them yourself
docs.text: Promptise sets these on the processes it starts to coordinate with them: PROMPTISE_RUN_CHILD, PROMPTISE_RUN_DEPTH, PROMPTISE_RUN_IPC, PROMPTISE_RUN_TUI (promptise run), PROMPTISE_RUNTIME_LAUNCH_ID (promptise runtime start --detach), PROMPTISE_EXEC_ID (sandbox commands) and _PROMPTISE_RELOAD_CHILD (MCP server hot reload).

docs.title: Your own variables in config files
docs.text: .superagent files and .agent manifests resolve ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} from the environment, so any name you choose works there. See Environment Resolver.

docs.title: Promptise Foundry Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to Promptise Foundry are documented here.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Sandbox: docker_network -- SandboxConfig(docker_network="agent-egress") (also in .superagent files) attaches the sandbox container to an existing Docker network instead of Docker's default bridge, with network="full" or "restricted". With an --internal network whose only way out is an egress proxy, sandboxed code reaches only the hosts the proxy allows; network="restricted" alone filters ports, not hosts. A network that does not exist stops the session from starting with a message that says how to create it, and the host's network, none and another container's network are refused. See "Allowing only some hosts" in docs/core/sandbox.md.
  • Guardrails: InjectionDetector(paragraphs=True) -- also classifies every paragraph (line of up to 512 characters) of the scanned text on its own and blocks on the highest score. The 512-character windows can dilute a short instruction: on a support page whose last paragraph was an instruction for AI assistants, its window scored 0.58 (below the 0.85 threshold) and the paragraph alone 0.99, so a tool result with it passed. Off by default: it costs one classification per paragraph, and the default model flags short lines of technical text (code, commands, headings) much more often than whole windows. See "Short instructions in longer text" in docs/core/guardrails.md.
  • MCP server: elicitation on the 2026-07-28 protocol -- 2026-07-28 has no server-to-client requests, so Elicitor.ask() there now asks in an input round: the tool call ends with an InputRequiredResult holding the question, the client (the mcp 2.x Client does this on its own) asks its user and sends the call again with the answer, and the tool runs again, where ask() returns the answer. A tool that asks several questions takes one round per question; the earlier answers travel in the result's request_state, encrypted and bound to the tool, its arguments and the server by the SDK's RequestStateBoundary. MCPServer(request_state_security=RequestStateSecurity(keys=[...])) shares the key between workers or replicas (by default it is made at startup and held by the process). The approval gate's ElicitationApprover works the same way. Code before ask() runs once per round, so side effects belong after the answer. Elicitor.last_failure says why ask() returned None. See "Elicitation on the 2026-07-28 protocol" in docs/mcp/server/advanced-patterns.md.
  • Runtime: local tools with ProcessConfig(extra_tools=[...]) and AgentProcess(..., extra_tools=[...]) -- an Agent Runtime process can now give its agent Python functions as tools without an MCP server, with the same semantics as build_agent(extra_tools=...): @tool functions, plain functions and LangChain tools, and TypeError for anything else when the config or process is created. The tools reach every agent the process builds (first start, restarts, hot reloads, new instructions), and budget, approval, health and journal apply to them as to MCP tools. They are code only, like a hook's callback: model_dump() and RuntimeConfig.to_dict() leave them out, and a manifest or YAML config can't set them. Processes spawned in open mode don't inherit them, and an open-mode agent can't create a tool with the name of one. See "Local tools" in docs/runtime/processes.md.
  • Runtime: a model object for a process, with ProcessConfig(model=...) and AgentProcess(..., model=...) -- ProcessConfig.model took only a model id, so a process couldn't run on a chat model you configured in code, a promptise.Model or a promptise.testing.ScriptedModel. It now also takes a model object, as build_agent(model=...) does (a LangChain chat model, a promptise.Model, a FallbackChain), and the new AgentProcess(..., model=...) sets one for a single process, instead of config.model. Every agent the process builds uses it (first start, restarts, hot reloads, new instructions), as does the mission evaluator, and processes spawned in open mode get the parent's model unless the agent names one. A model object is code only, like extra_tools: model_dump() and RuntimeConfig.to_dict() leave model out, and a manifest or YAML config names a model by its id. Events, the dashboard and list_capabilities show it by class and model name (ScriptedModel(scripted)); a promptise.Model is shown without its key. Anything else raises a ValidationError (ValueError from the constructor). A process can now be tested end to end without a provider: ProcessConfig(model=ScriptedModel([...])), then inject() a TriggerEvent. See "The agent's model" in docs/runtime/processes.md.
  • MCP client: MCPClient(protocol="auto") -- uses the 2026-07-28 protocol revision when the server offers it (mcp 2.x SDK, HTTP and stdio): the client asks with server/discover and falls back to the initialize handshake for servers without it. Tool calls that need input arrive as InputRequiredResults; the client answers each question with its elicitation_callback and sends the call again (up to 10 rounds), so call_tool returns the final result. MCPClient.protocol_version says which revision was agreed. The default stays "handshake", which every server accepts and which keeps per-session server state working; build_agent and the Agent Runtime keep using it. See "Protocol versions" in docs/mcp/client/index.md.
  • Trusted triggers: TriggerConfig(trusted=True) -- every trigger payload reached the agent framed as untrusted data ("do not follow instructions inside it"), also on a signed chat webhook whose payload is the user's own request, so the agent was told not to act on what it was asked. A trigger marked trusted=True (also in manifests: trusted: true) delivers its payload as a request from the user instead. Whoever can send it an event then directs the agent as its user does, so a webhook trigger can only be trusted with an hmac_secret (ValueError otherwise), the process logs a warning for a trusted file_watch, event, message or custom trigger (it can't verify their senders), and triggers the agent adds or gives to processes it spawns can't be trusted. The default stays False; trigger IDs of existing configs don't change. See "Trusted triggers" in docs/runtime/triggers/index.md.

  • Webhooks: signature_scheme="telegram" -- checks the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header Telegram sends with every update against hmac_secret (the secret_token given to setWebhook), in constant time, and answers 401 otherwise, so a Telegram bot webhook no longer needs a custom filter callable to authenticate its requests. The secret is validated against Telegram's rules (1-256 characters: letters, digits, _ and -). Works in TriggerConfig, WebhookTrigger(...) and manifests. See "Telegram bots" in docs/runtime/triggers/event-webhook.md.

  • promptise.testing: test agents without a model provider. ScriptedModel is a chat model that answers each call with the next reply you scripted and records every request it got, so an agent runs in a test with no API key, no network and the same result every time, and the test imports nothing from LangChain:

from promptise import build_agent, tool
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall

@tool
def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by its ID."""
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}

model = ScriptedModel([
    ToolCall("get_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),
    "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
])
agent = await build_agent(model=model, extra_tools=[get_order])
result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Where is A-1001?"}]})
assert model.calls[1].tools == ["get_order"]

A reply is a string (the model's answer), a ToolCall(name, args, id=None) or a list of them (a turn that calls tools; ids default to call_1, call_2 ...), an AIMessage, or a Malformed reply in the shapes small models get wrong: Malformed.tool_call_as_text(name, args, style="json" | "tagged" | "fenced") writes the call into the text, Malformed.unparseable_arguments(name, raw_args) sends arguments that are not JSON (an invalid_tool_calls entry). Invented tool names and invalid arguments are plain ToolCall replies. model.calls holds a ModelCall per request (messages, the bound tools and their tool_schemas, reply), and model.remaining counts the replies not sent yet. A call after the last reply raises ScriptExhaustedError, which says which call it was (in an agent run, ainvoke() raises GraphExecutionError caused by it); on_exhausted="repeat_last" repeats the last reply instead. The model supports ainvoke/invoke, astream/stream (text word by word, tool calls as tool-call chunks) and bind_tools, so it works with every agent pattern, astream_with_tools(), a FallbackChain and graph nodes. promptise.testing is not imported by import promptise. See docs/core/testing.md. - MCP server: tool versions with @server.tool(version=...) -- VersionedToolRegistry was exported, and its docstring showed @server.tool(version="1.0"), but the server never used it and tool() had no version parameter. Each version is now served under a pinned name, search_v1_0 (characters other than letters and digits become _, so LLM providers accept the name), and the bare name search runs the highest version, compared numerically per dot-separated part. Each version keeps its own schema, validation and options. Registering a version twice, or a version next to an unversioned tool of the same name, raises ValueError. @router.tool(version=...) works the same, with the router's prefix on every name. See "Tool Versioning" in docs/mcp/server/advanced-patterns.md. - MCP server: server.add_transform(...) -- the exported NamespaceTransform, VisibilityTransform, TagFilterTransform and the ToolTransform protocol were never applied by the server. add_transform() now applies them, in order, to tools/list and the docs://manifest resource, with the listing request's context (authenticated with the server's AuthMiddleware when there is one). A call by a renamed tool's listed name runs the tool: renaming transforms implement resolve_name(), which NamespaceTransform does. Transforms change discovery only; a hidden tool can still be called by its name, so access decisions stay in guards. apply() may be async, and a VisibilityTransform predicate that raises hides its tool. See "Tool Transforms" in docs/mcp/server/advanced-patterns.md.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Browser clients on the 2026-07-28 protocol were refused by CORS. A 2026-07-28 client sends mcp-method and mcp-name headers with every request, and the default CORSConfig.allow_headers did not list them, so the browser's preflight got 400 Disallowed CORS headers. Both are in the default list now. The SESSION_REQUIRED error also names how to connect with the handshake from Promptise's own client (MCPClient, whose default is protocol="handshake"), not only the MCP SDK's mode='legacy'.
  • Trace and webhook redaction missed most GitHub tokens. redact_sensitive (the sanitizer build_agent installs on its observability collector) and the event notifier's payload redaction knew only classic ghp_ personal access tokens, so a GitHub CLI token (gho_) in a tool result reached the HTML report, log files, webhooks and OpenTelemetry spans as it was. They now redact every GitHub token format: ghp_, gho_, ghu_, ghs_ (including the longer ghs_<app id>_<JWT> installation tokens GitHub is rolling out), ghr_ and github_pat_, with no fixed length. The same review added the credentials that also went through unredacted: temporary AWS access key IDs (ASIA…), an AWS secret access key after aws_secret_access_key=, Stripe (sk_live_…, rk_test_…) and Google (AIza…) API keys, GitLab and Slack tokens, JWTs and PEM private keys. The guardrails' CredentialDetector already knew gho_, ghu_ and ghr_; it now also detects ghs_ installation tokens (97 patterns), and its GitHub patterns take tokens longer than 40 characters whole.
  • The guardrails' bearer pattern left the token in the text. CredentialDetector's bearer_token pattern matched Authorization: Bearer and stopped at the space, so Authorization: Bearer 7f3c… was redacted to [BEARER_TOKEN] 7f3c…: the opaque token reached the model, and the trace sanitizer, which looked for the word Bearer, no longer recognised it either. The pattern now takes the whole value: Authorization: (or =) with any scheme (Bearer, Basic, Token...) or none, and a bearer token on its own (Bearer <token>, any case, at least 16 characters so prose such as "the bearer token expired" is not a finding). The trace and webhook sanitizer also redacts every Authorization value whatever its scheme (Authorization: Basic [REDACTED]), a lower-case bearer <token>, and the value of a credential key whatever it looks like: Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, X-API-Key, api_key, access_token, refresh_token, id_token, client_secret, password and passwd, as a dict key (a request's headers, a tool's arguments) or in JSON text (a tool result).
  • Sandbox network="restricted" no longer reaches link-local addresses. The egress filter allowed TCP 80 and 443 to every address, including 169.254.169.254, where cloud providers serve instance metadata and credentials over plain HTTP. It now drops 169.254.0.0/16, fe80::/10 and fd00:ec2::254 (DNS to a resolver there still works). It still filters ports, not hosts: DNS and TCP 80/443 reach any other host.
  • A memory provider left at the default SHARED scope gave one user's memories to another, without a word. With memory_auto_store=True the agent stores every exchange, and a provider created without scope= pools every caller's entries, so a note one employee gave a shared assistant ("Priya's new salary is 145,000") came back in a colleague's conversation. The default stays SHARED (changing it would break agents that share memory on purpose), but the agent (and MemoryAgent) now logs a warning the first time such a provider serves a second caller identity, saying what is shared and to pass scope=MemoryScope.PER_USER. A provider created with an explicit scope=MemoryScope.SHARED is a deliberate choice and is not reported. The memory page says this up front.
  • purge_user found nothing for a caller with a tenant. The agent stores a caller's memories under its isolation key, "acme::dana" for CallerContext(user_id="dana", tenant_id="acme"), and purge_user("dana") looked for "dana", so it removed nothing and returned 0. purge_user on every memory provider (and the MemoryProvider protocol) now takes tenant_id=, as SemanticCache.purge_user does: purge_user("dana", tenant_id="acme"). The new promptise.memory.owner_key(user_id, tenant_id) returns the key entries are stored under.
  • On a 2026-07-28 connection a question to the user was a silent "no", and per-session state was lost. Elicitor.ask() sent elicitation/create, which that protocol revision doesn't allow, and returned None with a warning in the server log only, so a confirmation step answered "cancelled" and an ElicitationApprover denied with "client declined", though nobody was asked. The question now goes to the client in an input round (see Added), and a client that did not declare the elicitation capability is told so: ask() returns None with last_failure set, and the approval denial says "the client did not declare the elicitation capability". A tool that takes a SessionState got new, empty state on every 2026-07-28 request (there is no session), so a cart kept one item; it now answers with a SESSION_REQUIRED error that names the protocol version and says to connect with the handshake. The same error answers every request to a server served with asgi_app(stateless=True), which also gave every call a fresh state. On handshake connections session state is kept per connection object and dropped with it; it was keyed by the object's id(), never removed, and a later connection could get the state of an earlier one whose address was reused. Sampler logs that sampling isn't available on 2026-07-28 instead of a transport error.
  • A tool that timed out told the model to "retry later", also when the call had done its work. @tool(timeout=...), @server.tool(timeout=...) and TimeoutMiddleware answered every timeout with retryable: true and a suggestion to retry, though a cancelled call may already have sent the email or charged the card, and a sync @tool function keeps running in its thread and completes. A model retried a timed-out send_invoice twice and three invoices went out. The TIMEOUT error now says the outcome is unknown (and that the call is still running, for a sync function), is retryable only for a tool marked read-only or idempotent, and otherwise tells the model to check whether the call took effect before calling the tool again. @tool takes read_only= and idempotent= for this (the MCP readOnlyHint / idempotentHint annotations, which the semantic cache and approval rules read too); MCP server tools use their read_only_hint / idempotent_hint. A TIMEOUT still counts as a failure for the circuit breaker when it is not retryable.
  • A tool call the budget refused left no trace in the journal. The refused call never ran, so it had no tool_call entry, even at journal level "full", and the violation the process then acted on was not journaled either: the journal showed only the state_transition to suspended with reason "budget". A refused call now writes a tool_denied entry (tool, kind, reason, limit_name, limit_value, current_value, and at level "full" the call's args, redacted like tool_call arguments), and every violation the process acts on (on_exceeded), including a run refused by max_runs_per_day, writes a budget_violation entry (limit_name, limit_value, current_value, tool_name, blocked, action). The permission_denied hook for a refused tool call also gets the call's arguments, and BudgetViolation has an arguments field. See docs/runtime/journal/index.md.
  • promptise.__version__ did not exist. import promptise; promptise.__version__ raised AttributeError; only promptise --version and importlib.metadata.version("promptise") gave the version. The package now sets __version__ from the installed package metadata, and to "0.0.0+unknown" when it is imported from a source tree that was never installed.
  • SIGTERM cut off the run in flight, and the run was lost on exit. AgentProcess.stop(), and with it AgentRuntime.run_forever() on SIGTERM or Ctrl+C, cancelled a run in the middle with no grace period, after its tools may already have acted, and the event went to the in-memory dead letters, which end with the program. run_forever() now stops gracefully: no new trigger event starts (a webhook answers 503, inject() dead-letters), runs in flight get up to ProcessConfig.drain_timeout seconds (default 5) to finish, and only the ones still running then are cancelled; a second signal cancels them at once. stop(drain_timeout=N) does the same for one process (None uses the config value), as do stop_all(drain_timeout=...) and shutdown(drain_timeout=...), where the processes drain at the same time; process.abort_drain() and request_shutdown(force=True) end the wait early. A run that is cancelled is logged, journaled as a run_interrupted entry at every journal level and kept in the journal checkpoint, so the next process object with the same name and journal lists it in dead_letters again (counted in recovered["interrupted_runs"]) and redeliver_dead_letters() can run it. The control API's POST /api/v1/processes/{name}/stop and POST /api/v1/runtime/stop-all take an optional drain_timeout in the JSON body (0 to 3600 seconds; anything else is 422 INVALID_FIELD) and answer once the processes have stopped, with interrupted_runs (the runs the stop cancelled) and, for one process, the drain_timeout used. POST /api/v1/runtime/shutdown passes a drain_timeout on to on_shutdown, and request_shutdown(drain_timeout=...) sets it for that shutdown. promptise runtime stop --drain-timeout SECONDS uses them, for one process and for a whole runtime (the wait for the runtime to exit then lasts at least the drain plus 10 seconds); OrchestrationClient.stop_process(), stop_all() and shutdown() and AgentRuntime.stop_process() take drain_timeout=. See "Graceful stop" in docs/runtime/processes.md.
  • build_agent(max_agent_iterations=...) above 15 still stopped the default agent after 15 model calls. The default ReAct graph's reason node had its own limit of 15 (and the engine a per-node ceiling of 25), so a run with max_agent_iterations=40 ended with "reached its iteration limit (15)". build_agent now gives the node the same limit as the run, so max_agent_iterations=N allows N model calls whatever N is.
  • A call to a tool that doesn't exist got no hint. The error result was Error: Unknown tool 'get_ordr', so a model that invented or misspelled a tool name had nothing to correct it with and often tried the same name again. It now lists the agent's tools, the names closest to the one called first, at most 20 of them followed by how many more there are, and suggests the tool whose name the called one looks like a misspelling of: Error: Unknown tool 'get_ordr'. Did you mean 'get_order'? Call one of the available tools: get_order, refund_order. A name that only shares a word with a tool (cancel_order and get_order) gets no suggestion. This applies to the tool calls of every built-in agent pattern and of a ToolNode. The text still starts with Error: Unknown tool '<name>'.
  • A tool call whose arguments were not valid JSON ended the run without an answer. LangChain keeps such a call (a Python-style dict with single quotes, a cut-off object) in the message's invalid_tool_calls, and the built-in agent patterns neither ran it nor answered it, so the run ended on that message with empty content, and a conversation continued from it was refused by OpenAI, since the call had no tool result. Every built-in pattern and a ToolNode now answer each such call with a tool error (status="error", the call's own tool_call_id) that says what is wrong and names the tool's parameters: Error: The arguments for 'get_order' were not valid JSON (Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes at line 1 column 2). Call the tool again with a JSON object that matches its parameters: order_id (required). A call to a tool the agent doesn't have gets the unknown-tool error. The tool loop goes on, so the model can call again; the call counts as a failed tool call (tool_calls_failed, and in NodeResult.tool_calls with success: False, invalid: True and the text the model sent as raw_args), callbacks get an on_tool_error with a ToolArgumentError, streams show it as a failed call, and iteration limits apply as before. A call without an id gets one, on the assistant message too, so every call has exactly one result. Context compaction keeps such an exchange, and a FallbackChain stream keeps the call.
  • OpenAPIProvider tools could not be called. Each generated tool's input schema was a single required kwargs field, so a call with the operation's real arguments failed with VALIDATION_ERROR, and the method-based annotations were computed and then dropped. A tool's input schema is now the operation's parameters (path-level ones included) and JSON request body from the spec, with every $ref inlined; calls are validated against it, and each argument is sent where the spec puts it (path, URL-encoded; query; header; cookie; body). Arguments the caller leaves out are not sent. Swagger 2.x in: body parameters and parameter types are read too. The tools carry the annotations (read_only_hint for GET/HEAD, destructive_hint for DELETE, idempotent_hint, open_world_hint=True, the summary as title).
  • A tool that returned a Pydantic model sent str(model). -> Book sent title='Dune' year=1965, and a list[Book] a JSON list of those strings. A model is now sent as its JSON (model_dump(mode="json")), also inside a dict or list, the same form a resource sends; resources now also serialise models inside a list or dict as JSON objects.
  • StructuredLoggingMiddleware(include_args=True) logged no arguments. The flag was stored and never used. The tool_call_start line now has args, the call's validated arguments after redact_sensitive (credential keys become [REDACTED], credentials and common PII in strings become placeholders).
  • WebhookMiddleware held up every tool call and kept every payload. The docstring said deliveries never block, but each one was awaited inside the call, so a slow endpoint added up to timeout seconds per event (twice per call with the default events), and sent grew for the life of the process. Events now go on a bounded queue (max_queue=1000) and are sent by background tasks (max_concurrency=4, one HTTP client each); a full queue drops the event with a warning and counts it in dropped. sent keeps the last history=100 payloads. New flush() waits for queued deliveries and aclose() stops the delivery tasks.
