  • Distributed: multi-node coordination

Build something real:

  • Building Agentic Runtime Systems: step-by-step guide from a single agent to a distributed deployment

Learn the concept

  • Autonomous AI Agent Runtime: Budgets, Crash Recovery, API: What an agent runtime adds: budgets, restarts and crash recovery.
  • Run Multiple AI Agents: One Runtime, Many Processes: One runtime, many processes, and a clean shutdown on SIGTERM.
  • Durable AI Agents: Crash Recovery and Safe Resume: Journal a process and continue where it stopped after a crash.
  • Topic hub: Runtime, triggers and deployment: Every guide on triggers, durable runs and deployment.

docs.title: Orchestration API
docs.text:
OrchestrationAPI is a REST API for a running AgentRuntime. Use it to deploy, start, stop and remove agent processes, change their instructions, budgets and triggers while they run, send them messages, rotate their secrets and read their journals, all over HTTP. OrchestrationClient is the matching typed Python client. promptise runtime start serves this API for you (see CLI Commands); in your own program you start it yourself.

import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import AgentRuntime, OrchestrationAPI, OrchestrationClient


async def main():
    runtime = AgentRuntime()
    api = OrchestrationAPI(runtime, port=9100, auth_token="change-me")
    await api.start()

    async with OrchestrationClient("http://127.0.0.1:9100", token="change-me") as client:
        await client.deploy(
            "monitor",
            {
                "model": "openai:gpt-5-mini",
                "instructions": "Watch the data pipelines and report problems.",
                "triggers": [{"type": "cron", "cron_expression": "*/5 * * * *"}],
                "inbox": {"enabled": True},
            },
            start=True,
        )
        status = await client.get_process("monitor")
        print(status["state"])  # running

        await client.send_message(
            "monitor", "Ignore staging alerts for 1 hour",
            message_type="directive", priority="high", ttl=3600,
        )

    await api.stop()
    await runtime.stop_all()


asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Creating the server
docs.text:
Signature
class OrchestrationAPI:
    def __init__(
        self,
        runtime,                          # the AgentRuntime to manage
        *,
        host: str = "127.0.0.1",
        port: int = 9100,
        auth_token: str | None = None,
        on_shutdown=None,
        allow_command_deploys: bool = False,
        allow_env_references: bool = False,
        allowed_env_vars=None,            # iterable of variable names
        data_dir=None,                    # str or Path; None = ./.promptise
    ) -> None: ...
Argument Default Description runtime required The AgentRuntime to manage host "127.0.0.1" Bind address port 9100 Port. 0 lets the OS pick a free port; read it from api.port after start() auth_token None Bearer token required on every route except GET /api/v1/health. Required when host is not a loopback address. "${VAR}" reads it from the environment on_shutdown None Sync or async callable. When set, POST /api/v1/runtime/shutdown exists: it answers 202 and then calls the callable (for example runtime.request_shutdown), without arguments or, when the request body has a drain_timeout, with drain_timeout=<seconds>. A callable without a drain_timeout parameter makes such a request 422 INVALID_FIELD. Without it the route answers 404 allow_command_deploys False Let POST /api/v1/processes deploy configs that run programs or code on the host (stdio MCP servers, command hooks, open mode with allow_tool_creation). See Deploys that run programs allow_env_references False Let deployed configs use ${VAR} references to any environment variable of the host. See Environment references allowed_env_vars None Names of the variables deployed configs may reference when allow_env_references is off, e.g. {"SEARCH_API_KEY"} data_dir ./.promptise The directory file system paths in deployed configs must lie in. See File system paths

await api.start() binds the port and serves; await api.stop() closes the server. The constructor raises ValueError when auth_token is an empty string, names an unset environment variable, or is missing for a non-loopback host, and TypeError when on_shutdown is not callable or allowed_env_vars is a single string.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
When auth_token is set, every request except GET /api/v1/health needs the token, including requests to unknown paths:

Authorization: Bearer <your-token>
  • Loopback (127.0.0.1, localhost, ::1): the token is optional.
  • Anything else: the token is required. The constructor refuses to build the API without one.
  • The comparison is timing-safe.
  • auth_token="${ORCHESTRATION_API_TOKEN}" reads the token from the environment; an unset variable raises ValueError.

A missing or wrong token gets 401 UNAUTHORIZED.

docs.title: Browsers can't drive a local API
docs.text:
A loopback bind is reachable by any web page open in a browser on the same machine. On a loopback bind the API therefore refuses:

Request Status Why Host header that isn't a loopback name 421 MISDIRECTED_REQUEST DNS rebinding: a page whose own host name resolves to 127.0.0.1 Origin header from a non-loopback site 403 CROSS_ORIGIN_REFUSED A cross-site fetch or form post from a page you visit

curl, scripts and the Promptise clients send a loopback Host and no Origin, so they are unaffected. A local web UI served from http://localhost:<port> is allowed. Set an auth_token even on loopback if other users share the machine. Behind a reverse proxy, keep the proxy's upstream Host on a loopback name, or bind the API to a non-loopback address with a token.

docs.title: Request bodies
docs.text: Request bodies must be JSON objects. Anything else (a list, a string, invalid JSON) gets 400 INVALID_JSON; routes that take no body accept an empty one. A body over 1 MiB gets 413 PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE.

docs.title: Securing the control API
docs.text:
Anyone with the token can deploy agents, so treat a token holder as someone who writes process configs on your machine. The API keeps such a config from reaching further than the agent itself:

Setting Default What it protects auth_token random with promptise runtime start, else None Every route except GET /health. Required off loopback Loopback bind (host="127.0.0.1") on Only local clients; browser pages are refused (421 / 403) allow_command_deploys False Deploys can't start programs or run agent-written code on the host allow_env_references / allowed_env_vars off / none Deploys can't read the host's environment through ${VAR} data_dir ./.promptise Deploys can't write journals, memory or watch files elsewhere open_mode.allowed_mcp_urls empty = no server for API deploys A deployed open-mode agent can't connect MCP servers you didn't list 
api = OrchestrationAPI(
    runtime,
    host="127.0.0.1",
    auth_token="${ORCHESTRATION_API_TOKEN}",
    allowed_env_vars={"SEARCH_API_KEY"},  # the only variable deploys may reference
    data_dir="/var/lib/promptise",
)

The same switches exist on the CLI: promptise runtime start --allow-command-deploys --allow-env-references --allow-env-var NAME. Processes you load from manifests on the host are yours and none of these checks apply to them. The process keeps the limits it was deployed with (secrets, MCP allowlist, paths) and passes them on to the processes it spawns.

docs.title: Deploys that run programs
docs.text:
A config that starts a program, or runs agent-written code, on the runtime's host can't be deployed over the API by default. POST /api/v1/processes answers 403 COMMANDS_NOT_ALLOWED when the config has:

  • a stdio MCP server (a server entry with a command, or type/transport "stdio"),
  • a command hook (a hooks entry with a command), or
  • open mode with open_mode.allow_tool_creation (the default in open mode). The agent's create_tool runs model-written Python inside the runtime's process, and its restricted builtins are not a sandbox, so it amounts to running commands. Deploy open-mode agents with "open_mode": {"allow_tool_creation": false}.

Anyone with the token could otherwise run any command as the runtime's user. Use HTTP MCP servers instead of stdio ones and leave out command hooks (a deploy is JSON, so it can't carry a Python callback hook either; register hooks on the host, in a manifest or in code), load such processes from manifests on the host, or, if every token holder may run commands there, enable it:

api = OrchestrationAPI(runtime, auth_token="${ORCHESTRATION_API_TOKEN}", allow_command_deploys=True)

promptise runtime start agents/ --allow-command-deploys

The check applies only to deploys. Processes loaded from manifests by the operator are not checked, and the other routes that change a process (triggers, PATCH sections, context, instructions) have no field that runs a program.

docs.title: Environment references
docs.text:
${VAR} references are resolved from the host's environment when a process starts (for example in secrets), and an agent can read a secret back with get_secret. So a deploy, a POST .../triggers or a PATCH of budget, health or mission whose body contains a ${VAR} reference anywhere gets 403 ENV_REFERENCES_NOT_ALLOWED, naming where the reference is. instructions are never resolved, so text there isn't checked. To allow references:

  • allowed_env_vars={"SEARCH_API_KEY"} (--allow-env-var SEARCH_API_KEY, repeatable): only these variables, or
  • allow_env_references=True (--allow-env-references): any variable.

Otherwise send the value itself as a literal secret. As a backstop, an API-deployed process's secret scope resolves only the allowed variables too. A reference that can't be resolved fails the start with a generic START_FAILED message that doesn't say whether the variable exists (the server log has the detail).

docs.title: File system paths
docs.text:
Paths in a deployed config must lie inside data_dir (default ./.promptise under the runtime's working directory, where the journal goes by default). Relative paths are resolved against the working directory, as the process uses them. 403 PATH_NOT_ALLOWED answers a deploy whose

  • journal.path (for a file journal that is on),
  • context.memory_persist_directory, or
  • a file-watch trigger's watch_path

is outside it, uses .. or ~, or is a symlink that leads out. POST .../triggers checks watch_path the same way, and the deployed agent's own add_trigger (open mode) is held to data_dir too.

docs.title: Route reference
docs.text: Every route the server registers. Paths start with /api/v1. All routes except GET /health need the bearer token when one is set; {name} is the process name.

docs.title: Runtime
docs.text: Method Path What it does Success GET /health Load-balancer probe, no auth: {"status": "healthy", "process_count"} 200 GET /runtime/status {"process_count", "processes": {name: status}} (plus cluster in distributed mode) 200 POST /runtime/start-all Start every process: {"status": "started"} 200 POST /runtime/stop-all Stop every process, optional body {"drain_timeout"} (see Stopping with a drain): {"status": "stopped", "interrupted_runs"} 200 POST /runtime/shutdown Only with on_shutdown: optional body {"drain_timeout"}; answers {"status": "shutting_down"} (plus the drain_timeout), then calls on_shutdown 202

docs.title: Processes
docs.text: Method Path What it does Success GET /processes {"processes": [{"name", "state", "process_id"}], "total"} 200 POST /processes Deploy: body {"name", "config", "start"} (see Deploying a process) 201 GET /processes/{name} Process status: state, counters, triggers, budget, health, mission state, active secret count 200 DELETE /processes/{name} Stop and close the process, then remove it (memory closed, secrets revoked, conversation cleared) 204 POST /processes/{name}/start Start: {"name", "state"} 200 POST /processes/{name}/stop Stop, optional body {"drain_timeout"} (see Stopping with a drain): {"name", "state", "drain_timeout", "interrupted_runs"} 200 POST /processes/{name}/restart Stop (if running), then start: {"name", "state"} 200 POST /processes/{name}/suspend Pause trigger processing: {"name", "suspended": true, "state"} 200 POST /processes/{name}/resume Resume a suspended process: {"name", "resumed": true, "state"} 200 GET /processes/{name}/metrics Same body as GET /processes/{name} 200

docs.title: Live configuration
docs.text: Method Path What it does Takes effect Success PATCH /processes/{name}/instructions Replace the instructions: {"instructions": "..."} Next run (effective_from: "next_invocation") 200 PATCH /processes/{name}/budget Change BudgetConfig fields Next budget check ("next_budget_check") 200 PATCH /processes/{name}/health Change HealthConfig fields Next check ("immediate") 200 PATCH /processes/{name}/mission Change MissionConfig fields Next evaluation and prompt ("immediate") 200 GET /processes/{name}/triggers Config and agent-added triggers with stable IDs; hmac_secret, credential-like custom_config values and URL user info masked : 200 POST /processes/{name}/triggers Add a trigger (body: a TriggerConfig) At once on an active process, else at the next start 201 DELETE /processes/{name}/triggers/{trigger_id} Stop and remove a trigger At once on an active process, else at the next start 200

docs.title: Messages
docs.text: Method Path What it does Success POST /processes/{name}/messages Queue a message: {"message_id", "status": "queued", "expires_at"} 201 POST /processes/{name}/ask Ask a question and wait for the answer (long poll; secret values in the answer are [REDACTED]) 200 GET /processes/{name}/inbox Pending messages and questions (redacted like the journal) 200 DELETE /processes/{name}/inbox Remove every message and cancel pending questions 204

docs.title: State, secrets, mission, health
docs.text: Method Path What it does Success GET /processes/{name}/context {"state", "writable_keys", "all_keys_writable"} 200 PATCH /processes/{name}/context Write state keys, all or none: {"state": {...}} 200 GET /processes/{name}/secrets Secret metadata, never values 200 PATCH /processes/{name}/secrets/{secret_name} Rotate one secret: {"value", "ttl"?} 200 DELETE /processes/{name}/secrets Revoke every secret (zero-fill): {"name", "secrets_revoked": true} 200 GET /processes/{name}/mission Mission state and evaluation history 200 POST /processes/{name}/mission/fail Fail an active or paused mission: {"reason"?} 200 POST /processes/{name}/mission/pause Pause an active mission 200 POST /processes/{name}/mission/resume Resume a paused mission 200 GET /processes/{name}/health/anomalies Anomaly history: type, description, timestamp 200 DELETE /processes/{name}/health/anomalies Clear the history and cooldowns: {"anomalies_cleared": n} 200

docs.title: Journal and rewind
docs.text:
Method Path What it does Success GET /processes/{name}/journal Newest entries, oldest first. ?limit= 1-500 (default 50), ?type= filters by entry type 200 GET /processes/{name}/rewind/plan Preview a rewind: ?target_entry_id= (required), ?mode= (default both). Changes nothing 200 POST /processes/{name}/rewind Rewind to just before a journal entry: {"target_entry_id", "mode"?, "actor"?} 200

Each journal entry is {"entry_id", "entry_type", "timestamp", "data"}; the entry_id is a rewind target. Without a journal the route answers {"name", "entries": [], "journal_enabled": false}, and the rewind routes answer 400 JOURNAL_DISABLED. Rewind modes are both, conversation_only, code_only, summarize and cancel; actor (default "api") is recorded in the journal. A running process is suspended for the rewind and resumed afterwards, and a run still in flight when the rewind times out gives 409 REWIND_BUSY. See Rewind Engine for what each mode restores.

docs.title: Deploying a process
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:9100/api/v1/processes \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "incident-handler",
    "config": {
        "model": "openai:gpt-5-mini",
        "instructions": "Handle infrastructure incidents.",
        "triggers": [{"type": "webhook", "webhook_path": "/incidents", "webhook_port": 9091}],
        "budget": {"enabled": true, "max_tool_calls_per_day": 500}
    },
    "start": true
  }'
  • name must match ^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_-]{0,63}$ (422 INVALID_NAME); a name already registered gets 409 PROCESS_EXISTS.
  • config is a ProcessConfig as JSON (422 INVALID_CONFIG when it doesn't validate). A valid config that still can't be turned into a process gets 422 DEPLOY_FAILED. The security checks answer 403 with COMMANDS_NOT_ALLOWED, ENV_REFERENCES_NOT_ALLOWED or PATH_NOT_ALLOWED.
  • start (default false) must be a boolean. When the start fails the answer is 500 START_FAILED and the process stays deployed: fix the cause and POST .../start, or DELETE it. A process whose start fails because of the process itself (a secret that can't be resolved, for example) is 500 START_FAILED on POST .../start too, never 404.
  • The answer is 201 with {"name", "process_id", "state", "created_at"}.

The config object follows ProcessConfig:

{
    "model": "openai:gpt-5-mini",
    "instructions": "Your agent instructions here.",
    "servers": {
        "tools": {"url": "http://tools:8080/mcp", "transport": "streamable-http"}
    },
    "triggers": [{"type": "cron", "cron_expression": "*/5 * * * *"}],
    "inbox": {"enabled": true, "max_messages": 50},
    "budget": {"enabled": true, "max_tool_calls_per_day": 500},
    "health": {"enabled": true, "stuck_threshold": 5},
    "mission": {
        "enabled": true,
        "objective": "Keep pipelines healthy",
        "success_criteria": "Zero critical alerts for 24h"
    }
}

docs.title: Stopping with a drain
docs.text:
POST /processes/{name}/stop and POST /runtime/stop-all stop gracefully, like SIGTERM (see Graceful stop): no new event starts, the runs in flight get up to drain_timeout seconds to finish, and only the ones still running then are cancelled. Each cancelled run is journaled as run_interrupted and kept in the dead letters for redeliver_dead_letters().

Body Effect none, {} or {"drain_timeout": null} Wait up to the process's ProcessConfig.drain_timeout (5 seconds unless set) {"drain_timeout": 30} Wait up to 30 seconds {"drain_timeout": 0} Cancel runs in flight at once

drain_timeout is a number from 0 to 3600; anything else (a negative number, a string, true) is 422 INVALID_FIELD and nothing is stopped. The default is the configured value rather than 0 so that a stop from a dashboard or a script treats a run the same way docker stop does; pass 0 when you want it gone now.

The request is answered once the process has stopped, so it takes at most the drain plus the teardown. The stop finishes even if the client disconnects. The answer says what happened:

{"name": "data-watcher", "state": "stopped", "drain_timeout": 5.0, "interrupted_runs": 0}

interrupted_runs counts the runs this stop cancelled (stop-all answers the total over its processes, which drain at the same time). OrchestrationClient.stop_process(name, drain_timeout=...) and stop_all(drain_timeout=...) wait for the answer as long as the drain may take, on top of the client's timeout.

POST /runtime/shutdown answers 202 at once and shuts down afterwards; a drain_timeout in its body is passed to on_shutdown (runtime.request_shutdown accepts it). promptise runtime stop --drain-timeout sends it.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: PATCH /instructions with {"instructions": "..."} (a non-empty string) replaces the process's instructions, including any an open-mode agent set for itself. The next run rebuilds the agent with them before it runs, keeping the connected MCP servers, the conversation history and the context state; a run already in progress finishes with the old instructions. A process that is not running uses them when it starts. In Python: process.update_instructions(text).

docs.title: Budget, health and mission
docs.text:
The body of a budget, health or mission patch holds the fields to change, named as in BudgetConfig, HealthConfig and MissionConfig.

curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9100/api/v1/processes/monitor/budget \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"max_cost_per_day": 500.0}'

{"name": "monitor", "budget_updated": true, "effective_from": "next_budget_check", "live": true}
  • The patched section is validated as a whole before anything changes, with the same limits as at deploy time and strict JSON types ("5" is not a number, 1 is not true). A field the model doesn't declare, including inside escalation or tool_costs, gets 422 UNKNOWN_FIELD; an invalid value gets 422 INVALID_CONFIG; an empty body gets 422 MISSING_FIELD. In every case nothing changes. null clears an optional field such as max_cost_per_day.
  • The process applies the change at once (live: true). Budget limits apply at the next budget check (the next tool call, LLM turn or run start) and the usage counted so far is kept. Health thresholds and window sizes apply at the next check, keeping the recorded history. A mission change applies to the next evaluation and the next [Mission] prompt block, keeping the mission's progress.
  • enabled works live too: {"enabled": true} builds the subsystem on a process that was deployed without it, and {"enabled": false} removes it.

The response always says when the change applies. live is false with effective_from: "redeploy", pending_fields and a note only for a process object that can't apply governance changes itself (a custom process class without apply_governance_config()).

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text:
Config triggers have stable IDs: <type>-<10-character digest of the trigger's config>, for example cron-6d904fd75c. An ID doesn't depend on the trigger's position, so removing one trigger leaves the other IDs unchanged, and the IDs are the same after a restart. Identical configs get -2, -3 suffixes. The ID is also the trigger_id of the events the trigger produces.

# List (config triggers include their config; agent-added ones have source "dynamic")
curl http://localhost:9100/api/v1/processes/monitor/triggers -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

# Add
curl -X POST http://localhost:9100/api/v1/processes/monitor/triggers \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"type": "cron", "cron_expression": "0 9 * * 1-5"}'
# {"name": "monitor", "trigger_added": true, "trigger_id": "cron-fb9fa7b826",
#  "trigger_type": "cron", "live": true, "effective_from": "immediate"}

# Remove by ID
curl -X DELETE http://localhost:9100/api/v1/processes/monitor/triggers/cron-6d904fd75c \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# {"name": "monitor", "trigger_removed": "cron-6d904fd75c", "live": true, "effective_from": "immediate"}
Operation Process starting, running, suspended or awaiting Process created, stopped or failed Add Created and started at once: live: true, effective_from: "immediate" Added to the config: live: false, effective_from: "next_start" Remove a config trigger Stopped at once and removed from the config: live: true, "immediate" Removed from the config: live: true, "next_start" Remove an agent-added trigger Stopped at once: live: true, "immediate" :

Adding a trigger identical to one already configured gets 409 TRIGGER_EXISTS; an invalid config or one that can't start gets 422 INVALID_CONFIG; a ${VAR} reference gets 403 ENV_REFERENCES_NOT_ALLOWED and a watch_path outside data_dir 403 PATH_NOT_ALLOWED; an unknown ID gets 404 TRIGGER_NOT_FOUND. In the listing, hmac_secret is masked, and so are the values of custom_config keys that look like credentials (names containing secret, token, password, api_key, auth, credential, signature or cookie) and the user info of any URL value (postgres://app:pw@db/x is listed as postgres://**********@db/x). The old position-based IDs (static_0, static_1, ...) are still accepted on DELETE; the response then carries a warning naming the stable ID to use instead.

docs.title: Context state
docs.text: PATCH /context with {"state": {key: value}} writes all keys or none: if any key is not writable the answer is 403 WRITE_DENIED naming them, and nothing is written. Writes are recorded with source "api" and journaled. Other top-level fields get 422 UNKNOWN_FIELD. See Agent Context.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: GET /secrets lists metadata, PATCH /secrets/{secret_name} rotates one value (404 SECRET_NOT_FOUND for a name the process doesn't have), DELETE /secrets revokes all. Values never appear in a response. See Secret Scoping.

docs.title: Mission
docs.text: GET /mission returns the state, objective, invocation count and evaluations; fail, pause and resume answer 409 MISSION_STATE when the mission is not in a state that allows them. See Mission Model.

docs.title: Messages and questions
docs.text:
A process with an inbox takes messages from people while it runs. The agent sees them in its prompt on its next run. Enable it in the process config:

{"inbox": {"enabled": true, "max_messages": 50, "default_ttl": 3600}}
InboxConfig field Default Description enabled false Enable the inbox max_messages 50 Most messages held at once (never exceeded) max_message_length 2000 Longer content is truncated to this many characters default_ttl 3600 Seconds a message lives when it has no ttl (0 = no expiry) max_ttl 86400 Cap on any message's lifetime (0 = no cap). default_ttl may not exceed it rate_limit_per_sender 20 Messages per sender_id per hour (messages without a sender_id are not limited) scan_with_guardrails true Scan messages for prompt injection when they arrive (see Guardrail scanning)

Without an inbox, /messages and /ask answer 400 INBOX_DISABLED and GET /inbox answers {"enabled": false, ...}. A stopped or failed process gets 409 PROCESS_NOT_RUNNING.

docs.title: Message types and priorities
docs.text:
Type Use case Example directive Tell the agent to do or stop doing something "Do not restart any services today" context Information the agent should know (the default for /messages) "Traffic spike is from a marketing campaign" question Ask the agent something; it answers in its reply "What's the current health status?" correction Tell the agent it was wrong "That alert was a false positive"

Priorities are low, normal (default), high and critical. The agent sees messages ordered by priority, then oldest first.

docs.title: Sending a message
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:9100/api/v1/processes/monitor/messages \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"content": "Ignore staging alerts for 1 hour", "message_type": "directive",
       "priority": "high", "sender_id": "alice", "ttl": 3600}'
# 201 {"message_id": "msg_...", "status": "queued", "expires_at": 1792445004.98}

Fields: content (required, non-empty string), message_type, priority, sender_id (string), ttl (seconds, >= 0; 0 or missing uses default_ttl, and max_ttl caps it) and metadata (object, stored with the message). An unknown message_type gets 422 INVALID_TYPE; another bad field gets 422 INVALID_FIELD.

docs.title: Asking a question
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:9100/api/v1/processes/monitor/ask \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"content": "How many alerts did you skip?", "timeout": 120}'

The request waits until the agent answers or timeout seconds pass (default 120, at most 3600). It always answers 200:

{"question_id": "msg_...", "status": "answered", "response": "Three staging alerts skipped.",
 "answered_at": 1792441406.1, "invocation_id": "2"}

or, when no answer came in time, {"question_id", "status": "timeout", "response": null}. The question stays in the inbox after a timeout (it lives for timeout + 60 seconds, capped by max_ttl), so a later run can still answer it, but nobody is waiting for that answer. The agent sees the question on its next run: if no trigger fires within timeout, it can't answer. priority, sender_id and metadata work as for /messages.

docs.title: What the agent sees
docs.text:
Before each run, the pending messages are added to the prompt as one system message, after the context state, budget and mission blocks and before the conversation history:

=== OPERATOR MESSAGES ===

[HIGH DIRECTIVE] (from: alice, just now, expires in 59 min)
Ignore staging alerts for 1 hour

[QUESTION] (just now, expires in 1 min)
How many alerts did you skip?
→ Please include your answer prefixed with "ANSWER Q1:"

=== END OPERATOR MESSAGES ===

Each message is a [<PRIORITY> <TYPE>] label (the priority is left out for normal) with the sender when known, its age (just now, <n> min ago, <n>h ago) and the time left before it expires, followed by the content. Questions are numbered Q1, Q2, ... in the order they appear in the block.

docs.title: Answers and consumption
docs.text:
After every run, the runtime:

  1. Reads ANSWER Q<n>: <text> parts from the agent's final reply and delivers each one to the question it numbers (the waiting /ask call returns it). Text after the marker up to the next ANSWER Q marker is the answer. Secret values in it are replaced by [REDACTED], as in the journal, so a question can't make the agent hand out a secret.
  2. Removes the messages that run saw: directives, context and corrections are gone after one run, and answered questions are removed. Unanswered questions stay until they are answered or expire.

So a directive is shown once. Send it again, or store the fact in the context state, when the agent must keep following it on later runs.

docs.title: Limits and refusals
docs.text:
Situation API answer Python (process.send_message) Empty content, unknown priority or type 422 INVALID_FIELD / 422 INVALID_TYPE InvalidInboxMessage Sender over rate_limit_per_sender this hour 429 RATE_LIMITED InboxRateLimitError Inbox full and nothing can be evicted 409 INBOX_FULL InboxFullError Flagged by the guardrail scan 422 MESSAGE_REJECTED InboxMessageRejected (with .reason)

All four exception classes are in promptise.runtime.inbox and subclass InboxError, a ValueError. Refused messages are not counted against the sender's rate limit.

When the inbox holds max_messages messages, a new message first replaces an answered question if there is one; otherwise it evicts the oldest message of the lowest priority present. Critical messages are never evicted, and a message never evicts one of higher priority: if every message is critical, or the new message has a lower priority than every evictable one, the new message is refused with INBOX_FULL. The inbox never holds more than max_messages. An /ask call waiting on an evicted question ends with 410 QUESTION_REMOVED.

docs.title: Guardrail scanning
docs.text:
With scan_with_guardrails: true (the default), each message is scanned when it arrives, in overlapping 500-character windows, and a flagged message is refused (422 MESSAGE_REJECTED). The scanner is, in order:

  1. ProcessConfig.guardrails, when it can scan text (a PromptiseSecurityScanner or any object with scan_text() or check_input()).
  2. The trigger payload scanner, when trigger_delivery.scan_payloads is on. It is loaded when the process starts; messages that arrived before (a created process already takes messages) are scanned then, and flagged ones are removed (an /ask waiting on one gets 422 MESSAGE_REJECTED).

With neither, messages are not scanned: the process logs a one-time warning and accepts them. Set guardrails (for example PromptiseSecurityScanner(detectors=[InjectionDetector()])) or trigger_delivery.scan_payloads=True to scan them, or scan_with_guardrails: false to accept messages unscanned without the warning. Only give inbox access to people you trust with the agent's instructions: a message lands in the agent's prompt.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
msg_id = await process.send_message(
    "Ignore staging alerts for 1 hour",
    message_type="directive", priority="high", sender_id="alice", ttl=3600,
)
response = await process.ask("How many alerts did you skip?", timeout=60)
print(response.content)  # an InboxResponse: question_id, content, answered_at, invocation_id

send_message returns the message ID. ask returns an InboxResponse and raises asyncio.TimeoutError when no answer arrives in time. Both raise RuntimeError when the process has no inbox or is stopped or failed, and ValueError (an InboxError) for a refused message.

docs.title: Using the inbox directly
docs.text:
The process builds its inbox from InboxConfig. The classes behind it are public in promptise.runtime, for tests or for your own message channel:

import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import InboxMessage, InboxResponse, MessageInbox, MessageType


async def main():
    inbox = MessageInbox(max_messages=10, default_ttl=600)
    await inbox.add(InboxMessage(
        content="Ignore staging alerts for the next hour.",
        message_type=MessageType.DIRECTIVE,
        priority="high",
        sender_id="alice",
    ))
    question_id = await inbox.add(InboxMessage(
        content="How many alerts did you skip?", message_type=MessageType.QUESTION,
    ))

    print([m.message_type.value for m in await inbox.get_pending()])  # ['directive', 'question']

    # What the process does when the agent's reply contains "ANSWER Q1: ..."
    await inbox.submit_response(question_id, InboxResponse(question_id=question_id, content="Three."))
    answer = await inbox.wait_for_response(question_id, timeout=5)
    print(answer.content)  # Three.
    print((await inbox.status())["pending_messages"])  # 1 (answered questions are not pending)


asyncio.run(main())

MessageInbox(*, max_messages=50, max_message_length=2000, default_ttl=3600, max_ttl=86400, rate_limit_per_sender=20, scanner=None) takes the InboxConfig limits (max_messages and max_message_length must be at least 1, else ValueError). scanner is an object with scan_text(text, direction=...) (such as a PromptiseSecurityScanner) or check_input(text); with one, add() refuses flagged content with InboxMessageRejected.

MessageInbox method Description await add(message) Stores the message (content truncated to max_message_length, expiry from default_ttl, capped by max_ttl) and returns its message_id. Raises InvalidInboxMessage, InboxRateLimitError, InboxFullError or InboxMessageRejected await get_pending() Unexpired, unanswered messages, by priority then age await get_questions() Pending questions only await submit_response(question_id, response) Answers a question and wakes its waiter await wait_for_response(question_id, timeout=300) Waits for the answer; KeyError for an unknown question, asyncio.TimeoutError on timeout, InboxQuestionRemoved after clear(), InboxFullError when the question was evicted await rescan() Scans the held messages again with the current scanner; removes and returns the flagged ones as (message_id, reason) await mark_processed(message_id) Removes one message await remove_consumed(delivered) Removes what a run has seen (all but unanswered questions); returns the count await purge_expired() Drops expired messages; returns the count await clear() Removes everything and ends waiting questions await status() pending_messages, pending_questions, oldest_message_age_seconds and a messages summary list InboxMessage field Default Description content required The message text message_type MessageType.CONTEXT MessageType.DIRECTIVE, CONTEXT, QUESTION or CORRECTION (values "directive", "context", "question", "correction") sender_id None Who sent it; the rate limit is per sender priority "normal" "low", "normal", "high" or "critical" message_id generated (msg_...) Unique ID created_at now (Unix time) When it was created expires_at None Unix time it expires; add() sets it from the TTL metadata {} Stored with the message

InboxResponse has question_id, content, answered_at (Unix time, default now) and invocation_id (default None). Both classes have to_dict(), and InboxMessage.is_expired() says whether its expiry has passed.

docs.title: Python client
docs.text:
OrchestrationClient has a typed method for every route. It uses httpx and is an async context manager.

from promptise.runtime import OrchestrationAPIError, OrchestrationClient

async with OrchestrationClient("http://localhost:9100", token="my-token") as client:
    await client.deploy("monitor", {"model": "openai:gpt-5-mini", "instructions": "Monitor pipelines."}, start=True)

    answer = await client.ask("monitor", "What anomalies have you found?", timeout=60)
    print(answer)  # the answer text, or None if the agent didn't answer in time

    result = await client.update_budget("monitor", max_cost_per_day=500.0)
    print(result["live"], result["effective_from"])  # True next_budget_check

    try:
        await client.rotate_secret("monitor", "api_key", "sk-new-key", ttl=3600)
    except OrchestrationAPIError as exc:
        print(exc.status_code, exc.code, exc.error_message)  # 404 SECRET_NOT_FOUND ...
Argument Default Description base_url required For example "http://localhost:9100" token None The server's auth_token, sent as Authorization: Bearer auth_token None Alias of token (passing both with different values raises ValueError) timeout 30.0 Default request timeout in seconds

Use it with async with, or call await client.aclose() when done.

Errors. A 4xx or 5xx answer raises OrchestrationAPIError, a subclass of httpx.HTTPStatusError, with status_code, code (the API error code, or None when the body was not an API error) and error_message. Network failures raise the usual httpx exceptions.

204 answers. remove_process() and clear_inbox() return {}.

/runtime/shutdown shutdown(*, drain_timeout=None) {"status": "shutting_down"}; 404 error without on_shutdown GET /processes list_processes() list[dict] POST /processes deploy(name, config, *, start=False) dict GET /processes/{name} get_process(name) dict DELETE /processes/{name} remove_process(name) {} POST .../start start_process(name) dict POST .../stop stop_process(name, *, ask() returns the answer text, or None when the server answered status: "timeout"; its HTTP timeout is timeout + 10 seconds, so the server's long poll ends first.

docs.title: Audit log
docs.text:
Every mutating request (POST, PATCH, PUT, DELETE) that passes the token and Host/Origin checks, successful or not, is logged at INFO to the promptise.runtime.api logger with its method, route, path parameters (process, trigger and secret names), status and client address. Requests those checks refuse (401, 403 CROSS_ORIGIN_REFUSED, 421) are logged as warnings, as are refused command deploys.

A successful mutating request is also written to the process's journal (when it has one) as an api_request entry:

{"method": "DELETE", "route": "/api/v1/processes/{name}/triggers/{trigger_id}",
 "params": {"name": "monitor", "trigger_id": "cron-6d904fd75c"}, "status": 200, "client": "127.0.0.1"}

Request bodies are never logged: they can hold secret values and message text.

docs.title: Error responses
docs.text:
Errors are JSON objects:

{
    "error": {
        "code": "PROCESS_NOT_FOUND",
        "message": "Process 'unknown-agent' not found"
    }
}

The codes come from promptise.runtime.api.ERROR_CODES (code -> (status, meaning)):

Status Code Meaning 400 HEALTH_DISABLED Health operation on a process without health monitoring 400 INBOX_DISABLED Inbox operation on a process without an inbox 400 INVALID_JSON Request body is not a JSON object 400 JOURNAL_DISABLED Rewind on a process without a journal 400 MISSION_DISABLED Mission operation on a process without a mission 400 RESUME_FAILED The process can't be resumed in its current state 400 ROTATION_FAILED The secret could not be rotated 400 SECRETS_DISABLED Secret operation on a process without secret scoping 400 SUSPEND_FAILED The process can't be suspended in its current state 401 UNAUTHORIZED Missing or wrong bearer token 403 COMMANDS_NOT_ALLOWED Deploy with a stdio MCP server, a command hook or open-mode tool creation while allow_command_deploys is off 403 CROSS_ORIGIN_REFUSED Cross-site Origin on a loopback bind 403 ENV_REFERENCES_NOT_ALLOWED Config with a ${VAR} reference the API doesn't allow (allow_env_references / allowed_env_vars) 403 PATH_NOT_ALLOWED Journal, memory or watch path outside the API's data_dir (or with '..') 403 WRITE_DENIED Context key(s) not writable (nothing was written) 404 ENTRY_NOT_FOUND Journal entry ID doesn't exist (rewind target) 404 NOT_FOUND No such route 404 PROCESS_NOT_FOUND Process name doesn't exist 404 SECRET_NOT_FOUND The process has no secret of that name 404 TRIGGER_NOT_FOUND Trigger ID doesn't exist 405 METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED The route doesn't accept this method 409 INBOX_FULL The inbox is full and nothing can be evicted for the message 409 MISSION_STATE Mission fail/pause/resume not valid in the mission's state 409 PROCESS_EXISTS Deploy with a name that's already registered 409 PROCESS_NOT_RUNNING Message or question to a stopped or failed process 409 REWIND_BUSY A run was still in flight when the rewind timed out 409 TRIGGER_EXISTS Adding a trigger identical to an existing one 410 QUESTION_REMOVED /ask: the question was cleared or evicted from the inbox before it was answered 413 PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE Request body over the server's size limit (1 MiB) 421 MISDIRECTED_REQUEST Non-loopback Host on a loopback bind (DNS rebinding) 422 DEPLOY_FAILED The process could not be created from a valid config 422 INVALID_CONFIG Config fails validation (deploy, trigger, PATCH sections) 422 INVALID_FIELD A field has the wrong type or an out-of-range value 422 INVALID_NAME Process name doesn't match ^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_-]{0,63}$ 422 INVALID_TYPE Unknown message_type 422 MESSAGE_REJECTED The inbox's guardrail scan flagged the message 422 MISSING_FIELD Required field missing from the request 422 UNKNOWN_FIELD PATCH names a field the config model doesn't declare 429 RATE_LIMITED Inbox rate limit exceeded varies HTTP_ERROR Another HTTP error from the server (400, 408, 411, 414, 431, ...); the response status says which 500 INTERNAL_ERROR Unexpected server error (details in the server log) 500 RESTART_FAILED The process failed to restart 500 START_FAILED The process failed to start 500 STOP_FAILED The process failed to stop

HTTP_ERROR has no fixed status (its ERROR_CODES status is None): it carries the status of the underlying HTTP error. An INTERNAL_ERROR message is generic; the details go to the server log.

When an error is caused by an exception inside the runtime (a failed deploy, start, stop, restart, suspend, resume or secret rotation, an inbox refusal, a rewind that failed, an unexpected error), the response never carries the exception's text, which can hold file paths, internal state or secret values. It carries a fixed message and an error_id, and the exception with its traceback is logged on promptise.runtime.api under the same id (ERROR for a 5xx, WARNING otherwise). OrchestrationAPIError.error_id holds it on the client side:

{
    "error": {
        "code": "START_FAILED",
        "message": "Process 'worker' failed to start",
        "error_id": "3f9c0a1b2d4e"
    }
}

Validation errors (INVALID_CONFIG from a config pydantic rejects) still list each offending field and what was expected of it.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Bearer token required on non-loopback binds, compared in constant time; GET /api/v1/health is the only route without auth (for Kubernetes probes).
  • On loopback binds, DNS-rebinding (421) and cross-site (403) requests are refused.
  • Deploys that would run programs or agent-written code on the host are refused unless allow_command_deploys=True.
  • ${VAR} references in deployed configs are refused unless allowed, and an API-deployed process resolves only the allowed variables; a failed resolution doesn't reveal whether a variable exists.
  • Journal, memory and watch paths in deployed configs stay inside data_dir.
  • An API-deployed open-mode agent connects only the MCP servers in allowed_mcp_urls (none when it is empty), and agent-connected servers never receive the process identity's credential (see Open Mode).
  • Process names are validated, and configs are validated before a process is created or changed; invalid changes change nothing.
  • Secret values never appear in responses (including /ask answers), error messages, the audit log or the journal.
  • Every mutating request is audited.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• An unanswered /ask is not an error. It answers 200 with status: "timeout", and client.ask() returns None. The agent only sees the question on its next run, so a process whose triggers don't fire within timeout can't answer. Inject an event or pick a trigger that runs often enough.
  • Directives are shown once. After the run that saw it, a directive is removed from the inbox. Put lasting rules in the instructions (PATCH /instructions) or the context state.
  • Messages are unscanned without guardrails. scan_with_guardrails defaults to true, but it needs a scanner; without guardrails or trigger_delivery.scan_payloads the process only logs a warning.
  • DELETE /inbox ends waiting questions. It removes pending questions; an /ask call still waiting on one answers 410 QUESTION_REMOVED (process.ask() raises InboxQuestionRemoved). Wait for open questions before clearing the inbox.
  • START_FAILED on deploy leaves the process registered. A retry with the same name gets 409 PROCESS_EXISTS; start it or delete it instead.
  • Secret rotations don't survive a restart (with the default revoke_on_stop=True). A restart revokes the secrets and resolves them from the config again; rotate the source value as well (see Secret Scoping).
  • An open-mode deploy gets 403 COMMANDS_NOT_ALLOWED. Open mode allows create_tool by default, which runs agent-written code on the host. Send "open_mode": {"allow_tool_creation": false}, or start the API with allow_command_deploys=True if every token holder may run code there.
  • A ${VAR} in a deploy gets 403 ENV_REFERENCES_NOT_ALLOWED. Send the value, or ask the operator to allow that variable (--allow-env-var NAME).
  • Use stable trigger IDs. Take the id from GET /triggers; position-based static_<n> IDs are deprecated.

docs.title: Runtime CLI
docs.text:
The promptise runtime command group runs agent processes from .agent manifests and controls them from another terminal. start runs a runtime (in the foreground or in the background); status, stop, restart, logs and rewind find it on their own and talk to its control API. validate and init work on manifest files.

# Start an agent in the background
promptise runtime start agents/watcher.agent --detach

# From any terminal on this machine
promptise runtime status
promptise runtime logs data-watcher --follow
promptise runtime restart
promptise runtime stop

docs.title: How the commands find a runtime
docs.text:
promptise runtime start serves the Orchestration API on 127.0.0.1 (a free port unless --api-port is given) with a random bearer token, and records how to reach it in a state file: ~/.promptise/runtime/<runtime name>.json. The file holds the PID, host, port, token, the manifest paths, each process's journal location, the start time and whether startup finished. status, stop, restart, logs and rewind read it. With one runtime running they need no name.

The state directory holds tokens, so it is private:

  • the directory is created with mode 0700, each file with 0600;
  • on POSIX, a directory or file owned by another user is refused, and so is a state file that other users can read or write; a directory you own that is too open is tightened to 0700;
  • a state file whose process is gone (a crash, kill -9) is stale and removed the next time a command lists the directory, and so is one that is not a valid state file; a file that can't be read at that moment (on Windows, while its runtime rewrites it) is left alone;
  • the runtime removes its own file when it exits.
Environment variable Effect PROMPTISE_RUNTIME_STATE_DIR Use this state directory instead of ~/.promptise/runtime PROMPTISE_RUNTIME_TOKEN start: use this API token instead of a random one (start then removes the variable from its own environment, so agents, hooks and stdio MCP servers don't inherit it). Client commands: the token for --url

docs.title: A runtime on another machine
docs.text:
Every client command also takes --url (the base URL of any Orchestration API) and --token. Prefer PROMPTISE_RUNTIME_TOKEN over --token: a token on the command line is visible to other users in ps. --token without --url is an error, because a local runtime's token comes from its state file.

export PROMPTISE_RUNTIME_TOKEN=...       # the token the remote runtime was started with
promptise runtime status --url http://10.0.0.5:9100
promptise runtime logs worker --url http://10.0.0.5:9100

To control a runtime remotely, start it with --api-host (for example 0.0.0.0) and a known PROMPTISE_RUNTIME_TOKEN, and put it behind TLS when the token crosses an untrusted network.

docs.title: promptise runtime start
docs.text:
Start agent process(es) from a .agent manifest or a directory of them.

promptise runtime start agents/watcher.agent                 # foreground
promptise runtime start agents/                              # every .agent file in a directory
promptise runtime start agents/watcher.agent --name my-watcher
promptise runtime start agents/ --runtime-name prod --detach # background
promptise runtime start agents/ --dashboard                  # live terminal dashboard
Argument / option Short Default Description MANIFEST required Path to a .agent file or a directory of .agent files --name -n : Override the process name (single manifest file only) --runtime-name -r process name (file) or directory name Name of this runtime for status, stop, restart, logs --detach/--no-detach -d off Run in the background; print the runtime name, PID and log file --dashboard/--no-dashboard off Live monitoring dashboard (foreground only) --api-host 127.0.0.1 Address the control API listens on --api-port 0 Port of the control API (0: a free port) --allow-command-deploys off Let the control API deploy processes with stdio MCP servers, command hooks or open-mode tool creation --allow-env-references off Let control-API deploys use ${VAR} references to any environment variable of this machine --allow-env-var NAME : Let control-API deploys reference this one variable as ${NAME}; repeatable --import MODULE -i : Import this Python module before loading the manifests, for example one that registers custom trigger types with register_trigger_type(); repeatable. The current directory is importable

In the foreground, start loads the manifests, starts the control API, writes the state file, starts every process and prints a status table:

Loaded process: notes
                        Agent Processes
┏━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Name  ┃ State   ┃ ID       ┃ Invocations ┃ Queue ┃ Uptime   ┃
┡━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ notes │ RUNNING │ 51a7550e │           0 │     0 │ 0h 0m 0s │
└───────┴─────────┴──────────┴─────────────┴───────┴──────────┘

Runtime notes (pid 23006), control API on http://127.0.0.1:53367
Press Ctrl+C to stop all processes, or run 'promptise runtime stop notes' from another terminal.

It runs until Ctrl+C, SIGTERM (docker stop, a process manager) or promptise runtime stop. Each stops every process gracefully (final checkpoint, dead letters, process.stopped), closes the API, removes the state file and exits with 0. A second Ctrl+C or SIGTERM during the shutdown exits at once with code 130.

A process that fails to start is reported and the others keep running. When none can start, the runtime shuts down with exit code 1.

Runtime names are 1-64 letters, digits, _, . or -, starting with a letter or digit; a default taken from a file or directory name is cleaned up to fit. A name is claimed when the runtime starts: a second start with the name of a running runtime fails (A runtime named 'notes' is already running (pid 18457)), so pick another with --runtime-name.

--detach starts the same command in the background (a new session, detached from the terminal), with its output in a log file next to the state file: ~/.promptise/runtime/<runtime name>.log (mode 0600, overwritten by the next detached start). It waits until startup has finished (every process started or reported as failed), then prints:

Started runtime notes in the background
  PID:         18457
  Processes:   notes
  Control API: http://127.0.0.1:52276
  Log file:    /home/me/.promptise/runtime/notes.log
  Status:      promptise runtime status notes
  Stop it:     promptise runtime stop notes

When the background runtime exits during startup, start prints the last 20 lines of its log and exits with 1. When it isn't ready after 60 seconds, start says so and exits with 0 (the runtime keeps starting; check status and the log). --detach can't be combined with --dashboard.

--allow-command-deploys. By default the control API refuses POST /api/v1/processes for a config with a stdio MCP server, a command hook or open mode with allow_tool_creation (403 COMMANDS_NOT_ALLOWED): anyone with the token could otherwise run any command on the machine. The flag lifts that; use it only when every token holder may run commands there. The manifests you start are never affected.

--import MODULE. A manifest trigger with a custom type needs the module that calls register_trigger_type() to be imported first, or start and validate report unknown trigger type. --import imports it (the current directory is on the import path, as with python -m); a module that fails to import ends the command with exit code 1. A --detach runtime gets the same --import options.

promptise runtime validate agents/ --import my_triggers
promptise runtime start agents/ --import my_triggers --detach

--allow-env-references and --allow-env-var NAME. By default the control API refuses a deploy (or a trigger or PATCH body) with a ${VAR} reference (403 ENV_REFERENCES_NOT_ALLOWED), because the deployed agent could read the value back through a secret. --allow-env-var SEARCH_API_KEY (repeatable) allows those variables only; --allow-env-references allows any. Both are passed on to a --detach runtime. Paths in deployed configs (journal, memory, watch paths) must lie in ./.promptise under the directory you start the runtime in (403 PATH_NOT_ALLOWED). See Securing the control API.

docs.title: promptise runtime status
docs.text:
Show the processes of running runtime(s), or the details of one process.

promptise runtime status                 # every runtime on this machine
promptise runtime status prod            # one runtime
promptise runtime status data-watcher    # a process name works too
promptise runtime status prod --process data-watcher
promptise runtime status --json
Argument / option Short Description NAME Runtime name, or a process name in a running runtime (omit for every runtime) --process -p Show this one process instead of the whole runtime --json Output as JSON: an object for one runtime or process, a list of runtimes otherwise --url, --token Talk to an Orchestration API instead of a local runtime

Each runtime is shown with its name, PID, API URL and start time ((starting) while processes are still starting), then its process table. The JSON output has runtime (name, pid, url, started_at, ready, manifests, log_file; never the token) and status (or process).

docs.title: promptise runtime stop
docs.text:
Stop a running runtime (every process, then the runtime exits), or one process.

promptise runtime stop                      # the only running runtime
promptise runtime stop prod
promptise runtime stop prod --process data-watcher
promptise runtime stop prod --process data-watcher --drain-timeout 0   # cancel its run now
promptise runtime stop prod --drain-timeout 30                         # let runs finish for 30 s
promptise runtime stop prod --timeout 60 --force
Argument / option Short Default Description NAME : Runtime to stop, or a process name in a running runtime; may be omitted when only one runtime runs --process -p : Stop only this process (the runtime keeps running) --force/--no-force off Kill the runtime if it hasn't stopped gracefully --drain-timeout each process's drain_timeout Seconds runs in flight may take to finish before they are cancelled (0 to 3600; 0 cancels them at once) --timeout 30.0 Seconds to wait for a graceful shutdown; with --drain-timeout at least the drain plus 10 --url, --token -- Talk to an Orchestration API instead of a local runtime

The stop is graceful (see Graceful stop): no new trigger event starts, and runs in flight get up to --drain-timeout seconds to finish. Without the option each process waits up to its own drain_timeout (5 seconds unless its config sets it), as on SIGTERM. A run still going after that is cancelled, journaled as run_interrupted and kept in the dead letters; for one process, stop says how many runs it cancelled.

How a runtime is stopped:

  1. stop asks it to shut down over its control API (POST /api/v1/runtime/shutdown, with the --drain-timeout if given) and waits up to --timeout seconds for it to exit. Keep --timeout above the processes' drain_timeout when you don't pass --drain-timeout: a SIGTERM during the drain (step 2) is a second signal, and the runtime exits at once without a clean shutdown.
  2. When the API can't be reached or the runtime is still running, it sends SIGTERM and waits again (up to 10 more seconds after a successful request, --timeout otherwise). Windows has no catchable SIGTERM, so this step is skipped there.
  3. Still running: with --force the process is killed (SIGKILL) and its state file removed; without it, stop exits with 1 and suggests --timeout or --force.

With --url, stop requests the shutdown and returns without waiting. A plain OrchestrationAPI (one not started by promptise runtime start, so without the shutdown route) gets stop-all instead: its processes stop, its server keeps running.

docs.title: promptise runtime restart
docs.text:
Restart every process of a running runtime, or one process.

promptise runtime restart
promptise runtime restart prod --process data-watcher
Argument / option Short Description NAME Runtime to restart, or a process name in a running runtime; may be omitted when only one runtime runs --process -p Restart only this process --url, --token Talk to an Orchestration API instead of a local runtime

The runtime itself keeps running, with the same control API and token. Restarted processes keep their context state and, unless context.conversation_clear_on_stop is set, their conversation. To load edited manifests, stop the runtime and start it again.

docs.title: promptise runtime logs
docs.text:
Show the newest journal entries of a process, each with its entry ID (the target promptise runtime rewind takes).

promptise runtime logs data-watcher                 # newest 20 entries
promptise runtime logs data-watcher --lines 50
promptise runtime logs data-watcher --follow        # keep printing new ones (Ctrl+C ends)
promptise runtime logs data-watcher --journal-path /var/lib/agents/journal
Argument / option Short Default Description NAME required Process name --lines -n 20 Number of most recent entries to show --follow/--no-follow -f off Keep printing new entries --journal-path see below Journal directory --url, --token : Read the journal through an Orchestration API

Where the entries come from:

  • --url: the API's GET /processes/{name}/journal (at most 500 entries per request; --follow polls every second);
  • --journal-path: <path>/<name>.jsonl;
  • otherwise, a process in a runtime on this machine: its journal file (read directly, so it works while the runtime is busy), or its API for a memory journal. A process with journal.level: none is an error that says so;
  • otherwise: .promptise/journal/<name>.jsonl in the current directory.

The output is a table of time, entry ID, type and data (cut at 80 characters). With --follow, new entries are printed one per line as they are written; a file that is truncated or replaced is read again from the start.

                                Journal: notes
 Time                     Entry ID                              Type               Data
 2026-10-19T20:25:02.077  b354d9ca-f7b7-4783-964a-970f9ae156b3  invocation_result  {"invocation": 1, ...
 2026-10-19T20:25:02.077  38b220ec-6b42-4c81-a0ca-f27f4f1a4767  checkpoint         {"state": {"context_state": {}, ...

docs.title: promptise runtime rewind
docs.text:
Roll a process's conversation and/or context state back to just before a journal entry. See Rewind for what each mode does.

promptise runtime rewind notes                                  # list recent entries with their IDs
promptise runtime rewind notes 7c7bee77-f518-41de-b250-d1b586819d7a --plan
promptise runtime rewind notes 7c7bee77-f518-41de-b250-d1b586819d7a        # plan, confirm, apply
promptise runtime rewind notes 7c7bee77-... --mode conversation_only --yes
Argument / option Short Default Description PROCESS required Process to rewind ENTRY_ID : Journal entry to go back to; omit it to list recent entries --mode -m both both, conversation_only, code_only (context state) or summarize (rewind nothing, add a summary to the conversation) --plan off Only show what the rewind would change --yes -y off Apply without asking for confirmation --runtime -r : Runtime the process runs in (needed when several runtimes run) --lines -n 20 Entries to list when no entry ID is given (1-500) --url, --token : Talk to an Orchestration API instead of a local runtime

The command shows the plan first (target entry, mode, how many entries are affected), then asks Rewind <process>? [y/N]. A running process is suspended for the rewind and resumed afterwards. The rewind is journaled with actor cli. It goes through the control API, so the process must run in a runtime and have a journal.

docs.title: promptise runtime validate
docs.text:
Validate a .agent manifest file, or every .agent file in a directory.

promptise runtime validate agents/watcher.agent
promptise runtime validate agents/
Argument / option Short Description PATH A .agent manifest file, or a directory of them --import MODULE -i Import this Python module first (repeatable), so custom trigger types it registers are known

Each file is checked against the manifest schema (field types, trigger settings, hooks, unknown keys) and warnings are printed for likely mistakes. A valid file gets a summary table: name, model, version, the start of the instructions, server count and trigger count. For a directory, a final line says how many manifests failed.

docs.title: promptise runtime init
docs.text:
Generate a template .agent manifest file.

promptise runtime init                                    # agent.agent, basic template
promptise runtime init --template cron --output agents/monitor.agent
promptise runtime init --output agent.agent --force       # overwrite
Option Short Default Description --output -o agent.agent Output file path --template -t basic basic, cron, webhook or full --force/--no-force off Overwrite an existing file Template Contents basic Model and instructions, no servers or triggers cron An HTTP MCP server and a cron trigger every 5 minutes webhook An HTTP MCP server and a webhook trigger full HTTP and stdio servers, cron, webhook and file-watch triggers, a full journal, restart and lifetime settings

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success (also a foreground runtime stopped with Ctrl+C, SIGTERM or stop) 1 An error with a message on stderr: no runtime running, unknown runtime or process, the API refused the request or the token, a manifest that fails to load or validate, no process could start, a runtime that didn't stop in time, a rewind that was not confirmed, an existing file for init 2 Usage error: an unknown option, a missing argument, a value out of range 130 A second Ctrl+C or SIGTERM while the runtime was shutting down (exits without a clean shutdown)

docs.title: Example workflow
docs.text:
# 1. Generate and edit a manifest
promptise runtime init --template cron --output agents/monitor.agent

# 2. Validate it
promptise runtime validate agents/monitor.agent

# 3. Start it in the background
promptise runtime start agents/monitor.agent --detach

# 4. Watch it
promptise runtime status
promptise runtime logs data-watcher --follow

# 5. Stop it
promptise runtime stop

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Commands that can't find the runtime. The state directory is per user (and per PROMPTISE_RUNTIME_STATE_DIR). A runtime started by another user, under sudo, or with a different state directory is invisible; use --url with its token.
  • Two runtimes running. stop, restart and rewind then need a name (or --runtime); the error lists the running ones.
  • Expecting restart to reload manifests. It restarts the processes with the loaded configuration. Stop and start the runtime to pick up edits.
  • logs reading the wrong journal. A relative journal.path is relative to the directory start ran in. Run logs with the runtime running (it then uses the recorded absolute path) or pass --journal-path.
  • A remote API without a known token. With --api-host 0.0.0.0 and no PROMPTISE_RUNTIME_TOKEN, the token is random and only in the local state file. Set the variable before start so remote clients can use it.
  • A killed runtime. After kill -9 the state file stays until the next command notices the PID is gone and removes it; the detached log file is kept.
