docs.title: Runtime Configuration
docs.text:
All runtime configuration is Pydantic models with defaults for every optional field. Small section configs (TriggerConfig, JournalConfig, BudgetConfig, ...) are composed into a ProcessConfig for one process, and ProcessConfigs into a RuntimeConfig for an AgentRuntime. This page lists every field with its exact type and default. You only set what you want to change.

from promptise.runtime import JournalConfig, ProcessConfig, RuntimeConfig, TriggerConfig

config = RuntimeConfig(
    processes={
        "watcher": ProcessConfig(
            model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
            instructions="Monitor data pipelines.",
            triggers=[TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *")],
            journal=JournalConfig(path=".promptise/journal"),
            restart_policy="on_failure",
        ),
    },
)

Every class on this page is importable from promptise.runtime.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
RuntimeConfig
  +-- processes: dict[str, ProcessConfig]
  |     +-- open_mode: OpenModeConfig
  |     +-- triggers: list[TriggerConfig]
  |     +-- trigger_delivery: TriggerDeliveryConfig
  |     +-- journal: JournalConfig
  |     +-- context: ContextConfig
  |     +-- hooks: list[HookConfig]
  |     +-- secrets: SecretScopeConfig
  |     +-- budget: BudgetConfig        (tool_costs: ToolCostAnnotation, escalation: EscalationTarget)
  |     +-- health: HealthConfig        (escalation: EscalationTarget)
  |     +-- mission: MissionConfig      (escalation: EscalationTarget)
  |     +-- inbox: InboxConfig
  +-- distributed: DistributedConfig

docs.title: Validation and unknown keys
docs.text:
Values are validated when the config is created: types, ranges, required trigger fields, cron expressions, time zones and cross-field rules raise pydantic.ValidationError at construction, not when the process first runs. What happens to a key the model doesn't know depends on the model:

Models Unknown key ProcessConfig, TriggerConfig, TriggerDeliveryConfig, InboxConfig, HookConfig Rejected: ValidationError ("Extra inputs are not permitted") RuntimeConfig, OpenModeConfig, JournalConfig, ContextConfig, SecretScopeConfig, BudgetConfig, HealthConfig, MissionConfig, ToolCostAnnotation, EscalationTarget, DistributedConfig Ignored with a FutureWarning naming the key and the valid keys; a future release will reject them 
HealthConfig(error_windw=5)
# FutureWarning: HealthConfig: unknown key(s) ['error_windw'] are ignored; valid keys are
# ['cooldown', 'empty_max_chars', ..., 'stuck_threshold']. Unknown keys will be rejected
# in a future release.

Manifests reject unknown keys in every section, and so does the Orchestration API. To catch typos in Python too, turn the warning into an error: warnings.simplefilter("error", FutureWarning).

docs.title: Secret fields
docs.text:
These fields are pydantic.SecretStr: TriggerConfig.hmac_secret, the values of SecretScopeConfig.secrets, the values of HookConfig.env and DistributedConfig.auth_token. You pass plain strings; repr() shows SecretStr('**********'), and code reads the value with .get_secret_value().

model_dump(mode="json") and RuntimeConfig.to_dict() write literal values as "**********". For SecretScopeConfig.secrets, HookConfig.env and DistributedConfig.auth_token, a ${VAR} reference carries no secret and is written as is. Loading a dict that holds the "**********" placeholder raises a ValidationError, so a dumped config can't silently start with a wrong secret; supply the real values (or references) again.

s = SecretScopeConfig(enabled=True, secrets={"api": "sk-live-123", "db": "${DB_PASSWORD}"})
s.model_dump(mode="json")["secrets"]
# {'api': '**********', 'db': '${DB_PASSWORD}'}

docs.title: RuntimeConfig
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description processes dict[str, ProcessConfig] {} Processes to register, by name. AgentRuntime(config) registers them at construction. distributed DistributedConfig DistributedConfig() Distributed mode (off by default) 
data = config.to_dict()                  # JSON-compatible; secrets masked
restored = RuntimeConfig.from_dict(data) # model_validate

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
DEFAULT_DEVELOPMENT_CONFIG and DEFAULT_PRODUCTION_CONFIG are identical: no processes and distributed.enabled=False. Production hardening is per process (journal, restart_policy, health, budget, trigger_delivery), and distributed mode needs your cluster's coordinator and token, so no preset turns either on.

from promptise.runtime import DEFAULT_DEVELOPMENT_CONFIG, DEFAULT_PRODUCTION_CONFIG

docs.title: ProcessConfig
docs.text:
Configuration for one agent process. Unknown keys are rejected.

Field Type Default Description model str or a model "openai:gpt-5-mini" LLM model ID. In code also a model object as build_agent(model=...) takes it (a LangChain chat model, a promptise.Model, a FallbackChain); a model object is not serialised. See The agent's model. instructions str \| None None System prompt execution_mode ExecutionMode ExecutionMode.STRICT "strict" or "open" (self-modifying, see Meta-Tools) open_mode OpenModeConfig OpenModeConfig() Open-mode limits; ignored in strict mode servers dict[str, Any] {} MCP servers: a dict per server (url for HTTP, command for stdio) or a server spec object triggers list[TriggerConfig] [] What wakes the process journal JournalConfig JournalConfig(level="none") Off unless set. JournalConfig() itself defaults to level="checkpoint". context ContextConfig ContextConfig() State, memory, conversation, environment concurrency int 1 Runs in parallel (1-100) heartbeat_interval float 10.0 Seconds between idle-timeout and lifetime checks (> 0) idle_timeout float 0.0 Seconds without a run before the process suspends with reason "idle" (0 = never). The next trigger event resumes it. max_lifetime float 0.0 Seconds after start at which the process stops, or is recycled with restart_policy="always" (0 = unlimited) max_consecutive_failures int 3 Failed events in a row before FAILED (> 0) restart_policy Literal["always", "on_failure", "never"] "never" See Restart policies drain_timeout float 5.0 Seconds a graceful stop (run_forever() on SIGTERM / Ctrl+C, stop(drain_timeout=None)) lets runs in flight finish before cancelling them (0 to 3600) max_restarts int 3 Automatic restart attempts in a row; the count resets after a successful run (>= 0) restart_backoff float 1.0 Seconds before the first restart; doubles per attempt, capped at 60 s (>= 0) secrets SecretScopeConfig SecretScopeConfig() Disabled budget BudgetConfig BudgetConfig() Disabled health HealthConfig HealthConfig() Disabled mission MissionConfig MissionConfig() Disabled inbox InboxConfig InboxConfig() Disabled approval Any \| None None ApprovalPolicy (or dict) for human approval of tool calls identity Any \| None None AgentIdentity: attributes the process's actions and presents its credential to MCP servers trigger_delivery TriggerDeliveryConfig TriggerDeliveryConfig() Retries, dead letters, payload scanning guardrails Any \| None None Passed to build_agent() (e.g. a PromptiseSecurityScanner) observe Any \| None None Passed to build_agent(): True or an ObservabilityConfig cache Any \| None None Passed to build_agent(): a SemanticCache optimize_tools Any \| None None Passed to build_agent(): semantic tool selection adaptive Any \| None None Passed to build_agent(): adaptive strategy max_invocation_time float 0 Per-run timeout in seconds, passed to build_agent() (0 = none) hooks list[HookConfig] [] Lifecycle hooks, registered on process.hooks when the process is created extra_tools list [] Local tools, as in build_agent(extra_tools=...): @tool functions, plain functions and LangChain tools. Code only: not serialised, and a manifest can't set them. See Local tools.

docs.title: ExecutionMode
docs.text: Value Description ExecutionMode.STRICT ("strict") The agent can't change itself. Default. ExecutionMode.OPEN ("open") The agent gets meta-tools to change its instructions, tools, MCP servers and triggers, and to spawn processes, within OpenModeConfig.

docs.title: OpenModeConfig
docs.text:
Limits for open mode. Unknown keys are ignored with a FutureWarning. Open mode lets the model change its own setup; see Meta-Tools: Security before you turn capabilities on.

Field Type Default Description allow_identity_change bool True modify_instructions tool allow_tool_creation bool True create_tool tool. Runs model-written Python in the runtime's process (not a sandbox); the control API refuses it without allow_command_deploys allow_mcp_connect bool True connect_mcp_server tool allow_trigger_management bool True add_trigger / remove_trigger tools allow_memory_management bool True store_memory / search_memory / forget_memory tools max_custom_tools int 20 Agent-created tools (>= 0) max_dynamic_triggers int 10 Agent-added triggers (>= 0) max_instruction_length int 10000 Characters of agent-written instructions (>= 100) max_rebuilds int \| None None Hot reloads per lifetime of the process object; restarts don't reset it. A refused change is not applied, now or after a restart. rollback() is not refused but counts. None = unlimited. allowed_mcp_urls list[str] [] URLs connect_mcp_server may use. Empty: any URL whose host resolves to public addresses (warning at start); for a process deployed through the control API, none identity_mcp_urls list[str] [] Agent-connected server URLs that may receive the process identity's credential and a caller's token (empty = none) sandbox_custom_tools bool True Run agent-written tools with restricted builtins and no imports (False: a fixed import allowlist). Not a security boundary either way allow_process_spawn bool False spawn_process / list_processes tools max_spawned_processes int 3 Processes this agent may spawn (>= 0) allow_public_webhooks bool False Webhook triggers the agent adds (or gives a spawned process) may bind a non-loopback webhook_host, with an hmac_secret

docs.title: TriggerConfig
docs.text:
One trigger. Each built-in type reads its own subset of fields; setting a field of another built-in type (for example watch_path on a cron trigger) to a non-default value is an error, because the trigger would ignore it. Custom types (registered with register_trigger_type()) receive the whole config and use custom_config. Unknown keys are rejected. See Triggers.

Field Type Default Applies to Description type str required all "cron", "webhook", "file_watch", "event", "message" or a registered custom type cron_expression str \| None None cron Required for cron. Five fields, or six with a trailing seconds field cron_timezone str \| None None cron IANA time zone (None = UTC) webhook_path str "/webhook" webhook URL path webhook_port int 9090 webhook Listen port (1025-65535) webhook_host str "127.0.0.1" webhook Bind address ("0.0.0.0" = all interfaces) hmac_secret SecretStr \| None None webhook Signature secret; unsigned or badly signed requests get 401 signature_scheme Literal["generic", "github", "stripe", "telegram"] "generic" webhook Signature format (telegram: the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header must equal hmac_secret); a non-default value needs hmac_secret signature_header str \| None None webhook Header with the signature (default: the scheme's header); needs hmac_secret signature_tolerance int 300 webhook Max age in seconds of a stripe signature timestamp (> 0) allowed_sources list[str] [] webhook Client IPs / CIDR ranges allowed (empty = any); others get 403 webhook_max_body_bytes int 1048576 webhook Largest request body (1 MiB; 1 to 1 GiB); larger bodies get 413 watch_path str \| None None file_watch Required for file_watch: the directory to watch watch_patterns list[str] ["*"] file_watch Glob patterns matched against the file name watch_events list[str] ["created", "modified"] file_watch Any of created, modified, deleted, moved (at least one) watch_debounce_seconds float 0.5 file_watch Events for one file within this window merge into one (>= 0) watch_recursive bool True file_watch Also watch subdirectories watch_backend Literal["auto", "watchdog", "polling"] "auto" file_watch auto: OS notifications through watchdog when installed, else polling. watchdog fails if it isn't installed. polling scans the directory (for network shares and bind mounts) watch_poll_interval float 1.0 file_watch Seconds between scans with polling (> 0, <= 3600) watch_max_pending_events int 10000 file_watch Changed files held while the process is busy; past that, new files are dropped and counted in dropped_events (>= 1) event_type str \| None None event Required for event: the event type to subscribe to event_source str \| None None event Only events from this source topic str \| None None message Required for message: the broker topic (wildcards allowed) custom_config dict[str, Any] {} all Settings for custom trigger types filter_expression str \| Callable \| None None all Safe expression string or a callable taking the TriggerEvent; events that don't match skip the agent (syntax) trusted bool False all Deliver payloads as the user's request, without the untrusted-data framing; a webhook needs hmac_secret (trade-off)

docs.title: TriggerDeliveryConfig
docs.text:
How a process handles trigger events it can't process (ProcessConfig.trigger_delivery). Unknown keys are rejected.

Field Type Default Description max_retries int 0 Extra attempts for an event whose run raised (0-10). A retry re-runs the whole agent turn, so tools with side effects may run twice. retry_backoff float 2.0 Seconds before the first retry; doubles per attempt (> 0) retry_backoff_max float 60.0 Upper bound for the retry delay (> 0) dead_letter_size int 100 Entries kept in process.dead_letters, oldest dropped first (>= 0) scan_payloads bool False Prompt-injection scan of each payload before the agent sees it; flagged events are dead-lettered. Uses guardrails when it is a scanner, otherwise an injection-only PromptiseSecurityScanner (needs transformers) max_payload_chars int 20000 Longest payload text placed in the prompt; longer payloads are truncated (>= 200). The payload scan reads exactly this text

docs.title: JournalConfig
docs.text:
The durable audit log and recovery source (ProcessConfig.journal). Unknown keys warn. See Journal.

Field Type Default Description level Literal["none", "checkpoint", "full"] "checkpoint" "none" disables the journal. "checkpoint" records transitions, run results, context updates and checkpoints. "full" also records trigger events and tool calls. backend Literal["file", "memory"] "file" Append-only JSONL files, or in memory (tests) path str ".promptise/journal" Base directory of the file backend recover_on_start bool True On the first start() of a process object, restore context state, mission, budget counters, conversation history and invocation count from the last checkpoint of the same process name. False always starts fresh.

ProcessConfig() uses JournalConfig(level="none"): no journal unless you set one. A manifest without a journal: section gets JournalConfig(), which journals at "checkpoint" level.

docs.title: ContextConfig
docs.text:
State, memory, conversation and environment (ProcessConfig.context). Unknown keys warn. See Context & State.

Field Type Default Description writable_keys list[str] [] State keys the agent may write (empty = all) memory_provider Literal["in_memory", "chroma", "mem0"] \| None None Long-term memory provider (None = off) memory_max int 5 Memories injected per run (>= 1) memory_min_score float 0.0 Minimum relevance score (0-1) memory_timeout float 5.0 Seconds to wait for a memory search or auto-store (> 0) memory_auto_store bool False Store each exchange in long-term memory memory_collection str "agent_memory" ChromaDB collection memory_persist_directory str \| None None ChromaDB persist directory memory_user_id str "default" Mem0 user scope conversation_max_messages int 100 Messages kept in the conversation buffer (0 = unlimited) conversation_history bool True False: every run sees only its trigger event conversation_clear_on_stop bool False Clear the conversation history on stop(). By default it survives stop() / start() and restarts; close() always clears it. state_tool bool False Give the agent an update_state(key, value) tool (limited to writable_keys when set) file_mounts dict[str, str] {} Logical name to filesystem path env_prefix str "AGENT_" Only environment variables with this prefix are exposed. Must not be empty (an empty prefix would expose the whole environment) initial_state dict[str, Any] {} State at the first start. Keys recovered from the journal replace these.

docs.title: HookConfig
docs.text:
One lifecycle hook (ProcessConfig.hooks): either an external command or an async Python callback, never both. Unknown keys are rejected.

Field Type Default Description event str required A HookEvent value, e.g. "user_prompt_submit"; an unknown event is rejected with the list of valid ones command str \| list[str] \| None None Program and arguments (a string is split like a shell would; no shell runs it). The event arrives on stdin as JSON. callback Any \| None None Async callable taking a HookContext (code only; never serialized) timeout float \| None None Seconds the hook may run: 5 for a command, 30 for a callback when unset (> 0, <= 3600) priority int 0 Higher runs first once bool False Run on the first matching event only tag str \| None None Group name for HookManager.remove_by_tag() fail_closed bool False An error or timeout of this hook blocks the action (blockable events only) cwd str \| None None Working directory of the command (command only) env dict[str, SecretStr] {} Extra environment variables for the command; ${VAR} values are resolved when the hook runs (command only) env_passthrough list[str] [] Host variables passed through; the command otherwise gets a minimal environment (command only) max_output_bytes int 65536 Largest stdout accepted from the command (> 0, <= 10 MiB)

docs.title: SecretScopeConfig
docs.text:
Per-process secrets (ProcessConfig.secrets). Unknown keys warn. See Secret Scoping.

Field Type Default Description enabled bool False Turn secret scoping on secrets dict[str, SecretStr] {} Name to value or ${VAR} / ${VAR:-default} reference. References are resolved from the environment when the process starts, so the config holds no secret value. default_ttl float \| None None Seconds until a secret expires (None = never; > 0) ttls dict[str, float] {} Per-secret TTLs; every name must be in secrets, every value positive revoke_on_stop bool True Zero-fill and drop the secrets on stop(); close() always revokes them

docs.title: BudgetConfig
docs.text:
Autonomy limits (ProcessConfig.budget). Unknown keys warn. See Autonomy Budget.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• A typo in a section config. HealthConfig(error_windw=5) or OpenModeConfig(max_rebuild=3) only warns and keeps the default. Check warnings in tests, or define the config in a manifest, which rejects unknown keys.
  • Governance without enabled=True. BudgetConfig(max_runs_per_day=10) alone tracks nothing.
  • JournalConfig() vs ProcessConfig(). A JournalConfig you create journals at "checkpoint" level, but a ProcessConfig without one has no journal.
  • Round-tripping secrets. to_dict() masks literal secrets; from_dict() of that dict raises until you put the real values (or ${VAR} references) back.
  • conversation_max_messages=0. It means unlimited, not disabled. Use conversation_history=False to turn short-term memory off.
  • Expecting DEFAULT_PRODUCTION_CONFIG to harden anything. It is the same as the development preset.

docs.title: Agent Context
docs.text:
AgentContext is the context every AgentProcess gives its agent: key-value state with an audit trail, optional long-term memory, a filtered view of the environment, and named file mounts. The state is how an agent keeps facts between runs (progress markers, counters, flags an operator sets): it is shown to the agent at the start of every run, written by the system, triggers, the control API and, if you allow it, the agent itself, and with a journal it survives a crash or a restart.

from promptise.runtime import AgentProcess, ProcessConfig
from promptise.runtime.config import ContextConfig, JournalConfig

process = AgentProcess("pipeline-watch", ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Check the pipeline. Record what you found with update_state.",
    context=ContextConfig(
        initial_state={"pipeline_status": "unknown", "check_count": 0},
        writable_keys=["pipeline_status", "check_count"],
        state_tool=True,                      # the agent gets update_state(key, value)
    ),
    journal=JournalConfig(path=".promptise/journal"),  # state survives restarts
))
await process.start()

process.context.put("pipeline_status", "degraded", source="operator")
print(process.context.state_snapshot())  # {'pipeline_status': 'degraded', 'check_count': 0}

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Four layers share one object:

Layer Purpose Example State Key-value store with an audit trail, shown to the agent every run ctx.get("status"), ctx.put("status", "ok") Memory Semantic long-term memory through a MemoryProvider await ctx.search_memory("error rate") Environment Filtered snapshot of os.environ ctx.env returns {"AGENT_MODE": "production"} Files Logical name to filesystem path mapping ctx.files returns {"data": "/mnt/data"}

The state works like a blackboard: several writers (initial config, triggers, operators over the API, the agent through its state tool) read and write the same keys, and every write is recorded as a StateEntry with a timestamp and a source.

You can also use AgentContext on its own:

from promptise.runtime.context import AgentContext

ctx = AgentContext(
    initial_state={"pipeline_status": "healthy", "check_count": 0},
    writable_keys=["pipeline_status", "check_count"],
    env_prefix="AGENT_",
    file_mounts={"data": "/mnt/data", "config": "/etc/agent"},
)

ctx.put("check_count", 1)
assert ctx.get("check_count") == 1
assert len(ctx.state_history("check_count")) == 2  # initial + put

docs.title: Reading and writing
docs.text:
status = ctx.get("pipeline_status")           # "healthy"
missing = ctx.get("nonexistent", "fallback")  # "fallback"

ctx.put("pipeline_status", "degraded", source="cron-trigger")

# Several keys, all or nothing
written = ctx.update({"pipeline_status": "ok", "check_count": 2}, source="operator")
# ["pipeline_status", "check_count"]

snapshot = ctx.state_snapshot()   # shallow copy of the current state
keys = ctx.state_keys()           # ["pipeline_status", "check_count"]
ctx.clear_state()                 # remove all state and history

put() records the write with source (default "agent"). update() checks every key before writing any: if one is not writable, it raises KeyError naming all of them and writes nothing.

docs.title: Writable keys
docs.text:
When writable_keys is set, put() and update() only accept those keys, whoever writes (agent, API or trigger code):

ctx = AgentContext(
    initial_state={"status": "ok", "owner": "ops"},
    writable_keys=["status"],
)

ctx.put("status", "error")    # works
try:
    ctx.put("owner", "me")
except KeyError as exc:
    print(exc)                # "Key 'owner' is not writable. Allowed: ['status']"
ctx.can_write("owner")        # False
ctx.denied_keys(["status", "owner"])  # ["owner"]

None or an empty list (the default) means every key is writable. initial_state and recovered state are loaded without the check. ctx.writable_keys returns the sorted list, or None when all keys are writable.

docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
Every write appends a StateEntry to the key's history:

for entry in ctx.state_history("check_count"):
    print(entry.value, entry.source, entry.timestamp)
Field Type Description key str The key that was written value Any A copy of the value stored (later in-place changes don't rewrite it) timestamp float Unix time of the write source str Who wrote it: "system" (initial state), "agent" (the state tool, and put()'s default), "api" (PATCH /context), "recovery" (restored from the journal), or any label you pass

StateEntry.to_dict() / StateEntry.from_dict() serialize an entry; to_dict() is also the data of the context_update journal entry.

docs.title: How the agent sees the state
docs.text:
Before every run, when the state is not empty, the process adds it to the prompt as a system message, first in the list (before the budget, mission and inbox blocks and the conversation history):

[Context State] {'pipeline_status': 'degraded', 'check_count': 2}

The whole state is shown on every run, so keep values short and JSON-friendly.

docs.title: Letting the agent write state
docs.text:
The agent has no way to write state unless you give it one. ContextConfig(state_tool=True) adds an update_state(key, value) tool to the agent, in any execution mode:

ContextConfig(
    initial_state={"tables_done": 0},
    writable_keys=["tables_done", "last_table"],
    state_tool=True,
)
  • The tool writes through put() with source "agent", so it obeys writable_keys; with writable keys set, the key is offered to the model as a fixed list of choices.
  • A value must be JSON (string, number, boolean, list or object) and at most 10,000 characters as JSON. Without writable_keys, the state may hold at most 100 keys; a write that adds a key beyond that is refused.
  • Refusals come back to the model as text starting with Error: (for example the allowed keys), never as exceptions.
  • Writes are journaled like any other.

state_tool is off by default. Turn it on together with writable_keys: without them the agent can write any key, including ones your code relies on.

To give your own agent the same tool, use create_state_tools(context, source="agent", max_value_chars=10_000, max_keys=100) from promptise.runtime.context; it returns [update_state].

docs.title: Changing state over the API
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:9100/api/v1/processes/pipeline-watch/context -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# {"state": {"pipeline_status": "degraded", "check_count": 2},
#  "writable_keys": ["check_count", "pipeline_status"], "all_keys_writable": false}

curl -X PATCH http://localhost:9100/api/v1/processes/pipeline-watch/context \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"state": {"pipeline_status": "ok"}}'
# {"name": "pipeline-watch", "updated_keys": ["pipeline_status"]}

PATCH /context is atomic: if any key is not writable, the answer is 403 WRITE_DENIED naming the denied keys and the allowed ones, and nothing is written. The writes are recorded with source "api" and journaled. GET /context returns writable_keys: [] with all_keys_writable: true when every key is writable. The Python client has get_context(name) and update_context(name, state).

docs.title: Persistence and recovery
docs.text:
Without a journal, the state lives in memory. It survives stop() / start() and restart_process() of the same process object, but a new process object (a new Python process, a redeploy) starts from initial_state.

With a journal (ProcessConfig.journal, off by default):

  1. Every write is journaled as a context_update entry with the StateEntry data (key, value, timestamp, source), including writes from the state tool and the API.
  2. Checkpoints with the whole state are written after every run, on stop() and after a rewind.
  3. Recovery on start. With JournalConfig.recover_on_start=True (the default), the first start() of a process object restores the state of the last checkpoint for its name plus the context_update entries written after it (or those entries alone when there is no checkpoint yet). Recovered keys replace the same keys of initial_state; other initial keys stay. Recovered values get a history entry with source "recovery".
process = AgentProcess("pipeline-watch", config)  # same name and journal path as before
await process.start()
print(process.recovered)
# {'lifecycle_state': 'stopped', 'entries_replayed': 1, 'context_keys': ['check_count', 'pipeline_status'],
#  'mission_restored': False, 'budget_restored': False, 'conversation_messages': 6, 'invocation_count': 3}

process.recovered is None when nothing was restored; the restore is also journaled as a recovered entry. Set recover_on_start=False to always start fresh. To go back to an earlier state, use rewind.

docs.title: Secret values in state
docs.text: With secret scoping on, the journal redacts secret values: a context_update entry or checkpoint never holds one in plain text, it holds [REDACTED]. A recovered value therefore comes back as [REDACTED], not as the secret. The live state is not redacted: the agent's prompt and GET /context show the value as stored. Keep secrets out of the state; read them with the secret scope where they are needed.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
ProcessConfig.context is a ContextConfig:

Field Default Description initial_state {} State the process starts with writable_keys [] Keys put() / update() may write; empty means all state_tool False Give the agent the update_state(key, value) tool env_prefix "AGENT_" Only environment variables with this prefix appear in ctx.env. An empty prefix is refused (it would expose the whole environment) file_mounts {} Logical name to filesystem path memory_provider None "in_memory", "chroma" or "mem0" for long-term memory memory_max 5 Memories injected per run memory_min_score 0.0 Minimum relevance score for injected memories memory_timeout 5.0 Seconds to wait for a memory search or auto-store write memory_auto_store False Store each exchange in long-term memory memory_collection "agent_memory" ChromaDB collection memory_persist_directory None ChromaDB persist directory memory_user_id "default" Mem0 user scope conversation_max_messages 100 Conversation buffer size (0 = unlimited); see Conversation conversation_history True False turns short-term conversation memory off conversation_clear_on_stop False Clear the conversation on stop()

Unknown keys are ignored with a FutureWarning.

In a .agent manifest, world: sets initial_state and the context: block takes any ContextConfig field:

name: pipeline-watch
model: openai:gpt-5-mini
instructions: Check the pipeline and record its status.
world:
  pipeline_status: unknown
  check_count: 0
context:
  writable_keys: [pipeline_status, check_count]
  state_tool: true
journal:
  level: checkpoint

Setting initial state both in world: and in context: initial_state is an error, as is an unknown context: key.

docs.title: Memory integration
docs.text:
When memory_provider is set, the agent gets semantic long-term memory: relevant memories are injected into each run, and memory_auto_store stores each exchange.

results = await ctx.search_memory("error rate", limit=3, min_score=0.5)
for r in results:
    print(f"[{r.memory_id}] score={r.score:.2f}: {r.content}")

memory_id = await ctx.add_memory("Pipeline had 5% error rate at 07:30", metadata={"severity": "warning"})
deleted = await ctx.delete_memory(memory_id)  # True if found and deleted

Without a provider, search_memory returns [], add_memory returns None and delete_memory returns False.

The provider stays open across stop() / start() and restarts of the process object. close() (and AgentRuntime.remove_process()) closes it; a later start() opens a new one, and an in_memory provider then starts empty. Use chroma with memory_persist_directory, or mem0, for memories that outlive the Python process.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
ctx.env is a filtered snapshot of os.environ with only the variables whose name starts with env_prefix. The prefix is not stripped:

ctx = AgentContext(env_prefix="AGENT_")
ctx.env  # {"AGENT_MODE": "production"}

docs.title: File mounts
docs.text:
ctx = AgentContext(file_mounts={"data": "/mnt/data", "config": "/etc/agent"})
ctx.files  # {"data": "/mnt/data", "config": "/etc/agent"}

The context does no file I/O itself; it provides the mapping for agents and tools.

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
snapshot = ctx.to_dict()
restored = AgentContext.from_dict(snapshot, memory_provider=my_provider)

The dict holds the state, the full history, the writable keys, the environment prefix and the file mounts. The memory provider is not serialized; pass it again with memory_provider. A process doesn't use these for recovery: it uses its journal (see Persistence and recovery).

docs.title: API summary
docs.text: Method / property Description get(key, default=None) Read a value put(key, value, *, source="agent") Write one key (audited, journaled); KeyError if not writable update(values, *, source="agent") Write several keys, all or nothing; returns the keys written can_write(key) / denied_keys(keys) Check keys against writable_keys writable_keys Sorted writable keys, or None when all are writable restore_state(state, *, source="recovery") Load recovered state: bypasses writable_keys, fires no update hooks add_update_hook(hook) Call hook(entry) on every write (sync, or returning an awaitable); returns a remover await flush_update_hooks() Wait for pending async hooks state_snapshot() Shallow copy of the state state_history(key) StateEntry list for a key state_keys() All keys clear_state() Remove all state and history memory The MemoryProvider, or None await search_memory(query, *, limit=5, min_score=0.0) Search long-term memory await add_memory(content, *, metadata=None) Store a memory await delete_memory(memory_id) Delete a memory env Filtered environment variables files File mount mapping to_dict() / AgentContext.from_dict(data, *, memory_provider=None) Serialize and restore

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• The agent can't write state by default. Without state_tool=True (or your own tool), only your code, triggers and the API write it.
  • state_tool without writable_keys lets the agent write any key. Name the keys it may change.
  • In-place changes bypass the audit trail. ctx.get("items").append(x) changes the stored list, but nothing is recorded or journaled. Write a new value with put().
  • Writes from another thread aren't journaled. put() called outside the process's event loop updates the state but skips the journal hook (with a warning).
  • Secrets in state come back redacted. With secret scoping, a recovered value that contained a secret is [REDACTED], while the live state and GET /context show the plain value.
  • The state is in every prompt. Large values cost tokens on every run; store summaries.
  • A new process object without a journal starts from initial_state. Configure a journal to keep state across redeploys and crashes.

docs.title: Conversation Buffer
docs.text:
ConversationBuffer is an agent process's short-term memory: a rolling window of the last messages exchanged, replayed to the agent on every run so it remembers what it saw and said on earlier runs. Each AgentProcess owns one. It keeps its history across stop() / start() and restarts, can be checkpointed and recovered with a journal, and never stores a secret value in plain text.

from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig
from promptise.runtime.config import ContextConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Triage incoming tickets.",
    context=ContextConfig(
        conversation_max_messages=50,      # keep the last 50 messages
        conversation_clear_on_stop=False,  # default: history survives stop()/start()
    ),
)

On its own:

from promptise.runtime.conversation import ConversationBuffer

buffer = ConversationBuffer(max_messages=50)
buffer.append({"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"})
buffer.append({"role": "assistant", "content": "Hi there!"})

history = buffer.get_messages()
# [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Hi there!"}]

docs.title: How a process uses it
docs.text:
On every run the process:

  1. Puts the buffer's messages into the prompt after the system blocks (context state, budget, mission, inbox) and before the new trigger message.
  2. After the run, appends two messages: the trigger message as the user message and the agent's final reply as the assistant message. Tool calls, tool results and the injected system blocks are not stored.
  3. Drops the oldest messages when the buffer is over conversation_max_messages.
ContextConfig field Default Description conversation_max_messages 100 Messages kept. 0 means unlimited, not off conversation_history True False turns the buffer off: every run sees only its own trigger message conversation_clear_on_stop False Clear the history on stop()

When an append makes the buffer drop old messages, the process fires the pre_compact hook (with the messages about to be dropped) and the post_compact hook. See Runtime Hooks.

docs.title: Lifetime
docs.text:
Event History stop() then start() on the same process object Kept (unless conversation_clear_on_stop=True) restart_process(), POST /restart (a stop, then a start) Kept (unless conversation_clear_on_stop=True) An automatic restart after a failure (restart policy) Kept An instructions change (update_instructions, PATCH /instructions) Kept: the agent is rebuilt with the same history close(), async with process: exit, AgentRuntime.remove_process(), DELETE /processes/{name} Cleared A new process object with the same name and a journal Restored from the last checkpoint (JournalConfig.recover_on_start, default True) A new process object without a journal Starts empty

With a journal, the conversation is part of every checkpoint (written after each run and on stop), and the first start() of a new process object restores it when conversation_history is on. process.recovered["conversation_messages"] says how many messages came back. A rewind can roll the conversation back to an earlier point.

Facts that must outlive all of this belong in long-term memory or in the context state.

docs.title: Secret values are redacted
docs.text:
With secret scoping enabled, both messages are stored with every secret value replaced by [REDACTED]: current values, and values replaced by a rotation or expired. An agent that echoes a secret in its reply doesn't carry it into later prompts, and the conversation in journal checkpoints holds no plain-text secret.

# The agent replied "the token is tok-SECRET-42"; the buffer holds:
{"role": "assistant", "content": "the token is [REDACTED]"}

docs.title: Adding messages
docs.text:
buffer = ConversationBuffer(max_messages=100)

buffer.append({"role": "user", "content": "Check the pipeline status."})
buffer.extend([
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Pipeline is healthy. No anomalies."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What about the error rate?"},
])

docs.title: Reading messages
docs.text:
messages = buffer.get_messages()  # list copy, oldest first
print(len(buffer))                # 3

docs.title: Replacing and clearing
docs.text:
buffer.set_messages(messages)  # replace the whole buffer (oldest dropped if over the limit)
buffer.clear()
assert len(buffer) == 0

docs.title: Turning it off
docs.text:
buffer = ConversationBuffer(max_messages=100, enabled=False)
buffer.append({"role": "user", "content": "Hello"})
assert len(buffer) == 0  # nothing is retained

docs.title: Async-safe operations
docs.text:
When several coroutines use the buffer (a process with concurrency > 1), use the async methods, which hold an internal asyncio.Lock:

snapshot = await buffer.async_snapshot()
await buffer.async_replace([{"role": "user", "content": "Fresh start"}])
await buffer.async_append({"role": "assistant", "content": "Ready."})

The synchronous methods take no lock; use them outside concurrent code (tests, serialization). The buffer is not thread-safe.

docs.title: Automatic eviction
docs.text:
When the buffer exceeds max_messages, the oldest messages are dropped:

buffer = ConversationBuffer(max_messages=3)

for i in range(1, 5):
    buffer.append({"role": "user", "content": f"Message {i}"})  # the 4th evicts Message 1

messages = buffer.get_messages()
assert len(messages) == 3
assert messages[0]["content"] == "Message 2"

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
data = buffer.to_dict()
# {"max_messages": 100, "enabled": True, "messages": [...]}

restored = ConversationBuffer.from_dict(data)

docs.title: API summary
docs.text: Method Sync/Async Description ConversationBuffer(max_messages=100, enabled=True) : max_messages=0 is unlimited; enabled=False retains nothing append(message) Sync Add one message dict extend(messages) Sync Add several message dicts get_messages() Sync All messages as a list copy, oldest first set_messages(messages) Sync Replace the whole buffer clear() Sync Remove all messages async_snapshot() Async Locked copy of all messages async_replace(messages) Async Locked replacement of the whole buffer async_append(message) Async Locked append of one message to_dict() Sync Serialize (max_messages, enabled, messages) ConversationBuffer.from_dict(data) Classmethod Rebuild from to_dict() output __len__() Sync Current message count

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• conversation_max_messages=0 keeps everything. It means unlimited, so the prompt grows with every run. Use conversation_history=False to turn the buffer off.
  • close() clears the history; stop() doesn't. Removing a process from a runtime closes it. To keep the conversation across a redeploy, configure a journal.
  • Each run adds two messages. max_messages=20 holds the last 10 runs, not 20.
  • Eviction is silent unless you hook it. Old messages are dropped without a log line; use the pre_compact hook to summarize or archive them, or store important facts in the context state or long-term memory.
  • Tool results aren't in the history. Only the trigger message and the final reply are kept; a value the agent read from a tool is gone on the next run unless the reply or the state holds it.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Agent Context: state and long-term memory around the conversation
  • Runtime Hooks: pre_compact / post_compact
  • Journal and Rewind Engine: checkpointing, recovery and rolling back the conversation
  • Secret Scoping: the values that are redacted

Learn the concept

  • AI Agent State Between Runs: Context, Keys and Audit: How state, conversation and memory differ, and what survives a restart.
  • Durable AI Agents: Crash Recovery and Safe Resume: Checkpoints that bring the conversation back after a crash.

docs.title: Runtime Dashboard
docs.text:
RuntimeDashboard is a full-screen terminal UI for watching a running AgentRuntime: process states and counters, configured triggers, each process's context state, and captured log output, refreshed several times a second. It is built on rich and is meant for local development and demos; for remote or scripted control use the Orchestration API or the CLI.

promptise runtime start agents/ --dashboard

from promptise.runtime import RuntimeDashboard, RuntimeDashboardState, RuntimeDataCollector

state = RuntimeDashboardState(runtime_name="my-runtime", manifest_names=["data-watcher"])
collector = RuntimeDataCollector(runtime, state, interval=0.5)  # runtime: your AgentRuntime
collector.start()

dashboard = RuntimeDashboard(state, runtime=runtime)
dashboard.start()   # takes over the terminal
...
dashboard.stop()    # restores the terminal
collector.stop()

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The dashboard has three parts:

  1. RuntimeDashboardState: the data the dashboard shows: process, trigger and context snapshots, plus ring buffers for invocations, events, commands and journal entries.
  2. RuntimeDataCollector: a background thread that reads the AgentRuntime every interval seconds and refreshes the process, trigger and context snapshots in the state. It also registers task_created / task_completed hooks on every process (for the event and run panels and the trigger fire counts) and reads each process's journal for the Logs tab.
  3. RuntimeDashboard: the renderer. It draws the state with rich.Live in the terminal's alternate screen, reads keys in a background thread, and captures Python log output for the Logs tab.

The collector fills every panel. Trigger events and finished runs arrive through the hooks it registers (removed again by collector.stop()); journal entries are read from each process's journal every fourth snapshot, on the runtime's event loop. Context values are shown with secret values [REDACTED], as in the journal. Create the collector on the runtime's loop (or pass loop=): without a loop the journal panel stays empty. state.record_invocation(), state.record_event() and state.record_journal() remain available to add records of your own.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
Switch tabs with the number keys 1-7, the left and right arrow keys, or Tab.

# Tab What it shows 1 Overview Counters (processes, running, failed, triggers, invocations, errors, throughput, uptime), a table of processes, and recent invocations (from state.invocations) 2 Processes Per process: name, state, process ID, model, invocations, failures, triggers, queue size, concurrency, heartbeat interval, uptime. On a narrow terminal the least important columns are left out first (heartbeat, process ID, concurrency, uptime...); name, state and model always show 3 Triggers Every config trigger: process, type, a configuration summary (cron expression, webhook port and path, watched path, event type or topic), fire count and last fire time (counted from task_created) 4 Context Per process: each state key, its value (secret values redacted, cut at 50 characters), whether it is writable and how many writes it has had, plus the number of environment variables, file mounts and whether memory is on 5 Logs Captured Python log records (runtime logs) and state.journal_entries, each in its own panel with a share of the height (newest first) 6 Events state.events (trigger events, with a one-line payload preview) and state.invocations (invocation results) 7 Commands The command line and the history of commands run

Process states are color-coded:

State Color running Bold green starting Yellow created Dim stopped Red failed Bold red suspended Yellow stopping Yellow awaiting Cyan

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Press : or / to type a command (the Commands tab opens), Enter to run it, Esc to cancel, Backspace to delete.

Command What it does help List the commands list Names of the processes in the dashboard state status Process count and how many are running status <name> One process's state, invocations and queue size start <name>, stop <name>, restart <name>, suspend <name>, resume <name> Lifecycle commands, run on the runtime's event loop (restart is AgentRuntime.restart_process()) inject <name> [payload_json] Inject a manual trigger event with the payload (non-JSON text becomes {"raw": "..."})

Lifecycle and inject commands are submitted to the runtime's event loop, which dashboard.start() captures, so call start() from that loop (as promptise runtime start --dashboard does). The command history shows Stopping <name>... at once; if the action then fails, a (result) entry with the error follows. Without a loop (or without runtime=), the command answers with an error and nothing runs.

docs.title: Via the CLI
docs.text:
# One manifest
promptise runtime start agents/watcher.agent --dashboard

# A directory of manifests
promptise runtime start agents/ --dashboard

The dashboard's title is the manifest file or directory name. Everything else promptise runtime start does still happens: the control API is served on loopback and the runtime is recorded, so promptise runtime status and promptise runtime stop work from another terminal. Press Ctrl+C to stop all processes and leave the dashboard. --dashboard can't be combined with --detach: the dashboard needs a terminal.

docs.title: Via Python
docs.text:
import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import (
    AgentRuntime,
    ProcessConfig,
    RuntimeDashboard,
    RuntimeDashboardState,
    RuntimeDataCollector,
    TriggerConfig,
)


async def main():
    runtime = AgentRuntime()
    await runtime.add_process("watcher", ProcessConfig(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions="Monitor pipelines.",
        triggers=[TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *")],
    ))

    state = RuntimeDashboardState(runtime_name="production", manifest_names=["watcher"])
    collector = RuntimeDataCollector(runtime, state, interval=0.5)
    dashboard = RuntimeDashboard(state, runtime=runtime)

    collector.start()
    dashboard.start()
    try:
        await runtime.run_forever()  # starts all processes; returns on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM
    finally:
        dashboard.stop()
        collector.stop()


asyncio.run(main())

runtime.run_forever() starts every process and, on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM, stops and closes them before it returns.

docs.title: Data types
docs.text: All of these are dataclasses in promptise.runtime._dashboard; the three main classes are also exported from promptise.runtime.

docs.title: RuntimeDashboardState
docs.text:
Field Default Description runtime_name "Agent Runtime" Title shown in the header started_at now Unix time the dashboard state was created (uptime) processes {} ProcessSnapshot per process name triggers [] TriggerInfo list contexts {} ContextSnapshot per process name invocations ring buffer (200) InvocationLog records events ring buffer (200) EventLog records commands ring buffer (100) CommandResult records journal_entries ring buffer (500) Journal entry dicts total_invocations, total_errors, total_events 0 Counters updated by the record_* methods manifest_names [] Names of the loaded manifests

Methods: record_invocation(log) (also counts errors), record_event(event), record_command(result), record_journal(entry).

docs.title: ProcessSnapshot
docs.text: Field Type Description name str Process name process_id str Unique process ID state str Current lifecycle state model str LLM model identifier invocation_count int Total invocations consecutive_failures int Current failure streak trigger_count int Number of running config triggers queue_size int Pending events in the queue uptime_seconds float \| None Time since the process started; None while it is not up (created, stopped, failed) concurrency int Max concurrent invocations heartbeat_interval float Heartbeat period

docs.title: TriggerInfo
docs.text: Field Type Description process_name str Owning process trigger_id str The trigger's stable ID, the same as the API's (for example cron-2721f2b845) trigger_type str cron, webhook, file_watch, event, message, ... config_summary str Short configuration text, or - fire_count int Times fired (default 0) last_fired float \| None Last fire time (default None)

docs.title: ContextSnapshot
docs.text: Field Type Description process_name str Owning process state dict The context state writable_keys list[str] \| None Writable keys, None when all are writable env_count int Environment variables exposed to the context file_mount_count int File mounts has_memory bool Whether a memory provider is set history_counts dict[str, int] Writes per key

docs.title: Log records
docs.text: Class Fields InvocationLog timestamp, process_name, trigger_type, trigger_id, success, duration_ms, error EventLog timestamp, process_name, trigger_type, trigger_id, event_id, payload_summary CommandResult timestamp, command, result, success

docs.title: RuntimeDataCollector
docs.text:
collector = RuntimeDataCollector(runtime, state, interval=0.5)
collector.start()   # daemon thread
collector.stop()    # ends the loop after the current sleep

Every interval seconds (default 0.5) it calls status() on each process of runtime.processes, reads its config and context, rebuilds the trigger list from the config triggers (with their stable IDs and the fire counts its hooks counted), and drops snapshots of processes that are no longer in the runtime. On each new process it registers a task_created and a task_completed hook (priority -1000, tag promptise-dashboard); every fourth snapshot it reads the newest 100 journal entries of each process. stop() ends the loop after the current sleep and removes the hooks.

docs.title: API summary
docs.text: Class Description RuntimeDashboardState Data container for everything the dashboard shows RuntimeDataCollector(runtime, state, interval=0.5, loop=None) Background thread that refreshes the snapshots from the runtime, registers the event/run hooks and reads the journals. loop defaults to the running loop when it is created RuntimeDashboard(state, runtime=None) Terminal renderer: start() (call it on the runtime's loop) takes over the terminal, stop() restores it. runtime is used by the commands ProcessSnapshot, TriggerInfo, ContextSnapshot Snapshots for display InvocationLog, EventLog, CommandResult Records for the ring buffers

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• The dashboard takes over the terminal. It draws in the alternate screen and reads keys directly; you can't use the same terminal for other commands. Always call dashboard.stop() (in a finally) so the terminal is restored.
  • Log output moves into the Logs tab. While the dashboard runs, the root logger is set to DEBUG and existing console handlers of the root, promptise.runtime, httpx, uvicorn and asyncio loggers are muted; stop() restores them.
  • An empty journal panel. The collector reads the journal on the runtime's event loop; create it there (or pass loop=), and give the process a journal.
  • Starting the dashboard off the runtime's loop. Commands then can't run and the journal panel stays empty; create the collector and call dashboard.start() inside the coroutine that runs the runtime.
  • Shorter intervals cost more. The collector polls every process each interval; 2.0 is plenty for a quiet runtime.
  • Not with --detach. The dashboard needs a foreground terminal.

docs.text:

  • Runtime Manager: the AgentRuntime the dashboard watches
  • Orchestration API: control the runtime while you watch it
  • Agent Context: what the Context tab shows

Learn the concept

  • Run Multiple AI Agents: One Runtime, Many Processes: Run and watch several agent processes in one runtime.
  • AI Agent Health Monitoring: Catch Silent Failures: What to watch in a running agent besides its state.

docs.title: Runtime Lifecycle Hooks
docs.text:
Runtime hooks let you react to what happens to an agent process (a session starting, a prompt about to reach the model, a tool approval being denied, a trigger event entering or leaving the queue) without changing the agent. Use them to audit prompts, add standing context, notify a chat channel, or refuse an action by policy. Every AgentProcess dispatches the 13 lifecycle events itself; you only register the hooks.

from promptise.runtime import (
    AgentProcess, HookBlocked, HookConfig, HookContext, HookEvent, ProcessConfig,
)

async def no_passwords(ctx: HookContext) -> None:
    if "password" in ctx.data["prompt"].lower():
        raise HookBlocked("prompts may not ask for passwords")

async def add_house_rules(ctx: HookContext) -> None:
    ctx.set("prompt", ctx.data["prompt"] + "\n\nAnswer in one sentence.")

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="You are a helpful assistant.",
    hooks=[
        HookConfig(event="user_prompt_submit", callback=no_passwords, priority=10),
        HookConfig(event="user_prompt_submit", callback=add_house_rules),
        HookConfig(event="task_completed", command=["./hooks/log-task.sh"], timeout=5),
    ],
)

process = AgentProcess("helper", config)

@process.hooks.on(HookEvent.SESSION_START)
async def started(ctx: HookContext) -> None:
    print("session started", ctx.data)   # {'restart': False, 'recovered': None}

await process.start()

A trigger event whose prompt mentions a password is refused before any budget is counted: it lands in process.dead_letters with reason "blocked by hook" and error "prompts may not ask for passwords". Every other prompt gets the extra sentence. After each event, ./hooks/log-task.sh receives the task_completed event as JSON on stdin.

Runtime hooks are not the reasoning graph hooks (Hook, LoggingHook, TimingHook): those run for every node and tool call inside one agent run. Runtime hooks fire at process-level moments, around runs.

docs.title: Registering hooks
docs.text:
Where How Accepts ProcessConfig.hooks A list of HookConfig Async callbacks and external commands Code process.hooks.on(event) decorator or process.hooks.register(event, fn) Async callbacks (or ShellHook(...).callback) Manifest The hooks: section of a .agent file External commands only Shared manager AgentRuntime(hooks=manager) or AgentProcess(..., hooks=manager) One HookManager whose hooks fire for every process

process.hooks is the process's own HookManager. It holds the hooks from config.hooks and whatever you register in code. A shared manager runs after the process's own hooks; ctx.process_id tells you which process dispatched the event.

A process spawned by an open-mode agent (spawn_process) inherits its parent's hooks manager (and whatever the parent inherited): they run for the child after the child's own hooks and before the shared manager, with ctx.process_id naming the child. So a permission_request or user_prompt_submit hook on the parent governs every process it spawns.

from promptise.runtime import AgentRuntime, HookEvent, HookManager

shared = HookManager()

@shared.on(HookEvent.SESSION_START)
async def announce(ctx):
    print(f"{ctx.process_id} is running")

runtime = AgentRuntime(hooks=shared)   # fires for every process the runtime starts

A callback must be an async function, or an object with an async __call__, that takes one HookContext. A sync function raises TypeError at registration. The event can be a HookEvent member or its value ("session_start"); an unknown value raises ValueError listing the valid ones.

docs.title: HookConfig
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description event str required A HookEvent value, for example "user_prompt_submit" command str \| list[str] \| None None External program and arguments, run as a ShellHook. A string is split like a terminal would (shlex.split); no shell runs it callback async callable None Python hook (code only; not serialized) timeout float \| None None Seconds the hook may run (> 0, at most 3600). Unset: 5 for a command, 30 for a callback priority int 0 Higher runs first once bool False Run on the first matching event only, then deregister tag str \| None None Group name for remove_by_tag() fail_closed bool False An error or timeout of this hook blocks the action (blockable events only) cwd str \| None None Working directory of the command env dict[str, SecretStr] {} Extra environment variables for the command. ${VAR} references are resolved from the host environment each time the hook runs; literal values are masked in JSON dumps env_passthrough list[str] [] Host environment variables passed through to the command max_output_bytes int 65536 Largest stdout accepted from the command (at most 10 MiB)

Set exactly one of command or callback; both or neither raises a validation error. Unknown keys are rejected.

docs.title: In a manifest
docs.text:
hooks:
  - event: user_prompt_submit
    command: ["./hooks/audit.sh"]
    timeout: 5
    fail_closed: true
  - event: task_completed
    command: "./hooks/notify.sh --channel ops"
    env_passthrough: [SLACK_TOKEN]

Each entry is a HookConfig with a command. A manifest resolves ${VAR} references when it is loaded, except in the secrets: section and in hook env: values: those stay ${VAR} references in the loaded config and are resolved each time the hook runs. Loading still checks that every variable they name is set, so env: {SLACK_TOKEN: ${SLACK_TOKEN}} needs the variable at load time but never puts its value into the loaded config. env_passthrough hands a host variable to the program as it is. A callback key in a manifest is an error (hooks[0]: a manifest hook runs a 'command'; Python callbacks are registered in code (process.hooks)). The old top-level entrypoint key is not read by the runtime; a manifest that sets it loads with a FutureWarning.

docs.title: Deploying command hooks over the control API
docs.text: A command hook runs a program on the runtime's host. The Orchestration API therefore refuses a POST /api/v1/processes whose config has a command hook (or a stdio MCP server, or open-mode tool creation) with 403 COMMANDS_NOT_ALLOWED, unless the API was created with OrchestrationAPI(..., allow_command_deploys=True) (promptise runtime start --allow-command-deploys). Anyone with the API token could otherwise run any command as the runtime's user. Callback hooks can't be sent over HTTP at all, and processes you load from manifests on the host are not checked.

docs.title: The 13 lifecycle events
docs.text:
ctx.data holds the keys listed for each event. Secret values (from secret scoping) are redacted before any hook sees them.

Event Fires when ctx.data Blockable: what a block does SESSION_START The process entered RUNNING (every start(), including automatic restarts) restart (bool), recovered (what journal recovery restored, or None) No SESSION_END The process is about to stop, before teardown: an explicit stop() or a restart reason ("stop" or "restart"), invocation_count No (a stop always proceeds) USER_PROMPT_SUBMIT A trigger event's prompt is about to be sent to the model prompt, event_id, trigger_id, trigger_type Yes: the run is skipped and the event dead-lettered ("blocked by hook"), before any budget is counted. A hook may also replace prompt PERMISSION_REQUEST A tool that needs approval (ProcessConfig.approval) is about to be sent to the approval handler tool_name, arguments (the reviewer's redacted copy), request_id Yes: the call is denied without asking the handler PERMISSION_DENIED Something the agent was about to do was refused kind, tool_name, request_id, reason, decided_by, plus per-kind keys (below) No SUBAGENT_START An open-mode agent is about to spawn a process (spawn_process meta-tool) process_name, execution_mode, trigger_count Yes: the spawn is refused SUBAGENT_STOP A process this one spawned stopped or failed process_name, state No PRE_COMPACT The conversation buffer is about to drop its oldest messages (context.conversation_max_messages) buffer_size, max_messages, dropping (the messages that will be dropped) No POST_COMPACT After that compaction buffer_size, dropped No FILE_CHANGED A file-watch trigger reported a change The event payload (path, event_type, ...), trigger_id, event_id Yes: the event is dropped and counted as filtered CONFIG_CHANGE The process's effective configuration changed source ("agent" or "operator"), change, plus details Only for source="agent": the agent's change is not applied. Operator changes always apply TASK_CREATED A trigger event is about to be queued (from a trigger or inject()) event_id, trigger_id, trigger_type, payload_summary (the payload as one line of JSON, at most 120 characters, secrets redacted) Yes: the event is dead-lettered ("blocked by hook") instead of queued TASK_COMPLETED A queued event finished event_id, trigger_id, trigger_type, outcome, duration_ms, error No

PERMISSION_DENIED covers three kinds of refusal:

kind What refused it Extra data "approval" The approval handler, a classifier rule, the gate, or a permission_request hook decided_by as in the ApprovalDecision "budget" A budget limit refused a tool call (tool_name set) or a run (max_runs_per_day; tool_name is None) decided_by="budget", limit_name, limit_value, current_value; arguments (redacted) for a refused tool call, event_id for a refused run "guardrail" The payload scan (decided_by="payload_scan") or the guardrail scanner (decided_by="guardrail") refused a trigger event's run tool_name is None; event_id, trigger_type

CONFIG_CHANGE names the change in change: "instructions", "tool", "mcp_server", "trigger_added", "trigger_removed", "budget", "health", "mission", "rollback" or "rewind".

TASK_COMPLETED's outcome is "success", "retrying", "failed", "blocked", "dead_lettered" or "refused" (the run did not start: max_runs_per_day was reached; the event is dead-lettered with reason "budget: max_runs_per_day"). The event is no longer the worker's when the hook runs: a stop() that arrives while a task_completed hook is still running doesn't dead-letter an event whose run has finished.

HookEvent values are the lowercase names (HookEvent.USER_PROMPT_SUBMIT.value == "user_prompt_submit"). BLOCKABLE_EVENTS is the frozenset of the six blockable events.

docs.title: HookContext
docs.text:
Every callback receives a single HookContext:

Field Type Description event HookEvent The event that fired process_id str The dispatching process's name timestamp datetime UTC time of the dispatch data dict[str, Any] The event payload (a copy; hooks may change it) metadata dict[str, Any] process_name and process_id (the process's UUID)

ctx.get(key, default) and ctx.set(key, value) are shorthands for ctx.data.

docs.title: Blocking, data and errors
docs.text:
Blocking. Raise HookBlocked(reason) to refuse the action. The remaining hooks for that dispatch don't run. Only the six blockable events can be refused; a block of any other event is logged as a warning and ignored.

Returned data. Hooks run one after another on the same ctx.data, so a later hook sees what an earlier one changed. The process reads one value back: the prompt of USER_PROMPT_SUBMIT. The hook sees the prompt with secrets redacted; only a prompt that a hook actually changed replaces the original. Changes to data of other events are not used.

Order. Hooks run by priority (highest first; ties in registration order). The process's own hooks run first, then those inherited from the process that spawned it, then the shared manager's. A once=True hook is removed before it runs, so it runs at most once even when dispatches overlap.

Timeouts. A hook that runs longer than its timeout is cancelled and recorded as an error. The manager an AgentProcess creates has a default timeout of 30 seconds; a standalone HookManager() has none unless you pass HookManager(default_timeout=...). A command hook's program is killed at its own timeout; the manager allows 5 seconds more as a backstop.

Errors. An exception other than HookBlocked never reaches the process: it is logged and recorded in DispatchResult.errors, and the next hook runs. A hook with fail_closed=True turns its error or timeout into a block (reason starts with "hook failed (fail_closed)"), which is what you want for a hook that enforces a policy. On a non-blockable event, fail_closed has no effect.

HookManager.dispatch() returns a DispatchResult when you dispatch yourself:

Field Description fired Number of hooks that ran blocked True if a hook raised HookBlocked (or a fail_closed hook failed) reason The block reason errors (hook_id, exception) pairs for hooks that raised or timed out data The payload after the hooks ran

docs.title: Managing registrations
docs.text:
hook_id = process.hooks.register(HookEvent.SESSION_END, notify, tag="ops")
await process.hooks.remove(hook_id)          # True if it was registered
await process.hooks.remove_by_tag("ops")     # number removed
process.hooks.registered(HookEvent.SESSION_END)  # hook IDs
process.hooks.clear()                         # everything (or clear(event))

process.status()["hook_count"] reports how many hooks the process's own manager holds.

docs.title: HookManager reference
docs.text:
HookManager(*, default_timeout=None) holds hook registrations and dispatches events. default_timeout (seconds) applies to every hook registered without its own timeout; None means no limit. The manager a process creates for process.hooks uses 30 seconds.

Method Description on(event, *, once=False, priority=0, tag=None, timeout=None, fail_closed=False) Decorator form of register(); returns the function unchanged register(event, callback, *, once=False, priority=0, tag=None, timeout=None, fail_closed=False) Registers an async callback; returns its hook ID. event is a HookEvent or its value await remove(hook_id) Removes one hook; True if it was registered await remove_by_tag(tag) Removes every hook with that tag; returns how many clear(event=None) Removes all hooks, or those of one event registered(event=None) Hook IDs, of all events or one has_hooks(event) Whether any hook is registered for the event await dispatch(event, *, process_id="", data=None, metadata=None) Runs the event's hooks and returns a DispatchResult

HookCallable is the type of a callback: Callable[[HookContext], Awaitable[None]]. Use it to type your own hook functions or helpers that return one:

from promptise.runtime import HookCallable, HookContext, HookEvent, HookManager


def make_logger(prefix: str) -> HookCallable:
    async def log(ctx: HookContext) -> None:
        print(prefix, ctx.event.value, ctx.process_id)
    return log


manager = HookManager(default_timeout=10)
manager.register(HookEvent.SESSION_START, make_logger("[ops]"), tag="ops")
result = await manager.dispatch(HookEvent.SESSION_START, process_id="demo")
print(result.fired, result.blocked)  # 1 False

docs.title: ShellHook: external commands
docs.text:
A command hook (HookConfig(command=...) or a manifest entry) runs as a ShellHook. You can also build one in code and register its callback:

from promptise.runtime import HookEvent, ShellHook

hook = ShellHook(command=["/opt/hooks/audit_prompt.sh"], timeout=5.0)
process.hooks.register(HookEvent.USER_PROMPT_SUBMIT, hook.callback, fail_closed=True)

The program receives the event as JSON on stdin:

{
  "event": "user_prompt_submit",
  "process_id": "support-bot",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-19T10:30:00+00:00",
  "data": {"prompt": "...", "event_id": "...", "trigger_id": "...", "trigger_type": "webhook"},
  "metadata": {"process_name": "support-bot", "process_id": "63712925-..."}
}

It may write one JSON object to stdout (all keys optional):

{
  "block": false,
  "reason": "",
  "data": {"prompt": "REWRITTEN"},
  "log": "anything"
}
Result Meaning Exit 0, empty stdout Success, nothing changed Exit 0, a JSON object data (an object) replaces the event data; "block": true refuses the action with reason; log is logged at debug level Non-zero exit Hook error (the message includes the exit code and up to 500 characters of stderr) Timeout The program is killed; hook error More than max_output_bytes on stdout The program is killed; hook error stdout that isn't a JSON object, or data that isn't an object Hook error

A hook error is logged and ignored, or blocks the action when the hook is fail_closed. Blocking is done with {"block": true}, not with an exit code.

No shell. The command runs directly: a list is used as is, a string is split with shlex.split (quotes work as in a terminal), and the executable is looked up on PATH. The event never appears on the command line. Only a ShellHook(shell=True) built in code runs its command string through /bin/sh -c; a manifest or HookConfig can't.

Minimal environment. The program does not inherit the host environment, so API keys and tokens in it don't reach hook programs. It gets:

  • these host variables, when they are set: PATH, HOME, USER, LOGNAME, SHELL, LANG, LANGUAGE, LC_ALL, LC_CTYPE, LC_MESSAGES, TZ, TMPDIR, TEMP, TMP, TERM, and on Windows SYSTEMROOT, SYSTEMDRIVE, WINDIR, COMSPEC, PATHEXT, USERPROFILE, APPDATA, LOCALAPPDATA, PROGRAMDATA, PROGRAMFILES (SAFE_ENV_VARS);
  • the host variables named in env_passthrough;
  • the values in env (${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} resolved when the hook runs);
  • PROMPTISE_HOOK_EVENT (the event value) and PROMPTISE_PROCESS (the process name).

ShellHook(inherit_env=True) (code only) passes the whole host environment instead.

ShellHook attribute Default Description command required List of program and arguments, or a string split with shlex.split timeout 5.0 Seconds before the program is killed cwd None Working directory env None Extra variables (values may be ${VAR} references) shell False Run a command string through the shell (code only) encoding "utf-8" stdin/stdout encoding inherit_env False Pass the whole host environment env_passthrough [] Host variables to pass through max_output_bytes 65536 Largest stdout accepted

ShellHook.run(ctx) runs the program and returns a ShellHookResult (block, reason, data, log, raw) without applying it, which is handy in tests.

Unless cwd is set, the program starts without fork() (CPython's posix_spawn path). That matters on macOS: a forked child of a multithreaded process that has used system frameworks (any httpx client does) can die with SIGSEGV before exec (exited -11). Prefer an absolute script path over cwd when you can.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Awaiting the process from its own hook. A hook must not await process.stop(), start() or rewind() of the process that dispatched it; that waits on itself. Schedule it with asyncio.create_task(process.stop()).
  • Expecting a block on an informational event. HookBlocked from SESSION_END, TASK_COMPLETED or PERMISSION_DENIED is ignored (with a warning). Refuse earlier: TASK_CREATED, USER_PROMPT_SUBMIT or PERMISSION_REQUEST.
  • A policy hook that fails open. Without fail_closed=True, a crashed or slow policy hook lets the action through. Set it on every hook that enforces something.
  • A hook script that needs a variable it doesn't get. Hook programs get a minimal environment. Name what they need in env_passthrough, or pass it through env with a ${VAR} reference.
  • A sync callback. def hook(ctx) raises TypeError at registration; use async def.
  • Deploying a command hook over the API. It answers 403 COMMANDS_NOT_ALLOWED unless the API allows command deploys; load the process from a manifest on the host, or use a callback hook in code.
  • A slow hook on a hot path. USER_PROMPT_SUBMIT, TASK_CREATED and TASK_COMPLETED run for every event, and the event waits for them. Keep them fast, or hand slow work to a background task.
