docs.title: Process Lifecycle
docs.text:
Every AgentProcess moves through a fixed set of states: created, starting, running, suspended, stopping, stopped and failed. The ProcessLifecycle state machine checks every transition against a transition map, rejects invalid ones with a StateError, and records each change with a timestamp and a reason. Use this page to know what a state means, what moves a process between states, and which event each change emits.

import asyncio

from promptise import CallbackSink, EventNotifier
from promptise.runtime import AgentProcess, ProcessConfig


def on_event(event):
    if event.event_type.startswith("process."):
        print(event.event_type, event.data.get("reason", ""))


async def main():
    notifier = EventNotifier(sinks=[CallbackSink(on_event)])
    process = AgentProcess(
        "watcher",
        ProcessConfig(model="openai:gpt-5-mini"),
        event_notifier=notifier,
    )
    await process.start()    # CREATED -> STARTING -> RUNNING
    await process.suspend()  # RUNNING -> SUSPENDED
    await process.resume()   # SUSPENDED -> RUNNING
    await process.stop()     # RUNNING -> STOPPING -> STOPPED
    print([t.to_state.value for t in process.lifecycle.history])


asyncio.run(main())

process.started
process.suspended manual
process.resumed manual
process.stopped
['starting', 'running', 'suspended', 'running', 'stopping', 'stopped']

docs.title: State diagram
docs.text:
The diagram shows every transition in VALID_TRANSITIONS (promptise.runtime.lifecycle) and nothing else. AWAITING is reserved: it is in the map, but AgentProcess never enters it.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CREATED
    CREATED --> STARTING
    CREATED --> STOPPED
    STARTING --> RUNNING
    STARTING --> STOPPING
    STARTING --> FAILED
    RUNNING --> SUSPENDED
    RUNNING --> STOPPING
    RUNNING --> FAILED
    RUNNING --> AWAITING
    SUSPENDED --> RUNNING
    SUSPENDED --> STOPPING
    SUSPENDED --> FAILED
    STOPPING --> STOPPED
    STOPPING --> FAILED
    STOPPED --> STARTING
    FAILED --> STARTING
    FAILED --> STOPPING
    AWAITING --> RUNNING
    AWAITING --> STOPPING
    AWAITING --> FAILED

docs.title: Valid transitions
docs.text:
From Allowed targets CREATED STARTING, STOPPED STARTING RUNNING, STOPPING, FAILED RUNNING SUSPENDED, STOPPING, FAILED, AWAITING SUSPENDED RUNNING, STOPPING, FAILED STOPPING STOPPED, FAILED STOPPED STARTING FAILED STARTING, STOPPING AWAITING (reserved) RUNNING, STOPPING, FAILED

Any other transition raises StateError. A transition to the current state is invalid too: calling suspend() on a suspended process raises.

docs.title: What each state means
docs.text: State Value Meaning CREATED "created" Constructed, never started. stop() moves it straight to STOPPED without an event. STARTING "starting" start() is running: journal recovery (first start only), secrets, agent build and MCP connections, triggers, workers and heartbeat. Trigger events that arrive wait until the process is RUNNING. RUNNING "running" Processing trigger events. An idle process with nothing to do is still RUNNING. SUSPENDED "suspended" Paused. Triggers keep firing and their events queue in arrival order; a run in flight finishes. See Why a process is suspended. STOPPING "stopping" Teardown in progress: workers cancelled, triggers stopped, queued events dead-lettered, agent and MCP clients closed. STOPPED "stopped" Stopped cleanly. start() can start it again; context state, long-term memory and conversation history are kept. FAILED "failed" max_consecutive_failures events in a row failed, or start() raised. New trigger events are dead-lettered ("process failed") and a webhook answers 503. start() (or an automatic restart) goes to STARTING; stop() goes to STOPPING, then STOPPED. AWAITING "awaiting" Reserved. The value and its transitions are kept for backward compatibility; AgentProcess never enters it.

docs.title: Why a process is suspended
docs.text:
SUSPENDED has several causes. process.suspend_reason (and status()["suspend_reason"]) says which one; it is None when the process is not suspended.

suspend_reason Who suspends How it resumes "manual" process.suspend() (default reason), the control API, the dashboard process.resume() "idle" idle_timeout seconds without a run, with nothing queued or running (checked every heartbeat_interval) By itself, when the next trigger event arrives or you call inject() (the process.resumed reason is "trigger") "budget" Autonomy budget with on_exceeded="pause" or "escalate" process.resume() "health" Behavioral health with on_anomaly="pause" or "escalate" process.resume() "rewind" process.rewind() on a running process, for the duration of the rewind By itself, when the rewind ends

resume() restarts the idle clock, so idle_timeout counts from the resume, and the queued events run in the order they arrived.

docs.title: What moves a process
docs.text:
Transition Caused by Event CREATED → STARTING start() : CREATED → STOPPED stop() before start() none STARTING → RUNNING Startup complete process.started STARTING → FAILED Startup raised (bad MCP server, missing secret, ...). start() re-raises the error; your own start() is not retried process.failed STARTING → STOPPING Allowed by the map. stop() called during start() waits for start() to finish first : RUNNING → SUSPENDED suspend(), idle_timeout, budget, health, rewind process.suspended RUNNING → STOPPING stop(), max_lifetime, budget on_exceeded="stop", health on_anomaly="stop", mission completion : RUNNING → FAILED max_consecutive_failures reached process.failed SUSPENDED → RUNNING resume(), or a trigger event for an idle-suspended process process.resumed SUSPENDED → STOPPING stop() : SUSPENDED → FAILED A run that was in flight when the process was suspended fails and reaches max_consecutive_failures process.failed STOPPING → STOPPED Teardown complete process.stopped (not during a max_lifetime recycle) STOPPED → STARTING start(), AgentRuntime.restart_process(), a max_lifetime recycle : FAILED → STARTING start(), restart_process(), start_all(), an automatic restart process.restarted (automatic restart only, before the attempt) FAILED → STOPPING stop() :

STOPPING → FAILED and the AWAITING transitions are allowed by the map but not used by AgentProcess.

Restarting a FAILED process (by start() or an automatic restart) first tears down what the failed run left: trigger listeners, triggers, heartbeat and agent. Nothing fires twice. See Restart policies for backoff and limits.

docs.title: Lifecycle events
docs.text:
With an event_notifier, the process emits these events. Every event's data holds process_name and process_id plus the keys below; agent_id is the process name, and metadata holds process_name, process_id and model (when the model is a string).

Event Severity When Extra data keys process.started info Entered RUNNING (every start, automatic restarts included) : process.stopped info A stop finished (not for CREATED → STOPPED) : process.failed critical Entered FAILED reason, error (the real error, "Type: message", at most 500 characters) process.restarted warning An automatic restart attempt begins (after its backoff), or a max_lifetime recycle reason, attempt (None for a recycle), max_restarts process.restart_exhausted critical A failure with max_restarts already used up; the process stays FAILED reason, restarts, max_restarts, error process.suspended warning Entered SUSPENDED reason ("manual", "idle", "budget", "health", "rewind") process.resumed info Left SUSPENDED reason ("manual", "trigger", "rewind"), suspended_for (the suspension's reason) process.rewound warning rewind() applied target_entry_id, mode, actor, entries_affected

A failed process that gets restarted and fails again emits process.failed each time, and process.restart_exhausted once the limit is hit:

process.started
process.failed             error="GraphExecutionError: ... RuntimeError: model down"
process.restarted          attempt=1, max_restarts=1
process.started
process.failed             error="GraphExecutionError: ... RuntimeError: model down"
process.restart_exhausted  restarts=1, max_restarts=1

The same process also emits invocation.* events from its agent and, when enabled, budget.*, health.* and mission.* events (see the governance pages). Journal entries mirror the lifecycle: a state_transition entry per transition (from_state, to_state, reason, process_id), plus restart, restart_exhausted and recovered entries.

The lifecycle hooks session_start (on entering RUNNING) and session_end (before a stop or restart) follow the same lifecycle.

docs.title: StateError and ProcessStateError
docs.text:
StateError is the one exception for an invalid transition. It subclasses ProcessStateError (which subclasses RuntimeBaseError) and ValueError, so any of these catches it:

from promptise.runtime import ProcessStateError, RuntimeBaseError, StateError

try:
    await process.start()  # already running
except ProcessStateError as exc:  # or StateError, ValueError, RuntimeBaseError
    print(exc)
    # Process 'watcher': Cannot transition from 'running' to 'starting'.
    # Allowed targets: ['awaiting', 'failed', 'stopping', 'suspended']
Attribute Type Value current ProcessState The state the transition started from target ProcessState The rejected target process_id str \| None The process name (an AgentProcess always sets it) current_state str current.value attempted_state str target.value

The message starts with Process '<name>': when the process is known and lists the allowed targets (sorted by value). The runtime never raises a bare ProcessStateError; it exists as the base class.

Which AgentProcess methods raise it:

Call Raises when start() The process is STARTING, RUNNING or SUSPENDED (already started) suspend() The process is not RUNNING resume() The process is not SUSPENDED stop() Never for a state reason: stopping a STOPPED or STOPPING process does nothing

docs.title: Using ProcessLifecycle directly
docs.text:
AgentProcess owns its ProcessLifecycle (process.lifecycle). You can use the class on its own, for example in tests:

from promptise.runtime import ProcessLifecycle, ProcessState, StateError

lc = ProcessLifecycle(process_id="demo")  # starts in CREATED
await lc.transition(ProcessState.STARTING, reason="CLI start command")
await lc.transition(ProcessState.RUNNING, reason="agent built")

if lc.can_transition(ProcessState.SUSPENDED):
    await lc.transition(ProcessState.SUSPENDED, reason="idle", metadata={"idle_s": 300})

try:
    await lc.transition(ProcessState.CREATED)
except StateError as exc:
    print(exc.current, exc.target)  # ProcessState.SUSPENDED ProcessState.CREATED

docs.title: Listeners
docs.text:
add_listener(callback) registers a sync or async callable that receives the ProcessTransition after every successful transition. Listeners run in registration order, after the state has changed and outside the lock, so they may read lc.state or start another transition. A listener that raises is logged and skipped; it never undoes the transition.

lc.add_listener(lambda t: print(f"{t.from_state.value} -> {t.to_state.value}: {t.reason}"))

docs.title: ProcessTransition
docs.text:
Field Type Description from_state ProcessState Previous state to_state ProcessState New state timestamp datetime When the transition happened (UTC) reason str Human-readable explanation metadata dict[str, Any] Extra context; AgentProcess puts the error under "error" for FAILED

to_dict() and ProcessTransition.from_dict(data) convert to and from JSON-compatible dicts.

docs.title: History and snapshots
docs.text:
for t in lc.history:  # a copy, oldest first
    print(t.from_state.value, "->", t.to_state.value, t.reason)

snapshot = lc.snapshot()  # {"state": "suspended", "history": [...]}
restored = ProcessLifecycle.from_snapshot(snapshot)
assert restored.state == lc.state

from_snapshot() restores the state and history only; listeners and the process_id are not part of a snapshot.

docs.title: API summary
docs.text: Method / property Description ProcessLifecycle(initial=ProcessState.CREATED, *, process_id=None) Create a state machine state Current ProcessState history Copy of all ProcessTransition records can_transition(target) Whether target is allowed from the current state await transition(target, *, reason="", metadata=None) Perform a transition; returns the ProcessTransition, raises StateError add_listener(callback) Call callback(transition) after every transition snapshot() {"state": ..., "history": [...]} ProcessLifecycle.from_snapshot(data) Rebuild from a snapshot

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Transitions are serialized with an asyncio.Lock. That makes ProcessLifecycle safe for concurrent tasks of one event loop; it is not thread-safe, so call it (and AgentProcess) from the loop that runs the process.

Serialized does not mean "only one wins". Concurrent transitions run one after another, and each is checked against the state the previous one left:

import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import ProcessLifecycle, ProcessState

lc = ProcessLifecycle(initial=ProcessState.RUNNING)
await asyncio.gather(
    lc.transition(ProcessState.SUSPENDED),  # RUNNING -> SUSPENDED
    lc.transition(ProcessState.STOPPING),   # SUSPENDED -> STOPPING, also valid
)
assert lc.state == ProcessState.STOPPING

A transition that is no longer valid when its turn comes raises StateError.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Waiting for AWAITING. It never happens. An idle process is RUNNING, or SUSPENDED with suspend_reason == "idle" after idle_timeout.
  • Treating every SUSPENDED the same. Only an idle suspension resumes by itself. A budget, health or manual suspension waits for resume(); its trigger events keep queueing (the queue holds 1000 events) and webhooks keep answering 202.
  • Treating FAILED as final. With restart_policy="on_failure" or "always" a failed process is restarted with backoff. Alert on process.restart_exhausted (it gave up), not only on process.failed.
  • Expecting process.stopped from a never-started process. stop() on a CREATED process moves it to STOPPED without an event.
  • Calling start() on a running process. It raises StateError. Use AgentRuntime.restart_process() to stop and start in one call.
  • Driving a process from another thread. The lifecycle lock is an asyncio.Lock; use asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe() to reach the process's loop.

docs.title: Agent Manifests
docs.text:
A .agent manifest is a YAML file that declares one agent process: model, instructions, MCP servers, triggers, initial state, governance, hooks and process settings. Manifests let you review and version an agent's definition like any other config, validate it before deploying, and start it from the CLI without writing Python. The loader is strict: an unknown key anywhere fails with the list of valid keys, so a typo never silently keeps a default.

# watcher.agent
version: "1.0"
name: data-watcher
model: openai:gpt-5-mini
instructions: |
  You monitor data pipelines and alert on anomalies.

servers:
  data_tools:
    type: http
    url: http://localhost:8000/mcp

triggers:
  - type: cron
    cron_expression: "*/5 * * * *"

config:
  restart_policy: on_failure

promptise runtime validate watcher.agent
promptise runtime start watcher.agent

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text:
AgentManifestSchema accepts exactly these keys. Only name is required.

Key Type Default Becomes version "1.0" "1.0" Schema version; any other value is rejected name str required The process name model str "openai:gpt-5-mini" ProcessConfig.model instructions str none ProcessConfig.instructions identity mapping none ProcessConfig.identity (see identity) servers mapping {} ProcessConfig.servers triggers list [] ProcessConfig.triggers (each a TriggerConfig) world mapping {} context.initial_state memory mapping none context.memory_* fields context mapping none Any ContextConfig field journal mapping JournalConfig() ProcessConfig.journal (see journal) execution_mode "strict" or "open" "strict" ProcessConfig.execution_mode open_mode mapping defaults OpenModeConfig secrets mapping disabled SecretScopeConfig budget mapping disabled BudgetConfig health mapping disabled HealthConfig mission mapping disabled MissionConfig hooks list [] ProcessConfig.hooks (command hooks) config mapping {} Any other ProcessConfig field entrypoint str none Reserved and not read; setting it emits a FutureWarning

Every field of every section is listed on the Configuration page.

docs.title: Strict validation
docs.text:
load_manifest() rejects:

Problem Error message (inside ManifestValidationError) Unknown top-level key (journal_level: full) manifest: unknown key(s) ['journal_level']; valid keys are [...] (did you mean 'journal_level' -> 'journal'?) Unknown key in a section (health:, context:, journal:, open_mode:, secrets:, budget:, mission:) health: unknown key(s) ['error_windw']; valid keys are ['cooldown', ..., 'stuck_threshold'] Unknown key in memory: memory: unknown key(s) ['provder']; valid keys are ['auto_store', 'collection', 'max', 'min_score', 'persist_directory', 'provider', 'timeout', 'user_id'] (did you mean 'provder' -> 'provider'?) Unknown key in config: config: unknown key(s) ['concurency']; valid keys are ['adaptive', 'approval', ...] (did you mean 'concurency' -> 'concurrency'?) A config: key that has its own section config: ['instructions'] also set by the manifest's own section(s); set each option in one place (the top-level section) world: and context: initial_state both set Initial state is set twice, in 'world:' and in 'context: initial_state'; use one of them The same option in memory: and context: 'memory: provider' and 'context: memory_provider' set the same option; use one of them Unknown key in a server entry servers.tools: timout: Extra inputs are not permitted A server without url or command servers.tools: needs 'url' (an HTTP server) or 'command' (a stdio server) A trigger without type Trigger at index 0 is missing required 'type' field An invalid trigger (an unknown key, a missing cron_expression, a bad time zone) triggers[0] (cron): unknown key(s) ['cron']; valid keys are [...] A hook with an unknown event hooks[0]: ... unknown hook event 'on_start'; valid events are ['session_start', ...] A hook with callback: hooks[0]: a manifest hook runs a 'command'; Python callbacks are registered in code (process.hooks) Invalid execution_mode execution_mode: 'auto' is not one of ['strict', 'open']

The exception message starts with Manifest validation failed:; exc.errors holds the Pydantic error details and exc.file_path the file.

Trigger entries are checked in full (unknown keys, the fields their type needs, a bad time zone) when the manifest is loaded, so load_manifest(), promptise runtime validate and promptise runtime start all report a bad trigger. Unknown keys, here and in every other section, come with "did you mean" hints.

A ${VAR} that is not set raises ManifestEnvVarError, which is both a ManifestError and an EnvVarNotFoundError. promptise runtime validate reports it for that file and goes on with the next one; promptise runtime start checks every manifest first and starts nothing when one fails.

docs.title: identity
docs.text:
Gives the process a stable, traceable Agent Identity. Same shape as the .superagent identity block: a local identity tags the process's actions for attribution; a verifiable identity (Entra, AWS, GCP, SPIFFE, OIDC, or auto) also presents a signed credential, scoped to each server's audience, to the MCP servers the process calls.

identity:
  provider: oidc                 # local|entra|aws|gcp|spiffe|oidc|auto
  agent_id: data-watcher
  owner: platform
  issuer: https://gitlab.com
  token_env_var: CI_JOB_JWT_V2

For provider: local only agent_id is required; for provider: oidc, issuer plus exactly one of token_file / token_env_var. See the .superagent reference for every field and the Agent Identity guide for the end-to-end flow.

docs.title: servers
docs.text:
MCP servers, the same format as .superagent files. type is http, streamable-http, sse or stdio; an HTTP server needs url, a stdio server command. Every key is passed to the server spec, and an unknown one fails.

servers:
  my_tools:
    type: http
    url: http://localhost:8000/mcp
    audience: api://my-tools     # optional: identity credential audience
  local_tools:
    type: stdio
    command: python
    args: ["-m", "mytools.server"]

docs.title: triggers
docs.text:
A list of trigger configurations, each with a type and the fields of that type (see Triggers):

triggers:
  - type: cron
    cron_expression: "0 9 * * 1-5"
    cron_timezone: Europe/Zurich
  - type: webhook
    webhook_path: /events
    webhook_port: 9090
    hmac_secret: ${WEBHOOK_SECRET}
  - type: file_watch
    watch_path: /data/inbox
    watch_patterns: ["*.csv", "*.json"]
    watch_backend: polling
  - type: event
    event_type: pipeline.degraded

docs.title: world and context
docs.text:
world: is the initial key-value state of the process's AgentContext. context: accepts any ContextConfig field, including initial_state; use one of world: or context: initial_state, not both. Keys recovered from the journal on start replace these initial values.

world:
  pipeline_status: unknown
  alerts_created: 0

context:
  writable_keys: [pipeline_status, alerts_created]
  conversation_max_messages: 50
  state_tool: true          # gives the agent an update_state(key, value) tool
  env_prefix: PIPELINE_

Equivalent, with the state inside context::

context:
  initial_state:
    pipeline_status: unknown
    alerts_created: 0
  writable_keys: [pipeline_status, alerts_created]

docs.title: memory
docs.text:
Short names for the long-term memory fields of ContextConfig:

memory: key Sets provider memory_provider (in_memory, chroma, mem0) auto_store memory_auto_store max memory_max min_score memory_min_score timeout memory_timeout collection memory_collection persist_directory memory_persist_directory user_id memory_user_id 
memory:
  provider: chroma
  collection: agent_memory
  persist_directory: .promptise/chroma
  max: 5

You can set the same options as memory_* keys under context: instead, but not both ways for one option.

docs.title: journal
docs.text:
journal:
  level: full             # none | checkpoint | full
  backend: file           # file | memory
  path: .promptise/journal
  recover_on_start: true

A manifest without a journal: section gets JournalConfig(): level: checkpoint, files under .promptise/journal, and recovery on start. A process loaded from a manifest therefore journals and, when started again under the same name, continues from its last checkpoint. Set level: none to turn the journal off, or recover_on_start: false to keep the journal but always start fresh. (A ProcessConfig built in Python has no journal unless you set one.)

docs.title: Governance
docs.text:
secrets:, budget:, health: and mission: take the fields of SecretScopeConfig, BudgetConfig, HealthConfig and MissionConfig. Each needs enabled: true.

secrets:
  enabled: true
  secrets:
    api_key: ${MONITORING_API_KEY}
  default_ttl: 3600

budget:
  enabled: true
  max_tool_calls_per_run: 20
  max_cost_per_day: 50
  on_exceeded: pause

health:
  enabled: true
  on_anomaly: escalate
  escalation:
    webhook_url: https://hooks.example.com/agent-alerts

mission:
  enabled: true
  objective: Keep every pipeline healthy.
  success_criteria: No pipeline degraded for more than 15 minutes.
  eval_every: 10

MissionConfig.success_check is Python only and can't be set in a manifest.

docs.title: hooks
docs.text:
A list of lifecycle hooks that run an external command. Each entry takes the HookConfig fields for a command hook: event, command, timeout, priority, once, tag, fail_closed, cwd, env, env_passthrough, max_output_bytes. The event arrives on the command's stdin as JSON; no shell runs it.

hooks:
  - event: user_prompt_submit
    command: ["./hooks/audit.sh"]
    timeout: 5
    fail_closed: true
  - event: session_end
    command: "python hooks/notify.py --channel ops"

Python callbacks are registered in code: process.hooks.on(...) or HookConfig(callback=...).

docs.title: Open mode
docs.text:
execution_mode: open

open_mode:
  allow_identity_change: true
  allow_tool_creation: true
  allow_mcp_connect: false
  allow_trigger_management: true
  allow_memory_management: true
  max_custom_tools: 5
  max_rebuilds: 10
  sandbox_custom_tools: true

allow_tool_creation: true lets the model run Python in the runtime's process; restricted builtins don't contain it. Keep it off unless that is acceptable. See Meta-Tools.

docs.title: config
docs.text:
Any ProcessConfig field that has no section of its own, for example:

config:
  concurrency: 2
  heartbeat_interval: 30
  idle_timeout: 3600
  max_lifetime: 86400
  max_consecutive_failures: 5
  restart_policy: on_failure
  max_restarts: 5
  restart_backoff: 2
  max_invocation_time: 300
  inbox:
    enabled: true
  trigger_delivery:
    max_retries: 2
    dead_letter_size: 200

A key that has its own section (model, instructions, identity, execution_mode, open_mode, servers, triggers, journal, context, secrets, budget, health, mission, hooks) is refused in config: when that section is also set; set each option in one place.

docs.title: Environment variables and secrets
docs.text:
${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} references are resolved from the environment when the manifest is loaded, in every value of the file, with one exception: the values under secrets.secrets. Those stay references in the loaded config and are resolved by the process's secret scope when it starts, so the config, repr() and any dump of it never hold the secret value. A reference to an unset variable without a default fails at load time in both cases:

ManifestEnvVarError: agents/monitor.agent: Environment variable 'MONITORING_API_KEY' not found (referenced in: secrets.secrets.api_key)

To keep a credential out of plain config, put it in secrets.secrets. In open mode the agent reads it with the get_secret tool; a strict-mode process has no such tool, so pass the credential to your own code or MCP server instead (see Secret scoping). Other secret-bearing values, such as a webhook's hmac_secret or a server's credential headers, are resolved at load time; they are stored as SecretStr (masked in repr() and JSON dumps) but held in memory in plain form.

secrets:
  enabled: true
  secrets:
    db_password: ${DB_PASSWORD}             # resolved when the process starts
    region: ${AWS_REGION:-eu-central-1}     # with a default

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
from promptise.runtime import (
    AgentProcess, load_manifest, manifest_to_process_config, save_manifest, validate_manifest,
)

manifest = load_manifest("agents/watcher.agent")       # AgentManifestSchema
config = manifest_to_process_config(manifest)          # ProcessConfig

# ['No MCP servers configured: agent has no tools']

Function Returns Raises load_manifest(path) AgentManifestSchema ManifestError (missing file, unreadable, invalid YAML, not a mapping), ManifestValidationError (schema), ManifestEnvVarError (unset ${VAR}; also an EnvVarNotFoundError) validate_manifest(path) list[str] of warnings: no instructions, no triggers, no MCP servers as load_manifest() manifest_to_process_config(manifest) ProcessConfig pydantic.ValidationError (for example an invalid trigger) save_manifest(manifest, path) None

save_manifest() writes the loaded manifest, so ${VAR} references outside secrets.secrets are written with their resolved values. AgentRuntime.load_manifest(path, name_override=None) and AgentRuntime.load_directory(dir) load and register in one step (see Runtime Manager).

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Expecting get_secret in strict mode. The agent's get_secret tool exists only in open mode; in strict mode secrets.secrets holds values for your code, not for the model.
  • A manifest process that "remembers" old state. Without a journal: section the process journals to .promptise/journal and recovers on start. Set journal: {level: none} or recover_on_start: false if each start should be fresh.
  • Putting an option in two places. config: {instructions: ...} next to a top-level instructions: fails; so do world: together with context: initial_state.
  • Secrets in plain values. Only secrets.secrets keeps ${VAR} references until start. A literal API key anywhere else is in the file and in the loaded config.
  • Old keys from earlier examples. journal_level, restart_on_failure and similar keys don't exist; the loader rejects them with the list of valid keys.
  • Using entrypoint. It is not read. Declare command hooks in hooks: and register Python hooks in code.

docs.title: Open Mode Meta-Tools
docs.text:
In open mode (execution_mode=ExecutionMode.OPEN) an agent process gets meta-tools: tools that change the process itself instead of the outside world. With them the agent can rewrite its instructions, write new Python tools, connect MCP servers, add and remove its own triggers, manage long-term memory and spawn helper processes. Every meta-tool goes through the same process methods an operator would use, so the limits in OpenModeConfig and your hooks apply to each change.

Open mode hands the model control of its own setup

Whoever can put text in front of the model (trigger payloads, inbox messages, tool results) can try to steer these tools. create_tool in particular runs model-written Python inside the runtime's process; its restricted builtins are not a sandbox. Read Security before you enable open mode, and switch off what the agent doesn't need.

import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import AgentRuntime, ExecutionMode, OpenModeConfig, ProcessConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="You are an adaptive monitoring agent. Improve your own tooling over time.",
    execution_mode=ExecutionMode.OPEN,
    open_mode=OpenModeConfig(
        allow_tool_creation=False,    # no model-written Python in this process
        allow_mcp_connect=False,      # no new servers
        allow_process_spawn=True,     # may start helper processes
        max_custom_tools=10,
        max_spawned_processes=2,
        max_rebuilds=20,
    ),
)


async def main():
    async with AgentRuntime() as runtime:  # spawn_process needs a runtime
        await runtime.add_process("monitor", config)
        await runtime.start_all()
        await asyncio.sleep(3600)


asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Available meta-tools
docs.text:
create_meta_tools() builds the list when the agent is built, filtered by OpenModeConfig. Strict-mode processes get none of them.

Meta-tool Present when What it does modify_instructions allow_identity_change Replace the system prompt (hot reload) create_tool allow_tool_creation Define a Python tool (hot reload). Runs in the runtime's process, not isolated connect_mcp_server allow_mcp_connect Connect an HTTP MCP server (hot reload) add_trigger allow_trigger_management Add a cron, event, message, webhook, file_watch or custom trigger remove_trigger allow_trigger_management Remove a trigger the agent added spawn_process allow_process_spawn Create and start a new process in the runtime list_processes allow_process_spawn List the runtime's processes store_memory allow_memory_management Store text in long-term memory search_memory allow_memory_management Search long-term memory forget_memory allow_memory_management Delete a memory by ID get_secret secret scoping enabled Read a scoped secret check_budget budget enabled Show the remaining budget check_mission mission enabled Show the mission state and latest evaluations list_capabilities always (in open mode) Show the agent's current instructions, tools, triggers and counters

The update_state(key, value) tool is not a meta-tool: ContextConfig(state_tool=True) gives it to a process in either mode (see Context).

docs.title: How changes are applied
docs.text:
Each meta-tool calls a process method, and every method enforces the limits and dispatches the config_change hook (source="agent"), which can refuse the change:

Meta-tool Calls Limits checked modify_instructions process.set_dynamic_instructions() max_instruction_length, max_rebuilds create_tool hot reload max_custom_tools, duplicate names, max_rebuilds connect_mcp_server hot reload duplicate names, http(s) URL, allowed_mcp_urls (or a public address when it is empty), max_rebuilds add_trigger process.add_dynamic_trigger() max_dynamic_triggers, trigger validation, loopback-only webhooks, the API's data_dir for watch paths, process state remove_trigger process.remove_trigger(trigger_id, source="agent") only triggers the agent added spawn_process process.spawn_process() max_spawned_processes, unique name, loopback-only webhooks; the subagent_start hook can refuse it

A refused or failed change is not applied, now or after a restart. Tools report problems as text starting with Error, so the model can read them and carry on.

docs.title: modify_instructions
docs.text:
Parameter Type Description new_instructions str The complete new system prompt

The agent is rebuilt with the new instructions. rollback() restores the configured ones, and an operator's process.update_instructions() replaces whatever the agent set.

Result When Rebuild successful Applied Error: instructions exceed max length (12000 > 10000) Longer than max_instruction_length Error: max rebuilds (N) reached; the change was not applied max_rebuilds used up Error: the change was blocked by a hook: <reason> A config_change hook refused it

docs.title: create_tool
docs.text:
Parameter Type Description tool_name str Unique name for the new tool tool_description str What the tool does parameters dict JSON object schema of the tool's parameters (empty: one free-form input string) python_code str Python code defining run(...), which returns a string

parameters shapes the new tool's inputs. Each property of the object schema is a parameter, offered to the model with its type and constraints, and passed to run as a keyword argument:

create_tool(
    tool_name="add",
    tool_description="Add two integers.",
    parameters={
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"a": {"type": "integer"}, "b": {"type": "integer"}},
        "required": ["a", "b"],
    },
    python_code="def run(a, b):\n    return str(a + b)",
)
# The new tool is called as add(a=2, b=3) -> "5"
  • Arguments are validated against the schema before run is called. Invalid arguments raise ToolArgumentError (the model sees each problem and can correct the call), and run is not called.
  • run gets the arguments the caller gave, as plain JSON (nested objects are dicts), plus each property's schema default when the caller left it out. An optional parameter without a schema default that the caller left out is not passed, so run's own default applies.
  • Property names must be usable as Python keyword arguments (identifiers, not keywords, not starting with _), and required may only name declared properties. A schema that is not an object schema, or that lists parameters without properties, is refused and no tool is created.
  • With empty parameters (or an object schema without properties), the tool takes one free-form input string: run(input="...").

The new tool can be called from the agent's next run, not in the run that creates it (the current run keeps the tools it started with). The tool's description and its result say so, so the model finishes the current task without it instead of looking for it or creating it again.

Result When Tool 'add' created. You can call it from your next run, not in this one: this run keeps the tools it started with, so finish the current task without it. Created Error: max custom tools (20) reached max_custom_tools reached Error: tool 'add' already exists Duplicate name Error creating tool: <reason> Unusable parameters schema, or the rebuild failed Error: max rebuilds (N) reached; the change was not applied max_rebuilds used up Error: the change was blocked by a hook: <reason> A config_change hook refused it

docs.title: Sandbox execution
docs.text:
With sandbox_custom_tools=True (the default), agent-written code runs with restricted builtins:

  • Allowed: len, range, str, int, float, list, dict, set, sorted, enumerate, zip, map, filter, max, min, sum, print, round, abs, bool, type, isinstance, common exceptions and other safe builtins.
  • Blocked: open, exec, eval, __import__, file I/O, network access and all imports.

With sandbox_custom_tools=False, the code runs with the same restricted builtins (no open, exec, eval, file I/O or network access) but may import a fixed allowlist of standard-library modules: base64, collections, copy, datetime, functools, hashlib, itertools, json, math, re, string, urllib.parse, uuid. Any other import (os, decimal, ...) fails with Import of '...' is not allowed, and each call logs a warning. No setting gives agent-written code full Python builtins; give the agent such capabilities as reviewed MCP tools.

This is not a sandbox, with either setting. The code runs in the runtime's own process, and Python's object model lets code walk from any object back to modules like os, so agent-written code can run commands as the runtime's user, read its memory and environment, and reach anything the runtime can. The restrictions only stop honest code from reaching for files and imports by accident. Treat allow_tool_creation=True as "the model may run arbitrary code here":

  • the control API refuses to deploy such a config unless allow_command_deploys is on (403 COMMANDS_NOT_ALLOWED);
  • for code from the model, prefer the Docker sandbox (build_agent(sandbox=...)), which runs each command in an isolated container, or give the agent reviewed MCP tools instead.

docs.title: connect_mcp_server
docs.text:
Parameter Type Default Description server_name str required Unique name for the server url str required http:// or https:// URL of the MCP server transport str "streamable-http" streamable-http or sse

Only HTTP(S) servers: the agent can't start a stdio server (a program on the host). Which URLs are accepted depends on allowed_mcp_urls:

allowed_mcp_urls Operator-configured process Process deployed through the control API Listed URLs Only those (compared with a lowercase scheme and host, default ports dropped, no trailing slash); a listed private or loopback URL is fine The same Empty Any URL whose host resolves to public addresses only: loopback, private, link-local (cloud metadata) and other internal addresses are refused. A warning is logged when the process starts None: the agent can't connect servers

The address check resolves the host when the agent connects and again at every agent build, like escalation webhooks, but it can't stop a host whose DNS answer changes in between; list the servers in allowed_mcp_urls where that matters. After connecting, the agent is rebuilt with the server's tools, which are available from the next run.

A server the agent connected never receives the process identity's credential (ProcessConfig.identity) or a caller's token, so the agent can't send them to a server it picked. List the URLs that may receive it in open_mode.identity_mcp_urls.

Result When Connected to MCP server 'x' at <url>. Its tools are available from your next run, not in this one: this run keeps the tools it started with. Connected Error: the MCP server URL must start with http:// or https:// Not an HTTP(S) URL Error: URL not in allowed whitelist (open_mode.allowed_mcp_urls) Not in allowed_mcp_urls Error: refused: '<host>' resolves to private/internal IP <ip> (...) No allowlist, and the host is internal Error: this process was deployed through the control API and has no open_mode.allowed_mcp_urls, ... API-deployed process without an allowlist Error: the MCP server host did not resolve (...) No allowlist, and the host doesn't resolve Error: server 'x' already connected Duplicate name Error connecting to MCP server: <reason> The connection or rebuild failed Error: max rebuilds (N) reached; the change was not applied max_rebuilds used up Error: the change was blocked by a hook: <reason> A config_change hook refused it

docs.title: add_trigger
docs.text:
Parameter Type Description trigger_type str "cron", "event", "message", "webhook", "file_watch" or a registered custom type cron_expression str \| None For cron event_type str \| None For event topic str \| None For message webhook_path str \| None For webhook webhook_port int \| None For webhook watch_path str \| None For file_watch watch_patterns list[str] \| None For file_watch custom_config dict \| None For custom trigger types

The trigger is validated like any TriggerConfig, started at once with its listener, and counts toward max_dynamic_triggers. It is not added to config.triggers: it lives until remove_trigger, rollback() or the next stop() (a restart drops it too).

A webhook the agent adds listens on loopback only. process.add_dynamic_trigger() refuses a non-loopback webhook_host unless open_mode.allow_public_webhooks is on, and then requires an hmac_secret. For a process deployed through the control API, a file_watch watch_path must lie in the API's data_dir.

Result When Trigger 'cron-36042769' (cron) added and listening. Added; the ID is what remove_trigger takes Error adding trigger: max dynamic triggers (10) reached Limit reached Error adding trigger: Invalid trigger config: <details> Invalid fields Error adding trigger: Adding the cron trigger was blocked: <reason> A config_change hook refused it Error adding trigger: Trigger could not start: <reason> The trigger failed to start (for example a port in use) Error adding trigger: a webhook trigger on '0.0.0.0' would accept requests from other machines; ... Non-loopback webhook (see above) Error adding trigger: watch_path '...' is outside the data directory ... API-deployed process, path outside data_dir

docs.title: remove_trigger
docs.text:
Parameter Type Description trigger_id str ID returned by add_trigger

The agent can only remove triggers it added; config triggers stay. The trigger's listener is cancelled with it.

Result When Trigger 'cron-36042769' removed. Removed Error: trigger 'x' not found in dynamic triggers Not an agent-added trigger Error removing trigger: Removing trigger 'x' was blocked: <reason> A config_change hook refused it

docs.title: spawn_process
docs.text:
Parameter Type Default Description process_name str required Unique name in the runtime instructions str required System prompt for the new process model str \| None None Model ID; None uses the parent's model triggers list[dict] [] Trigger configs (each with type and its fields) execution_mode str "strict" "strict" or "open"

The new process is registered in the parent's AgentRuntime, started, and listed in process.spawned_processes. It inherits the parent's guardrails:

Inherited from the parent Not inherited budget, health, trigger_delivery and journal settings (copies: the child has its own counters) Secrets approval policy and guardrails scanner MCP servers max_invocation_time Identity open_mode limits, with allow_process_spawn switched off config.hooks entries, mission, inbox, context settings The parent's hooks: its hooks manager (and what the parent inherited) is dispatched for the child after the child's own, so permission_request, user_prompt_submit and every other hook the parent has also govern the child (ctx.process_id names the child) The deploy policy: a child of an API-deployed process is limited like its parent (env references, MCP allowlist, data_dir)

So a spawned process can never spawn more processes, even in open mode. Its triggers follow the add_trigger rules: webhooks listen on loopback unless open_mode.allow_public_webhooks is on (then with an hmac_secret), so the model can't open a public, unsigned endpoint. The subagent_start hook runs before the spawn and can refuse it; subagent_stop runs when the child stops or fails. The child runs independently: stopping the parent does not stop it. allow_process_spawn defaults to False.

Result When Process 'helper' spawned and started. Mode: strict. Triggers: 1. Spawned Error: process is not running inside an AgentRuntime. spawn_process requires a runtime. The process has no runtime Error spawning process: max spawned processes (3) reached Limit reached Error spawning process: process 'helper' already exists in the runtime Name taken Error spawning process: invalid process config: <details> Bad trigger or mode Error spawning process: spawning 'helper' was blocked by a hook: <reason> A subagent_start hook refused it Error spawning process: can't spawn 'helper': a webhook trigger on '0.0.0.0' ... A non-loopback (or unsigned public) webhook trigger

A child that fails to start is removed from the runtime again, and the error is returned.

docs.title: list_processes
docs.text:
No parameters. Lists every process in the runtime:

Processes in runtime:
  - monitor: state=running, invocations=12 (this process)
  - helper: state=running, invocations=3 [spawned by this process]

Without a runtime: Error: process is not running inside an AgentRuntime. list_processes requires a runtime.

docs.title: store_memory, search_memory, forget_memory
docs.text:
These need a long-term memory provider (ContextConfig.memory_provider); without one each returns Error: no memory provider configured.

Tool Parameters Result store_memory content: str, tags: list[str] = [] Stored in memory (id=<id>). search_memory query: str, limit: int = 5 (1-20) Found memories: and one - [<id>] (score=0.87) <content> line each, or No relevant memories found. forget_memory memory_id: str Memory '<id>' deleted. or Memory '<id>' not found.

docs.title: Governance tools
docs.text:
These appear in open mode when the subsystem is enabled.

Tool Parameters Result get_secret name: str The secret value, or Error: secret '<name>' not found or expired. Each access is logged in the audit trail. check_budget none Budget remaining: and one line per limit (Tool Calls Run: 5, Cost Day: unlimited, ...) check_mission none The mission summary and up to the latest 10 evaluations (- #<run> [<source>] achieved, confidence=0.82: <reasoning>)

docs.title: list_capabilities
docs.text:
No parameters. Returns the process name, mode and model, the current instructions (first 200 characters), custom tool names, config and dynamic trigger IDs, spawned processes, memory status, conversation size, and the invocation and rebuild counts:

Process: monitor
Mode: open
Model: openai:gpt-5-mini
Instructions: You coordinate carefully.
Custom tools: ['add']
Static triggers: []
Dynamic triggers: []
Spawned processes: ['helper']
Memory: disabled
Conversation buffer: 0 messages

Rebuilds: 2

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Open mode gives the model the same levers an operator has, within OpenModeConfig. Plan for a model that has been talked into misusing them.

Capability Risk What limits it create_tool (allow_tool_creation, on by default) Runs model-written Python in the runtime's process: effectively any command as the runtime's user Nothing contains it. Switch it off unless that is acceptable; the control API refuses it without allow_command_deploys connect_mcp_server (allow_mcp_connect) Sends requests (and tool arguments) to a server the model picked allowed_mcp_urls; without it, internal addresses are refused and API deploys get none. Agent-connected servers never get the process identity's credential or a caller's token (identity_mcp_urls opts a URL in) add_trigger (allow_trigger_management) Opens new entry points (webhooks, file watchers) Webhooks on loopback only unless allow_public_webhooks (then signed); unsigned loopback webhooks refuse browser cross-site requests; API deploys keep watch paths in data_dir spawn_process (allow_process_spawn, off by default) New processes with their own triggers Children inherit the guardrails, hooks and deploy policy, can't spawn further, and follow the add_trigger webhook rules get_secret (secret scoping on) The model reads secret values Secret values are redacted from the journal, the prompt history, /ask answers and inbox listings; an API deploy can't make a secret out of a host environment variable unless the operator allows it

Hooks are the place for your own policy: a config_change hook (source="agent") can refuse any self-modification, subagent_start any spawn, and permission_request any approval-gated tool call, for spawned children too.

docs.title: Hot reload
docs.text:
modify_instructions, create_tool and connect_mcp_server rebuild the agent:

  1. The limits are checked and the config_change hook runs; a refusal stops here, with nothing changed.
  2. The change is staged and the conversation history saved.
  3. The agent is rebuilt from the static config plus the dynamic state, with a fresh connection to each MCP server.
  4. The previous agent and its MCP connections are closed (stdio servers exit) once the run that asked for the reload has finished; until then that run keeps the tools it started with.
  5. The conversation history is restored and rebuild_count goes up.

If the rebuild fails, the process keeps the previous agent and the change is undone, so a later start doesn't apply it either.

docs.title: max_rebuilds
docs.text: With OpenModeConfig.max_rebuilds set, the process refuses further changes once that many hot reloads have happened. The limit counts over the lifetime of the AgentProcess object: stop() / start(), recovery and automatic restarts don't reset it (status()["rebuild_count"]). A refused change is not made at all; the limit is checked before the change is staged, under the same lock as the rebuild.

docs.title: rollback
docs.text: await process.rollback() is the operator's undo: it removes the agent's instructions, tools, MCP servers and triggers and rebuilds from the original config. It is not refused by max_rebuilds but counts as a rebuild, and it returns Rebuild successful. It keeps the context state and conversation; use rewind() to roll those back. Strict-mode processes raise RuntimeError.

docs.title: What survives a restart
docs.text: Agent-written instructions, custom tools and MCP servers stay on the process object, so stop() / start() and automatic restarts rebuild the agent with them. Agent-added triggers end at stop(). A new process object (a redeploy) starts from the config only.

docs.title: Programmatic use
docs.text:
from promptise.runtime.meta_tools import create_meta_tools

tools = {t.name: t for t in create_meta_tools(process, runtime=runtime)}
print(await tools["add_trigger"].ainvoke({"trigger_type": "cron", "cron_expression": "*/5 * * * *"}))
# Trigger 'cron-36042769' (cron) added and listening.

create_meta_tools(process, *, runtime=None) returns LangChain StructuredTools filtered by process.config.open_mode. Without runtime, spawn_process and list_processes answer with the "not running inside an AgentRuntime" error. Calling the tools directly is useful in tests; the process adds them to its own agent by itself.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Spawning without a runtime. A bare AgentProcess can't spawn; register it with AgentRuntime.add_process() (which passes the runtime) or pass runtime=.
  • Expecting the new tool in the same run. Created tools and connected servers are available from the next run.
  • Leaving max_rebuilds unset. Each hot reload reconnects every MCP server. A cap bounds both the cost and how far the agent can drift.
  • Assuming a child has the parent's secrets or tools. A spawned process gets the parent's limits and hooks, not its secrets or servers.
  • Treating the sandbox as isolation. Restricted builtins don't contain hostile code: create_tool can run any command as the runtime's user. Set allow_tool_creation=False unless that is acceptable, and use the Docker sandbox or MCP tools for anything sensitive.
  • Empty allowed_mcp_urls. For your own process it means any public HTTP(S) URL (a warning says so at start); for an API deploy it means none. List the servers the agent may use, or set allow_mcp_connect=False.
