docs.title: Agent Processes
docs.text:
AgentProcess turns an agent into a long-running process. It builds the agent, connects its MCP servers, starts its triggers, runs the agent once per trigger event, and keeps state, memory and conversation history between runs. It also restarts itself after failures when you ask it to. It is the core unit of the Agent Runtime; AgentRuntime manages many of them.

import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import AgentProcess, ProcessConfig, TriggerConfig, TriggerEvent


async def main():
    process = AgentProcess(
        name="health-checker",
        config=ProcessConfig(
            model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
            instructions="You monitor infrastructure health.",
            triggers=[TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *")],
        ),
    )
    await process.start()  # runs on the cron schedule from now on

    # Run it once now, without waiting for the schedule
    await process.inject(TriggerEvent(
        trigger_id="manual", trigger_type="manual", payload={"reason": "ad-hoc check"},
    ))
    await asyncio.sleep(5)

    status = process.status()
    print(status["state"], status["invocation_count"])  # running 1
    await process.stop()


asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Creating a process
docs.text:
Signature
class AgentProcess:
    def __init__(
        self,
        name: str,                    # unique process name; the journal files entries under it
        config: ProcessConfig,        # every setting of the process
        *,
        process_id: str | None = None,  # auto-generated UUID if omitted
        event_bus=None,               # shared bus for "event" triggers
        broker=None,                  # shared broker for "message" triggers
        runtime=None,                 # parent AgentRuntime (open mode's spawn_process needs it)
        event_notifier=None,          # EventNotifier for process.* and agent events
        hooks=None,                   # shared HookManager, dispatched after the process's own hooks
        deploy_policy=None,           # set by the Orchestration API for configs it deploys
        extra_tools=None,             # local tools, added after config.extra_tools
        model=None,                   # the agent's model, instead of config.model
    ) -> None: ...

deploy_policy is internal: the Orchestration API passes it for configs deployed over HTTP, so that ${VAR} references, open_mode.allowed_mcp_urls and file paths are limited to what the operator allowed. Leave it at None in your own code.

The constructor checks each entry of config.servers and raises ValueError for one it can't use. Every setting lives in ProcessConfig; see Configuration for all fields and defaults. Inside an AgentRuntime, use runtime.add_process(name, config) instead: it passes the runtime's bus, broker, notifier and hooks.

docs.title: Local tools
docs.text:
Python functions the agent can call need no MCP server: pass them in extra_tools, on ProcessConfig or the AgentProcess constructor (or both; the constructor's come after the config's). They take what build_agent(extra_tools=...) takes: functions made tools with @tool, plain functions (made tools as if decorated) and LangChain tools.

from promptise import tool
from promptise.runtime import AgentProcess, BudgetConfig, ProcessConfig

@tool
def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Look up an order's status."""
    return f"{order_id}: shipped"

process = AgentProcess(
    "orders",
    ProcessConfig(
        instructions="Answer questions about orders.",
        extra_tools=[lookup_order],
        budget=BudgetConfig(enabled=True, max_tool_calls_per_run=10),
    ),
)

They sit next to the MCP servers' tools, and budget, approval, health and the journal treat them the same way. Every agent the process builds has them: after a restart, a hot reload or new instructions. Anything that is not a tool raises TypeError when the config or process is created.

They are code only, like a hook's callback: model_dump() and RuntimeConfig.to_dict() leave them out, and a manifest or YAML config can't name them (serve such tools from an MCP server instead). Processes spawned in open mode don't get them, and the agent can't create a tool with the name of one.

docs.title: The agent's model
docs.text:
ProcessConfig.model is usually a model id such as "openai:gpt-5-mini". In code it can also be a model object, as build_agent(model=...) takes it: a LangChain chat model you configured yourself, a promptise.Model with its provider settings, a FallbackChain, or a ScriptedModel in a test. AgentProcess(..., model=...) does the same for one process and wins over config.model. Every agent the process builds uses it (after a restart, a hot reload or new instructions), and so does the mission evaluator.

import asyncio

from promptise import tool
from promptise.runtime import AgentProcess, ProcessConfig, TriggerEvent
from promptise.testing import ScriptedModel, ToolCall


@tool
def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Look up an order's status."""
    return f"{order_id}: shipped"


async def main():
    model = ScriptedModel([
        ToolCall("lookup_order", {"order_id": "A-1001"}),
        "Order A-1001 has shipped.",
    ])
    process = AgentProcess(
        "orders",
        ProcessConfig(model=model, instructions="Answer questions about orders.", extra_tools=[lookup_order]),
    )
    await process.start()
    await process.inject(TriggerEvent(trigger_id="manual", trigger_type="manual", payload={"order": "A-1001"}))
    while process.status()["invocation_count"] < 1:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    await process.stop()

    print(len(model.calls), model.calls[1].messages[-1].content)


asyncio.run(main())

Output:

2 A-1001: shipped

A model object is code only, like extra_tools: model_dump() and RuntimeConfig.to_dict() leave model out, so a config read back from them has the default model id, and a manifest or YAML config names a model by its id. Events, the dashboard and the open-mode list_capabilities tool show a model object by its class and model name, such as ChatOpenAI(gpt-5-mini); a promptise.Model is shown without its key. Processes spawned in open mode run on the parent's model unless the agent names another one. Anything that isn't a model id or a model object raises a ValidationError (ValueError from the AgentProcess constructor).

docs.title: Lifecycle methods
docs.text:
Method Transition What it does await start() CREATED, STOPPED or FAILED → STARTING → RUNNING Recovers from the journal (first start only), resolves secrets, builds the agent and connects MCP servers, starts triggers, workers and the heartbeat await stop(*, drain_timeout=0.0) → STOPPING → STOPPED (from CREATED: straight to STOPPED) Cancels workers and runs in flight (with drain_timeout: lets runs in flight finish first, see Graceful stop), stops triggers, dead-letters queued events, writes a journal checkpoint (with a journal), closes the agent and its MCP connections, revokes secrets await close() as stop() stop(), then closes long-term memory, revokes secrets and clears the conversation history await suspend(reason="manual") RUNNING → SUSPENDED Pauses processing; triggers keep queueing events await resume(reason="manual") SUSPENDED → RUNNING Runs the queued events in order; restarts the idle clock async with process: start() on enter, close() on exit

The Lifecycle page has the full state diagram, which transitions raise StateError, and every process.* event.

docs.title: start()
docs.text:
start() works from CREATED, STOPPED and FAILED. On FAILED it first tears down what the failed run left (trigger listeners, triggers, heartbeat, agent) and cancels a pending automatic restart, so nothing runs twice. If startup raises, the process goes to FAILED, process.failed is emitted, and start() raises the error to you; your own start() call is never retried automatically.

Calling start() on a process that is already STARTING, RUNNING or SUSPENDED raises StateError.

docs.title: stop()
docs.text:
stop() works from every state:

  • RUNNING, SUSPENDED, FAILED: STOPPING → STOPPED, then process.stopped.
  • CREATED (never started): straight to STOPPED, no event.
  • STOPPED or STOPPING: does nothing.

An explicit stop() never triggers an automatic restart and cancels one that is pending. A run in flight is cancelled, and every event that hasn't run goes to the dead letters with reason "process stopped": events still in the queue, events a suspended worker or a trigger listener was holding, events still inside a trigger (a file watch's backlog, a webhook's accepted requests), and the cancelled run's event (with error "run cancelled"). An automatic restart keeps the queue instead, and adds the triggers' leftover events to it.

docs.title: Graceful stop
docs.text:
stop(drain_timeout=N) lets the runs in flight finish before the process stops. From the moment it is called, no new event starts: trigger events and inject() go to the dead letters ("process stopped"), a webhook answers 503, and queued events are not picked up. The runs in flight get up to N seconds; only the ones still running then are cancelled. drain_timeout=None uses ProcessConfig.drain_timeout (default 5 seconds), and process.abort_drain() ends the wait early. A plain stop() keeps cancelling at once.

await process.stop(drain_timeout=30)    # wait up to 30 s for the current run
await process.stop(drain_timeout=None)  # wait up to config.drain_timeout
await process.stop()                    # cancel at once

AgentRuntime.run_forever() stops this way on SIGTERM and Ctrl+C (see Runtime Manager).

The control API and promptise runtime stop stop this way too. There the default is the process's configured drain_timeout, as on SIGTERM, so an operator's stop doesn't cut off a run by surprise; 0 cancels at once:

promptise runtime stop prod --process data-watcher --drain-timeout 30
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"drain_timeout": 0}' \
    http://127.0.0.1:9100/api/v1/processes/data-watcher/stop

A cancelled run may have called tools that already took effect, so it is not dropped silently: the process logs a warning, writes a run_interrupted journal entry (at every journal level) with the event, and keeps the event in its journal checkpoint. A new process object with the same name and journal lists it in dead_letters again after start() (and counts it in recovered["interrupted_runs"]), so you can inspect it and call redeliver_dead_letters() if it should run again. Once redelivered or cleared, it is no longer carried over.

docs.title: suspend() and resume()
docs.text:
suspend() pauses the process without tearing anything down. Triggers keep firing; their events wait in the queue in arrival order, and a run in flight finishes. resume() runs them in that order and restarts the idle clock, so idle_timeout counts from the resume.

A process suspended by idle_timeout resumes by itself when the next trigger event arrives (or you call inject()); you don't need to call resume(). Budget, health and manual suspensions wait for resume(). process.suspend_reason tells them apart: "manual", "idle", "budget", "health" or "rewind".

await process.suspend()  # e.g. during a maintenance window
print(process.suspend_reason)  # "manual"
await process.resume()

docs.title: close()
docs.text: close() stops the process and releases what lives as long as the process object: it closes the long-term memory provider, revokes secrets (whatever revoke_on_stop says) and clears the conversation history. async with process: and AgentRuntime.remove_process() call it. A closed process can be started again; start() opens a new memory provider, and an in_memory one starts empty.

docs.title: What survives stop and start
docs.text:
stop() and start() on the same object (including automatic restarts) keep the process's state, so the next run continues where the last one stopped. close() releases it.

Item After stop() / start() After close() In a new process object Context state Kept Kept Restored from the journal (see Recovery on start) Conversation history Kept (cleared if context.conversation_clear_on_stop=True) Cleared Restored from the journal Long-term memory Provider stays open Provider closed; start() opens a new one Whatever the provider persists (Chroma, Mem0) Secrets Revoked on stop (unless secrets.revoke_on_stop=False), resolved again on start Revoked Resolved on start Invocation count, budget counters, mission Kept Kept Restored from the journal Dead letters Kept Kept Runs a stop cancelled are restored (with a journal); the others are not Agent-added triggers (open mode) Stopped and dropped Dropped Not restored

docs.title: Recovery on start
docs.text:
With a journal, a new AgentProcess continues from the last checkpoint of the same process name. On the first start() of a process object, when JournalConfig.recover_on_start is True (the default) and the journal holds state for that name, the process restores the context state (the last checkpoint plus the context_update entries written after it; without a checkpoint, for a crash before the first run ended, the context_update entries alone), the mission, the budget counters (a restart can't reset the daily limits), the conversation history and the invocation count. Recovered keys replace the same keys of context.initial_state.

The process writes a checkpoint after every run, on stop() and after a rewind, so this works after a clean stop and after a crash.

from promptise.runtime import AgentProcess, JournalConfig, ProcessConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    journal=JournalConfig(path=".promptise/journal"),  # level="checkpoint"
)
process = AgentProcess("pipeline-watcher", config)
await process.start()
print(process.recovered)
# {'lifecycle_state': 'stopped', 'entries_replayed': 1, 'context_keys': ['counter'],
#  'mission_restored': False, 'budget_restored': False,
#  'conversation_messages': 2, 'invocation_count': 1}

process.recovered is None when nothing was restored. lifecycle_state is the last state the journal recorded: "stopped" after a clean stop, "running" after a crash. A journal that can't be read is logged and the process starts fresh. Set recover_on_start=False to always start fresh. ProcessConfig has no journal by default (level="none"); see Journal and Replay Engine.

docs.title: Trigger events and the queue
docs.text:
Each trigger's events go into one queue per process (1000 events). concurrency workers take events from it in arrival order and run the agent once per event; with concurrency=1 (the default) runs never overlap.

ProcessConfig(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", concurrency=3)  # up to 3 runs in parallel

await process.inject(event) puts a TriggerEvent into the queue by hand, as if a trigger had fired: it resumes an idle-suspended process, passes the file_changed / task_created hooks, and is dead-lettered ("queue full") when the queue is full.

A run that raises is retried when trigger_delivery.max_retries is above 0 (default 0); an event that has used up its retries counts as one consecutive failure. Events blocked by the payload scan, the guardrail scanner or a user_prompt_submit hook are dead-lettered without counting as failures. See Triggers for trigger types, filters and payload handling.

docs.title: Dead letters
docs.text:
process.dead_letters lists the events that were not processed, oldest first. Each entry has event (the TriggerEvent), reason, error, attempts and dead_lettered_at. The list keeps the last trigger_delivery.dead_letter_size entries (default 100).

Reason When "process stopped" Not run yet at stop() (queued, held, running or still inside a trigger), or arriving while the process is stopping or stopped. A run that finished (its task_completed hooks may still be running) is not dead-lettered "budget: max_runs_per_day" The run was refused because max_runs_per_day was reached; redeliver it after the daily reset "process restarting" Held by a worker, or waiting for a retry, when an automatic restart or recycle tears the process down "trigger removed" Still buffered in a trigger, or held by its listener, when the trigger was removed (remove_trigger(), DELETE .../triggers/{id}, the agent's remove_trigger) "process failed" Queued when the process failed, or arriving while it is FAILED "retries exhausted" The run raised and used up trigger_delivery.max_retries "queue full" inject() or a retry found the queue full "trigger buffer full" An event or message trigger's 100-event buffer was full (also counted in the trigger's dropped_events) "flagged by payload scan" trigger_delivery.scan_payloads flagged the payload "blocked by guardrails" The guardrail scanner blocked the run "blocked by hook" A user_prompt_submit hook refused the run 
for entry in process.dead_letters:
    print(entry["reason"], entry["event"].payload)

await process.start()
requeued = await process.redeliver_dead_letters()  # or event_ids=[...]
process.clear_dead_letters()

redeliver_dead_letters(event_ids=None) puts the events back on the queue and returns how many it re-queued; events that don't fit stay in the list. Like inject(), it wakes a process suspended for idle_timeout.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
process.status() returns a JSON-serializable dict:

Key Description name, process_id Identity state Lifecycle state value, e.g. "running" suspend_reason "manual", "idle", "budget", "health", "rewind", or None execution_mode "strict" or "open" invocation_count Completed runs (restored by journal recovery) consecutive_failures Current streak of failed events restart_count Automatic restart attempts in the current failure streak journal_enabled Whether the process has a journal trigger_count, dynamic_trigger_count Running config triggers, agent-added triggers triggers One dict per trigger: id, type, source ("config" or "dynamic"), for a file watch dropped_events and pending_events, and for an event or message trigger dropped_events custom_tool_count, rebuild_count, spawned_process_count Open-mode counters conversation_messages Messages in the conversation buffer has_memory Whether a long-term memory provider is configured queue_size Events waiting in the queue dead_letter_count Entries in dead_letters filtered_count Events skipped by a trigger's filter_expression pending_retries Events waiting for a retry uptime_seconds Seconds since the last start() while the process is up; None before the first start and while it is stopped or failed hook_count Hooks registered on process.hooks recovered Only after a journal recovery: the recovered dict budget Only with a budget: remaining limits health_anomalies, health Only with health monitoring: anomaly count and health status mission_state Only with a mission: its state active_secrets Only with secret scoping: number of active secrets

Other read-only properties: state (ProcessState), context (the AgentContext), lifecycle (the ProcessLifecycle), recovered, suspend_reason, dead_letters, spawned_processes and hooks.

docs.title: Restart policies
docs.text:
When a running process enters FAILED (after max_consecutive_failures failed events in a row), restart_policy decides what happens next.

Policy Behavior "never" The process stays FAILED (default) "on_failure" Tear the process down and start it again, up to max_restarts attempts in a row "always" Same as "on_failure", and a process that reaches max_lifetime is recycled (stopped and started again) instead of stopped 
ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    restart_policy="on_failure",
    max_restarts=5,
    restart_backoff=2.0,          # 2 s, 4 s, 8 s, ... (max 60 s)
    max_consecutive_failures=3,
)

How restarts behave:

  • The first attempt waits restart_backoff seconds; each further attempt in a row doubles the wait, capped at 60 s. A restart whose start() fails counts as an attempt.
  • The attempt count (restart_count) resets after a successful run, so max_restarts limits a streak of failures, not the process's lifetime. A restarted process also starts a fresh max_consecutive_failures streak. max_lifetime recycling doesn't count as an attempt.
  • When max_restarts is used up, the process stays FAILED: a restart_exhausted journal entry is written and process.restart_exhausted is emitted.
  • An explicit stop() never triggers a restart and cancels a pending one. Stops the process makes on purpose (budget on_exceeded="stop", health on_anomaly="stop", mission completion, max_lifetime without "always") are not restarted either.
  • A restart keeps the context state, conversation history, invocation count and process_id. Each restart shuts the old agent down and closes its MCP connections (stdio servers exit) before starting again.
  • A failure of your own start() call is raised to you and not retried.
  • Each attempt emits process.restarted (attempt, max_restarts); each failure emits process.failed with the error.

Only an event whose run raised (after its retries) counts as a failure. A tool that raises does not fail the run: the model sees the error and carries on.

docs.title: Live triggers
docs.text:
add_trigger() and remove_trigger() change a process's config triggers while it runs:

trigger_id = await process.add_trigger({"type": "cron", "cron_expression": "0 * * * *"})
await process.remove_trigger(trigger_id)

On a RUNNING or SUSPENDED process the new trigger starts at once (its events queue while suspended); otherwise it starts with the next start(). Trigger IDs are stable (<type>-<digest of the config>), so removing one trigger leaves the others' IDs unchanged. An invalid config raises ValueError and nothing is added; an unknown ID raises KeyError. See Triggers.

docs.title: Instructions, messages and hooks
docs.text:
• process.update_instructions(text) replaces the system prompt from the next run on. The agent is rebuilt before that run, reusing the connected MCP tools; no restart.
  • await process.send_message(content, ...) and await process.ask(content, timeout=120) reach the agent through its inbox (InboxConfig(enabled=True)); both raise RuntimeError on a stopped or failed process. See Orchestration API.
  • process.hooks is the process's HookManager. It holds the hooks from ProcessConfig.hooks (or a manifest's hooks: section); register more in code:
from promptise.runtime import HookEvent

@process.hooks.on(HookEvent.SESSION_START)
async def announce(ctx):
    print(ctx.process_id, "started; restart:", ctx.data["restart"])

docs.title: Other methods
docs.text:
Method What it does apply_governance_config(section) Applies a changed config.budget, config.health or config.mission to the running process (section is "budget", "health" or "mission"; anything else raises ValueError). Enabling builds the subsystem, disabling drops it, and an enabled one keeps its counters, history or progress. The API's PATCH routes call it await record_operator_action(action, data) Writes a journal entry of type action (for example "api_request") with secret values redacted. Does nothing without a journal; a journal error is logged, never raised fail_mission(reason) Fails the mission as an operator decision and emits mission.failed. Raises RuntimeError without a mission and ValueError when the mission is already completed or failed. See Mission Model await add_dynamic_trigger(config) Adds a trigger on the agent's behalf (open mode). It is not added to config.triggers and lives until stop(), rollback() or remove_trigger() await set_dynamic_instructions(text) Replaces the instructions on the agent's behalf (open mode; what modify_instructions calls). Returns "Rebuild successful" or an "Error: ..." message await spawn_process(name, *, instructions, model=None, triggers=None, execution_mode="strict", runtime=None) Starts a child process in the parent runtime (open mode; what the spawn_process meta-tool calls). The child inherits the parent's limits, hooks and deploy policy await rollback() Undoes the agent's self-modifications (instructions, tools, servers, dynamic triggers) and rebuilds from the original config. Raises RuntimeError in strict mode. It does not touch context state or conversation; use rewind() for those

The open-mode methods are covered on Meta-Tools.

docs.title: Rewind
docs.text:
With a journal, rewind() rolls the context state and/or conversation history back to just before a journal entry. rewind_plan() previews it without changing anything.

plan = await process.rewind_plan(entry_id, mode="both")
print(plan.entries_affected)
result = await process.rewind(entry_id, mode="both")  # also: conversation_only, code_only, summarize, cancel

A running process is suspended (reason "rewind") for the duration, waits for a run in flight, and is resumed afterwards. Long-term memory, budget counters, the mission, secrets and the outside effects of tool calls are never rolled back. Without a journal it raises RuntimeError. From the command line: promptise runtime rewind <process> [<entry_id>] [--mode both|conversation_only|code_only|summarize] [--plan]. See Rewind Engine.

docs.title: Governance
docs.text:
Budget, health, mission, secrets and the inbox are opt-in and add no overhead while disabled. Each has its own config object on ProcessConfig:

Field Config Page budget BudgetConfig(enabled=True, ...) Autonomy Budget health HealthConfig(enabled=True, ...) Behavioral Health mission MissionConfig(enabled=True, ...) Mission Model secrets SecretScopeConfig(enabled=True, ...) Secret Scoping inbox InboxConfig(enabled=True, ...) Orchestration API 
from promptise.runtime import (
    BudgetConfig, HealthConfig, JournalConfig, MissionConfig, ProcessConfig,
    SecretScopeConfig, ToolCostAnnotation, TriggerConfig,
)

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Monitor the data pipeline and respond to incidents.",
    servers={"tools": {"type": "http", "url": "http://localhost:8000/mcp"}},
    triggers=[
        TriggerConfig(type="webhook", webhook_path="/alerts", webhook_port=9090),
        TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *"),
    ],
    concurrency=2,
    restart_policy="on_failure",
    journal=JournalConfig(path="./pipeline-journal"),
    budget=BudgetConfig(
        enabled=True,
        max_tool_calls_per_run=20,
        max_cost_per_day=50.0,
        on_exceeded="pause",
        tool_costs={"restart_service": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=5.0, irreversible=True)},
    ),
    health=HealthConfig(enabled=True, stuck_threshold=3, on_anomaly="escalate"),
    mission=MissionConfig(
        enabled=True,
        objective="Keep all services above 99.9% uptime.",
        success_criteria="No unresolved P1 incidents for more than 15 minutes.",
        eval_every=10,
    ),
    secrets=SecretScopeConfig(
        enabled=True,
        secrets={"api_key": "${MONITORING_API_KEY}"},
        default_ttl=3600,
    ),
)

Start with governance disabled

For local development, leave governance off. Turn it on one subsystem at a time as you move toward production: budget first (runaway cost), then health (stuck agents), then mission (long-running goals).

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Forgetting enabled=True. Every governance config defaults to enabled=False; SecretScopeConfig(secrets={...}) without enabled=True resolves no secrets.
  • Expecting a new process object to start empty. With a journal, a process with the same name continues from its last checkpoint. Use a new journal path, a new name, or recover_on_start=False for a clean start.
  • Losing events at stop. Events that were queued when you stopped are in dead_letters, not lost. Call redeliver_dead_letters() after start() if they should still run.
  • Calling resume() for an idle process. Not needed: the next trigger event wakes it. resume() is for manual, budget and health suspensions.
  • Relying on stop() to free memory. stop() keeps long-term memory and the conversation for the next start(). Use close() (or async with) when you are done with the process.
  • Leaving restart_policy at "never" in production. A failed process then stays FAILED until someone restarts it.

docs.title: Runtime Manager
docs.text:
AgentRuntime runs several agent processes together in one Python process. It keeps a registry of named AgentProcess instances, starts and stops them together or one by one, shares an event notifier, hooks and an event bus between them, and shuts everything down cleanly on SIGTERM or Ctrl+C. Use it when you have more than one agent, or when one agent should run as a long-lived service.

import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import AgentRuntime, ProcessConfig, RuntimeConfig, TriggerConfig

config = RuntimeConfig(
    processes={
        "watcher": ProcessConfig(
            model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
            instructions="You monitor data pipelines and report anomalies.",
            triggers=[TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *")],
            restart_policy="on_failure",
        ),
        "responder": ProcessConfig(
            model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
            instructions="You handle alerts.",
        ),
    },
)


async def main():
    runtime = AgentRuntime(config)  # registers "watcher" and "responder"
    await runtime.run_forever()     # starts both; stops cleanly on SIGTERM / Ctrl+C


asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Creating a runtime
docs.text:
Signature
class AgentRuntime:
    def __init__(
        self,
        config: RuntimeConfig | None = None,  # processes to register, distributed settings
        *,
        event_bus=None,        # shared bus for "event" triggers
        broker=None,           # shared broker for "message" triggers
        event_notifier=None,   # EventNotifier shared by every process
        hooks=None,            # HookManager whose hooks fire for every process
    ) -> None: ...

The processes in config.processes are registered when the runtime is created, in CREATED state; nothing starts until you call start_all(), start_process() or run_forever(). await AgentRuntime.from_config(config, ...) takes the same arguments and is equivalent.

runtime = AgentRuntime(config)
print(runtime.list_processes())
# [{'name': 'watcher', 'state': 'created', 'process_id': '67b6...'},
#  {'name': 'responder', 'state': 'created', 'process_id': '86e2...'}]

docs.title: Shared resources
docs.text:
• event_notifier: every process emits its process.*, invocation.* and governance events through it. A process never stops a shared notifier; stop_all() drains it after the last process has stopped, so every process.stopped is delivered before stop_all() returns.
  • hooks: a HookManager whose hooks run for every process's lifecycle events, after each process's own hooks. ctx.process_id names the process.
  • event_bus and broker: objects you provide; AgentRuntime does not create them. promptise.runtime.InProcessEventBus is a ready-made bus for processes in one Python process, and promptise runtime start gives its runtime one. event triggers call await event_bus.subscribe(event_type, handler) and await event_bus.unsubscribe(event_type, handler); message triggers call await broker.subscribe(topic, handler) (which returns a subscription ID) and await broker.unsubscribe(subscription_id). See Event & Webhook triggers.

docs.title: Registering processes
docs.text:
from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, TriggerConfig

process = await runtime.add_process(
    "data-watcher",
    ProcessConfig(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        instructions="You monitor data pipelines.",
        triggers=[TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/5 * * * *")],
    ),
)

add_process(name, config, *, process_id=None, deploy_policy=None) returns the new AgentProcess (in CREATED state). deploy_policy says where the config came from; the control API passes its own for deploys (limited ${VAR} references, MCP allowlist, data_dir), and code you write leaves it out. Names are unique; a duplicate raises RuntimeBaseError:

Process 'data-watcher' already exists. Use remove_process() first or choose a different name.

await runtime.remove_process(name) works in every state. It stops the process (a FAILED one too, so its triggers, listeners and heartbeat end), closes it (long-term memory closed, secrets revoked, conversation cleared) and removes it from the registry. An unknown name raises KeyError.

docs.title: Loading manifests
docs.text:
process = await runtime.load_manifest("agents/watcher.agent")
process = await runtime.load_manifest("agents/watcher.agent", name_override="watcher-2")

names = await runtime.load_directory("agents/")  # every *.agent file, in name order

load_directory() raises ManifestError when the path is not a directory, and stops at the first manifest that fails to load (re-raising its error); the manifests loaded before it stay registered. See Agent Manifests.

docs.title: Starting and stopping
docs.text:
Method What it does await start_all() Starts every CREATED, STOPPED and FAILED process. A process that fails to start is logged and skipped. With distributed.enabled, the cluster node starts first, and its failure raises. await stop_all() Stops every process that is not STOPPED or CREATED (FAILED and SUSPENDED ones too), then drains the shared event notifier await start_process(name) get_process(name).start() await stop_process(name, *, drain_timeout=0.0) get_process(name).stop(drain_timeout=...) await restart_process(name, *, stop_timeout=30.0) Stops a running or suspended process, then starts it. A FAILED process is torn down by start() itself (old triggers, listeners and heartbeat end first), so nothing fires twice. A process that is already stopping (another stop or restart) is waited for, up to stop_timeout seconds; after that it raises RuntimeError and starts nothing. Context state, long-term memory and conversation history carry over. await shutdown() stop_all(), then closes every process (memory, secrets, conversation), then stops the cluster node. The processes stay registered.

Each method that takes a name raises KeyError for an unknown one.

docs.title: run_forever()
docs.text:
run_forever() is the entry point for a service. It starts every process, waits until shutdown is requested, then calls shutdown(), so every process gets its process.stopped event, a final journal checkpoint and its dead letters before the program exits.

The shutdown is graceful: no new trigger event starts, and runs in flight get up to drain_timeout seconds to finish (default: each process's ProcessConfig.drain_timeout, 5 seconds) before they are cancelled. The processes drain at the same time. A run that is cancelled is journaled and comes back as a dead letter in the next process object (see Graceful stop). A second SIGTERM or Ctrl+C during the wait cancels the runs at once; a third one gets the default action. Keep the drain shorter than your platform's kill deadline: docker stop sends SIGKILL after 10 seconds unless you pass --time, Kubernetes after terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 by default).

await runtime.run_forever()                               # handles SIGTERM and SIGINT
await runtime.run_forever(install_signal_handlers=False)  # you handle signals
await runtime.run_forever(drain_timeout=20)               # wait up to 20 s for runs in flight
await runtime.run_forever(drain_timeout=0)                # cancel runs in flight at once

It returns after:

  • SIGTERM (docker stop, Kubernetes, systemd) or SIGINT (Ctrl+C), when install_signal_handlers=True (the default). The handlers are installed on the running loop for the duration of the call, including the shutdown, and removed afterwards. Where the loop can't install them (Windows, or a thread other than the main one) they are skipped.
  • runtime.request_shutdown(), which is safe to call from your own signal handler or another task. request_shutdown(force=True) also ends a graceful wait that is in progress, and request_shutdown(drain_timeout=N) replaces run_forever()'s drain_timeout for that shutdown.
  • Cancellation of the task running it.
AgentRuntime: received SIGTERM, shutting down

docs.title: async with
docs.text:
async with AgentRuntime(...) as runtime: calls shutdown() on exit, even when the block raises. It does not install signal handlers; a SIGTERM kills the program without a clean stop unless you use run_forever() or call request_shutdown() from your own handler.

async with AgentRuntime() as runtime:
    await runtime.add_process("watcher", config)
    await runtime.start_all()
    await asyncio.sleep(60)
# every process is stopped and closed here

From the command line, promptise runtime start agents/ runs a runtime with the same clean shutdown on SIGTERM and Ctrl+C, and --detach runs it in the background. See CLI Commands.

docs.title: Running several processes
docs.text:
Each process has its own agent, triggers, queue, context, conversation and journal entries. One process failing, restarting or being suspended does not affect the others, and start_all() keeps starting the rest when one fails to start.

All processes share one asyncio event loop. Agent runs and tool calls are async, but a blocking call (a synchronous HTTP request, time.sleep()) in a tool or callback stalls every process until it returns. Each webhook trigger opens its own HTTP server, so give each one its own port.

for name, info in runtime.status()["processes"].items():
    print(name, info["state"], info["invocation_count"], info["restart_count"])

docs.title: Status and monitoring
docs.text:
runtime.status()
# {"process_count": 2,
#  "processes": {"watcher": {...process status...}, "responder": {...}},
#  "cluster": {...}}            # only in distributed mode

runtime.process_status("watcher")  # one process's status() dict
runtime.list_processes()           # [{"name", "state", "process_id"}, ...]
runtime.get_process("watcher")     # the AgentProcess (KeyError if unknown)
runtime.processes                  # dict copy: name -> AgentProcess
print(runtime)                     # AgentRuntime(processes=2, 2 running)

The per-process fields are listed under Status.

docs.title: Distributed mode and presets
docs.text:
With RuntimeConfig(distributed=DistributedConfig(enabled=True, ...)), start_all() and run_forever() first start this node's management transport and then, depending on the config, the cluster coordinator or the registration with one. shutdown() stops them, and runtime.cluster is the running ClusterNode (or None). See Distributed Coordinator and Discovery & Transport.

DEFAULT_DEVELOPMENT_CONFIG and DEFAULT_PRODUCTION_CONFIG are identical: no processes, distributed mode off. Production hardening is set per process (journal, restart_policy, health, budget, trigger_delivery), and distributed mode needs your cluster's coordinator and token, so no preset turns either on.

docs.title: API summary
docs.text: Method / property Description AgentRuntime(config=None, *, event_bus, broker, event_notifier, hooks) Create a runtime; registers config.processes await AgentRuntime.from_config(config, ...) Same as the constructor await add_process(name, config, *, process_id=None, deploy_policy=None) Register a process; returns it await remove_process(name) Stop, close and unregister a process get_process(name) The AgentProcess processes Dict copy of all processes list_processes() name, state, process_id per process await load_manifest(path, *, name_override=None) Register a process from a .agent file await load_directory(path) Register every *.agent file in a directory await start_all() / await stop_all(*, drain_timeout=0.0) Start / stop every process (drain_timeout: let runs in flight finish first; None = each process's drain_timeout) await start_process(name) / await stop_process(name, *, drain_timeout=0.0) / await restart_process(name, *, stop_timeout=30.0) Control one process await shutdown(*, drain_timeout=0.0) Stop and close every process, stop the cluster node await run_forever(*, install_signal_handlers=True, drain_timeout=None) Start everything and run until a signal or request_shutdown(), then stop gracefully request_shutdown(*, force=False) Make run_forever() return (force=True: cancel runs still draining) status() / process_status(name) Status dicts cluster The running ClusterNode, or None await start_distributed() / await stop_distributed() Start / stop the cluster node (start_all() and shutdown() call them)

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Not checking after start_all(). A process that fails to start is only logged. Check status() (or watch for process.failed) to see that every process reached running.
  • Using async with in a container. It does not handle SIGTERM; docker stop then kills the program mid-run. Use run_forever().
  • Reusing a name after a failure. add_process() with an existing name raises. remove_process() first, or use restart_process().
  • Blocking the event loop. A synchronous call in one agent's tool pauses every process in the runtime.
  • Two webhook triggers on one port. Each webhook trigger binds its own server, so two of them on the same port conflict.
  • Expecting the production preset to change behavior. DEFAULT_PRODUCTION_CONFIG is the same as the development preset; configure each process instead.

docs.title: Distributed Mode
docs.text:
Distributed mode lets several AgentRuntimes on different machines (or ports) work as one cluster. Each runtime runs a small management transport (an HTTP API for its processes); one runtime also hosts the coordinator, which knows every node and checks its health. You turn it on with RuntimeConfig.distributed; start_all() and run_forever() start it, shutdown() stops it. Use it when one machine is not enough, or when agents must run close to the systems they work on.

# coordinator.py: hosts the cluster coordinator and one process
import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import AgentRuntime, DistributedConfig, ProcessConfig, RuntimeConfig

config = RuntimeConfig(
    processes={
        "planner": ProcessConfig(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", instructions="Plan the work."),
    },
    distributed=DistributedConfig(
        enabled=True,
        coordinator=True,               # this runtime hosts the coordinator
        node_id="coordinator",
        transport_port=9100,
        auth_token="${CLUSTER_TOKEN}",  # resolved when the transport starts
        heartbeat_interval=5,
    ),
)

asyncio.run(AgentRuntime(config).run_forever())

# node.py: a worker node that registers with the coordinator
import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import AgentRuntime, DistributedConfig, ProcessConfig, RuntimeConfig

config = RuntimeConfig(
    processes={
        "worker": ProcessConfig(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", instructions="Do the work."),
    },
    distributed=DistributedConfig(
        enabled=True,
        node_id="worker-1",
        transport_port=9101,
        coordinator_url="http://127.0.0.1:9100",
        auth_token="${CLUSTER_TOKEN}",
        heartbeat_interval=5,
    ),
)

asyncio.run(AgentRuntime(config).run_forever())

Run both with the same token, then ask the coordinator:

export CLUSTER_TOKEN=$(python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))")
python coordinator.py &
python node.py &

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9100/health
# {"status": "healthy", "node_id": "coordinator", "process_count": 1}

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLUSTER_TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:9100/cluster/nodes
# {"node_id": "coordinator", "nodes": [
#    {"node_id": "coordinator", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:9100", "status": "healthy",
#     "process_count": 1, "metadata": {"role": "coordinator"}, ...},
#    {"node_id": "worker-1", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:9101", "status": "healthy",
#     "process_count": 1, "metadata": {"processes": 1}, ...}], "count": 2}

# Send the worker a trigger event through its transport
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLUSTER_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"payload": {"task": "hello"}}' http://127.0.0.1:9101/processes/worker/event
# {"status": "injected", "event_id": "5650beaa-...", "process": "worker"}

Without the token, /cluster/nodes answers 401. When node.py stops (Ctrl+C or SIGTERM), it unregisters, and the coordinator lists only itself again.

docs.title: What a node runs
docs.text:
With distributed.enabled=True, AgentRuntime.start_all() (and run_forever()) first starts a ClusterNode, then the processes. A failure to start it (a port in use, an unset token variable) raises; the processes don't start. AgentRuntime.shutdown() stops the processes, then the node. runtime.cluster is the running ClusterNode (or None), and runtime.status()["cluster"] summarizes it.

Role Config Runs Coordinator coordinator=True The transport with the /cluster routes, a RuntimeCoordinator that health-checks every node each heartbeat_interval, and its discovery (registry or static). The coordinator lists itself Node coordinator_url=... The transport, plus registration: register at start, re-register every heartbeat_interval (so a restarted coordinator finds the node again), unregister at stop Stand-alone neither The transport only (a static coordinator elsewhere can list it)

A node that can't reach the coordinator still starts; it logs the failure and keeps trying every heartbeat_interval (runtime.status()["cluster"]["last_registration_error"] shows why).

docs.title: Discovery: registry or static
docs.text:
discovery_method How the coordinator learns about nodes "registry" (default) Nodes register themselves at POST /cluster/nodes on the coordinator's transport. A node that hasn't re-registered for node_timeout seconds is dropped "static" The coordinator lists the nodes in static_nodes (node_id -> URL). Nodes don't register (POST /cluster/nodes answers 409) "multicast" Rejected: discovery_method='multicast' is not implemented. Use 'registry' (nodes register with the coordinator at coordinator_url) or 'static' (list the nodes in static_nodes on the coordinator).

A static coordinator:

DistributedConfig(
    enabled=True,
    coordinator=True,
    discovery_method="static",
    static_nodes={
        "worker-1": "http://10.0.0.11:9100",
        "worker-2": "http://10.0.0.12:9100",
    },
    transport_host="0.0.0.0",
    advertise_url="http://10.0.0.10:9100",
    auth_token="${CLUSTER_TOKEN}",
)

The workers then run stand-alone (enabled=True, no coordinator_url) with the same token.

docs.title: DistributedConfig
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description enabled bool False Start the transport (and the coordinator or registration) with the runtime coordinator bool False This runtime hosts the coordinator coordinator_url str \| None None Base URL of the coordinator's transport; this node registers there node_id str \| None None This node's ID. Default <hostname>-<port> transport_host str "127.0.0.1" Interface the transport binds transport_port int 9100 Port of the transport; 0 picks a free port. Ports 1-1024 are rejected advertise_url str \| None None URL other nodes reach this one at. Default http://<transport_host>:<port>. Required with a wildcard transport_host on a coordinator or a registering node auth_token SecretStr \| None None The cluster bearer token, or a ${ENV_VAR} reference resolved when the transport starts allow_unauthenticated bool False Allow a non-loopback transport or coordinator without auth_token discovery_method "registry" \| "static" \| "multicast" "registry" How the coordinator finds nodes ("multicast" is rejected) static_nodes dict[str, str] {} node_id -> URL, for a coordinator with discovery_method="static" allowed_node_hosts list[str] [] For a registry coordinator: the hosts a registering node's URL may name (*.example.com matches subdomains); others get 403. Empty: any host heartbeat_interval float 15.0 Seconds between the coordinator's health checks and between a node's re-registrations node_timeout float \| None None Seconds without a successful health check (or re-registration) before a node counts as unhealthy (or is dropped from the registry). Default 3 * heartbeat_interval

URLs must be http:// or https:// with a host; a trailing slash is removed. Unknown keys are ignored with a FutureWarning. In a JSON dump (RuntimeConfig.to_dict()), a literal auth_token is written as "**********" and a ${VAR} reference as is; loading the masked placeholder back is an error.

Inconsistent combinations fail when the config is built, each with a message that says what to change:

  • coordinator=True together with coordinator_url;
  • static_nodes without coordinator=True and discovery_method="static";
  • discovery_method="static" with coordinator_url (static nodes don't register);
  • a non-loopback transport_host, or a coordinator_url on another host, without auth_token (unless allow_unauthenticated=True);
  • a wildcard transport_host (0.0.0.0, ::) without advertise_url on a coordinator or registering node;
  • an empty auth_token.

DEFAULT_DEVELOPMENT_CONFIG and DEFAULT_PRODUCTION_CONFIG both leave distributed mode off: it needs your cluster's addresses and token, which no preset can know.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
One cluster token authenticates everything:

  • requests to every node's transport (all routes except GET /health need Authorization: Bearer <token>; compared in constant time);
  • a node's registration with the coordinator;
  • the coordinator's health checks and requests to the nodes.

Generate it once (secrets.token_urlsafe(32)), give it to every node through an environment variable, and reference it as auth_token="${CLUSTER_TOKEN}" so it never sits in code or config files. A transport without a token logs a warning at start: any local process could manage that runtime. A node started with the wrong token is refused by the coordinator (401) and keeps retrying, logging the failure.

The transport speaks plain HTTP. Across an untrusted network, put the nodes behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy and use https:// URLs for coordinator_url, advertise_url and static_nodes.

The coordinator calls every registered node URL with the cluster token, so a token holder could register an internal address and have the coordinator send requests there. On a registry coordinator, set allowed_node_hosts to your nodes' hosts (see Security).

docs.title: ClusterNode
docs.text:
ClusterNode(runtime, config) is what AgentRuntime creates; you rarely build one yourself.

Member Description await start() Start the transport, then the coordinator (and its prune loop for registry discovery) or the registration. Raises ValueError when the token's ${ENV_VAR} is not set, OSError when the port can't be bound. Calling it twice does nothing await stop() Unregister (best effort), stop the coordinator's health monitor and the transport role "coordinator", "node" or "standalone" node_id, url This node's ID and advertised URL (known after start()) transport, coordinator, discovery The RuntimeTransport, and on a coordinator the RuntimeCoordinator and its discovery registered, last_registration_error Registration state of a node status() node_id, role, url, discovery_method, authenticated; plus coordinator_url, registered (and last_registration_error) on a node, nodes and healthy_nodes on a coordinator await prune() On a registry coordinator: unregister nodes whose registration expired; returns their IDs

AgentRuntime.start_distributed() and stop_distributed() start and stop the node on their own, without the processes.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Port 9100 twice. DistributedConfig.transport_port and OrchestrationAPI(port=...) both default to 9100. On one host, give each node and each control API its own port.
  • 0.0.0.0 without advertise_url. Other nodes can't connect to a wildcard address; the config refuses it on a coordinator or registering node.
  • An unset token variable. auth_token="${CLUSTER_TOKEN}" is resolved at start; when the variable is missing, start_all() raises ValueError: distributed.auth_token: Environment variable 'CLUSTER_TOKEN' not found and no process starts.
  • A short node_timeout. A registry node that misses re-registrations for node_timeout seconds is dropped. Keep it at least two or three heartbeat_intervals (the default is three).
  • Expecting failover. The coordinator monitors health; it does not move processes. When a node fails, your code picks a healthy node (coordinator.healthy_nodes) and starts the process there (start_process_on_node).
  • Expecting promptise runtime start to join a cluster. The CLI runs a runtime without a RuntimeConfig, so distributed mode is configured in Python, as above.
  • The coordinator as a single point. It is not replicated. If it goes away, nodes keep running and keep trying to register; a restarted coordinator finds them again within one heartbeat_interval.

docs.title: Distributed Coordinator
docs.text:
The RuntimeCoordinator is the part of a cluster that knows every node: it keeps a registry of runtime nodes, checks their health periodically, aggregates their status, and runs remote operations (start, stop, inject events) on them. It does not move processes on its own: when a node fails, your code picks a healthy node (healthy_nodes) and starts the process there (start_process_on_node).

In a cluster built with distributed mode, you don't create it yourself: DistributedConfig(enabled=True, coordinator=True) makes the runtime host one, exposes it on its transport (/cluster/nodes, /cluster/status), and lets nodes register. Use the class directly to monitor or drive nodes from your own code:

from promptise.runtime.distributed.coordinator import RuntimeCoordinator

async with RuntimeCoordinator(
    health_check_interval=15.0,
    node_timeout=45.0,
    auth_token="cluster-token",  # bearer token for the nodes' RuntimeTransport
) as coordinator:
    coordinator.register_node("node-1", "http://host1:9100")
    coordinator.register_node("node-2", "http://host2:9100")

    # Check cluster health
    health = await coordinator.check_health()
    print(health)
    # {"node-1": {"status": "healthy"}, "node-2": {"status": "healthy"}}

    # Get aggregated cluster status
    status = await coordinator.cluster_status()

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
In a distributed deployment, agent processes run across multiple machines (nodes). Each node runs an AgentRuntime with a RuntimeTransport HTTP server. The coordinator sits at the center, providing:

  • Node registry: track which nodes exist and their URLs.
  • Health monitoring: periodic HTTP health checks to detect node failures.
  • Cluster status: aggregate process counts and health across all nodes.
  • Remote operations: start/stop processes and inject events on remote nodes.
         ┌──────────────┐
         │  Coordinator  │
         └──────┬───────┘
          ┌─────┼─────┐
          │     │     │
     ┌────▼──┐ │  ┌──▼────┐
     │Node 1 │ │  │Node 3 │
     │Runtime │ │  │Runtime │
     └───────┘ │  └───────┘
          ┌────▼──┐
          │Node 2 │
          │Runtime │
          └───────┘

docs.title: Hosted by a runtime
docs.text:
With DistributedConfig(coordinator=True), the runtime's ClusterNode builds the coordinator with health_check_interval=heartbeat_interval, node_timeout=node_timeout (default three heartbeat intervals) and the cluster auth_token, registers itself (metadata {"role": "coordinator"}) and every entry of static_nodes, and starts the health monitor. Its transport then serves:

Route Description GET /cluster/nodes The registered nodes (NodeInfo.to_dict() each) and count. With registry discovery, expired registrations are pruned first POST /cluster/nodes Register or refresh a node: {"node_id": "...", "url": "http://...", "metadata": {...}}. 422 for a bad node_id (^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._:-]{0,127}$), URL (http/https with a host) or metadata; 403 for a host not in allowed_node_hosts; 409 for the coordinator's own ID or with static discovery DELETE /cluster/nodes/{node_id} Unregister a node (404 when unknown, 409 for the coordinator itself) GET /cluster/status cluster_status() plus "coordinator": <node_id>

Every /cluster route needs the cluster bearer token. runtime.cluster.coordinator is the RuntimeCoordinator object, for the remote operations below.

docs.title: Registering nodes
docs.text:
from promptise.runtime.distributed.coordinator import RuntimeCoordinator

coordinator = RuntimeCoordinator()

# Register nodes with their transport URLs
node1 = coordinator.register_node("node-1", "http://host1:9100")
node2 = coordinator.register_node(
    "node-2",
    "http://host2:9100",
    metadata={"region": "us-east", "capacity": "high"},
    auth_token="node-2-token",  # overrides the coordinator's auth_token
)

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Nodes that bind a non-loopback address must run RuntimeTransport(auth_token=...). The coordinator sends Authorization: Bearer <token> on every request: the node's own auth_token from register_node(), or else the coordinator's auth_token. Tokens are never included in NodeInfo.to_dict() or cluster_status().

docs.title: Unregistering nodes
docs.text:
coordinator.unregister_node("node-1")

Raises KeyError if the node is not registered.

docs.title: Querying nodes
docs.text:
# Get a specific node
node = coordinator.get_node("node-1")
print(node.url)       # "http://host1:9100"
print(node.status)    # "healthy" or "unhealthy" or "unknown"
print(node.is_healthy)  # True/False

# All registered nodes
all_nodes = coordinator.nodes  # dict[str, NodeInfo]

# Only healthy nodes
healthy = coordinator.healthy_nodes  # list[NodeInfo]

docs.title: NodeInfo
docs.text:
Information about a runtime node in the cluster:

Field Type Default Description node_id str required Unique node identifier url str required Base URL for the node's transport API last_heartbeat float now (time.monotonic()) Monotonic time of the last successful health check status str "unknown" "healthy", "unhealthy", or "unknown" process_count int 0 Number of processes on this node metadata dict[str, Any] {} Additional node metadata

is_healthy is status == "healthy", and to_dict() gives the JSON form (never the node's token). NodeUnreachableError(message, *, node_id) carries the node in .node_id.

from promptise.runtime.distributed.coordinator import NodeInfo

node = NodeInfo(
    node_id="node-1",
    url="http://host1:9100",
    metadata={"region": "us-east"},
)
print(node.is_healthy)  # False (status defaults to "unknown")

docs.title: Automatic monitoring
docs.text:
The coordinator runs a background health check loop when used as a context manager:

async with RuntimeCoordinator(
    health_check_interval=15.0,  # Check every 15 seconds
    node_timeout=45.0,           # Consider unhealthy after 45s
) as coordinator:
    coordinator.register_node("node-1", "http://host1:9100")
    # Health checks run automatically in the background

docs.title: Manual health checks
docs.text:
# Check all nodes now
health = await coordinator.check_health()
# {
#     "node-1": {"status": "healthy", "process_count": 3},
#     "node-2": {"status": "unhealthy", "error": "Connection refused"},
# }

Health checks make HTTP GET requests to each node's /health endpoint. Nodes that respond with status 200 are marked healthy. A node that has never answered, or has failed checks for longer than node_timeout since its last successful one, is marked unhealthy. A healthy node that misses a check within node_timeout stays healthy (its entry in the result carries "missed_check": true and the error), so one dropped request does not flap the cluster view.

A failing health round is logged and the background monitor keeps running.

docs.title: Starting and stopping the monitor
docs.text:
coordinator = RuntimeCoordinator()
await coordinator.start_health_monitor()
# ... health checks run in background ...
await coordinator.stop_health_monitor()

docs.title: Cluster Status
docs.text:
Aggregate status across all nodes:

status = await coordinator.cluster_status()
# {
#     "total_nodes": 3,
#     "healthy_nodes": 2,
#     "unhealthy_nodes": 1,
#     "total_processes": 8,
#     "nodes": {
#         "node-1": {
#             "node_id": "node-1",
#             "url": "http://host1:9100",
#             "status": "healthy",
#             "process_count": 3,
#             "health": {"status": "healthy"},
#             ...
#         },
#         ...
#     },
# }

docs.title: Single node status
docs.text:
Get detailed status from a specific node via HTTP:

node_status = await coordinator.get_node_status("node-1")
# Full runtime.status() response from the remote node

Like the remote operations, it raises RuntimeError when the node answers with an error status and NodeUnreachableError (a RuntimeError subclass) when the node can't be reached.

docs.title: Remote Operations
docs.text:
Remote operations raise RuntimeError when the node answers with an error status (401 wrong token, 404 unknown process, 500 failed start, ...), so a failure is never mistaken for success. A node that can't be reached at all (connection refused, a DNS failure, a timeout) raises NodeUnreachableError, a RuntimeError subclass with the node_id, so except RuntimeError handles both and failover code can tell a down node apart:

from promptise.runtime.distributed import NodeUnreachableError

try:
    await coordinator.start_process_on_node("node-1", "data-watcher")
except NodeUnreachableError:
    await coordinator.start_process_on_node("node-2", "data-watcher")

docs.title: Start a process on a remote node
docs.text:
result = await coordinator.start_process_on_node("node-1", "data-watcher")
# {"status": "started", "name": "data-watcher"}

docs.title: Stop a process on a remote node
docs.text:
result = await coordinator.stop_process_on_node("node-1", "data-watcher")
# {"status": "stopped", "name": "data-watcher"}

docs.title: Inject a trigger event on a remote node
docs.text:
Send a trigger event to a specific process on a remote node:

result = await coordinator.inject_event_on_node(
    "node-1",
    "data-watcher",
    payload={"alert": "high_error_rate", "rate": 0.15},
    trigger_type="remote",
)
# {"status": "injected", "event_id": "...", "process": "data-watcher"}

docs.title: API Summary
docs.text: Method / Property Description RuntimeCoordinator(*, health_check_interval=15.0, node_timeout=45.0, auth_token=None) Create a coordinator (all keyword-only) register_node(node_id, url, metadata=None, *, auth_token=None) Register (or replace) a runtime node; returns its NodeInfo unregister_node(node_id) Remove a node get_node(node_id) Get NodeInfo for a node nodes Read-only dict of all nodes healthy_nodes List of healthy nodes await start_health_monitor() Start background health checks await stop_health_monitor() Stop health checks await check_health() Check all nodes now await cluster_status() Aggregate status across all nodes await get_node_status(node_id) Detailed status from a remote node await start_process_on_node(node_id, name) Start a remote process await stop_process_on_node(node_id, name) Stop a remote process await inject_event_on_node(node_id, name, payload, trigger_type="remote") Inject event into remote process

docs.title: Tips and Gotchas
docs.text:
Use the context manager

async with RuntimeCoordinator() as coordinator: automatically starts the health monitor on entry and stops it on exit. This is the recommended pattern.

Keep node_timeout at about 3x health_check_interval

A node that misses three consecutive health checks (45s with 15s intervals, the defaults) is likely down, not just experiencing a transient network issue. DistributedConfig.node_timeout defaults to 3 * heartbeat_interval for the same reason.

aiohttp shipped with base install

All HTTP-based operations (health checks, remote commands, status queries) use aiohttp, which is included in the base pip install promptise.

Plain HTTP

The coordinator authenticates with bearer tokens but talks to nodes over plain HTTP unless the node URLs are https://. Across an untrusted network, put the nodes behind a TLS reverse proxy.

Coordinator is a single point of failure

The coordinator itself is not replicated. If it stops, the nodes keep running their processes and keep trying to register; a restarted coordinator (registry discovery) finds them again within one heartbeat_interval, but its health history starts over.

docs.title: Service Discovery and Transport
docs.text:
The distributed runtime uses two complementary systems: service discovery for nodes to find each other, and transport for remote management via HTTP. Together, they enable multi-node agent deployments where processes can be started, stopped, monitored, and triggered across machines.

With distributed mode (DistributedConfig(enabled=True)), every runtime builds its own RuntimeTransport, and the coordinator its discovery, from the config. This page documents the pieces themselves: the HTTP routes every node serves, and the discovery classes, for when you call them directly or assemble a cluster by hand.

from promptise.runtime.distributed.discovery import StaticDiscovery, RegistryDiscovery
from promptise.runtime.distributed.transport import RuntimeTransport
from promptise.runtime import AgentRuntime

# Discovery: nodes find each other
discovery = StaticDiscovery(nodes={
    "node-1": "http://host1:9100",
    "node-2": "http://host2:9100",
})
nodes = await discovery.discover()

# Transport: expose a node for remote management
runtime = AgentRuntime()
async with RuntimeTransport(runtime, port=9100) as transport:
    # HTTP API now available at http://127.0.0.1:9100/ (this machine only)
    ...

docs.title: Service Discovery
docs.text: Service discovery provides mechanisms for runtime nodes to find each other. Two implementations are provided:

docs.title: ProcessDiscovery Protocol
docs.text:
All discovery implementations satisfy this protocol:

Protocol (promptise.runtime.distributed.discovery)
from typing import Protocol

from promptise.runtime.distributed.discovery import DiscoveredNode


class ProcessDiscovery(Protocol):
    async def discover(self) -> list[DiscoveredNode]:
        """Discover available runtime nodes."""
        ...

    async def register(self, node_id: str, url: str, metadata: dict | None = None) -> None:
        """Register this node for discovery by others."""
        ...

    async def unregister(self, node_id: str) -> None:
        """Remove this node from discovery."""
        ...

docs.title: DiscoveredNode
docs.text:
Each discovered node is represented as a DiscoveredNode dataclass:

Field Type Default Description node_id str required Unique node identifier url str required Base URL for the node's transport API discovered_at float now (time.monotonic()) Monotonic time the node was discovered or last refreshed metadata dict[str, Any] {} Additional node metadata

to_dict() returns the fields as a dict.

docs.title: StaticDiscovery
docs.text:
A simple discovery mechanism for fixed-topology deployments where all node addresses are known at configuration time.

from promptise.runtime.distributed.discovery import StaticDiscovery

discovery = StaticDiscovery(nodes={
    "node-1": "http://host1:9100",
    "node-2": "http://host2:9100",
    "node-3": "http://host3:9100",
})

# Discover all nodes
nodes = await discovery.discover()
for node in nodes:
    print(f"{node.node_id}: {node.url}")

# Add a node dynamically
await discovery.register("node-4", "http://host4:9100")

# Remove a node
await discovery.unregister("node-2")

Best for:

  • Development and testing environments
  • Small, fixed-size clusters
  • Deployments where node addresses are known at startup

docs.title: RegistryDiscovery
docs.text:
A dynamic registry where nodes register themselves and discover each other. Stale registrations are pruned after a TTL (default 60 seconds). The object lives in one Python process; a coordinator started with distributed mode holds one (with ttl=node_timeout) and exposes it over HTTP as POST /cluster/nodes, so nodes on other machines register by calling that route.

from promptise.runtime.distributed.discovery import RegistryDiscovery

registry = RegistryDiscovery(ttl=60.0)  # 60-second TTL

# Nodes register themselves at startup
await registry.register("node-1", "http://host1:9100", metadata={"region": "us-east"})
await registry.register("node-2", "http://host2:9100", metadata={"region": "eu-west"})

# Discover all active nodes
nodes = await registry.discover()  # Prunes stale entries first

# Nodes send periodic heartbeats to stay registered
await registry.heartbeat("node-1")

# Unregister on shutdown
await registry.unregister("node-1")

docs.title: TTL and stale pruning
docs.text:
Nodes that do not refresh their registration within the TTL are automatically removed:

registry = RegistryDiscovery(ttl=30.0)

await registry.register("node-1", "http://host1:9100")
# ... 30+ seconds pass without heartbeat ...
nodes = await registry.discover()  # node-1 is pruned

docs.title: Thread safety
docs.text:
RegistryDiscovery uses an asyncio.Lock for all operations, making it safe for concurrent use.

Best for:

  • Dynamic clusters where nodes come and go
  • Single-process testing with multiple logical nodes
  • The coordinator of a cluster (discovery_method="registry", the default)

Over HTTP, a node refreshes its registration by posting it again (a ClusterNode does that every heartbeat_interval); heartbeat() is the in-process equivalent.

docs.title: RuntimeTransport
docs.text: The RuntimeTransport exposes an AgentRuntime as an HTTP API for remote management. It runs an aiohttp server that handles process control, status queries, and event injection.

docs.title: Creating a transport
docs.text:
import os

from promptise.runtime import AgentRuntime
from promptise.runtime.distributed.transport import RuntimeTransport

runtime = AgentRuntime()
transport = RuntimeTransport(
    runtime,
    host="0.0.0.0",                     # reachable from other machines
    port=9100,
    node_id="node-1",
    auth_token=os.environ["PROMPTISE_NODE_TOKEN"],  # required off loopback
)

await transport.start()
# HTTP API available on port 9100 of every interface
await transport.stop()

The default host is 127.0.0.1 (this machine only). Pass port=0 to let the OS pick a free port; transport.port reports it after start().

Argument Default Description runtime required The AgentRuntime to manage host "127.0.0.1" Interface to bind port 9100 Port (0: a free one) node_id "node-1" This node's ID (in /health and /status) auth_token None Bearer token for every route except GET /health; required off loopback allow_unauthenticated False Allow a non-loopback bind without a token coordinator None A RuntimeCoordinator: adds the /cluster routes (this node hosts the coordinator) discovery None The coordinator's discovery (RegistryDiscovery or StaticDiscovery) allowed_node_hosts None Hosts a node registering at POST /cluster/nodes may name in its URL (*.example.com matches subdomains); others get 403. None or empty: any host

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The transport can start, stop and drive your agents, so it is locked down by default:

Rule Behaviour Bearer token With auth_token set, every endpoint except GET /health requires Authorization: Bearer <token> (compared in constant time). Missing or wrong token, including a header with non-ASCII bytes: 401. Public bind needs a token RuntimeTransport(host="0.0.0.0") (or any non-loopback address) without auth_token raises ValueError. If an authenticating proxy or a private network you control already protects the port, opt out explicitly with allow_unauthenticated=True (a warning is logged at start). Loopback bind blocks browsers On 127.0.0.1 / localhost / ::1, a request whose Host header is not a loopback name gets 421 (DNS rebinding), and a request with an Origin header from a non-loopback origin gets 403. A web page you visit cannot drive the local runtime. Non-browser clients (the coordinator, curl, scripts) send no Origin and are unaffected. Empty token auth_token="" raises ValueError. Node URLs POST /cluster/nodes takes http:// or https:// URLs with a host only (422 otherwise), and only hosts in allowed_node_hosts when it is set (403).

Registered URLs receive the cluster token

The coordinator sends health checks and management calls, with the cluster token, to every URL registered at POST /cluster/nodes. Anyone holding the token can register a URL, and so make the coordinator send requests (and the token) to any host it can reach, internal services included. Set allowed_node_hosts (DistributedConfig.allowed_node_hosts) to your nodes' host names or a domain such as *.cluster.internal, or use static discovery, where only your config lists nodes.

Use TLS (a reverse proxy) when the token crosses an untrusted network: the transport itself speaks plain HTTP.

Changed in 1.3.0

A non-loopback bind without auth_token used to log a warning and serve every endpoint unauthenticated. It now raises ValueError unless you pass allow_unauthenticated=True.

docs.title: Context manager
docs.text:
async with RuntimeTransport(runtime, port=9100, auth_token="node-token") as transport:
    # Server running
    ...
# Server stopped automatically

docs.title: HTTP API Endpoints
docs.text: The transport exposes the following REST endpoints:

docs.title: Health check
docs.text:
GET /health

Response:

{
    "status": "healthy",
    "node_id": "node-1",
    "process_count": 3
}

docs.title: Runtime status
docs.text:
GET /status

Returns the full runtime.status() dict including per-process status, plus the node_id.

docs.title: List processes
docs.text:
GET /processes

Response:

{
    "node_id": "node-1",
    "processes": [
        {"name": "watcher", "state": "running", "process_id": "abc123"},
        {"name": "handler", "state": "stopped", "process_id": "def456"}
    ]
}

docs.title: Process status
docs.text:
GET /processes/{name}/status

Returns the status dict for a single process. Returns 404 if the process does not exist.

docs.title: Start a process
docs.text:
POST /processes/{name}/start

Response (200):

{"status": "started", "name": "watcher"}

docs.title: Stop a process
docs.text:
POST /processes/{name}/stop

Response (200):

{"status": "stopped", "name": "watcher"}

docs.title: Restart a process
docs.text:
POST /processes/{name}/restart

Response (200):

{"status": "restarted", "name": "watcher"}

docs.title: Inject event
docs.text:
POST /processes/{name}/event

Request body (a JSON object; payload and metadata must be objects when given and default to {}):

{
    "trigger_id": "remote",
    "trigger_type": "remote",
    "payload": {"alert": "high_error_rate"},
    "metadata": {}
}

Response (202):

{
    "status": "injected",
    "event_id": "...",
    "process": "watcher"
}

docs.title: Cluster routes (coordinator only)
docs.text: A transport created with coordinator= also serves GET /cluster/nodes, POST /cluster/nodes (register or refresh {"node_id", "url", "metadata"}), DELETE /cluster/nodes/{node_id} and GET /cluster/status. See Coordinator for the request and response details.

docs.title: Error responses
docs.text:
All endpoints return appropriate HTTP error codes:

Code Meaning 200 Success 202 Accepted (async operations like event injection) 400 Bad request (invalid JSON, body or payload/metadata not an object) 401 Missing or wrong bearer token 403 Cross-origin browser request (loopback bind) 404 Process (or, on /cluster, node) not found 409 Cluster routes: registering with static discovery, or the coordinator's own ID 421 Host header is not a loopback name (loopback bind) 422 Cluster routes: a bad node_id, url or metadata 500 Internal server error

docs.title: Putting It Together
docs.text:
For a real cluster, let the config wire everything: see the two-node setup in Distributed Mode. By hand, the same pieces look like this (a node with a transport, and a coordinator that knows it):

import asyncio
import os

from promptise.runtime import AgentRuntime, ProcessConfig
from promptise.runtime.distributed.coordinator import RuntimeCoordinator
from promptise.runtime.distributed.transport import RuntimeTransport

TOKEN = os.environ["CLUSTER_TOKEN"]

async def run_node() -> None:
    runtime = AgentRuntime()
    await runtime.add_process("watcher", ProcessConfig(
        model="openai:gpt-5-mini", instructions="Monitor data.",
    ))
    await runtime.start_all()
    async with RuntimeTransport(runtime, port=9101, node_id="node-1", auth_token=TOKEN):
        await asyncio.Event().wait()   # serve until cancelled
    await runtime.shutdown()

async def run_coordinator() -> None:
    async with RuntimeCoordinator(auth_token=TOKEN) as coordinator:
        coordinator.register_node("node-1", "http://127.0.0.1:9101")
        while True:
            status = await coordinator.cluster_status()
            print(status["healthy_nodes"], "of", status["total_nodes"], "nodes healthy")
            await asyncio.sleep(15)

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text: Class Description ProcessDiscovery Protocol for discovery implementations DiscoveredNode Dataclass for discovered nodes StaticDiscovery(nodes=None) Fixed-topology discovery (node_id -> URL) RegistryDiscovery(ttl=60.0) Dynamic registry with TTL; heartbeat(node_id) refreshes an entry

docs.title: Transport
docs.text: Method / Property Description RuntimeTransport(runtime, *, host="127.0.0.1", port=9100, node_id="node-1", auth_token=None, allow_unauthenticated=False, coordinator=None, discovery=None, allowed_node_hosts=None) Create a transport server node_id This node's unique identifier port The port being listened on (the OS-assigned one after start() with port=0) await start() Start the HTTP server await stop() Stop the HTTP server

docs.title: Tips and Gotchas
docs.text:
Let distributed mode host the registry

DistributedConfig(coordinator=True) gives the coordinator a RegistryDiscovery and serves it as POST /cluster/nodes; nodes with coordinator_url register at start and re-register every heartbeat_interval. Stale nodes are pruned.

Event injection for cross-node coordination

Use the POST /processes/{name}/event endpoint to trigger processes on remote nodes. This enables cross-node agent coordination without shared message brokers.

aiohttp shipped with base install

The RuntimeTransport uses aiohttp, which is included in the base pip install promptise.

One token per node, plain HTTP

auth_token is a single shared secret with full control of the node, and the transport does not terminate TLS. In production, put nodes behind a TLS reverse proxy or on a private network, and give each node its own token (RuntimeCoordinator.register_node(..., auth_token=...)).

RegistryDiscovery lives in one Python process

The registry is in memory. Across machines, nodes reach it through the coordinator's transport (/cluster/nodes); a restarted coordinator starts with an empty registry and fills it as nodes re-register.

Trailing slashes are stripped

Both StaticDiscovery and RegistryDiscovery strip trailing slashes from URLs to ensure consistent URL construction.
