docs.title: Autonomy Budget
docs.text:
An autonomy budget puts explicit limits on what an agent may do on its own: tool calls, LLM turns, abstract cost units and irreversible actions, per run and per day. The runtime refuses a tool call that would cross a limit before the tool runs, and then pauses, stops or escalates the process. The agent can see what is left of its budget, so it can plan around it.

from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, BudgetConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Process customer support tickets.",
    budget=BudgetConfig(enabled=True, max_tool_calls_per_run=20, max_runs_per_day=200),
)

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: Without a budget, an autonomous agent can loop indefinitely, call expensive APIs without limit, or take irreversible actions at 3am with no guardrails. The autonomy budget defines the envelope within which the agent operates freely. Anything outside that envelope stops the agent until a human looks at it.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, BudgetConfig, EscalationTarget, ToolCostAnnotation

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Process customer support tickets.",
    budget=BudgetConfig(
        enabled=True,
        max_tool_calls_per_run=20,
        max_llm_turns_per_run=10,
        max_cost_per_run=25.0,
        max_tool_calls_per_day=500,
        max_cost_per_day=100.0,
        tool_costs={
            "stripe_charge": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=5.0, irreversible=True),
            "send_email": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=2.0, irreversible=True),
            "search": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=0.5),
        },
        on_exceeded="escalate",   # "pause", "stop", or "escalate"
        daily_reset_hour_utc=6,   # the budget day runs 06:00-06:00 UTC
        inject_remaining=True,    # Show budget in agent context
        escalation=EscalationTarget(
            webhook_url="https://hooks.slack.com/...",
        ),
    ),
)

Or in a .agent manifest:

name: support-agent
model: openai:gpt-5-mini
budget:
  enabled: true
  max_tool_calls_per_run: 20
  max_cost_per_day: 100.0
  on_exceeded: escalate
  inject_remaining: true
  tool_costs:
    stripe_charge:
      cost_weight: 5.0
      irreversible: true
    search:
      cost_weight: 0.5
  escalation:
    webhook_url: "https://hooks.slack.com/..."

An unknown key under budget: is rejected in a manifest; in Python, BudgetConfig ignores it with a FutureWarning.

docs.title: Per-run and daily tracking
docs.text:
The budget system tracks two scopes:

  • Per-run: Resets at the start of every invocation. Limits how much the agent can do in a single trigger-driven execution.
  • Per-day: Limits total daily activity. The budget day runs from daily_reset_hour_utc (default 0, midnight UTC) to the same hour the next day.

The daily counters are reset when a run starts and the last reset happened before the most recent reset hour. With daily_reset_hour_utc=6, a run at 05:59 UTC still counts toward the previous day, and the first run at or after 06:00 UTC resets the counters and emits budget.daily_reset. Nothing resets while no run starts, so process.status()["budget"] can show the previous day's usage until the next run.

docs.title: Counters survive restarts
docs.text:
Within one process object, the counters live in memory: stop() / start() and restart_process() keep them.

With a journal, they also survive a new process object (a restarted runtime, a redeploy under the same name). Every checkpoint stores the budget counters: after each run, after a failed run, after a run refused by max_runs_per_day, and on stop(). On the first start(), with journal.recover_on_start on (the default), the daily counters and the time of the last daily reset are restored, so a restart can't reset the daily limits. The per-run counters start at zero. process.recovered["budget_restored"] says whether it happened.

from promptise.runtime import BudgetConfig, JournalConfig, ProcessConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    journal=JournalConfig(level="checkpoint", path=".promptise/journal"),
    budget=BudgetConfig(enabled=True, max_tool_calls_per_day=500),
)

If the restored counters are from before the most recent reset hour, the next run resets them as usual. A journal that has no checkpoint for the process name, or a checkpoint without budget counters, leaves them at zero.

docs.title: Understanding cost_weight
docs.text:
Critical: cost_weight is NOT real money

Budget cost is measured in abstract weight units that you define, not dollars. A cost_weight=5.0 means "5 budget units", not $5. The framework does not connect to any LLM provider's pricing API, does not know your token rates, and does not track actual monetary spend.

You are responsible for defining what the numbers mean and keeping them aligned with reality.

docs.title: What the budget tracks and what it does NOT
docs.text:
Tracked Not tracked Tool calls (counted and weighted by cost_weight) LLM API costs (token pricing from OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) LLM turns (counted, but with zero cost) Actual dollar spend on any provider Irreversible actions (counted) Infrastructure costs (compute, network, storage) Abstract cost units (sum of cost_weight values) Real-time exchange rates or dynamic pricing

This means: An agent with max_cost_per_day=100.0 and zero tool cost annotations can make unlimited LLM API calls, whatever they cost in tokens: the budget system will not stop it, because LLM turns have no cost weight. Use max_llm_turns_per_run to cap them by count.

The budget system controls what the agent does (which tools it calls, how many times), not how much it costs the provider.

docs.title: Default behavior for unannotated tools
docs.text:
Any tool without a ToolCostAnnotation entry defaults to cost_weight=1.0. This means:

# These two are identical:
tool_costs={"search": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=1.0)}
# vs. not listing "search" at all (it defaults to 1.0)

If you want a tool to be "free" (not consume budget), set cost_weight to a very small value:

tool_costs={"health_check": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=0.01)}

docs.title: Approach 1: Relative risk weighting (recommended)
docs.text:
Assign weights based on how expensive or risky the tool is relative to a baseline read operation (weight 1.0). This is the simplest approach, and it holds up when prices change: you don't need to know actual dollar costs.

tool_costs={
    # Baseline: internal reads, cheap and low risk
    "search_docs": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=0.5),
    "get_user": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=1.0),       # 1.0 = baseline

    # Write operations, moderate risk
    "update_record": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=2.0),
    "send_email": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=3.0, irreversible=True),

    # External API calls, expensive and high risk
    "stripe_charge": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=10.0, irreversible=True),
    "deploy_production": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=20.0, irreversible=True),
}

How to set limits with this approach:

Think in terms of operations, not dollars:

  • max_cost_per_run=50.0 → the agent can do 50 searches, or 5 Stripe charges, or 25 email sends, or any mix
  • max_cost_per_day=500.0 → daily limit of ~500 baseline operations

This approach works because you're limiting agent behavior, not monetary spend. You don't need to update weights when provider prices change.

docs.title: Approach 2: Dollar-based approximation
docs.text:
If you want cost units to roughly map to real money, assign weights based on the actual cost you incur per tool call:

tool_costs={
    # ~$0.01 per call (internal DB query, negligible infrastructure cost)
    "search": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=0.01),

    # ~$0.10 per call (third-party geocoding API with per-request pricing)
    "geocode_address": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=0.10),

    # ~$2.50 per call (Stripe processing fee)
    "stripe_charge": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=2.50, irreversible=True),

    # ~$0.50 per call (email delivery service fee)
    "send_email": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=0.50, irreversible=True),
}
# max_cost_per_day=50.0 → approximately $50/day in tool-related costs

Dollar-based weights require manual maintenance

The framework does NOT validate these weights against real pricing. If Stripe raises their fee to $3.00, you must manually update cost_weight=3.00. If your email provider changes pricing tiers, the weights become inaccurate silently.

Dollar-based weights also do NOT include LLM API costs. Whatever the model calls cost in tokens is not tracked by the budget.

docs.title: Approach 3: Combined with external cost tracking
docs.text:
For production systems that need real monetary limits, combine the budget system with external cost tracking:

from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, BudgetConfig, ToolCostAnnotation

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    budget=BudgetConfig(
        enabled=True,

        # Use relative weights for tool budget
        max_cost_per_day=500.0,
        tool_costs={
            "stripe_charge": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=10.0, irreversible=True),
            "search": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=0.5),
        },

        # Use quantity limits for LLM cost control
        max_llm_turns_per_run=15,     # Cap LLM turns per invocation
        max_tool_calls_per_day=1000,  # Cap total daily tool calls

        on_exceeded="pause",
    ),
)

For actual dollar-level cost control, track LLM spending through:

  • Your LLM provider's dashboard (OpenAI usage page, Anthropic console, etc.)
  • OpenAI/Anthropic API usage headers (x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens, usage metadata)
  • Promptise observability: token counts are tracked per invocation via get_stats() and can be exported to Prometheus/Grafana for alerting on real spend

The budget system handles behavioral limits (what the agent is allowed to do). External systems handle monetary limits (how much the infrastructure costs).

docs.title: Context injection
docs.text:
When inject_remaining=True, the agent sees remaining budget in a system message before every invocation. It lists every limit, None for one that is not set (with max_tool_calls_per_run=20, max_irreversible_per_run=2 and max_runs_per_day=50, at the start of a run):

[Budget Remaining] {'tool_calls_run': 20, 'llm_turns_run': None, 'cost_run': None, 'irreversible_run': 2, 'tool_calls_day': None, 'runs_day': 49, 'cost_day': None}

The values are what is left of each limit (BudgetState.remaining()); the run that is starting already counts toward runs_day. The same dict is process.status()["budget"].

This lets the agent prioritize: if it's running low on budget, it can choose cheaper tools or skip non-essential operations. In open mode, the agent can also call check_budget to inspect remaining limits.

docs.title: Per-call enforcement
docs.text:
Tool-call, cost and irreversible-action limits are checked before each tool call runs. A call that would push a counter past its limit (or any call once max_llm_turns_per_run is exceeded) is refused: the tool body never executes, the call is not counted, and the agent receives a BudgetExceededError as the tool's result, telling it to stop calling tools and answer. Parallel tool calls in one turn are checked one by one, so a limit of 2 lets exactly 2 of 3 parallel calls through.

from promptise.runtime import BudgetExceededError  # error the agent sees as the tool result

The message the agent gets looks like this:

Budget limit max_tool_calls_per_day reached (limit 5); tool call 'send' was not executed. Stop calling tools and give your final answer.

LLM turns are counted but not blocked: the turn that exceeds max_llm_turns_per_run still runs, and every tool call after it is refused.

A refused call never runs, so the journal has no tool_call entry for it. It gets a tool_denied entry instead (with the call's args at journal level "full"), and the permission_denied hook fires with kind="budget" and the call's arguments. The violation the process acts on is journaled as budget_violation.

After the invocation finishes, the first violation of the run triggers the action configured in on_exceeded (below). max_runs_per_day is checked when an invocation starts; a run over that limit does not start, and on_exceeded is applied at once. Its event goes to the dead letters with reason "budget: max_runs_per_day" (the task_completed hook reports outcome "refused"), so redeliver_dead_letters() can run it after the daily reset.

Changed in 1.3.0

Earlier versions counted tool calls and applied on_exceeded only after the invocation had finished, so an agent could exceed max_irreversible_per_run (or any per-run limit) within a single run.

docs.title: Enforcement actions
docs.text:
When a limit is exceeded (after the invocation in which it happened, or when a run is refused by max_runs_per_day):

Action Behavior "pause" (default) Suspend the process (suspend_reason == "budget"). Resume it with resume() or the API. "stop" Stop the process. Start it again by hand. "escalate" Send the escalation notification when escalation is set (webhook and/or event bus), then suspend.

A process paused by the budget does not resume by itself, not even after the daily reset hour: the reset only happens when a run starts. Its trigger events keep queueing and run in order after resume().

Escalation sends a POST to the configured webhook URL (and emits the same payload as escalation.event_type on the runtime's event bus) with the violation:

{
  "type": "budget_violation",
  "process_id": "0c8e5d0a-6b8f-4c56-9a52-0f4f3c1e9b7d",
  "process_name": "support-agent",
  "violation": {
    "limit_name": "max_cost_per_day",
    "limit_value": 100.0,
    "current_value": 102.5,
    "tool_name": "send_email"
  }
}

limit_name is the BudgetConfig field that was exceeded; current_value is the value the refused call would have produced; tool_name is the tool whose call exceeded it, or null when no tool call did (a run over max_runs_per_day, or a model turn over max_llm_turns_per_run).

The webhook URL must resolve to a public address (SSRF protection). The host is resolved before every notification, the notification is dropped with a warning if any address is private, loopback, link-local (cloud metadata) or otherwise internal, and the POST goes to the address that was checked, so a DNS record that changes in between (DNS rebinding) cannot send it to an internal service. Redirects are not followed. The same applies to health and mission escalations.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event Severity When Payload budget.warning warning After a run, for each limit at warning_threshold (default 80%) or more of its value (and not over it) at the run's last budget check process_name, limit_type, current, limit, percentage budget.exceeded critical After a run with a violation (once per run, for the first one), and when a run is refused by max_runs_per_day process_name, limit_type, current, limit budget.daily_reset info When a run start resets the daily counters process_name

limit_type is the BudgetConfig field name, for example max_tool_calls_per_day. The threshold is warning_threshold (default 0.8). A run refused by max_runs_per_day emits budget.exceeded with limit_type: "max_runs_per_day" and then applies on_exceeded; when on_exceeded suspends the process ("pause" or "escalate"), process.suspended follows with reason: "budget". Events reach the runtime's event notifier sinks.

docs.title: Changing limits while it runs
docs.text:
Every BudgetConfig field can change on a running process through PATCH /api/v1/processes/{name}/budget (or client.update_budget(name, **fields)):

curl -X PATCH http://127.0.0.1:9100/api/v1/processes/support-agent/budget \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"max_tool_calls_per_day": 1000}'
# {"name": "support-agent", "budget_updated": true, "effective_from": "next_budget_check", "live": true}

The patch is validated as a whole first (422 UNKNOWN_FIELD for a misspelt field, 422 INVALID_CONFIG for a bad value; nothing changes then). The counters are kept, and each value applies at the next check that reads it:

Field Takes effect Tool-call, cost and irreversible limits, tool_costs The next tool call, also inside a run already in progress max_llm_turns_per_run The next LLM turn max_runs_per_day, daily_reset_hour_utc, inject_remaining The next run start on_exceeded, escalation The next violation warning_threshold The warnings computed after the next run enabled: true Builds the budget with zero counters; applies from the next run enabled: false Drops the budget and its counters

Lowering a limit below what was already used blocks the next tool call. Raising a limit does not resume a process that the budget paused; call resume().

In Python, change process.config.budget and call process.apply_governance_config("budget").

docs.title: Irreversible action tracking
docs.text:
Tools marked irreversible=True are tracked separately. Use max_irreversible_per_run to limit how many destructive actions the agent can take per invocation:

budget=BudgetConfig(
    max_irreversible_per_run=2,  # Max 2 irreversible actions per invocation
    tool_costs={
        "delete_record": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=3.0, irreversible=True),
        "send_email": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=1.0, irreversible=True),
        "search": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=0.5),  # Not irreversible
    },
)

The agent can call search as many times as the cost budget allows, but it can only call delete_record and/or send_email a combined total of 2 times per invocation.

A call an approval gate denies did nothing irreversible, so it gives its irreversible action back: with max_irreversible_per_run=2, two denied delete_record calls still leave room for two approved ones. It still counts as a tool call and against the cost budget.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• cost_weight is not money. LLM token spend is not tracked at all; see Understanding cost_weight.
  • No journal, no persistence across runtimes. Without a JournalConfig, a new process object starts with zero daily counters.
  • A daily limit pauses until someone resumes. With on_exceeded="pause", a process that hits max_runs_per_day stays suspended past the reset hour. Resume it on a schedule, or use "stop" and restart it, if that is what you want.
  • escalate without a target. The process is suspended, but nobody is notified. Set escalation.
  • Disabling to "reset". PATCH {"enabled": false} drops the counters; enabling again starts from zero. That defeats the daily limit.
  • Tool names in tool_costs. Keys must match the tool names the agent sees (MCP tool names); an unmatched key has no effect and the tool costs 1.0.

docs.title: BudgetConfig
docs.text: Field Type Default Description enabled bool False Enable budget tracking max_tool_calls_per_run int \| None (>= 1) None Per-invocation tool call limit max_llm_turns_per_run int \| None (>= 1) None Per-invocation LLM turn limit max_cost_per_run float \| None (> 0) None Per-invocation cost limit (abstract units) max_irreversible_per_run int \| None (>= 0) None Per-invocation irreversible action limit max_tool_calls_per_day int \| None (>= 1) None Daily tool call limit max_runs_per_day int \| None (>= 1) None Daily invocation limit max_cost_per_day float \| None (> 0) None Daily cost limit (abstract units) tool_costs dict[str, ToolCostAnnotation] {} Per-tool cost annotations on_exceeded "pause" \| "stop" \| "escalate" "pause" Action on violation escalation EscalationTarget \| None None Where "escalate" sends violation notifications daily_reset_hour_utc int (0-23) 0 UTC hour at which the budget day starts inject_remaining bool True Show remaining budget in agent context warning_threshold float (0-1, above 0) 0.8 Fraction of a limit at which budget.warning is emitted

docs.title: ToolCostAnnotation
docs.text: Field Type Default Description cost_weight float 1.0 Abstract cost units consumed per call. Must be > 0. irreversible bool False Whether this tool performs an irreversible action (delete, send, charge).

docs.title: BudgetState
docs.text:
BudgetState(config); the process creates it for you.

Method Description .record_tool_call(tool_name, *, enforce=False) Record a tool call and add its cost_weight to run and daily totals. Returns a BudgetViolation if any limit is exceeded, or None. With enforce=True the call is checked first: if it would exceed a limit it is not counted and the violation has blocked=True (the caller must not run the tool). .record_tool_call_sync(tool_name, *, enforce=False) Thread-safe synchronous form, used by the runtime's budget guard (synchronous tools run on worker threads). .record_llm_turn() Record an LLM turn (counts toward max_llm_turns_per_run only, no cost). Returns a BudgetViolation if the limit is exceeded. .record_run_start() Count a run toward max_runs_per_day; returns a violation when it is over the limit. .reset_run() Reset per-run counters. Called automatically at the start of each invocation. .check_daily_reset() Reset the daily counters if a reset hour has passed since the last reset; returns True when it did. .remaining() Dict of what is left per limit (tool_calls_run, llm_turns_run, cost_run, irreversible_run, tool_calls_day, runs_day, cost_day); None = no limit, negative = exceeded. .snapshot() The counters as a JSON-safe dict (what checkpoints store). .restore(data) Load a snapshot: the daily counters and last_daily_reset; per-run counters start at zero. Raises ValueError for a malformed snapshot, changing nothing. .pending_warnings BudgetWarnings for limits at warning_threshold or more after the latest check. .refund_irreversible(tool_name) Give back the irreversible action of a call that did not run (what the runtime does when an approval gate denies it); tool-call and cost counters keep the attempt. .budget_context() The limits that are set, as one line ([Budget] Tool Calls Run: 5 \| Cost Day: 40.0), or "" when none is set. .to_dict() / BudgetState.from_dict(data, config) Same as snapshot(), and rebuild a state from it. 
import asyncio

from promptise.runtime import BudgetConfig, BudgetState, ToolCostAnnotation


async def main():
    state = BudgetState(BudgetConfig(
        enabled=True,
        max_tool_calls_per_run=2,
        tool_costs={"send_email": ToolCostAnnotation(cost_weight=2.0, irreversible=True)},
    ))
    await state.record_tool_call("search", enforce=True)
    await state.record_tool_call("send_email", enforce=True)
    violation = await state.record_tool_call("search", enforce=True)  # a third call
    print(violation.limit_name, violation.blocked)  # max_tool_calls_per_run True
    print(state.remaining()["tool_calls_run"])       # 0


asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: BudgetViolation
docs.text:
Field Description limit_name The BudgetConfig field that was exceeded limit_value The configured maximum current_value The counter value that exceeded it (for a refused call: the value the call would have produced) tool_name The tool that triggered it, or None blocked True when the tool call was refused before it ran arguments The refused call's arguments (a refused call only), or None

BudgetWarning has limit_name, limit_value, current_value and percentage (0.0-1.0).

docs.title: BudgetEnforcer
docs.text: Method Description .handle_violation(violation, process) Execute the configured enforcement action (pause, stop, or escalate).

docs.title: Behavioral Health Monitoring
docs.text:
Behavioral health monitoring catches an agent that runs but no longer does useful work: stuck on the same tool call, looping through the same sequence, giving empty replies, or failing run after run. Detection is pure pattern matching on the tool calls, final replies and run outcomes the process records; it makes no LLM calls. When it finds an anomaly, the process logs it, pauses, escalates or stops, as you configure.

from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, HealthConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Monitor data pipelines.",
    health=HealthConfig(enabled=True, on_anomaly="pause"),
)

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text: System monitoring watches CPU and memory. Nobody watches whether the agent is actually doing what it should be doing. A stuck agent calling the same tool in a loop burns compute silently until it hits context limits, and a scheduled agent that answers "ok" to every run looks healthy from the outside. Behavioral health catches both.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, HealthConfig, EscalationTarget

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Monitor data pipelines.",
    health=HealthConfig(
        enabled=True,
        stuck_threshold=3,        # 3 identical calls in a row = stuck
        loop_window=20,           # check the last 20 tool calls for loops
        loop_min_repeats=2,       # a sequence repeated 2+ times = loop
        empty_threshold=3,        # 3 trivial final replies in a row = anomaly
        empty_max_chars=10,       # a reply of at most 10 chars is trivial
        error_window=10,          # error rate over the last 10 runs
        error_rate_threshold=0.5, # 50%+ failed runs = anomaly
        on_anomaly="escalate",    # "log", "pause", "escalate" or "stop"
        cooldown=300,             # 5 min before the same anomaly is reported again
        escalation=EscalationTarget(
            webhook_url="https://hooks.slack.com/...",
        ),
    ),
)

Or in a .agent manifest:

name: pipeline-monitor
health:
  enabled: true
  stuck_threshold: 3
  loop_window: 20
  error_window: 10
  on_anomaly: escalate
  cooldown: 300
  escalation:
    webhook_url: "https://hooks.slack.com/..."

An unknown key under health: is rejected in a manifest; in Python, HealthConfig ignores it with a FutureWarning.

docs.title: How the process feeds the monitor
docs.text:
Signal Recorded when Tool call (name + hash of the arguments) Each tool call starts, through the process's callback handler Final reply length A run finishes without raising; the agent's final answer, not tool results Run success A run finishes without raising Run failure A run raised and used up its retries (trigger_delivery.max_retries)

Tool history starts fresh at every run (stuck and loop detection look for repetition inside a run). Reply lengths and run outcomes carry over between runs. Runs blocked by a guardrail, a hook or the payload scan are not recorded.

docs.title: Stuck detection
docs.text:
When the agent calls the same tool with the same arguments stuck_threshold times in a row within one run, it's stuck. A scheduled agent that checks the same queue once per cron tick is behaving normally and is not reported.

details: tool_name, consecutive_count.

docs.title: Loop detection
docs.text:
Examines the last loop_window tool calls of the run (at least 4) for a repeating sequence of two or more calls. If a sequence like search → read → analyze → search → read → analyze repeats loop_min_repeats times back to back, it's a loop.

details: pattern (tool names), repeat_count, pattern_length.

docs.title: Empty response detection
docs.text:
Counts consecutive final replies of at most empty_max_chars characters after stripping whitespace. With the default 10, a 10-character reply counts as empty and an 11-character one doesn't; 0 counts only blank replies. After empty_threshold such replies in a row, the anomaly fires. Tool results are not replies: a tool that returns [] because a queue is empty does not count.

details: consecutive_count, max_chars, lengths.

docs.title: Error rate detection
docs.text:
Once error_window run outcomes are recorded, the error rate is the share of failed runs among the last error_window. It fires when the rate is at or above error_rate_threshold. Before the window is full, nothing fires, so with the defaults a process needs 10 recorded runs first.

details: error_rate, error_count, window_size, threshold.

docs.title: Enforcement actions
docs.text:
on_anomaly Behavior "log" (default) Log the anomaly and emit health.anomaly; the process keeps running "pause" Suspend the process (suspend_reason == "health") "escalate" Send the escalation notification when escalation is set, then suspend the process. Without escalation it still suspends "stop" Stop the process

The action runs once, when the run that produced the anomaly ends, whether the run succeeded or raised (a stuck tool loop often ends in GraphIterationLimitError), and however long the run went on after the anomaly was detected. An anomaly detected when a failure is recorded (high_error_rate) is acted on right then. Each anomaly is handled once: a later healthy run does not pause the process again for it. pause and escalate suspend only a RUNNING process.

A process suspended for health does not resume by itself. Its trigger events keep queueing; resume() (or POST /api/v1/processes/{name}/resume) lets it continue in order. To stop a process outright on a hard limit, use on_anomaly="stop" or the Autonomy Budget with on_exceeded="stop".

The escalation is a POST to escalation.webhook_url and/or an escalation.event_type event on the runtime's event bus, with the latest anomaly of the run:

{
  "type": "health_anomaly",
  "process_id": "0c8e5d0a-6b8f-4c56-9a52-0f4f3c1e9b7d",
  "process_name": "pipeline-monitor",
  "anomaly_type": "stuck",
  "details": {"tool_name": "search", "consecutive_count": 3}
}

The webhook URL must resolve to a public address; see escalation delivery for the SSRF rules, which apply here too.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event Severity Payload health.anomaly warning process_name, anomaly_type (stuck, loop, empty_response, high_error_rate), details health.recovered info process_name

Events reach the runtime's event notifier sinks; their metadata carries process_name, process_id and the model. health.anomaly is emitted for every new anomaly, whatever on_anomaly is.

health.recovered is emitted once per incident: on the first run after an anomaly that finishes without raising. That can be the same run that produced a stuck or loop anomaly, if that run then finishes cleanly; the health.recovered event is then emitted before the health.anomaly event of that run. The reply of the recovering run may itself still be empty.

docs.title: Cooldown
docs.text:
cooldown (default 300 s) stops the same anomaly from being reported over and over, so a stuck agent does not send an escalation per call. "The same" means the same kind and the same evidence:

Anomaly Same anomaly when STUCK the same tool with the same arguments LOOP the same repeating sequence, whichever call it is caught at (A, B and B, A are one loop) EMPTY_RESPONSE, HIGH_ERROR_RATE always (one signal per process)

A different stuck call or a different loop is a new anomaly and is reported at once, also within the cooldown and in the same run. The cooldown carries over between invocations: a scheduled agent that gets stuck on the same call in every run reports it once per cooldown.

clear_anomalies() (and DELETE /api/v1/processes/{name}/health/anomalies) forgets the anomaly history and resets the cooldowns: after a clear, the next occurrence of any anomaly is reported and acted on at once.

docs.title: Reading health status
docs.text:
process.status()["health"]
# {'is_healthy': False,
#  'anomaly_count': 1,
#  'anomalies_by_type': {'stuck': 1, 'loop': 0, 'empty_response': 0, 'high_error_rate': 0},
#  'latest_anomaly': {'type': 'stuck',
#                     'description': "Agent stuck: tool 'search' called 3 times consecutively with identical arguments",
#                     'timestamp': '2026-10-19T20:21:57.600765+00:00'}}

process.status()["health_anomalies"]  # 1: anomalies in the history

status()["health"] is HealthMonitor.health_status():

Key Meaning is_healthy True when no anomaly was reported within the last cooldown seconds anomaly_count Anomalies reported since the start or the last clear anomalies_by_type The same count per type latest_anomaly type, description and ISO timestamp of the newest one, or None

Both keys are present only when health monitoring is enabled. GET /api/v1/processes/{name} returns the same status over HTTP.

The anomaly history keeps the latest 1000 anomalies (HealthMonitor.MAX_ANOMALIES), oldest dropped first; anomaly_count counts all of them.

Over the orchestration API:

Route Response GET /api/v1/processes/{name}/health/anomalies {"name", "health_enabled": true, "anomalies": [{"type", "description", "timestamp"}], "count"}; {"health_enabled": false, "anomalies": []} when monitoring is off DELETE /api/v1/processes/{name}/health/anomalies {"name", "anomalies_cleared": n}; 400 HEALTH_DISABLED when monitoring is off PATCH /api/v1/processes/{name}/health {"name", "health_updated": true, "live": true, "effective_from": "immediate"}

docs.title: Changing the configuration while it runs
docs.text:
Every HealthConfig field can change on a running process, through PATCH /api/v1/processes/{name}/health or the client:

async with OrchestrationClient("http://127.0.0.1:9100", token=TOKEN) as client:
    await client.update_health("pipeline-monitor", error_window=20, on_anomaly="pause")

The patch is validated as a whole before anything changes (422 UNKNOWN_FIELD or 422 INVALID_CONFIG otherwise) and applies at the next recorded signal:

  • Thresholds and actions apply to the next check.
  • Window sizes (error_window, loop_window, stuck_threshold, empty_threshold) resize the monitor's windows and keep the most recent data. Growing error_window from 10 to 20 keeps the 10 outcomes recorded so far; the error rate is checked again once 20 are recorded.
  • enabled builds the monitor (true) or drops it with its history (false).

In Python, change process.config.health and call process.apply_governance_config("health"), or give a standalone monitor a new config with monitor.apply_config(config). A monitor also picks up window-size changes made directly on the config object it reads.

The monitor's history lives in memory. It survives stop() / start() and restart_process() of the same process, but it is not written to the journal, so a new process object (a new runtime, a redeploy) starts with an empty history.

docs.title: As an in-run guard
docs.text:
HealthMonitor also works on its own, outside AgentProcess, as a guard inside a run: a pre_tool engine hook records every call and blocks the one that keeps the agent stuck. Set cooldown=0 for this. With the default cooldown, record_tool_call() returns the anomaly only the first time, so the guard would block the third identical call and let every later one through.

from promptise.runtime import HealthConfig, HealthMonitor


class LoopGuard:
    """Blocks a tool call while the agent is repeating itself."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        # cooldown=0: report every call that continues the anomaly
        self.monitor = HealthMonitor(
            HealthConfig(enabled=True, stuck_threshold=3, cooldown=0),
            process_id="my-agent",
        )

    async def pre_tool(self, tool_name, args, state):
        anomaly = await self.monitor.record_tool_call(tool_name, args)
        if anomaly:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"{anomaly.description}. The result will not change in this run: "
                "stop calling it and continue with what you have."
            )
        return args

Pass it in hooks=[LoopGuard()] of a PromptGraphEngine. The error goes back to the model as the tool's result. Use one guard per run, or call monitor.begin_invocation() at the start of each run, because stuck and loop detection look at the calls of one run.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• on_anomaly="escalate" with no target. The process is suspended, but no one is notified. Set escalation with a webhook_url or an event_type.
  • A suspended process doesn't resume itself. After pause or escalate, resume it once you have looked at the cause; until then its events queue up.
  • Sparse schedules and the error window. An agent that runs twice a day needs five days to fill the default error_window=10. Use a smaller window for rare runs.
  • Short legitimate replies. An agent whose normal answer is "OK" or "none" trips the empty-response detector. Lower empty_max_chars (or set 0) for such agents.
  • cooldown=0 in a process. Every repeat is reported, so is_healthy turns True again right away and a stuck agent sends one escalation per run.
  • Clearing anomalies resets cooldowns. After DELETE /health/anomalies, an ongoing problem is reported (and acted on) again on its next occurrence.

docs.title: HealthConfig
docs.text: Field Type Default Description enabled bool False Enable health monitoring stuck_threshold int (>= 2) 3 Consecutive identical calls (same tool and arguments) that count as stuck loop_window int (>= 4) 20 Recent tool calls examined for loops loop_min_repeats int (>= 2) 2 Back-to-back repeats of a sequence that count as a loop empty_threshold int (>= 2) 3 Consecutive trivial final replies that count as an anomaly empty_max_chars int (>= 0) 10 A final reply of at most this many characters (after stripping whitespace) is trivial error_window int (>= 2) 10 Recent runs the error rate is computed over; checked once the window is full error_rate_threshold float (> 0, <= 1) 0.5 Error rate at or above which the anomaly fires on_anomaly "log" \| "pause" \| "escalate" \| "stop" "log" Action when a run produced an anomaly cooldown float (>= 0) 300.0 Seconds before the same anomaly (same kind and evidence) is reported again; 0 reports every repeat (in-run guards) escalation EscalationTarget \| None None Where "escalate" sends its notification

docs.title: HealthMonitor
docs.text:
HealthMonitor(config, process_id)

Member Description .record_tool_call(tool_name, args) Record a call; return the anomaly it completes, unless the same anomaly was reported less than cooldown seconds ago .record_response(text) Record the agent's final reply for empty detection (not tool results) .record_success() Record a successful run; returns True once, on the first success after an anomaly .record_error() Record a failed run for error-rate detection; returns the anomaly, if any .begin_invocation() Start a new run: clears the tool history used by stuck/loop detection (the runtime calls it) .take_new_anomalies() Anomalies detected since the previous call, each returned once (the runtime calls it when a run ends to apply on_anomaly) .apply_config(config) Switch to another HealthConfig, resizing the windows and keeping data, history and cooldowns .clear_anomalies() Forget the history, counts and cooldowns; returns how many anomalies were cleared .health_status() The summary dict shown as process.status()["health"] .config The HealthConfig the monitor reads .anomalies Detected anomalies, oldest first (the latest MAX_ANOMALIES) .latest_anomaly Most recent anomaly, or None .tool_history The run's recorded calls as (tool_name, args_hash) .to_dict() / HealthMonitor.from_dict(data, config) Serialize and restore the windows and counts MAX_ANOMALIES 1000, the size of the anomaly history

docs.title: Anomaly
docs.text: Field Description anomaly_type An AnomalyType description Human-readable explanation timestamp When it was detected (UTC) details Evidence; keys per detector above

docs.title: AnomalyType
docs.text:
A str enum; the value is what events and the API show.

Member Value Description STUCK "stuck" Same tool + args repeated consecutively LOOP "loop" Repeating pattern in the tool call sequence EMPTY_RESPONSE "empty_response" Consecutive trivial final replies HIGH_ERROR_RATE "high_error_rate" Error rate at or above the threshold

docs.title: Mission-Oriented Process Model
docs.text:
A mission turns an agent process from "run when triggered" into "work toward a goal until it is done". You give the process an objective and success criteria; after its runs, an LLM judge (or your own check) decides whether the mission is achieved, how confident it is, and whether to pause and escalate. The process completes, fails on a time or run limit, or is failed by an operator, and the mission's progress survives restarts when the process has a journal.

from promptise.runtime import AgentProcess, EscalationTarget, MissionConfig, ProcessConfig
from promptise.runtime.config import JournalConfig, TriggerConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Migrate all tables to the new schema, one per run.",
    triggers=[TriggerConfig(type="cron", cron_expression="*/10 * * * *")],
    mission=MissionConfig(
        enabled=True,
        objective="Migrate all database tables to the v2 schema",
        success_criteria="All tables pass v2 schema validation with zero errors",
        eval_every=3,              # judge after every 3rd successful run
        confidence_threshold=0.7,  # below this: pause and escalate
        timeout_hours=24,          # fail after 24 hours
        max_invocations=50,        # fail after 50 successful runs
        eval_model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
        escalation=EscalationTarget(webhook_url="https://hooks.slack.com/..."),
    ),
    journal=JournalConfig(path=".promptise/journal"),  # mission survives restarts
)

process = AgentProcess("schema-migrator", config)
await process.start()

The same in a .agent manifest:

name: schema-migrator
model: openai:gpt-5-mini
instructions: Migrate all tables to the new schema, one per run.
triggers:
  - type: cron
    cron_expression: "*/10 * * * *"
mission:
  enabled: true
  objective: "Migrate all database tables to the v2 schema"
  success_criteria: "All tables pass v2 schema validation with zero errors"
  eval_every: 3
  confidence_threshold: 0.7
  timeout_hours: 24
  max_invocations: 50
  escalation:
    webhook_url: "https://hooks.slack.com/..."
journal:
  level: checkpoint

docs.title: States
docs.text:
A mission (MissionState) is in one of four states:

State Meaning active The agent works on the mission and evaluations run (the initial state) paused An evaluation was below confidence_threshold, or an operator paused it. No evaluations run until it is resumed; the process keeps running its triggers completed Achieved. Final: later runs are skipped failed timeout_hours or max_invocations reached, or failed by an operator. Final: later runs are skipped

Evaluations never change a completed or failed mission: a judge verdict that arrives after an operator failed the mission doesn't complete it, and a failed mission can't be completed. The API fails only active or paused missions. Only an active mission can be paused, and only a paused one resumed.

docs.title: Evaluation cycle
docs.text:
Every eval_every successful runs (after each one by default), while the mission is active, the process:

  1. Collects the evidence (MissionEvidence): the conversation, the context state, the run's tool calls (recorded when health monitoring is on) and the trigger event.
  2. Runs your success_check first, when you set one (see Programmatic success checks).
  3. Otherwise asks the judge: a tool-less agent built with eval_model (or the process's model) that gets the objective, the success criteria and the evidence (the state as JSON up to 1,000 characters, the last 20 tool calls, the trigger up to 300 characters, the last 10 conversation messages up to 500 characters each) and must answer with JSON: achieved, confidence (0.0-1.0, clamped), reasoning, progress_summary.
  4. Applies the verdict:
    • Achieved: the mission is completed, a mission.complete event is emitted, and with auto_complete=True (the default) the process stops.
    • Not achieved, confidence below confidence_threshold: the mission is paused, a mission.progress event is emitted, and when escalation is set it receives {"type": "low_confidence", "process_id", "process_name", "confidence", "reasoning"}.
    • Otherwise: a mission.progress event; the mission stays active.

If the judge call fails or its reply is not valid JSON, the evaluation counts as not achieved with confidence 0.5 and reasoning starting with Evaluation failed:, so with the default threshold it pauses the mission. Every evaluation is journaled as a mission_evaluation entry (achieved, confidence, reasoning, progress_summary, mission_state, invocation_number, source).

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
With an event notifier on the process or runtime:

Event Severity Data mission.complete info process_name, confidence, invocations mission.progress info process_name, confidence, achieved (false), invocations mission.failed critical process_name, process_id, reason, message, objective, invocation_count, previous_state, failed_at

In mission.failed, reason says who failed it ("timeout", "max_invocations" or "manual") and message says why (for example "Mission timeout reached", "Mission reached max_invocations (50)", or the operator's reason). failed_at is ISO UTC.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: timeout_hours and max_invocations fail the mission with a mission.failed event. Both are checked before each run and again after it, once its evaluation has run, so max_invocations=50 lets 50 runs happen and the mission is failed right after the 50th unless that one completed it. Only successful runs count. The timeout clock starts when the process object is created and, after a restart with a journal, continues where it stopped. A failed or completed mission doesn't stop the process: its later runs are skipped.

docs.title: Failing a mission
docs.text:
An operator can fail an active or paused mission with a reason:

data = process.fail_mission("Requirements changed, migration cancelled")
# {"process_name": "schema-migrator", "process_id": "...", "reason": "manual",
#  "message": "Requirements changed, migration cancelled", "objective": "...",
#  "invocation_count": 6, "previous_state": "active", "failed_at": "2026-10-19T20:23:26+00:00"}

fail_mission() stores the reason with the mission (MissionTracker.failure_reason, the [Mission] prompt block, checkpoints), journals a mission_failed entry, emits mission.failed and returns the event data. It raises RuntimeError when the process has no mission, and ValueError when the mission is already completed or failed (The mission is already failed; a failed mission can't be failed). Over the API: POST /mission/fail (see Over the API).

docs.title: Context injection
docs.text:
Before every run the agent sees its mission as a system message:

[Mission] Objective: Migrate all database tables to the v2 schema
Success Criteria: All tables pass v2 schema validation with zero errors
Status: active
Progress: 6 invocations/50, 2.3/24.0 hours
Last Evaluation: confidence=0.82 — Tables users..orders migrated; invoices and payments remain.
Progress Summary: 6 of 8 tables migrated

/50 and the hours appear only when max_invocations and timeout_hours are set; the last two lines appear after the first evaluation. A failed mission adds a Failure Reason: line after Status.

docs.title: Evaluation history
docs.text:
The tracker keeps the latest 100 evaluations (MissionTracker.MAX_EVALUATIONS), oldest first, in tracker.evaluations; evaluation_count counts all of them. In open mode the agent can call check_mission, which returns the mission block above followed by the latest 10 evaluations:

Evaluation History (1):
- #3 [llm] not achieved, confidence=0.90: Two tables remain.

GET /api/v1/processes/{name}/mission returns the kept evaluations.

docs.title: Restore after a restart
docs.text: With a journal, the mission is part of every checkpoint: its state, invocation count, elapsed time, failure reason and evaluation history. The first start() of a new process object with the same name restores it (JournalConfig.recover_on_start, default True), and process.recovered["mission_restored"] is True. A snapshot made for a different objective is not restored (a warning is logged) and the mission starts fresh. A completed or failed mission stays completed or failed after a restart.

docs.title: Programmatic success checks
docs.text:
When success can be measured in code, set success_check in Python. It is called with the MissionEvidence before the judge:

from promptise.runtime import MissionConfig
from promptise.runtime.mission import MissionEvidence


def migration_done(evidence: MissionEvidence) -> bool | None:
    left = evidence.state.get("tables_left")
    if left == 0:
        return True    # achieved: no judge call
    if left is None:
        return False   # not achieved: no judge call
    return None        # inconclusive: ask the LLM judge


mission = MissionConfig(
    enabled=True,
    objective="Migrate all tables",
    success_criteria="tables_left is 0",
    success_check=migration_done,
)

True completes the mission and False records "not achieved", both with confidence 1.0 and source: "programmatic", without a judge call. None falls through to the judge. A check that raises is logged and the judge decides. success_check is Python only: it can't be set in a manifest or over the API, and it is never serialized.

docs.title: Over the API
docs.text:
Method Path What it does GET /api/v1/processes/{name}/mission {"name", "mission_enabled": true, "mission": {"state", "objective", "invocation_count", "evaluations": [...]}}; {"mission_enabled": false} without a mission POST /api/v1/processes/{name}/mission/fail Fail an active or paused mission: body {"reason": "..."} (optional, default "Manually failed via API"). Emits mission.failed with reason: "manual" POST /api/v1/processes/{name}/mission/pause Pause an active mission POST /api/v1/processes/{name}/mission/resume Resume a paused mission PATCH /api/v1/processes/{name}/mission Change MissionConfig fields; applies to the next evaluation and prompt

Each evaluation in GET /mission has achieved, confidence, reasoning, progress_summary, invocation_number, source and timestamp. fail, pause and resume answer 409 MISSION_STATE when the mission's state doesn't allow them (for example pausing a completed mission) and 400 MISSION_DISABLED without a mission. The Python client has get_mission, fail_mission, pause_mission, resume_mission and update_mission.

curl -X POST http://localhost:9100/api/v1/processes/schema-migrator/mission/fail \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"reason": "Requirements changed, migration cancelled"}'
# {"name": "schema-migrator", "mission_failed": true, "reason": "Requirements changed, migration cancelled"}

docs.title: MissionConfig
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description enabled bool False Enable mission tracking objective str "" What the agent is trying to achieve success_criteria str "" How the judge decides completion eval_model str \| None None Model for the judge (None = the process model) eval_every int 1 Evaluate every N successful runs (>= 1) confidence_threshold float 0.7 Below this (not achieved): pause and escalate (0-1) timeout_hours float 0.0 Fail after this many hours (0 = no timeout) max_invocations int 0 Fail after this many successful runs (0 = unlimited) auto_complete bool True Stop the process when the mission is achieved. False keeps it running (its later runs are skipped) on_complete "stop" \| "continue" \| "suspend" \| None None Deprecated, ignored. Setting it emits a FutureWarning; use auto_complete escalation EscalationTarget \| None None Where to notify on low confidence (webhook_url, event_type) success_check Callable[[MissionEvidence], bool \| None] \| None None Programmatic check run before the judge. Python only, never serialized

Unknown keys are ignored with a FutureWarning (manifests and the API reject them).

docs.title: MissionTracker
docs.text:
Created by the process when mission.enabled=True (or when a PATCH /mission enables it).

Member Description .state Current MissionState .evaluations Kept evaluations, oldest first (at most MAX_EVALUATIONS = 100) .evaluation_count Total evaluations, including ones no longer kept .evaluation_history(limit=10) The latest limit evaluations .history_summary(limit=10) context_summary() plus the latest evaluations (what check_mission returns) .invocation_count Successful runs counted .failure_reason Why the mission failed, or None .should_evaluate() Whether an evaluation is due now await .evaluate(evidence, model) Run success_check and/or the judge; model is used when eval_model is not set .context_summary() The [Mission] block text .is_timed_out() / .is_over_limit() The timeout_hours / max_invocations checks .fail(reason, *, source="manual") Fail the mission; returns the mission.failed data (without process_name). On a process, use process.fail_mission(), which also emits the event .pause() / .resume() / .complete() State changes (no effect from a state that doesn't allow them) .to_dict() / .restore(data) / MissionTracker.from_dict(data, config) Snapshot and restore (restore raises ValueError for a snapshot with another objective)

docs.title: MissionEvaluation
docs.text: Field Type Description achieved bool Whether the mission is complete confidence float 0.0-1.0 confidence in the verdict reasoning str Why the evaluator decided this progress_summary str Current progress timestamp datetime When the evaluation ran (UTC) invocation_number int The run count it covers source str "llm" or "programmatic"

docs.title: MissionEvidence
docs.text: Field Type Description conversation list[dict] The conversation buffer state dict The context state tool_calls list[tuple[str, str]] Tool calls of the run as (name, args_hash) (with health monitoring on) trigger_event dict {"type", "payload"} of the trigger event invocation_count int Successful runs of the process so far

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Every evaluation is an LLM call. With eval_every=1 the judge runs after every run. Raise eval_every, use a cheaper eval_model, or add a success_check that answers without the judge.
  • A failed judge call pauses the mission. It scores confidence 0.5, below the default threshold. A paused mission stays paused until someone calls resume; check the Evaluation failed: reasoning first.
  • Paused doesn't mean idle. A paused mission skips evaluations, but the process keeps running its triggers (and spending budget). Suspend the process if it should stop working.
  • Completed and failed are final. Restarting the process doesn't reopen the mission when a journal restores it; its runs keep being skipped. Use a new objective, a new journal, or recover_on_start=False to start a new mission.
  • on_complete does nothing. Use auto_complete.
  • success_check only exists in Python. A manifest or API deploy can't set it; those missions always use the judge.
  • Tool calls are only evidence with health monitoring on. Without health.enabled, the judge sees state, conversation and trigger only.

docs.title: Secret Scoping
docs.text:
Secret scoping gives each agent process its own credentials, with expiry, rotation without a restart, an access log and revocation. Environment variables are shared by every agent on a host; a secret scope holds only the secrets one process needs, keeps them encrypted in memory, and makes sure their values never reach the journal, checkpoints, the conversation history or API responses in plain text.

import os

from promptise.runtime import AgentProcess, ProcessConfig, SecretScopeConfig
from promptise.runtime.config import JournalConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Process payments.",
    secrets=SecretScopeConfig(
        enabled=True,
        secrets={
            "stripe_key": "${STRIPE_API_KEY}",                 # resolved from the environment at start
            "db_url": "postgres://app:${DB_PASSWORD}@db/app",  # references inside text work too
        },
        default_ttl=3600,           # every secret expires after 1 hour...
        ttls={"stripe_key": 1800},  # ...this one after 30 minutes
    ),
    journal=JournalConfig(path=".promptise/journal"),  # access log
)

process = AgentProcess("payments", config)
await process.start()  # resolves the references; a missing variable fails the start

Operators rotate and revoke a running process's secrets over the API. The scope itself is a SecretScope, which you can also use on its own:

from promptise.runtime.secrets import SecretScope

scope = SecretScope(config.secrets, process_id="payments")
await scope.resolve_initial()
key = scope.get("stripe_key")                              # None once expired
await scope.rotate("stripe_key", "sk_live_new", ttl=1800)  # new value, new 30-minute lifetime
print(scope.list_metadata())                               # names, sources, expiry, counts: never values
print(scope.sanitize_text(f"charged with {key}"))          # "charged with [REDACTED]"

The same in a .agent manifest:

name: payments
model: openai:gpt-5-mini
instructions: Process payments.
secrets:
  enabled: true
  secrets:
    stripe_key: "${STRIPE_API_KEY}"
    db_url: "postgres://app:${DB_PASSWORD}@db/app"
  default_ttl: 3600
  ttls:
    stripe_key: 1800
  revoke_on_stop: true
journal:
  level: checkpoint

docs.title: Where values come from
docs.text:
Each value in secrets is either a literal or contains environment references:

Form Example Resolved to Reference "${STRIPE_API_KEY}" The variable's value Reference with default "${DB_PASSWORD:-devpw}" The variable, or devpw when it is unset Text with references "postgres://app:${DB_PASSWORD}@db/app" The text with each reference replaced Literal "tok-abc123" The text as written
  • References are resolved when the process starts (SecretScope.resolve_initial()), not when the config is built, so a ProcessConfig or a loaded manifest holds the reference, never the value. Loading a manifest checks that the referenced variables exist and fails early when one is missing.
  • A variable that is unset (and has no default) when the process starts raises SecretResolutionError (a KeyError) naming the variable and the secret; the process ends up failed.
  • A process deployed through the control API may only reference the variables the operator allowed (OrchestrationAPI(allowed_env_vars=...) or allow_env_references=True): the API refuses other references with 403 ENV_REFERENCES_NOT_ALLOWED, and the process's scope won't resolve them either. Its resolution errors are generic (they don't say whether a variable exists), so a token holder can't probe the host's environment.
  • Values are stored as pydantic.SecretStr: repr() shows SecretStr('**********'), and a JSON dump (model_dump(mode="json")) shows ********** for literal values and references as written. Passing the masked placeholder ********** back as a value is refused, so a dumped config with literal values can't be loaded again by mistake.
  • Every name in ttls must be a key of secrets, and every TTL must be positive.

For production, deliver secrets as environment variables (from your secret manager, Kubernetes or Docker secrets) and reference them; avoid literal values in configs and manifests.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Resolve. Every start() resolves all secrets from the config again and starts their TTLs. A value set by a rotation is replaced by the configured value on the next start.
  2. Access. scope.get(name) returns the value, or None when the secret doesn't exist or has expired. Every successful access is logged (name only).
  3. Expiry. A secret with a TTL expires that many seconds after it was resolved or rotated (monotonic clock). An expired secret is removed on the next access or listing, and its value stays redacted.
  4. Rotation. await scope.rotate(name, new_value, ttl=None) replaces a value at once, without a restart. ttl sets a new lifetime from now; without it the secret keeps its current expiry. An expired secret can be rotated: it becomes active again, with ttl or else its configured TTL. A name that isn't configured raises SecretNotFoundError (a KeyError); an empty value or a TTL <= 0 raises ValueError.
  5. Revocation. await scope.revoke_all() overwrites every value with null bytes, removes all secrets, forgets rotated values and replaces the encryption key. It runs on stop() when revoke_on_stop=True (the default), always on close() (and so on AgentRuntime.remove_process()), and on DELETE /api/v1/processes/{name}/secrets. With revoke_on_stop=False, a stopped process keeps its secrets until it is closed; the next start() resolves them again either way.

Values are kept Fernet-encrypted in memory with a key per scope. Python strings can't be wiped, so zero-filling is a best effort: copies may stay in the interpreter's memory until they are garbage-collected.

docs.title: Access log
docs.text:
With a journal, the scope writes a secret_access entry for every access, rotation, expiry and revocation:

{"entry_type": "secret_access", "data": {"action": "access", "secret_name": "stripe_key"}}

action is "access", "rotation", "expired" or "revoke_all" (with secret_name "*"). The value is never logged. Without a journal (JournalConfig(level="none"), the ProcessConfig default) there is no access log.

docs.title: Redaction
docs.text:
Secret values are replaced by [REDACTED] wherever the runtime stores or shows text:

Where What is redacted Journal entries and checkpoints Every string in the entry data and the checkpoint state, including tool arguments and results (level="full"), invocation results, context updates and the conversation snapshot. The result of the get_secret tool is always journaled as [REDACTED] Conversation history The stored trigger message and the agent's reply, so an echoed secret never reaches a later prompt Lifecycle hooks The data passed to hooks, including the prompt a user_prompt_submit hook sees Inbox answers The answer to a question (ANSWER Qn: in the reply), so POST /ask and process.ask() return [REDACTED] instead of a value the agent was talked into repeating; GET /inbox too Control API Responses never contain values; a failed rotation answers ROTATION_FAILED without echoing the error

Redaction covers the current values and values that were rotated away or expired (the last 10 per secret), longest first. It is an exact text match: a value that was encoded, split or reformatted is not recognized.

Two things are not redacted: the live context state (the agent's [Context State] prompt block and GET /context show values as stored; a value recovered from the journal comes back as [REDACTED]), and what the model itself receives, such as the get_secret result. Keep secrets out of the context state.

scope.sanitize_text(text) and scope.sanitize(value) (nested dicts, lists and tuples; returns a copy) do the same replacement for your own logs and output.

docs.title: Open mode: get_secret
docs.text:
When secret scoping is enabled and the process runs in open mode, the agent gets a get_secret(name) meta-tool. It returns the value (or an error text when the secret is missing or expired), so the agent can pass it to the tool that needs it; the tool's description tells the agent never to repeat it. Each call is access-logged. The agent never sees secrets in its system prompt.

Prefer giving credentials to the tool instead of the model: put tokens in the MCP server spec (bearer_token, api_key, or env of a stdio server), where the model never sees them.

docs.title: Over the API
docs.text:
Method Path What it does GET /api/v1/processes/{name}/secrets {"name", "secrets": [...], "enabled": true}; {"secrets": [], "enabled": false} without secret scoping PATCH /api/v1/processes/{name}/secrets/{secret_name} Rotate: body {"value": "...", "ttl": <seconds, optional>}. Answers {"name", "secret_rotated", "secret": <metadata>} DELETE /api/v1/processes/{name}/secrets Revoke all: {"name", "secrets_revoked": true}

Each item of the listing (and secret in the rotation answer) is the secret's metadata plus expires_at:

{"name": "stripe_key", "active": true, "source": "rotation", "ttl": 60,
 "expires_in": 59.999, "rotation_count": 1, "rotated_at": "2026-10-19T20:23:26.797891+00:00",
 "access_count": 0, "expires_at": 1792441466.79}
Error When 400 SECRETS_DISABLED Rotate or revoke on a process without secret scoping 404 SECRET_NOT_FOUND Rotating a name the process has no secret for 422 MISSING_FIELD / INVALID_FIELD value missing or not a string; ttl not a number > 0 422 UNKNOWN_FIELD A body field other than value and ttl 400 ROTATION_FAILED The rotation failed for another reason (the message never contains the value)

The Python client has list_secrets(name), rotate_secret(name, secret_name, value, *, ttl=None) and revoke_secrets(name). GET /api/v1/processes/{name} shows active_secrets, the number of active secrets.

docs.title: SecretScopeConfig
docs.text:
Field Type Default Description enabled bool False Enable secret scoping secrets dict[str, SecretStr] {} Secret name to literal value or ${VAR} reference default_ttl float \| None None TTL in seconds for every secret (None = no expiry; must be > 0) ttls dict[str, float] {} Per-secret TTL overrides (names must be in secrets) revoke_on_stop bool True Revoke all secrets on stop()

Unknown keys are ignored with a FutureWarning.

docs.title: SecretScope
docs.text:
SecretScope(config, process_id, journal=None, *, source="operator", env_references=True) from promptise.runtime.secrets. env_references limits which variables ${VAR} may read (True any, False none, or a set of names); source="api" makes resolution errors generic. A process with secrets.enabled creates its own (it is not a public attribute of the process); reach a running process's secrets over the API.

Member Description await .resolve_initial(*, missing_only=False) Resolve every secret from the config and start its TTL (again on each call). missing_only=True resolves only the secrets the scope doesn't hold, keeping rotated values (what a process start uses). Raises SecretResolutionError .get(name) The value, or None when missing or expired (access-logged) await .rotate(name, new_value, *, ttl=None) Replace a value now; SecretNotFoundError for an unknown name await .revoke_all() Zero-fill and remove all secrets, forget rotated values, new encryption key .list_metadata() One dict per configured secret: name, active, source ("env", "literal" or "rotation"), ttl, expires_in (seconds left, None = no expiry or not active), rotation_count, rotated_at (ISO UTC or None), access_count. Never a value .list_names() Names of the active secrets .active_secret_names / .active_secrets Names of the non-expired secrets (active_secrets is an alias) .active_secret_count Number of non-expired secrets .sanitize_text(text) text with known values replaced by [REDACTED] .sanitize(value) The same for every string in a nested value (a copy)

SecretNotFoundError subclasses KeyError and has .name and .known (the configured names).

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• A rotation lasts until the next stop. With the default revoke_on_stop=True, stop() (and so a restart) revokes every secret and the next start resolves them from the config again. With revoke_on_stop=False a start only resolves missing secrets, so the rotated value survives. Rotate the value at its source (the environment variable or your secret manager) as well.
  • The model sees what get_secret returns. Redaction keeps the value out of storage, not out of the model's context. Prefer server-side credentials in MCP server specs.
  • Secrets in the context state come back as [REDACTED]. The journal stores the redacted value, so recovery restores the placeholder.
  • No journal, no access log. The ProcessConfig default journal level is none.
  • A missing environment variable fails the start. The process goes to failed with a KeyError naming the variable; set it or give a default (${VAR:-default}).
  • Masked dumps can't be reloaded. A JSON dump shows literal values as **********, which is refused as a value. Use references for anything you serialize.
  • Redaction is exact-match. A value the agent encodes or splits is not recognized.

docs.title: Journal System
docs.text:
The journal is a process's durable, append-only record: state transitions, context writes, run results, errors, restarts, and a checkpoint of the recoverable state after every run. It powers three things: you can see what a process did (promptise runtime logs, GET /processes/{name}/journal), a process picks up where it left off after a crash or restart, and you can rewind a process to an earlier point.

from promptise.runtime import AgentProcess, JournalConfig, ProcessConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="You write release notes.",
    journal=JournalConfig(level="checkpoint", backend="file", path=".promptise/journal"),
)

process = AgentProcess("notes", config)
await process.start()
process.context.put("stage", "draft")
# ... trigger events run ...
await process.stop()

# Next time (a new Python process, after a crash or a deploy):
again = AgentProcess("notes", config)
await again.start()
print(again.recovered)
# {'lifecycle_state': 'stopped', 'entries_replayed': 1, 'context_keys': ['stage'],
#  'mission_restored': False, 'budget_restored': False,
#  'conversation_messages': 2, 'invocation_count': 1}
print(again.context.get("stage"))   # 'draft'

The entries land in .promptise/journal/notes.jsonl, and the latest checkpoint in .promptise/journal/notes.checkpoint.json. Entries are filed under the process name, not its internal ID, so a restarted process (which gets a new process_id) and promptise runtime logs notes find them.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Journaling is off by default for a process: ProcessConfig.journal defaults to JournalConfig(level="none"). Pass a JournalConfig to turn it on; JournalConfig() itself defaults to level="checkpoint".

Field Type Default Description level "none" \| "checkpoint" \| "full" "checkpoint" How much is recorded (see below). "none" creates no journal at all backend "file" \| "memory" "file" FileJournal (JSONL on disk) or InMemoryJournal (lost when the Python process exits) path str ".promptise/journal" Directory of the file backend, relative to the working directory recover_on_start bool True Restore the recorded state on the process object's first start() (see Recovery on start)

In a manifest:

journal:
  level: checkpoint
  backend: file
  path: .promptise/journal
  recover_on_start: true

Unknown keys are ignored with a FutureWarning.

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
Level What the process records "none" Nothing (no journal object; rewind and recovery are unavailable) "checkpoint" State transitions, every context write (context_update), each run's result, run errors, restarts, recovery and rewind markers, operator actions from the API, secret accesses, mission evaluations, and a checkpoint after every run "full" Everything above, plus each trigger event, each run's start, and every tool call and tool result

A failing journal backend is logged and never stops the process.

The levels are also the JournalLevel enum (promptise.runtime.journal.JournalLevel, a str enum: NONE, CHECKPOINT, FULL), which JournalConfig.level accepts as well as the strings:

from promptise.runtime import JournalConfig, JournalLevel

config = JournalConfig(level=JournalLevel.FULL)
print(config.level)  # full

docs.title: Entry types
docs.text:
Every record is a JournalEntry:

Field Type Description entry_id str Unique ID (a UUID). This is what rewind targets process_id str The process name the entry is filed under timestamp datetime When it was recorded (UTC) entry_type str One of the types below data dict[str, Any] Type-specific payload

What an AgentProcess writes:

entry_type Level When data state_transition checkpoint Every lifecycle transition from_state, to_state, reason, process_id context_update checkpoint Every write to the context state (by your code, the API's PATCH /context, or the agent's state tool) key, value, timestamp, source invocation_result checkpoint A run finished invocation, event_id, trigger_type, duration_ms, response (first 2000 characters) checkpoint checkpoint After every run, after a failed or refused run when a budget is enabled, when the mission's state changes, on stop(), after a rewind {"state": {...}}, see Checkpoints error checkpoint A run raised event_id, error_type, error (first 1000 characters) restart checkpoint An automatic restart begins reason, attempt (None for a max_lifetime recycle) restart_exhausted checkpoint max_restarts reached reason, restarts, max_restarts, error recovered checkpoint Journal recovery restored state at start The same dict as process.recovered rewind checkpoint A rewind was applied target_entry_id, mode, actor, entries_affected, conversation_affected, code_affected, summary_note api_request checkpoint A successful mutating request to the Orchestration API Method, route, path parameters, status and client address (never the body) secret_access checkpoint Secret scoping read, rotated, revoked or expired a secret action ("access", "rotation", "revoke_all", "expired"), secret_name (never the value) mission_evaluation checkpoint The mission judge evaluated progress achieved, confidence, reasoning, progress_summary, mission_state, invocation_number, source tool_denied checkpoint The budget refused a tool call before it ran tool, kind ("budget"), reason, limit_name, limit_value, current_value; at level "full" also args (redacted) budget_violation checkpoint The process acts on a budget violation (on_exceeded), also for a run refused by max_runs_per_day limit_name, limit_value, current_value, tool_name, blocked, action trigger_event full A run starts for a trigger event trigger_id, trigger_type, event_id, payload invocation_start full Before the model is called invocation, event_id tool_call full The agent called a tool tool, args (redacted) tool_result full A tool returned tool, result (first 2000 characters). Results of get_secret are never journaled

Every entry has an entry_id, so any entry can be a rewind target.

Your own code can append any other type with journal.append(JournalEntry(...)). Entries serialize with entry.to_dict() and JournalEntry.from_dict(data).

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
A checkpoint is a full snapshot of what a process can recover:

Key Content context_state The context key-value state lifecycle_state The process state when it was written invocation_count Runs so far conversation The conversation buffer (short-term memory) budget The budget counters (when a budget is enabled) mission The mission's state and evaluation history (when a mission is enabled)

The context writes made before a checkpoint are journaled before it, so the journal's order matches what the checkpoint contains.

docs.title: Recovery on start
docs.text:
With recover_on_start=True (the default), the first start() of a process object reads the journal for its name and restores what it recorded, before its own first transition is journaled:

  • the context state: the last checkpoint's context_state plus the context_update entries written after it (replayed with ReplayEngine); recovered keys replace the same keys of context.initial_state;
  • the mission (MissionTracker.restore), when a mission is enabled;
  • the budget counters, when a budget is enabled, so a restart can't reset the daily limits;
  • the conversation history, when context.conversation_history is on;
  • the invocation count.

Without a checkpoint (a crash before the first run ended), the context_update entries alone are replayed. A journal that holds neither restores nothing, and a journal that can't be read is logged and the process starts fresh.

process.recovered reports what was restored (or is None): lifecycle_state ("stopped" after a clean stop, "running" after a crash), entries_replayed, context_keys, mission_restored, budget_restored, conversation_messages and invocation_count. The same dict is journaled as a recovered entry and passed to SESSION_START hooks as recovered.

Not recovered from the journal: long-term memory (its provider persists it), secrets, queued trigger events and dead letters, and anything a tool did outside the process. Later starts of the same object (an automatic restart, restart_process) keep the live state and don't read the journal again. Set recover_on_start=False to always start fresh.

docs.title: Secrets never reach the journal in plain text
docs.text:
When secret scoping is enabled, the process wraps its journal in a RedactingJournal. Every string in an entry's data and in a checkpoint passes through the secret scope's redactor before it reaches the backend, so tool arguments, run results and the conversation snapshot store [REDACTED] instead of a secret value, also after a rotation. get_secret results are never journaled at all.

To redact your own journal the same way:

from promptise.runtime.journal import FileJournal, RedactingJournal

journal = RedactingJournal(FileJournal(".promptise/journal"), scope.sanitize)

The redactor must return a redacted copy and leave its input unchanged. Values that were stored redacted come back redacted on recovery and rewind.

docs.title: Reading entries
docs.text:
From How The terminal promptise runtime logs notes (newest entries, with their entry IDs; --follow for more), see CLI The Orchestration API GET /api/v1/processes/{name}/journal?limit=50&type=checkpoint; OrchestrationClient.get_journal(name, limit=, entry_type=) Python await journal.read(name, since=..., entry_type=..., limit=...) on a backend 
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from promptise.runtime.journal import FileJournal

journal = FileJournal(".promptise/journal")
entries = await journal.read("notes")
errors = await journal.read("notes", entry_type="error",
                            since=datetime(2026, 10, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc))
checkpoint = await journal.last_checkpoint("notes")

Backends implement the JournalProvider protocol: append(entry), read(process_id, *, since, entry_type, limit), checkpoint(process_id, state), last_checkpoint(process_id) and close(). See Journal Backends.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Expecting a journal by default. A ProcessConfig without journal= writes nothing, so logs, recovery and rewind have nothing to work with. Set JournalConfig() (checkpoint level).
  • Two processes with the same name and path. Entries are filed under the name, so they share one file and recover each other's state. Give each process its own name or path.
  • A relative path and a different working directory. .promptise/journal is relative to where the process starts. A process started from another directory finds no journal and starts fresh; use an absolute path in services.
  • backend: memory and recovery. The in-memory journal disappears with the Python process, so nothing survives a crash. Use it for tests.
  • recover_on_start and a fresh run. A test or a new deployment that should start clean must set recover_on_start=False or use a new journal directory; otherwise it continues the old state.
  • full level and storage. Tool results and payloads can be large, and JSONL files are never rotated by Promptise. Rotate or archive them externally.

docs.text:
