docs.text: Field Description topic The subscribed topic message_id The message's message_id sender The message's sender content The message's content

docs.title: WebhookTrigger
docs.text: An aiohttp HTTP server that listens for POST requests and turns each accepted request into a TriggerEvent. Each webhook trigger runs its own server on its own port.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
import os
from promptise.runtime import TriggerConfig

TriggerConfig(
    type="webhook",
    webhook_path="/github",
    webhook_port=9090,
    webhook_host="127.0.0.1",          # default: loopback only
    hmac_secret=os.environ["GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET"],
    signature_scheme="github",         # generic | github | stripe | telegram
    allowed_sources=["203.0.113.0/24"],  # the sender's published IP ranges
    webhook_max_body_bytes=256 * 1024,   # default 1 MiB
    filter_expression="payload['action'] == 'opened'",
)
Field Default Description webhook_path "/webhook" URL path that accepts POST requests webhook_port 9090 TCP port (1025–65535) webhook_host "127.0.0.1" Interface to bind. The default only accepts local connections; use "0.0.0.0" to accept requests from other machines hmac_secret None Shared secret; when set, requests without a valid signature get 401 signature_scheme "generic" How the signature is computed (table below); requires hmac_secret signature_header scheme default Override the header the signature is read from; requires hmac_secret signature_tolerance 300 Max age in seconds of a stripe signature timestamp; inside that window each signed request is accepted once (replay protection) allowed_sources [] (any) Client IPs or CIDR ranges allowed to call the webhook; others get 403 webhook_max_body_bytes 1048576 (1 MiB) Largest request body accepted, 1 byte to 1 GiB; larger bodies get 413 filter_expression None Skip events before the agent runs (see Filtering) trusted False Deliver the payload as the user's request instead of untrusted data; needs hmac_secret (see Trusted triggers)

In a manifest, keep the secret out of the file with an environment reference: hmac_secret: ${GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET}. The secret is a SecretStr: it is masked in repr(), in config dumps and in GET /triggers.

docs.title: Authentication: HMAC signatures
docs.text:
With hmac_secret set, every request must carry an HMAC-SHA256 signature of the raw body, made with the shared secret. The comparison is timing-safe.

signature_scheme Header Value generic X-Webhook-Signature sha256=<hex HMAC of body> github X-Hub-Signature-256 sha256=<hex HMAC of body>, as GitHub sends it stripe Stripe-Signature t=<unix ts>,v1=<hex HMAC of "<ts>.<body>">, as Stripe sends it; rejected when the timestamp is older than signature_tolerance, or when the same signed request was already accepted telegram X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token The secret itself, as Telegram sends the secret_token given to setWebhook; not a signature of the body. The secret must be 1-256 characters of A-Z, a-z, 0-9, _ and -

generic and github signatures cover only the body, with no timestamp, so anyone who captures a signed request can send it again. Serve the webhook over TLS (a reverse proxy in front of it) so requests can't be captured, and make the agent's actions safe to repeat where you can.

Signing a request for the generic scheme:

import hashlib, hmac, json, urllib.request

body = json.dumps({"order_id": 42}).encode()
signature = "sha256=" + hmac.new(b"my-secret", body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(
    "http://127.0.0.1:9090/webhook",
    data=body,
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/json", "X-Webhook-Signature": signature},
))

For other providers that sign the body with HMAC-SHA256 and a sha256= prefix, keep signature_scheme="generic" and set signature_header to their header name.

docs.title: Telegram bots
docs.text:
Telegram doesn't sign updates; it sends the secret_token you register with setWebhook in the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header. signature_scheme="telegram" checks that header against hmac_secret (constant-time) and answers 401 otherwise:

triggers:
  - type: webhook
    webhook_path: /telegram
    hmac_secret: ${TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET}
    signature_scheme: telegram
    trusted: true   # the message text is the user's request

Register the same value with Telegram: https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/setWebhook?url=https://<your host>/telegram&secret_token=<secret>. Telegram calls only HTTPS URLs, so put a TLS reverse proxy in front of the webhook (it listens on loopback by default). As with generic, there is no timestamp: anyone who captures a request (and so the secret) can send more, which TLS prevents. The secret proves the request came through your bot's webhook, not who wrote the message; check payload["message"]["from"]["id"] in a filter_expression if only some users may talk to the agent.

docs.title: Stripe replay protection
docs.text:
A stripe signature is accepted once. The webhook records it only when it takes the event, so a sender's retry is not mistaken for a replay:

  • after a 503 (process unavailable or queue full), the signature was never recorded and the retry goes through;
  • after a 500 (an unexpected error while handling the request), the signature is released again, so the retry goes through;
  • after a 202 or a 200 ignored, the same signature gets 401.

Recorded signatures are kept for twice signature_tolerance.

Set a secret before you expose the port

Without hmac_secret, anyone who can reach the port can make the agent run, and pick what it reads. The trigger logs a warning at start-up in that case. Always set a secret (and ideally allowed_sources) when webhook_host isn't loopback.

Unsigned loopback webhooks refuse browser requests. A webhook on a loopback address can also be reached by any web page open in a browser on the same machine (a cross-site form post or fetch, or DNS rebinding). Without hmac_secret, a loopback webhook therefore answers 421 to a request whose Host header is not a loopback name and 403 to one with a cross-site Origin header, like the control API. Local senders such as curl, scripts and other services send a loopback Host and no Origin, so they are unaffected. A signed webhook skips this check: the signature already proves the sender.

Agent-added webhooks. A webhook trigger an open-mode agent adds (add_trigger), or gives a process it spawns, must listen on loopback unless open_mode.allow_public_webhooks is on, and then needs an hmac_secret (see Open Mode).

allowed_sources is checked against the TCP peer address. Behind a reverse proxy that is the proxy's address, so list the proxy and do the provider IP check there.

docs.title: Direct instantiation
docs.text:
from promptise.runtime.triggers.webhook import WebhookTrigger

trigger = WebhookTrigger(
    path="/webhook",
    port=9090,
    host="127.0.0.1",
    hmac_secret="my-secret",
    signature_scheme="generic",
    max_body_bytes=256 * 1024,
)

await trigger.start()
# HTTP server now listening at http://127.0.0.1:9090/webhook

event = await trigger.wait_for_next()
print(event.payload)   # POST body (JSON or text)
print(event.metadata)  # {"method": "POST", "path": "/webhook", ...}

await trigger.stop()

event_filter= takes a callable (the TriggerEvent in, a bool out); TriggerConfig.filter_expression is compiled into it. WebhookTrigger raises ValueError for an unknown signature_scheme or a max_body_bytes below 1.

docs.title: How requests are handled
docs.text:
1. A POST request arrives at the configured path.
  2. The client address is checked against allowed_sources → 403 if not allowed. Without hmac_secret on a loopback bind, a non-loopback Host header → 421 and a cross-site Origin → 403.
  3. The body size is checked against webhook_max_body_bytes → 413 if larger. The Content-Length header is checked before the body is read; a chunked body without one is cut off at the limit while it is read.
  4. With hmac_secret set, the signature (for telegram, the secret token) is verified → 401 if missing or wrong (or a stripe replay).
  5. If the owning process can't take the event (it is FAILED, stopping or stopped, or its queue is full) → 503 with Retry-After: 30.
  6. The body is parsed as JSON (falling back to plain text) and a TriggerEvent is created with the body as payload and request details in metadata.
  7. If a filter_expression is set and doesn't match → 200 {"status": "ignored", "event_id": ...}; the agent doesn't run.
  8. The event is queued → 202 {"status": "accepted", "event_id": ...}. If the webhook's own queue is full at that moment → 503.

A suspended process still accepts events: they wait in the queue until it resumes, and a process suspended by idle_timeout resumes by itself.

Status Body Meaning 202 {"status": "accepted", "event_id": …} Queued for the agent 200 {"status": "ignored", "event_id": …} Didn't match filter_expression 401 {"status": "error", "message": "Missing or invalid signature"} Missing, wrong or replayed signature 403 {"status": "error", "message": "Source not allowed"} Source address not in allowed_sources 403 {"status": "error", "message": "Cross-origin request refused"} Unsigned loopback webhook, cross-site Origin 421 {"status": "error", "message": "Misdirected request"} Unsigned loopback webhook, non-loopback Host (DNS rebinding) 404 (aiohttp) Wrong path 405 (aiohttp) Method other than POST on the webhook path 413 {"status": "error", "message": "Request body too large (limit … bytes)"} Body larger than webhook_max_body_bytes 500 {"status": "error", "message": "internal error"} Unexpected error while handling the request; the event was not queued 503 {"status": "unavailable", "message": …} + Retry-After: 30 message is process failed, process stopped, queue full or webhook stopped; retry later

The 202 is sent when the event is queued, before the agent runs. If the run later fails, the sender is not told; the event ends up in the process's dead letters. Stripe retries 5xx answers automatically (for up to three days in live mode); GitHub doesn't retry failed deliveries by itself, but you can redeliver them from the webhook's settings page.

Sensitive headers (Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie) and the signature header are stripped from the metadata.

docs.title: Health check endpoint
docs.text:
The webhook server also exposes GET /health on the same port. It returns 200 while events are accepted and 503 when they aren't:

{
    "status": "healthy",
    "reason": null,
    "trigger_id": "webhook-1f0c9e2a7b",
    "queue_size": 0
}

When unavailable, status is "unavailable" and reason is the same text the POST route returns in message.

docs.title: Webhook payload
docs.text:
The payload field contains the raw POST body:

  • If the body is valid JSON, it is stored as parsed JSON (usually a dict).
  • Otherwise, it is stored as a string.

The agent sees it inside a delimited untrusted-data block; see Trigger payloads are untrusted input. A signed webhook with trusted=True delivers it as the user's request instead.

docs.title: Webhook metadata
docs.text:
Field Description method HTTP method (always POST) path Request path query Query parameters dict headers Safe headers (auth and signature headers excluded) remote Client IP address signature_verified True when the request passed the HMAC check

The agent sees only the payload, not the metadata.

docs.title: Queue-based decoupling
docs.text:
All three triggers use asyncio.Queue to buffer events:

  • EventTrigger: maxsize=100 (when full, a new event is counted in dropped_events and dead-lettered)
  • MessageTrigger: maxsize=100 (when full, a new message is counted in dropped_events and dead-lettered)
  • WebhookTrigger: maxsize=1000 (answers 503 when full)

docs.title: Graceful stop
docs.text:
When stop() is called, each trigger:

  1. Unsubscribes from its event source (event bus, broker), or shuts down the HTTP server.
  2. Enqueues a sentinel event with metadata={"_stop": True}.
  3. Any wait_for_next() call receiving the sentinel raises asyncio.CancelledError.

Events still in the trigger's queue are returned by drain_pending(). A process calls it when it stops (the events are dead-lettered with reason process stopped) or restarts (they move to the process queue), so an accepted 202 webhook event is not lost.

docs.title: API Summary
docs.text:
Class Description EventTrigger(event_bus, event_type, *, source_filter, trigger_id) Event-bus trigger MessageTrigger(broker, topic, *, trigger_id) Message-broker trigger WebhookTrigger(path, port, host, hmac_secret, *, signature_scheme, signature_header, signature_tolerance, allowed_sources, event_filter, max_body_bytes) HTTP webhook trigger

All implement the BaseTrigger protocol: start(), stop(), wait_for_next(). WebhookTrigger.set_availability_check(callback) installs the check behind the 503 answers; AgentProcess sets it for you.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Large payloads. Bodies over webhook_max_body_bytes (1 MiB by default) get 413, and a retry of the same body gets 413 again. Raise the limit for providers that send big payloads.
  • Two webhooks on one port. Each webhook trigger binds its own server, so a second trigger on the same port fails to start (address already in use). Give each one its own port, or use one webhook with a filter_expression per event kind.
  • Reverse proxy and allowed_sources. Behind a proxy the peer address is the proxy's. List the proxy, or filter by IP in the proxy.
  • 200 ignored is final. Senders treat a 2xx as delivered. A filtered request is not retried later, even if you change the filter.
  • A 202 is not a successful run. Watch dead letters and the process status; the sender only knows the event was queued.
  • Event bus not shared. EventTrigger and MessageTrigger only see events emitted on the same bus or broker instance you passed to AgentRuntime.

Use EventTrigger for inter-process coordination

When one process needs to trigger another, use EventTrigger with a shared event bus. This is simpler than a webhook for in-process communication.

Webhook security

The webhook server binds to 127.0.0.1 by default, so only local clients can reach it. When you bind 0.0.0.0, set hmac_secret (and allowed_sources where the sender publishes its IP ranges), and put a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy) in front for TLS. The trigger doesn't terminate TLS itself.

docs.title: File Watch Trigger
docs.text:
The FileWatchTrigger runs an agent when files in a directory are created, modified, deleted or moved. Use it for drop folders, data ingestion and file-based workflows. It uses native OS notifications through watchdog, or scans the directory on an interval when you choose polling (network shares, bind mounts).

from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, TriggerConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Summarise each new CSV file in /data/inbox.",
    triggers=[
        TriggerConfig(
            type="file_watch",
            watch_path="/data/inbox",
            watch_patterns=["*.csv"],
        ),
    ],
)

On its own, outside a process:

import asyncio
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from promptise.runtime.triggers.file_watch import FileWatchTrigger


async def main():
    inbox = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
    trigger = FileWatchTrigger(watch_path=str(inbox), patterns=["*.csv", "*.json"])
    await trigger.start()

    (inbox / "new_data.csv").write_text("id,value\n1,42\n")
    event = await asyncio.wait_for(trigger.wait_for_next(), timeout=10)
    print(event.payload["filename"], event.payload["event_type"])  # new_data.csv created
    # payload: {"path": ".../new_data.csv", "filename": "new_data.csv",
    #           "event_type": "created", "event_types": ["created", "modified"]}

    await trigger.stop()


asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
When files appear in or change within a watched directory, the trigger produces TriggerEvent objects that wake the agent. The payload carries the path, not the content: the agent reads the file with its own tools.

Two backends detect changes:

  • watchdog: native OS notifications (inotify on Linux, FSEvents on macOS, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows), near-instant. watchdog ships with pip install promptise.
  • polling: scans the directory every watch_poll_interval seconds and compares each file's modification time and size. Works everywhere, including network shares and container bind mounts where OS notifications are unreliable, at the cost of latency and CPU.

docs.title: Via TriggerConfig
docs.text:
from promptise.runtime import ProcessConfig, TriggerConfig

config = ProcessConfig(
    model="openai:gpt-5-mini",
    instructions="Process new data files as they arrive.",
    triggers=[
        TriggerConfig(
            type="file_watch",
            watch_path="/mnt/share/inbox",
            watch_patterns=["*.csv", "*.json"],
            watch_events=["created", "modified", "moved"],
            watch_debounce_seconds=1.0,
            watch_recursive=False,
            watch_backend="polling",     # network share: don't rely on OS notifications
            watch_poll_interval=5.0,
            watch_max_pending_events=5000,
        ),
    ],
)
Field Default Description watch_path required Directory to monitor (created at start if missing) watch_patterns ["*"] Glob patterns matched against the file name watch_events ["created", "modified"] Which (merged) events run the agent: any of created, modified, deleted, moved; at least one watch_debounce_seconds 0.5 Window in which events for the same file are merged into one (>= 0) watch_recursive True Also watch subdirectories watch_backend "auto" "auto" (watchdog when installed, otherwise polling), "watchdog" (fail if it isn't installed) or "polling" watch_poll_interval 1.0 Seconds between scans with the polling backend (> 0, at most 3600) watch_max_pending_events 10000 How many changed files may wait for the process before new changes are dropped (>= 1); see Back-pressure filter_expression None Extra filter on the event (see Filtering)

Unknown event names, an unknown backend, watch_backend="watchdog" without watchdog installed, and out-of-range numbers are rejected when the config is created. Setting a watch_* option on another trigger type is a validation error too.

Inside a process, the trigger's ID is a stable ID such as file_watch-06bfa13759.

docs.title: Direct instantiation
docs.text:
from promptise.runtime.triggers.file_watch import FileWatchTrigger

trigger = FileWatchTrigger(
    watch_path="/data/inbox",
    patterns=["*.csv", "*.json"],
    events=["created", "modified", "deleted"],
    recursive=True,
    debounce_seconds=0.5,
    poll_interval=1.0,
    backend="auto",
    max_pending_events=10_000,
)
Parameter Type Default Description watch_path str required Directory to monitor patterns list[str] ["*"] Glob patterns to match file names events list[str] ["created", "modified"] Merged events that fire the trigger recursive bool True Watch subdirectories debounce_seconds float 0.5 Window in which events for one file are merged poll_interval float 1.0 Seconds between scans (polling backend) backend str "auto" Keyword-only: "auto", "watchdog" or "polling" max_pending_events int 10000 Keyword-only: most files waiting before changes are dropped

The constructor raises ValueError for an unknown event type or backend, backend="watchdog" without watchdog, a poll_interval that isn't positive, a negative debounce_seconds, or a max_pending_events below 1.

docs.title: Supported Events
docs.text:
Event Description created A new file was created in the watched directory modified An existing file's content was changed deleted A file was removed moved A file was moved or renamed into place (watchdog backend only)

Configure which events to react to via events / watch_events. The check runs on the merged event for each file (see Debouncing), so watch_events=["deleted"] fires only when a file is gone, never for a new or changed one.

Editors and many upload tools save atomically: they write a temporary file and rename it over the target. With the watchdog backend that shows up as moved (to the target name) rather than created or modified, so the default watch_events miss it. Add "moved" to watch_events if files arrive that way. The polling backend sees a rename as a deleted event for the old name and a created event for the new one.

Directory events are ignored; only files fire the trigger.

docs.title: Pattern Matching
docs.text:
Patterns use standard glob syntax and are matched against the file name (not the full path):

# Match CSV and JSON files
patterns=["*.csv", "*.json"]

# Match all Python files
patterns=["*.py"]

# Match everything (default)
patterns=["*"]

# Match specific prefixes
patterns=["report_*.xlsx"]

docs.title: Event Payload
docs.text:
When the trigger fires, the TriggerEvent.payload contains:

Field Description path Full file-system path of the changed file filename Just the file name (basename) event_type The merged change: "created", "modified", "deleted", or "moved" event_types The raw events merged into this one, in arrival order (e.g. ["created", "modified"])

The metadata includes:

Field Description watch_path The configured watch directory patterns The configured glob patterns

Example:

event = await trigger.wait_for_next()
print(event.payload)
# {
#     "path": "/data/inbox/report_2026.csv",
#     "filename": "report_2026.csv",
#     "event_type": "created",
#     "event_types": ["created", "modified"],
# }
print(event.metadata)
# {
#     "watch_path": "/data/inbox",
#     "patterns": ["*.csv", "*.json"],
# }

docs.title: Debouncing
docs.text:
The operating system often reports one logical change as several events: writing a new file usually produces created and modified, and copying a large file can produce several modified. Without merging, the agent would run once per raw event.

The trigger therefore collects every event for the same path during a debounce_seconds window (starting with the first event) and then emits one trigger event describing the net change:

What happened in the window event_type File no longer exists deleted (nothing at all if it was also created in the window) File was created (or deleted and recreated) created File was moved/renamed into place moved Anything else modified

That merged type is then checked against events / watch_events. One write_text() to a new file therefore runs the agent once, with event_type="created" and event_types=["created", "modified"].

# Merge everything that happens to a file within 1 second
trigger = FileWatchTrigger(
    watch_path="/data/inbox",
    debounce_seconds=1.0,
)

A larger window coalesces tools that write in several steps; the trade-off is that events arrive that much later. The window is fixed: it does not wait for the file to stop changing, so a slow upload can still be half-written when the agent runs.

docs.title: Back-pressure
docs.text:
Changes are not dropped when the process is busy. The trigger's own queue holds up to 1000 events; once it is full, further changes wait in a per-file backlog and move to the queue, oldest first, as the process takes events. A second change to a file that is already waiting is merged into its event, so a busy file costs one slot, not one per write.

Only when watch_max_pending_events different files are waiting (queued plus backlog) is a change to a new file dropped. Each drop is counted, and the first drop and every hundredth after it are logged as errors:

FileWatchTrigger file_watch-06bfa13759: 5000 files are waiting for the process
(max_pending_events=5000); dropped the change to /data/inbox/f5001.csv (1 dropped so far).
Raise watch_max_pending_events or process events faster.

The counters are on the trigger and in the process status:

Counter Meaning pending_events Events waiting for the process (queued plus backlog) dropped_events Changes dropped because max_pending_events files were waiting 
process.status()["triggers"]
# [{'id': 'file_watch-06bfa13759', 'type': 'file_watch', 'source': 'config',
#   'dropped_events': 0, 'pending_events': 12}]

A suspended process keeps the backlog; the events run after resume(). A process suspended by idle_timeout resumes by itself when a file event arrives.

docs.title: Directory Creation
docs.text:
If the watch_path does not exist when start() is called, the trigger creates it (with parent directories):

trigger = FileWatchTrigger(watch_path="/data/new_inbox")
await trigger.start()  # Creates /data/new_inbox if missing

docs.title: Backend Selection
docs.text:
backend / watch_backend picks how changes are detected; trigger.backend reports the one in use:

trigger = FileWatchTrigger(watch_path="/data/inbox")
print(trigger.backend)  # "watchdog" (or "polling" when watchdog isn't installed)
print(trigger)
# FileWatchTrigger(path='/data/inbox', patterns=['*'], events=['created', 'modified'],
#                  backend='watchdog', recursive=True)

docs.title: Watchdog backend
docs.text:
• Uses native OS notifications for near-instant detection.
  • Handles created, modified, deleted, and moved events.
  • Runs an Observer thread that hands events to the event loop with call_soon_threadsafe.

docs.title: Polling backend
docs.text:
• Takes a snapshot of the directory at start(), then scans every poll_interval seconds.
  • Compares each file's modification time (nanoseconds) and size, so a rewrite inside the file system's timestamp resolution is still seen.
  • Detects created, modified, and deleted events (not moved).
  • Use it for NFS/SMB shares and container bind mounts, where native notifications may not arrive.

Neither backend reports files that already exist when the trigger starts. Process those at start-up yourself (for example with a one-off process.inject() per file).

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
trigger = FileWatchTrigger(
    watch_path="/data/inbox",
    patterns=["*.csv"],
)

await trigger.start()

# Process events in a loop
while True:
    try:
        event = await trigger.wait_for_next()
        print(f"File: {event.payload['filename']} ({event.payload['event_type']})")
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        break

await trigger.stop()

When stop() is called:

  1. The watchdog observer is stopped and joined (or the polling task is cancelled).
  2. Changes still waiting (the backlog and open debounce windows) are turned into events that drain_pending() returns. In a process, they are dead-lettered with reason process stopped, or kept for the next run when the process restarts.
  3. A sentinel event is enqueued; it makes wait_for_next() raise asyncio.CancelledError.

In a process, add or remove a file watch while it runs with process.add_trigger() / process.remove_trigger(). A FILE_CHANGED hook sees every file event before it is queued and can drop it (counted in filtered_count).

docs.title: API Summary
docs.text: Method / Property Description FileWatchTrigger(watch_path, patterns, events, recursive, debounce_seconds, poll_interval, *, backend, max_pending_events) Create a file watch trigger trigger_id Identifier (standalone default: file_watch-{path}; in a process: the stable config ID) backend The backend in use: "watchdog" or "polling" pending_events Events waiting for the consumer (queued plus backlog) dropped_events Changes dropped because max_pending_events files were waiting await start() Start watching (creates the directory if needed) await stop() Stop watching and release resources await wait_for_next() Block until a matching file change occurs

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Atomic saves and uploads. Files renamed into place arrive as moved with watchdog. Add "moved" to watch_events, or the agent never runs for them.
  • Half-written files. The debounce window is fixed. For slow uploads, have the producer write to a temporary name that doesn't match watch_patterns and rename it when done, or raise watch_debounce_seconds.
  • The agent triggers itself. An agent that writes output into the watched folder (or a subfolder, with watch_recursive=True) wakes itself up. Write elsewhere, narrow watch_patterns, or set watch_recursive=False and write to a subfolder.
  • Network shares and bind mounts. Native notifications are often missing there. Use watch_backend="polling".
  • Large trees with polling. Every scan walks the whole tree. Watch a narrower directory, set watch_recursive=False, or raise watch_poll_interval.
  • A growing pending_events. The process can't keep up. Raise concurrency, narrow watch_patterns, or raise watch_max_pending_events; watch dropped_events for losses.
  • Files that were there before start. They don't fire the trigger.

File contents are untrusted input

The trigger passes only the path and file name, but an agent that then reads the file reads whatever someone dropped into the folder. Treat that content like a webhook body: gate side-effecting tools with approval (see Trigger payloads are untrusted input).
